articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s annual 4th of July celebration will begin at 11:00 a.m. on Friday, July 4, running eight blocks along Highland Avenue from Park Way past Piedmont Park. One of Piedmont’s oldest and most beloved traditions, the parade features floats from neighborhoods and community organizations, an array of antique and classic cars, and several bagpipe bands in keeping with Piedmont’s Scottish traditions. This year’s theme is “Traditions Thrive in 2025.” Following the parade, festivities will continue in Piedmont Park with a community picnic and music by David Martin’s House Party band from 12-3:00 p.m. The City asks the following: • Do not place chairs at bus stops • Do not block access from the street to the sidewalk with chairs • Use blankets rather than tarps for picnics in the park, as tarps damage the grass Block Party applications due June 26 Neighborhoods wanting streets to be closed for block parties on July 4 must complete an online application: • Applications are due at City Hall by 5 p.m. on Thursday, June 26. • If a permit is not approved, the City will contact you by Tuesday, July 1. The online application can be found at https://docs.google. com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSft5rOOsPm3rkBAvpFhbfWWNJjUfN6xdfNc1FDjv2gPpHHR2A/viewform. Public Works will deliver barricades to streets with approved closures on Thursday, July 3rd.

articles.text: Artist Walter Hood talks about the preliminary design for the upcoming Sidney and Irene Dearing Memorial project. The City of Piedmont has released the preliminary conceptual design for the long-discussed Sidney and Irene Dearing Memorial Project, created by Oakland-based artist Walter Hood, a nationally renowned designer and chair of the Department of Landscape Architecture and Environmental Planning at UC Berkeley. The Dearing Memorial began in concept in 2022, after research by local resident Meghann Bennett brought renewed attention to the injustice faced by Piedmont’s first Black homeowners. Sidney and Irene Dearing were subjected to a harassment campaign that ultimately forced them to sell their home to the city and leave. In a video accompanying the announcement, Hood explains the vision behind the design— what he calls the “Dearing Portal.” The concept features a two-person loveseat inside a tall, angular structure set among the redwood trees in Triangle Park, near the site of the Dearing home. ADAM TRIKI, 9th grade I’ll be attending the Piedmont Fourth of July Parade. I might even be able to be in the parade with my older cousin. Messed up times By Pastor Jim Hopkins The near consensus of biblical scholars is that though there is a Mark 16: 9-20 these verses were not in the earliest manuscripts of the gospel and were likely added by scribes who found the original ending, Mark 16:8, unsatisfactory because of its emphasis on the fear, confusion and bewilderment of the followers of Jesus who visited his tomb and found it empty. The verse reads — So they went out and fled from the tomb, for terror and amazement had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. One can see why the scribes wanted a happier ending. Yet, the ending original ending is consistent with the way Mark frequently describes the disciples, easily confused and often afraid, understandable in light of an event as shocking as the resurrection and connected to the lives of the hearers and readers of the gospel. We too are often confused, bewildered and afraid. I would argue that Mark ends his gospel the way he does to teach us that our faith is that the love of God meets us in our fear and carries us to God’s new day. We are living in a time in which fear, confusion and bewilderment abound. They seem to be our constant companions. They show up in our waking and in our sleeping. Many of us would describe our world as messed up. Mark would most certainly understand this. He would not, however, want us to be stuck in our fear. He would argue that though fear is real, it need not rule. He would urge us not to let the messed up times we live in mess us up. He would point out that though there are many reasons to be confused and bewildered, we have the resources of our faith to turn to and these resources, the way of Jesus, the community of the church, the promise of resurrection and the hope of God’s new day, sustain and shape us and the communities of faith of which we are a part. In these times I find the prayer I offer to begin my day ever more meaningful. Loving God, Help me to be a blessing to someone today. For my family I pray safety. For my enemies I pray grace. For the world I pray peace. It is my intent to live mindfully and gratefully and to walk in the way of Jesus Amen. Messed up times need not mess us up. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. SANDI HUTCHINSON, Sea View Ave. No plans yet, except for making sure to see the fireworks. IAN STOCK, 5th grade I’ll be in Rome, Italy for a fencing camp. It’ll be my first time in Italy. CALEB SEIDER, 5th grade We will be in Malibu for the Fourth of July. We will probably be on the beach, chilling. articles.text: The following letter was written by community members and read by Susy Struble at the City Council Meeting on Monday, June 16. Editor: We are writing as concerned residents to request further clarification of the City of Piedmont’s policies, practices, contracts and MOUs regarding the sharing of data collected through our 58 Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs). This surveillance includes images and license plate data for all vehicles entering Piedmont, along with time and location information. This surveillance data can be used to infer the identity, associations, and movement patterns of a car’s occupants. We are deeply alarmed over recent problematic immigration raids in California and in our local area and worry that our local surveillance system is being used to support civil immigration enforcement, potentially in violation of state and federal protections. This is not an unwarranted concern. There are numerous, well documented instances of ICE and other federal agencies accessing surveillance systems – directly and indirectly – to inform immigration raids, many of which are of dubious legality and increasing militarization. Given this context, we believe the City of Piedmont should conduct a thorough review of all ALPR-related governance documents and agreements to ensure compliance with state law and alignment with our community’s values. The goal is to: • Identify any gaps, conflicts or inconsistencies in policies, practices, contracts and MOUs. • Update as needed. Specifically, we recommend the City conduct a review of: • Policy 422 (Immigration Violations) • Policy 438 (Automated License Plate Readers) • The Master Services Agreement (MSA) with Flock Safety • Any related MOUs, including any that have not been publicly shared Some areas to review include, but are not limited to: • Our relationship with the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC, aka “fusion center”). According to the ALPR transparency portal, NCRIC has access to our surveillance data. When residents raised concerns about this a decade ago, Piedmont cited NCRIC’s free surveillance data hosting as a justification. However, Flock now hosts this data. If there is an MOU between NCRIC and the City of Piedmont, do its terms and oversight and enforcement mechanisms align with CA law and our community’s values? • Flock’s data sharing capabilities. These might present a risk of unauthorized access by federal agencies in ways that could violate the California Values Act or our department’s commitment to non-cooperation with civil immigration enforcement. For example, Flock MSA §5.3 states Flock may disclose footage to law enforcement or federal officials if “legally required” or based on “good faith belief” of necessity. This could bypass local oversight and possibly violate CA law. • Oversight gaps with the ALPR transparency portal. Again, it’s unclear if Flock must disclose external queries, such as from a federal agency like ICE or DHS. Moreover, while we appreciate Piedmont’s early adoption of this feature from Flock, the data presented does not help the public understand who has queried our ALPR data, what data is collected and tagged (it’s more than “vehicles, license plates”) and for what purpose in each instance. We applaud Chief Bowers’ thoughtful, consistent leadership and his team’s efforts to ensure their essential work aligns with our community’s values. We also recognize the City must navigate a complex and often ambiguous legal landscape. Still, we believe more should be done to ensure no part of our surveillance infrastructure is used to support civil immigration enforcement in a way that violates state law or community trust. We urge the City to adopt, publish, and actively enforce stronger, clearer policies that prevent misuse of local surveillance data and uphold our community values of the rule of law, civil liberties, and democratic accountability. Thank you for your time, attention and continued transparency on this important issue. With respect and gratitude, Fairuz Abdullah Shanti Brien Irene Cheng David Cole Maya Guzdar Diana Lee Jonah Sachs Susy Struble Liz Tahawi Katy Bradford Vosburg
articles.title: Questions about license plate readers

articles.text: Editor The Piedmont Post of June 4 had a startling headline, “Pool Construction Pushed Back with no clear end in sight.” I was stunned at such a direct and bold statement and fully expected to see some pushback or rebuttal from the Piedmont City staff or Council the following week, but there was no such response. Over the course of the construction narrative, various causes have been put forth regarding delays and additional costs on the pool project; PG&E approvals, underground surprises, supply chain delays, even winter rains? So, in July 2024, the three primary consultants, Wickman Construction, Griffin Structures and ELS Architects jointly received a $1.5 million Extension of Time for the claimed delays. In the July 2024 Status Report, the project was 72% complete and the Grand Opening was “expected Spring 2025.” In the Dec. 2, 2024 City Staff Update, the project was about 82% complete and the completion date was said to be late Spring 2025. Several delays were detailed: contaminated soil, underground tanks and ground water intrusion – most of which could have and should been identified at the start of the project with core samples. In the March 3, 2025 City Staff Update, the project was about 86% complete and “the project completion date is currently estimated as Summer of 2025.” The next update is scheduled 4th of July Parade Date: Address:

Will the delays result in requests for additional Project Costs from the design/construction team? Stay tuned for the July 7th update. We also recognize the City must navigate a complex and often ambiguous legal landscape. Still, we believe more should be done to ensure no part of our surveillance infrastructure is used to support civil immigration enforcement in a way that violates state law or community trust. We urge the City to adopt, publish, and actively enforce stronger, clearer policies that prevent misuse of local surveillance data and uphold our community values of the rule of law, civil liberties, and democratic accountability. Thank you for your time, attention and continued transparency on this important issue. With respect and gratitude, Fairuz Abdullah Shanti Brien Irene Cheng David Cole Maya Guzdar Diana Lee Jonah Sachs Susy Struble Liz Tahawi Katy Bradford Vosburg READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to adopt the proposed budget for FY2025-26 after a second hearing at their regular meeting on Monday, June 16. The budget provisions City funds starting on July 1. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. This year’s budget was presented by retired Finance Director Michael Szczech, performing interim duties while the City awaits the arrival of its next appointed Finance Director, Kiran Bawa. The budget, first presented in Council Chambers on June 2, features a General Fund of approximately $40 million. A $8.3 million spending plan for the Facilities Capital Fund was included for work finishing projects to include the community pool and police/fire dispatch center. The adopted budget includes a “modest” change from the first hearing of $10,300. The budget hearing reported a current status with expected revenue $1.2 million above the current year’s budget, with expenditures expected to be lower than budgeted by $1.6 million. With an expected surplus around $3.6 million, City staff recommended that $850,000 of it be transferred from the General Fund to the City’s Equipment fund, keeping the remainder for next year’s budget. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorses the proposed plan, stating: “The proposed budget for FY 25-26 reflects the City’s continued commitment to conservative budgeting and financial discipline. This approach ensures that the City can continue to provide high quality public services, replace aging equipment, and address infrastructure repairs, while retaining a strong General Fund.” The Committee’s report encourages the City to further quantify and plan for future infrastructure costs. The Committee also reiterates their call from previous reports for the City to explore options for additional revenue sources, including an increase in the Transfer Tax. Councilmember Tom Ramsey asked at the meeting about how much funding would be needed to bring Piedmont streets up to higher standards, revisiting a previous discussion of paving and road maintenance costs from the previous Council meeting. “That is a question I think we’ll be able to better answer once we develop our new pavement management program, which is something we’ll look to certify by the end of August,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “...we’re about two to three months away from having those numbers finalized.” Gonzales confirmed that it is likely that additional funds will be required to properly maintain or improve existing road conditions in Piedmont. Gonzales estimated this funding gap to be around $800,000-850,000 per year. The overall budget is meant to embrace priorities presented in a series of City Council Study Sessions, including completion of the community pool, completion of the dispatch center project, the undertaking of the Dearing Memorial Project, and planning for the future public safety building project. articles.text: David Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont Park on the 4th of July this year immediately following the parade. The concert will begin at approximately 12:00 p.m. on a large stage in the park. One of San Francisco’s premier party bands for 25 years, this interactive 11-piece all-star group has gained a national reputation for their high energy performances, incredible musical variety, and “anything-can-happen” hi-jinx. Past appearances include The Waldorf Astoria in New York City, special Napa Valley performances for Wine Spectator Magazine, concertizing in Maui at the Hyatt Regency Kaanapali and La Costa Resort in Carlsbad; selling out in Reno at the Grand Sierra Resort’s VIP New Years Eve 2010; and entertaining at numerous benefit galas in the greater Bay Area. David Martin is a Bay Area native who began his musical career at the age of six. Known for his powerful vocals and sparkling guitar work, David was a founding member of legendary San Francisco “New Wave” faces The Lloyds and The Buzztones. Martin has assembled a remarkable group of established musician/entertainers including Bobby Strickland (Todd Rundgren, Phil Lesh), Byron Allred (Steve Miller, Todd Rundgren), Gerald Goudeau (Race & Rhythm), Christina Sabatelli (Tubes, Starship), Tim Allen (Silvercreek), Timo Guierrez (Viva Brazil), John Mader (Booker T, Pee Wee Ellis), and Rob Russ (Eddie Money). Rounding out the group’s lineup are the dance artists Sandra Leathley and Stephanie Romano. Dave Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont on the 4th of July.
articles.title: Dave Martin’s House Party Band returns to Piedmont Park on 4th of July

articles.text: Piedmont elementary schools will teach English and language arts with a new curriculum next year, Fishtank Learning, a knowledge-based curriculum. The change formally began two years ago and moves away from Lucy Calkins’ “Units of Study” towards a “science of reading” based curriculum. In the May 28 Piedmont School Board meeting the first reading of the action item was conducted and on June 11, the change was approved with a second reading. “Really, this is a paradigm shift for our district,” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. “This committee does not make this recommendation lightly. We recognize the shift that it will entail moving forward, but feel confident with the recommendation.” Dolowich described the report to the board, beginning by summarizing some of the former curricula’s problems. “A few [limitations of Calkins’ system] include a lack of sufficient systematic and explicit instruction in foundational skills such as phonics and fluency, inadequate opportunities to engage in complex and rich texts, and, thirdly, a lack of building background knowledge and vocabulary development for our students,” he said. This past school year, the English Language Arts Adoption Committee, which included nine teachers, evaluated eight alternative curriculum, before narrowing the options down to two, Benchmark and Fishtank, to pilot with students. Twenty-one elementary teachers participated in the piloting of the two new options, of which Fishtank Learning was selected. Wildwood School first grade teacher Amiee Peri spoke for the pilot teachers on May 28. “The main difference is that Benchmark uses short stories, many of which are authored by curriculum writers, and Fishtank uses full length novels that are high quality, rich literature and capture authentic voices of authors of varied cultures and backgrounds,” said Peri. School Board President Lindsay Thomasson explained the process which took two years. “DIBELS was the very first step, and then ‘From Phonics to Reading’ and Spellography adopting those, and then this is the final step in the curriculum adoption process,” said Thomasson. From Phonics to Reading has already been implemented for Piedmont K-3 students. “We’ve seen a lot of success with [From Phonics to Reading] over the last two years. It’s pretty exciting, especially at a first grade level, to see reading and spelling grow for kids,” said Peri. School Board Vice President Ruchi Medhekar spoke in superlatives about the change. “This will be one of the moments that I will remember the most, when I look back at my time on the board,” said Medhekar. Piedmont teachers at all elementary sites will be using Fishtank Learning’s texts and lessons in the fall.
articles.title: Changes to reading and language arts for K-5 students

articles.text: Even though summer vacation is in full swing, the Piedmont Board of Education will meet tonight, Wednesday, June 25, to take up several key topics. The regularly scheduled meeting will begin at 7 p.m. in City Hall. On the agenda: approval of a new policy on artificial intelligence, one-year contract extensions for top district leaders, review of the Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP), and adoption of several district budgets. The board is expected to approve next year’s general fund budget. Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) projects $56,578,194 in revenue for the upcoming school year, with expenditures coming in $618,690 below that total. The district anticipates ending the year with a $4.3 million reserve. Budget forecasts for future years will also be presented. If approved, one-year contract extensions for the superintendent, chief business officer, and assistant superintendent would keep them in their roles through 2028. Contract negotiations with employee unions will not address salaries at this time but will reopen discussions on other areas, including work hours and committee participation. According to board documents, the district wants to revisit topics such as the structure of the professional day, the seven-period schedule, field trips, collaboration time, online training, bell schedules—including the Academy program—as well as union release time and grading timelines. articles.text: First year Piedmont High School Athletic Director Tyler Small provided a report on the recent year of athletics to the school board on June 11. The report included the status of Title IX compliance. Title IX efforts focused on improvement to weight room access, locker room usage, more tournament participation, and more concession sales during home events for girls’ teams with the overarching goal of balancing participation. In total, there were 373 female students at PHS and 413 males. Females account for 47.5% of the student body. When counting two- and three-sport athletes multiple times, there were 365 female athletes and 431 male athletes. Girls sports teams would need to add 24 athletes onto their rosters to achieve equal participation with the boys. To balance participation Small is focusing 2025-26 efforts on increasing participation in girls water polo and swimming when the new community pool opens. The district will also continue to search for local opportunities for beach volleyball practice and competitions. “Traveling to Santa Rosa, or to Santa Cruz or to somewhere on the coast for [beach volleyball] matches, it wears on the athletes, the coaches, the families that are transporting the athletes,” said Small. “The closest competition [girl’s beach volleyball] had was Livermore.” Two strength and conditioning coaches were hired at the start of the year for the weight room, and designated times were allotted for female athletes and middle school athletes. Small said locker room usage was improved by increasing communication around scheduling and by giving more coaches keys to the Witter Field weight room. New to the school, girls’ JV basketball team went to a tournament in Reno, while both girls’ and boys’ golf teams played in invitational tournaments. The varsity girls and boys sports teams each participated in 14 tournaments each. Small highlighted the revitalization of the football program. “Our football program has continued to grow. Hats off to the amazing coaches, who took a program that was almost non-existent and almost cut, due to a lack of interest, and have grown that to over 60 athletes. Next year’s numbers look very similar,” said Small. Small called 2024-25 a “banner year” with four WACC12 Players of the Year and one CIF Norcal Championship in boys soccer. Small also highlighted the 58 first-team WACC12 selections, 54 second-team selections and 35 honorable mention selections. “For a school of 800 students going up against Berkeley, a school of 4000, and going against O’Dowd, a private school, to be able to have those numbers within our league is pretty astounding,” he said. Piedmont’s Title IX compliance was sparked by a gender equity audit of the high school athletic program in 2021-22.
articles.title: Athletics end of year and Title IX report

articles.text: When most people think of a speech therapist, they imagine someone helping a child say their “R” sounds or overcome a lisp. While articulation therapy is one important aspect of the field, it’s only the tip of the iceberg. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) are trained to assess and treat a broad spectrum of communication and swallowing challenges across the lifespan. Here are ten lesser-known— but equally important—areas where SLPs make a difference: • Language Delays and Disorders SLPs help children who struggle to understand language (receptive) or use language to express themselves (expressive). This includes kids who speak in very short phrases, have trouble following directions, or are late to talk. • Social Communication Individuals with autism, ADHD, or social anxiety may need support learning conversational skills, reading body language, or understand humor and sarcasm. These “hidden rules” of communication are crucial for building friendships. • Feeding and Swallowing Disorders Yes, we help with eating too! Children who choke, gag, or have difficulty transitioning to solids may benefit from feeding therapy. SLPs also work with medically complex infants and children who use feeding tubes. Adults may benefit from swallowing therapy post stroke, head injury or other neurological conditions. • Stuttering and Fluency Fluency disorders like stuttering can cause emotional stress for both children and adults. SLPs provide strategies to improve speech flow, manage tension, and build confidence. • Voice Disorders A hoarse or breathy voice that persists could signal a voice disorder. SLPs work with children who strain their voices, speak too loudly, or have vocal nodules— often caused by yelling or poor vocal habits. • Literacy and Pre-Reading Skills SLPs address phonological awareness, decoding, spelling, and reading comprehension. Many children with language impairments also struggle with reading, and early intervention can change their academic trajectory. • Cognitive Communication After brain injuries or neurological conditions, people may need help with memory, attention, problem-solving, or organizing their thoughts. SLPs help rebuild these skills. • Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) When speaking isn’t possible, SLPs help children and adults communicate through devices, picture boards, or sign language. AAC gives a voice to those who don’t use verbal speech. • Accent Modification and Voice Coaching Some individuals seek help modifying an accent or refining their speaking voice for professional or personal reasons. SLPs offer evidence-based strategies for achieving clear, confident communication. • Selective Mutism and Anxiety-Related Disorders Some children speak comfortably at home but remain silent in school or public. SLPs work collaboratively with psychologists and families to gently increase communication in different settings. Speech therapy is a dynamic and evolving field that touches nearly every aspect of communication—from birth through adulthood. If you or someone you love struggles with speech, language, or swallowing, know that help is available. It’s not just about saying “S” or “R” correctly—it’s about making sure every voice is heard. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .
articles.title: Summer Thoughts Not just articulation: 10 things speech therapists treat

On the agenda: approval of a new policy on artificial intelligence, one-year contract extensions for top district leaders, review of the Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP), and adoption of several district budgets. The board is expected to approve next year’s general fund budget. Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) projects $56,578,194 in revenue for the upcoming school year, with expenditures coming in $618,690 below that total. The district anticipates ending the year with a $4.3 million reserve. Budget forecasts for future years will also be presented. If approved, one-year contract extensions for the superintendent, chief business officer, and assistant superintendent would keep them in their roles through 2028. Contract negotiations with employee unions will not address salaries at this time but will reopen discussions on other areas, including work hours and committee participation. According to board documents, the district wants to revisit topics such as the structure of the professional day, the seven-period schedule, field trips, collaboration time, online training, bell schedules—including the Academy program—as well as union release time and grading timelines. The board meeting agenda with background documents is available online at Simbli. e b o a r d s o l u t i o n s . c o m / S B _ Meetings/ViewMeeting.aspx- ?S=36030373&MID=41888 At 7:00 p.m. tonight, head over to 120 Vista Avenue, watch on channel 27 KCOM, or participate remotely via Zoom. us/j/86287493134. Summer Thoughts Not just articulation: 10 things speech therapists treat By Katie Penguilly When most people think of a speech therapist, they imagine someone helping a child say their “R” sounds or overcome a lisp. While articulation therapy is one important aspect of the field, it’s only the tip of the iceberg. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) are trained to assess and treat a broad spectrum of communication and swallowing challenges across the lifespan. Here are ten lesser-known— but equally important—areas where SLPs make a difference: • Language Delays and Disorders SLPs help children who struggle to understand language (receptive) or use language to express themselves (expressive). This includes kids who speak in very short phrases, have trouble following directions, or are late to talk. • Social Communication Individuals with autism, ADHD, or social anxiety may need support learning conversational skills, reading body language, or understand humor and sarcasm. These “hidden rules” of communication are crucial for building friendships. • Feeding and Swallowing Disorders Yes, we help with eating too! Children who choke, gag, or have difficulty transitioning to solids may benefit from feeding therapy. SLPs also work with medically complex infants and children who use feeding tubes. Adults may benefit from swallowing therapy post stroke, head injury or other neurological conditions. • Stuttering and Fluency Fluency disorders like stuttering can cause emotional stress for both children and adults. SLPs provide strategies to improve speech flow, manage tension, and build confidence. • Voice Disorders A hoarse or breathy voice that persists could signal a voice disorder. SLPs work with children who strain their voices, speak too loudly, or have vocal nodules— often caused by yelling or poor vocal habits. • Literacy and Pre-Reading Skills SLPs address phonological awareness, decoding, spelling, and reading comprehension. Many children with language impairments also struggle with reading, and early intervention can change their academic trajectory. • Cognitive Communication After brain injuries or neurological conditions, people may need help with memory, attention, problem-solving, or organizing their thoughts. SLPs help rebuild these skills. • Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) When speaking isn’t possible, SLPs help children and adults communicate through devices, picture boards, or sign language. AAC gives a voice to those who don’t use verbal speech. • Accent Modification and Voice Coaching Some individuals seek help modifying an accent or refining their speaking voice for professional or personal reasons. SLPs offer evidence-based strategies for achieving clear, confident communication. • Selective Mutism and Anxiety-Related Disorders Some children speak comfortably at home but remain silent in school or public. SLPs work collaboratively with psychologists and families to gently increase communication in different settings. Speech therapy is a dynamic and evolving field that touches nearly every aspect of communication—from birth through adulthood. If you or someone you love struggles with speech, language, or swallowing, know that help is available. It’s not just about saying “S” or “R” correctly—it’s about making sure every voice is heard. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C . Athletics end of year and Title IX report By Jay Russell First year Piedmont High School Athletic Director Tyler Small provided a report on the recent year of athletics to the school board on June 11. The report included the status of Title IX compliance. Title IX efforts focused on improvement to weight room access, locker room usage, more tournament participation, and more concession sales during home events for girls’ teams with the overarching goal of balancing participation. In total, there were 373 female students at PHS and 413 males. Females account for 47.5% of the student body. When counting two- and three-sport athletes multiple times, there were 365 female athletes and 431 male athletes. Girls sports teams would need to add 24 athletes onto their rosters to achieve equal participation with the boys. To balance participation Small is focusing 2025-26 efforts on increasing participation in girls water polo and swimming when the new community pool opens. The district will also continue to search for local opportunities for beach volleyball practice and competitions. “Traveling to Santa Rosa, or to Santa Cruz or to somewhere on the coast for [beach volleyball] matches, it wears on the athletes, the coaches, the families that are transporting the athletes,” said Small. “The closest competition [girl’s beach volleyball] had was Livermore.” Two strength and conditioning coaches were hired at the start of the year for the weight room, and designated times were allotted for female athletes and middle school athletes. Small said locker room usage was improved by increasing communication around scheduling and by giving more coaches keys to the Witter Field weight room. New to the school, girls’ JV basketball team went to a tournament in Reno, while both girls’ and boys’ golf teams played in invitational tournaments. The varsity girls and boys sports teams each participated in 14 tournaments each. Small highlighted the revitalization of the football program. “Our football program has continued to grow. Hats off to the amazing coaches, who took a program that was almost non-existent and almost cut, due to a lack of interest, and have grown that to over 60 athletes. Next year’s numbers look very similar,” said Small. Small called 2024-25 a “banner year” with four WACC12 Players of the Year and one CIF Norcal Championship in boys soccer. Small also highlighted the 58 first-team WACC12 selections, 54 second-team selections and 35 honorable mention selections. “For a school of 800 students going up against Berkeley, a school of 4000, and going against O’Dowd, a private school, to be able to have those numbers within our league is pretty astounding,” he said. Piedmont’s Title IX compliance was sparked by a gender equity audit of the high school athletic program in 2021-22. READ IT IN THE POST

8 8 Wednesday, June 25, 2025 POSTCARDS FROM CAMP - MAIN Postcards from Camp Postcards from Camp Letters sent home by kids at Camp Augusta Enjoy some glimpses into a day at Camp Augusta. Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. Our first week of summer camp was full of Piedmont children ready to start their summer off with time in nature, and also enjoying so much more with almost 150 different clinic activities. There were more than 75 “Playstation” activities, which are the opposite of the console — whimsical, natural games played with real humans, in real time, with collective creative joy. The campers created their own cabin activities which test the bounds of imagination, creativity, and expression. Want to be a zombie hoard? How about creating your own Mission Impossible scenarios? For something different how about building a cardboard city and then torching it with a flame thrower. The first week of summer camp was greeted by 100 campers enjoying the magic that only occurs on the shores of Lake Vera at Camp Augusta. The new counselors were excitedly nervous for their first campers, even after 25 days and nearly 300 hours of training. The returning staff were excited to see old campers, and greet the new ones. articles.text: Enjoy some hide-and-seek fun designed to encourage residents and visitors to get to know their Rockridge businesses. Finding Waldo is a wonderful way to support shopping local. There is no charge to participate and all ages are welcome. Families will love joining the scavenger hunt to find the iconic children’s book character, with his red-and-white-striped shirt and black glasses, hidden in 25 local businesses. To join in the fun, simply pick up a “Find Waldo Passport” at Pegasus Books (5560 College Avenue) or at one of the participating stores during the month of July. You can also download it here at home (be sure to include both pages stapled together). Get a Stamp (ie. stamp, sticker, signature) on your passport from a shopkeeper where you find a miniature Waldo. Collecting store stamps at 20 or more businesses will entitle diligent seekers entry into prize drawings! On Thursday, July 31 at 6 p.m., Pegasus Books will host a Where’s Waldo party with treats for anyone who participated. Books, stickers, and prizes will be raffled. You don’t have to be present to win a prize, but we’d love for you to come. articles.text: Piedmont City Council received an update on the city’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and progress on its Climate Action Plan at its regular meeting on Monday, June 16. While the report shows that Piedmont continues to make significant reductions in emissions, it also warns that the city is unlikely to meet its 2030 target without further action. The update follows the city’s 2018 adoption of Climate Action Plan 2.0 (CAP 2.0), which set a goal of reducing emissions 50% from 2005 levels by 2030, and reaching carbon neutrality by 2045. The presentation was delivered by Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz, who authored this year’s GHG inventory. Kaplowitz joined the city through the Sustainability Service Corps Fellowship Program, which had previously supplied climate fellows to Piedmont for nine years. Fellows have played key roles in emissions reporting, public outreach, and development of the city’s REACH building codes. “For nine years, fellows have been vital to advancing the climate action here in Piedmont,” said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “Fellows have worked on developing the city’s REACH codes, annual greenhouse gas emissions inventories, and have been essential in public engagement.” Kaplowitz’s own fellowship was nearly cut short. On April 26, the federal AmeriCorps program suspended the fellowship as part of broader national budget cuts. The City quickly responded, hiring Kaplowitz as a part-time temporary Sustainability Clerk using unspent Planning Department salary funds to ensure continuity and completion of his work. 2023 Greenhouse Gas Inventory According to the 2023 GHG inventory, Piedmont has reduced its total emissions by 32.1% compared to 2005. Transportation and building energy continue to dominate the city’s emissions profile, accounting for roughly 97% of all emissions. Among transportation sources, passenger vehicles made up 90.5% of the sector’s emissions—representing about 45% of total citywide emissions. In the building energy category, residential natural gas usage made up 92.6%— another 44% of the total. Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz presents the Climate Action Update. Municipal operations, such as the city’s vehicle fleet and employee commutes, made up just 3.5% of Piedmont’s total emissions. However, overall emissions ticked up slightly—by 1.35% from 2022. Kaplowitz attributed the increase largely to a rise in residential natural gas use, as more residents spent time at home due to remote work. Warmer weather and more hot days likely drove higher use of air conditioning as well. These trends, Kaplowitz noted, underscore the urgency of electrification efforts identified in CAP 2.0. Despite the uptick, other emissions categories showed improvement from 2022: • Transportation emissions declined 2.2% • Water and wastewater emissions dropped 41.2%, hitting their lowest levels since 2016 • Electricity-related emissions fell 20.9% Looking Ahead Despite encouraging trends, Piedmont remains off track to meet its 2030 emissions target, according to analysis provided by ICLEI – Local Governments for Sustainability. Kaplowitz’s report emphasized several key strategies for bridging the gap: • Encourage EV adoption and green transportation • Amplify home electrification and energy efficiency • Promote climate-related rebates and public engagement • Incentivize low-carbon commuting options for city staff • Upgrade when and where suitable for efficiency The city also plans to finalize its Electrification Strategy, conduct an energy audit of city facilities, and increase climate-oriented community outreach in the coming year. The Hidden Carbon Footprint The report also noted that the city’s annual inventories do not include lifecycle emissions—the greenhouse gases associated with the production, transportation, and disposal of goods and services consumed outside Piedmont’s borders. If included, emissions would be seven times higher than the current inventory suggests. “If included, Piedmont is the highest emitter per capita in Alameda County due to higher consumption of goods,” the report reads. “While these immense consumption-based emissions pose a significant challenge, they also demonstrate the power Piedmonters yield to curb climate change with their purchasing decisions.” Future Growth as a Climate Variable One major upcoming decision with climate implications is the city’s Moraga Canyon Housing Project, which proposes building up to 199 units on cityowned land. In a June 13 newsletter, local climate advocacy group Piedmont Connect warned that emissions from the housing development could offset most of the gains the city has made over the past decade. The project has not yet been formally evaluated in the city’s climate models, but its potential to increase demand for transportation and energy will likely factor into future CAP updates. As Piedmont plans for a growing population, its climate strategy faces a central challenge: how to accommodate that growth while continuing to drive emissions down. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team’s season continued for an additional week when 10 athletes competed at the Nike Outdoor Nationals at the University of Oregon’s historic Hayward Field Thursday through Sunday, June 19-22. The 35-year old event is a premier postseason meet, with 5,000 athletes from high schools, middle schools, and club teams throughout the country. “There’s a series of postseason events outside of the score of your respective state competitions. Some individuals compete with their high school, some compete with their club, or some compete independently. You have to hit a minimum mark to apply and then you go through an acceptance round,” described PHS track coach Pouyan Assadi. Putting a bow on his high school career was Miguel Long, who will be a freshman at Chico State in the fall. Long placed fourth of 41 athletes in the Emerging Elite triple jump category, notching a new personal record of 45 feet, 10.5 inches and improving his previous best by two inches. Long was named Athlete of the Year by the Piedmont Post. “You must have a good season in order to qualify. Miguel was able to PR and broke his own school record,” Assadi said. Fellow Athlete of the Year, Nia Kim, also left her mark on the 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams with teammates Ella Yasar, Kyla Williams, Claire Aubrecht, and Daniela Lucaccini. Their 4x100 team finished fourth of nine teams in the Emerging Elite category finals with a time of 49.73. To get there, they placed sixth of 37 teams in the preliminary round in 50.45. Lucaccini replaced Williams in the 4x400, finishing 22nd of 32 in 4:10.15 “We cut our teeth in the relays. In order to be good at the relays, you need a standout athlete and have depth. If our coaches do our job right, the depth runners can become the star. Our goal is to create that pipeline. The girls 4x1 had all of that; Nia became a star, Ella is a seasoned-vet, Claire could have the highest trajectory, and Kyla is someone we’re still learning about,” Assadi said. Piedmont also featured its girls’ 4x800 relay team with Nikita Gorelik, Skylar Best, Caroline Taylor, and Leighton Mand. The team placed 17th of 29 teams with a time of 10:09.39. Of the group, Taylor is the only graduating member with the Class of 2025. Gorelik is a rising sophomore and was in consideration for our Freshman of the Year award. Mand is a rising junior and the winner of our 2025 Sophomore of the Year award, while Best enters her senior year. Assadi highly praised Gorelik’s impact as a freshman. “Internally, we awarded Nikita our Freshman of the Year. She competed on the team the whole season and was on the DMR team that qualified for the Miguel Long capped off his high school career by finishing fourth in the triple jump at the Nike Outdoor Nationals in Oregon. Stanford Invitational and Sacramento Meet of Champions. She has super stardom written on her,” Assadi said. Piedmont’s 4x100 relay team placed fourth. articles.text: On June 14, Jasper and Josie Schuetz strongly represented Piedmont Mountain Bike Team at the Lost and Found Gravel Festival, an annual gravel-bike showcase held in Portola set among the rugged backcountry of the Lost Sierra by the Feather River. The festival features three challenging routes – 40, 64, and 96 miles, each demanding a mix of pavement, dirt, and gravel. Riders traverse scenic ranchlands, high-Sierra valleys, mountain lakes, wildflower meadows, and historic railroad tracks along the Feather River, offering both physical challenge and natural beauty, all at nearly 5,000 feet in elevation. The race and festival is a fundraiser for Sierra Buttes Trail Stewardship, supporting sustainable trail development and the “Connected Communities” network across 15 mountain towns. Jasper Schuetz, 17, co-captain of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team, has been on a remarkable streak, racking up wins this year. After the regular NICA NorCal Mountain Bike Season ended, he kicked off summer racing on May 30 at the Wente 8-Hour Mountain Bike Race. He teamed up with Sophia Tripovich (Team Schmirk Zone) to claim first place in the Co-Ed 2-Person category, completing 11 laps by beating out pro cyclist Levi Leipheimer and his partner. He followed up that win by taking first place in the Men’s Junior Division (13–18) at Lost and Found, riding the “Full Bull” Jasper Schuetz (middle) atop the podium of the Lost and Found “Full Bull” Course Junior Men’s category. Josephine Schuetz (middle) on top of the Lost and Found “Half Calf” Course Junior Women’s podium.
articles.title: Schuetz siblings shine in Mountain Bike races

articles.text: In this week’s edition of the Piedmont Post we take a look at Nina Schwab of Carleton College’s diving team, JoJo Murphy of Seattle University’s basketball team, and Natalia Martinez of San Diego State’s basketball team. At the NCAA Division III Swimming & Diving Championships in March, Schwab finished third of 29 in the 1-meter dive with a score of 438.20, earning All-American honors in the process. Nina also made school history when winning the MIAC Championship in the 1-meter dive. She wound up twice setting the school and MIAC Championship record at the event in February, scoring 464.10 points in the preliminary round and 475.40 points to claim the title in a field of 23. She was also second of 22 in the 3-meter dive with a score of 471.35. Schwab was Piedmont High’s only diver and competed in the 2024 CIF State Swimming Diving Championship in the 1-meter dive. She finished 16th of 28 athletes with a score of 429.55. To get there, Nina finished fourth of 16 at the NCS Championships with a final score of 423.35. game and a .395 3-point shooting percent. He scored 20 or more points 16 times, was a three-time CCAA Men’s Basketball Player of the Week winner and earned CCAA All-Tournament honors. The Wildcats went 24-6 last season with Murphy leading the team with 279 total minutes and 155 points. He’s converting 44 percent from the field and 34 percent from 3-pointers. He was named the CCAA’s Freshman of the Year in 2023 and was first-team All-CCAA. He was an honorable mention for All-CCAA in 2024. Murphy was a top recruit for Seattle University in the transfer portal. He’s now set to play Division 1 basketball in the Western Athletic Conference with the Redhawks. Photo courtesy of Carleton College Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, finished her freshman year as a record-setter and All-American at Carleton College. JOJO MURPHY Basketball NINA SCHWAB Diving Carleton College Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, closed her freshman on Carleton College’s diving team in Minnesota. She proved to be one of the best divers in Division 3 collegiate diving, earning firstteam All-American honors in her debut year. Seattle University JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, just finished his junior year on Chico State and recently completed a transfer to Seattle University. With the Wildcats, Murphy won the California Collegiate Athletic Association Player of the Year award and the Division 2 California Collegiate Athletic Association’s Men’s Basketball West Region Player of the Year. Murphy led the entire CCAA with an average of 20.5 points per Photo courtesy of San Diego State Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, helped San Diego State win the Mountain West Conference basketball championship as a freshman. NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Photo courtesy of Chico State JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, recently transferred to Seattle University after winning the CCAA Player of the Year at Chico State. San Diego State Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, closed an impressive freshman season on the San Diego State women’s basketball team. They won the Mountain West Conference as the No. 4 seed and earned the No. 14 ranking in the NCAA’s Spokane 1 bracket. The Aztecs finished its season with a 25-10 record. San Diego State went up against No. 2 LSU, which made it to the Elite Eight, losing 103- 48. Martinez was in the starting five, playing 27 minutes for seven points, one rebound, and one assist. As the No. 4 seed in the Mountain West Tournament, SD State beat No. 5 New Mexico 63-53, upset No. 1 UNLV 71-59, and won the title against No. 2 Wyoming 72-68. She logged six points and two assists on Wyoming. She set a Mountain West Conference record on January 18’s 85-66 win over Utah State, where she became the first player to ever sink six 3-pointers in a conference game when the, to go along with nine rebounds and seven assists. In her record-setting performance, Martinez finished with 22 points, converting 7/8 from the field and 6/7 for 3-pointers. She also added one steal and a block, and hit one of her 3-pointers from nearly 30 feet. Martinez finished her debut year with 252 points shooting with 39 three pointers and a sterling 41 percent shooting percentage from beyond the arc and 44 percent from the field. She also logged 68 rebounds, 49 assists, 20 steals, and seven blocks.

articles.text: Sophomore Cole Carnazzo made history as a member of PHS’ 200 and 400 relay teams to reach the State Championship. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. Photo by Becky Spies Skylar Best is a distance runner in cross-country and track. He was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in May, our honorable mention for 2024 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Freshman of the Year. Smolko defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Neo Chai in three sets for the 2025 WACC singles title, dominating the first and third sets toward a 6-1, 4-6, 6-2 win. At the NCS Individual Tournament, Smolko fought to three sets against Head Royce’s Dylan Donovan, but lost 5-7, 6-1, 6-3. It became Smolko’s second appearance in the NCS championship match after last playing in the 2023 final as a sophomore. Skylar Best is a four-year varsity athlete in both cross country and track. She earned second-team All-League honors in cross country last fall, was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in October, and was our honorable mention for Freshman of the Year in 2023. In cross country, Best helped Piedmont finish fourth of 19 schools in the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship at Hayward HS. articles.text: Preview of this year’s course and favorite riders This year’s Tour de France marks the 112th edition of La Grande Boucle. Starting with the Grand Départ in Lille on Saturday, July 5, the tour will once again feature its iconic finish along the Champs-Élysées in Paris on July 27. The race concluded last year due to the Olympic Hames underway in Paris. This year’s race will be entirely on French soil, the first time since 2020 that the entirety of the race wo;; ne within France. Lille hosts its first Grand Départ since 1994. Day 1 opens with a 184.9 kilometer flat course around the city. Stage 2 to Boulogne marks the longest stage of the entire tour at 209.1 km on a hilly course, while Stage 3 is a 178.3 km flat course to Dunkirk, while Stage 4 is another hilly course on a 174.2 km ride to Rouen. Stages 5 is one of two individual time trials on a 33 km sprint through Caen. Stages 6-7 provides a collective 398.5 km of hilly riding, while Stages 8-9 are continuous flat courses with 345.5 km collectively. Le Tour turns up in Stage 10 on Bastille Day, July 14, for the first mountain course, 165.3 km from Ennezat to Le Mont Dore with 4,400 meters of climbing. After a rest day, Stage 11 is a 156.8 km ride through the city of Toulouse, which is a precursor to a return to the mountains. Stage 12 is a 181 km ride from Auch to Hautacam with three different steep ascents, including a summit finish. Stage 13 is a unique 10 km time trial on a mountain course that’s completely uphill. Stages 14 is another mountain ride, 182.6 km from Pau to Superbagnères, featuring four steep ascents and a third consecutive summit finish. Stage 15 is another 169.3 km hilly stage followed by their second rest day. They’ll need the rest with three of the next four stages on mountain courses. Stage 16 rides 171.5 km from Montpellier up Mont Ventoux, where the course will have just one huge ascent with a gradient of 8.8 percent to a summit. After a 160.4 km Stage 17, Stages 18-19 provides 301.4 km of mountain riding. Stage 18 has three steep ascents with grades of 5.5 percent, 7.9 percent, and 6.5 percent and a summit finish. Stage 19 also has three steep climbs and another summit finish. Stage 20 is a 185 km hilly course with fluctuating ascents and descents throughout the ride. The finale on July 27’s Stage 21 is a 132.3 km flat ride from Mantes la Ville to Paris. Provided are the five riders to watch based on odds makers. • Tadej Pogačar UAE Team Emirates Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar is the hands-down favorite after winPhoto courtesy of LeTour.com Map of the 112th Tour de France winding 3,338.8 km through France. ning his third Grand Tour last year and seeking to become the first four-time winner since Chris Froome. He goes to France with a head of steam after winning the Critérium du Dauphiné earlier this month. • Jonas Vingegaard Visma–Lease a Bike Danish rider Jonas Vingegaard won the Yellow Jersey in 2022 and 2023, and finished second in last year’s tour. He is the No. 2 candidate to win this year’s General Classification. • Remco Evenepoel Soudal–Quick-Step A 25-year-old Belgian, Remco Evenepoel, is odds makers’ third favorite after finishing third in last year’s Tour de France. He recently finished fourth in the Critérium du Dauphiné and won the Brabantse Pijl in April. • João Almeida UAE Team Emirates João Almeida is odds makers’ No. 4 favorite, but winning the tour seems less likely given he’s teammates with Pogačar, meaning he’ll likely be a role player in helping push his teammate toward the Yellow Jersey. Helping his cause is several wins this year, including the Tour de Suisse, Tour of the Basque Country, and the Tour de Romandie • Primož Roglič Bora–Hansgrohe Fellow Slovenian Primož Roglič, 35, was leading the 2020 Tour de France entering the second-to-last stage before his countryman Pogačar took the lead in a breathtaking Stage 20 time trial. The veteran rider is the oldest of the bunch, but is coming off a win of the Volta a Catalunya in March. Get your FREE estimate today from Piedmont’s most trusted auto body shop. pages.text: Wednesday, June 25, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Eagle Lake, a pristine alpine lake near Lake Tahoe’s Emerald Bay By Jonathan Comeaux Welcome back. Hiking with Jon has returned for the summer months, starting the summer series with a batch of hikes around the popular summer getaway for Bay Area residents at Lake Tahoe. Eagle Lake is a 0.9 mile outand-back trail near Emerald Bay and South Lake Tahoe, making just 1.8 miles of hiking to a quiet and awe-striking alpine lake. It is considered a moderately challenging route with 429 feet of elevation gain and a starting point of 6,570 feet in elevation. It’s considered a very popular trail with hundreds of visitors each day given the proximity to South Lake Tahoe just 10 miles away. In May there was still snow lacing the mountainside feeding Eagle Lake, Eagle Creek, and Eagle Falls. A bluejay poses for a picture by Eagle Lake. Eagle Lake is an achievable hike in the spring to see a magnificent frozen lake. Eagle Lake is a 1.8 mile out-and-back trail with 429 feet of elevation gain. PRIVATE, LOCALLY OWNED CARE FOR YOUR BEST FRIEND Looking for the best in veterinary care services? Come to The Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital for personalized, compassionate care. The view from the Eagle Lake trail toward Lake Tahoe’s Emerald Bay After parking off of CA-89, the day starts with a jaunt past Eagle Falls, a huge cascading waterfall along Eagle Creek that feeds into Lake Tahoe. You’ll walk alongside Eagle Creek as you trek toward Eagle Lake. After a healthy winter of snow, the foliage around Lake Tahoe is lush with vegetation. Eagle Lake trail takes hikers beneath groves of pine trees, while there are portions with beautiful views of Emerald Bay beneath you for when you’d like to catch a breath. Eagle Lake requires entering the Desolation Wilderness, which you can get a permit for near the parking lot. Given the amount of foot traffic, hiking in the morning is your best bet to if you want to avoid a highway of hikers. There are portions less than three-feet wide, which will require patience when passing other at times. It’s an achievable hike to see a frozen lake in the winter and spring. On a visit in May, Eagle Lake still was covered in a thin layer of frost and ice. More adventurous minds have taken their ice skates during the winter time to skate across the hard frozen surface. Punch “Eagle Falls” or “Eagle Falls Lake” into your GPS device to find this hike. articles.text: Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 18, marking the 56th anniversary of the eclectic music celebration along Highway 4 that brings together renowned artists and ensembles across genres including classical, jazz, rock, pop and more. The annual summer event is held in the picturesque Bear Valley, nestled in the Sierra Nevada mountains about halfway between Lake Tahoe and Yosemite. Concerts take place under an outdoor tent that seats more than 500 guests. This year’s lineup features everything from ‘80s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy,” said Board of Directors President Julia Mee. “From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone.” Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off the festival Friday, July 18. They are followed Saturday by San Francisco’s Super Diamond, a Neil Diamond tribute band, performing hits from “Sweet Caroline” to “I Am…I Said.” After a week of tribute performances, the festival shifts to classical with Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Friday, July 25. The program also features guitarist Lyle Sheffler performing Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez and a work by 18th-century composer Marianna Martines. Soprano singer Carrie Hennessey closes out this year’s festival on August 3. A program featuring music by Mozart and Haydn, interspersed with contemporary pop tunes, takes place Sunday, July 27. The symphonic finale, featuring works by Leonard Bernstein, Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Sergei Rachmaninoff, is scheduled for Friday, Aug. 1. The festival’s annual gala is held Saturday, Aug. 2. Guests are encouraged to wear period attire from the late 19th to early 20th century for an evening of music from the era. Gala tickets include concert admission, a welcome glass of champagne or themed cocktail, dinner with wine, and a live auction. Soprano Carrie Hennessey closes the festival Sunday, Aug. 3. Back by popular demand after last summer’s performance, she will perform fan-favorite songs from Broadway and Hollywood, including music from Les Misérables, The Lion King and The Sound of Music. Visit https://www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org to see the full festival lineup and purchase tickets. Single day tickets are now available. Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off Bear Valley Music Festival on July 18.

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform its annual Independence Day themed-program on July 4 at Shoreline Amphitheatre, an outdoor venue in Mountain View, playing alongside ukulele virtuoso Taimane. Conductor Edwin Outwater returns to Shoreline Amphitheatre to lead the symphony with a lineup of popular Independence Day classics. The Symphony will be joined by special musical guest Taimane, a Hawaiiborn ukulele virtuoso and songwriter, who makes her Stern Grove debut performing alongside the world-class orchestra on July 6. Taimane is renowned for her unique and inventive style of playing the four-string island instrument and has garnered critical acclaim for her signature stage presence. She is the recipient of the 2023 Nā Hōkū Hanohano Instrumental Album and Instrumental Composition of the Year award, and was recognized as the Nā Hōkū Hanohano Favorite Entertainer of the Year in 2023 and 2019. The concert begins at 8 p.m. and traditionally concludes with a grand finale of spectacular fireworks. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2024-25/SWTSShoreline-4th.

articles.text: Ruth Asawa: Retrospective, the first posthumous retrospective of the groundbreaking work of Californian modernist artist Ruth Asawa, is on display at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) through September. Organized by SFMOMA and New York’s Museum of Modern Art, the exhibition features over 300 works of art including looped-wire hanging sculptures for which Asawa is best known, as well as sculptures, drawings, prints, paintings and archival material from public and private collections. “Ruth Asawa: Retrospective is deeply aligned with SFMOMA’s vision to be both local and global—presenting Bay Area artists with profound significance that also have the potential to be highly impactful and relevant on an international scale,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “This exhibition provides an opportunity to celebrate the legendary Ruth Asawa, who was both a widely acclaimed artist and a hometown inspiration whose impact can be very much felt today.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective spans over six decades of the artist’s celebrated career and highlights how her longtime San Francisco home and garden served as a muse for her artwork and informed her public sculpture commissions and dedication to arts advocacy in the city. The posthumous retrospective is co-curated by Janet Bishop, Thomas Weisel Family Chief Curator and Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. “It is an immense privilege to present the full range of Ruth Asawa’s life’s work through this retrospective,” said Bishop. “Not only was Asawa an exceptionally talented artist, among the most distinguished sculptors of the 20th century and a major contributor in so many other mediums, but she lived her values in everything she did, modeling the importance of the arts and opening up creative opportunities for others at every turn.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective will be on view at SFMOMA through September 2. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415. 357.4000 for more information. Patrons view the Ruth Asawa retrospective at SFMOMA. Photo courtesy of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, June 25, 2025 Arts & Entertainment Bear Valley Music Festival runs July 18 to August 3 By Allyson Aleksey Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 18, marking the 56th anniversary of the eclectic music celebration along Highway 4 that brings together renowned artists and ensembles across genres including classical, jazz, rock, pop and more. The annual summer event is held in the picturesque Bear Valley, nestled in the Sierra Nevada mountains about halfway between Lake Tahoe and Yosemite. Concerts take place under an outdoor tent that seats more than 500 guests. This year’s lineup features everything from ‘80s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy,” said Board of Directors President Julia Mee. “From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone.” Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off the festival Friday, July 18. They are followed Saturday by San Francisco’s Super Diamond, a Neil Diamond tribute band, performing hits from “Sweet Caroline” to “I Am…I Said.” After a week of tribute performances, the festival shifts to classical with Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Friday, July 25. The program also features guitarist Lyle Sheffler performing Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez and a work by 18th-century composer Marianna Martines. Soprano singer Carrie Hennessey closes out this year’s festival on August 3. A program featuring music by Mozart and Haydn, interspersed with contemporary pop tunes, takes place Sunday, July 27. The symphonic finale, featuring works by Leonard Bernstein, Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Sergei Rachmaninoff, is scheduled for Friday, Aug. 1. The festival’s annual gala is held Saturday, Aug. 2. Guests are encouraged to wear period attire from the late 19th to early 20th century for an evening of music from the era. Gala tickets include concert admission, a welcome glass of champagne or themed cocktail, dinner with wine, and a live auction. Soprano Carrie Hennessey closes the festival Sunday, Aug. 3. Back by popular demand after last summer’s performance, she will perform fan-favorite songs from Broadway and Hollywood, including music from Les Misérables, The Lion King and The Sound of Music. Visit https://www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org to see the full festival lineup and purchase tickets. Single day tickets are now available. The concert traditionally concludes with a grand finale of spectacular fireworks. SF Symphony performs at Shoreline Amphitheatre July 4 By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Symphony will perform its annual Independence Day themed-program on July 4 at Shoreline Amphitheatre, an outdoor venue in Mountain View, playing alongside ukulele virtuoso Taimane. Conductor Edwin Outwater returns to Shoreline Amphitheatre to lead the symphony with a lineup of popular Independence Day classics. The Symphony will be joined by special musical guest Taimane, a Hawaiiborn ukulele virtuoso and songwriter, who makes her Stern Grove debut performing alongside the world-class orchestra on July 6. Taimane is renowned for her unique and inventive style of playing the four-string island instrument and has garnered critical acclaim for her signature stage presence. She is the recipient of the 2023 Nā Hōkū Hanohano Instrumental Album and Instrumental Composition of the Year award, and was recognized as the Nā Hōkū Hanohano Favorite Entertainer of the Year in 2023 and 2019. The concert begins at 8 p.m. and traditionally concludes with a grand finale of spectacular fireworks. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2024-25/SWTSShoreline-4th. articles.text: Oakland artist King Isis will take the stage at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) this Friday, June 27, showcasing their unique take on Afrofuturism in music—a blend of R&B, alternative rock, and boho indiepop. King Isis is an emerging pop artist steadily gaining momentum in Oakland’s queer arts scene, known for a fresh, acoustic-forward sound. Their tracks “Dissonance,” “Make it Up,” and “Im fine, thx 4 asking” have garnered hundreds of thousands of views on YouTube. They’ll be joined Friday by DJ Ignacia, whose genre-blending set is designed to get guests dancing. The performance is part of OMCA’s Friday Nights series, a free weekly community event held every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout the spring and summer. The series features live music, hands-on art activities, and late-night museum access with the purchase of a general admission ticket. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s expansive lawn, where live entertainment continues into the evening. Attendees may bring their own food and nonalcoholic beverages or purchase from on-site food trucks. A rotating selection of vendors will be stationed on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon streets, adjacent to the museum. Outside alcohol is not permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-kingisis/ to learn more. King Isis

articles.text: Visit the Legion of Honor in San Francisco any Saturday afternoon and enjoy a free organ concert by local, classically trained organists Jonathan Dimmock, Joy-Leilani Garbutt or Christopher Keady. Dimmock, a graduate of Oberlin and Yale, was the first American to hold the prestigious position of organ scholar at Westminster Abbey. He has served as resident organist at St. John the Divine in New York City, St. Mark’s in Minneapolis and Grace Cathedral in San Francisco. He is currently principal organist at the Legion of Honor, organist for the San Francisco Symphony and director of music at Congregation Sherith Israel. He has also recorded a Grammy-winning album with the San Francisco Symphony. Garbutt is an organist and co-founder of the Boulanger Initiative, a nonprofit that supports female composers. She spent a year in France researching early 20th-century organ music by women composers and currently Organist Joy-Leilani Garbutt performs free concerts on Saturday at Legion of Honor. serves as director of music at St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in San Francisco. Keady is the interim director of music at Grace Cathedral, where he serves as principal accompanist for the Cathedral Choir of Men and Boys and performs on the cathedral’s Alexander Memorial Organ. Concerts begin at 4 p.m. in Gallery 10 and are free to all museum patrons. Residents of all nine Bay Area counties — Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano and Sonoma — receive free admission to the Legion of Honor on Saturdays. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ events/organ-concert to learn more and to register.

articles.text: The historic Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside welcomes visitors every Wednesday and Thursday evening throughout the summer for its aptly named “Summer Nights.” Filoli typically closes its grounds at 5 p.m., but on Wednesdays and Thursdays, visitors can explore the historic house and gardens well into the evening. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides an idyllic backdrop for watching the sun set on a pleasant summer evening. The weekly event features live music by the pool, a pop-up wine and cocktail stand, and a food truck. Some visitors nestle on blankets, while others explore the Estate Trail — a one-mile, self-guided walk through Filoli’s nature preserve. There, it’s not uncommon to spot a family of deer or a gaggle of turkeys along the trail’s five distinct native ecosystems. Filoli’s mission is to “connect [its] rich history with a vibrant future through beauty, nature, and shared stories,” and there is no shortage of natural beauty at the estate. The property is surrounded by more than 23,000 acres of protected Peninsula watershed, and on warm summer evenings, fog can be seen rolling down the mountains. The house was constructed in 1917 and is a notable example of Georgian Revival architecture. Designed by Willis Polk, it took three years to complete and cost $425,000 — roughly $8.5 million in today’s dollars. Built under the direction of William and Agnes Bourn, the estate was originally conceived as a “humble” country home. The Bourn family’s wealth came from gold — specifically the Empire Gold Mine, California’s most productive. “When [the Bourns] built Filoli they were in their 50’s, and were looking to construct a country estate, a common thing for wealthy San Franciscans to do at the time. They chose this spot because of its beautiful location,” explained Susan O’Sullivan, chief external relations officer at Filoli. The Bourns, two of the founding board members of the San Francisco Symphony, loved to entertain. The massive two-story mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. The same Baccarat crystal chandeliers from 1917 remain in the ballroom — six-foot-tall glass fixtures that are meticulously cleaned and maintained by Filoli staff. The house spans 54,256 square feet and includes 16 bathrooms, 10 main bedrooms, 14 staff bedrooms and 17 fireplaces. When the Bourns passed away in the 1930s, the house was purchased by William and Lurline Roth, heiress to the Matson Navigation Company. The Roths expanded the gardens to include collections of camellias, rhododendrons and azaleas, and added a swimming pool and screened-in teahouse. Lurline Roth passed away in 1976, and her wish was to donate Filoli so it could be open to the public. In 1977, the estate was given to the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Today, the site is both a California Historical Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. “Lurline’s wish was that Filoli would be a cultural center for the Bay Area,” O’Sullivan said. “Summer Nights” ends September 18. Learn more about “Summer Nights” at Filoli, and book your visit at https://filoli. org/summer-nights/. Visitors can enjoy live music by the pool during “Summer Nights” events.
articles.title: “Summer Nights” events at Filoli House and Garden every Wed & Thurs
