articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Bob Houser currently has an exciting exhibit of wood sculptures at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “I grew up on the edge of a woods in New England and I spent all my free time wandering amongst the trees. Though I have been living in California for all of my adult life, you cannot take the New Englander out of me. It is a part of me. I’m determinedly independent, critically frugal, I don’t take myself too seriously, and yes, there’s the sarcasm. For over 30 years I have been making portraits of people, real people, as a photographer for advertising and editorial clients worldwide. Along the way, I have pictured large sculptural pieces in my mind – pieces I never had the space to create. “Fast forward a few decades of city life, and I’m back living on a farm, this time in the Oakland hills. When I started to make sculpture under the shade of a 60-year-old Cedar, I was back home again, back in the woods of New England, back playing with trees.” Robert Houser
articles.title: Robert Houser exhibit of wood sculptures now at PCA

articles.text: 2nd show added at 5:30 p.m. on Saturday, July 12 Derek Gripper is a South African classical guitarist and composer renowned for his unique ability to transcribe and perform complex West African kora music on the classical guitar. His work bridges the gap between different musical traditions and has garnered international recognition for its innovation and virtuosity. Gripper’s journey began with the challenge of how to bring the intricate, flowing music of West Africa’s griots — traditionally played on the 21-string kora — on the guitar? His album One Night on Earth was the answer, a recording so unexpected that celebrated guitarist John Williams said, “It seemed absolutely impossible until I heard Derek Gripper do it.” But this project wasn’t just about technical mastery. It was about creating connection — between African oral traditions and Western classical music, between different ways of listening and understanding. Along the way, Gripper has performed with legendary musicians John Williams and Toumani Diabaté’s Symmetric Orchestra, sharing stages from Carnegie Hall to Shakespeare’s Globe. In his concerts he weaves together the works of composers like Toumani Diabaté, Ali Farka Touré, J.S. Bach, and Arvo Pärt, creating a dialogue where different musical traditions meet. His adventurous spirit and artistry have been recognized by Songlines Magazine more than once: his 2016 album Libraries on Fire was named Best Album in Africa & the Middle East, and his 2024 collaboration with kora master Ballaké Sissoko won Songlines’ Best Album award for that year. Recent projects like A Year of Swimming and his ongoing work with Sissoko blend original compositions, improvisations, and West African and European musical lineages. His recordings of Bach’s solo works reveal surprising links between classical music and the improvisational spirit of the griots. Book your tickets now and be part of the conversation. You can learn more about him through the below videos: • NEW YORK GUITAR FESTIVAL: https://youtu.be/ HvqYZ5sOjI8 • TINY DESK CONCERT: https://youtu.be/55QnOlXckOk • TEDx: https://youtu.be/ TD2I_Q9dkac • 56 – Derek Gripper and Guy Buttery play this classic by Ali Farka Touré: https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=qwPIGM_yPG4 laughing. Live music filled the fairgrounds. A marching band paraded through, while a country-western band played twangy favorites on a nearby stage. And speaking of country flair, Leapin’ Louie delivered cowboy comedy with style and skill. Equal parts clever and athletic, he wowed the crowd with rope tricks and slapstick. I spoke to him after his set—turns out he’s performed in 35 countries. The miniature railroad museum was like something out of The Twilight Zone—an odd, mesmerizing little world in motion. On a more humorous note, one small restaurant served an entire menu built around Spam. Oddly enough, Monty Python was nowhere to be found. Spam aside, a friend of mine grilled up a surprisingly good steak. His method broke with tradition: make a marinade with salt and brown sugar (pepper optional), rub it onto the meat, seal it in a plastic bag, and cook it like a regular steak. The result? A delicious detour from the expected.
articles.title: Guitarist Derek Gripper to perform at PCA

articles.text: Excitement was everywhere— that’s just how it is when the circus comes to town. PT Barnum, Bailey, and the Ringling Brothers may be long gone, but their spirit was alive and well at the Alameda County Fair. Families crowded the grounds, creating a true cross-section of America. It felt like a fairground collided with a three-ring circus. First, you pay to park, then there’s a nominal admission fee— and then it’s off to the races, so to speak. There was something for everyone. Naturally, we started with food. One of the first stands we passed offered giant turkey legs, billed as “Texas-sized,” for nearly $23. We paired that with a heaping pile of French fries. Everything was oversized. You’d think PT Barnum himself was still running the show. Among the attractions was a breathtaking trapeze act, and the motorcycle acrobatics show was downright heart-stopping. “Terrifying” might be more accurate. The only downside was the announcer’s nonstop shouting of “Let’s make some noise!”— repeated ad nauseam. The piglet races were a surprise hit—those little guys can really move. The announcer laced his commentary with puns and wordplay that kept the crowd The Alameda County Fair is running now through July 6 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds in Pleasanton.
articles.title: Critic’s Day Off

On a more humorous note, one small restaurant served an entire menu built around Spam. Oddly enough, Monty Python was nowhere to be found. Spam aside, a friend of mine grilled up a surprisingly good steak. His method broke with tradition: make a marinade with salt and brown sugar (pepper optional), rub it onto the meat, seal it in a plastic bag, and cook it like a regular steak. The result? A delicious detour from the expected. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 The Musical Gourmet Critic’s Day Off By Joe Gold Excitement was everywhere— that’s just how it is when the circus comes to town. PT Barnum, Bailey, and the Ringling Brothers may be long gone, but their spirit was alive and well at the Alameda County Fair. Families crowded the grounds, creating a true cross-section of America. It felt like a fairground collided with a three-ring circus. First, you pay to park, then there’s a nominal admission fee— and then it’s off to the races, so to speak. There was something for everyone. Naturally, we started with food. One of the first stands we passed offered giant turkey legs, billed as “Texas-sized,” for nearly $23. We paired that with a heaping pile of French fries. Everything was oversized. You’d think PT Barnum himself was still running the show. Among the attractions was a breathtaking trapeze act, and the motorcycle acrobatics show was downright heart-stopping. “Terrifying” might be more accurate. The only downside was the announcer’s nonstop shouting of “Let’s make some noise!”— repeated ad nauseam. The piglet races were a surprise hit—those little guys can really move. The announcer laced his commentary with puns and wordplay that kept the crowd The Alameda County Fair is running now through July 6 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds in Pleasanton.

articles.text: Perhaps it began with the COVID confinement, but how we now watch movies—and find a variety of other entertainment— is nothing short of revolutionary. Streaming has transformed film access, once the domain of art house theaters and rare screenings, into something extraordinarily available. The review that follows is a good example of what this shift has made possible. Gentleman’s Agreement, directed by Elia Kazan, was released in 1947. Based on the novel of the same name by Laura Z. Hobson, the film was bold for its time in addressing anti-Semitism and earned eight Academy Award nominations in 1948, winning three. Gregory Peck stars as journalist Phillip Green, a respected writer who accepts a provocative assignment for a national magazine based in New York: to investigate and expose anti-Semitism in American society. Eager to begin, he initially struggles to find the right angle. Then it dawns on him—the angle is the experience itself. To write the article with authenticity and empathy, he decides to pose as a Jewish man. As a newcomer to the magazine and the city, Green embarks on his now deeply personal investigation. Through a series Dorothy McGuire, Gregory Peck and Sam Jaffe in Gentleman’s Agreement of everyday interactions, he encounters subtle and not-sosubtle prejudice. In one striking example, he’s turned away from a “restricted” New York hotel once the staff assumes he’s Jewish. These moments lead to increasing awareness. The bigotry is not always loud or obvious—it’s often embedded in the culture, coded in silence or social exclusion. Green’s relationships become strained, especially with Kathy Lacey (Dorothy McGuire), a colleague and love interest. Though she recognizes the prejudice around her, she prefers to remain quiet. When Phillip challenges her passivity, insisting that silence is a form of consent, the film doesn’t shy away from the discomfort that follows. Gentleman’s Agreement is a powerful, well-acted film that remains sadly relevant today. Its unflinching look at casual and institutional prejudice offers a reminder of how deeply such attitudes can linger—and how necessary it is to name them. Gentleman’s Agreement. Directed by Elia Kazan. Starring Gregory Peck, Dorothy McGuire, John Garfield. 1 hr., 58 min. Not rated. Released in 1947. Streaming on Prime/Apple TV/Fandango.

articles.text: What Peter Jackson achieves in They Shall Not Grow Old is extraordinary—bordering on magical. Given access to hundreds of hours of archival footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum, he set out to make a 30-minute short. The project instead became a years-long restoration feat that transforms how we see World War I. Using cutting-edge technology, Jackson and his team meticulously cleaned and restored the original film—most of it handcranked, shot at varying speeds. They stabilized it to modern 24-frames-per-second, then undertook the painstaking work of colorizing the black-and-white footage. They traveled to original battlefield sites to capture reference photos, ensuring accuracy in landscapes, uniforms, and detail. Lip-readers deciphered what soldiers were saying, and voice actors from the same regions recreated their speech, dialects intact. No narration was added; instead, the film uses excerpts from more than 600 hours of BBC interviews with WWI veterans—100 voices telling their own story. The result feels almost surreal, as if time has folded and we are seeing 1914 through the eyes of those who lived it. The story unfolds chronologically. In the beginning, we see black-and-white footage of young enlistees—some as young as 14 or 15—arriving at boot camp, wide-eyed and eager. The voiceovers reflect a mix of excitement and national pride. Many believed they were embarking on a grand adventure that would be over by Christmas. Britain buzzed with war fever. Men not in uniform were shamed on the streets and handed white feathers—symbols of cowardice—by young women. Posters urged them to enlist and “do their part.” Then, abruptly, the screen shifts to color. The transformation is stunning. Now we are in the trenches with these young An example of how original World War I footage was restored and colorized for Peter Jackson’s documentary, They Shall Not Grow Old.

articles.text: Whisper of the Heart is the first and only film by director Yoshifumi Kondo, a protégé of Hayao Miyazaki. The narrative is based on the manga story of the same name, written by Hiragi Aoi. It is an engaging and sensitive tale, meant to carry on the Studio Ghibli tradition. Sadly, however, Kondo died unexpectedly in 1998 and Miyazaki returned to the Studio from an all too brief retirement. The film’s protagonist is Shizuku (Brittany Snow), a self-conscious, often shy 14-yearold girl, as well as the characters that surround her, all created with an aura that is often dreamlike. Shizuku lives in the Tama New Town suburb of Tokyo. articles.text: The weather was beautiful last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group, which enjoyed its final spring walk of 2025. A large turnout of 52 walkers—and three K-9 best friends—gathered at the Exedra to take part. The morning was a celebration of the beautiful day and the arrival of summer. Friday, June 20, marked the first astronomical day of summer in the Northern Hemisphere—also known as the summer solstice. The group discussed the significance of the day, which brings the longest period of daylight each year—approximately 15 hours and 9 minutes in Piedmont. This year’s solstice occurred at 7:42 p.m. PDT, when the Earth tilts north to its farthest point (23.5 degrees from the celestial equator) and the sun appears directly overhead at noon above the Tropic of Cancer. The region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn is known as the tropics, an area that receives more direct sunlight and often has warmer, wetter climates. The Tropic of Cancer passes through countries such as Mexico, the Bahamas, Western Sahara, Algeria, Egypt, India, and Taiwan. The word “solstice” comes from the Latin sol (sun) and sistere (to stand still), referring to the point where the sun appears to pause in the sky before reversing direction. For six months the sun appears to move north; the solstice marks the turning point southward until the winter solstice. People have observed solstices for centuries. At England’s Stonehenge, for example, the summer solstice sunrise aligns with the monument’s ancient entrance, illuminating its center. While Piedmont doesn’t host a solstice celebration, the city recently marked another milestone. On June 4, it held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new pedestrian bridge in Piedmont Park. The project began in mid-February, and the bridge was installed over Bushy Dell Creek on March 20 in the park’s southwest section. The old bridge, more than 30 years old, had needed repeated repairs and was patched with plywood after its railings collapsed in 2023. The new bridge features a weathered steel frame and pressure-treated wood decking for long-term durability. Built off-site and lowered into place by crane, the bridge was installed with minimal disruption to the creek’s natural environment. pages.text: Wednesday, June 25, 2025 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays greets summer and a new park bridge By Dick Carter The weather was beautiful last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group, which enjoyed its final spring walk of 2025. A large turnout of 52 walkers—and three K-9 best friends—gathered at the Exedra to take part. The morning was a celebration of the beautiful day and the arrival of summer. Friday, June 20, marked the first astronomical day of summer in the Northern Hemisphere—also known as the summer solstice. The group discussed the significance of the day, which brings the longest period of daylight each year—approximately 15 hours and 9 minutes in Piedmont. This year’s solstice occurred at 7:42 p.m. PDT, when the Earth tilts north to its farthest point (23.5 degrees from the celestial equator) and the sun appears directly overhead at noon above the Tropic of Cancer. The region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn is known as the tropics, an area that receives more direct sunlight and often has warmer, wetter climates. The Tropic of Cancer passes through countries such as Mexico, the Bahamas, Western Sahara, Algeria, Egypt, India, and Taiwan. The word “solstice” comes from the Latin sol (sun) and sistere (to stand still), referring to the point where the sun appears to pause in the sky before reversing direction. For six months the sun appears to move north; the solstice marks the turning point southward until the winter solstice. People have observed solstices for centuries. At England’s Stonehenge, for example, the summer solstice sunrise aligns with the monument’s ancient entrance, illuminating its center. While Piedmont doesn’t host a solstice celebration, the city recently marked another milestone. On June 4, it held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new pedestrian bridge in Piedmont Park. The project began in mid-February, and the bridge was installed over Bushy Dell Creek on March 20 in the park’s southwest section. The old bridge, more than 30 years old, had needed repeated repairs and was patched with plywood after its railings collapsed in 2023. The new bridge features a weathered steel frame and pressure-treated wood decking for long-term durability. Built off-site and lowered into place by crane, the bridge was installed with minimal disruption to the creek’s natural environment. The project came in under budget at $202,661, with $119,000 funded by a California Proposition 68 grant. The walkers had been meaning to visit the new bridge and decided this week was the time. They headed behind the Exedra, entered the park’s upper trail, and followed the lower path along Bushy Dell Creek. Towering eucalyptus trees, nourished by the creek for decades, shaded their way. The group paused to read park history trail markers about the Sulphur Springs Grotto, the Eucalyptus Amphitheater, and “the Cascade,” a lush tropical landscape created by Frank C. Havens in the early 1900s. They reached the new bridge, crossed it, and took a group photo. Later, walker Mark Davis researched the creek’s name, which came from the “rural and romantic” character of its surrounding ravine, once called Bushy Dell. In early Piedmont history, the creek was known for its mineral springs and may also have been referred to as “Red Rock.” With time left in the morning, the group visited more nearby landmarks. They stopped at the PHS softball field, located on the former site of Havens’ Amphitheater, built in 1908 for Shakespearean and other performances. Nancy DeRoche shared that the Piedmont Play School—a two-room building once run by the Recreation Department— later stood there before moving to Hampton Park in 1998 when the Witter Sports Complex was developed. From there, the walkers visited one of Piedmont’s lesser-known fields—Bern Field. Tucked above Witter Field, this small turf space sits along a service road. Cathy Laymon explained that June Bern, who once lived nearby, made the land available to the school district. A local soccer club later developed the field for young athletes. The group then descended to the walkway above the stadium and climbed to Wildwood Avenue for a warm, sunny return to the Exedra. Along the way, Sherry Jacobs pointed out two small paths in the bushes—wellworn deer trails that local wildlife still use. The walk gave the group a chance to celebrate both the city’s newest park improvement and the seasonal shift from spring to summer in quintessential Piedmont style. articles.text: Jeanne Lorraine Gordon passed away on February 15, 2025 after a brief illness. Jeanne was born in Oakland on November 3, 1939 and moved with her family to Piedmont as a teenager. She graduated from Piedmont High School with the class of 1957 and resided in Piedmont her entire life. She loved the lush greenery and parks and only looked forward to leaving Piedmont for family trips to her beloved Grants Pass, Oregon. Jeanne graduated from California College of Arts in Oakland. She did not end up pursuing a career in the arts and later chose to attend UC Berkeley to receive her Masters degree in Social Work. She worked as a social worker for the County of Alameda for 35 years. She spoke of how hard as well as rewarding the work was. Jeanne had a flair about her. She was both highly organized and meticulous in all things, while also being a creative artist at heart. She was quite the wordsmith and was a very talented, wellrounded woman, who appreciated her friends and family. Jeanne was extremely dedicated to helping animals in need. If she knew of an injured cat or dog, she would jump into action. She wanted to help all animals, wild and domestic. She was supportive of The Oakland Zoo’s conservation programs and community cat spay-neuter programs. Jeanne was preceded in death by her parents, Ruth and Leonard Gordon, and half-sister Kathy. Her father was the owner of Gordon Pumps, in Oakland. Jeanne was beloved by her many friends, and cousin Al. Neighbors and friends are planning to have an outdoor gathering in Jeanne’s memory.

By Deborah Quok Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on Nov.5, 2014 Bring the flavors of Spain to your table with this dish that comes together fairly easily. A few weeks remain for local tomatoes and red bell peppers, and new crop California almonds are readily found at local farmers’ markets. These fresh ingredients make up the popular Romesco sauce that originated in Catalonia. Our Bay Area climate is similar to theirs, offering the opportunity to share the same flavors from our kitchens. Catalan-Style Pork and Shrimp “Mar y Montano” (Sea and Mountain) Adapted from España – James Campbell Caruso Serves 6 INGREDIENTS • 1 pork tenderloin, about 1½ pounds; sinew removed and cut into ¾-inch thick medallions • 12 colossal shrimp, 15 count/ • • • pound; peeled and deveined 2 tablespoons lemon juice, freshly squeezed ¼ cup extra virgin olive oil; plus 2 tablespoons more for cooking and finishing Flat leaf parsley, chopped Romesco sauce For the spice mix, thoroughly mix together: • 2 teaspoons salt • 1 teaspoon each granulated garlic and freshly ground black pepper • ½ teaspoon each sweet paprika and smoked paprika • ¼ teaspoon piment d’Esplette or cayenne pepper, to taste. INSTRUCTIONS Coat the pork pieces with 2 tablespoons olive oil, then toss with 2 teaspoons of the spice mix. Set aside in the refrigerator for 15-20 minutes. Coat the shrimp with lemon juice and 2 tablespoons olive oil, then toss with 2 teaspoons of the spice mix. Set aside in the refrigerator for not longer than 15 minutes. Heat a heavy skillet over medium high heat. Coat with about 1 tablespoon of olive oil. Sear the pork first and cook for about 4 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate and keep warm. In the same pan, add a bit more olive oil if needed, and sear the shrimp; about 2 minutes per side. TO SERVE: Spread some Romesco sauce on a plate, then place the pork and shrimp on top. Drizzle a bit more sauce and olive oil over the top, if desired. Garnish with plenty of chopped parsley. Enjoy! Quick Romesco Sauce Adapted from Chow – Kate Ramos Makes: About 1½ cups • • • • • • • • • INGREDIENTS 1 medium tomato, halved 2 medium garlic cloves, peeled 1 slice crusty bread (about 1 ounce) ¼ cup whole raw almonds 2 red bell peppers 2 tablespoons Sherry vinegar ¼ cup olive oil ½ teaspoon sea salt ½ teaspoon paprika INSTRUCTIONS Place oven rack on middle rung. Preheat the oven to 450°F. Arrange the peppers, tomato (cut side up), garlic, bread and almonds on a rimmed baking sheet and roast until the bread and almonds are lightly toasted, about 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the bread and almonds and set aside. Return the peppers, tomato and garlic to the oven and roast an additional 10–12 minutes; until softened and some browning occurs. Transfer the roasted ingredients to a food processor or blender and pulse to coarsely chop. Add vinegar, olive oil, salt, and paprika and pulse again until well combined and relatively smooth. NOTES: Reserve any remaining spice mix and Romesco sauce for future use. The spice mix may be used on any meats, vegetables, rice and potatoes. Romesco is a classic dipping sauce for vegetables. The spacious dining room offered first-class dining on white linen tablecloths to visitors and residents in a room filled with potted palms. Large windows looked out to the park and a wide, open veranda offered outside dining. Once again, beef from nearby ranches, and fresh seafood and fine wine from San Francisco were served in Piedmont Park. The Clubhouse was open for luncheons only and was available for catered dinners. Havens cleared out the underbrush and thinned trees to allow light to filter into the ravine. He transformed the once rustic ravine to a Victorian strolling park. Victorians loved exotic plants, and Havens planted Queen palms, Canary Island date palms, cordyline trees (cabbage palms) The veranda at the Piedmont Clubhouse offered outside dining. and other exotics throughout the park. Just east of the clubhouse, Havens built a rustic teahouse. Stickwork formed the railings, posts and roof of this first teahouse. Thatch and later vines covered the roof, providing shade. That evening hundreds of small twinkling lights in the trees created a fantasy parkland for partygoers. Only the Clubhouse and the mineral spring grottoes were built at this time. The beauty of the wooded ravine, the cascading water, bucolic pathways, rustic bridges and exotic plantings were the Park attractions. articles.text: men—shoulder to shoulder— as their “adventure” descends into unthinkable hardship. They endure mud, cold, and the constant threat of death. Trenches are flooded, littered with corpses, and filled with the stench of decay. Blackened arms protrude from the walls of earth. The soldiers spend sleepless nights in dugouts, while the ground shakes from relentless shelling. When the order comes to go “over the top,” they climb out of the trenches and into machinegun fire. Casualties are immense. Those who survive suffer disfigurement, trauma, and loss. Some stare directly into the camera with brittle smiles—already aware of what awaits them. WWI lasted from 1914 to 1918 and was once called “The War to End All Wars.” After watching They Shall Not Grow Old, it becomes painfully clear why people believed it had to be. The scale of devastation is staggering: 5.5 million military dead, 12 million wounded, and more than 4 million civilian casualties. Poison gas alone caused 1.3 million injuries. One million British soldiers—boys, many of them—never returned. For a small island nation, the loss was overwhelming. Yet Jackson offers no commentary—no on-screen text, no judgment. The soldiers speak for themselves. And that silence is powerful. When the final frame fades, it’s all but impossible not to see this as an anti-war film. That we are watching restored footage

articles.text: her curiosity peaked, she begins to search for him, instead of studying for her final exams and preparing to graduate from her junior high school with her best friend Kuko (Ashley Tisdale). One day she follows a strange cat to an antique shop. It’s a wondrous place, she discovers, owned by an old man named Nishi, who turns out to be the grandfather of Seiji, the boy she’s been obsessively looking for. Of course, the two meet and become friends and Shizuki soon learns that Seiji nurtures a dream of becoming a world-class maker of violins; however, he explains, in order to fulfill his dream he must travel to Italy and serve a kind of apprenticeship. Shizuki is inspired by Seiji’s commitment to his goal, and comes to realize that more than anything she wants to write stories. Amazing stories. And so, she too begins to research, sitting at a table, hunched over a sheet of paper, worrying whether she has the right stuff to tell a compelling story. Meanwhile, her parents worry that her grades might suffer as they watch their daughter devote herself relentlessly to her task.
articles.title: Whisper of the Heart

articles.text: mance by Stenberg as she give fulsome substance to what is, in essence, a coming of age tale, one in which she conveys the duality of her life and its code-shifting demands. She is incandescent as Starr, and it’s a portrayal in which she inhabits a bright, vital girl who is carefully navigating a journey that soon becomes both harrowing and life altering. Tillman is unflinching, refusing to pull back from revelations large and small that America has yet to overcome the painful realities of racism and socioeconomic inequality. He also acknowledges that life for many Americans, especially those of color, is replete with grays. In a friend way, Starr’s life is an awkward but delineated metaphor that captures this perpetual, sometimes surreal dilemma, meaning that the prisms through which most of us peer are prone to an inherent distortion. To Tillman’s credit he rarely lapses into polemics; rather, he relies in The Hate U Give on point of view from the inside out. There is one tragic moment when Starr bears witness to the death of her childhood friend, Khalil (Algee Smith). Drivshort ing Starr home from a party, he is stopped (something that we immediately know will not end well) and then is devastatingly shot by a white police officer. As the singular witness, Starr is forced to make a moral choice regarding stepping forward or remaining silent. For her it is a nexus of the rock and the hard place and she is tormented by indecision. Her mother (Regina Hall) counsels retreat. Her father, Maverick Carter (an outstanding Russell Hornsby), insists she speak her truth. It’s at this point in the film that a myriad of issues are crystalized as Starr faces questions of identity and morality that up to this point have never intruded into her young life. There is a backstory scene that takes place not long after the film begins. It’s one where her father sits his young children down at the dining room table (Starr is 10, her brother 9), and gives them “the talk,” one that consists of what to do and how to behave if stopped by a white police officer. Put your hands on the dashboard, he tells them, do not resist, and obey all commands. The children sit silently, looking at their father

articles.text: Several crosswalks on Grand Avenue have re-opened for pedestrian traffic, as construction crews wrapped up another phase of the Grand Avenue Repavement Project last week. New concrete bulb-outs— designed to shorten crossing distances and improve safety—were completed at the intersections of Grand and Greenbank and Grand and Linda. The first concrete pours took place Saturday, June 14, with crews finishing the final ramp on Monday, June 16. Temporary asphalt was laid later in the week, allowing the city to reopen the crosswalks. Though back in use, the crossings still require finishing touches before the full project wraps. Final improvements—including new flashing beacons and fresh pavement along Piedmont’s stretch of Grand—are expected by the end of August. “The completion of the bulbouts is an important milestone on the Grand Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “The contractor’s activities are now shifting to the Grand/Fairview intersection, where they will relocate a sewer pipeline and install new storm drainage pipelines that will service the newly installed green infrastructure facilities. This will take approximately five weeks to complete. We remain on schedule to complete the paving and striping of Grand Avenue by the end of August.” The project will move next to the Grand and Fairview intersection, where crews will begin work on Piedmont’s first bioswale—a vegetated channel designed to naturally filter stormwater. Partial road closures will be in place while this work is underway. New concrete bulb-outs were poured last week, on the corner of Grand and Greenbank Avenues. Concrete work added new features to the sidewalks along Grand Avenue last week. articles.text: unusual in the winter here and should have been anticipated. My experience in two Southern states, where they really have a lot of rain, is seeing many projects with crews spreading roofing type membranes over sites much larger than our pool to protect the soil and employing pumps to drain the collected water. Was that type of mitigation discussed here? If there is a claim for this for an extension or for additional services or for the underground issues noted above (Dec.2, 2024 report), I would hope that there would be pushback from the City and the same for all claims where we ask the question; Were alternatives sought which could have mitigated the delay or additional cost? Why do I Care? I opposed the pool project in 2020 because I and others felt that the upgrade of the Essential Services Buildings (ESB) should have the highest priority because of their basic function and that they serve all Piedmont residents not just a segment. I still hold that view, but the pool project is the reality, and I do, of course, want the project to be successful. The project has staggered around a bit from the first bid process to finally finding a low bidder who met the City’s budget estimate. I’ve been critical to the Council of the City’s iterative design process rather than a more controlled model (see piedmontcivic.org – opinion) because of the time lost and the additional fees incurred by design process to date. I want to see an efficient fair project management process – even if only in parts. The ESB project is right ahead of us and will probably triple the cost of the pool. Managing that process and budget in an efficient and prudent way will be paramount. What do I hope will happen? As the pool project appears to wobble along toward some future opening date, I hope the City Council and Staff will be a strong, demanding and fair Owner/Client when the design construction team comes before them on July7th. And that they require more frequent updates. (I say wobble because if you visit the site you will see a jobsite that doesn’t resemble any 90% complete jobsite I have ever been involved in. On Friday, June 20, there were four earth moving vehicles, one major excavation still open, several walls and steps ready for a concrete pour, incomplete cladding on the building exterior. When I dropped by about 2:30 p.m. that afternoon, the site was totally buttoned up. What’s the rush?). I fear that the low bidder served the City well financially at the start of the project but that we may now be paying for that decision with the lackluster performance by the construction team to forecast and meet critical dates which are so important for the City to manage its role in opening the pool. And one personal comment. The Piedmont Post article mentioned “one factor contributing to the recent delays is the unexpected death of project executive George Sanen of Griffin Structures.” That remark is beyond the pale, and I would hope whoever is the source of that comment would retract it and sincerely apologize to Mr. Sanen’s family for it. Sincerely, Donald Chandler, AIA

articles.text: Senior Speaker for the PHS Class of 2025, Ella Hughes For what I’m sure is the 100th time you’re all hearing this, congratulations, everyone. I hope you all got the joy, heartbreak, success, and failure out of high school that you wanted. I hope if anything, you leave with an innate sense of progress. If not, this is only the beginning, and we still have our whole lives to take life between our teeth. With that specific statement in mind, this speech is, in short, a speech in defense of chalance, I’m aware it’s a back-formation, not a real word, but I think today being proper is a lot less important than being real. Quiet luxury. Nonchalance. Keeping everything high-brow and chic. We are entering an era of rising social neoconservatism, but why does that matter, why do we care? Because it means that as we venture into this next era of life, we are being constantly told one thing: it’s not cool to be too much! Too passionate, too invested: too chalant. But I’m here today to argue the opposite. I want you to take a moment to think of a friend, family member, writer, musician, politician, you love- hell, think of your favorite memory or story. Do you love these people, these moments, because they’re subtle, diminutive, nonchalant? No. You love them because they carry enough

articles.text: Piedmont residents participated in a community wildfire evacuation drill Saturday morning, June 14, beginning at 9 a.m. The exercise had residents of the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood evacuate on foot or in cars, while residents elsewhere in Piedmont participated in an at-home family exercise. Immediately following the drill, community members gathered at Piedmont Fire Station for a debrief and to hear firsthand accounts of wildfire evacuations from residents, firefighters and emergency managers. Attendees listened to speakers with experience in recent wildfires, including Piedmont firefighters who provided mutual aid during the L.A. fires, and words from Eaton Fire evacuee Diane Jimenez. “Go with your gut feeling,” said Jimenez. “I should have left a lot sooner. I could see the fire—I mean it was right there in front of me. It came within a block of my street, so it was flames galore.” Jimenez spoke about the rapid spread of the fires, plainly visible from the windows of her home in Altadena. articles.text: Piedmont Cub Scouts enjoyed a wide array of scouting activities last week, including arts and crafts, STEM learning, cooking and more, at the Piedmont Council’s annual Cub Scout Day Camp. A tradition for more than 55 years, the day camp welcomes first through fifth graders for five afternoons of activities in Dracena Park. The highlight each year is the Egg Drop facilitated by the Fire Department and its 75-foot extension ladder. This year’s camp rook place from Monday-Friday, June 9-13. Each day the campers cycled through six stations – crafts, Den time, Scout skills, sports, STEM activities, and cooking. Each station showed unique daily activities inspired by this year’s camp theme, “Invention Convention.” The crafts station had Cubs making a rubber band-powered rocket out of a pool noodle, as Cub Scouts in the Purple Den raise the flag to start off the last day of camp. Staff photo
articles.title: Egg Drop & Cub Scout Day Camp in Dracena Park

Religion Corner - main Some things are best done in community By Pastor Jim Hopkins Father’s Day coincides with Trinity Sunday this year. Besides sharing June 15 on the 2025 calendar the connection I see between the two is an emphasis on community. The doctrine of the Trinity teaches that divinity is best done in community. Father’s Day recognizes that fathering, and all parenting, is best done in community. Trinity with its description of God as three yet one, one yet three, is best understood not as an invention of Christianity but as a discovery of Christianity. As the community of followers of Jesus experienced the love of God, the grace of Jesus and the strength of the Holy Spirit it came to understand that Trinity described their experience. Finding just the right language to describe Trinity was, and is, difficult and sometimes contentious. Yet, the emerging majority opinion was, in the words of Eugene Peterson, that “Trinity is a sacred mystery, not a mystery that keeps us in the dark, but a mystery in which we are taken by the hand and gradually led into the light.” Brazilian theologian Leonardo Boff notes the centrality or community to this experienced based doctrine. “Believing in the Trinity means that truth is on the side of communion rather than exclusion; consensus translates truth better than imposition; the participation of many is better than the dictate of a single One.” Again, divinity is best done in community. So it is with fathering. Fathering is a calling, a job, a practice, an identity best done in community. Solitary fathering is not impossible. It is, however, exhausting and lonely. While overused, the saying “It takes a village to raise a child,” remains almost impossible to refute. As I look back on my experience as a father, I am profoundly grateful to my wife Karen, our friends, our parents, our siblings, the teachers, the coaches and the mentors who parented with us. Our church was a tremendous help. Churches are imperfect, but they are generally a great help in the work of parenting. articles.text: Editor: When the City of Piedmont considered developing new sports fields in Blair Park from 2008 to 2012, there were years of studies, a lawsuit and much controversy. Neighbors and I attended meetings and read reports where experts and citizens explained why development was too dangerous, even with a pedestrian bridge and/or a crosswalk and/ or a traffic light to have persons crossing busy Moraga Ave by Coaches field. Inadequate sightlines were a big part of that calculation. Identified safety issues weren’t limited to the Coaches field site but also linked to challenges farther up the hill looking at traffic impacts and projected dangers of bottlenecks all along Moraga Avenue which serves as an important emergency escape route for both Piedmont and Oakland residents. An environmental impact study in 2010 found that stopping sight distances for the former development plan did not meet Caltrans safety standards. What has changed in 15 years to make Moraga Canyon a safe location for major development? I attended the April 30 presentation by project consultants where traffic issues related to proposed Moraga Canyon development were discussed. The consultant acknowledged traffic sightlines are a continuing concern yet was dismissive of projected impacts, saying they would be quite minimal. The report did not address any impacts along the length of Moraga Avenue outside the boundaries of Piedmont, even knowing how close Highway 13 is to the border and the challenges of the intersection at Harbord Drive. I appreciate the thoughtful questions to the consultants I observed at the Council meeting on April 30, though there were few people in attendance to hear. Development of Moraga Canyon was not deemed safe in 2010 or 2012. Please continue to question how it can be safer now with more density and traffic. This could be a life-or-death decision.
articles.title: Moraga Canyon development not safe in 2010 & 2012. Why now?

articles.text: Editor: Recently, several parents shared their heartfelt concerns about changes to our elementary instrumental music program in a letter to the editor. Their passion for music education is admirable and reflects our community’s deep commitment to the arts. After reviewing the district’s plan, I’d like to share an alternative viewpoint. I believe these changes represent an exciting opportunity to strengthen our performing arts program. The district is thoughtfully reimagining elementary performing arts to provide more diverse opportunities for our students beyond instrumental music. They’ll be evaluating this new approach alongside existing programs in visual arts, technology, and library, with the goal of also introducing world language in 5th grade the following year. Here’s what’s actually happening next year: 4th graders will receive 60 minutes of theater arts weekly (replacing the current 40-minute instrumental music class), while 5th graders receive a full 60 minutes of dedicated instrumental music instruction. Previously, students received 40 minutes of instrumental music in both 4th and 5th grades (80 minutes total). Now they’ll receive 60 minutes in each grade—120 minutes total across their elementary years. That’s a 50% increase in performing arts instruction! Additionally, instrumental music class sizes will be cut in half with increased staffing, allowing for more individualized attention and meaningful instruction time. As the parent of a recent 4th grade instrumental music student most of the instructional period was spent on logistics rather than actual playing and learning. Theater arts will provide tremendous benefits, including building confidence, empathy, creativity, and collaboration skills—all backed by extensive research which was cited by the district in their evaluation. By introducing theater in 4th grade while strengthening instrumental music in 5th grade, we’re helping more children discover their unique talents and passions in the performing arts. The district spent months developing this proposal through a collaborative process involving teachers, administrators, and performing arts staff. While change can feel uncomfortable, our administration has demonstrated remarkable success in improving programs, increasing enrollment, and enhancing communication across the district. They’ve found a way to consistently give parents and students more of what they want and need while communicating about it transparently. I encourage our community to embrace a new approach that seeks to expand opportunities for all our students. Let’s support our district as they work to create a more comprehensive and inclusive performing arts education for every child. Sincerely, Adam Fishman Dad to a rising 5th grader (WW) and 7th grader (PMS)
articles.title: Piedmont dad in favor of “theater arts”

articles.text: Piedmont’s upcoming Shell Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Station at 29 Wildwood Avenue has issued a notice of Environmental Assessment Activities to neighbors. Work on additional environmental investigation at the site of the former Shell service station was scheduled to begin on Tuesday, June 17, with samples being retrieved on July 1. According to the notice, the work will examine the extent of contamination in the property’s soil vapor, or air spaces between particles of soil. Four soil vapor sampling devices will be buried three feet deep along the northern property boundary and near the former tank areas where chlorinated solvents have previously been detected. The samples will be retrieved on July 1 and submitted to a lab for analysis. The work, overseen by Alameda County Environmental Health Department (ACEHD), will take place from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. each day and activities include use of a handheld drill and a support vehicle. Dust and odors are expected to be controlled, but the notice encourages any concerns to be directed immediately to Tracy Craig at (510) 334-4866. Once this work is complete, the site will be secured until approval is given for abatement of lead/ asbestos and demolition of the existing building. ACEHD will issue a work notice with details about the abatement and demolition prior to work occurring. However, ACEHD may require cleanup actions based on the results of the environmental investigation. Community members may review the case file for the 29 Wildwood Ave. project, including all technical documents, online at the State Water Resources Control Board GeoTracker website at https://geotracker.waterboards. ca.gov and searching for the address “29 Wildwood Avenue, Piedmont.” For more information, contact Tracy Craig ay Shell Community Outreach at (510) 334-4866 or tracy@craig-communications. com. A map of digging locations for environmental samples
articles.title: Shell EV Station issues Environmental Digging Notice

articles.text: Vader is an affectionate 11-year-old cuddle bug with a speckled coat that’s simply out of this world. Once this loyal boy bonds with you, greet you at the door, he’ll follow you from room to room, and curl up in your lap the moment you sit down. articles.text: Last date is June 30 Consumer Affairs Reporter Everyone in Piedmont should be familiar with Republic Services, the company that does weekly trash, recycling, and green recycling pickups. However, people may not know – or they may have forgotten – that residents get two free large item pickups each year. “Each year” is not the calendar year, though; it runs from July 1st to June 30th. And unused large item pickups don’t go into a bank like PTO at work. Instead, they expire every June 30th, and the So, if you’ve been meaning to clean out the garage and haven’t used both pickups since last July 1st, you’d better hurry and schedule one. It’s usually done on the day of your regular pickup and needs to be scheduled in advance. Fortunately, there’s a customer service line for Piedmont, Monday-Friday, 8AM-5PM. A quick call to 800-320-8077 will get your large items whisked away and leave you wondering why you haven’t taken advantage of this service in the past. In case you need more information, the main web page for Republic Services is https://www. republicservices.com/municipality/piedmont-ca, and it’s full of useful facts (such as what happens when a holiday falls during the week). An even more detailed narrative on residential service can be found at https://www. republicservices.com/cms/documents/municipality/ca/PIEDMONT/Piedmont-CA-Residential-Service-Guide.pdf. There may be no such thing as a free lunch, but we all get two free pickups, so take advantage of them before they vanish like the Oakland Athletics. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

Large item pickups by Republic Services – Use it or lose it Last date is June 30 By Wiley Hoag, Consumer Affairs Reporter Everyone in Piedmont should be familiar with Republic Services, the company that does weekly trash, recycling, and green recycling pickups. However, people may not know – or they may have forgotten – that residents get two free large item pickups each year. “Each year” is not the calendar year, though; it runs from July 1st to June 30th. And unused large item pickups don’t go into a bank like PTO at work. Instead, they expire every June 30th, and the counter gets reset. So, if you’ve been meaning to clean out the garage and haven’t used both pickups since last July 1st, you’d better hurry and schedule one. It’s usually done on the day of your regular pickup and needs to be scheduled in advance. Fortunately, there’s a customer service line for Piedmont, Monday-Friday, 8AM-5PM. A quick call to 800-320-8077 will get your large items whisked away and leave you wondering why you haven’t taken advantage of this service in the past. In case you need more information, the main web page for Republic Services is https://www. republicservices.com/municipality/piedmont-ca, and it’s full of useful facts (such as what happens when a holiday falls during the week). An even more detailed narrative on residential service can be found at https://www. republicservices.com/cms/documents/municipality/ca/PIEDMONT/Piedmont-CA-Residential-Service-Guide.pdf. articles.text: Workers prepare to lift the backup generator into place with a crane. A backup generator and Motor Control Center electrical panel for Piedmont’s new 911 Dispatch Center arrived and were put into place using a crane on Monday, June 9. The generator and the electrical panel are items listed as “critical path” on the construction schedule, and their installation marks a milestone on the completion schedule for the Dispatch Center. This equipment serves as an independent and secure power source to continue operations during outages and challenging conditions. Piedmont’s Dispatch Center will be located in the former Emergency Operations Center and the Police Department conference room. The Dispatch Center functions as the “nerve center” for the Piedmont public safety services, fielding over 13,000 calls annually for the Police and Fire Departments. According to the City, the former space was severely undersized, unable to accommodate modern technologies, and located in an area that has not been seismically retrofitted. Concurrent with the building improvements, the City recently increased dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978. Two new Construction workers with a crane Workers guide the generator to its place of installation. A crane carries heavy electrical equipment high in the air. dispatcher positions were added last year, a staffing increase made possible by the March 2024 passage of Measure F. Renovation of the dispatch center was identified by the City Council as the highest and best use for American Rescue Plan Act funding in October 2021. Design work for the relocated dispatch center began in 2022, and the City Council awarded a $1.8 million construction contract for the project in March of 2023. Construction began in June 2024. Construction on the dispatch center is scheduled to complete this Fall. Prior to delivery, a worker prepares the site for the city’s backup generator.

articles.text: Oakland Animal Services staff say one-year-old Otterbear is the total package – easy to handle, affectionate, and mellow. Otterbear is a red Husky mix and weighs 60 pounds. He walks well on leash, knows “sit,” and how to give his paw. He recently went to live temporarily in a foster home. In his doggie playgroups at the shelter, he’d greet new friends, then happily find a sunny spot to lounge. He’s easygoing and ideal for a home with a well-matched dog or as a solo pup with some canine buddies. On a recent field trip, Otterbear strolled through a neighborhood and was curious about squirrels and dogs, but never pulled or barked. Even in a busy environment, he stayed Otterbear is a mellow red Husky mix calm and collected. To meet Otterbear, fill out an adoption application online and you will be contacted by his foster who can provide you with more info about how Otterbear behaves in a home environment. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Every summer, Piedmont’s population diminishes significantly as soon as the final school bells signal the arrival of summer vacation. The most popular and time-honored migration from Piedmont is to Camp Augusta in Nevada City. On Saturday, June 8, two large buses picked up campers at Piedmont Park and headed to camp on the shores of Lake Vera. Camp Augusta was donated to the girls of Piedmont in 1931 by Edwin William Ehmann and Charlotte Ehmann. For at least the last 80 years, the site has operated as a summer camp and provided a favorite home away from home, for tens of thousands of Piedmont kids and any interested kids aged 8-16, regardless of city origin. Camp Augusta’s success is unrivaled. It has been fully booked since 2009. The camp provides more than the beauty of a Sierra Nevada forest; youth receive the opportunity to try out and explore hundreds of new activities, skills and passions, like swimming, horseback riding, canoeing, and rock climbing. The first session of camp began last week. Each weekend of the summer the buses will be back in town, returning satiated campers and collecting new busloads of kids heading to a wonderland called Camp Augusta. A line down Highland Avenue forms as parents say goodbye to their kids headed to the first session of Camp Augusta. Families wait in line to load their kids and camp gear onto buses headed for Camp Augusta.
articles.title: It’s off to Camp Augusta – by the busload

articles.text: Piedmont Makers co-founder Dave Ragones (left), with Vaughn and Ken Khouri In recognition of their extraordinary contributions to the Maker community over the past decade, Piedmont Makers has honored father and son team Ken and Vaughn Khouri as Makers of the Year during an end-of-year gathering in June. Ken, a board member of Piedmont Makers since 2018, has played many important roles. He served on the Advisory Committee for the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab, was a Mechanical Mentor for Highlander Robotics, and was Commissioner for FIRST Tech Challenge. Vaughn, the outgoing captain of Highlander Robotics, has been a dedicated participant in FIRST Robotics through Piedmont Makers for seven years. Over his four years as driver for Highlander Robotics, he led the team to four consecutive appearances at the FIRST World Championship – including a run as Division Finalist – while being a familiar face at both the Piedmont School Maker Fairs and the East Bay Mini Maker Fair. Together, they’ve built everything from t-shirt slingshots to rocket launchers, enriching our community with their creative spirit. This year, they have outdone themselves: over six months, Vaughn and Ken designed and led the fabrication of a 27’×54’ welded steel and polycarbonate field perimeter needed for FIRST Robotics Competition events. They secured more than $30,000 in in-kind donations from material suppliers and coordinated a team of 35 volunteers, who together logged over 1,000 hours building the new practice field infrastructure. Today, the field stands as a vital resource for 19 regional teams who have spent countless hours there refining their robots. They were thanked for their dedication to improving our community. Vaughn will be a freshman at MIT this fall.
articles.title: Ken and Vaughn Khouri honored as Makers of the Year

articles.text: Do you ever just look down and wonder, when on earth did the floor get so far away? Or, realize that you’ve somehow grown into the huge shirt your parents bought you “for the future” — and now, “the future” is…now?? Or, personally, I get the feeling that Witter Field’s looking smaller every PE class, but somehow expands again when we’re told its mile day. All of these are reminders that time is ticking…. And now: Boom, it’s the last Wednesday of middle school. Like, ever. In retrospect, it’s been quite the rollercoaster ride. Maybe for you it’s been getting to know yourself or others better, discovering new passions, or trying (and failing) to cut down that 7 hour screentime. Maybe you’re just mourning the tragic fact you aged out of the“kids eat free” IHOP deal. Whatever steps we’ve taken on this journey, middle school has definitely had its share of ups, downs, and everything in between. After all, it hasn’t just been having real homework and somehow getting used to not having recess — it’s been a period of self exploration. And we can’t forget the cheerleaders that have been with us every leap, wobble, and step of the way. To our teachers, staff, parents and everyone who has been part of this wild ride — thank you for all of the Sophia Li delivering her student speech for Piedmont Middle School’s 8th grade graduation. kindness you have shown us. People love to compare life to a lot of things: a road, a game, a play. But for me, I’ve always thought life is most like writing a book. You can write pretty much anything you want to, but every new chapter builds on the ones from before. Especially going through middle school, the journey of self-discovery is also one that’s shaped by who you currently are, who you want to be, and the steps you take to get there. And here’s what I’ve learned: you don’t need to do what everyone else is doing in order to be at the top of your game. If everyone’s emptying their wallets on Jellycats and Lululemon, and that’s your cup of tea, go for it. But if it isn’t, don’t sweat it. However cliche it sounds, a one-size-fitsall for humanity doesn’t exist and it’s a good thing that it never will. Taylor Swift once said, “I promise that you’ll never find another like me.” Turns out, she’s right. You are your own greatest strength. So, as we close the chapter of middle school, let’s not be afraid to throw ourselves out there. Take that hard class. Join that club. Spend time on the things you enjoy. I can’t wait to write the next chapter with you all and embrace whatever high school throws at us. So, to my fellow middle school graduates, cheers to the bright road ahead! • Inclusion, and Belonging Council. Someone who always shows up to help people with her whole being. Also, Tommy Ashton, whom I frequently see down at the weight room putting in the extra mile in strength and mobility training, who always shows up as his best on the field, even when his only audience was my weight room class, most of whom were barely making it through their mandatory PE credits. These are just a few of many examples of my exceptional classmates who portray what it is that makes humanity so lovely. What makes people dynamic and compelling is the ability to find passion and live it out in full, unapologetically, with chalance. So what does this mean for us, going forward? It means going into the rest of our lives that we can’t be afraid to experiment, innovate, exist loudly: take that 101 class you’re not sure you’ll like, join that intramural team, apply for the internship, talk to that girl at the cafe or the football game. Take a chance on life. The fear of being perceived as alive and invested should never stop you from exploring, rather showing those around just how alive and invested you are is what makes you powerful. So I want to extend a thank you to all our teachers, classmates, families, administrators, and everyone who has shown us the power of a full life. We are the class of 2025, and if we let ourselves live fully, there’s no telling what we can accomplish, what legacies we can make ring, because human potential isn’t in the moments of nonchalance and deflection, but in the times we let ourselves find connection through our passion, let ourselves be seen, and let ourselves be unapologetically chalant.

articles.text: A small crowd filled the Piedmont Unified School District Wellness Center on Thursday, May 29, to honor Piedmont High School counselor Amanda Carlson as winner of the Brooke Zimmerman Award. Carlson was given the award for her outstanding service to Piedmont students and her partnership with the Wellness Center, the district’s hub for student mental health support. The Brooke Zimmerman plaque stands as a testament to the counselors, staff and volunteers who show up for Piedmont students every day. With Amanda Carlson’s name now engraved alongside last year’s inaugural honoree the award continues to spotlight individuals whose compassion, expertise and commitment make the Wellness Center a vital resource for Piedmont students. “I could not do my job or serve my students without the partnership of the Wellness Center,” said Carlson. Wellness Center co-founder and former Piedmont Middle School Counselor Brooke Zimmerman attended the celebration with her grandson, Cy Leonard, a recent fifth-grade graduate of Beach Elementary. Zimmerman and a small committee founded the Center in 2007 to address rising student stress and anxiety levels. Today, the Wellness Center has become a regional model, inspiring schools such as Castro Valley High School to open wellness centers based on Piedmont’s example. Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn and Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich also joined the ceremony in affirmation of PUSD’s dedication to student well-being. “We are committed to supporting the Wellness Center as a thriving part of our school programs,” said Hawn. Millennium High School Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels opened the awards ceremony by reminding attendees why the Center’s mission matters. “The work of supporting student mental health is not just important – it is essential,” she said. The Wellness Center, located behind the library at Piedmont High School, provides free mental health services to Piedmont Middle, High and Millennium students. The support given there PHS Counselor Amanda Carlson, has been named the 2025 Brooke Zimmerman Award honoree for her outstanding service to students. Wellness Center co-founder Brooke Zimmerman is pictured with her grandson Cy Leonard. is in high demand. During the 2024-2025 school year, the Wellness Center provided over 2,000 hours of student therapy, and 150 Piedmont students received ongoing support. These numbers reflect the Center’s reach and its critical role in meeting student’s mental health needs. Sustaining the Wellness Center requires ongoing community involvement. Each year, the Wellness Center Support Committee – a dedicated group of Piedmont parents – raises the funds necessary to maintain current service levels. Their efforts, combined with district support, ensure that the Center remains a cornerstone of the PUSD’s holistic approach to education. Mr. Mockel, Ms. Black, Dr. Marks, it’s your fearless passion which drove me to challenge, edit, and find the bravery to put myself out there to start my writing path again. Without you there is no doubt in my mind I would never have found my love of language again. Your choices to give me space to write, help me with editing, teach me how to acknowledge an idea I disagree with and respectfully challenge it, and make me realize how fascinating peat bogs can be in relation to Chaucer shaped me. It’s your passion for the subject that taught me it’s always worthwhile to pursue what you love, even if it’s not cool to anyone else. or you know, even if that passion is dusty books and dissecting perspective shifts in mid century poetry. articles.text: Brynne Jones stands with the Terracotta Army during a spring break trip to China in April. After finishing her sophomore year at Piedmont High School, Brynne Jones will study Mandarin this summer in Taiwan on a National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI‑Y) scholarship. Jones was one of 440 students selected from thousands of high school applicants across the United States to receive a scholarship. While in Taiwan, Jones will live with a host family and engage with local peers to enhance language learning. The program will last around seven weeks, and participants receive a minimum of 120 hours of classroom instruction in intensive language classes. “To prepare, I’ve been using Duolingo, especially for speaking, and watching Chinese movies to practice my Mandarin. The program also had several virtual information sessions to help us prepare, which have been super helpful,” said Jones. Jones visited China with six students and Piedmont Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia during Spring Break in early April, giving her valuable experience about living in there. The rich culture in Taiwan captured her interest to study abroad this summer, especially the lively night markets, great street food and seeing local temples. “I’m most excited to meet my host family and experience everyday life in Taiwan,” said Jones. The program is part of the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, which promotes the study of Chinese (Mandarin), Hindi, Indonesian, Korean, Persian (Tajiki), Russian, Turkish, and Arabic. Launched in 2006 as part of a multi-agency U.S. Government initiative, the program increases the number of young Americans with the critical language skills necessary to contribute to U.S national security and economic competitiveness. Many program alumni go on to pursue education and careers vital to the U.S. NSLI‑Y is administered by American Councils for International Education in cooperation with AFS‑USA, American Cultural Exchange Service, Amideast, iEARN‑USA, Stony Brook University, and the University of Delaware. Applications for NSLI‑Y programs are available at Nsliforyouth.org each fall. The U.S. Department of State provides additional study abroad opportunities for both American and international high school students. Americans can welcome a new language and culture into their home by hosting an international exchange student, which is a life-changing experience for students, host families, schools, and communities. Visit Exchanges.state.gov and Hosting. state.gov for more.

articles.text: The Beach Dads Club hosted its end-of-year celebration, the “BBQ Boogie,” at Beach Field to the delight of hundreds of attendees. The Dads Club, known affectionately as the Baja Padres, celebrated in style on the evening of Friday, May 30, while raising $5,100 for the Beach Parents Organization. The event was billed as a kids’ dance party, as the Beach Revue Band played summer classics for a crowd of several hundred partygoers. The sun stayed up seemingly forever, and the warm weather kept the energy high as the band performed songs from Beach Dad Richie Przybyla (left), and four past Padre Grandes Michael Gross, Peter Jaeschke, Arash Ghassemi, and Will Rogan serve up wine at the Beach Dads BBQ Boogie. The Beach Revue Band played eclectic tunes before reprising the favorites from the 2025 Beach Revue. Beach Elementary Dads cook up enough hot dogs for a small army. the 2025 Beach Revue, with kids singing along. Fifty Padre volunteers—and a number of moms—contributed time and talent to help the event run smoothly. The barbecue station was set up on the hill near the Howard Avenue entrance to the field. In total, 465 hot dogs, including 65 veggie dogs, were grilled and enjoyed, along with several tables’ worth of barbecue sides. “It’s always my favorite Dads Club event of the year because it’s a celebration of the end of the school year. It’s warm, the sun sets late, and the vibe is so good,” said former club president Michael Gross. Below the field, in the shadow of the Oakland Avenue Bridge, the Padres set up a libations area that paired perfectly with the food, watermelon and sunshine. John Karnay and his team at Oakland United generously donated two kegs of beer, and Alder Yarrow donated seven cases of wine. Grace from Tea on Piedmont provided boba tea. Band members of the Beach Revue Band included Ried Steiner, Tara Levy, Brandon Garibaldi, Susan Landau and Lucas Jones. Kids chased an enormous beach ball across the field while parents enjoyed time with fellow Beach families over drinks. The BBQ Boogie welcomed summer in grand fashion—with laughter, music and full bellies. A giant beach ball commanded an enormous following of kids all from start to finish. A long afternoon of sun and fun at Beach Elementary’s Grassy Field

articles.text: The full-sized model of the Mercury capsule at the Chabot Space & Science Center We are living through a space renaissance: an era defined by groundbreaking innovation, historic achievements, and big questions about our future. What’s remarkable about this moment in time is that it isn’t limited to distant launchpads or orbiting satellites. The space renaissance is unfolding right here on Earth, in labs, classrooms, studios, and observatories—including right here in the Bay Area. Silicon Valley startups are developing next-generation satellites and NASA Ames is helping develop the Vented Fly Box, a specialized research chamber used aboard the International Space Station to study DNA repair in fruit flies (tiny organisms whose genetic similarities to humans make them powerful models for understanding the impacts of space travel on human health). Our region is at the center of this exciting new chapter in space exploration and Chabot Space & Science Center, a longtime hub for science, technology, engineering, art, and math (STEAM) education, is proud to be part of this movement. The technologies developed for space exploration are already enhancing life on Earth in remarkable ways. NASA Aqua and Terra satellites have collected years of data on wildfire behavior, allowing scientists to potentially improve the future of wildfire management. The camera in your smartphone? It exists because of NASA research into compact imaging systems. These examples, and so many more, show how pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in space leads to practical solutions at home. But innovation flows in both directions. Artists, designers, and creators on Earth are influencing how we explore the universe. Origami-inspired folding techniques have been used to design reduced size and weight antennas and solar arrays, which are not only space-saving, but less costly to boot. This interplay between art and science is one of the defining features of the space renaissance. Chabot Space & Science Center believes that everyone (a curious kid, a seasoned engineer, or someone who simply loves to look up at the stars and be in nature) has a place in this story. Through hands-on activities, live science demonstrations, telescope viewings, conversations with experts, NASA and more, we’ll connect people of all ages to the innovations and ideas transforming our understanding of the universe and our place in it. Space Week is more than a celebration. It’s an invitation to see yourself as part of this moment in history. The decisions we make and the technologies we develop today will shape the future of life on Earth and beyond. Chabot Space & Science Center is here to spark curiosity, inspire discovery, and support the next generation of explorers. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team won the D5 CIF NorCal title on Mach 8. The 2024-25 school year is has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite moments from the recent sports seasons. 1. Boys’ Soccer’ wins CIF NorCal Championship As the No. 5 seed in the Division 5 CIF NorCal tournament, Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team battled its way to claim the title. They opened with a 1-nil upset over No. 4 Orland and also kept a clean sheet in the semifinals in a 2-nil win over No. 8 Colusa. Then in the Final, Piedmont defeated No. 7 Williams 4-1 for the championship including a first-half hat trick by Gianluca Bini and Bosco Lorin scoring Piedmont’s final goal. 2. Girls’ Basketball’s competes in Open Div. in State Tourney The girls’ basketball team received the No. 5 seed in the NCS Open Division, which is considered the top echelon of the section with a batch of freshmen like Andrea Martin, Jenelle Solis, and Savannah Dennig, and sophomore Taylor White. They lost 51-45 to No. 4 Cardinal Newman in the opening round but won 70-48 over No. 6 Salesian in the fifth-place final. They received the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 CIF State Tournament, dominating No. 8 Oakland Tech 60-29 in the first round and won 62-60 over No. 16 San Joaquin Memorial at Binks Rawlings Gym. They lost to No. 4 St. Mary’s of Stockton 61-48 in the regional semifinals. 3. Sebastien Swain in 2 State Championships Sophomore distance runner Sebastien Swain was one of our honorable mention for Athlete of the Year recipients after his monumental 2024-campaign. In the spring track season, Swain ran his way to the 2025 CIF State Track and Field Championship in Clovis, where he placed 18th of 29 runners in the 800 in 1:53.15. Back in the fall for cross country, he finished 96th of 201 in the 2024 CIF State Cross Country Championship at Woodward Park. 4. Sophomores at State Cross Country Championship Along with Swain reaching the CIF State Cross Country Championship, Piedmont also sent two sophomores from the girls’ team: Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray. Mand finished the race in 74th of 201 runners with a time of 19:52.7 on the 5,000 meter course, while Gray placed 101st in 20:24.5. We named Mand this year’s Sophomore of the Year. 5. Miguel Long wins Del Campo Decathlon & Stanford Invitational Miguel Long won our 2025 Athlete of the Year thanks in part to a monumental run in April. On April 5, Long won the prestigious Stanford Invitational by reaching 45 feet, 8.5 inches—marking his personal record while in a field of 18 athletes. Then on April 18-19, he won the Del Campo Decathlon with a score of 5,369 points in a field of 19. He finished in the top-10 of every event, including winning the long jump in 21 feet, 3 inches, the high jump in 6 feet, 7.5 inches, and the 110 meter hurdles in 16.69 seconds. 6. Nia Kim’s breakout season Nia Kim was also our 2025 Athlete of the Year after her breakout year on track and field. She became a WACC champion on May 7 in the 100 meter hurStaff Photos dles with a time of 15.62 seconds and won the NCS Bayshore Area title in 15.19 on May 17. Nia also placed second of 15 at the WACC Championship in the high jump with a height of five feet. She jumped the same height at the NCS Bayshore Area Championship to place third of 18. Her 4x400 team placed second of 14 at the Bayshore in 4:09.20. 7. PHS swim team’s lights-out relay team Piedmont’s boys’ swim team became the first team in school history to send two relay teams to the CIF State Championship: Owen Blanford, Cole Carnazzo, Nik Costello, Dima Secor, and Asher Takazawa. Both the 200 and 400 freestyle teams won the WACC Championship, clocking respective times of 1:34.27 and 3:11.09. Then at the NCS Championship, the 200 team was fifth of 16 in 1:33.24, while the 400 team was seventh of 16 in 3:07.68. At State, the 200 medley relay team posted a time of 1:33.84, finishing 23rd out of 40 teams. Secor replaced Costello in the 400 freestyle relay, finishing 21st of 40 in 3:07.38. 8. Girls’ Lacrosse loses NCS in overtime The girls team battled to the D2 NCS Championship as the No. 6 seed before losing to No. 4 College Park 8-7 in sudden death overtime for the title. This year marked Piedmont’s first NCS semifinals and finals appearance since winning the 2019 title. To reach the finals, Piedmont obliterated No. 11 Cardinal Newman 16-3 in the first round, upset No. 3 Lick-Wilmerding 5-4 in the quarterfinals, and dominated arch-rivals No. 2 Bishop O’Dowd 16-8 in the semifinals. 9. Boys’ Basketball team in near comeback in NCS Championship The Highlanders went 15-16 and reached the D4 NCS Finals as the No. 1 seed before losing No. 11 St. Patrick 75-70. To get there, PHS beat No. 16 Ukiah 87-49 in the first round, No. 9 Bethel 78-69 in the quarterfinals and No. 12 Windsor 60-53 in the semifinals. They qualified for the D4 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed, losing to No. 8 Natomas 84-71. Staff Photos Sebastien Swain competed at the State meet in both cross-country and track. Photo by Becky Spies Sophomore Amalia Gray qualified for the State Cross Country Championship. Staff Photos Girls’ Basketball was one of the best teams in the state, reaching the NCS Open Division and D1 CIF State Tournament. Photo courtesy of PHS Swim Team PHS swimmers Owen Blanford (left), Asher Takazawa, Cole Carnazzo and Nik Costello with an underwater photo at the CIF State Championship.
