articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost in the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on three athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included senior Briana Webb of the girls’ basketball team, junior Xavier Henderson of the football team, and Edie Elmquist of the softball and flag football teams. We’ll provide more athletes in the coming weeks. Staff Photos Briana Webb was a senior leader on the basketball team after transferring from Moreau. BRIANA WEBB Basketball Briana Webb joined Piedmont High as a senior and made an instant impact on Bryan Gardere’s basketball team. She was a first-team All-League recipient and was our Athlete of the Month in January. Webb logged a double-double in Piedmont’s 70-48 win over Salesian in the NCS Open Division’s Fifth-Place Final. She also led scoring with 15 points in a 50-47 regular season win over arch rival Bishop O’Dowd on February 5. She had important performances in some of Piedmonts more critical games, including 13 points in Piedmont’s overtime 61-52 win over Clayton ValXavier Henderson was a star on the football team on offense, defense, and special teams. ley on, she logged 19 points and eight rebounds in their 54-44 win over Alameda, had 19 points and seven boards in their narrow 53-51 loss to Antelope, and led scoring Webb also led scoring with 22 points in an 81-66 loss to Centennial, a top three rated team in Nevada. XAVIER HENDERSON Football Edie Elmquist was a freshman starter on the softball and flag football teams. Xavier Henderson burst onto the team as a do-it-all type player on offense, defense, and special teams. He earned first-team AllLeague honors on special teams. an honorable mention on defense as a linebacker, and also contributed as a running back and receiver. Henderson had two kickoff returns for a touchdown, including a 90-yard return to the house in the third quarter in Piedmont’s 42-26 win over Fortuna in the D7 NCS Quarterfinals. On defense, Xavier had at least five tackles for loss and led the team. Offensively, Henderson had 169 rushing yards and one touchdown, to go along with 19 receptions for 312 yards and six touchdowns. EDIE ELMQUIST Softball, Flag Football Edie Elmquist was a freshman who made a quick impact on the softball team in the spring and flag football team in the fall. She earned second-team All-League honors on softball and was the flag football team’s starting quarterback which finished 6-10. On softball, Elmquist helped the team reach the D4 NCS Quarterfinals at the No. 11 seed before falling 6-5 to No. 3 Piner. Their opening round 15-5 win over No. 6 California School of the Deaf marked the team’s first NCS victory since 2022. She hit for a .317 batting average on 20 hits, three doubles, her three triples. Her 39 runs were second place on the team, while she also logged 17 RBIs.
articles.title: Breakout stars: Briana Webb, Xavier Henderson, Edie Elmquist

articles.text: Audrey Lam is a Piedmont High graduate from the Class of 2023 and was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a senior. Lam just finished her sophomore year at Brown University and is currently playing locally with Oakland Soul’s pre-professional W League team. Lam recently logged her first assist with Soul in the club’s 2-1 loss to Stockton Cargo on June 7 while playing in front of thousands of spectators at the Oakland Coliseum. The W League is considered one of the top semi-professional leagues in the country, often featuring players who are competing in other Division 1 colleges or are on the fringe of top leagues around the world. Playing alongside Lam includes former Stanford national champion Sam Tran, former Thailand National Team forward Miranda Nild, and fringe NWSL talent Shaelan Murison, who got time with the Utah Royals. “Everyone at Brown is asked to play in the summer to prepare for the fall season. I was looking at all my options and tried to determine what would be a high-performance team and give me good competition. It’s been a great experience; all these players are really great,” said Lam. “The coaching staff and everyone at Soul has been amazing.” With Soul, Lam received four straight starts as a central midfielder, proving her playmaking ability. She takes almost all of the team’s free kicks and corners. “Audrey had a short stint with us last year and it’s great to have her back,” said Soul head coach Jessica Clinton. “You really see what she brings to the game. The goal is to see what our core players look like going forward and Audrey Lam had an assist for Oakland Soul at the Oakland Coliseum on June 7. Staff Photos Audrey Lam, PHS Class of 2023, is competing professionally on Oakland Soul’s W League team. Audrey certainly can be that,” Appearing earlier with Oakland Soul was Piedmont grad Aubrey Turner (Class of 2020). She finished her collegiate career at the University of Portland and played for F.C. Famalicão in the top tier of Portuguese football in 2024. “It’s great to play with Aubrey,” said Lam. “I haven’t seen her in a while so it was great to see her with Soul. We carpool every now and again to practice and games, so it’s very nice to have a familiar face there.” Lam came to Soul with the intention of getting minutes before returning to Brown’s soccer program in the fall. In 2023 as a freshman, Audrey helped Brown go 12-2-3 and earn the No. 3 seed in its bracket for the 2023 NCAA Tournament. They beat Quinnipiac 3-nil in the first round, but lost to No. 6 Mississippi State 2-1 in the second round. Lam elected to take the following year off, but is looking to remerge on Brown’s lineup come the fall. “I made a difficult decision. But at the end of the day, it was the best decision to get back in the right mindset ahead of the fall,” Lam said. Soul has three matches left in its season. They host San Juan FC at Merritt College in Oakland on June 22, host Olympic Club at Merritt College on June 26, and visit SF Glens at Treasure Island Stadium on June 29. Lam was the Post’s Honorable Mention for 2023 Athlete of the Year after helping lead Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team go 13-1-6 (W-T-L) and win its first Division 4 NCS championship in 20 years. She was named the WACC’s Player of the Year. Audrey Lam has three games remaining in Oakland Soul’s season. You can watch her play at Merritt College.

Three who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included senior Briana Webb of the girls’ basketball team, junior Xavier Henderson of the football team, and Edie Elmquist of the softball and flag football teams. We’ll provide more athletes in the coming weeks. Staff Photos Briana Webb was a senior leader on the basketball team after transferring from Moreau. BRIANA WEBB Basketball Briana Webb joined Piedmont High as a senior and made an instant impact on Bryan Gardere’s basketball team. She was a first-team All-League recipient and was our Athlete of the Month in January. Webb logged a double-double in Piedmont’s 70-48 win over Salesian in the NCS Open Division’s Fifth-Place Final. She also led scoring with 15 points in a 50-47 regular season win over arch rival Bishop O’Dowd on February 5. She had important performances in some of Piedmonts more critical games, including 13 points in Piedmont’s overtime 61-52 win over Clayton ValXavier Henderson was a star on the football team on offense, defense, and special teams. ley on, she logged 19 points and eight rebounds in their 54-44 win over Alameda, had 19 points and seven boards in their narrow 53-51 loss to Antelope, and led scoring Webb also led scoring with 22 points in an 81-66 loss to Centennial, a top three rated team in Nevada. XAVIER HENDERSON Football Edie Elmquist was a freshman starter on the softball and flag football teams. Xavier Henderson burst onto the team as a do-it-all type player on offense, defense, and special teams. He earned first-team AllLeague honors on special teams. an honorable mention on defense as a linebacker, and also contributed as a running back and receiver. Henderson had two kickoff returns for a touchdown, including a 90-yard return to the house in the third quarter in Piedmont’s 42-26 win over Fortuna in the D7 NCS Quarterfinals. On defense, Xavier had at least five tackles for loss and led the team. Offensively, Henderson had 169 rushing yards and one touchdown, to go along with 19 receptions for 312 yards and six touchdowns. EDIE ELMQUIST Softball, Flag Football Edie Elmquist was a freshman who made a quick impact on the softball team in the spring and flag football team in the fall. She earned second-team All-League honors on softball and was the flag football team’s starting quarterback which finished 6-10. On softball, Elmquist helped the team reach the D4 NCS Quarterfinals at the No. 11 seed before falling 6-5 to No. 3 Piner. Their opening round 15-5 win over No. 6 California School of the Deaf marked the team’s first NCS victory since 2022. She hit for a .317 batting average on 20 hits, three doubles, her three triples. Her 39 runs were second place on the team, while she also logged 17 RBIs. Audrey Lam competing with Oakland Soul W League team By Jonathan Comeaux Audrey Lam is a Piedmont High graduate from the Class of 2023 and was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a senior. Lam just finished her sophomore year at Brown University and is currently playing locally with Oakland Soul’s pre-professional W League team. Lam recently logged her first assist with Soul in the club’s 2-1 loss to Stockton Cargo on June 7 while playing in front of thousands of spectators at the Oakland Coliseum. The W League is considered one of the top semi-professional leagues in the country, often featuring players who are competing in other Division 1 colleges or are on the fringe of top leagues around the world. Playing alongside Lam includes former Stanford national champion Sam Tran, former Thailand National Team forward Miranda Nild, and fringe NWSL talent Shaelan Murison, who got time with the Utah Royals. “Everyone at Brown is asked to play in the summer to prepare for the fall season. I was looking at all my options and tried to determine what would be a high-performance team and give me good competition. It’s been a great experience; all these players are really great,” said Lam. “The coaching staff and everyone at Soul has been amazing.” With Soul, Lam received four straight starts as a central midfielder, proving her playmaking ability. She takes almost all of the team’s free kicks and corners. “Audrey had a short stint with us last year and it’s great to have her back,” said Soul head coach Jessica Clinton. “You really see what she brings to the game. The goal is to see what our core players look like going forward and Audrey Lam had an assist for Oakland Soul at the Oakland Coliseum on June 7. Staff Photos Audrey Lam, PHS Class of 2023, is competing professionally on Oakland Soul’s W League team. Audrey certainly can be that,” Appearing earlier with Oakland Soul was Piedmont grad Aubrey Turner (Class of 2020). She finished her collegiate career at the University of Portland and played for F.C. Famalicão in the top tier of Portuguese football in 2024. “It’s great to play with Aubrey,” said Lam. “I haven’t seen her in a while so it was great to see her with Soul. We carpool every now and again to practice and games, so it’s very nice to have a familiar face there.” Lam came to Soul with the intention of getting minutes before returning to Brown’s soccer program in the fall. In 2023 as a freshman, Audrey helped Brown go 12-2-3 and earn the No. 3 seed in its bracket for the 2023 NCAA Tournament. They beat Quinnipiac 3-nil in the first round, but lost to No. 6 Mississippi State 2-1 in the second round. Lam elected to take the following year off, but is looking to remerge on Brown’s lineup come the fall. “I made a difficult decision. But at the end of the day, it was the best decision to get back in the right mindset ahead of the fall,” Lam said. Soul has three matches left in its season. They host San Juan FC at Merritt College in Oakland on June 22, host Olympic Club at Merritt College on June 26, and visit SF Glens at Treasure Island Stadium on June 29. Lam was the Post’s Honorable Mention for 2023 Athlete of the Year after helping lead Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team go 13-1-6 (W-T-L) and win its first Division 4 NCS championship in 20 years. She was named the WACC’s Player of the Year. Audrey Lam has three games remaining in Oakland Soul’s season. You can watch her play at Merritt College.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Pomona-Pitzer Jack Stein (4201), PHS Class of 2022, runs for Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams. In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at Jack Stein of Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams, Breah Bell of Chico State’s track team, and Max Wagener of University of Redlands. JACK STEIN Track & Cross-Country Pomona-Pitzer Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, was the Post’s Co-Athlete of the Year in 2022 and just finished his junior year at Pomona-Pitzer. In cross-country Stein competed in a few 8K events last fall for the Sagehens. He finished the season by helping his school place third of 32 schools in the Division 3 NCAA Championship on November 23. Stein finished the race 28th of 294 runners with a time of 24:34.3 on the 8k course. With the track team this past Spring Stein competed in the 5k and 10k events at the SCAIC Track and Field Championship on April 26-27. He was second of 16 runners in the 10k with a time of 30:57.88, and was seventh in a field of 44 runners in the 5K. His time was 14:57.80. Stein helped his team win the Division 3 NCAA Championship in 2023, defeating Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point. 158- 159, where the former Highlander star finished as Pitzer’s fifth-best runner—meaning his time of 25:49.3 was what they ultimately needed to win the title. Stein graduated from Piedmont High as its all-time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 with respective times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. He also won the WACC Cross Country championship Photo courtesy of Chico State Breah Bell, PHS Class of 2024, just finished he freshman year on the track team at Chico State. with a time of 15:34.76, was second of 144 in the NCS Championship in 15:29.4 and placed 12th of 209 at the CIF Championship, clocking a 15:43.4. BREAH BELL Track Chico State Breah Bell, PHS Class of 2024, just finished her freshman year at Chico State. She was The Posts’ 2024 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year. She concluded her year at the CCAA Track and Field Championship on May 1-3. She competed in the 100 at the championship meet, finishing 18th of 30 with a time of 12.63 seconds. Her best time was a 12.47 at the Sac State Hornet Invitational on March 21-22, where she finished 31st of 74. Bell was a four-year starter on Piedmont’s track and field team and concluded her senior year as one of the most re;;iable athletes on coach Pouyan Assadi’s roster as a sprinter and long jumper.
articles.title: Three former PHS athletes in college

articles.text: Here is the Gold Cup’s 2025 bracket. Who do you have winning it? Summer soccer is here! The CONCACAF Gold Cup has already returned over the past week with the United States opening with a 5-nil shellacking of Trinidad and Tobago on Sunday, June 15 to open Group D’s action. FIFA rankings are shown for each team, and our final predictions of how the tournament plays out. We’ll start with the United States’ Group C and go from there. Group D: No. 16 USA, No. 58 Saudi Arabia, No. 83 Haiti, No. 100 Trinidad and Tobago The United States has caught some flak for missing some of their top talent for the Gold Cup, including AC Milan’s Christian Pulisic. Juventus’ Weston McKennie and Tim Weah are unavailable because of the FIFA Club World Cup. Despite being without several of their best players, this should be an easy qualification into the knockout stages. No. 100 Trinidad and Tobago clearly didn’t post much of a problem for the Stars and Stripes. Haiti opened the tournament with a 1-nil loss to Saudi Arabia, which looks like the U.S.A.’s biggest threat in the group. I’m taking USA to win the group and Saudia Arabia to take the second spot. USA and Saudi Arabia play on Thursday, while the U.S. Men’s national team closes the group stage against Haiti on June 22. Group A: No. 17 Mexico, No. 54 Costa Rica, No. 137 Suriname, No. 139 Dominican Republic Mexico walks into the tournament arguably with the best 26-man roster, including West Ham midfielder Edson Álvarez, AC Milan forward Santiago Gimenez, and Fulham striker Raul Jiménez. Although they looked lackluster against Dominican Republic in a 3-2 win on June 14, I’m still taking El tri as 1A. Costa Rica had a high-scoring affair against Suriname in a surprising 4-3 shootout. Costa Rica still looked like a high-powered bunch with 19 shots, so I’m not taking any surprises; Costa Rica as 2A. Group B: No. 30 Canada, No. 75 Honduras, No. 81 El Salvador, No. 90 Curacao Although Canada is without Bayern Munich star Alphonso Photos courtesy of CopaAmerica.com Can the United States win this year’s Gold Cup without key players involved? Davies, they’ll still be led by Lille striker Jonathan David. I’m taking them to win the group. Picking the second team gets a bit more difficult. Honduras played Canada on Tuesday, along with Curacao and El Salvador. Honduras against El Salvador on June 21 will likely determine the fate. Honduras comes into the tournament on three straight wins, so I’m taking them as 2B. Group C: No. 33 Panama, No. 63 Jamaica, No. 106 Guatemala, Unranked Guadeloupe Guatemala pulled off a pretty shocking 1-nil upset of Jamaica on June 16, putting the Reggae Boyz in danger of getting knocked out. Panama got the job done with a 5-2 whooping of Guadeloupe, so I’m taking them as 1C. The question is whether Jamaica can recover. I’m thinking Guatemala pulls it off and gets out the group. Quarterfinals predictions (2A) Costa Rica beats (1D) USA; (1A) Mexico beats (2D) Saudi Arabia; (1C) Panama beats (2B) Honduras; (1B) Canada beats (2C) Guatemala. I’m starting with an update. I’m not convinced that the USA can beat Costa Rica, so I’m taking USMNT to get ousted from the first stage of the knockout rounds. Costa Rica has talented athletes playing in Europe, and I’m thinking they are good enough to beat a shaken United States program. Semifinals Canada beats Costa Rica; Mexico beats Panama. I like Canada. Jesse Marsch’s bunch beat the United States 2-1 back in March and I think Jonathan David is good enough to lead them past Costa Rica. As for Mexico, I stand by my words that they have the best roster of the tournament. Finals Mexico defeats Canada. El Tri lifts their second straight Gold Cup trophy and 10th overall in the competition. Who do you have winning it all? Fill out your bracket in the attached image. articles.text: In addition to covering all Piedmont High School sports, the Piedmont Post strives to produce high quality photographs of the Highlanders’ student athletes. Provided is a collection of some of our favorite shots from the 2024-25 school year. Xavier Henderson looks at a Kennedy defender after stiff-arming him on his way to the end zone on November 2. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s football team resumed hosting Homecoming Night after a two-year hiatus due to the prolonged renovation of Witter Field. Pictured is the Piedmont student-section on September 20 against Encinal. Eliza Hammond runs to celebrate with her teammate following a goal. Diego Delventhal celebrates the game-winning run against Alameda on April 18. Friedie Schickedanz storms downfield in the NCS Championship game on May 18. 11. Lucas Smolko’s WACC tennis title & NCS run Lucas Smolko won his second consecutive WACC Tennis Championship as a junior and reached the D2 NCS Individual Tournament singles final. For the WACC title, Smolko defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Neo Chai in three sets, dominating the first and third sets toward a 6-1, 4-6, 6-2 win. At the NCS Individual Tournament, Smolko fought to three sets against Head Royce’s Dylan Donovan, but lost 5-7, 6-1, 6-3. To get there, Smolko opened with a 6-3, 6-1 win over Sonoma Academy’s Alex Sae and defeated Head Royce’s Jackson Stowell 6-2, 6-2. 12. Golfer Mei Assalian’s NCS run Senior Mei Assalian leaves Piedmont as the one of the school’s best golfers of all time. Assalian finished 13th of 144 at the D2 NCS Tournament at Rooster Run in Santa Rosa with an 18-hole round of 82 strokes. She went on to the D1 NCS Championship at Paradise Valley Golf Course in Fairfield, shooting a round of 89. Girls’ basketball team members celebrate after beating Bishop O’Dowd on February 6. San Joaquin Memorial head coach Jordan Whitfield shown with her newborn in a baby-carrier at Piedmont’s 62-60 win in the second round of the Division 1 CIF State tournament. Staff Photo Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Mission Division title, marking their second straight league title. Boys’ lacrosse coach Paul Pappas, a PHS Class of 2020 graduate, shouts out instructions in Piedmont’s 8-7 win over Bishop O’Dowd on April 4.
articles.title: The Post’s favorite photos from 2024-25

Football team wins WACC Mission Division title Back in the fall, Piedmont’s football team won its second consecutive WACC title by going 10-2 and perfect 5-0 against league teams on their way to the Mission Division title by going 5-0 against league teams. They were given the No. 3 seed in the D7 NCS playoffs, reaching the semifinals before falling to No. 2 Ferndale. Their 42-26 win over No. 6 Fortuna as the No. 3 seed in the Quarterfinals marked the program’s first NCS victory since 2017.

articles.text: Markets feature live music and extended museum hours The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting this month’s Night Market, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft, on Friday, June 27. Night Market events feature live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. Night Markets are held on the following dates: June 27, July 18, August (Date TBA), September 5, October 17, November (Date TBA), and December 12, 2025. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2025/. Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason next Friday. ®
articles.title: Fort Mason hosts artisan Night Market June 27

articles.text: Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art, the first exhibition to highlight Thiebaud’s extensive reinterpretations of works by his artistic heroes, is on display at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco now through August. Thiebaud was an American painter known for his colorful works depicting commonplace objects like pies, pastries, and hot dogs, most often associated with the Pop art movement because of his interest in objects of mass culture. Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art is the first exhibition to spotlight his extensive involvement with art history throughout his six-decade-long career until his death in 2021. The exhibition is a facet of the “Legion of Honor 100,” a yearlong centennial celebration of San Francisco’s fine arts museums and its collections. The exhibition includes 65 pieces by Thiebaud, representing his wide-ranging reinterpretations of old and new European and American artworks spanning the years 1957 to 2020. “As a self-identified ‘thief,’ who mined the work of his predecessors and contemporaries, Wayne Thiebaud’s practice was deeply rooted in his study of art history, but this aspect of his work has never been explored,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Over the course of the next year, as we reflect upon the Legion of Honor’s legacy as a center of art historical research and inspiration, Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art couldn’t be more timely.” Exhibition curator Timothy Anglin Burgard said Thiebaud’s engagement with art history at large “revealed his belief that the world of art transcended limiting definitions of time and place, as well as progress. Viewed from this perspective, the entire global history of art, encompassing every movement and style, was as accessible, relevant, and inspiring to Thiebaud as contemporary art,” he said. The exhibition is on display through August. Visit https:// www.famsf.org to learn more and to plan your visit.
articles.title: Wayne Thiebaud exhibit on view at Legion of Honor

articles.text: Festival Napa Valley’s 2025 summer season kicks off July 5 at outdoor venues and popular wineries throughout Napa Valley, including Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena and Nickel & Nickel in Oakville. The festival, now in its 19th season, is presented annually by the nonprofit Napa Valley Festival Association, governed by a board of vintners and local business owners. More than 200 musicians, wineries, resorts, theaters, restaurants, chefs and vintners participate each year, showcasing a range of classical and orchestral live music with Napa Valley’s iconic vineyards as a backdrop. This year’s highlights include the North American debut of Versailles Royal Opera with The Daughter of the Regiment, a tribute to composer Ennio Morricone, and performances by renowned artists such as New Orleans singer-songwriter Jon Batiste, mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato, pianist Tianxu An, soprano Alexandra Armantrading, baritone Lester Lynch and more. The festival spans the Napa Valley region and presents performances at many wineries that are rarely open to the public. Taste of Napa, a signature event within the summer festival, showcases wine and culinary delicacies from approximately 80 local wineries, restaurants and food artisans. Festival Napa Valley also presents year-round school programming and is the leading private funder of arts education in Napa County public schools, offering programs for students, tuition-free academies for young emerging artists and scholarships for students studying music. This year, Festival Napa Valley is also introducing a “Choose Your Price” ticket model for select concerts during the 2025 summer season, allowing attendees to choose ticket prices starting as low as free to $5, with the option of contributing more. Festival Napa Valley runs from July 5 to 20. Visit https://festivalnapavalley.org for the full summer lineup and to purchase tickets. Festival Napa Valley returns to wine country for its 19th season on July 5.
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley begins July 5

pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, June 18, 2025 Arts & Entertainment Fort Mason hosts artisan Night Market June 27 Markets feature live music and extended museum hours By Allyson Aleksey The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting this month’s Night Market, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft, on Friday, June 27. Night Market events feature live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. Night Markets are held on the following dates: June 27, July 18, August (Date TBA), September 5, October 17, November (Date TBA), and December 12, 2025. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2025/. Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art exhibition at Legion of Honor. Wayne Thiebaud exhibit on view at Legion of Honor By Allyson Aleksey Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art, the first exhibition to highlight Thiebaud’s extensive reinterpretations of works by his artistic heroes, is on display at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco now through August. Thiebaud was an American painter known for his colorful works depicting commonplace objects like pies, pastries, and hot dogs, most often associated with the Pop art movement because of his interest in objects of mass culture. Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art is the first exhibition to spotlight his extensive involvement with art history throughout his six-decade-long career until his death in 2021. The exhibition is a facet of the “Legion of Honor 100,” a yearlong centennial celebration of San Francisco’s fine arts museums and its collections. The exhibition includes 65 pieces by Thiebaud, representing his wide-ranging reinterpretations of old and new European and American artworks spanning the years 1957 to 2020. “As a self-identified ‘thief,’ who mined the work of his predecessors and contemporaries, Wayne Thiebaud’s practice was deeply rooted in his study of art history, but this aspect of his work has never been explored,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Over the course of the next year, as we reflect upon the Legion of Honor’s legacy as a center of art historical research and inspiration, Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art couldn’t be more timely.” Exhibition curator Timothy Anglin Burgard said Thiebaud’s engagement with art history at large “revealed his belief that the world of art transcended limiting definitions of time and place, as well as progress. Viewed from this perspective, the entire global history of art, encompassing every movement and style, was as accessible, relevant, and inspiring to Thiebaud as contemporary art,” he said. The exhibition is on display through August. Visit https:// www.famsf.org to learn more and to plan your visit. Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason next Friday. Festival Napa Valley begins July 5 By Allyson Aleksey Festival Napa Valley’s 2025 summer season kicks off July 5 at outdoor venues and popular wineries throughout Napa Valley, including Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena and Nickel & Nickel in Oakville. The festival, now in its 19th season, is presented annually by the nonprofit Napa Valley Festival Association, governed by a board of vintners and local business owners. More than 200 musicians, wineries, resorts, theaters, restaurants, chefs and vintners participate each year, showcasing a range of classical and orchestral live music with Napa Valley’s iconic vineyards as a backdrop. This year’s highlights include the North American debut of Versailles Royal Opera with The Daughter of the Regiment, a tribute to composer Ennio Morricone, and performances by renowned artists such as New Orleans singer-songwriter Jon Batiste, mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato, pianist Tianxu An, soprano Alexandra Armantrading, baritone Lester Lynch and more. The festival spans the Napa Valley region and presents performances at many wineries that are rarely open to the public. Taste of Napa, a signature event within the summer festival, showcases wine and culinary delicacies from approximately 80 local wineries, restaurants and food artisans. Festival Napa Valley also presents year-round school programming and is the leading private funder of arts education in Napa County public schools, offering programs for students, tuition-free academies for young emerging artists and scholarships for students studying music. This year, Festival Napa Valley is also introducing a “Choose Your Price” ticket model for select concerts during the 2025 summer season, allowing attendees to choose ticket prices starting as low as free to $5, with the option of contributing more. Festival Napa Valley runs from July 5 to 20. Visit https://festivalnapavalley.org for the full summer lineup and to purchase tickets. ® R&S OVERHEAD R&S OVERHEAD GARAGE DOOR, INC. GARAGE DOOR, INC. articles.text: Play ends June 21 San Francisco Playhouse’s production The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, based on the novel by Mark Haddon and adapted by Simon Stephens, is playing onstage now through June 21. Haddon’s 2003 mystery novel has been critically acclaimed for its portrayal of neurodivergence, featuring a main character who is described as a “bright mathematician with behavioral problems.” The novel is narrated by 15-yearold Christopher John Francis Boone and chronicles his investigation into the murder of his neighbor’s dog. The book won the Whitbread Book Awards for Best Novel and Book of the Year, the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize for Best First Book, and the Guardian Children’s Fiction Prize. Brendan Looney makes his San Francisco Playhouse debut as protagonist Christopher, who discovers his neighbor’s dog dead, stabbed by a kitchen fork, and launches his own guerrilla investigation. Christopher is determined to solve the mystery of who murdered Wellington and carefully records each fact of the crime. But his detective work, forbidden by his father, takes him on a thrilling journey that upturns his world. Mark P. Robinson also makes his Playhouse debut as Ed Boone, Christopher’s father. Cassidy Brown, Laura Domingo, Whit K. Lee, Catherine Luedtke, Renee Rogoff, and Wiley Naman Strasser round out the ensemble. San Francisco Playhouse Producing Director and co-founder Susi Damilano leads the production with movement direction by Bridgette Loriaux. The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time is playing onstage through June 21 at San Francisco Playhouse 450, Post Street. For tickets and more information, visit sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677- 9596. Photo by Jessica Palopoli Mark P. Robinson and Brendan Looney in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time

articles.text: Marah Sotelo (Maria) and Lucy Fisch as Liesl, Jaxon Hunt as Friedrich, Miranda Klein as Louisa, Ray Khalili as Kurt, Sage Luu as Brigitta, Kaylee Lopez as Marta, Erin Koh as Gretl in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Sound of Music Berkeley Playhouse closes its current season with The Sound of Music, playing onstage now through June 29. The musical, based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers, premiered years before the widely-popular 1965 American musical film. Berkeley Playhouse director Danny Cozart said the beloved, timeless musical is one of his all-time favorites that “continues to become more relevant day by day.” “The themes we are looking to explore in this production are the choices a person must make when the different structures of society [including] family, religion, and the state, are imposing conflicting demands on them.” Cozart said. “Our focus for this production is to drive home the real-world consequences of political action and the impact on a family trying to stay together in the face of looming tyranny.” The cast includes Marah Sotelo as Maria Rainer, Teressa Foss as Mother Abbess, Chloe Angst as Sister Berthe, Sage Alberto as Sister Margaretta, Akshaya Lakshmi as Sister Sophia, Robert Lopez as Captain Georg Von Trapp and Phillip Leyva as Franz. A cast of young musicians perform the musical’s key songs. Musical numbers feature Lucy Fisch as Liesl, Jaxon Hunt as Friedrich, Miranda Klein as Louisa, Ray Khalili as Kurt, Sage Luu as Brigitta, Kaylee Lopez as Marta and Erin Koh as Gretl, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 (extension 351) or visit www. berkeleyplayhouse.org. Showtimes vary.

articles.text: Picnic tables still available, space is limited The San Francisco Symphony performs its annual concert at Stern Grove Festival, a free summer music festival in San Francisco, on Sunday, July 6. The Symphony has performed at the festival every year since its inception 88 years ago. Stern Grove Festival includes 10 summer concerts on Sundays from mid-June through August at a natural amphitheater in San Francisco surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees. The grove’s natural acoustics have been preserved as a park in which the public can enjoy admission-free music, dance, and theatre performances. The Symphony will be joined by special musical guest Taimane, a Hawaii-born ukulele virtuoso and songwriter, who makes her Stern Grove debut with the world-class orchestra. Taimane is renowned for her unique and inventive style of playing the fourstring island instrument and has garnered critical acclaim for her signature stage presence. She is the recipient of the 2023 Nā Hōkū Hanohano Instrumental Album and Instrumental Composition of the Year award and was recognized as the Nā Hōkū Hanohano Favorite Entertainer of the Year in 2023. Free registration is now closed, but concert goers may still purchase picnic tables or stageside lounges. Visit https://www.sterngrove.org/sfsymphony-taimane to purchase seating. articles.text: Thursday, June 19, 6:00 p.m. La Speranza String Quartet La Speranza makes their highly anticipated California debut with Mozart’s Contemporaries, a concert program featuring works from their upcoming album — a program of historically informed performances of chamber music string quartet gems by French prodigy Hyacinthe Jadin (1776-1800), the highly respected Paul Wranitzky (1756- 1808), and the masterful Joseph Eybler (1765-1846) that will delight and inspire in an unforgettably engaging performance. Named after the Italian word for hope, La Speranza was founded in 2016. A collective of some of the top musicians in the Bay Area – including Grammy®-award-winners and nominees, Vitamin Em brings a wealth of experience, creativity and fearless improvisation to each performance. Members are steeped in an abundance of musical traditions, from jazz, blues, and rock to Balkan, fiddle, and classical, and present a harmonious blend of clever arrangements and first-class original music for each concert – all delivered with fun-loving spontaneity and infectious enthusiasm. This concert features Vitamin Em’s masterfully inventive string players Matt Szemela and Evan Price, violins; Emily Onderdonk, viola; Michael Graham, cello; and bassoonist Paul Hanson. With Bay Area ties both professional and personal, the duo is thrilled to return in June for two concerts, bringing uniquely joyful energy to the art of four-hand piano music. These Denver-based pianists began their collaboration in 2018 and have delighted audiences at recitals and house concerts ever since. articles.text: History is like the hall of mirrors. There are many facets. It can be viewed from many directions. The accounts can be compelling, especially when brought on by knaves and phonies. Six of us attended the dress rehearsal of the musical Anastasia at Woodminster Amphitheater in the Oakland hills. Anastasia is a full bodied musical, best described as “a drama played after a tragedy for the purpose of entertainment.” It was all of those things. Musicians of all ages will love this musical, and it will also appeal to historians. Let me tell you why. First of all, Woodminster is a beautiful location now celebrating its 50th anniversary. The productions are fine tuned. A live orchestra is in the pit and the musicians are very proficient. The actual story of Anastasia Romanoff (the youngest daughter of the last czar of Russia) is a fantasy of the highest order. The musical is based on history… in part factual, in part fantasy and in part false history. There are imposters everywhere. The plot has many sub plots. It is almost impossible to tell where history leaves off and fantasy begins. That is the very nature of the true story of Anastasia. Dramatically speaking, this musical is worth seeing. All of the history is explained in dialogues and musically. When the singers perform their arias, the story comes together quite clearly. All of the leading characters have excellent voices and the staging is beautiful. Drama came at the appropriate time and was often riveting. In addition, there is a fabulous ballet scene. Unfortunately, there were no printed programs so I am not able to provide the names of the performers. Nevertheless, Anastasia the musical will appeal to historians and music lovers. My only suggestion is that this Russian story should have had some Russian-sounding music. Meredith explained what the young people’s choral Orchestra does and Von Stade was on stage to give the audience a sense of the storyline. From the start, it was obvious that these two top-flight musicians deserve their good reputations. All of the young singers showed promise. And then von Stade stood to sing. It was obvious from the start that she was not in good health, vocally speaking. That hardly mattered. Even when she clears her throat, it is obvious that she is a real superstar. What an inspiration she is. Just watching her stage deportment is illuminating. That’s the way it is with great entertainers. Meredith’s accompaniment was equally fine. The choral orchestra has been at the forefront of education since 1968. YPSO concert on Sunday On Sunday, the Young Peoples’ Symphony Orchestra played a Pops concert. This great organization is now in its 88 year. Conductor David Ramadanoff is a real inspiration. As a conductor, he is a real maestro. As a teacher, he knows exactly what to say, and how to say it. All of his young musicians proceed to careers in music as well as in other admirable professions. All we have to do is open our eyes – and ears. History allows us to look at events which happened “then”. “Now” is experienced as we live it. The “future” offers many possibilities. articles.text: Fried Green Tomatoes is based on the 1987 novel Fried Green Tomatoes at the Whistle Stop Café, written by Fannie Flagg. The film is extraordinary, filled with humor, wonderful portrayals, Oscar nominated, a kaleidoscope of wonderful characters, each giving outstanding performances. The narrative is set in real time Alabama, and opens with Evelyn Couch (Kathy Bates) and her husband, Ed (Gailard Sartain), visiting his aunt at a nearby nursing home. Banished from the visit by Ed’s very cranky aunt, Evelyn goes to the waiting room where she meets an elderly woman seated alone on a sofa. Happy for the company, she introduces herself as Ninny Threadgoode (Jessica Tandy). Small talk quickly evaporates and Ninny begins to share stories from her past, a series of vignettes set in a whisper of a place called Whistle Stop and a café of the same name. She begins telling Evelyn about a young girl named Idgie (later played by an older Mary Stuart Masterson), willful, best described as a Tomboy. It’s at this point that the film cuts to Alabama in the early 1920s. The tale, told by Ninny, initially in the form of introductory voice-over, immediately captures Evelyn’s imagination, and so the audience is introduced to a young Idgie and a slightly older, very feminine Ruth Jamison (Mary Louise Parker), a family relative. Though this brief tale ends in a heartbreaking tragedy, Evelyn, expecting to be rejected by Ed’s aunt, returns to the same waiting room and once again finds Ninny there, alone. And so the soulful story of Idgie and Ruth continues, two women who eventually share a deep bond, and together run the Whistle Stop Café. What the narrative does at this point is weave two stories together: the first involves Evelyn who is attempting to improve her marriage with Ed while acquiring a budding sense of empowerment. She finds inspiration from Ninny and the close relationship that existed between Idgie and Ruth. The audience is reminded that rural Alabama in the 1920s was plagued by a malignant racism. Yet, at the Whistle Stop Café there was a prevailing color-blindness and an abiding humanity, made evident through the remarkable and pivotal performances by cicely Tyson as Sipsy and Stan Shaw as Big George who both worked at the café. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Grave of Fireflies Grave of Fireflies is a mustsee if you have been captured by the extraordinary animation and storytelling that has come to define Studio Ghibli. It is, without hesitation, an achingly beautiful film that transcends all expectations. However know that its story is profoundly sad and emotive, bordering on the traumatic. Because it is animated, and its two main characters are children, it is easy to assume that its subject matter will reflect the fanciful innocence associated with the animé genre. But while this narrative is, to be sure, an allegory of sorts, it also challenges our assumptions about animation. Grave of Fireflies is set in Kobe, Japan. The year is 1945, and WWII is coming to a close, despite the unwillingness of the Japanese to stand down. Told in a long flashback, the tale focuses on a 14-year-old boy named Seita (J. Robert Spencer) and his 5-year-old sister, Setsuko (Rhoda Chrosite). Orphaned by allied fire-bombings, they go to live with their aunt (Amy Jones) whose initial charitable response to the children turns surprisingly bitter until, finally, Seita decides that they must leave. The two find a cave in the hills and for a brief time all is well. But before long malnutrition stalks them. Seita is beaten while looking for food and Setsuko falls ill. Their struggle is the struggle of the vulnerable who must confront events not of their making and the arc of the story is wrenchingly inevitable. pages.text: Wednesday, June 18, 2025 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Fried Green Tomatoes an extraordinary film By Chris Honoré Fried Green Tomatoes is based on the 1987 novel Fried Green Tomatoes at the Whistle Stop Café, written by Fannie Flagg. The film is extraordinary, filled with humor, wonderful portrayals, Oscar nominated, a kaleidoscope of wonderful characters, each giving outstanding performances. The narrative is set in real time Alabama, and opens with Evelyn Couch (Kathy Bates) and her husband, Ed (Gailard Sartain), visiting his aunt at a nearby nursing home. Banished from the visit by Ed’s very cranky aunt, Evelyn goes to the waiting room where she meets an elderly woman seated alone on a sofa. Happy for the company, she introduces herself as Ninny Threadgoode (Jessica Tandy). Small talk quickly evaporates and Ninny begins to share stories from her past, a series of vignettes set in a whisper of a place called Whistle Stop and a café of the same name. She begins telling Evelyn about a young girl named Idgie (later played by an older Mary Stuart Masterson), willful, best described as a Tomboy. It’s at this point that the film cuts to Alabama in the early 1920s. The tale, told by Ninny, initially in the form of introductory voice-over, immediately captures Evelyn’s imagination, and so the audience is introduced to a young Idgie and a slightly older, very feminine Ruth Jamison (Mary Louise Parker), a family relative. Though this brief tale ends in a heartbreaking tragedy, Evelyn, expecting to be rejected by Ed’s aunt, returns to the same waiting room and once again finds Ninny there, alone. And so the soulful story of Idgie and Ruth continues, two women who eventually share a deep bond, and together run the Whistle Stop Café. What the narrative does at this point is weave two stories together: the first involves Evelyn who is attempting to improve her marriage with Ed while acquiring a budding sense of empowerment. She finds inspiration from Ninny and the close relationship that existed between Idgie and Ruth. The audience is reminded that rural Alabama in the 1920s was plagued by a malignant racism. Yet, at the Whistle Stop Café there was a prevailing color-blindness and an abiding humanity, made evident through the remarkable and pivotal performances by cicely Tyson as Sipsy and Stan Shaw as Big George who both worked at the café. Fried Green Tomatoes is a funny, moving story, rich in characters, and is, as well, an intriguing mystery, one that is not answered until the final scenes of this marvelous movie that deftly winds through the past and present. As an aside, Jessica Tandy did win a Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her role as Ninny Threadgoode. She is superb. As well the film won a BAFTA award and three Golden Globe Awards. Fried Green Tomatoes. Directed by John Avnet. Starring Kathy Bates, Jessica Tandy, Mary Stuart Masterson, Mary Louise Parker. 2 hrs., 10 min. PG-13. Released in 1991. articles.text: Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. And parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, well, start there before heading on to Lightyear. Here is some backstory: in 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. Loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy Story. So far so good? The question then begged is, what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination? First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board a Star Trek-like deep space star ship, akin to the iconic EnterA scene from Disney-Pixar animation’s Lightyear prise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission, all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, hey decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however the ship is damaged on landing, plus there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear, a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk Lightyear. Directed by Angus MacLane. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Chris Evans, Taika Waititi, Keke Palmer. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG. Released in 2022. articles.text: If you happen to have a tween or an early teen girl as a member of your family, well, Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret is a must see film. It’s extraordinary, superbly acted, comedic, and honest to a fault while touching on a spectrum of concerns and issues that confront young girls as they approach early adolescence and the many exigent changes that define this emotive period. The story is based on the hugely popular, award-wining novel, written by Judy Blume and published in 1970. The film is initially set in New York City and opens with 11-year-old Margaret Simon (Abby Ryder Fortson) returning from summer camp. She lives in a two-story brownstone with her parents, Herbert (Benny Safdie) and Barbara (Rachel McAdams) and her grandmother, Sylvie (Kathy Bates). Soon after giving affectionate hugs all around and then unpacking her camp gear, her parents sit Margaret down and tell her that Herb has gotten a promotion and as a result they are moving to a split-level ranch house in a suburb of New Jersey. Of course she is not happy and asks her parents, “What about all my friends?” But move they do and thus begins her journey to a new school where she will enter the 6th grade and unexpectedly joins a group of girls (four in all) named the Preteen Sensations. articles.text: Previously printined in the Piedmont Post on June 15, 2022. The French Riviera in the South of France is continuous to the Italian Riviera, sharing the same climate and geology, but the French refer to La Côte d’Azur as the famous seaside resort region from Saint Tropez to the border. The azure-blue coastline has been the playground of the rich since the Brits believed the sea air cured consumption (tuberculosis). It was previously a coastline of impoverished villagers who fished and farmed for a living, but when the Nice-Paris train route opened in the 1860s, English aristocrats infused wealth and built luxury villas. Celebrities and royalty followed, including Queen Victoria who made repeat visits. The region of ProvenceAlpes-Côte d’Azur was known to ancient mariners as Land’s End. Proof of ancient tribes is derived from artifacts and excavation, Voyagers dazzled by the blue sea date to the pre-historic era. Ancient paths became roads cut from the great walls of rock from the southern flank of the Alps, which abruptly rises from the eastern shoreline. The lower Rhône River drains into the Mediterranean, and following westward, the sea is pinched through the Straits of Gibraltar, then empties into the North Atlantic. The Greeks, already settled at Marseilles, moved eastward to found Nicaia, or Nice, around 350 BCE. The Greeks were swept out by the Romans around 150 BCE, and when Rome fell in 476 A.D., the Goths defended the coastline. Many historical peoples fought to control the mystically calm Mediterranean Sea. During the Middle Ages, Nice was part of Italy under the control of citystate Genoese, From the Renaissance and for the next five centuries, Nice was ruled by the Duchy of Savoy. France’s Emperor Louis Napoléon III courted Nice to join France. By1860, the port of Genoa had gained immense importance over Nice’s seaport, and Italy let go without a fight. Nice and La Côte d’Azur Visitors to Nice may detect the strong Italian influence, noticed by native French speakers. The café americano is annoyingly served as an espresso, among other useful facts. Nice is a View from terrace at Villefranche-sur-Mer and Les Baies des Anges. deep-water seaport that surprises with sharp, sudden drop-offs, and the coastline hotels cordon off the danger points with ropes and buoys. The Mediterranean is so calm that the tidal waves barely vary between high and low, barely a 20-inch variation (50 cm). Marseilles, Lyon, and Toulouse are larger cities than Nice, and most visitors elect to stroll Promenade des Anglais, named for the English who transformed it from a modest muddy and stony path to a respectable road that burgeoned into the urban freeway it is now. Old Nice (Vieux-Nice) is also a destination, a mostly walking district that draws visitors to its produce markets and cafés. The Alps protect Nice from the heat of summer and the frost of winter, keeping it temperate almost yearround. The Nice art museums are small and intimate, and an hour is sufficient for the typical visit. Upon the best-known hill of Nice, the Cimiez quarter, is where the Chagall and Matisse museums are set in peaceful gardens. They are nearby to a Roman excavation and archeological museum. Seaside Resorts, La Côte d’Azur While on an eight-day holiday, we lodged at the small seaside resort of Villefranche-surMer, carved into the limestone cliffs. We sat back on the terrace to glimpse the sea, rooftops, and roadway switchbacks across the cliffs. One felt nestled into the trees, branches rustling in the sea breeze, in a manner unruffled by the passage of time. We were on the Bay of Angels (Les Baies des Anges) watching the sea from only about a hundred feet as the pelican flies. The reclusive, billionaires’ village Saint Jean Cap-Ferrat to the east is a jutting peninsula densely populated with extravagant, heavily secluded homes. Property owners are serious about privacy, they armor up with gnarly hedges and cyclone fences to discourage prying eyes. The peninsula is surrounded by a pleasant 3-mile (5 km.) walkway that may be started at the historical landmark lighthouse. Bring track shoes, mine were leather that day. The Three Corniches The coastline (corniche) has a hundred beaches accessed from the low coastal road, the Basse Corniche, a route served by fine seaside resorts. La Basse is a Bay of Nice, the South of France. Saint-Jean Cap-Ferrat pathway around the peninsula’s periphery near the historic lighthouse. passable road built for seeing the sights and not for speed. The corniches are the coastline roads connecting Nice to Menton (east of Monaco). The Moyenne Corniche is the “average” or “middle” coastline road and the most direct route, except when deciding to bail on traffic. Our rental, an automatic, which seemed not as agile as the spiffy French mini or compact, but with the benefit of being stingy on petrol. It does keep the driver busy with six forward gears. The “automatics” are a rare find, so Go Stick and drive a mini. Or trust the bus: we bussed to Nice and sat back to enjoy the ride. Motorcyclists shorn of mufflers seem to have invaded the idyllic coastline, and we could hear their revved engines at all times of the day and night, making an otherwise luxe hillside apartment reverberate with their engine noise to the highest maximum decibels. I read a recent Riviera poll that 82% of the French say the noise is a nuisance, but who are the 18% who are fine to go with the flow? Michael noticed the oddity of the bedroom’s double set of heavyweight steel sliding doors opening to the night air, apparently a halfway attempt at tamping down the noise. The coastline has another popular bike culture: bicyclists of great skill and courage riding the tight cliffside with cars passing in both directions. The lanes are so narrow that wide loads can’t help their turns crossing briefly into oncoming traffic, like a daredevil course. As an alternative to commuter traffic on the Moyenne, we turned onto the Grande Corniche. Instantly the ride turned tranquil with astonishing sea vistas, a never-ending continuum of blues of the deep blue sea against white clouds against the blue of the sky. articles.title: AMERICANS IN PARIS The South of France, La Côte d’Azur, and Nice

pages.text: Wednesday, June 18, 2025 21 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Previously printined in the Piedmont Post on June 15, 2022. The French Riviera in the South of France is continuous to the Italian Riviera, sharing the same climate and geology, but the French refer to La Côte d’Azur as the famous seaside resort region from Saint Tropez to the border. The azure-blue coastline has been the playground of the rich since the Brits believed the sea air cured consumption (tuberculosis). It was previously a coastline of impoverished villagers who fished and farmed for a living, but when the Nice-Paris train route opened in the 1860s, English aristocrats infused wealth and built luxury villas. Celebrities and royalty followed, including Queen Victoria who made repeat visits. The region of ProvenceAlpes-Côte d’Azur was known to ancient mariners as Land’s End. Proof of ancient tribes is derived from artifacts and excavation, Voyagers dazzled by the blue sea date to the pre-historic era. Ancient paths became roads cut from the great walls of rock from the southern flank of the Alps, which abruptly rises from the eastern shoreline. The lower Rhône River drains into the Mediterranean, and following westward, the sea is pinched through the Straits of Gibraltar, then empties into the North Atlantic. The Greeks, already settled at Marseilles, moved eastward to found Nicaia, or Nice, around 350 BCE. The Greeks were swept out by the Romans around 150 BCE, and when Rome fell in 476 A.D., the Goths defended the coastline. Many historical peoples fought to control the mystically calm Mediterranean Sea. During the Middle Ages, Nice was part of Italy under the control of citystate Genoese, From the Renaissance and for the next five centuries, Nice was ruled by the Duchy of Savoy. France’s Emperor Louis Napoléon III courted Nice to join France. By1860, the port of Genoa had gained immense importance over Nice’s seaport, and Italy let go without a fight. Nice and La Côte d’Azur Visitors to Nice may detect the strong Italian influence, noticed by native French speakers. The café americano is annoyingly served as an espresso, among other useful facts. Nice is a View from terrace at Villefranche-sur-Mer and Les Baies des Anges. The South of France, La Côte d’Azur, and Nice deep-water seaport that surprises with sharp, sudden drop-offs, and the coastline hotels cordon off the danger points with ropes and buoys. The Mediterranean is so calm that the tidal waves barely vary between high and low, barely a 20-inch variation (50 cm). Marseilles, Lyon, and Toulouse are larger cities than Nice, and most visitors elect to stroll Promenade des Anglais, named for the English who transformed it from a modest muddy and stony path to a respectable road that burgeoned into the urban freeway it is now. Old Nice (Vieux-Nice) is also a destination, a mostly walking district that draws visitors to its produce markets and cafés. The Alps protect Nice from the heat of summer and the frost of winter, keeping it temperate almost yearround. The Nice art museums are small and intimate, and an hour is sufficient for the typical visit. Upon the best-known hill of Nice, the Cimiez quarter, is where the Chagall and Matisse museums are set in peaceful gardens. They are nearby to a Roman excavation and archeological museum. Seaside Resorts, La Côte d’Azur While on an eight-day holiday, we lodged at the small seaside resort of Villefranche-surMer, carved into the limestone cliffs. We sat back on the terrace to glimpse the sea, rooftops, and roadway switchbacks across the cliffs. One felt nestled into the trees, branches rustling in the sea breeze, in a manner unruffled by the passage of time. We were on the Bay of Angels (Les Baies des Anges) watching the sea from only about a hundred feet as the pelican flies. The reclusive, billionaires’ village Saint Jean Cap-Ferrat to the east is a jutting peninsula densely populated with extravagant, heavily secluded homes. Property owners are serious about privacy, they armor up with gnarly hedges and cyclone fences to discourage prying eyes. The peninsula is surrounded by a pleasant 3-mile (5 km.) walkway that may be started at the historical landmark lighthouse. Bring track shoes, mine were leather that day. The Three Corniches The coastline (corniche) has a hundred beaches accessed from the low coastal road, the Basse Corniche, a route served by fine seaside resorts. La Basse is a Bay of Nice, the South of France. Saint-Jean Cap-Ferrat pathway around the peninsula’s periphery near the historic lighthouse. passable road built for seeing the sights and not for speed. The corniches are the coastline roads connecting Nice to Menton (east of Monaco). The Moyenne Corniche is the “average” or “middle” coastline road and the most direct route, except when deciding to bail on traffic. Our rental, an automatic, which seemed not as agile as the spiffy French mini or compact, but with the benefit of being stingy on petrol. It does keep the driver busy with six forward gears. The “automatics” are a rare find, so Go Stick and drive a mini. Or trust the bus: we bussed to Nice and sat back to enjoy the ride. Motorcyclists shorn of mufflers seem to have invaded the idyllic coastline, and we could hear their revved engines at all times of the day and night, making an otherwise luxe hillside apartment reverberate with their engine noise to the highest maximum decibels. I read a recent Riviera poll that 82% of the French say the noise is a nuisance, but who are the 18% who are fine to go with the flow? Michael noticed the oddity of the bedroom’s double set of heavyweight steel sliding doors opening to the night air, apparently a halfway attempt at tamping down the noise. The coastline has another popular bike culture: bicyclists of great skill and courage riding the tight cliffside with cars passing in both directions. The lanes are so narrow that wide loads can’t help their turns crossing briefly into oncoming traffic, like a daredevil course. As an alternative to commuter traffic on the Moyenne, we turned onto the Grande Corniche. Instantly the ride turned tranquil with astonishing sea vistas, a never-ending continuum of blues of the deep blue sea against white clouds against the blue of the sky. Mountaintop views are awe-inspiring, and La Grande is my favorite travel route, even with its many road twists and loopbacks. Our brains are what makes the sea appear a vivid blue, of course. Millions of glints of light reflect stone pebbles of the sea floor, where tidal waves constantly churn and shave infinitesimally small particles from the galets (stones), and these reflect too. Meanwhile, the stones are worn flat and smooth. The cost of keeping the galets groomed falls upon the beachfront businesses, and they frown on visitors pocketing a souvenir stone. People know to not walk the pebble beach without practical shoes like rubber flat soles, An extra benefit is the workout exercising our feet. La Promenade de Croisette, Cannes We were not invited to the 75th Cannes Film Festival, nor did we attend, but we did stand on the sidewalk in front of the theater. The massive screen perched on the metallic-sided convention hall is the world’s biggest projector. Impromptu players in a frenzy of humanity, we were amassed into the jumbles of people rushing, crushing, waiting, posing. Our planned promenade on La Boulevard Croisette slipped past, like water circling down the drain, and despite backtracks and zigzags to get by Security, we faced the reality: no laminated lanyard, no entry. Se headed home to Villefranche-sur-Mer. The Cannes film festival See Americans in Paris on page 28

articles.title: From Havens to Witter Field: Walkers Trace the Roots of Piedmont High

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 18, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday From Havens to Witter Field: Walkers Trace the Roots of Piedmont High By Richard F. Carter With school out for summer, last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group enjoyed a guided walk through the Piedmont High School campus. Forty-one walkers (plus two K-9 best friends) gathered at the Exedra to explore notable features and local history. Before the walk, the group learned about the origins of Piedmont High. In 1916, land developer Frank C. Havens faced financial ruin. A onetime real estate speculator, he returned to California with little left, attempting to sell land to settle debts. Piedmont Park was heavily mortgaged, and Havens was unable to pay interest or principal. He auctioned his art collection and hoped to sell the parkland. The Piedmont School Board wanted 13 acres for a new high school and athletic field, but Havens refused to split the 27-acre parcel. The City also wanted to preserve the park but lacked funds. In November 1916, voters rejected a measure to purchase the remaining land. Havens died in 1918. In 1921, philanthropist Wallace Alexander stepped in. He and other donors bought 14 acres on the condition the City would later reimburse them. The deal allowed the School District to purchase its desired 13 acres. The next year, voters approved a bond to repay Alexander and his partners, securing the entire 27 acres. The walkers followed a path behind the Exedra to the high school’s rear entrance and continued past the student center and library, where more history was shared. Construction of Piedmont High began in 1921, designed by architect William Weeks. The reinforced concrete structure with terra cotta trim included an auditorium, two classroom wings, and separate science and cooking labs. Piedmont Junior High and the athletic field were added in 1924, with further additions in 1937 and 1939. In 1974, the original building was declared unsafe under new earthquake laws and demolished—though the process was slow due to the building’s sturdy construction. Three new classroom buildings and a gym replaced it, while the original library, quad, and administration buildings were preserved. That era’s “back-to-nature” wooden buildings, popular in the 1970s, were later deemed earthquake unsafe and also removed. With the passage of Measure H1, voters approved $56 million in bonds for safe, modern facilities. A new STEAM building and theater opened in fall 2021. The walkers also heard that Piedmont High was the last school in California to drop its enforced dress code, which required girls to wear middy blouses and pleated skirts until the early 1960s. Alumna Sherry Jacobs remembered the uniform’s upside—it made dressing for school simple. The group made a brief stop at the under-construction aquatics center, where fresh concrete had been poured but swimming likely won’t resume this summer. They continued past Millennium High, Binks Rawlings Gym, and Piedmont Middle School, then down “PE Hill” to the locker rooms and Witter Field. At Witter Field, the group paused at the monument to Jean C. Witter Jr., a 1940s PHS football captain and Cal player who died in WWII aboard the USS San Francisco. The field was named for him in 1948. The scoreboard also honors Charles Williams, a 1948 team member. Nearby, walkers passed Humphries Diamond, named for longtime teacher and coach Mike Humphries, who led PHS baseball for 33 years and freshman football for 43. Emerging on lower El Cerrito Avenue, the group climbed Jerome Avenue, detoured through Keefer Court to admire a unique cactus garden and Santa Fe– inspired front yards, and posed for a group photo. The final stretch took them across Oakland Avenue and up Latham Street—famously the only “street” in Piedmont—then on to Cambridge Way, Ricardo Avenue, and Blair Avenue. They finished the loop via Carmel Avenue and Bonita Vista back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call at (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: As our country navigates a multitude of challenges, service dogs are bringing hope and relief to many struggling to cope with the stress of everyday life. Protected by federal law under the Americans With Disabilities Act, these highly trained animals are more than just pets – they’re lifesavers. Service dogs are trained to actively mitigate an individual’s disability. These specially trained canines provide critical support to individuals struggling with a wide range of disabilities, both visible and invisible. Curious how service dogs improve their owners’ lives every day? Musubi, a Miniature Golden Doodle, alerts his owner to the sound of the smoke alarm, ensuring her safety despite her hearing loss. Other trained service dogs, like the Great Dane Scooter, provide mobility assistance in the form of balance support and fall recovery to their owners. And still more, like June and Nala, are currently in training to remind their owner to take medication or alert them to oncoming panic attacks. Facility dogs, while not protected by federal law, also make a difference in the lives of many. These dogs partner with working professionals to serve their clients, often going into schools, healthcare centers, and even family court. Dogs like Missy, the Australian Shepherd, partner with a therapist and are trained to help decrease anxiety in children. Stinson, a Labradoodle, spends time in schools as a reading dog to help children build confidence and improve their reading skills. These specially trained animals respond to specific needs, performing tasks such as deep pressure therapy to decrease anxiety, medication reminder and retrieval, allergen alert, migraine alert, mobility assistance, and more. As the need for service dogs and facility dogs continues to rise, it is essential that we raise awareness about their importance and impact. These are challenging times as we attempt to navigate political and social challenges; more people than ever may find themselves needing extra support and unconditional care. By recognizing the value of these unsung heroes, we can work towards creating a more inclusive and supportive community for all. With the right training, a service dog or facility dog could be a game-changer for anyone in this uncertain world. Sierra Berrick is a local service dog and behavioral trainer. She started Oak Hills Dog Training in Oakland mid pandemic in 2020 and helped to found the Alpha Dog Assist service dog training program in Mill Valley in 2021. She has supported the training of over 40 service dogs since, and currently specializes in training psychiatric, allergen alert, migraine alert, and mobility assistance service dogs, as well as facility dogs.

articles.text: Join Us for 4th of July Food & Fun Like many mature dowagers, the Pardee Home, has a few extra lines, worn skin, and some achey parts. Liposuction, Botox and radio frequency microneedling are not options. However, a rhytidectomy is. The second floor rooms of the Pardee Home Museum are undergoing a facelift. Ceiling leaks, general cracks and water stains have been all addressed with new wall surfacing applied. While messy and curtailing some public access during the process, the results will be stunning. Although these repairs will not be visible to the public once fresh paint and wallpaper (Bradbury & Bradbury, no less!) are applied, the old lady’s structural integrity has been protected and her internal health will glow and shine through the makeup applied. Soon tours will include part of the upstairs while the “procedure” continues! If you have never been or haven’t visited in a long time, please visit http://www.pardeehome.org and come visit. The next great opportunity will be resurrection of the traditional Fourth of July BBQ. This is the perfect venue for a fun, safe destination to enjoy the holiday. Pianist Frederick Hodges will provide Ragtime music in the shaded back garden amid tables and chairs for our guests. A barbeque of burgers, Impossible burgers, hot dogs, corn-on-the-cob plus other tasty treats will be served. Guests will be able to enjoy the beautiful blooming garden with mature oak trees overhead. Vintage attire encouraged. Please call Richelle Lieberman 510 381.1973 to make reservations so we know how much food and seating to offer. The Pardee Museum is located at Castro between 11th & 12th St. Enter at gate on Castro St. Reservations are also available on Eventbrite.com Prices are $20 for Adults (12 and older), $5 for those 5-11 years old and Free for children under 5. For additional information check the Pardee Home Museum website http://pardeehome.org. Full tours will not be given at this event, just come to enjoy the music and food.
