articles.text: Order of the Arrow is an honor society within Scouting America to promote cheerful service above self. It recognizes Scouts who best exemplify and live by the Scout oath, law, motto and slogan. Piedmont’s lodge is called Hungteetsepoppi, meaning ‘bird with red head’, a reference to the bird that represents our lodge. Year round the lodge helps the Piedmont Scout Council with various aspects of Piedmont scouting, such as the Cub Scout Webeloree, where we prepare dinner and a campfire on the first night. We also help set up and take down the Tree Lot at the end of the season. In addition, the OA participates in larger events, such as the section-wide Conclave, a gathering of multiple lodges from the area. Similar to Camporee, Conclave is usually a larger event and features master classes on certain aspects of the OA, such as ceremonies and membership retention. Events also take place at the regional and national level, such as the National Leadership Seminar and exclusive experiences at the four national high adventure bases. On June 8th, our lodge celebrated a successful year of leadership, community service, and new members with a lodge-wide barbecue, and a brotherhood ceremony. Brotherhood is recognition you receive after being an active member of the lodge for six months, and show a strong understanding of the ideals of the OA. It’s not a rank to progress through, but rather an indicator of your commitment to the highest ideals of Scouting The celebration was followed by a barbeque before beginning the elections for the upcoming year. One unique aspect of the OA is that it’s fully youth led. While Scouting has a large amount of youth input and leadership, the OA is only restrained by what the youth leaders can put into place and organize. Everything, down to the elections of lodge officers are entirely youth run. Vice Chief of Program Caleb Canada (left), Vice Chief of Membership Sean McKee, Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson, and Vice Chief of Communication Samantha Pell For me, this is a testament to the truest displays of character, and an excellent foundation for lifelong connections and valuable lessons on leadership. To quote our National Chief, Samuel Crowder’s Chiefly Thoughts “...such a simple display of his appreciation and love for his friends, but it spoke volumes on what he truly enjoyed, and I would argue most love about the Order of the Arrow: the people”. The people are what truly make the OA an enjoyable and formative experience, one that is certainly worth being a part of. If you are an active Scouter in Piedmont and interested in joining the Order of the Arrow, please reach out to your Scoutmaster for additional information. Samantha Pell is the Vice Chief of Communications for the Hungteetsepoppi Lodge serving the 2025-26 year. Lodge members gather around the barbeque. Brotherhood Sashes Lodge with new officers

Vice Chief of Program Caleb Canada (left), Vice Chief of Membership Sean McKee, Lodge Chief Theo Ferguson, and Vice Chief of Communication Samantha Pell For me, this is a testament to the truest displays of character, and an excellent foundation for lifelong connections and valuable lessons on leadership. To quote our National Chief, Samuel Crowder’s Chiefly Thoughts “...such a simple display of his appreciation and love for his friends, but it spoke volumes on what he truly enjoyed, and I would argue most love about the Order of the Arrow: the people”. The people are what truly make the OA an enjoyable and formative experience, one that is certainly worth being a part of. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently visited the historic Elliston Winery in Sunol, where they toured the estate and enjoyed an elegant tea featuring open-faced sandwiches, scones, and decadent desserts. Tucked away in the Sunol hills, Elliston Vineyards offers a picturesque setting for outdoor tea or special events. Its lush grounds, historic stone mansion, and secluded Terrace Room create a memorable backdrop for any occasion. The Elliston estate was established by Henry Hiram Ellis, who came to California in 1849 during the Gold Rush. He later served as San Francisco’s last elected chief of police from 1875 to 1877, and Ellis Street was named in his honor. In 1885, Ellis purchased a scenic, oak-studded property in Sunol for his retirement. Between 1885 and 1890, he built Elliston—a 17-room, three-story neo-Romanesque mansion constructed with 32-inch-thick blue sandstone walls quarried nearby in Niles Canyon. In 1890, Ellis planted three acres of vineyards on the propThe Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a beautiful day and a lovely tea at Elliston Winery in Sunol. Pictured (L to R): Fred Pemberton, Jim Ayotte, Greg Jurin, Mary Buller, Mona Jamieson, Nancy Hinsch, Elene Manolis, Gloria Wilmer, Carole Jones, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Yorkman Lowe, Edith Hereso, Jan Yager, and Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein. erty, which remain in production today. The estate is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Following their tea, the Seniors headed to Niles, where they strolled through the Town Plaza, browsed antique shops, and enjoyed ice cream from a local parlor. With more than 40 antique and specialty stores, the area offers plenty of unique finds. Niles also boasts a rich history. Established in the 1850s, it served as a key junction for Southern Pacific Railroad lines connecting Oakland, San Jose, and points south. It once housed the state’s largest rose plantation and later became a hub for early filmmaking. In 1912, Essanay Studios brought national attention to Niles. Led by Bronco Billy Anderson, the studio filmed silent-era classics with stars like Charlie Chaplin, Wallace Beery, and Ben Turpin. Many westerns were shot in Niles Canyon and on the town’s main streets. Strolling through the neighborhood, the Piedmont Seniors appreciated Niles’ historic charm, friendly shops, and relaxed, welcoming vibe. It was, all in all, a peaceful and thoroughly enjoyable day. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. The Piedmont Seniors received a guided tour of Elliston Winery, including the historic Elliston mansion. Pictured (L to R): Nancy Hinsch, Jim Ayotte, Fred Pemberton, Carole Jones, Yorkman Lowe, tour guide Kathleen, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, and Jan Yager. A lazy, hazy, almost-summer day found the Piedmont Seniors relaxing in the heart of Niles Town Plaza. articles.text: Ever wished you could bring a slice of nature indoors but worried about the commitment of a full-fledged houseplant? Terrariums offer the perfect solution. These miniature ecosystems housed in glass containers are a captivating display of greenery that requires minimal care. Choosing the perfect container: Select a clear glass container to allow plenty of sunlight to reach your plants. Bowls, apothecary jars or even recycled fish tanks with wide openings are all great options. Choose a container that’s large enough to comfortably fit the drainage layers, potting mix and your plants at their mature size. Picking the perfect plants: When choosing plants, consider both their mature size and the limitations of your container. Here are some low-maintenance options that thrive in drier environments: • Pincushion cactus • Air plants • Hens and chicks • Button fern Pro tip: Select plants with similar light and watering needs to ensure a harmonious environment within your terrarium. Building a foundation for success: Terrariums don’t have drainage holes, making it extra important to create a well-draining base to prevent root rot. Drainage layer: • Add a layer of coarse gravel, sea glass or beach stones to the bottom of your container. A good foundation made up of different layers of material is essential for the well being of the terrarium. Succulents, air plants, cacti and ferns work great in open terrariums. Barrier layer: • Next, add a quarter- to halfinch layer of activated charcoal on top of the gravel. This will help prevent fungus growth. • Then, cover the stones and charcoal with a layer of sphagnum moss. This will prevent the potting soil from mixing in with the drainage layers. (Do not use peat moss for this layer.) Soil layer: • Add sterile potting mix on top of the moss. The soil should be formulated for the plants you’ve picked, such as a cactus and succulent mix. Planting and design: Here’s where you can unleash your creativity. Before planting, take some time to design the layout of your terrarium. Carefully remove your plants from their pots, loosen the roots and gently brush away any excess dirt. Play with the arrangement to create a visually interesting composition. Once you’re happy with the layout, use a spoon or your fingers to carefully plant each one in your terrarium. Fill in any gaps with moss for a natural, finished look. Caring for your terrarium: Light: Terrariums prefer bright, indirect sunlight. Avoid direct sunlight, which can scorch your plants. Rotate your terrarium occasionally for even growth. Watering: Less is more when it comes to watering your terrarium. Use a spray bottle or tablespoon to add water sparingly when the soil is dry. Upkeep: Remove yellowing or dead plants right away. Occasionally wipe down the glass with damp newspaper or a lint-free cloth. Adding your personal touch: Finally, it’s time to decorate. Add elements like small rocks, figurines or colorful gravel to personalize your miniature world. Enjoy your thriving little world! Debbi DiMaggio Debbi. Cunamacué: Family Dance Program Wednesday, June 18 — 6:00 p.m. – 6:45 p.m. Cunamacué, is an Oakland arts organization dedicated to promoting Afro-Peruvian culture through its music and dance. This intergenerational class is an introduction to Afro-Peruvian culture through dance. The name Cunamacué is a reminder that their work is based on ancestral roots and meant to be left for future generations. The word macué is representative of the ancestors; it is a stream in Mozambique, one of the places from which Africans were uprooted and taken to Perú. Cuna is the Spanish word for crib, representing future. Cunamacué contributes to a more just world by amplifying the history, culture, voices, and ideas of African descendants from Peru using music and dance as the vehicle for transformation, Build Make Play/Construir Hacer Jugar Saturday, June 21 — 10:30 a.m. – 11:30 a.m. Join us for an afternoon of hands-on activities. articles.text: MAX WAGENER Water Polo University of Redlands Max Wagener, PHS Class of 2021, wrapped up his senior year on University of Redlands’ water polo team as a National Champion, helping his school defeat No. 2 Chapman 14-13 on December 8 as the No. 1 seed. Wagener is breathing rarified air as a two-time Division 3 NCAA title winner after helping his team win the D3 NCAA title once before in 2022 as a sophomore. He ended the season as the Southern California Intercollegiate Athletic Conference Player of the Year. Wagener finished the year with a team-leading 73 goals, to go along with 16 assists. It marked the third straight time for Redlands to reach the D3 NCAA title game, winning it all in 2022 as the No. 2 seed, losing in 2023 as the No. 2 seed, and claiming this year’s championship as the top seed. The Bulldogs finished their season with an 18-12 overall record and captured the SCIAC title as well with a similar 14-13 sudden death overtime win over Chapman back on November 23.

And thus Margaret’s once narrow world begins to expand as she spends after school hours with the sisterhood, discussing in detail all the changes and anxieties that confront them. They worry about their bust size (or lack thereof), chanting “We must, we must, develop our busts.” Margaret asks her mother to take her shopping in order to buy her first brassiere. It’s a wonderful vignette framed with self-conscious sizing. The girls worry about menstruation, wondering who will be first. They attend their first teen party and play spin the bottle, and Margaret receives her first kiss. They discuss boys intensely, and are unexpectedly overwhelmed by emotions. Meanwhile, Margaret, who has been raised absent any religious affiliation, (Herb is Jewish and Barbara is Christian), begins an ongoing monologue with God, asking questions, sharing random thoughts, while undeterred when no answers are forthcoming. What makes Are You There God? remarkable and courageous is its explicit frankness.

At the sports station, Cubs participated in group frisbee golf and balloon volleyball. For Scout skills, a tent-pitching competition saw Dens racing to be the fastest to set up their tent and a class on basic first aid. At the cooking station, campers enjoyed the chef’s relay race and solar-cooked s’mores. The STEM station included bottle rockets using only air and water, as well as aluminum foil boats. One camper’s boat held a record 200 pennies before sinking. Campers played plenty of games in between the activities, like “Duck Duck Goose” and “Captain’s Coming,” which has campers pretending to look out of a crow’s nest, searching for a man overboard, and dining in a ship’s mess hall. The Day Camp presents leadership opportunities for older Scouts. This year’s camp had scout volunteers of various ranks from Piedmont’s five troops. As per tradition, the camp culminated in its much-anticipated egg drop contest, where Scouts put their creative minds to the test by finding the best way to drop a raw egg from a height of seven stories without the egg breaking. Members of the Piedmont Fire Department assisted by dropping the eggs, one by one, in homemade protective enclosures from the engine’s 75-foot extension ladder. The contest is unique in that Scouts are given very few limitations on how to achieve their goal. The container’s dimension must measure less than 8” x 8” x 8”, the egg must be raw, and campers may not affix anything to the egg itself. Other than that, anything goes. Photos courtesy of Piedmont Scout Council Scouts and family members gather in Dracena Park for the camp’s crowning event – The Egg Drop. An egg floats down from the drop on a parachute. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to provide feedback on the June 14 community wildfire evacuation exercise. Whether residents participated in the practical exercise for the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood, completed the at-home family exercise, or did not participate in either, the City wants to know: • If you received the “THIS IS A DRILL” AC Alert notification on Saturday morning • How well the activity helped you think through your own evacuation planning • What, if any, actions the exercise prompted you to take • What was confusing or didn’t work well • What types of preparedness programs, resources, or activities you would like to see in the future The feedback survey is available online at piedmont.ca.gov/WildfireSurvey. At-Home activity still available The at-home evacuation activity that was developed for the June 14 exercise will remain available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/wildfiredrill. The Fire Department encourages those who were not able to participate this weekend to plan a time to complete the exercise soon. The at-home activity is designed for families, housemates, or neighbors to complete together. A short video guides residents through a realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont. It also includes discussion prompts and a printable worksheet to help households plan and reflect. Participants should plan about 30 to 45 minutes to complete the exercise. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/wildfire for more information and resources on preparing for wildfires, including packing a go bag, preparing yards for fire season, and hardening homes against wildfires.

Some people never got that notice.” Fire Captain Mike Carlisle, who led the team of Piedmont firefighters that responded to the Palisades Fire in Southern California earlier this year, gave advice on preparing for emergency alerts. “You’re either going to get a warning or a mandatory evacuate order. If you get a warning, heed that warning. Start preparing yourself—prepare your home, prepare the things that you need to take with you, your car, all the rest of that stuff,” said Carlisle. articles.title: Congratulations to the Class of 2025

articles.text: Millennium High School (MHS) graduated 18 seniors in the class of 2025 on Wednesday, June 4. Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels presided over her second class of graduates as the ceremony format modeled Millennium’s close knit family form. Every student walked to the podium and delivered thoughtful insights after staff introduced each at length, leaving no dry eyes in the Alan Harvey Theater. The ceremony allots for personal touches all through out, students spoke from their hearts through suppressed tears about overcoming challenges on and off campus, delving into personal lives in a way larger ceremonies cannot. English teacher Elise Marks provided background on three of her graduates, reading an impressive passage from soon to be UC Santa Cruz freshman Maile Imburg’s essay on Paradise Lost. “[Miley] takes on leadership roles not for power, but to genuinely solve problems,” Marks said. Millennium succeeds in providing a private school personal environment to students, in contrast to the pressure cooker that can be Piedmont High. Some Millennium students are heading to prestigious universities in the fall. Shakila Zuberi heads to UC Irvine, Ellie Willats will study at Lewis & Clark, Grace Rego is on her way to Chapman U., and Axé Johnson will be a freshman at Loyola University of Chicago. articles.title: Millennium grads honored in style

articles.text: The Piedmont High School (PHS) Class of 2025 bonded together one last time on Witter Field, Thursday, June 5, for the finishing act of their educational journey, Graduation Day. With broad support from parents, teachers, siblings and friends, the 205 students from the Class of 2025 received high school diplomas and entered summer as graduates. Those watching above kept temperatures not too hot, and not chilly, a perfect day by all accounts, inviting free wardrobe choices for all in attendance. Graduates, in purple caps and gowns, sat in chairs on Witter Field for the graduation ceremony. PHS Principal David Yoshihara showed a knack for the microphone and made a positive impression after his first year in the role. “Yo-sh” as his students call him, introduced student speakers Ellen Gudiksen, Salutatorian; August von Metzsch, Valedictorian; Ella Hughes, Senior Speaker; and Dean Olliphant, Senior Class President. “Life is about that resonance. Like a gong, it requires force to truly ring. To craft a legacy that rings, is to let yourself go,” said Hughes. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Graduates share a laugh on Witter Field.

Spiritual practices in the electronic age By Pastor Jim Hopkins If you are a Facebook friend or an X (formerly Twitter) follower of mine you know that for almost a decade I have shared my daily spiritual practice publicly. That practice is quite simple. After offering a prayer I read a portion of scripture and write a short response. Here are some my most responded to postings from the month gone by. Exodus 2:19 “An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they answered, “and he even drew water for us and watered our animals.” There is much irony in this verse. Moses is identified as an Egyptian. Jethro’s daughters need to he rescued from shepherds, a term that often described political and religious leaders. Moses, who was pulled from the water, now provides water. Luke 18:13 But the tax collector stood at a distance and would not even raise his face to heaven, but beat on his breast and said, ‘God, have pity on me, a sinner!’ In Jesus’ vision of the world put right, he called it the Reign of God, widows win justice from corrupt judges and tax collectors are praised for their spiritual insight. Matthew 18:20 [Jesus] For where two or three come together in my name, I am there with them. As churches gather in Jesus’ name this 4th of July weekend, may we pray for the country rather than to it. Psalm 32:3 When I did not confess my sins, I was worn out from crying all day long. As we begin the Fourth of July holiday, there is a lesson here for us as a nation. Romans 14:19 So then, we must always aim at those things that bring peace and that help strengthen one another. Kind of sounds like me taking care of the grandsons - “Do you think your brother appreciated you poking him like that?” Romans 12:21 Do not let evil defeat you; instead, conquer evil See Religion Corner on page 31 LEVYCHI KULUVA, 8th grade It was awesome. I’m looking forward to trying and learning new things. DYLAN JEREZ, 8th grade Today was fun. I really like my teachers this year and have lots of friends in my classes. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting the community to hear firsthand experiences of wildfire evacuations from community members, firefighters, and emergency managers at a community preparedness event this Saturday, June 14, at 10:00 a.m. at the Piedmont Fire Department. The event will follow the Fire Department’s citywide wildfire evacuation exercise and will also act as a debrief. At the event, community members will be invited to share their observations and questions from the morning’s evacuation exercise. Attendees will also have a chance to learn from speakers with real world experiences in recent wildfires, including an Eaton fire evacuee and Piedmont firefighters who provided mutual aid in Southern California. Piedmont Chief Dave Brannigan will discuss some of the City’s current initiatives related to wildfire mitigation and preparedness and how community members can get involved. Exercise instructions to be delivered via AC Alert Community members should look for an AC Alert notification around 9:00 a.m. on Saturday, June 14 with instructions for completing the exercise. Residents in the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood will be asked to physically evacuate their homes. Elsewhere in the city, residents will receive instructions for an evacuation exercise they can complete at home. The at-home exercise is designed to be simple, easy to complete, and high impact. AC Alert is the mass notification system used by City and County agencies throughout Alameda County to rapidly disseminate emergency alerts to people who live, work in, or visit the County. AC Alert is capable of sending alerts by voice, text and email, posting to social media pages and sending FEMA Wireless Alerts. Those not yet signed up for AC Alert notifications can register at bit.ly/ACAlert. For more information, or to let the City know you plan to participate, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ EvacDrill.
articles.title: Speakers to share Firsthand Wildfire Experiences at Community Preparedness Event on Saturday, June 14

articles.text: Meet Jhene a shepherd mix at Oakland Animal Services. Jhene is a stunning, snuggle-seeking shepherd mix who walks nicely on leash and is very people focused. She is 2-years-old and weighs 60 pounds. Staff and volunteers at Oakland Animal Services report Jhene is affectionate and has mastered the art of the gentle hug, placing her paws on people ever so sweetly just to be close. She’s eager to say hello to everyone she sees, even from across the shelter yard. She’s still learning her doggy social skills and would be great as your one and only pet or could potentially live with another dog with a slow and careful introduction. Come meet Jhene at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 7 pm, or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Jhene must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, June 11, 2025 Local Items Adoptable Dog of the Week Speakers to share Firsthand Wildfire Experiences at Community Preparedness Event on Saturday, June 14 By Tony Simons The City of Piedmont is inviting the community to hear firsthand experiences of wildfire evacuations from community members, firefighters, and emergency managers at a community preparedness event this Saturday, June 14, at 10:00 a.m. at the Piedmont Fire Department. The event will follow the Fire Department’s citywide wildfire evacuation exercise and will also act as a debrief. At the event, community members will be invited to share their observations and questions from the morning’s evacuation exercise. Attendees will also have a chance to learn from speakers with real world experiences in recent wildfires, including an Eaton fire evacuee and Piedmont firefighters who provided mutual aid in Southern California. Piedmont Chief Dave Brannigan will discuss some of the City’s current initiatives related to wildfire mitigation and preparedness and how community members can get involved. Exercise instructions to be delivered via AC Alert Community members should look for an AC Alert notification around 9:00 a.m. on Saturday, June 14 with instructions for completing the exercise. Residents in the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood will be asked to physically evacuate their homes. Elsewhere in the city, residents will receive instructions for an evacuation exercise they can complete at home. The at-home exercise is designed to be simple, easy to complete, and high impact. AC Alert is the mass notification system used by City and County agencies throughout Alameda County to rapidly disseminate emergency alerts to people who live, work in, or visit the County. AC Alert is capable of sending alerts by voice, text and email, posting to social media pages and sending FEMA Wireless Alerts. Those not yet signed up for AC Alert notifications can register at bit.ly/ACAlert. For more information, or to let the City know you plan to participate, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ EvacDrill. articles.text: Hello everyone! What a beautiful day to celebrate such an important milestone. How’s everyone doing? Before I go any further, I want to take a moment to recognize and thank the PUSD Board of Education, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, Principal David Yoshihara, and the Parent Club selection committee for inviting me to speak today. I’m deeply grateful for the opportunity. And now, let’s give a huge round of applause to the parents and guardians, the teachers, coaches, counselors, band leaders, drama directors – everyone who supported and guided these graduates to this moment. Their dedication and love helped make today possible. I have three children of my own. Two of them have already walked across this field—one in 2021, the other just recently in 2024. So, to be perfectly honest, I thought the next (and likely final) time I’d be back at a Piedmont graduation would be in 2027, when my youngest is set to graduate… hopefully. Just kidding – she’s a great student. Most days. So yes, I’ve been here before – sitting up in the stands, squinting into the sun, thinking things like: “Wow, it’s hot,” “I hope the speaker is brief and brilliant,” and of course, feeling that overwhelming mix of pride, excitement, and a little nervousness about what lay ahead for my kids as they closed one chapter and prepared to open another. When Principal Yoshihara asked me to speak, I said yes— but with one request. I asked for the chance to sit down with some seniors and ask an important and not so simple of a question: What are your thoughts, feelings, goals, and concerns as you prepare to leave high school and begin the next phase of your life? I wanted to do this because no words I could offer would have meaning without first listening to you [students]. You are the heart of today. And the insights some of you shared with me were, in some cases, exactly what I expected. But in many others, they were surprising, thought-provoking, and deeply honest. While the views shared by the groups of students I spoke with may reflect the sentiments of many in the class, I also recognize that there are likely other perspectives that weren’t represented. Each graduate’s journey is unique, and I want to acknowledge and honor that diversity of experience. Among the predictable views shared were the excitement for newfound freedom, the anticipation of college life, the desire to explore new passions, and the bittersweet feeling of leaving behind the familiar comhow we live, work, and connect. These changes are not abstract— they are happening in real time, Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers was the 2025 Commencement Speaker at Piedmont High School graduation. forts of high school. The concerns echoed some of those feelings – the anxiety of the unknown, the pressure to succeed, the fear of making the wrong choices, and the sadness of parting ways with close friends. But what truly resonated with me were the unpredictable responses, the insights that spoke to the unique character of this graduating class. Some expressed a profound desire to make a tangible difference in the world, whether by helping others, contributing to their communities, or engaging in causes and careers they feel passionate about. Others spoke with a quiet determination to pursue unconventional paths, to forge their own definitions of success, and to prioritize personal well-being. One student shared a powerful metaphor: “High school was like walking a challenging but familiar path which has, to an extent, been paved for them. Now we’re at a point where the path must now be paved by us.” Others spoke eloquently about the importance of authenticity, exploration, and vulnerability and the courage to embrace failure as a necessary step towards growth. Several articulated a deep appreciation for the teachers and mentors who had guided them, not just academically, but as young adults finding their way. And others spoke about importance of community, specifically the importance of being part of one, with all of its good points and areas for improvement, nevertheless community was important. Graduates of Piedmont High School, your responses revealed a depth of self-awareness, a sense of purpose, and a refreshing blend of idealism and pragmatism. You are not just moving on; you are moving forward with intention. I want to take a moment to acknowledge the elephant in the room, something we talked about. Your next steps, whether they be to college, a gap year, the work force, the military, some mixture, or none of those, are happening at a time marked by extraordinary uncertainty and rapid transformation. The political climate is turbulent, social dynamics are shifting, the environment is under immense pressure, and technological advances are reshaping

articles.text: and they are shaping the world you are inhabiting. To add to that, many of you may soon find yourselves in places very different from the Bay Area. You may encounter perspectives, cultures, and values that challenge what you’ve known. That can feel disorienting. It’s natural to have doubts, to feel apprehensive about what lies ahead. But here’s what I want to say to you: Uncertainty is not just a challenge, it’s also an invitation. An invitation to be curious, to grow, to lead with empathy, and to adapt. And as you do, hold tightly to the values that define you. Let them be your compass, not your anchor, guiding you without limiting your ability to engage with others, particularly others with different views. Values rooted in integrity, compassion, equity, and respect—these are not to be sacrificed for the sake of fitting in or going along. They are the foundation on which you will build meaningful relationships and a purposeful life. You’ve been educated in one of the most dynamic and forward-thinking regions in the country. You are equipped with the tools to think critically, to ask bold questions, and to build bridges where others see divides. So as you enter this next chapter, don’t back away from the unknown. Face it with courage to explore, humility to learn, and a steady commitment to growing, without losing sight of the values that define you. The future is uncertain by nature, but that’s your call to step forward, stay grounded in your values, and meet it with the resilience it requires. Carry forward the lessons you’ve learned here, both in and outside the classroom. And don’t hesitate to lean on your support systems, your family, your friends, your teachers, as you navigate what comes next. Give yourself room to stumble. Be willing to take detours. Redefine success as you go because life is rarely a straight path, and it’s often in the unexpected twists and turns that you discover who you really are. And finally, lead with kindness. Let empathy and service guide your actions. The world needs your talents, your perspective, and your heart. Use what you’ve learned not just to succeed—but to uplift others and build stronger communities. Graduates, I stand before you today not just as the Chief of Police, but as a proud parent of Piedmont students, a neighbor, and someone who sees in each of you the strength, insight, and compassion that our future depends on. Class of 2025, you did it! Celebrate this milestone with pride, carry your values with confidence, and step boldly into the future you will help shape. The world is waiting, and I, for one, can’t wait to see what you’ll do with it. articles.text: Valedictorian Good afternoon everyone, and thank you, Ellen. As she said, I’m Gus, and I’m honored to be standing here in front of the class of 2025! On behalf of my whole class, I’d like to reiterate our gratitude to everyone who is here today—our entire Piedmont family—family, remember that—for the time and energy you have invested to get us to this point! Most of all, thank you to our parents. As much as your snarky 17 or 18-year-old might have told you they don’t care if you show up to their events— and I’m sure they have: I got a lot of texts before prom from kids who really wanted me to give them an out by telling them that their parents were not invited to my house to take photos of them; we truly do appreciate you all. Special shoutout to my mom, who has not only sacrificed so much for me but also for the entire Piedmont community. I know it’s an odd image now, but I remember when she would physically put me on her shoulders so I could see over a crowd. She was not the first person to put someone on her shoulders. Sir Issac Newton once said “If I have seen further than others, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants,” and our parents are the prime example of this. Literally and metaphorically, they’ve lifted us up throughout our childhoods. It’s not just them, either. I remember in fourth grade at Wildwood when we first got access to the computer lab and were doing the most basic of things, but to us, Scratch was like magic, imparted upon us by Ms. Cheung. Of course, a few of us, instead of paying attention, immediately installed Minecraft on our computers. Still, we must have learned something, because now we have a robotics team—go 8033—that goes to world championships every year. Another thing from the computer lab: do you all remember TypingAgent? I hated it. I used to poke at the keyboard like Nevertheless, the quote has weight, and the translation is where Durant built from Aristotle: condensing, adding his own spin, and most importantly for us, translating into English. When Durant stood on Aristotle’s shoulders, he added value by allowing us to derive meaning from unintelligible (to most of us) Ancient Greek. He understood that his translation wasn’t direct and that the ideas were not originally his, but he built nonetheless. That’s the most important part of progress. It’s imperfect, but it builds on what was before, inching forward. I look to how so many of us like Cash, Nia, and myself embodied this by trying out new sports for our senior years. We started from nothing, no expectations, and after our friends prodded us to become their teammates, we opened up to their feedback, and they supported us to win championships, receive all-league honors, and break school records. Similarly, the work that Leila, Ava, Olivia, and everyone else involved with peer tutoring does not only helps their students, but allows the tutor to gain a deeper understanding. As a class, we provide our shoulders for our peers to stand on, but the metaphor isn’t entirely accurate. They don’t weigh us down: instead, we collectively grow. As we go out into the world, I urge us all to keep building upon ourselves, upon others, and to eventually become the shoulders for others to stand upon, without forgetting the family— families—we came from. Now, as I finish up here, I need everyone with me as we break it down for the last time. If you’ve been paying attention you’ll remember how I emphasized the word family earlier, and if you played a sport here, you might know where I’m going. If you haven’t, it doesn’t matter, just follow along as we close out our time on each other’s shoulders as a Piedmont family. Piedmont on three, family on six: one, two, three PIEDMONT, four, five, six FAMILY. Gus von Metzsch, Valedictorian this. It was horrible. I got better though, and though we didn’t realize it then, that practice would make a huge difference when we needed to crank out our senate bills for civics at the last minute. Anyway, there are a lot of shoulders we’ve stood on, way more than you might think. Even in middle school. You could say I was a little awkward in middle school. I mean, everyone was, but I went to Rubik’s cube competitions in my free time. I was really into it. Looking back on it, that doesn’t have to be a bad thing, of course, but I think it says something about my social skills. I think that awkward phase was essential for all of us to mature as we have. In a way, we stand on the shoulders of our past selves. We’ve done that a lot this year, even ways as mundane as reading back our senior quotes we had forgotten about from when we picked them a few months ago. I was in bio a few weeks ago when we were getting our yearbooks, and Samantha Ronen off-hand said something along the lines of “Gus, I bet you quoted Aristotle or someone like that.” I begrudgingly had to admit that yes, I did quote Aristotle. Specifically, the quote is “We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” Seems normal enough, right? One issue: Aristotle didn’t speak English. The English translation of that quote is correctly attributed to the American historian Will Durant.

articles.text: Salutatorian, Class of 2025 Welcome everyone to the graduation of Piedmont High School’s class of 2025 at Witter Field, where we’re all glad to not be running the mile today. Instead, we’re here to celebrate, and I would like to extend the biggest thank you to everybody gathered. Teachers, faculty, family, friends, mentors, your support to all of us during the 18 some years of our lives has been invaluable in getting us to this finish line. I have a confession to make. I have been staring at the glowing green reminders widget on my to-do list, particularly the looming word graduation and feeling sick to my stomach. In fact, it was more on my to-do list than anything else. I’m sure all of us discovered the never-ending nature of a to-do list, constantly growing, lurking, demanding our attention. Though, it’s clear we’ve gotten very good at getting things done. It’s a relatively universal experience to have finally taken the Chem test hanging over your head for weeks just to be assigned an essay on All Quiet on the Western Front in the next period. And it becomes obvious quickly that just checking off items and watching them disappear from a list is an unfulfilling existence, although for one moment it’s pretty glorious. With an already overwhelming and unconquerable list of tasks and obligations, it becomes easy to shy away from doing more. In my quest to be a more ‘productive’ person, every year I hop on the New Year’s resolution trend. And while my bed might be made for the month of January, after a few weeks it’s all but forgotten. This year, though, I did something different. My New Year’s resolution was a mantra: “I will not avoid doing something out of fear of embarrassment.” As small as raising my hand in English, or say, giving a speech at graduation to hundreds of people… This 2025 resolution unlocked something in me beyond the to-do list, another realm of opportunities: the “YOLO list” and the “what is important to me” list. For the “YOLO” list, anyone over 50 can turn to a younger audience member to explain onto the “what is important to me” list. It is for tuning into our interests and aptitudes. These lists hold the items that make our lives meaningful and unique, which translates into how we give back to the world around us. Ellen Gudiksen, Salutatorian When it comes to giving back, I know Piedmont would look very different if Juliana DeYoung had not decided all of her Title IX work was important on top of varsity athletics. Or imagine if Oliver Greenebaum didn’t choose to use his enthusiasm to brighten every space, from school dance circles to every single classroom. Alma Ruberto is so deserving of the Gail Dryden award for community service, and the ways she has changed and inspired our community are innumerable. These contributions may have started in some way as a task to complete, but these people continued because they found a purpose not from simply completing the tasks set in front of them, but from following a spark within them. In truth, every single person in this class has developed a unique excellence guided by their own values. Our happiness relies more on not getting caught up in the stuff we need to do, so we can find joy in the things we get to do. And sometimes to-dos are actually things we need to do (unfortunate right?), and sometimes we have to get it done and it’s going to suck. But we can’t forget to live outside of those parameters, because life itself is NOT a to-do list. We make meaning of our lives by daring to challenge ourselves, following our passions, and using that to find our individual roles within our communities. And sometimes, life should just be enjoyable. Today is a collective finish line for the class of 2025, and it is absolutely cause to celebrate; be proud, and savor the feeling. Ohmygosh. I cannot believe we made it. I encourage every one of you to ask yourselves as we step forward into the future, what are you choosing to do for yourself? Okay graduation speech. CHECK. Markos Lagios walks towards Principal Yoshihara to receive his diploma on Witter Field.

articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board will meet tonight, Wednesday, June 11, at 7 p.m. in City Hall for a regularly scheduled meeting. Following the graduations, the board will discuss Title IX and athletics, a status update on next year’s dual enrollment program, a public hearing on the current Local Control and Accountability Plan (LCAP), and next year’s budget. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich will explain the dual enrollment program, which will involve 22 Piedmont high school students taking Calculus III at Berkeley City College during period six. Dual enrollment for second semester will consider Business Entrepreneurship and possibly Discrete Mathematics. The Title IX and athletics year-end report will be presented by Athletic Director Tyler Small. Last year 373 girls and 413 boys participated in sports. Piedmont’s teachers’ union, APT, has informed the district they would like to reopen negotiations to develop agreements related to hours and professional responsibilities and class sizes. PUSD and APT previously agreed that contract salary and benefits will not be available for negotiations in 2025 and 2026. Year-end iterations of district Personnel Action Reports are on the consent calendar and include information on which teachers and staff members will be departing and joining the district. articles.text: With the rise of the internet and social media, building and investing time in community and in-person connection is more important now than ever before. Fostering moments of intergenerational learning and frequenting places apart from home and work are effective ways to support overall wellbeing. Intergenerational learning is the way in which all ages can come together and learn with and from one another. The concept goes beyond just a transfer of knowledge; it fosters social and emotional growth for all. Different generations spending time together in and outside of the classroom helps to cultivate skills, build self-esteem and encourage mutual respect and empathy. Engaging in learning opportunities with people outside your generation is something to which not all of us have access; this is where the significance of a “third place” applies. The concept of a third place was first referenced by sociologist Ray Oldenburg in his 1989 novel, The Great Good Place. It is a space, separate from home (first place) and work (second place) that we can go to unwind, connect, and socialize. Such spaces can be hubs for intergenerational learning, providing the connection we crave and setting us on a path of lifelong learning. A third place can be the local coffee shop where you are a regular customer, a bookstore around the corner that you like to sneak away to after work, or even a park Check out Chabot workshops where you can relax and decompress with others after a long day. It is any space that facilitates social interaction where your attendance is not required. We have many places like this available to us right in our own backyards. East Bay Regional Park District is made up of 73 parks throughout Alameda and Contra Costa counties to the east of San Francisco. They are committed to facilitating learning outside the classroom and they provide fun, informative, and healthy things to do year-round. Chabot Space & Science Center aims to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and Planet Earth. The museum itself is a base for intergenerational learning with its volunteers and staff eager and willing to pass on their knowledge to Photo courtesy of JPJ Pictures aspiring scientists, space enthusiasts, members, and visitors. Chabot hosts a variety of programs and events that help you to engage with the world around you and deepen your societal roots: Family nature workshops, paint and sips, hike and sips, First Fridays, and so much more. These spaces and relationships enrich our joint well-being, reinforce the importance of education, and remind us that learning does not stop with age—it strengthens with connection. Let us build and support local environments where curiosity is lifelong, generations learn together, and everyone has a place they belong. articles.text: ANDREA MARTIN Basketball, Track and Field Andrea Martin becomes our first-ever freshman to become an Athlete of the Year awards after becoming a star on the basketball court and league champion in the shot put for track and field. She was our Athlete of the Month in December, February, and March. The girls’ basketball team proved to be one of the best in the state, finishing with a 25-6 record and Co-League champions with Bishop O’Dowd. They received a berth in the NCS Open Division, finishing fifth, and reached the Regional Semifinals of the D1 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed. Martin led scoring with 22 points and 10 rebounds in Piedmont’s 62-60 win over No. 16 San Joaquin Memorial, along with 11 points and 11 rebounds in their 60-29 win over No. 8 Oakland Tech in the state tournament. She helped dominate No. 6 Salesian 70-58 in the Open Division with 23 points, 11 rebounds, and two blocks. In track, Martin proved excelled in the shot put. Her distance of 34 feet, 1.5 inches to win the WACC Championship is a school record. PEYTON WATSON Lacrosse, Golf Peyton Watson is a junior and led the lacrosse team to being runners-up in the Division 2 NCS Championship. She also played on the golf team in the fall. We named her our Athlete of the Month for May and March, and honorable mention in April. She was a major part of Piedmont’s postseason run with 24 goals over four playoff games.

articles.text: MARKOS LAGIO Football Markos Lagios was the football team’s quarterback and won the WACC Mission Division’s Offensive Player of the Year. Lagios led the team to a 10-2 season and undefeated Mission Division title at 5-0. Markos finished the season with 2,136 passing yards, completing 62 percent of his passes for 25 touchdowns, to go along with 608 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns. He also helped lead the baseball team to a successful season this spring. He was our 2024 Athlete of the Year, our honorable mention for 2023 Sophomore of the Year, our 2022 Freshman of the Year, and the school’s 2025 Outstanding Senior Athlete. MEI ASSALIAN Golf Mei Assalian graduates from Piedmont High as perhaps the program’s best golfer in the last decade. At the Antioch Invitational on October 14, she finished third of 37 athletes with 81 strokes, helping Piedmont finish second of seven schools. Then at the WACC Tournament at Monarch Bay on October 21, Assalian finished ninth overall with a round of 87, helping PHS finish second overall. She went onto the D2 NCS Tournament at Rooster Run in Santa Rosa on October 28, finishing 13th of 144 athletes with an 82—Piedmont finished ninth of 14. She was our Athlete of the Month in October. Assalian is continuing her golf career at Wesleyan.

articles.text: First seminar “The World of a Play” launches July 28 Shotgun Players, a community-focused theater company based in Berkeley, recently announced the launch of a new, six-part seminar series entitled Miriam’s Place with engagements beginning July 28. The new program series is dedicated to an in-depth exploration and community discussion about local live theater, held at Shotgun Studios, the company’s rehearsal space in Berkeley. Seminars are led by Shotgun Players’ artistic directors, performers, artists and other key theater staff members and creatives. T he si x sem i na r s a re designed to give audience members an inside-look at how a production comes together while getting access to a design run, rehearsals, and a preview show. Coffee, tea and light refreshments will be served at every session, and visitors will gain exclusive access to a live production. Miriam’s Place gatherings are hosted in memory of Miriam Schiffman, “a life-long learner with an insatiable curiosity and passion for bringing people together” said Artistic Director Patrick Dooley. Dooley leads the seminar series, offering an immersive look into his process as Shotgun Players’ founder and director, leading up to the premiere of Christopher Chen’s newest play The Motion. “[Miriam’s Place is] a great opportunity for theatre-lovers to really get a deeper understanding and appreciation for the production process,” Dooley added. The series runs from July 28 to September 29. Sessions take place on Mondays from 10:30 a.m. to 12 p.m. Enroll for seminars at https://shotgunplayers.org/ show/miriam/ or by calling the box office at 510-841-6500 x 303.
articles.title: Shotgun Players launches seminar series Miriam’s Place this summer

articles.text: Photo by Laurie Gordon Entrance to Building One, Treasure Island, location of Treasure Island Museum, featuring “Pacific Unity” sculptures by Adaline Kent, Jacques Schnier and Helen Philips Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known Pacific-themed heritage, welcomes Bruce Marwick, president of the Sacramento Art Deco Society, this Saturday to lead a discussion on the island’s historic sculptures. Visitors will learn more about the Gladding McBean artists who created many of the public art pieces for the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition. The exposition was held on Treasure Island, between San Francisco and Oakland, to celebrate the city’s two newly built bridges. Photo courtesy of Rebecca Schnier Jacques Schnier working on a large bar relief artwork for the Fair — unfortunately, the artwork no longer exists. Jacques Schnier’s artwork created for the World Fair Gladding McBean was the largest maker of architectural terra cotta in the western United States and remains one of California’s oldest operating companies and a pioneer in ceramics technology. The company’s artists created sculptures and bas-reliefs for buildings around the country during the 1920s and early 1930s. In the late 1930s, they were commissioned to create monumental sculptural works for the exposition on Treasure Island. While almost all traces of the World’s Fair have disappeared, the City of San Francisco has made efforts to preserve the island’s history—including the surviving sculptures—since the museum’s founding in 1975. The event will also explore the life, work and legacy of artist Carlo Taliabue, who immigrated from Milan in 1924 to work for Gladding McBean in Lincoln, California. Taliabue created monumental sculptures for the exposition while in residence. The event is free, but registration is encouraged. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/single-post/treasure-island-sculptors-from-gladding-mcbean to register. The program begins at 10:30 a.m. this Saturday, June 14.
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum hosts sculpture speaker event this Saturday

articles.text: Photo by Stefan Cohen The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus returns to the city’s Curran Theatre for its annual Pride engagement. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus (SFGMC) and Grammy Award-nominated nonbinary songwriter Justin Tranter will perform at the city’s annual Pride concert on Saturday, June 21, at BroadwaySF’s Curran Theatre. Founded in 1978, the choral group remains one of the most iconic and influential LGBTQ arts organizations in the world. SFGMC was the first openly gay chorus globally and has played a pivotal role in the gay rights movement through both music and activism. articles.text: San Francisco Opera premieres Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Idomeneo this Saturday, June 14, as part of its 2025 Summer Season at the War Memorial Opera House. Set in Crete following the Trojan War, the opera begins with King Idomeneo making a desperate vow to the god Neptune: to sacrifice the first living being he sees if he survives a perilous storm at sea. When Idomeneo returns to shore, the first person he sees is his son, Idamante— sending him into a moral crisis. The opera follows the king’s struggle with this promise, featuring performances by American tenor Matthew Polenzani and Argentine mezzo-soprano Daniela Mack as Idomeneo and Idamante. Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducts Mozart’s early masterpiece, marking her second Mozart opera at the company following The Magic Flute. This season’s production includes new staging by Australian director Lindy Hume, making her San Francisco Opera debut. Her staging emphasizes the tension between people and their environment, with projections of craggy coastlines and raging seas that mirror Mozart’s dramatic score. The cast also includes bass-baritone Jongwon Han as the Voice of the Oracle, tenor Samuel White as the High Priest of Neptune, and Olivier Zerouali, Georgiana Adams and Mary Hoskins in supporting roles. Five performances of Idomeneo will be sung in Italian with English supertitles and are scheduled for June 14 (7:30 p.m.), 17 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (2 p.m.) and 25 (7:30 p.m.). The June 20 performance will be livestreamed at 7:30 p.m. Tickets are available at the San Francisco Opera Box Office (301 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco), by calling (415) 864-3330 or online at sfopera.com. Box office hours are Monday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Matthew Polenzani in the title role of Mozart’s Idomeneo for the Metropolitan Opera

articles.text: The chamber music festival Music in the Vineyards (MITV) kicks off its 31st season in Napa Valley on August 1. The series of live performances traditionally showcases distinguished chamber musicians as well emerging young talent during its four-week season, with concerts held at popular wineries and vineyards throughout the valley. This year’s featured artists include the Borromeo String Quartet, Pacifica Quartet and Ariel Quartet, as well as Pavone String Quartet, a group of undergraduate students at the world-renowned Shepherd School of Music at Rice University. The Pavone Quartet are winners of Music in the Vineyards’ 2025 Fellowship Quartet competition and perform on August 11. Since the festival’s inception in 1995, wineries in Napa Valley continue to lend their space for MITV musicians to perform live, offering a uniquely Northern Californian festival experience. With complimentary wine tastings at each intermission and breathtaking views of the Napa Valley, this unique combination of wine country ambiance and great musicianship allows audiences to experience chamber music in small intimate settings. Music venues this year include Clos Pegase Winery, Frog’s Leap Winery, Hess Persson Estates, Domaine Carneros, Louis M. Martini Winery, Maxville Winery, Stag’s Leap Wine Cellars, Hudson Ranch, Ehlers Estate, Markham Vineyards, Hudson House – Beringer Vineyards, Spottswoode Estate, Silverado Vineyards, and Inglenook. For more information on Music in the Vineyards and to purchase tickets, visit www. musicinthevineyards.org. Music in the Vineyards returns to Napa Valley this August.

The contradiction here is that, while he was one of the greatest leaders of all time, he was illiterate. Another great leader at the forefront of education was Napoleon. Music is important in every aspect of human endeavor. Human beings have turned to music since the beginning of time. Perhaps we should increase music education, rather than reduce it. That is my proposal. If you have some time, I suggest reading the research done by the neuroscientist Daniel J. Levitin. He suggests that music Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts Charlemagne can diminish anxiety and depression, reduce blood pressure, improve body flexibility and speech, while improving intelligence. His research was done on Alzheimer’s patients and others. It has been proved that music accomplishes these things with young people. I did my own study many years ago and found that his research is absolutely true. Perhaps education should require all students to participate in music. articles.text: The Big Sleep is one of many films shot in the 1940s and into the 1959s which is referred to as Film Noir or American Pulp, a genre created in post-WWII Hollywood and recognized for its dark, even ominous contrasting black and white tones and images. The stylized narrative usually features cynical, antihero cops or P.I.s, flashy villains, guns and murder. Women are considered femme fatales, often called “angel” or “sister,” some hard-boiled and able to push back when engaging in a distinctive double entendre repartee. The Big Sleep, directed by Howard Hawks, is based on the book written by Raymond Chandler, and adapted for the screen by William Faulkner. The film opens with private investigator Philip Marlowe (Humphrey Bogart), looking a bit rumpled, narrow tie and the iconic fedora. He is called to the elegant manor of an aging, wealthy individual General Sherwood. Of course, a butler greets Marlowe and asks him to wait in an expansive foyer while he goes to announce his arrival to the General. A young woman, named Carmen (Martha Vickers), comes slowly down a wide staircase and pauses to give Marlowe a provocative hello. And so the story begins. Marlowe is soon taken into an adjoining glass hothouse where the General is waiting, confined to a wheelchair, formally dressed and legs covered with a blanket. While Philip begins to perspire, he listens to the backstory explaining why the General needs his services. He has two daughters, wild-child teenage Carmen, and the older sister, Vivian (Lauren Bacall). It’s Carmen who has signed a number of gambling debt IOUs, and the holder of the notes wants to be paid. Part of this dialogue is exposition, and the words blackmail and photographs are mentioned. Marlowe agrees to look into the matter. His rate is twenty-five dollars per day. Typical of film noir is its complex, even convoluted plot. The Big Sleep is no exception. Just when the mystery seems about to be resolved, another character appears, and a new thread is pulled creating a new mystery within a mystery. Lots of cigarettes are smoked, guns are pulled, some are shot. Marlowe gets worked over in an alley, then tied up, and is rescued by Vivian. Outside it’s dark, heavy rain falling, wispy fog swirling, and headlights appear, coming down a narrow road. There’s gunplay. A gangster-type is shot and falls slowly to the wet pavement. This is all classic noir, and you don’t have to know what you don’t know to enjoy the very clipped, suggestive, fast-paced dialogue revealing the obvious chemistry between Marlowe and Vivian. Don’t miss Marlowe and Vivian driving off down a country road, thus ending the noir tale. The Big Sleep. Directed by Howard Hawks. Starring Humphrey Bogart, Lauren Bacall, Martha Vickers. 1 hr., 54 min, Rated R. Made in 1946, Now streaming on Fandango/apple tv/ prime. articles.text: Daniel Craig and Léa Seydoux in Spectre The James Bond film, Spectre, is the 24th in ne of Hollywood’s longest-running franchises. The first was Dr. No, released in 1962, starring the debonair and iconic Sean Connery. It’s been more than 50 years since Bond took stage center and captured moviegoers’ imaginations and there have been, over the decades, multiple incarnations of 007, secret agent, licensed to kill. Daniel Craig was the most recent actor to don the Bond mantle (now retired) and though initially he seemed a risky choice (he followed the intensely classy, upper crust Pierce Brosnan), Craig proved to be perfect, in a blunt, well-toned, thuggish way. In fact, Craig’s Bond was a hammer and every encounter with the seriously bad guys proved to be a nail, no matter that he is wearing designer tuxes, white dinner jackets, or elegant bespoke suits (his wardrobe is part of his allure. Regarding the film Spectre, it’s a wonderful ride. But one that requires the audience to pay attention, for its plot is at times maddeningly convoluted with twists that require perhaps more exposition than is necessary in a Bond film. This fourth Craig film (Casino Royale, then Quantum of Solace followed by Skyfall) is as solid as the previous Bond films and includes a threading backstory that ultimately leads to Spectre, a worldwide crime organization headed by a Franz Oberhauser (Christoph Walz, doing what has become his signature psychopath). pages.text: Wednesday, June 11, 2025 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Big Sleep a classic with Bogie and Bacall By Chris Honoré The Big Sleep is one of many films shot in the 1940s and into the 1959s which is referred to as Film Noir or American Pulp, a genre created in post-WWII Hollywood and recognized for its dark, even ominous contrasting black and white tones and images. The stylized narrative usually features cynical, antihero cops or P.I.s, flashy villains, guns and murder. Women are considered femme fatales, often called “angel” or “sister,” some hard-boiled and able to push back when engaging in a distinctive double entendre repartee. The Big Sleep, directed by Howard Hawks, is based on the book written by Raymond Chandler, and adapted for the screen by William Faulkner. The film opens with private investigator Philip Marlowe (Humphrey Bogart), looking a bit rumpled, narrow tie and the iconic fedora. He is called to the elegant manor of an aging, wealthy individual General Sherwood. Of course, a butler greets Marlowe and asks him to wait in an expansive foyer while he goes to announce his arrival to the General. A young woman, named Carmen (Martha Vickers), comes slowly down a wide staircase and pauses to give Marlowe a provocative hello. And so the story begins. Marlowe is soon taken into an adjoining glass hothouse where the General is waiting, confined to a wheelchair, formally dressed and legs covered with a blanket. While Philip begins to perspire, he listens to the backstory explaining why the General needs his services. He has two daughters, wild-child teenage Carmen, and the older sister, Vivian (Lauren Bacall). It’s Carmen who has signed a number of gambling debt IOUs, and the holder of the notes wants to be paid. Part of this dialogue is exposition, and the words blackmail and photographs are mentioned. Marlowe agrees to look into the matter. His rate is twenty-five dollars per day. Typical of film noir is its complex, even convoluted plot. The Big Sleep is no exception. Just when the mystery seems about to be resolved, another character appears, and a new thread is pulled creating a new mystery within a mystery. Lots of cigarettes are smoked, guns are pulled, some are shot. Marlowe gets worked over in an alley, then tied up, and is rescued by Vivian. Outside it’s dark, heavy rain falling, wispy fog swirling, and headlights appear, coming down a narrow road. There’s gunplay. A gangster-type is shot and falls slowly to the wet pavement. This is all classic noir, and you don’t have to know what you don’t know to enjoy the very clipped, suggestive, fast-paced dialogue revealing the obvious chemistry between Marlowe and Vivian. Don’t miss Marlowe and Vivian driving off down a country road, thus ending the noir tale. The Big Sleep. Directed by Howard Hawks. Starring Humphrey Bogart, Lauren Bacall, Martha Vickers. 1 hr., 54 min, Rated R. Made in 1946, Now streaming on Fandango/apple tv/ prime. Spectre – more adventures with James Bond Daniel Craig and Léa Seydoux in Spectre By Chris Honoré The James Bond film, Spectre, is the 24th in ne of Hollywood’s longest-running franchises. The first was Dr. No, released in 1962, starring the debonair and iconic Sean Connery. It’s been more than 50 years since Bond took stage center and captured moviegoers’ imaginations and there have been, over the decades, multiple incarnations of 007, secret agent, licensed to kill. Daniel Craig was the most recent actor to don the Bond mantle (now retired) and though initially he seemed a risky choice (he followed the intensely classy, upper crust Pierce Brosnan), Craig proved to be perfect, in a blunt, well-toned, thuggish way. In fact, Craig’s Bond was a hammer and every encounter with the seriously bad guys proved to be a nail, no matter that he is wearing designer tuxes, white dinner jackets, or elegant bespoke suits (his wardrobe is part of his allure. Regarding the film Spectre, it’s a wonderful ride. But one that requires the audience to pay attention, for its plot is at times maddeningly convoluted with twists that require perhaps more exposition than is necessary in a Bond film. This fourth Craig film (Casino Royale, then Quantum of Solace followed by Skyfall) is as solid as the previous Bond films and includes a threading backstory that ultimately leads to Spectre, a worldwide crime organization headed by a Franz Oberhauser (Christoph Walz, doing what has become his signature psychopath). A much-anticipated trope in these films is the first twenty of so minutes, which are meant to captivate the audience, telegraphing that the games have begun. Spectre doesn’t disappoint. articles.text: Alpha is a wonderful merging of old-fashioned story telling and state-of-the art filmmaking, creating a solidly engaging, even riveting tale about a boy who out of kindness and then necessity befriends an injured wolf. But this narrative is not of the Lassie Come Home genre. The film is set in southwestern Europe, just as the Ice Age is coming to a close, meaning some 20,000 years ago. The story opens with Tau (Johannes Haukur Johannesson), the clan’s chief, leading a small cohort of hunters, to include his teenage son, Keda (Kodi Smit McPhee), on a bison hunt. Actually the strategy is to charge at the animals, herd them toward a cliff where some will drop to their deaths and can then be butchered and skinned later. During the stampede, Keda is thrown off the same cliff by a massive bison, A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Porco Rosso Porco Rosso (Crimson Pig) begins in a carefree, unselfconscious manner and for some 20 minutes going in there is not a hint that that the protagonist, Porco Rosso, is a pig wearing a trench coat, aviator goggles, and a discrete mustache. In other words, yes, indeed, according to writer/ director Hayao Miyazaki, pigs can fly. In Porco’s case, it’s a vintage airplane. Porco (Michael Keaton) was an ace Italian flyer during WW I, known then as Marco Pagot. For reasons never explained, he has been cursed to live the rest of his life as an anthropomorphized pig. There is, however, one flashback where Marco fights an air duel with Austro-Hungarian planes; however, it hardly qualifies as backstory. But that was then. And now is the 1930s, the place is all that surrounds the Adriatic Sea. Porco is a mercenary- bounty hunter pilot, hired to fight the menacing air pirates (aka Mamma Aiuto) who roam the local skies. In a brief air battle, Porco’s plane is damaged and he finds his way to Milan for repairs. In Milan is a young girl, Flo (Kimberly Willia Paisley), who happens to be an airplane mechanic and engineer and Porco hires her to fix his plane. As it turns out, there is another girl, Madame Gina (Susan Egan), and despite Porco’s piggishness, crushes on him. Meanwhile a pilot named Donald Curtis (Gary Ewles), a rival of Porco’s, is crazy about Gina. And so a competitive triangle is formed. Much of the interaction takes place in the Hotel Adriano where all the local flyers hang out, good guys and bad. The hotel is also where Gina sings. It all sounds a bit strange and convoluted, even eccentric, but it isn’t. In fact, the plot is spare, straight-forward, comedic and ideal for young audiences. Kids will enjoy immensely the premise of Porco and will find the handdrawn animation – skies filled with airplanes, floating among billowing porcelain clouds – truly breathtaking and poetic. Miyazaki has demonstrated repeatedly in his work a love of flight: airplanes soaring through cobalt blue skies, symbols of freedom. As Flo says in one scene, “These old planes are works of art.” And its those flying machines that border on the mythic encompassing excitement and fantasy and good-hearted fun. Porco Rosso. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Studio Ghibli animé. Starring Michael Keaton, Susan Egan and David Ogden Stiers. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Bow streaming on Hulu/Fandango/Prime/MAX/Roku. articles.text: It used to be that there was just Napa Valley – one appellation. Over the years folks have recognized that there are distinct geographic regions within the valley, creating wines with a distinct and separate character. First it was the difference between the mountain regions like Mt. Veeder and Howell Mountain from the valley floor vineyards. Then it became apparent that the wines of Calistoga were different from those of Carneros or Rutherford. Today there are 17 different AVA’s (American Viticultural Areas) in Napa Valley and this week we focus on one of the lesser-known regions – Atlas Peak. The Atlas Peak AVA is located within the Soda Canyon and Foss Valley areas northeast of the town of Napa, east of Yountville, and above the foothills of the Stags Leap District. Vineyards were first planted on Atlas Peak in 1870, and the terrain saw steady vineyard and acreage growth between 1880 and 1901. Historically the region grew many grape varieties, but today Atlas Peak is known for its expressive mountain Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux varietals. The first winery was established in the early 1980’s, and the appellation was given official status in 1992. Atlas Peak growers supply fruit to dozens of wineries in Napa and Sonoma counties, the largest being the gigantic Stagecoach Vineyard started by the Dr. Jan Krupp in 1991. He spent years developing the site undertaking what many local experts had claimed was an impossible task. It took seven years to clear more than one billion pounds of volcanic rock. In 2016 the E.& J. Gallo Winery purchased Stagecoach Vineyard. Today with over 600 acres planted to vines, the Cabernet -focused Stagecoach is the largest contiguous vineyard in the Napa Valley and the fruit is used by over 80 different wineries. The Atlas Peak AVA has about 25 member wineries in the association. This year they held their annual tasting event at William Hill Winery on May 17. While there were many outstanding wines poured, the following wines stood out above the crowd. They are the cream of the crop of the Atlas Peak AVA. • 2021 En Garde Cabernet Sauvignon Hendrickson Vineyard The En Garde Cabernet shows beautiful blueberry and black raspberry fruit, a cool, almost floral note, medium to full body and sensational purity and texture. Found in this big boned wine are classic Atlas Mountain characteristics. This is a beauty of finesse and restraint, yet intensity. Drink over the next 25 years. • 2023 Pahlmeyer Chardonnay This is a nod to the old school style of California Chardonnay.

The nose is jubilant with apricots, peaches and honeysuckle blossoms with a good lashing of vanilla oak. The stone fruit flavors explode in the mouth with gobs of full-bodied weighty fruit and the finish is full and satisfying. While this wine would pair with many foods, I almost prefer it as a meal in itself. • 2022 Vin Roc Cabernet Sauvignon The deep garnet-purple colored 2022 Vin Roc Cab sashays out of the glass with provocative warm blackcurrant, blueberries, and raspberry scents with an undercurrent of violets, graphite, and forest floor. The full-bodied palate is laden with fragrant black and blue fruits, framed by firm, finely grained tannins and seamless freshness, finishing long and perfumed. Built for the ages, this wine has a long life ahead of it. • 2021 Beaulieu Vineyards Georges de la Tour Cabernet Sauvignon This esteemed BV Cabernet is one of California’s classic wines. It reveals an earthy/meaty nose with herbal notions over a core of cassis, plums and blackberries, plus cedar chest and menthol hints. There is enough acidity and some tannin, but the wine’s purity and equilibrium are hallmarks of this smashing effort.
