articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a lovely morning last Wednesday for a special walk. Recent news reports said there have been a higher-than-normal number of eagle sightings in the Bay Area. Air quality improvements in the area and a year of plentiful rain that have filled the reservoirs where eagles seek food could be behind the increase. A pair of bald eagles have been nesting in a eucalyptus tree at the edge of Mountain View Cemetery near one of the cemetery’s reservoirs. Their eaglets had hatched, but since they typically don’t leave the nest, or “fledge,” for 10 to 14 weeks, the new family would still be in residence. Additionally, a pair of owls in Dracena Park were the subject of a recent naming contest by the city. The walkers went down Highland Avenue to and up Moraga Avenue. Bird watchers had been on the corner of Monte and Moraga Avenues, but State Fish & Wildfire guidelines instruct viewers to stay at least 330 feet from nests. While eagles can be curious about humans and even seem to recognize individuals who regularly observe them, they are not inherently “friendly” with people. Bald eagles are territorial, particularly during nesting season, and can be aggressive when they feel threatened, especially when defending their nests or young. Moraga Avenue traffic isn’t bothering them, but eagles are generally scared by loud noises, large, moving objects, and the presence of humans, so it is good to view them from a safe distance. The walkers stopped at Mesa, the street before Monte, for some information about eagles. Bald eagles weigh 10-14 pounds and have wing spans of 6.5 to 7 feet. Males are smaller than females. Eagles are not built for speed flying, but they can fly at about 30 mph and dive at over 100 mph. Their large, broad wings suit them for soaring and scanning, not chasing and maneuvering. Bald eagles typically live between 20 and 30 years in the wild. The oldest bald eagle on record lived to be 47 years old. Young bald eagles are dark in color but develop their characteristic white head and tail at about four to five years. Eagles only live in North America and are especially prevalent near coastal regions or large inland lakes and rivers with healthy fish populations. They mainly eat fresh fish, which they snatch out of the water with their sharp, curved talons. When eagles can’t find fish, they will eat ducks, small mammals, and decaying animal flesh, often considered roadkill. . Nests are built with large sticks and may be lined with moss, grass, plant stalks, lichens, seaweed, and sod. They are usually about 4 to 6 feet in diameter and 3 feet deep, although larger nests have been seen. Eagles primarily sleep on tree perches, not in their nests, either at them or nearby, especially during the breeding season to guard their young. Eagles have a specialized mechanism in their foot that allows them to lock it while they are sleeping. Bald eagles come out during the daytime. They often eat after sunrise but can hunt anytime in daylight. Eagles’ eyesight is incredible. They can see a rabbit running up to three miles away or a fish down in the water, but eagles don’t have good night vision. They need to find a branch and tuck in at night until the morning. This is different from another type of raptor, owls, who are nocturnal and have excellent night vision. Eagles’ hearing is similar to humans, okay, but not great. They also do not have a very well-developed sense of taste and smell. This benefits them because they are scavengers. Their breeding season lasts from January through July or August. Bald eagles mate for life. Both the male and female work together to construct a nest, usually high in a living tree. They typically return to the same nest each year, adding new material with every breeding season, so Piedmont’s eagles may be back next year. Males and females share incubation responsibilities, but the female typically spends more time on the nest. The process of eaglets leaving the nest can be gradual, with the young ones initially branching out to nearby areas before fully taking flight. Before leaving the nest, eaglets may start going to nearby branches but still remain in the area. They often remain nearby for several weeks or even months, learning to hunt and fly from their parents. The parent eagles continue to feed their young even after they leave the nest. While bald eagles once nested along the entire Pacific Coast, from the Aleutians to Baja California, there were only 487 nesting pairs remaining in the lower United States in 1963. The decline was a result of habitat destruction and degradation, the use of DDT, and illegal shooting. In 1976, the eagle was officially listed as an endangered species, and conservationists took steps to save them. Bald eagles are protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act which prohibits hunting, selling, possessing eagles, or taking their feathers, nests, and eggs. A 1972 nationwide DDT ban and restrictions on lead birdshot and lead fishing weights also helped restore eagle populations. By 1995, bald eagles were relisted as threatened. Seeing a bald eagle now is no longer considered rare. Populations have significantly recovered and they are now common in many regions of North America. Alaska has the most bald eagles in the United States, with an estimated population of around 30,000 birds, and about five now in Piedmont. The Piedmont walkers continued up to Monte and found three bird enthusiasts. Many of the walkers had brough binoculars, and one of the three let others view the nest through his telescope. The group also wanted to find the owls in Dracena Park too, so they retraced their steps on Moraga and Highland and then to Park Way and the top of the park. Bald eagles typically live between 20 and 30 years in the wild. The oldest bald eagle on record lived to be 47 years old. Young bald eagles are dark in color but develop their characteristic white head and tail at about four to five years. Eagles only live in North America and are especially prevalent near coastal regions or large inland lakes and rivers with healthy fish populations. They mainly eat fresh fish, which they snatch out of the water with their sharp, curved talons. When eagles can’t find fish, they will eat ducks, small mammals, and decaying animal flesh, often considered roadkill. . Nests are built with large sticks and may be lined with moss, grass, plant stalks, lichens, seaweed, and sod. They are usually about 4 to 6 feet in diameter and 3 feet deep, although larger nests have been seen. Eagles primarily sleep on tree perches, not in their nests, either at them or nearby, especially during the breeding season to guard their young. Eagles have a specialized mechanism in their foot that allows them to lock it while they are sleeping. Bald eagles come out during the daytime. They often eat after sunrise but can hunt anytime in daylight. Eagles’ eyesight is incredible. They can see a rabbit running up to three miles away or a fish down in the water, but eagles don’t have good night vision. They need to find a branch and tuck in at night until the morning. This is different from another type of raptor, owls, who are nocturnal and have excellent night vision. Eagles’ hearing is similar to humans, okay, but not great. They also do not have a very well-developed sense of taste and smell. This benefits them because they are scavengers. Their breeding season lasts from January through July or August. Bald eagles mate for life. Both the male and female work together to construct a nest, usually high in a living tree. They typically return to the same nest each year, adding new material with every breeding season, so Piedmont’s eagles may be back next year. Males and females share incubation responsibilities, but the female typically spends more time on the nest. The process of eaglets leaving the nest can be gradual, with the young ones initially branching out to nearby areas before fully taking flight. Before leaving the nest, eaglets may start going to nearby branches but still remain in the area. They often remain nearby for several weeks or even months, learning to hunt and fly from their parents. The parent eagles continue to feed their young even after they leave the nest. While bald eagles once nested along the entire Pacific Coast, from the Aleutians to Baja California, there were only 487 nesting pairs remaining in the lower United States in 1963. The decline was a result of habitat destruction and degradation, the use of DDT, and illegal shooting. In 1976, the eagle was officially listed as an endangered species, and conservationists took steps to save them. Bald eagles are protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act which prohibits hunting, selling, possessing eagles, or taking their feathers, nests, and eggs. A 1972 nationwide DDT ban and restrictions on lead birdshot and lead fishing weights also helped restore eagle populations. By 1995, bald eagles were relisted as threatened. Seeing a bald eagle now is no longer considered rare. Populations have significantly recovered and they are now common in many regions of North America. Alaska has the most bald eagles in the United States, with an estimated population of around 30,000 birds, and about five now in Piedmont. The Piedmont walkers continued up to Monte and found three bird enthusiasts. Many of the walkers had brough binoculars, and one of the three let others view the nest through his telescope. The group also wanted to find the owls in Dracena Park too, so they retraced their steps on Moraga and Highland and then to Park Way and the top of the park. They scoured the treetops, looking for the owls, who recently were named Ramona and Blair, but the nocturnal birds were not to be seen. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Anything can be famous. If you don’t think so, picture the most famous subway grate in New York City – actually the most famous subway grate in the world. How can a subway grate become famous? By being the one that sends up busy gusts of air just as Marilyn Monroe stands over it in the movie, The Seven Year Itch. Monroe’s provocatively blowing skirt became emblematic of the film, and of her, but if your visual memory fails you, you can refresh it at Piedmont’s monthly Flix Fest next week, because The Seven Year Itch is on the bill. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The hit 1954 Cinemascope comedy, directed by Billy Wilder, begins as middle aged publishing executive, Richard Sherman (Tom Ewell) sends his wife and son off to Maine, to spend the summer away from New York’s summer heat. Without his family to anchor him, his thoughts start to drift – he’s afflicted with, to put it politely, a waning interest in staying monogamous, known to psychologists, and to the rest of us, as “the seven year itch.” Dream fulfillment shows up in the form of a curvaceous blonde model (Marilyn Monroe) who has moved into the apartment upstairs. Pondering infidelity, Richard hones in on his scrumptious new neighbor—but will his technicolor fantasies about her become a reality? Comedy ensues. The Seven Year Itch will be shown tomorrow, Thursday, June 12 at 4:15 p.m. in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors for this showing will open at 4:00. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is suggested at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the 2004 martial arts action comedy film, Kung Fu Hustle, to be screened on July 10th.

The group was pleased that Linda Sigel was with them for the first time. Discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus was away, so Phil Witte filled in for her. The readers were there to talk about How We Got to Now: Six Innovations That Made the Modern World by Steven Johnson, which was published in 2014, and in which he explores the history of innovation over centuries. The book presents stories of accidental wonders and beneficial mistakes. Specifically, the author examines the unexpected connections within six technologies: Glass, Cold, Sound, Clean, Time, and Light. He traces aspects of the development of modern life from discoveries in these areas to their often unintended and surprising consequences. For example, Johnson presents glass as the material that he feels has most changed human existence. He traces the consequences of its discovery to the invention of printing, the adoption of reading glasses, and the creation of the microscope and telescope. These advancements led to understanding the patterns of the stars and observing microorganisms. One reader also noted we probably wouldn’t have pet goldfish if there weren’t glass bowls. The invention of air-conditioning enabled history’s largest human migration to cities like Dubai and Phoenix, which would have otherwise been uninhabitable. Johnson stressed that many innovations were not the result of a sudden moment, but rather they were usually a long process involving a network of inventors and entrepreneurs. Radio was an important exception: it was developed in one place at one time. Almost all the readers enjoyed it. The topics that Johnson covers are certainly ones that have changed how our civilization has advanced and how we live today. We tend to take much for granted, but it was fun to have a fuller understanding of what got us here. There was a lot of trivia in the book, but readers found it enlightening to see how one invention led to another and then to another. It made the readers aware of how fickle the flow of history and life can be with both good and bad consequences. There were some reservations about the book. The writing style seemed derived from television, and in fact the book has been developed into a PBS broadcast series. The importance of people with different skill sets in close proximity in order to collaborate and cross cross-pollinate ideas was noted. So was the importance of places, like the Bell Labs and Silicon Valley, that fostered communication. The book’s concluding statement reasoned with the readers. Johnson says, “There is … risk in being true to your own sense of identity … Better to explore uncharted terrain … Better to make new connections than to remain comfortably situated in the same routine.… If you want to improve the world slightly, you need focus and determination.” The group had previously selected The Immortalists by Chloe Benjamin for July and Tender At The Bone: Growing Up At The Table by Ruth Reichl for August. After Dick Carter’s presentation of three fiction books. the group selected The Women by Kristin Hannah for September. articles.text: Compiled Reporting on the Shortcomings of Tesla’s Electric Pickup Since its release in late 2023, Tesla’s electric pickup truck has been making headlines — not always for the right reasons. The Cybertruck’s weight, power and speed make it a formidable presence on American roads, but its futuristic design and unconventional features have raised serious questions about safety and practicality. In just 18 months on the market, the Cybertruck has already been recalled eight times. The most recent recall, in March, involved more than 46,000 vehicles after reports that an exterior trim panel could detach and create hazardous driving conditions. The safety concerns don’t stop there. According to a February report by Mother Jones, analysis suggests the Cybertruck has a higher fatality rate than even the infamous Ford Pinto. As of February, the Cybertruck’s fatality rate stood at 14.5 per 100,000 units — 17 times that of the Pinto. Rough around the Edges The Cybertruck remains a technological accomplishment among electric vehicles. It accelerates from zero to 60 mph in just 2.6 seconds and weighs nearly 7,000 pounds, with its distinctive stainless steel paneling and armored glass adding to its futuristic image. While the vehicle boasts a 5-star safety rating from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), concerns about pedestrian safety have followed it since launch. The sharp, rigid body panels that give the Cybertruck its signature look fail to meet European pedestrian protection standards, effectively banning it from European roads. Auto reviewers at Throttle House even tested the vehicle’s edges using carrots to simulate human fingers — and showed how easily the sharp steel peeled the carrot and how quickly the automatic trunk could snap one in half. “Borderline dangerous. I don’t care how much it costs, you’ve got to round these edges The memorial site of last November’s tragic auto-accident involving a Cybertruck. An image taken from crash tests on the Tesla Cybertruck by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). out,” said reviewer Thomas Holland. Visibility is another issue. Holland called the Cybertruck’s blind spots “God-awful,” noting large gaps between the windshield and side windows, along with a rearview mirror blocked when the truck bed is covered. The rear camera provides some help, but not always reliably. Safety by Software — and Its Limitations Like much of Tesla’s product line, the Cybertruck relies heavily on its computer system to operate even basic functions — including opening the doors. If the system fails or loses power, doors may remain locked, forcing passengers to locate a hidden emergency release that Jalopnik called “a dangerous nightmare.” That release is buried under a plastic panel and rubber mat at the bottom of the rear door. While instructions are available in the owner’s manual, most passengers wouldn’t know where to look — especially in a crisis, where seconds can matter. A Local Tragedy In Piedmont, these safety concerns took a tragic turn. Early on the morning of Nov. 27, 2024, a single-car Cybertruck crash took the lives of three recent graduates of Piedmont High School. The wrecked vehicle was soon engulfed in flames, leaving the community in mourning. As reported by Chase Hunter for the East Bay Times, witness testimony and the California Highway Patrol (CHP) report revealed harrowing rescue attempts. The Cybertruck’s doors could not be opened after the crash. Initial attempts to break a window with fists failed. A tree branch — about 4 to 5 feet long — was then used to strike the passenger-side window 10 to 15 times before it cracked. The window was pulled from its frame, and one passenger was rescued. Another passenger in the back seat tried to escape through the same opening but was unable to make it past the growing fire. The CHP investigation into the crash remains ongoing. Consumer Frustrations Mount Beyond safety concerns, Cybertruck owners have shared frustrations online. Videos of Cybertruck malfunctions have gone viral, and an entire Reddit community — “Cyberstuck” — documents breakdowns and glitches. In one widely shared story, a Cybertruck entered “limp mode” due to a front trunk alignment issue and had to be towed from a child’s baseball game. Tesla’s top-of-the-line Cyberbeast model sells for $100,000. Yet sluggish sales reflect the growing skepticism. As of June 9, International Business Times reported that Tesla was offering interest-free loans — essentially a $10,000 discount — to move inventory. Meanwhile, more than 100 unsold Cybertrucks reportedly sit in storage at a disused shopping center in Farmington Hills, Michigan. Once Promised, Now Stalled While the Cybertruck initially promised to revolutionize the pickup truck market, reality has proven more complicated. Parking lots are filling with unsold inventory in the U.S., while European countries have banned the vehicle entirely. And despite Tesla’s loyal fan base, many truck shoppers remain unconvinced. The Cybertruck remains a marvel of design and engineering — but increasingly, it’s also a case study in how innovation can collide with real-world safety, regulation, and consumer trust. In Farmington Hills, Michigan, Tesla stores over 100 unsold Cybertrucks in a disused shopping center.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Linda G. Arellano passed away peacefully at home on May 23rd surrounded by her loving family. Linda was kindhearted, outgoing, engaging and stylish, always with a flower on her lapel or pinned to her dress. She loved her family deeply and would light up any room the minute she walked in. An encounter with her always included her warm smile, a twinkle in her eyes, often a touch or hug, and the feeling of being loved. Born on December 26, 1939 and raised in Altadena, CA with two brothers, she was a true California girl. In 1957 she was named a Princess in the Pasadena Rose Parade. Linda attended UC Berkely and served as President of the Delta Gamma Sorority house after which she married her first husband of 12 years and settled in Piedmont. For the last 38 years, she shared a beautiful life with her treasured husband, Rick. While raising her three children as a single parent, she was engaged in interior design and worked as an Office Manager at Grey Advertising, as an Executive Director at Easter Seals of the East Bay, and as Senior VP of Communications at Grubb & Ellis, ringing the bell on Wall Street when they went public. In later years, she assisted Rick in his financial advisory business. She was also known for her culinary skills and catered events with her friend Nancy Martz. Linda and Rick were members of Claremont Country Club since 1987 where she served as Chair of the House Committee for several years. She enjoyed sailing as Rick’s first mate as well as tennis, golf, travel, and frequent games of dominoes. She was a knowledgeable and diehard football fan, cheering for the Cal Bears and the San Francisco 49ers. Linda Arellano died on May 23 at age 85. Linda was a woman of deep faith. She served as a Eucharistic Minister and a choir member at St. Theresa Catholic Church in Oakland. She also was a Dame of the Knights of the Holy Sepulcher. She is survived by her beloved husband, Rick (J. Richard) Arellano, and her three devoted children, Lisa Clawson (Steve), Geoff Greenlee (Sonia), and Phyllis Walker (John) and her two treasured granddaughters, Sydney Rae Greenlee and Justine Linda Greenlee. In addition, she leaves behind her five stepchildren Lorelei (Koby), Chris, David (Michelle), Pamela, Gregory (Terry), and their eight children. A funeral mass will be held at St. Theresa Catholic Church, 30 Mandalay Rd, Oakland, on Friday, June 20 at 11:00 a.m. with a reception immediately following. In lieu of flowers. the family suggests a donation to your favorite charity or the Susan G. Komen Foundation.
articles.title: Linda Arellano dies on May 23

articles.text: A Mon Chateau was a quiet restaurant at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Note the horse trough in Fenton, Maloney and Jennings ran A Mon Chateau in 1907 and 1908. Note the arched opening to the beer garden on the far right. The building was the Grand Avenue Grocery Company in 1915. The grocery enclosed the porch and added large windows. The distinctive gabled roofs of A Mon Chateau are recognizable. (Photo, c. 1915) Avenue, and the Leisz grocery closed in 1935. The old A Mon Chateau building was torn down in 1936 when the Richfield Oil Company built a gas station on the corner lot. In the late 1960s, the business became the Phillips Gas station run by O.N. articles.text: Part 11 in a series In the history of Piedmont, two saloons have quenched the thirst of residents and visitors. One saloon was in a respected hotel. The other was fraught with problems. The Piedmont Springs Hotel was built to serve visitors to the Piedmont hills and the mineral springs in Piedmont’s Bushy Dell Creek. Built in 1871 as a first class resort, the hotel had 20 rooms and a main dining room with a crystal chandelier and velvet drapes. The Grand Saloon (for gentlemen only) had a long mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove in the corner. The Grand Saloon gained brief notoriety in 1891 when the wives of some of Piedmont’s more prominent businessmen petitioned the county to rescind the hotel’s liquor license. The women objected to their husbands stopping for a drink on their way home. The license was never rescinded, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel continued to serve liquor for another year before it burned to the ground in 1892. A Mon Chateau Piedmont’s other saloon was A Mon Chateau. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran through a very pleasant valley – sunny, free of wind, rolling hills, scattered trees – that extended from Lake Merritt into the Piedmont hills. It was the route that many early Oakland residents took from downtown Oakland to picnic in the Piedmont hills. Today, that road is Grand Avenue until it crosses the city line near Rose Avenue. It continues as Pleasant Valley Road in Oakland until it crosses Broadway and becomes 51st Street. In 1892, Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at the southwest corner of today’s Grand and Linda Avenues and served refreshments to these travelers into the Piedmont countryside. He called it “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) and advertised it as a family resort and French restaurant. Taking advantage of the mild weather, he built a beer garden on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. During its first years, A Mon Chateau was a quiet, slow-paced retreat, but that changed with the 1906 earthquake. With the influx of San Francisco refugees to the East Bay, the surrounding land began to fill with new houses and residents. From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket at the other end of the block at Sunnyside and Grand This early photo of A Mon Chateau shows a horse trough in front, Pleasant Valley Road before it was paved, and open rolling hills beyond. “A Mon Chateau” is painted on the gable, and the sign announces “Family Resort.”

articles.text: Piedmont’s quiet and respectful community of birders have been gathering on the sidewalk of Moraga Avenue to see a bald eagle nest above the nearby cemetery, complete with two recently-hatched eaglets. The nest was first seen by neighborhood residents in late summer of last year. The nesting eagles frequented the area for the following months, appearing to settle into place around April of this year. On May 18, the birders observed two of America’s national birds feeding their young and captured long-distance photos of the eaglets and their parents. Knowledgeable birders at the scene estimate that the young birds were about two weeks old at the time. “I’m astounded every day I come out,” said one local resident. “I get goosebumps. My favorite is when they fly into or out of the nest – they’re just majestic birds. A bald eagle feeds one of its eaglets on May 18. Knowledgeable Piedmont birders estimated the chicks to be about two weeks old at the time. And then it’s been fun to watch the development of the eaglets.” Currently, one of the parents can sometimes be found in a tree adjacent to the nest, appearing to stand watch. According to nearby bird watchers, the most popular viewing spot is frequented by a retired Harvard professor who graciously answers questions about the nesting eagles. For residents interested in seeing the birds themselves, the Post asks its readers to be respectful of the birds habitat and safety, and to follow the lead of the more experienced birders for bird-watching etiquette. An adult bald eagle stands guard in a nearby tree. A young eagle stands atop its nest on June 9. Interested birders watch the nest carefully.
articles.title: Birders Flock to Bald Eagle Nest visible from Piedmont

articles.text: Piedmont High School sophomore Mikey Swei won the 2025 VEX Worlds Robotics Championship in Dallas, Texas on May 8 with teammate Jacob Jung, a senior at Dublin High. Swei’s team, Double Play, and their alliance partners, Jackson Area Robotics, outlasted a field of 800 teams to become the high school world champions. There are 11,400 VEX high school teams world-wide, and Swei’s team qualified for the World Championship by winning a tournament in January held in Salt Lake City, Utah. Double Play made it through the qualifying rounds in Dallas and was the No. 1 seed going into the single elimination Championship playoffs. In the finals, Double Play and its alliance partner competed a best of three match. It lost the first but won Round Two to stay alive. In the pivotal rubber match. The robot Swei constructed in Piedmont and the alliance partner’s machine outscored their two opponents to win the VEX World Championship. “Our strategy was based around securing the doubled corner points, and then the very high climbing robot climbing up to the tier three of the ladder,” said Swei.
articles.title: PHS sophomore Mikey Swei wins VEX robotics World Championship

articles.text: Progress on Piedmont’s longawaited community pool has stalled again, with the previously announced June 2 completion date now quietly pushed back. The city has not provided a new target date, saying that construction is expected to finish sometime this summer. The project’s $34.9 million budget remains unchanged, funded by $25.1 million in Measure UU bonds and associated interest. The last formal update came at the March 3 City Council meeting, when officials projected a June 2 construction end date. Now, city staff say a more detailed timeline will be shared at the next council update, scheduled for July 7. Work still to be completed includes deck work, concrete pours, and exterior finishes. Once the site is built out and the pools are filled with water, the facility will enter a “commissioning” period—at least four weeks of testing critical systems like the electric heat pump. An opening date will be announced only after this process is underway. The facility will also need to obtain approval permits from Alameda County Environmental Health prior to opening. One factor contributing to recent delays is the unexpected death of project executive George Sanen of Griffin Structures. Joshua Kaiser has stepped in as the new project executive and will oversee the remainder of the build. Kaiser brings more than 25 years of experience managing complex public construction projects and has assumed full leadership. Griffin Structures President Jon Hughes will remain involved to provide continuity. According to the city, Sanen’s name will be included on the final facility signage honoring key staff and officials who contributed to the project. articles.text: Piedmont’s Jazz and Orchestral Bands picked up the beat together in the Spring Concert in the Alan Harvey Theater on Thursday, May 22. Selections from the evening performance brought the year’s music program into reverie and treated the audience to an evening of auditory excellence. The leader of Piedmont’s music program, Trevor Meseroll, directed the Spring performance for the high school musicians. Meseroll’s student musicians brought to life the music from Chuck Mangione to Gustav Holst. The PHS Symphonic Band started off the evening with highlights from Ratatouille, before giving lively rendition to selections from the musical Grease. The full Orchestra then took over, the jazz and orchestral bands playing together on stage for the first time in a decade. The Full Orchestra performed Duel of Fates from John Williams’ Star Wars, and then teamed up to tackle Gustav Photos by Sophie Hess Barber Shop Quartet featuring juniors Nate McKenzie (left) and Theo Ferguson, freshman Zayd Mahmood, and junior Collin Cameron Senior Claire Weiss’s vocals steer the performance with grace. Holst’s Jupiter. In the audience, Piedmont parent Ellen Lee reflected on the journey of the musicians on stage. “You can see how much progress they’ve made since the kids were in elementary school, with their ability to play a sophisticated piece of music (Jupiter). It’s a culmination of years and years of practice,” said Lee. Soon to graduate, senior Clare Weiss sang all evening with various jazz combos. A Barbershop Quartet brought an energy of showmanship to the stage as well. Standing microphones were stationed for juniors Nate McKenzie, Collin Cameron, and Theo Ferguson, and freshman Zayd

articles.text: Piedmont’s Park Commission will be discussing the landscaping and open space components of the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan at their meeting tonight at 5:30 p.m. in Piedmont City Hall. The presentation and discussion will focus on elements of the Specific Plan that relate to the Park Commission’s charge, addressing proposed improvements to the public realm, preservation of significant open space and scenic views, and wildfire safety provisions. articles.text: From the music of Grease to Gustav Holst’s Jupiter performed recently by Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School musicians, an inspiring musical celebration capped the school year. But the school district’s sterling music program is now being threatened. Recently, the school board approved a program to end instrumental music education for fourth graders next year, a move that is short-sighted and will limit the musical potential of our students. Learning an instrument takes time, and it requires repeated hands-on practice to become proficient enough to play more than just “Hot Cross Buns.” Delaying instrumental music education to 5th grade means that students will have less of an opportunity to master an instrument, and this could have a major impact on middle school and high school band and orchestra. Students also lose out on all the cognitive benefits that come from learning an instrument. Current and recent elementary and middle school students have complained about a challenging and frustrating music experience. Instead of fixing this problem — such as hiring a full-time music teacher, asking for parent volunteers, or incorporating other kinds of classroom support — the school board threw the baby out with the bathwater. Next year, our fourth graders will get 60 minutes a week of “theater arts” in a program that has yet to be defined or developed. The school board heralded this as an exciting change. While we love theater and all that it offers for kids, we don’t understand why it must come at the expense of music. There are plenty of ways to incorporate theater arts into our classrooms – indeed, many of our elementary teachers have already done this – but there are very few opportunities for students to try a variety of instruments and perform in groups. Now they won’t have that chance until 5th grade. Next year has been called a “bridge year.” This only adds to the uncertainty around the future of Piedmont’s music program. Furthermore, this change was made with little transparency and was unnecessarily rushed. Parents and students were scolded for raising their concerns, and there was a fallacy about the collaboration of teachers and staff. Our neighboring school districts – including Berkeley, Orinda, Lafayette, and Moraga – introduce instruments in the fourth grade, and with regression such as this, we will continue to lose students to private schools. With this shift, our district is not being innovative. It is taking a step back in the musical education it offers to our students. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department will host an Alice in Wonderland-themed event at Piedmont Park on Saturday and Sunday, June 7 and 8, with performances at 10:30 a.m. and 2 p.m. each day. The interactive show is designed for children ages two to eight and their parents, though attendees of all ages are welcome. Participants will follow Alice down the rabbit hole and through the park to encounter the magical beings of Wonderland on a 1.5- mile walking journey. Characters from the story will guide families along the path as the show unfolds with clowning, inventive puppetry and live music. Presented by Pinecones and Portals Hiking Theater Company, the Alice in Wonderland production has been an East Bay family favorite for two consecutive years. The Piedmont Recreation Department will also offer a wheelchair- and stroller-accessible version of the experience. Compa ny fou nder a nd director Juliana Frick is an award-winning physical theater artist, acrobat and former musician. Frick toured with the acclaimed youth troupe Circus Smirkus from ages nine to 15. In 2017, she was diagnosed with a rare illness that led to profound hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction. As a chronically ill and late-deafened adult, Frick is a proud disabled artist committed to making the creative process and live performance accessible to all. Tickets can be purchased for $35 per child on the Recreation Department’s Community Pass website, or at https://register. capturepoint.com/reg/cat_program_class_detail.cfm?s=&t=&- season_id=24069&program_ id=2471789&family_mbr_str=. ADA Tickets are available on a limited basis. Wonderland characters lead families on a walking theater adventure.
articles.title: Alice in Wonderland event in Piedmont Park

articles.text: Sign up for AC Alert to participate The City of Piedmont encourages all community members to sign up—or confirm their registration—for AC Alert before Saturday, June 14, when the Piedmont Fire Department will conduct a community wildfire evacuation exercise and preparedness town hall, beginning at 9 a.m. The exercise will include a live evacuation drill in the Blair, Scenic, and Alta neighborhoods, along with an at-home preparedness exercise for the rest of the community. The at-home component is designed to be simple, easy to complete, and high impact. Instructions will be delivered via AC Alert, the emergency notification system used by Piedmont and Alameda County. Community members can sign up to receive AC Alert notifications at bit.ly/ACAlert. This exercise is intended to help residents improve their readiness to evacuate in the event of a wildfire, while also giving first responders an opportunity to test emergency protocols. The Fire Department encourages all residents to participate. On the morning of June 14: • Look for an AC Alert emergency notification around 9 a.m. • Follow the instructions provided in the alert • Attend the community debrief at the Fire Station at 10 a.m. The more residents who take part, the more resilient the community will be. For more information, or to let the City know you plan to participate, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ EvacDrill.
articles.title: Community Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday, June 14

articles.text: Droves of kids on the way to school stopped by the City’s energizer station on Highland Ave for Bike to Work Day on May 15. The city’s bike racks were packed full as hundreds of Piedmont residents brought their bikes out on Thursday, May 15, for the Bay Area’s annual Bike to Work Day. Joining thousands across the Bay Area in biking to work, to school, or to run errands, the yearly celebration of pedal-powered transportation aims to help fledgling riders find new routes and experience what it’s like to use a bike for daily mobility while also building community among active cyclists. Over 20,000 East Bay residents each year pedal to visit over 100 energizer stations and celebrate the joy of biking. Whether For this cyclist, taking his bike out doesn’t mean he can’t still bring his dog. biking to the office, accompanying the kids to school, or just taking a coffee break, community members rolled over to the Piedmont energizer station on Highland Avenue to say hello. The station, run by City staff and community volunteers, was open in the morning from 7:30- 9:30 a.m. in front of Havens Elementary. Energizer station visitors enjoyed free tote bags as well as treats, fruits and refreshments courtesy of Mulberry’s Market. A mother and her children grab snacks and a free tote bag from the City’s energizer station. A Piedmont child carefully picks his favorite snack. Children and adults alike put on their helmets to go where they needed to on May 15.
articles.title: Piedmonters Roll Out for Bike to Work Day

articles.text: Piedmont City Council held the first of two public hearings on Piedmont’s proposed FY2025-26 budget at their regular meeting on Monday, June 2. City Council is expected to adopt the budget following a second public hearing on June 16. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. This year’s budget was presented by retired Finance Director Michael Szczech, performing interim duties while the City awaits the arrival of its next appointed Finance Director, Kiran Bawa. The proposed FY2025-26 budget aims to maintain existing service levels citywide, prioritizing high quality service delivery, fiscal responsibility, and planning for the future while bringing several multi-year major projects to completion, including the City’s new community pool, 9-1-1 dispatch center relocation, and the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The proposed budget features a General Fund of $40 million. A $8.3 million spending plan for the Facilities Capital Fund is also included for work on finishing projects such as the community pool, dispatch center, and more. The budget hearing reported a current projection with expected revenue $1.2 million above the current year’s budget and expenditures expected to be lower than budgeted by $1.6 million. With an expected surplus around $3.6 million, City staff recommended that $850,000 of it be transferred from the General Fund to the City’s Equipment fund, keeping the remainder for next year’s budget. Frank Ryan, Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee chair, spoke at Monday’s budget hearing. A $8.3 million spending plan for the Facilities Capital Fund is also included for work on finishing projects such as the community pool, dispatch center, and more. articles.text: Congratulations to the Piedmont National and State Top-20 winners of the International Math Kangaroo competition. In March, the Piedmont ALPS parent support group hosted 113 community students to compete in the National Math Kangaroo competition that took place at sites across the country. USA Math Kangaroo has a mission to motivate students towards a love of math and has hosted a yearly competition for K-12 students for the past 27 years with 53,562 US students competing this year. National and state winners were announced in May and local Top-20 finishers were honored Wednesday in a prize ceremony in Piedmont Park. Piedmont School District Assistant Superintendent, Ariel Dolowich presided and was joined by Wildwood Elementary School Principal, Beth Rhine to present the winners with prizes from the National Math Kangaroo organization. School Board Member and former ALPS co-lead Michael Malione attended as the test center host. This year there were 20 winners from Piedmont, including three 1st place winners. Michael Chu (Grade 3, Wildwood), Clio Khatri (Grade 4, Wildwood), and James Phung (Grade 4, Wildwood) all finished first at the National and State levels. The Top-20 winners were honored at the event. articles.text: For many students, summer means turning off the alarm, sleeping late, and enjoying an unstructured day. While freedom from the routine of the academic year provides a mentally refreshing break, summer is a great time to practice executive functioning and life skills. Becoming more competent at managing the logistics of life carries over into improved academics and increased confidence. Here are three simple ways kids can work on these important life skills: Field trip fun day Give your kids the opportunity to plan a fun day out to a local museum or outdoor activity. They can research opening times, entry fees, and transport logistics. Will you drive or take BART? Public transportation is a fantastic way to practice realworld skills like reading a schedule, determining fares, and navigating public spaces. By giving kids control over this activity, they are invested in making it a fun day for everyone. Plan and cook a simple meal Cooking requires a tremendous amount of executive functioning. From planning ingredient lists to carving out time to go to the grocery store to understanding how to time different meal components so everything is ready simultaneously is a big learning curve. The multiple steps involved in cooking can be overwhelming, so starting simple and age-appropriate can help build these skills and grow confidence. Pack your bags Regardless of if your child is going to day camp or on a vacation, give them the opportunity to pack their own bag. Not only can they have the experience of thinking through what they might need for different weather conditions or activities, they can also think about what food and drink they might want. You can help them be aware of any restrictions — like liquids on airlines or allergens at camp — they need to consider. While it takes time and patience to let kids pack their own bags, remember that independence for them is independence for you. Using the summer to practice executive functioning skills gives your child the opportunity to build cognitive pathways that correlate with better academic performance during the school year. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. articles.text: Piedmont Mountain Bike Team concluded its five-race season at the 2025 NorCal Cycling League Championship at Six Sigma Ranch and Winery in Lower Lake on Sunday, May 18. Piedmont featured 13 riders for the high school championship. The championship course was a difficult 4.9-mile loop with an elevation gain of 800 feet. Leading the way for Piedmont was Jasper Schuetz, finishing his four-lap race in 21st of 61 riders with a time of 1:34:12.52. He finished his first lap in 22:14 minutes, logged a time of 23:11 on his second lap, 24:19 on his third, and 24:26 to close. Varsity member Cary Ward placed 55th in 1:44:58.29. Josephine Schuetz finished off her impressive freshman season by finishing 13th of 29, clocking a time of 1:08:44.93 over her twolap race. She finished her laps with respective times of 33:15 and 35:29. Piedmont had three other riders in the freshman girls’ race: Mina Herrgott, 19th in 1:14:01.52, Rose Reining, 21st in 1:17:11.16, Olivia Bailey 24th in 1:21:29.57, and Gracey Ann Hatchell in 2:06:46.06. Zachary Carter had a strong run in the freshman boys’ division 1 race. Over his two-lap event, Carter finished 20th of 71 athletes, clocking a 52:28.91. He notched times of 25:16 and 27:12 for his two laps. Jack Mendelsohn also rode in the race, finishing 60th in 1:08:27.53. Kai Hsu was 64th in 1:13:05.49, while William Carter was 68th in 1:18:29.49. In the JV2 girls’ race, Olive Reining was 45th of 48 with a time of 1:28:21.89 for her twolap race. As for the JV2 boys, Caleb Canada was 44th of 60 in 1:00:07.77 for his two-lap event. Photos courtesy of Piedmont MTB Jasper Schuetz finished 21st of 61 riders in the NorCal Cycling League Championship’s varsity race. Josephine Schuetz was 13th of 29 in the freshman girls’ race. Zachary Carter finished 20th of 71 riders in the freshman boys’ division 1 race.

articles.text: Sophomore is 2 seconds away from school record Piedmont High sophomore Sebastien Swain, the only member of the track team to qualify for the State Championships, came within two seconds of setting a school record in the 800 meters. Competing at Veterans Memorial Stadium at Buchanan High School in Clovis on Friday, May 30, he posted a time of 1:53.15, two seconds off the Piedmont school record set by Gordon Johnson in 1988. Competing at State pits together hundreds of California’s top runners along with their family and friends into the large high school stadium. It’s a championship atmosphere unlike almost every high school track event. “It’s definitely a special meet,” said Swain. “I’m just super happy Sebastien Swain’s CIF State Championship marks his third State Championship appearance and first for the track team. Sebastien Swain is less than two seconds behind Gordon Johnson’s 1988 school record of 1:51.69 in the 800. Sophomore Sebastien Swain (#6) represented Piedmont at the 2025 CIF State Championship, finishing the 800 meters in 18th. to make it there. You have the atmosphere, all the people, and the opportunity to see what you can do against the top runners in the state. I’m just a sophomore, so it’s a chance to see what it takes and what I need to do to match up with my competition.” Swain placed 18th in a field of 29 half milers. “Because I’m racing all these fast people, my goal was to just put myself in a good position. I wanted to get out early so I’m not stuck at the back early in the race. I wanted to come through to the line one a second faster than I normally would,” Swain said. Though a sophomore, Swain has now completed the third CIF State Championship of his running career. He qualified for State in the fall for two years on the cross-country team. “It’s exciting. I’m looking forward to building off this success and maybe next year, not just qualify for State, but to actually place in the finals. That’s my plan,” he added. With a personal record time of 1:53.15, Swain is less than two seconds back of Gordon Johnson’s 1988 record of 1:51.69. Swain is well-aware that he’s nipping at Gordon’s heals with two years of eligibility left. “Oh, I’m thinking about it; Gordon’s going down,” Swain said with a laugh. “My mom and my dad actually know Gordon. He’s still around Piedmont, so it’s really neat to have that connection,” he added. Swain also won the Western Alameda County Conference title in the 1600 at the league championship on May 9. He opted to only compete in the 800 at the NCS’ Bayshore Area Championship and Meet of Champions. “The 800 has definitely been my focus. In order to run a 1600 well and close, you have to run a good 800. I felt a good way to improve in the 1600 was to get the shorter distance down. It also had to do with working on the short-end because that’s more difficult. I know I can run with endurance, especially after cross country. As the season progressed, I dealt with an injury that made long aerobic fitness more difficult. Because I wasn’t getting that work in, it made more sense to focus on the 800.” Swain said. Now entering the summer, Swain will return to toe the line in the fall for the cross country season.
articles.title: Swain sets PR in 800 at CIF State Championship

Piedmont had three other riders in the freshman girls’ race: Mina Herrgott, 19th in 1:14:01.52, Rose Reining, 21st in 1:17:11.16, Olivia Bailey 24th in 1:21:29.57, and Gracey Ann Hatchell in 2:06:46.06. Zachary Carter had a strong run in the freshman boys’ division 1 race. Over his two-lap event, Carter finished 20th of 71 athletes, clocking a 52:28.91. He notched times of 25:16 and 27:12 for his two laps. Jack Mendelsohn also rode in the race, finishing 60th in 1:08:27.53. Kai Hsu was 64th in 1:13:05.49, while William Carter was 68th in 1:18:29.49. In the JV2 girls’ race, Olive Reining was 45th of 48 with a time of 1:28:21.89 for her twolap race. As for the JV2 boys, Caleb Canada was 44th of 60 in 1:00:07.77 for his two-lap event. Sebastien Swain’s CIF State Championship marks his third State Championship appearance and first for the track team. Sebastien Swain is less than two seconds behind Gordon Johnson’s 1988 school record of 1:51.69 in the 800. Sophomore Sebastien Swain (#6) represented Piedmont at the 2025 CIF State Championship, finishing the 800 meters in 18th. to make it there. You have the atmosphere, all the people, and the opportunity to see what you can do against the top runners in the state. I’m just a sophomore, so it’s a chance to see what it takes and what I need to do to match up with my competition.” Swain placed 18th in a field of 29 half milers. “Because I’m racing all these fast people, my goal was to just put myself in a good position. I wanted to get out early so I’m not stuck at the back early in the race. I wanted to come through to the line one a second faster than I normally would,” Swain said. Though a sophomore, Swain has now completed the third CIF State Championship of his running career. He qualified for State in the fall for two years on the cross-country team. “It’s exciting. I’m looking forward to building off this success and maybe next year, not just qualify for State, but to actually place in the finals. That’s my plan,” he added. With a personal record time of 1:53.15, Swain is less than two seconds back of Gordon Johnson’s 1988 record of 1:51.69. Swain is well-aware that he’s nipping at Gordon’s heals with two years of eligibility left. “Oh, I’m thinking about it; Gordon’s going down,” Swain said with a laugh. “My mom and my dad actually know Gordon. He’s still around Piedmont, so it’s really neat to have that connection,” he added. Swain also won the Western Alameda County Conference title in the 1600 at the league championship on May 9. He opted to only compete in the 800 at the NCS’ Bayshore Area Championship and Meet of Champions. “The 800 has definitely been my focus. In order to run a 1600 well and close, you have to run a good 800. I felt a good way to improve in the 1600 was to get the shorter distance down. It also had to do with working on the short-end because that’s more difficult. I know I can run with endurance, especially after cross country. As the season progressed, I dealt with an injury that made long aerobic fitness more difficult. Because I wasn’t getting that work in, it made more sense to focus on the 800.” Swain said. Now entering the summer, Swain will return to toe the line in the fall for the cross country season. articles.text: The original article was written by Owen Blanford, then a Bronco division player and 5th grader at Havens Elementary School. It first appeared in the Piedmont Post in May 2018 and has been updated with the 2025 Award recipients. Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation (PBSF) is proud to be a community league dedicated to providing opportunities for players of all skill levels. PBSF’s mission emphasizes that the games are an opportunity to learn life lessons and skills that have meaning beyond the game of baseball or softball, such as sportsmanship, character, confidence, resilience, being part of a team, and building memories that last a lifetime. Former PBSF President Murray Davis was instrumental in the development of the PBSF mission with his own youth baseball experience as his personal guide. Murray played youth baseball with hall-of-famer Robin Yount. While Murray didn’t have the same skills of the future hall of famer, Murray was fond of telling anyone that his love of the game helped Robin Yount fulfill his achievements in baseball. Former PBSF Board member Barry Barnes said, “Every time I asked, ‘how are you doing, Murray?’ His response was almost always, ‘I’m living the dream man, living the dream.’” Murray carried the positive attitude from youth baseball throughout his life. After his passing in late 2012, PBSF created the “Livin’ the Dream” award in his honor. The “Livin’ the Dream” award is given to one player on each team. The award is not a MVP award, rather is given to a player who embodies positive, intangible contributions to the team, sportsmanship, perseverance, and a positive infectious attitude. It’s like giving the award to a person who is most like Murray Davis. When Former PBSF President Chris Hart gave out the “Livin’ the Dream” award he looked for a player who enjoyed playing on the team and whose teammates enjoyed with him, who gave full effort and a player who showed a desire to improve.
articles.title: Baseball, Softball Foundation announces winners of Murray Davis Livin’ the Dream Awards

articles.text: The Piedmont Gummy Bears, a team of 6- to 9-year-old girls, recently won the 2025 Softball League Championship. They powered through four tough playoff games, including an extra-inning thriller against the Oakland Dancing Bananas, in the semifinals. Throughout the postseason, the Gummy Bears leaned on grit, teamwork, and contributions from every player. Ten different girls pitched over the course of the season — an incredible feat made possible with the help of high school volunteer and pitching coach Elsa Chun, who supported and inspired the team’s youngest arms. “The way these kids supported each other, stayed focused, and rose to the challenge was something special,” said Coach Annalee Gould. “They played for each other and trusted their teammates every step of the way.” Standing Row: Assistant Coach Anand Patel, Head Coach Annalee Gould, Lydia Bowman, Brianna Ackerman, Leila Patel, Amelia Kolstad, Elena Dean, Maya Torrey, Assistant Coaches Elsa Chun and Tim Souva. Kneeling Row: Ariana Drury, Layla Souva, Nora Holder, Paloma Sahuc (with dog, Ginger) Summer Booth, Maddie Chew (not pictured Maya Levinsohn)
articles.title: Piedmont Gummy Bears win softball League Championship

articles.text: Recently three brothers – Cooper, Ramsey, and Dillon Stull – accomplished the rare feat of winning the championship of their respective Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation tournaments. Ramsey and Dillon both play on the Space Cowboys in the Mustang Division and are coached by their dad, Jonathan Stull. Although the Space Cowboys finished in eighth place, the squad came alive in the tournament. They opened by upsetting the No. 1 seed Sea Wolves on Wednesday, May 14. Then they followed up by beating No. 4 Biscuits on Saturday, May 17, and then winning the championship the same day by beating the No. 3 seed Iron Birds 7-5. Ramsey pitched as the closer in every game, while Dillon grabbed the final out in both the semifinals and finals – snagging a high fly ball to end semis and a grounder in the championship The Stull brothers pulled off a rare feat by taking home three championship medals in the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation tournament. Pictured are Ramsey Stull (left), Cooper Stull, and Dillon Stull. game. Ramsey is 10-years-old, while Dillon is two years younger but plays up in the higher age division. 12-year-old Cooper plays on the Gators in the Bronco Division. He entered as a relief pitcher for the final three innings of the championship game. The Gators, ironically, also won 7-5. Ramsey, Dillon and dad Jonathan drove straight from the Mustang medal ceremony at Hampton Field to the Bronco game at Coaches Field to catch the final few innings.
articles.title: Three brothers win PBSF championships

articles.text: Bancroft Garden curator Brian Kemble Join Ruth Bancroft Gardens curator Brian Kemble this Saturday, June 7, in a guided tour of the garden’s unique spring blooms. Visitors will get a closer look at columnar, barrel, and Opuntia (paddle) cacti and learn more about their short but spectacular flowering stages. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees thousands of cacti and succulent species that grow in the garden’s three acres. As curator, he is in charge of hybridizing plants and finding two plants that have complementary characteristics and combining them to create new species. Kemble worked closely with Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, who was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Kemble will share Bancroft’s legacy with tour attendees and offer his decades of firsthand experience, having traveled extensively through the U.S., Mexico, and Chile in search of wild cactus populations. The garden will also be hosting a pop-up sale of unique cacti. Artisan crafts and refreshments will be available for purchase. The tour begins at 12:30 p.m. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/cactuscrawl-guided-tour-with-our-curator/ to learn more and to register.
articles.title: Guided tour of Bancroft Gardens with curator Brian Kemble held this Saturday

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony has announced its 2025–26 season, featuring four dynamic symphonic programs and four intimate chamber music performances. Following the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful six-year tenure, Berkeley Symphony will welcome an exceptional lineup of conductors to the podium for a season that promises to be both innovative and inspiring. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Executive Director Marion Atherton. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage. For the 2025–26 season, we’re excited to shine a light on stirring masterpieces from the classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works. From Dvořák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’s spirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ Symphony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” New subscription packages are available now. Returning subscribers may renew online, by mail, or by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800. Individual concert tickets will go on sale in mid-July. All Symphonic Series concerts will be held at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley; all Chamber Series concerts will take place at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Symphonic Series The Symphonic Series opens with Visions of Elysium on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025, at 4 p.m. Guest conductor Dina Gilbert, currently principal conductor of Les Grands Ballets Canadiens, associate conductor of the Orchestre symphonique de Montréal, and music director of the Walla Walla Symphony, will make her Berkeley Symphony debut. Known for her “contagious dynamism and audacious programming,” Gilbert will lead a powerful program featuring Beethoven’s monumental Symphony No. 3, Eroica, and Samy Moussa’s ethereal Elysium for Orchestra. The series continues with Refracted Light on Sunday, Oct. 5, 2025, at 4 p.m. Edwin Outwater, described by Michael Tilson Thomas as “one of the most innovative conductors on the scene today,” will lead the orchestra. Violinist Helen Kim is featured as soloist in Samuel Adams’ textured Chamber Concerto. The program also includes Yaz Lancaster’s Gender Envy and Haydn’s celebratory Symphony No. 100, Military. On Sunday, Nov. 16, 2025, at 4 p.m., Ming Luke will conduct Worlds Beyond, a program exploring reflection and transformation. Luke, noted for his “energy, creativity, and charisma,” opens with the West Coast premiere of Juan Pablo Contreras’ Alma Monarca, co-commissioned by Berkeley Symphony. Soprano Laquita Mitchell makes her Berkeley Symphony debut in Strauss’s evocative Four Last Songs. The evening continues with Missy Mazzoli’s cosmic Sinfonia (for Orbiting Spheres) and concludes with Shostakovich’s spirited Symphony No. 9. The symphonic season concludes with Fables and Folklore on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026, at 4 p.m. Internationally acclaimed conductor Carolyn Kuan, known for her “extraordinary versatility, innovative programming, and dedication to contemporary music,” will lead a program inspired by cultural traditions from around the world. Guitarist Marc Teicholz will perform Clarice Assad’s colorful Concerto for Guitar and Chamber Orchestra, O Saci-Pererê. The program also includes Huang Ruo’s vibrant Folk Songs for Orchestra and Dvořák’s lush Symphony No. 8. Chamber Series The Chamber Series begins with Roots and Resonances on Sunday, Feb. 22, 2026, at 4 p.m. Curated by acclaimed composer Samuel Adams, the concert features percussionist Haruka Fujii alongside a Berkeley Symphony string quartet in works that explore texture and timbre. The program includes music by Salina Fisher and Osvaldo Golijov, as well as Haruka Fujii’s Divisions and Adams’ Sundial. The series continues with French Connections, curated by Dianne Nicolini, the voice of Classical California KDFC, on Sunday, March 22, 2026, at 4 p.m. The concert will feature works by Francis Poulenc and Lili Boulanger, along with Gabriel Fauré’s Piano Quartet No. 1 in C minor. On Sunday, April 12, 2026, at 4 p.m., composer Juan Pablo Contreras—also featured in this season’s Symphonic Series— curates The Music of Muses, a program exploring artistic inspiration. In addition to works by Reena Esmail, Jennifer Higdon, and Bedřich Smetana, the concert will include Contreras’ own Musas Mexicanas, a tribute to three influential Mexican women who helped shape the country’s history. The Chamber Series concludes with I, Too, Sing America on Sunday, May 31, 2026, at 4 p.m., curated by James Parrish Smith, organist and music director of Berkeley’s First Presbyterian Church. The program features works by Brian Raphael Nabors and Anna Clyne—both past collaborators with Berkeley Symphony—as well as Dvořák’s seminal “American” String Quartet. About Berkeley Symphony For more than 50 years, Berkeley Symphony has established itself as a cultural cornerstone of the East Bay through its commitment to artistic excellence, community engagement, and introducing audiences to new and lesser-known works. Berkeley Symphony takes pride in crafting thoughtfully balanced programs that pair contemporary voices with beloved classics, creating meaningful musical experiences that resonate with the East Bay’s diverse community. Ticket Information Subscriptions to the Symphonic Series and the Chamber Series are on sale now. For the Symphonic Series, four-concert subscriptions range from $48 to $280. The Chamber Series subscriptions are $120. Subscriptions can be purchased by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800 or visiting berkeleysymphony.org.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) newest exhibition Students on Strike highlights the 1968 student-led strike at San Francisco State University (SFSU) and other noteworthy movements that established the nation’s first Black Studies Department and first College of Ethnic Studies at the university. The exhibition features historical and contemporary posters and photographs to draw comparisons between the strike at SFSU and the recent campus protests against the war in Gaza. In October 2024, San Francisco University State University students protested the Israel-Hamas war and the statewide school system’s ongoing investments in weapons manufacturers. Student-led demonstrations were seen at campuses across the state and at University of California schools. Museum visitors will be presented with an opportunity to integrate local historical context with more recent student strikes. Students on Strike is on view through May 31, 2026. Visit https://museumca.org/ on-view/students-on-strike/ to learn more. The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA)

pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, June 4, 2025 Arts & Entertainment Guided tour of Bancroft Gardens with curator Brian Kemble held this Saturday Bancroft Garden curator Brian Kemble By Allyson Aleksey Join Ruth Bancroft Gardens curator Brian Kemble this Saturday, June 7, in a guided tour of the garden’s unique spring blooms. Visitors will get a closer look at columnar, barrel, and Opuntia (paddle) cacti and learn more about their short but spectacular flowering stages. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees thousands of cacti and succulent species that grow in the garden’s three acres. As curator, he is in charge of hybridizing plants and finding two plants that have complementary characteristics and combining them to create new species. Kemble worked closely with Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, who was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Kemble will share Bancroft’s legacy with tour attendees and offer his decades of firsthand experience, having traveled extensively through the U.S., Mexico, and Chile in search of wild cactus populations. The garden will also be hosting a pop-up sale of unique cacti. Artisan crafts and refreshments will be available for purchase. The tour begins at 12:30 p.m. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/cactuscrawl-guided-tour-with-our-curator/ to learn more and to register. articles.text: Photo by Jeremy Daniel Broadway In Chicago’s production of “A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical,” stars Hannah Jewel Kohn and Nick Fradiani. The smash-hit musical and biographical drama A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical is now playing at San Francisco’s Golden Gate Theatre for a limited engagement through Sunday, June 22. Created in collaboration with singer-songwriter Neil Diamond himself, the musical tells the true story of a kid from Brooklyn’s meteoric rise to fame and how he became an American rock icon. “Some of my most thrilling nights have been while I was on tour, bringing my music to audiences across the world,” said Diamond. “Having A Beautiful Noise go on tour is an honor and I can’t wait for audiences across North America to experience this show. I hope they enjoy it as much as I have.” Including a catalogue of classics like “America,” “Forever in Blue Jeans,” and “Sweet Caroline,” Diamond’s story is portrayed by Nick Fradiani, who. played the title role in “American Idol” in 2015 and has since released his debut album “Hurricane” featuring the hit single “Beautiful Life.” Joining Fradiani are Tony Nominee Robert Westenberg (Neil Diamond – Now), Hannah Jewel Kohn (Marcia Murphey), Lisa Reneé Pitts (Doctor), Michael Accardo (Bert Berns/ Kieve Diamond), Tuck Milligan (Fred Weintraub/ Tommy O’Rourke), Kate A. Mulligan (Ellie Greenwich/ Rose Diamond) and Tiffany Tatreau(Jaye Posner). The show is produced by Ken Davenport and Bob Gaudio. “I couldn’t imagine a more perfect way to honor [Diamond’s] legacy than having A Beautiful Noise touring North America, visiting the same cities where he gave so many people so much joy,” Davenport said. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.broadwaysf.com/ events/a-beautiful-noise/golden-gate-theatre/calendar.

articles.text: Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 18, marking the 56th anniversary of the iconic, eclectic music festival along Highway 4 that brings together renowned artists and ensembles from various genres, including classical, jazz, rock, pop and more. The annual summer event is held in the picturesque Bear Valley nestled within the Sierra Nevada Mountains. All concerts are tucked inside an outdoor tent that holds over 500 guests This year’s lineup features an eclectic variety of music from 80’s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy,” said Board of Directors president Julia Mee. “From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone.” Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off the music festival with a performance on Friday, July 18. They are followed on Saturday by San Francisco’s Super Diamond, A Neil Diamond tribute band, delivering a dazzling show of Neil Diamond‘s hits from “Sweet Caroline” to “I Am…I Said.” After a week of tribute bands, the festival offers a performance of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Friday, July 25. The program includes guitarist Lyle Sheffler performing Spanish composer Joaquin Rodrigo’s evocative Concierto de Aranjuez, plus a piece by the relatively unknown 18th-century composer Marianna Martines. The July 27 program features music by Mozart and Haydn interspersed with contemporary pop tunes. A symphonic finale consists of the music of Leonard Bernstein, Erich Wolfgang Korngold, and Sergei Rachmaninoff on Friday, August 1. Bear Valley Music Festival’s annual gala event is on Saturday, August 2. Guests are invited to sport their finest period attire from the late 19th to early 20th century for an evening filled with music from that era. Gala ticket purchases include concert admission, a welcome glass of champagne or the evening’s themed cocktail, dinner with wine, and a live auction. Soprano Carrie Hennessey closes out this year’s festival on Sunday, August 3. Back by popular demand after last summer’s performance, Hennessey returns to perform favorite songs from Broadway and Hollywood, including music from Les Miserable, Lion King and The Sound of Music. Visit https://www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org to see the full festival lineup and purchase tickets. Single day tickets are now available. Bear Valley Music Festival runs from July 18 to August 3.

articles.text: Shutter Island, just off the coast of Massachusetts, is a federal maximum-security prison for the criminally insane. In the opening scene of Martin Scorsese’s film, Shutter Island, a small ferryboat slides out of a wispy fog and bears down on the only harbor on the island. Beyond stand dark, hunched buildings from another century. There is something foreboding, even ominous about the place, long ago named Ashecliffe Asylum. Terry Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo), both United States Marshals, have been sent to the island to search for an escaped patient, Rachel Soldano (Patricia Clarkson). Immediately, as the Marshals, in the company of grim prison guards, enter through the gates of the asylum, the noir mood of the film is established and then is slowly ratcheted up. Patients stand silently watching, some raking the lawns, other tending plants. All have a chilling, vacuous look. Soon it becomes evident, through a series of flashbacks, that Daniels is struggling with demons of his own. He explains to Chuck that his wife died in a fire, a tragedy that haunts him still, causing him severe migraines. Shutter Island is a series of set pieces in which Daniels discovers that the asylum is a labyrinth of elusive truths, long corridors, and dark rooms. A force 5 hurricane Leonardo DiCaprio in Shutter Island lashes the island and strands the two marshals until ferry service can be restored. Soldandos nowhere to be found and the staff, headed by Dr. Cawley (Ben Kingsley), can offer no explanation. She has literally vanished. And so the hunt continues. There are countless moments in the film where Scorsese pays explicit homage to Alfred Hitchcock, especially to the classic North by Northwest. And there’s a shower scene with Daniels letting the water sluice over his face that mirrors Psycho. Like so many of Hitchcock’s films, Shutter Island is a psychological thriller that twists and turns growing ever more convoluted and enigmatic. The cast is superb. Clarkson delivers a powerful and understated cameo as Soldando. Max Von Sydow, an extraordinary character actor, portrays a psychiatrist with allusions to a Nazi past. And Ben Kingsley, as the chief physician, is, again, exceptional. It’s DiCaprio’s most powerful role since The Aviator. It’s all but impossible to say more about this film without flirting with the ending, which surprises. Shutter Island will find its core audience – cinephiles who have followed the work of Martin Scorsese over these many decades. They will not be disappointed. Shutter Island. Directed by Martin Scorsese. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Ben Kingsley, Mark Ruffalo, Michele Williams and Max Von Sydow. 2 hrs., 18 min. Rated R. Released in 2010. articles.text: Rear Window, directed by Alfred Hitchcock, is widely regarded as a masterclass in suspenseful storytelling and cinematic craftsmanship. Tightly scripted and brilliantly staged, the film features four standout performances: James Stewart as L.B. “Jeff” Jeffries, a globe-trotting photographer confined to a wheelchair with a broken leg; Grace Kelly as Lisa Fremont, his elegant, high-society girlfriend; Thelma Ritter as Stella, Jeff’s wisecracking insurance nurse; and Wendell Corey in a supporting role as Detective Lieutenant Thomas, Jeff’s skeptical friend from his WWII days. The entire film unfolds within the walls of Jeff’s Manhattan apartment during a sweltering late summer. With windows wide open, Jeff spends his recovery observing the lives of neighbors across a shared courtyard. Their daily routines are mundane, almost comforting—until one evening, things change. Jeff notices something odd in the apartment of a salesman, Lars Thorwald. His wife, previously seen bedridden, suddenly vanishes. Thorwald’s suspicious behavior – late-night errands with a suitcase, frequent phone calls, the use of kitchen knives –draws Jeff’s attention.
