Beyond stand dark, hunched buildings from another century. There is something foreboding, even ominous about the place, long ago named Ashecliffe Asylum. Terry Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo), both United States Marshals, have been sent to the island to search for an escaped patient, Rachel Soldano (Patricia Clarkson). Immediately, as the Marshals, in the company of grim prison guards, enter through the gates of the asylum, the noir mood of the film is established and then is slowly ratcheted up. Patients stand silently watching, some raking the lawns, other tending plants. All have a chilling, vacuous look. Soon it becomes evident, through a series of flashbacks, that Daniels is struggling with demons of his own. He explains to Chuck that his wife died in a fire, a tragedy that haunts him still, causing him severe migraines. Shutter Island is a series of set pieces in which Daniels discovers that the asylum is a labyrinth of elusive truths, long corridors, and dark rooms. A force 5 hurricane Leonardo DiCaprio in Shutter Island lashes the island and strands the two marshals until ferry service can be restored. Soldandos nowhere to be found and the staff, headed by Dr. Cawley (Ben Kingsley), can offer no explanation. She has literally vanished. And so the hunt continues. There are countless moments in the film where Scorsese pays explicit homage to Alfred Hitchcock, especially to the classic North by Northwest. And there’s a shower scene with Daniels letting the water sluice over his face that mirrors Psycho. Like so many of Hitchcock’s films, Shutter Island is a psychological thriller that twists and turns growing ever more convoluted and enigmatic. The cast is superb. Clarkson delivers a powerful and understated cameo as Soldando. Max Von Sydow, an extraordinary character actor, portrays a psychiatrist with allusions to a Nazi past. And Ben Kingsley, as the chief physician, is, again, exceptional. It’s DiCaprio’s most powerful role since The Aviator. It’s all but impossible to say more about this film without flirting with the ending, which surprises. Shutter Island will find its core audience – cinephiles who have followed the work of Martin Scorsese over these many decades. They will not be disappointed. Shutter Island. articles.text: Felicity Jones and Eddie Redmayne in The Aeronauts When I first saw the trailer for The Aeronauts, I was immediately captivated. What evokes a sense of adventure more than a towering, colorful balloon (or better yet, a sky full of them) drifting away on invisible currents of wind? The film stars Felicity Jones as Amelia Wren, a daring balloon pilot, and Eddie Redmayne as James Glaisher, an aspiring meteorologist. Set in 1862, a time when weather prediction meant little more than stepping outside, the film promises a thrilling ascent into the unknown. Jones and Redmayne, who previously charmed audiences in The Theory of Everything, reunite here with high expectations. Their mission: to rise higher than anyone before –above 23,000 feet – aboard a striking red-and-white gas balloon. The balloon, built specifically for the film, stands 80 feet tall and 55 feet wide, with a roomy wicker basket below packed with sandbags, ropes, and scientific instruments. At launch, Wren and Glaisher are far from harmonious. He’s a meticulous, rule-bound scientist; she’s a reluctant pilot, skeptical of his gadgets and ambitions. After a brief setup, they ascend straight into a turbulent storm that sets the tone for their journey –breathtaking, but fraught with danger. As they climb to unprecedented altitudes, the temperature plummets and the air thins dangerously. No one has been this high before. While the film occasionally stalls during these airborne sequences – at times lacking dramatic tension beyond the sheer vastness of the sky – it regains momentum when the pair realizes they must descend or risk death. The valve to release gas is frozen shut, triggering a suspenseful final act that redeems the slower middle stretch. Ultimately, The Aeronauts is a visual spectacle with moments of true peril and awe. While it drifts now and then, its climactic payoff is worth the ride. The Aeronauts. Directed by Tom Harper. Starring Felicity Jones, Eddie Redmayne, Tom Courtenay. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: Benji the Hunted is a family-friendly adventure that finds its heart in the wild and delivers an engaging story for young viewers. As dogs go, Benji is extraordinary. The film opens with Benji’s trainer (Frank Inn, portraying himself) refusing to believe his beloved dog was lost at sea following a shipwreck. He hires a helicopter to search for him. Sure enough, Benji survives and washes ashore on a remote, forested island. So begins Benji’s breathtaking wilderness journey. The island turns out to be inhabited. Benji witnesses a hunter shoot a mother cougar, only to soon discover her four orphaned cubs. With unwavering loyalty, Benji takes it upon himself to protect them. After finding them shelter, he sets out to gather food. Spotting a quail roasting over a campfire near a cabin, Benji steals it for the cubs. Along the way, he faces off with the hunter again, evades a threatening wolf, and is briefly captured and tied up. One close call follows another, but Benji always manages to escape, keeping young viewers on the edge of their seats and cheering for their heroic pup. Meanwhile, Frank hasn’t stopped searching. As the helicopter reappears overhead, Benji realizes rescue may be near. Help is on the way. Benji the Hunted. Directed by Joe Camp. Starring Red Steagall, Frank Inn, Nancy Francis. 1 hr 28 min. Rated G. Released 1987. Streaming on Disney+, Prime Video, Apple TV, Fandango at Home. A scene from Benji the Hunted

articles.text: Saturday, June 7, 7:30 p.m. Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Left Coast Chamber Ensemble (LCCE) presents Spring Contrasts. The contrasting timbres of the violin, clarinet, and piano bring to life a vibrant variety of musical imaginations. The program includes Hannah Kendall’s Processional for solo piano, Kevin Day’s virtuosic Unquiet Waters, Mel Bonis’ lyrical Suite en Trio, Op. 59 for piano, violin, and clarinet, and selections from Roberto Sierra. The centerpiece is Béla Bartók’s Contrasts for violin, clarinet, and piano, a work written for American bandleader Benny Goodman. It incorporates Hungarian and Romanian folk music and Bulgarian rhythms. Tickets may be purchased at the door for $38/general, $18/students. Subsidized ARTS ACCESS tickets invite concertgoers to pay what they can. Advance tickets are available at $35/general and $15/student. For details visit www.leftcoastensemble.org/spring-contrasts or call 415/617-LCCE (5223). Sunday, June 8, 3:00 p.m. Breshears String Trio The Breshears String Trio will perform works by Mozart, Handel/Halvorsen, Vivaldi/Colton and von Dohnányi. The Trio consists of violinist Valery Breshears (15), violist Colin Breshears (12) and cellist Starla Breshears (17). They reside at their family home in San Pablo, California. Valery and Starla are currently members of the San Francisco Symphony Youth Orchestra. All are students at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. The family in various combinations has been performing as soloists, duets, trios and quartets for 12 years. Tickets will be available at the door or in advance at www.Brownpapertickets.com/e/6652231. Sunday, June 15, 3:00 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio This month’s Sunday afternoon Jazz Club event celebrates the summer solstice, Fathers’ Day, and William Jackman’s 81st birthday with an assortment of familiar songs mostly from the early and mid-20th century, including some jazz, some latin, ballads, and two more contemporary blues pieces, including Blues for Michael Morgan, written and premiered in 2021 shortly after his untimely passing. Sit back at a table, enjoy the music and some complimentary snacks as you listen to the music. Advance tickets are $25 at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6214927, or $30 at the door, cash/check only. Thursday, June 19, 6:00 p.m. La Speranza String Quartet La Speranza makes their highly anticipated California debut with Mozart’s Contemporaries, a concert program featuring works from their upcoming album. The music includes string quartet gems by French prodigy Hyacinthe Jadin (1776- 1800), the highly respected Paul Wranitzky (1756-1808), and the masterful Joseph Eybler (1765-1846). Named after the Italian word for hope, La Speranza was founded in 2016. Violinists Joanna Becker and Maria Lin, founder and violist Yvonne Smith, and cellist Fran Koiner are La Speranza’s core musicians. Find out more at www.la-speranza.com, and buy tickets at https://tinyurl.com/4zdscsca. Friday, June 20, 7:30 p.m. Vitamin Em Chamber Concert Vitamin Em returns to PCA by popular demand. A collective of some of the top musicians in the Bay Area – including Grammy-award-winners and nominees, Vitamin Em brings a wealth of experience and fearless improvisation, with music ranging from jazz, blues, and rock to Balkan, fiddle, and classical. This concert features Vitamin Em’s masterfully inventive string players Matt Szemela and Evan Price, violins; Emily Onderdonk, viola; Michael Graham, cello; and bassoonist Paul Hanson. Enjoy a casual reception afterwards for drinks and conversation with the musicians. Buy advance tickets at https:// www.simpletix.com/e/215100. Jason Sia is a pianist from Sacramento with an international career. His program felt like a personal and intimate concert. I like to arrive early and listen to the musicians as they warm up. Many secrets are revealed in warm-ups. I also enjoy speaking with the musicians. Fortunately, they do not know that I intend to write a review. Sia has a very relaxed way at the piano. He plays a little bit and then walks around and socializes. Then he plays some more and socializes some more. His personality is quiet but warm. Those characteristics are imparted in his music. He began by playing two pieces by Debussy. The composer drew his inspiration from paintings by impressionist artists. We were treated to an out of the ordinary interpretation of the 2nd movement from the Polish master’s Second Piano Concerto. This was an arrangement for solo piano by Carl Reinecke and was romantic in every way. Next came the heroic Pianist Jason Sia plays beautifully and eloquently. His music has no need for histrionics; his virtuosity comes through.

It’s all about inspiration By Joseph Gold You can’t go wrong when you attend an event at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The piano concert on Saturday evening is a perfect example. Jason Sia is a pianist from Sacramento with an international career. His program felt like a personal and intimate concert. I like to arrive early and listen to the musicians as they warm up. Many secrets are revealed in warm-ups. I also enjoy speaking with the musicians. Fortunately, they do not know that I intend to write a review. Sia has a very relaxed way at the piano. He plays a little bit and then walks around and socializes. Then he plays some more and socializes some more. His personality is quiet but warm. Those characteristics are imparted in his music. He began by playing two pieces by Debussy. The composer drew his inspiration from paintings by impressionist artists. If you closed your eyes, you could envision the paintings; that’s how vivid the performance was. The music was painted by velvet fingers on the keys. Next came three pieces by Chopin. We were treated to an out of the ordinary interpretation of the 2nd movement from the Polish master’s Second Piano Concerto. This was an arrangement for solo piano by Carl Reinecke and was romantic in every way. Next came the heroic Polonaise. Modern interpreters The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet have forgotten everything about the polonaise, nut Jason Sia does not play like other modern players. He knows his history. The polonaise was intended to be an aristocratic processional dance. An aristocrat never hurries. Sia’s interpretation was truly noble with an impressive crescendo at the end. All of the pieces during the first half were played at a high level. A Liszt Hungarian Rhapsody was like being in a gypsy café in Budapest. The piano erupted with virtuosity. And then, in an instant the pianist changed his tone colors to be gentle, delicate, and intimate. After intermission came the Porgy and Bess Fantasy by American pianist-composer Earl Wild. Sia played with superlative virtuosity. Warm applause greeted the concert, and Sia glanced at his wristwatch. I noticed a sly sense of humor in his demeanor. He responded by playing two encores. After the program, the audience was treated to a table set with beautiful desserts and drinks. That’s the way it is at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, thanks largely to the deft, quiet touch of the Center’s president, Sue Malick. It was a reasonable price to attend an outstanding concert and an elegant post-concert meal. It’s always fun to talk with the performers after the concert. Sia is a very friendly fellow. He told me that he began his piano studies at the age of six. It sure helps to begin musical studies at an early age. That’s the way things should be. Unfortunately in the letters to the editor section of the Piedmont Post of May 28 we were told of a “regression” in Piedmont’s public schools. The letter states that the people on the school board have approved a program to end instrumental music for fourth graders. What a misguided change. When I taught in the San Francisco public schools, 100% of the students received weekly music lessons. and Instrumental class lessons began in the third grade. I went to every class beginning with kindergarten. I hope that the Piedmont Post will re-print the letter from the concerned parents. Music education is very important in our public schools and we must speak up. The future of our children is at stake. Pianist Jason Sia plays beautifully and eloquently. His music has no need for histrionics; his virtuosity comes through. Your Personal Driver I’ll take You where you need to go: Shopping, Doctor, Airport... articles.text: When it comes to wine, Mendocino County has often lived in the shadow of Napa and Sonoma its neighbors to the south. Yet that obscurity has turned out to be a plus for today’s wine consumer because Mendocino County is home to some of the greatest values in the California wine world. And no winery fits this description better than McNab Ridge. Its winery has a very rich heritage. Mendocino County’s first vineyards were planted during the Civil War by immigrants seeking to carve out new lives in this fertile part of Northern California. McNab Valley just north of Hopland is named after the Scottish immigrant Alexander McNab who raised sheep on a 10,000-acre land grant in 1866. He became well known locally for the skill of his herding dogs which he developed into a breed, the McNab, which is still a beloved working breed in the area. Adolph Parducci was one of many Italian immigrants who settled in Mendocino County arriving in 1912. He sold grapes for home winemaking during prohibition, and later when it became legal his descendants started Parducci winery. John Parducci and his family became one of the go to wineries in California in the 1970’s. In the 1980’s the Parducci brand sold, and John Parducci founded the McNab Ridge Winery in 1999 to continue his love for making Mendocino County wine. John Parducci’s grandson Rich Parducci grew up in the Mendocino County wine industry like his grandfather and studied enology at California State University in Fresno. And no winery fits this description better than McNab Ridge. Its winery has a very rich heritage. Mendocino County’s first vineyards were planted during the Civil War by immigrants seeking to carve out new lives in this fertile part of Northern California. McNab Valley just north of Hopland is named after the Scottish immigrant Alexander McNab who raised sheep on a 10,000-acre land grant in 1866. He became well known locally for the skill of his herding dogs which he developed into a breed, the McNab, which is still a beloved working breed in the area. Adolph Parducci was one of many Italian immigrants who settled in Mendocino County arriving in 1912. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had a cloudy, cool morning last Wednesday and a special walk. Piedmont Fire Chief Brannigan was with them. He had been with the group in March to tell them about what they should do to be prepared if an emergency evacuation is required. The fire department doesn’t have enough resources to do it alone and will need to rely on the community to evacuate in a wildfire and help keep Piedmont safe. Chief Brannigan said there were two parts to this effort. First, there will be a citywide Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday, June 14th at 9 AM. The Fire Department will send instructions for the at-home activity via AC Alert on the morning of June 14. The Fire Department has designed the at-home exercise to be simple, easy-to-complete, and high impact, with clear instructions and discussion prompts, things like: What route would you take if roads were closed? Who grabs the pets? Where will you go if you can’t come home? Taking the time to talk through these questions now would save critical minutes in a real evacuation emergency and help you feel confident that you know what to do if the worst happens. At the top, on the narrow Scenic, Chief Brannigan shared more fire information. Wildfires can come from different directions and you don’t know where a fire could be coming from. You should have two ways out of your residence and two modes of transportation. Autos may not do it. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 4, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers head to the hills By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group had a cloudy, cool morning last Wednesday and a special walk. Piedmont Fire Chief Brannigan was with them. He had been with the group in March to tell them about what they should do to be prepared if an emergency evacuation is required. The fire department doesn’t have enough resources to do it alone and will need to rely on the community to evacuate in a wildfire and help keep Piedmont safe. Chief Brannigan said there were two parts to this effort. First, there will be a citywide Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday, June 14th at 9 AM. It will be a scenario in which Piedmont’s firefighters and police will be practicing a real-world evacuation scenario with residents in the Blair/Scenic neighborhood. This will be followed by a community debrief and conversation around 10 AM at the Piedmont Fire Station. Chief Brannigan said the second part of the effort is an at-home exercise for everyone outside of the Blair/Scenic area, which guides people in a verbal walk-through of an evacuation scenario. The Fire Department will send instructions for the at-home activity via AC Alert on the morning of June 14. The Fire Department has designed the at-home exercise to be simple, easy-to-complete, and high impact, with clear instructions and discussion prompts, things like: What route would you take if roads were closed? Who grabs the pets? Where will you go if you can’t come home? Taking the time to talk through these questions now would save critical minutes in a real evacuation emergency and help you feel confident that you know what to do if the worst happens. If you aren’t yet registered for AC Alert, the emergency notification system for Piedmont and Alameda County, you can sign up http:// bit.ly/ACAlert. After this introduction, Chief Brannigan joined the walkers on their climb to Scenic Avenue. They went up Highland and Pala Avenues, and enjoyed roses in front yards and lovely cedar shake shingle homes along the way. The group arrived at the 161-foot, somewhat hidden set of stairs that go up to Scenic and made their ascent one step at a time. At the top, on the narrow Scenic, Chief Brannigan shared more fire information. Wildfires can come from different directions and you don’t know where a fire could be coming from. You should have two ways out of your residence and two modes of transportation. Autos may not do it. Abandoned cars have blocked roads in emergencies. Piedmont has about four to six high danger “Red Flag” days each year and extra fire personnel are on duty during them. The narrow Scenic Avenue with cars parked all along it made clear the almost impossibility of all residents evacuating by car at the same time. The walkers continued up Scenic to Alta Avenue and then back to Scenic. They regrouped at the EBMUD “Reservoir Number 2” at Scenic and Blair Avenue and talked about it. It occupies more than nine acres straddling the Oakland-Piedmont border with 8.3 acres in Piedmont. Its 22.8-million-gallon water storage tank provided water for Piedmont from 1905 to 2003. The facility was decommissioned and drained in 2003 as part of EBMUD’s facility modernization program, and Piedmont’s water now comes from other large tanks in the Oakland Hills. The group then started their descent and return to the city center via Mountain, Hagar, Pacific, and Dormidera Avenues. On the way down, they realized that walker Diane Jimenez, who as with them, had to evacuate her Southern California home as a result of the Eaton Fire. She shared her first-hand experience. They knew there was fire in the area, but thought the fire department would give them a warning and tell them to evacuate if it was necessary. So, they stayed put until three in the morning when the warning and evacuation order were issued. Then, everyone made a rush to get out. Diane’s advice was: if you see fire, get out. Don’t wait. Besides the important papers you need, take the things, like pictures, that you will need emotionally. Many of her friends’ homes burned down and the loss of these items has been traumatizing. It was also suggested that people scan important photos. The walkers thanked Chief Brannigan for being with them and sharing this important information. The message was clear. Wildfire risk in Piedmont is real, but so is our ability to prepare. The Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday, June 14th, will be a good start. articles.text: The 11th Annual Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival returns Saturday, June 14, from noon to 6 p.m. in Oakland’s Montclair Village. The event, presented by the Ken Betts Company and Montclair Village Association, features live music, beverage tastings, family activities, and community programming. Admission is free and open to all ages. Tasting packages are available for $55 in advance or $65 at the event, and include access to samples from more than 50 craft beer, wine, and cider producers, along with a commemorative festival glass. Festival manager Jacob Cohen noted the continued collaboration with local producers. “It’s been a rare pleasure working with local breweries and wineries these last three years,” he said. With curatorial input from Farmstead Cheeses & Wines and CaDraftTech, the event showcases a range of regional beverages. Live music will be performed on the Mister Beever’s Paws & Claws stage, powered by Meet Your Core Pilates. Performers include Dos Four, Namorados Da Lua, the Khalil Abdullah Quartet, and a cast performance from the upcoming Woodminster Summer Musicals production of Anastasia. Dos Four, the festival headliner, features Cuban-American artist Leyder Chapman. Namorados Da Lua, a Bay Area band, blends Brazilian rhythms with influences from jazz, reggae, and funk. The Khalil Abdullah Quartet, led by guitarist and educator Brother Khalil, opens the festival with a jazz-infused set. New this year, the Flair Travel & Adventure Zone will offer family-friendly activities and interactive experiences related to global travel and culture. Additional programming will take place in the Play-Palooza Family Fun Zone, sponsored by F&M Bank. The Oakland Fire Department’s Random Acts Parade Rig will also be onsite. Food will be available from local chefs and vendors, with offerings ranging from Thai street food and Mexican fare to classic festival options. Montclair Village restaurants and shops will remain open during the event, and artisan vendors will be featured throughout the festival area. Get discounted drink packages today at MontclairVillage.com. The Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival in 2022 Photo credit Peter Marcus.

articles.text: In mid-May, Troop 1 embarked on a kayaking and camping trip at Elkhorn Slough, one of the largest estuaries in California along the coast of Monterey Bay between Santa Cruz and Monterey. Elkhorn Slough has the highest sea otter concentration in the state, along with dozens of other aquatic species. Scouts paired up in double kayaks, and after a short lesson on kayaking, ventured out of the harbor and into the slough. While many Scouts zoomed off, a few pairs stayed behind in a small cove, sheltered from the wind. Regardless of their location, all Scouts encountered a plethora of wildlife. Rafts (groups) of otters lounged on their backs in the seagrass munching away on crabs and clams and massaging air bubbles into their fur to stay afloat. Small harmless jellyfish called Velella Velella floated along by the hundreds, blown into the slough by an unlucky wind. Seals Troop 1 Scouts ready for their kayaking adventure sped through the water, investigating the kayaks, while sea lions lounged on the beach. While exploring, the scouts in the cove saw what appeared to be a large rock in the middle of the seagrass. It turned out to be a dead seal on its back! After enjoying the beauty of the slough however, came the arduous journey back. Winds reached over 20mph and many Scouts struggled to fight the wind funneling into the Slough. Everyone eventually made their way back, tired, bedraggled, but smiling. The Scouts continued on to their campsite at Sunset Beach State Park and set up camp. Fortunately, the campsite was close to the water, so everyone was able to enjoy the beach. Some fished in the surf while others played with large pieces of driftwood they found on the beach. The Scouts enjoyed a hearty taco dinner before lighting a fire, roasting marshmallows and battling each other to see who could make the most ridiculous s’more creation possible. The next morning the Scouts packed up, ate a delicious breakfast, and set off for home. The trip was not only a memorable adventure with California sea life, but also a great bonding experience, especially for the newer Scouts, who got a warm and adventurous introduction to Troop 1. Theodore Cost is a member of Piedmont Scouts Troop 1. Troop 1 Scouts Jonathan Pell (left), Ryan Morrison, Alex Dean, Cade Ogles, Theodore Cost, Adrien Messina, Ciaran Gallagher, Zeke Stein, and Finn Holder enjoying their time on the beach. Rafts of otters could be seen relaxing in the seagrass, massaging air bubbles into their fur to stay afloat. Scouts Zeke Stein (left), Adrien Messina, Finn Holder, Ciaran Gallagher, Theodore Cost, Cade Ogles, and Alex Dean enjoy a gorgeous sunset atop a sand dune on the beach.

articles.text: Book review by Lawrence Siskind In 1868, Alexander Gardner, famous for photographing a timeworn Abraham Lincoln, traveled to Wyoming to photograph the work of six peace commissioners who were negotiating treaties with the local Indians. At Fort Laramie, Gardner posed the commissioners: three on the left and three on the right. Between them, he posed a small, dark-skinned girl. Collections of Gardner’s photographs identify the six men, all distinguished military and political leaders. But who was that girl in the middle? How did she find herself standing between the six imposing white warriors? Thomas Carlyle deemed history the story of great men. For retired Princeton professor Martha Sandweiss, history can also be the story of a small, shy girl. A self-described “truffle hunter,” Sandweiss rooted about in town libraries, school archives, and family living rooms, searching for clues about the girl in the middle. She found her. Along the way she also found a throng of others – white settlers, Indians, halfbreeds, rogues, idealists, utopians, murderers – all with their own fascinating accounts. The girl in the middle was Sophie Mousseau, known as Little Flower, the eight-year old daughter of an Oglala Lakota woman and her French Canadian husband. Sophie’s mother was wounded at Blue Water Creek in Nebraska during a bloody raid led by General William Harney in 1855. Harney’s Lakota nickname was “Woman Killer” – which tells us much about the man. After the massacre, Harney rounded up the survivors and marched them to Fort Laramie, where Sophie’s mother met and married her future father. Thirteen years after serving as the unwitting matchmaker of her parents, this same General Harney returned to Fort Laramie as a peace commissioner. As he posed with Sophie for Gardner’s photograph, he had no idea who the girl was, or how he had affected her life. In describing Harney’s life, Sandweiss introduces us to Judge Charles “Horse” Allen, who presided over an earlier trial of Harney for murdering a slave. The judge was typical of the colorful characters populating the book. According to a contemporary reporter: “The Judge’s educational advantages were certainly very limited and he never improved himself much by study, for he had but little relish for books, and his knowledge of the law was very superficial.” He also “had a taste for fights” and would “adjourn his court to go watch a good one.” Harney was acquitted. Alexander Gardner was not the first photographer to visit Fort Laramie. Two years earlier, an idealistic Quaker named Ridgeway Glover had arrived. Convinced that the Indians would not harm so earnest a visitor, he defied the locals’ warning and wandered outside the Fort alone. His body was discovered later. Reports differed on whether he had been beheaded, disemboweled, or burned, but all agreed that he had been scalped. diers who found Glover’s corpse was a Civil War veteran named Posey Ryan. A decade later, he would meet and marry Sophie, who bore him five children. Ryan left Sophie for another woman – taking all five children with him. Sophie was fortunate. After marrying the woman for whom he left Sophie, Ryan later quarreled with her over money, and shot her and a step-daughter dead in a restaurant. “I didn’t have the slightest idea of killing them when I went into the restaurant,” Posey told a friend. “But … I was mad.” What of Sophie herself? She remarried, this time to a mixed-race medicine show performer, who later served as a translator for prominent anthropologists. Sophie bore him eight children. Having brought a total of 13 children into the world, she lived out her life on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, where she found work as a laundress at a boarding school. She took advantage of her location to learn to read and write. This is not a book for the genteel or delicate. The Indians are no more idealized than the white invaders. In 1906, Sophie’s father, embittered by Indian raids on his business, told an interviewer that the Indians “ought to be killed and burned as the whites were by them.” His Indian daughter’s reaction to this grim opinion is not reported. Nor is this a book for advocates of “intersectionality.” Minorities did not find common cause with each other. A peace commissioner’s wife hears Frederick Douglass declare that black people deserved civil rights more than Indians, because “the negro is more like the white man than the Indian in his tastes and tendencies, and disposition to accept civilization.” Professor Sandweiss narrates her story in an easy, friendly manner. She is not above leavening her reporting with literary flourishes now and then. Describing Sophie’s death, she writes: “She passed away in her simple dugout home alongside a trout stream. The bearskin hanging over her front door flapped in the winds blowing from the west.” Perhaps the bearskin flapped, but that’s prose, not history. In an age when lives were nasty, br utish, and short, Sophie’s longevity is astonishing. She survived poverty, wars, massacres, and natural disasters to live to 1936, midway through Franklin Roosevelt’s second term. General Harney, the oldest of her fellow photographic subjects, had been born in 1800, in the last days of John Adams’s presidency. The collective lifespans embodied in Gardner’s photograph cover more than half of the nation’s history. In traversing the long, convoluted trail to Sophie, we are fortunate to have a guide as indefatigable as Professor Sandweiss. The Girl in the Middle: A Recovered History of the American West. By Martha A. Sandweiss. Princeton University Press, 351 pages.

In VEX, drivers can’t destroy or intentionally tip opponents, but opponents can be pinned and pushed around. “VEX is very easy to do from your home,” said Swei. “Because of the small team size, and you don’t need as many resources.” The game winning score by the Double Play and Jackson Area Robotics alliance in the World Championship finals. Swei does the programming and building of the robot, Jung is the driver, and the team’s mentor is Ali Muhammad. When deciding how to build his robot. Swei chose to put six of the eight allotted motors into the main drive and two to score the rings, prioritizing speed. “There are definitely a ton of applied concepts from physics, like force. You have to start the match in a certain size, and we aimed to maximize the geometry of our arm, so it could reach out as far as possible,” said Swei. Swei’s cousins and uncle introduced him to robotics in elementary school and Mikey started up his own team in fourth grade. Seven years later, Swei has earned a world championship and still has two more years of high school left. “For the programming aspects I took computer science classes in middle school and high school and that helped me understand some of the concepts. There’s a lot you can do with just simple, basic programming,” said Swei. More that 30,000 students from 50 states and 50 countries participated in the tournament, with the final rounds held in the Hutchison Convention Center in Dallas, Texas. articles.text: Around 145 Piedmont High School (PHS) seniors participated in the first “Cap and Gown Day” on May 21, returning to the elementary school sites where their Piedmont education began. Soonto-be graduates donned their purple caps and gowns and took a walk down memory lane, stopping to visit former teachers and current students at Beach, Wildwood and Havens. Senior Class President Dean Olliphant and Vice President Juliana DeYoung were the masterminds behind the event. They coordinated with the three elementary school principals, arranged for seniors to be excused from their second-period classes for 45 minutes, and ensured caps and gowns could be picked up in time. “The graduates got this full-circle moment, being able to go back to where their education started and the place where they grew up,” said DeYoung. articles.text: American f lags lined the walkways of Mountain View Cemetery on Monday, May 26, as a crowd of nearly 300 people attended its 101st Annual Memorial Day Ceremony. Audience members came to pay tribute to American servicemen and women who lost their lives in the line of duty. The morning’s program included a guest speaker, music, a color guard provided by Piedmont Scout Council Troop 6, and the annual release of doves. Scouts from Troop 6 prepare to act as the event’s color guard.
articles.title: Mountain View Cemetery marks 101st Memorial Day Ceremony

articles.text: Three key presentations are scheduled for the May 28 school board meeting, including recognitions for retiring staff and this year’s four school board members. The board will also hold a first reading of proposed changes to next year’s elementary English Language Arts curriculum, a process that has been years in the making. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich will join seven elementary teachers and a reading specialist to present findings from the district’s pilot program, which included 21 teachers. Following the presentation, the ELA Adoption Committee will formally recommend replacing the current Lucy Calkins-authored curriculum with Fishtank Learning at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood. The Class of 2025’s gift will also be announced during the meeting. The proposed project will add a green wall between the 20s and 30s buildings at Piedmont Middle School as part of a broader campus beautification effort. Also on the agenda is a second reading of the Mobile Communication Device policy, which seeks to finalize rules around student cell phone use in future school years. Lastly, the board will address inconsistencies between the district’s LGBTQ Resolution and current flag practices. Although the resolution directs the district to fly the Pride flag only during June, since October 2024 the current practice has been to display it year-round. Trustees will consider aligning the resolution with current practice. Review board background documents at https://simbli.eboard solutions.com/SB_Meetings/ ViewMeeting.aspx?S=36030373 &MID=40531&Tab=Agenda. The meeting will start at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall at 120 Vista Avenue, and can also be participated in remotely via Zoom. us/j/84569929618. articles.text: On Friday, May 23, fourthgrade students from Ben Spencer and Alicia Martinez’s classes at Beach School participated in a community service field trip, collecting 120 pounds of trash. In small groups led by parent volunteers, students fanned out across neighborhoods in Piedmont and Oakland, gathering 4,690 individual pieces of litter in just two hours. Back on campus, students cataloged every item before weighing the total haul. Among the debris were paper plates, cigarette butts, food wrappers and orange peels—evidence that even everyday waste can end up in unexpected and unwanted places. Wearing gloves, tongs and safety goggles, students explored local parks and streets, including the Rose Garden, Piedmont Avenue, Grand Avenue, Pleasant Valley and Dracena Park. After the cleanup, students Beach fourth grade trash pickers and community beautifiers circle around the 4,690 pieces of trash collected on May 23.

articles.text: Editor: From the music of Grease to Gustav Holst’s Jupiter, the Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School bands and orchestras performed last week, an inspiring musical celebration to cap the school year. But our district’s sterling music program is now being threatened. Recently, the school board approved a program to end instrumental music education for fourth graders, an unnecessarily rushed move that is short-sighted and will limit the musical potential of our students. Learning an instrument takes time, and it requires repeated hands-on practice to become proficient enough to play more than “Hot Cross Buns.” Delaying instrumental music education means that students will have less of an opportunity to master an instrument. It will have a major impact on middle and high school band and orchestra. And students will lose out on the cognitive benefits that come from learning an instrument. Elementary and middle school students have recently complained about a frustrating music experience. Instead of fixing this problem – such as hiring a full-time music teacher or incorporating more classroom support – Piedmont threw the baby out with the bathwater. Our fourth graders will now get 60 minutes a week of “theater arts.” The school board heralded this as an exciting change. While we love what theater offers for kids, it should not come at the expense of music. Our kids already have ready access to theater, including in the classroom. But there are few opportunities for students to try a variety of instruments and perform in groups. Now they won’t have that chance until 5th grade. Our neighboring school districts – including Berkeley, Orinda, Lafayette, and Moraga – introduce instruments in the fourth grade. With regression such as this, we will continue to lose students to private schools. Our district is not being innovative. It is taking a step back in the musical education it offers to our students. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District awarded Cory Smegal the 2025 Arthur Hecht Award as the school volunteer of the year. She was presented with the award during the May 14 school board meeting. Smegal served two terms on the school board from 2016-2024. During her eight year tenure on the school board Smegal bridged the gap from pre- to post-pandemic education in Piedmont. Education and volunteering is a family tradition. Cory’s mother in-law, Sue Smegal, won the award in 2020 and was a member of the school board. “Thanks to Sue, for not only convincing Tom [husband] and me to move to Piedmont but she was also so inspiring with her years of service,” said Cory. “Thanks for being such a strong example of leadership and community involvement and community support.” Cor y’s legacy includes reopening the schools after the pandemic and pushing for the building of the STEAM building and Alan Harvey Theater. Before holding public office she volunteered tirelessly by raising money for the Giving Campaign and the middle school via March Mingle. “Cory is optimistic and enthusiastic. She believes in the best of people and thinks creatively to solve problems. She is ridiculously smart and has forgotten more about the district than others could aspire to know,” said Vice President Ruchi Medhekar. Piedmont Mayor, Betsy Smegal Andersen is Cory’s sister-inlaw. “When you ran for school board you knew it was going to be a lot of work but you didn’t know Covid was coming. But the second time you ran, you did know Covid was coming,” said Andersen. term in 2020, Smegal provided continuity in leadership and a steady hand when the schools were closed due to Covid. Smegal sought reelection to the board despite the microscope upon school board members and education decision makers across the globe. “Some of our meetings during Covid had several hundred people. There’s nothing like an experience of breaking down in tears and sobbing in front of hundreds of people, so I’m trying not to cry tonight,” said Cory. Smegal’s fingerprints on the district are easy to see. She served on the board while hiring Interim-Superintendent Donald Evans, and current Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. The award is named for Art Hecht, a former school Board member and a tireless community volunteer in Piedmont and Oakland schools. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. He was very active with the founding of the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by school board member Dewey Watson in his memory.

articles.text: Limited-edition Library card now available In celebration of Children’s Fairyland’s 75th anniversary, the beloved storybook theme park has partnered with Oakland Public Library to debut a limited-edition library card designed by 12-year-old Ezekiel Ramos, the winner of a citywide youth art contest. Beginning May 30 the card will be available at all Oakland Public Library branches while supplies last. Only 4,000 limited-edition cards will be distributed. Community members can request one with a valid ID at any Oakland Public Library location. Existing cardholders may transfer their account to the new card. The release coincides with the kickoff of Summer at Oakland Public Library, which offers a wide range of educational and creative programs for all ages— giving families even more reasons to visit their local library and celebrate the joy of reading. As part of its milestone year, Fairyland invited local chilLibrary Card Image dren to enter the “Library Card Contest: Fairyland Edition.” Bay Area youth ages 5–12 were asked to submit original artwork inspired by Fairyland, storytelling, and imagination. Ezekiel’s colorful design—featuring park icons Willie the Whale and Ching Lung, the Happy Dragon—was selected from more than 100 submissions. “I thought entering the competition would be a great chance to showcase my artwork,” said Ezekiel Ramos, Fairyland’s limited-edition library card artist. “I’ve been to Fairyland many times since I was little. I took two of the most iconic figures I could think of and made it my project for a few weeks. I’m proud to know that people will use my art in their everyday lives, and I hope other kids see it and feel like they can do something like this, too.” To learn more about upcoming programming, visit fairyland. org/75. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Construction, road work block both sides of Piedmont’s busiest street Signage now marks detours for temporary sidewalk closures on Grand Avenue, between Oakland and Linda Avenues. The closure prevents pedestrian traffic on both sides of the street due to an apparent breakdown of communication between a housing construction project and the ongoing Grand Avenue Repavement Project. Piedmont resident and Greenbank Neighborhood Watch Coordinator Mark Herrick first noticed the safety issue presented by the sidewalk closures three weeks ago. “It caught me off-guard that they weren’t aware of this problem,” he said. After almost three weeks of correspondence with the City, Herrick sent in a video after repeatedly being told that the sidewalk should still be accessible from the other side. The City has since updated the signage to include detours on both sides of the street. “It sure took a lot of effort and frankly a lot of broken glass, because I had to jump up and down and send some hard emails to get them to listen to me,” said Herrick about the City’s less-than-satisfactory response. Herrick reported difficulty getting members of City Council involved, with one excepNew detour signage directs pedestrians away from construction areas. tion. While Herrick struggled to get the City to understand and recognize the safety issue, Councilmember Lorrell Plimier seemed to show genuine concern. “She was sensitive to the issues, she responded to me directly, she came down to my house… and she saw the problems and she saw that there was really poor signage that was not clear. And as a result of her coming, things got better,” said Herrick. With construction of new pedestrian bulb-outs on Grand Avenue underway, officials remind community members to follow instructions on safety signage and use marked detours. The pedestrian crossings will remain closed at the intersections of Grand Avenue with Linda and Greenbank Avenues while electrical infrastructure is being installed to support flashing safety beacons. Closures will continue until bulb-out construction is complete, expected in June. The work is part of a $1.5 million roadway improvement and pedestrian safety project on Grand Ave., funded in part by a $500,000 grant from the Alameda County Transportation Commission. The work includes bulb-outs and flashing beacons at the Linda and Greenbank intersections, as well as bicycle safety enhancements and ADA curb ramps at all street crossings. Once bulb-outs at Linda and Greenback Avenues are complete, construction will begin at the intersection of Grand and Fairview. There, the City will install permanent bulb-out islands and a bioswale – a landscaped channel that improves drainage and supports soil filtering of storm water. The final phase of the project, scheduled for August, will re-pave Grand Avenue from Fairview to Greenbank. Roadside construction has caused changes to pedestrian pathways along Grand Avenue.
articles.title: Temporary sidewalk closure on Grand Ave.

articles.text: Meet Black Tie, a dapper 10-pound Chihuahua mix. Black Tie is about 8, but he is still full of spunk. On walks he happily trots along with one ear perked up and his tail wagging. He lives in a foster home and enjoys playing with his foster brothers, napping while his foster mom is at work, and snuggling on the couch. Black Tie shines when he feels safe and loved. articles.text: Beautiful Odessa is a playful 5-year-old with a perfect mix of curiosity and coziness. She loves chasing wand toys, napping on sunny windowsills, and trailing her favorite person around the house. She’s looking for a quiet, adult home where she can be the only cat. Odessa is sensitive to loud noises and too much stimulation, so she takes a daily anti-anxiety med (easily mixed into breakfast) to stay relaxed and content. She’ll do best with a calm routine and a catsavvy guardian who can tune into her cues. Independent but loyal, Odessa is always nearby, ready to follow you from room to room. pages.text: Wednesday, May 28, 2025 5 Temporary sidewalk closure on Grand Ave. Construction, road work block both sides of Piedmont’s busiest street By Tony Simons Signage now marks detours for temporary sidewalk closures on Grand Avenue, between Oakland and Linda Avenues. The closure prevents pedestrian traffic on both sides of the street due to an apparent breakdown of communication between a housing construction project and the ongoing Grand Avenue Repavement Project. Piedmont resident and Greenbank Neighborhood Watch Coordinator Mark Herrick first noticed the safety issue presented by the sidewalk closures three weeks ago. “It caught me off-guard that they weren’t aware of this problem,” he said. After almost three weeks of correspondence with the City, Herrick sent in a video after repeatedly being told that the sidewalk should still be accessible from the other side. The City has since updated the signage to include detours on both sides of the street. “It sure took a lot of effort and frankly a lot of broken glass, because I had to jump up and down and send some hard emails to get them to listen to me,” said Herrick about the City’s less-than-satisfactory response. Herrick reported difficulty getting members of City Council involved, with one excepNew detour signage directs pedestrians away from construction areas. tion. While Herrick struggled to get the City to understand and recognize the safety issue, Councilmember Lorrell Plimier seemed to show genuine concern. “She was sensitive to the issues, she responded to me directly, she came down to my house… and she saw the problems and she saw that there was really poor signage that was not clear. And as a result of her coming, things got better,” said Herrick. With construction of new pedestrian bulb-outs on Grand Avenue underway, officials remind community members to follow instructions on safety signage and use marked detours. The pedestrian crossings will remain closed at the intersections of Grand Avenue with Linda and Greenbank Avenues while electrical infrastructure is being installed to support flashing safety beacons. Closures will continue until bulb-out construction is complete, expected in June. The work is part of a $1.5 million roadway improvement and pedestrian safety project on Grand Ave., funded in part by a $500,000 grant from the Alameda County Transportation Commission. The work includes bulb-outs and flashing beacons at the Linda and Greenbank intersections, as well as bicycle safety enhancements and ADA curb ramps at all street crossings. Once bulb-outs at Linda and Greenback Avenues are complete, construction will begin at the intersection of Grand and Fairview. There, the City will install permanent bulb-out islands and a bioswale – a landscaped channel that improves drainage and supports soil filtering of storm water. The final phase of the project, scheduled for August, will re-pave Grand Avenue from Fairview to Greenbank. Roadside construction has caused changes to pedestrian pathways along Grand Avenue. articles.text: 2-week trip to raise awareness of autism A group of students from Piedmont High School, HeadRoyce School, and other high schools will travel to Ethiopia this June for a two-week service and advocacy trip focused on autism awareness and education. The initiative is being led by Nathan Bekele, a junior at Piedmont High School, as a part of his membership in the Piedmont Community Service Crew and in partnership with the Melu’e Foundation. Through the Ethiopian Ministry of Health, Bekele was able to establish the connection and secure a partnership with the foundation that supports children with autism and their families. The goal of the trip is to raise awareness of the stigma of autism in Ethiopia where affected children are often isolated from their communities. The local students will visit schools and community centers in Addis Ababa to host educational workshops, volunteer at the Melu’e Foundation’s multidisciplinary treatment center – one of only two autism centers in the entire country – and deliver equipment and the supplies needed by the center for children and families. Joaquin Fierro, a freshman at Piedmont High School, says, “I’m looking forward to making a meaningful impact on those in need, while also being able to explore a new and exciting culture. “I really want to help kids that need it the most. I am also excited to share this experience with my friends,” said Bekele. The trip will begin on June 10 and conclude on June 29. The service trip was made possible in part by Bekele’s “Taste of Ethiopia with Jazz” fundraiser dinner hosted at Lemat Restaurant in Berkeley, which raised over $35,000 to support the initiative. Tax deductible donations may be made to: https://givebutter. com/NathanforAutism The students look forward to reporting their experiences after they return from the trip. To learn more about Piedmont Community Service Crew and how we encourage youth leadership development among teens, visit PCServiceCrew.org, or contact Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net.
articles.title: Local students plan summer trip to Ethiopia

articles.text: Volunteers for Nature Program Manager, California Academy of Sciences Get involved: rediscover local nature through volunteering Volunteering is more than lending a hand—it’s a meaningful way to connect with your community, spend time outdoors, and make a tangible difference close to home. Whether you’re newly retired, raising a family, or simply looking to give back, nature-based volunteer opportunities offer a chance to support the environment while boosting your own well-being. At the California Academy of Sciences, we offer a variety of local volunteer programs—both inside the museum and out in the community. One of our recent pilots, Volunteers for Nature, engaged college students and early-career professionals in regeneration projects across the Bay Area. In our latest initiative with the Presidio Trust, volunteers helped restore San Francisco’s sand dunes by supporting the silvery blue butterfly, a species that symbolizes the extinct Xerces blue, last seen in the Presidio in the 1940s. Efforts like these help revive local ecosystems—and they’re open to everyone. which is essential to supporting pollinators. Search for local conservation organizations to see what’s happening near you. If plants aren’t your thing, consider joining Snapshot Cal Coast, a statewide effort to document coastal biodiversity—either solo or at a local bioblitz. Or, join Wild Oyster Project in Alameda for monthly volunteer days working to restore native oysters to the Bay. Why volunteer? Beyond the measurable impact on ecosystems, research shows that volunteering can improve mental health, enhance physical wellness, and develop skills like empathy and patience. For those early in their careers, it can even boost employment prospects. According to the Corporation for National and Community Service, volunteers are 27% more likely to find a job. Volunteering invites us to connect—with nature, with others, and with ourselves. As John Muir once said, “Go out to go in.” So let’s get to work. You don’t need to travel far to make a difference. Whether it’s a local park, shoreline cleanup, or community garden, your efforts matter. If we don’t know our local nature, how can we protect it? Let’s rediscover it—together. Ready to get started? June is Pollinator Month, the perfect time to jump into volunteering. Many opportunities focus on native plant restoration, If you are interested in more information about CAL Academy, check out calacademy.org or call at (415) 379-8000 Volunteers for Nature participants help install native plant species in the Presidio.

articles.text: The distant hum of the freeway and the occasional train horn could faintly be heard all the way to Palm Drive. Birds chirped in the trees to greet the early sun, filling the quiet morning. Palm trees towered over the still-sleeping houses. A blue-and-gold lawn sign that read, “Congratulations Class of ’25,” stood in front of the house with a crawling bougainvillea still wet with dew from the night before. Somewhere inside that house, a faucet turned on, an alarm rang, and a dog barked. The sun rose higher in the sky. At the end of the street, the red stop sign saw more and more cars as the world began to wake. A squirrel perched on a tree branch watched dogs and their owners emerge from their homes for morning walks. It remained unseen—its sworn enemies oblivious as they passed below. It chittered once and leapt to another tree. In front of the house with the blue-and-gold sign, a car engine sputtered to life—a gray Volkswagen, to be exact. It made its way past the red stop sign, up Oakland Avenue, across Highland, through Moraga Canyon, and onto Highway 13. From there, it merged onto Highway 24 and passed through the Caldecott Tunnel into Orinda. The greenand-yellow hills rolled above the morning commuters. The Volkswagen took Exit 11, turned right, went down the hill past the “Bentley Upper School” sign, and pulled through the campus gates. The student lot wasn’t full yet—classes wouldn’t start for another 15 minutes. The metallic roofs of the gym and English buildings began to glow as the sun’s rays danced across them. More cars arrived, more students walked up the steps to campus. The clock ticked closer to 8:30. When it finally struck 8:30, teachers began their morning lessons—everything from the principles of statistics to the fall of the Roman Empire. The campus was quiet, or as quiet as it could be with a freeway nearby. Aside from that, only the occasional buzz of a leaf blower or the sound of a tardy slip printing in the front office broke the silence. From the commons came the smell of lunch and the chatter of students enjoying a free period away from the chilly morning air. The day unfolded. Classes began and ended, homework turned in and new assignments handed out. Above the school, vultures circled in the sky, riding the wind currents, looking down at the people below. Then the wind shifted, and the vultures drifted off. Lunch came. Seniors with off-campus privileges left with friends. Students lay on the field in the warm sun. The gym echoed with shouts and friendly competition. Tables in the quad filled with conversation and food. The commons, as always, held its familiar lunch line. It was a break from academics, and students made the most of it. The seniors talked about life after high school. Graduation felt near. The final classes of the day began. Inside air-conditioned classrooms, teachers handed out more readings, more worksheets, more instructions. At the front office, small talk spilled through open doors. Another off-campus pass was dated and signed. Pleasantries exchanged, a student began the walk back to the parking lot. The gray Volkswagen’s lights flashed as it unlocked. The engine came to life once more, and the car exited through campus and headed back toward the hilltop gate. Its left blinker came on, the accelerator pressed, and the journey home began—through the hills, through the tunnel, back onto Highway 13, down Moraga Canyon, across Highland, down Oakland, and finally to the house with the blue-and-gold sign and the blooming red bougainvillea. The day began to wind down. The stop sign welcomed home the same cars it had seen in the morning. The squirrel had vanished into the trees. The sun dipped lower. Another day had wound down. In the house with the blue-and-gold sign, two sisters were about to graduate: one ready to toss her high school cap, the other her college one. A plane ride to a university in Scotland waited for one. A new job to start for the other. Things were ending, yes—but just as many things were beginning. When both graduates finally walk across their separate stages and receive their diplomas, their parents’ applause will rise above all the rest—as it always has, and always will. It’s frightening when the routines and places we’ve grown used to fall away, but that only means there are new places to discover, and new routines to create. To the graduating class of 2025: congratulations. We finally made it. As we head to different corners of the world, remember the places and patterns you once called home—for they’ll always be there to welcome you back. Piedmont resident Larissa Edel is a graduating senior at Bentley School, an intern with the Post and a contributing writer for six years.
articles.title: As the school year winds down

articles.text: The Roman Empire was back in command at Wildwood—if only briefly—on Wednesday, May 21, as twin third graders Malcolm and Beazy Roman shadowed Principal Beth Rhine for the day. The special opportunity, “Principal for a Day,” was a Spring Fling auction item. As the winning bidders, the Romans enjoyed a full day of duties, including a lunch meeting with the superintendent, a visit to a fifth grade classroom, and even Malcom holds a script for Beazy to read into Principal Rhine’s microphone in the school auditorium. Beazy Roman (left), Principal Beth Rhine and Malcolm Roman with Malcolm Roman hammers away at some of the Wildwood Principal’s emails in the Principal’s office. speaking at a school assembly. Rhine, who stepped in as interim principal mid-year, welcomed the company—both in her office and during her rounds through the halls. “I hope I shared with them that it’s a busy job with lots of moving parts. One asked if they would have to do paperwork and I assured them that they wouldn’t have to do any,” said Rhine. She also crafted custom Wildwood staff lanyards for the twins and had them help lead her weekly meeting with Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Beazy described the experience: “We loved having lunch in [the principal’s] office with a friend.” Superintendent Hawn, take note—you made quite the impression. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn meets with 3rd grade Principals for the Day Beazy and Malcom Roman. Later, a fifth grade class invited the trio to visit. The older students were amused and slightly envious, asking, “How come someone who’s younger than us gets to be principal?” and “Can you suspend people?” After their taste of leadership, the twins had ideas of their own for school improvements. “I would put in a vending machine—well, lots of them!” said Malcolm. Beazy’s campaign platform was equally ambitious: “Longer recess, you get to choose your own teacher, and better lunch for all.” They also had a few kind words for their real-life principal. “She is nice, and the school will really miss her,” said Beazy. Seniors visited classrooms and shared their experiences with wide-eyed younger students. “I saw some tears from people, embraces from past teachers, and lots of reminiscing,” said DeYoung. At Beach, graduates looked at photos from their time as 8- and 9-year-olds. At each site, memories came flooding back, and the reality of their next chapter came into focus—even through dewy eyes. “It was really nice for students to reconnect with teachers they remembered in the building where they spent so much time. The seniors did not want to leave, having too much fun playing with students on the playground,” said Beach Principal Anne Valva. A time to reminisce and a time to celebrate, the event proved itself a success. Future graduating classes would be wise to ensure Cap and Gown Day becomes Piedmont’s newest annual tradition. pages.text: Wednesday, May 28, 2025 9 Beach Cleanup Continued from page 1 Parker Johnson and Cormac Bell carrying an air filter found on the street gathered on the blacktop to reflect on environmental stewardship and the human impact on local ecosystems. Nancy Kent, parks and project manager for the City of Piedmont, praised the students’ efforts in a heartfelt message thanking them for helping to clean up the city. The cleanup also served a dual purpose—raising funds for the Marine Mammal Center. Families were invited to donate one cent for each piece of trash collected. Founded in 1975, the center has rescued and rehabilitated tens of thousands of marine mammals, including sea lions, elephant seals, harbor seals, fur seals and sea otters. Now in its third year, the walking field trip continues to grow in impact. The total weight of trash collected has increased from 85 pounds in 2023, to 106 pounds in 2024, and now 120 pounds in 2025—waste that will no longer enter local waterways. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Senior Awards ceremony occurred the evening of Monday, May 19, in the Alan Harvey Theater. Three dozen seniors walked across the stage and received awards for their achievements. Their teachers, counselors and coaches shared with the audience some the most distinguished accolades of the soon to be graduates. Six perpetual awards hold extra weight in the PHS halls of history. Some of the kind words spoken on stage for the perpetual award winners, are included below. Susan Kawaichi Diversity Plaque – Dahlia Saffouri The perpetual award is named for Susan Kawaichi, a former school board member who co-founded the Appreciating Diversity Committee in Piedmont. The award honors students who are deeply committed to the work of diversity, equity, inclusion and belonging. Saffouri was the co-president of the Diversity Club, an ASB Social Justice leader, and an Affinity Mentor. She also spoke at the History of Piedmont Assembly and was a Consent Speaker at the “I am Here” assembly. “[She] is unequivocally committed to social justice, to equity, and action. She is fearless, bold and articulate,” said PHS DEI Director Jean Takazawa. Gail Dryden Community Service Plaque – Alma Ruberto The Gail Dryden Community Service Plaque honors former School Board member Gail Dryden who displayed a strong commitment to community service. Ruberto logged more than 300 hours volunteering at the Chabot Space and Science Center. “She helped meet the needs of the community through her involvement in Piedmont Community Service Crew and spreading joy by helping out at the Chabot Elementary Spring Festival,” said Counselor Michelle Hoang. Eric Swart Rachesky Memorial Certificate – Teresa McKay Jurgens Named after the late Eric Swart Rachesky, a class of 2000 Piedmont High School graduate, the memorial award is presented Dahlia Saffouri: Susan Kawaichi Diversity Plaque Alma Ruberto: Gail Dryden Community Service Plaque Teresa McKay Jurgens: Eric Swart Rachesky Memorial Certificate Mary Schickendanz: League of Women Voters Civics in Action Medal Genevieve Hiller: Daughters of the American Revolution Good Citizen Award each year to a student who makes significant academic leaps, while overcoming obstacles and hardships along the way. Rachesky died at age 21 by contracting an infection after receiving a tattoo. articles.text: Piedmont High hosted a College Recognition ceremony on Wednesday, May 21 at the school’s amphitheater, where 20 Highlanders were honored prior to officially signing their collegiate letters of intent. Players were honored by coaches in front of family and fellow classmates. Piedmont track head coach and football assistant Pouyan Assadi introduced Sam Shelby, Jordan Alemania, Tommy Ashton, Miguel Long, and Gus Von Metzsch. Ashton will play rugby at the University of California in Berkeley, Long will continue his track career at Chico State, Shelby and Alemania will play at Princeton, and Von Metzsch will play lacrosse at Princeton. Assadi also honored senior Nia Kim, who is set to join UC Santa Cruz’s track and field team. Kim was a breakout star on the track team as a first-year varsity runner, breaking the school’s 100 meter hurdles record. Baseball coach Eric Olson introduced stalwarts Will Parker, who heads to Pomona Pitzer, and Markos Lagios who remains undecided, but will continue playing baseball. Softball coach Gene Denard introduced two four-year stars who are off to the next level. articles.text: Swain only athlete to qualify for State Championship Piedmont High’s track and field team took to Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 23-24 for the 2025 North Coast Section Meet of Champions. The Highlanders brought a total of 19 athletes to compete across 18 different events, while athletes with top three finishes qualify for the prestigious CIF State Championship in Clovis. Sophomore Sebastien Swain was Piedmont’s only athlete to qualify for the State meet after finishing 2nd in the 800 meters with a time of 1:54.67. He was a half second behind the winning runner, Caeden Gardner, a senior from Tamalpais. Swain was in a field of 12 runners. The previous day he was fifth of 22 half milers in the prelims in 1:57.08. “Seb put together back to back weeks with beautifully executed races, said coach Pouyan Assadi. “He runs the event like a veteran. He’ll have his work cut out for him next week, but none of us ever doubted what he’s capable of,” RT Reaching the State Championship puts a bow on another strong athletic campaign. In the fall Swain also reached the CIF State Cross Country Championship in November, making the upcoming State run the third of his two-year high school career thus far. Swain also ran the third leg of the 4x400 relay team alongside Maddox Ma, Eric Venner, and Sam Shelby. The foursome finished sixth of 22 teams in the prelims with a time of 3:27.66, then advanced to the finals to finish ninth in 3:30.57. Here’s a rundown of all results from the NCS Meet of Champions. In her first year on the varsity team, Nia Kim made the NCS Meet of Champions finals in the 100 meter hurdles. Photos by Becky Spies Sebastien Swain (#5) qualified for the CIF State Championship by finishing second in the 800 meters at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions. Meet Recap Nia Kim reached the finals of the 100 meter hurdles, finishing sixth of eight with a time of 15.19 seconds. To reach the finals, Kim was fifth of 23 in the prelims in 15.30. Kim has been a standout story on this year’s track and field team. She joined the team as a senior after being a gymnast in her earlier years in high school. Initially joining track with the intention of being a sprinter, coach Assadi noticed she had a quick understanding of hurdling after seeing her in practice. ‘ “This season was the first step in what will certainly be a wonderful track and field career for Nia. We’re excited that UC Santa Cruz is going to take a shot on her. I said to her on Saturday that all of this is a stepping stone for the next level,” Assadi said. Kim also competed on two relay teams. She was the first leg in the 4x100 with Ella Yasar, Kyla Williams, and Claire Aubrecht, which finished the prelims 17th of 24 in 50.18. On the 4x400 relay team, Kim, Aubrecht, Daniela Lucaccini, and Yasar were 13th of 23 in the prelims in 4:09.06. Miguel Long came 10 inches away from qualifying for the CIF State Championship in the triple jump, placing fifth with a distance of 45 feet, 1.5 inches. Sam Shelby also qualified for the 400 meter finals but did not compete in Saturday’s race. In the prelims, Shelby placed sixth of 21 with a time of 49.64. Shelby also ran the second leg of the 4x100 relay team, which finished ninth of 24 in 42.89. He ran alongside Rehan Mumtaz, Ma, and Venner. In the girls’ 4x800, Nikita Miguel Long reached the finals in the triple jump at the NCS Meet of Champions Gorelik, Skylar Best, Caroline Taylor and Leighton Mand finished 12th of 16 in 10:07.33. Mand was also 17th of 24 in the 1600 prelims with a time of 5:23.46. Taylor placed 22nd in 5:32.76. Saniyah Johnson placed 12th of 24 in the shot put finals with a distance of 33 feet, 5 inches. She was also 21st of 24 in the discus in 93 feet, 3 inches. In the boys’ pole vault, Meg Foster was 19th of 20 at 11 feet. articles.text: Season ends in North Coast Section Quarterfinals Piedmont High’s baseball season came to an end on Friday, May 23, falling as the No. 2 seed to No. 10 Northgate 5-0 at Humphries Diamond in the quarterfinals of the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs. The game was similar to PHS’ WACC Semifinals loss to Encinal on May 12, where a pitcher threw lightsout baseball. This time, NAME pitched 6.1 innings for the Broncos, recording 10 strikeouts and two hits allowed. “We’ve faced some really good left-handed pitchers this year. That kid threw hard and he tossed like 107 pitches, we couldn’t get him out of the game. Give him credit, we just couldn’t get consecutive at bats,” coach Eric Olson said. PHS gave up individual runs in the top of the first, third, and fifth innings before allowing two in the seventh. The Highlanders won six games in come-from-behind fashion this season, including their recent 7-6 win over No. 15 Archie Williams in the first round, but they couldn’t reactivate the comeback on Friday. “It was the strength of our team because we always had hope, character, and heart. But she finally bucked us off, we got down and couldn’t claw back. That’s a well-coached quality team. But I’m super proud of our guys. To be bumped up to Division 3 and play bigger schools when we’ve always been D4, it’s a feather in the cap of our guys,” Olson said. “Basically all four of my years, we’ve been a team that crept up on guys, but today we couldn’t do it. It was still a strong year, I don’t think we’ve ever played in Division 3 before. Hopefully, we left an impact on younger freshmen to keep this going,” added senior outfielder Markos Lagios. Piedmont had a chance to make some damage when Will Parker cracked a triple off the right-center field fence with no outs in the fourth inning, but the Highlanders went down with three straight strikeouts. “He was jamming me, so I stepped off the plate. He was tough though, I think our approach was a little bit off today, but that’s baseball. We had a few good comebacks, but going down 5-0 makes things tough and it’s easier to put up a run here and there. If I’m brought in, it becomes 2-1 and you never know how that changes a game. We just didn’t get those runs today,” Parker said. Will Parker celebrates after sliding into third base with at triple. Markos Lagios wraps up his illustrious athletic career at Piedmont High. Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end on May 23, losing to Northgate in the D3 NCS Quarterfinals. “We always work to get a guy [on base] and get him in. We just didn’t execute. We’ve had trouble with lefties all year. He just kept throwing strikes and did well mixing his curveballs and changeups. We had runners on base almost every inning, but we just didn’t capitalize,” Lagios said. Game Recap Northgate scored once in the top of the first, third, and fifth, while tacking on two in the top of the seventh. The Broncos capitalized on mistakes, scoring in the fifth by way of a balk and one more in the seventh due to an error. Piedmont gained a runner in the bottom of the first when Diego Delventhal drew a leadoff walk, but PHS went down in order. Vo also drew a leadoff walk the following inning, but they the next three went out in order, once again. In the bottom of the fourth, Parker stepped to the plate as the leadoff man and turned on a pitch in a 2-2 count all the way to the right-center field wall. He legged his way all the way to third base, but Nate Luehs struck out two batters and forced a lineout to close the inning. Shafer Dando got a two-out single in the bottom of the sixth, but was left stranded. Michael Martin reached on an error with one out in the final inning of action, but Northgate retired the next two batters to end the game. Final stats: Parker went 1-for-3 with a triple. Dando went 1-for-3. Vo drew two walks. Delventhal drew a walk.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 28, 2025 13 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s track and field team took to Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 23-24 for the 2025 North Coast Section Meet of Champions.
