articles.text: MARKOS LAGIOS Football & Baseball At the annual Senior Awards ceremony, Piedmont High named Markos Lagios and Miya Fujimoto as the school’s 2025 Outstanding Senior Athletes recipients, noting their academic success, student leadership, and prowess in their sports. Both athletes competed in two sports. to the Mission Division for 2024 last fall, Lagios led Piedmont to a 10-2 record and 5-0 in league— eventually named the league’s Player of the Year. As the No. 3 seed in the Div.7 NCS playoffs, Piedmont beat No. 6 Fortuna 42-26, which marked the school’s first NCS win since 2017. On the baseball team, Lagios was a four-year starter as Eric Olson’s center fielder. This year’s team finished its season 16-10 and reached the NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 2 seed in Division 3. He was a member of Piedmont’s regular season Foothill Division title run in 2024, reached the D4 NCS Semifinals in 2023, and helped PHS go 19-9 in 2022 toward the WACC Shoreline title. This season, Lagios finished with a .325 batting average with 26 hits, six doubles, one triple, one home run, 11 RBIs, 19 runs scored, and nine stolen bases. He was the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2024, the 2023 honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year, and 2022 Freshman of the Year. in the school’s first two years with the sport. She finishes her time at the school as a WACC Shoreline Division champion in 2022 with multiple all-league honors on the softball diamond and football gridiron. She helped the softball team go 14-11 overall and finish first place in the WACC Shoreline B division, receiving the league’s Player of the Year award. The Highlanders reached this year’s Division 5 NCS Quarterfinals with the No. 11 seed after beating No. 6 California School of the Deaf 15-5 in the first round— marking the team’s first postseason win since 2022. She was also a member of the 2022 team which went 18-7 and 10-0 against WACC Shoreline teams on their way to the title. This season, Fujimoto hit for a sterling .508 batting average with 20 RBIs, scored 43 runs, hit 10 doubles, three triples, and stole 31 bases. On the flag football team, Fujimoto was a starter in both of the program’s first two seasons of activity. Using her speed an mobility, Fujimoto typically lined up at receiver and running back. The team went 4-6 in her first season and 6-10 in the fall of 2024. She received second-team All-League honors both seasons. Fujimoto was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2022. Markos Lagios was an influential member of Piedmont High’s football team in the fall and baseball team in the spring. He finishes his time at the school as a two-time Western Alameda County Conference champion on football, while he was a starter on the baseball team’s WACC regular season Foothill Division title in 2024 and the Shoreline Division playoff title as a freshman in 2022. Last year’s baseball team reached the D4 NCS championship to qualify for the CIF NorCal tournament for the first time, reaching the D4 championship game. In football, Lagios was a three-year starter as the quarterback. In 2023, the Highlanders won the WACC’s Shoreline Division, finishing 7-4 overall and 5-1 in league. After getting promoted MIYA FUJIMOTO Softball & Flag football Miya Fujimoto was a four-year varsity member and captain of Piedmont’s softball team and was a starter of the flag football team Markos Lagios was a two-sport athlete at Piedmont High with baseball and football. He’s pictured here with his mother, Alexis and father, dad John. Miya Fujimoto was a two-sport athlete in softball and flag football and a four-year starter on the softball team.

Each troop rotated through a series of space-themed activities. One of the most popular events was the Mars Buggy, also known as the Lizzigator, where Scouts have to work together to navigate a challenging course while on a wooden board on top of pipes used as rollers. Another highlight was Zero Gravity, also known as spiderweb, involving the task of getting teammates through a complex spiderweb of ropes — an excellent exercise in teamwork and strategy. The Scouts also had a blast at the Alien Shootout, which showcased their archery skills, and at night built impressive fires during the fire-building competition. Their creativity truly shined during the spaceship race, where they fashioned “spaceships” by lashing three poles together and then carrying a teammate on top. After a weekend of competition, challenges, and plenty of fun, Troop 1 emerged victorious by a narrow margin of just 0.3 points. This year’s winner was determined by calculating the average scores by troop rather than patrol, making every event count even more. Overall, this year’s Camporee at Camp Tamarancho was a success particularly as the first outing for many of the Scouts who had just joined. The competition is a fun way for Scouts to get to know one another, and show their Scout skills in a friendly competition, building bonds and providing opportunities to make new friends. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse closes out its 2024/25 season with The Sound of Music playing onstage now through June 29. The musical, based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers, premiered years before the widely-popular 1965 American musical drama film. Berkeley Playhouse director Danny Cozart said the beloved, timeless musical is one of his all-time favorites that “continues to become more relevant day by day.” “The themes we are looking to explore in this production are the choices a person must make when the different structures of society [including] family, religion, and the state, are imposing conflicting demands on them.” Cozart said. “Our focus for this production is to drive home the real-world consequences of political action and the impact on a family trying to stay together in the face of looming tyranny.” Cast includes Marah Sotelo as Maria Rainer, Teressa Foss as Mother Abbess, Chloe Angst Danny Cozart directs Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Sound of Music as Sister Berthe, Sage Alberto as Sister Margaretta, Akshaya Lakshmi as Sister Sophia, Robert Lopez as Captain Georg Von Trapp and Phillip Leyva as Franz. A cast of young musicians will perform the musical’s key songs. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 (extension 351) or visit www. berkeleyplayhouse.org. Showtimes vary. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony is hosting a concert this Sunday, June 1, at 4:00 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall. The concert will be conductor Joseph Young’s last concert as Music Director of Berkeley Symphony. The concert includes the Bay Area Premiere of Gity Razaz’ Methuselah (In Chains of Time), a piece that Berkeley Symphony co-commissioned. The piece promises to be a lush and poignant reflection on the endurance of life, inspired by an ancient Great Basin bristlecone pine tree growing high in the White Mountains of Inyo County in eastern California. Concert goers will enjoy Astor Piazzolla’s Concerto for Bandoneon, Aconcagua, featuring virtuoso Hanzhi Wang on the accordion. Drawing inspiration from the majestic peaks of the Andes, Piazzolla’s composition captures the fiery spirit of Argentine tango with its lush melodies and pulsating rhythms. To close out the season, Shostakovich’s monumental Symphony No. 5 serves as a stirring testament to the triumph of the human spirit over oppression and tyranny. From its brooding opening to its victorious finale, Shostakovich’s symphony resonates with themes of resilience, redemption, and the enduring promise of hope. Tickets may be purchased at https://www.berkeleysymphony. org/event/triumph/. Accordionist Hanzhi Wang will perform with Berkeley Symphony on Sunday, June 1.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony concert this Sunday

articles.text: The Breshears String Trio will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, June 8, at 3:00 p.m. Imagine a family in which the first four children, all just a year or two apart, were eager to learn to play stringed instruments at an early age. All succeeded so well in the mastery of their instruments that as pre-teens and teenagers they performed frequently before paying audiences as soloists, duets, trios and quartets. The statistical unlikelihood of such a story is mind-boggling. And yet that is the story of the Breshears family. In the Piedmont concert they will perform works by Mozart, Handal/Halvorsen, Vivaldi/ Colton and von Dohnányi. The Breshears trio consists of violinist Valery Breshears (15), violist Colin Breshears (12) and cellist Starla Breshears (17). They reside with their family home in San Pablo. Valery and Starla are currently members of the San Francisco Symphony Youth Orchestra, which Colin will join in September. All are currently students at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. The family in various combinations has been performing as soloists, duets, trios and quartets for 12 years. The sibling artists of the Breshears Trio also perform as soloists with orchestras all over California. These appearances have included California Youth Symphony, Kalamazoo Junior Symphony in Michigan, Palo Alto Philharmonic, Sonoma County Philharmonic, Symphony Parnassus, Nova Vista Symphony, Fremont Symphony Orchestra, Prometheus Symphony, Livermore-Amador Symphony, South Valley Orchestra, Diablo Symphony, and Diablo College Orchestra. As ensembles, they have performed throughout the world, including concerts in Argentina, Mexico, and Italy. In 2023, along with older brother and violinist Dustin Breshears, they performed as the Breshears Quartet at Piedmont Center for the Arts in a program entitled Beethoven, Borodin and Brazil. Tickets to the Breshears Trio concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on June 8 are available at brownpapertickets. com/e/6652231.
articles.title: Breshears String Trio at PCA on June 8

articles.text: San Francisco Opera presents John Caird’s acclaimed production of Giacomo Puccini’s most adored opera La Bohème onstage June 3 through 21. Puccini’s classic was the very first opera to be presented by the San Francisco Opera a century ago. The famous opera returns to San Francisco on Tuesday, June 3, taking audiences into the bohemian world of nineteenth century Paris to follow a group of ‘starving artists’ falling in and out of love and living for the moment. The libretto of La Bohème is based on Henri Murger’s 1851 novel, Scènes de la vie de bohème, a collection of vignettes portraying young bohemians living in Paris in the 1840’s. La Bohème’s debut at San Francisco Opera in 1923 catapulted it as a world-class opera company in the Bay Area, and was a favorite of General Director Gaetano Merola. Between 1943 and 1954, it was performed every season. This year’s cast includes Rene Pati and Evan LeRoy Johns as Rodofolo, Karen Ho and Nicole Car as Mimi, Lucas Meachem and Will Liverman as Marcello, and Andrea Carroll and Brittany Renee as Musetta. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/operas/la-boheme to learn more and to purchase tickets online. Call the box office for latest seating availability at (415) 864- 3330 for the June 7 and June 15 performances. Puccini’s masterpiece returns to the San Francisco Opera stage on June 3. Photo courtesy of SF Opera
articles.title: SF Opera presents La Boheme June 3 - 21

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Randall Museum Randall Museum has something for kids of all ages. Randall Museum, a children’s science and art museum located in the heart of San Francisco, is offering discounted workshops for kids and teens throughout June in addition to free admission Tuesday through Saturday. The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages, from pine needle basket-weaving to scrapyard robotics. Along with ongoing Saturday drop-in workshops for families, the museum is offering a new program entitled “Craft and Cinema” for craft enthusiasts aged 16 and up. Held on Saturday, June 21 from 2 pm to 4pm, this workshop invites craft enthusiasts and artists to bring a current craft project to work on while enjoying a screening of Chasing Coral in the Randall Museum’s theater. Crafters are encouraged to bring their crochet, knitting, embroidery or other projects to the movie screening and stay after to socialize and learn about Randall Museum’s many arts and crafts programs. In addition to a rotating list of art and science workshops held every Saturday morning, the museum also offers popular yearround exhibits open to the public throughout the week. The Museum’s live animal exhibit, Wild in California, offers an up-close look at California’s natural wildlife and is one of its most popular displays. Every Saturday morning, visitors can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Lyra and Scarlet have been rehabilitated by staff and are now animal ambassadors for the museum. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. Visit https://randallmuseum. org to learn more. The Museum is open every Tuesday through Saturday, 10 am to 5 pm. Randall Museum will be closed on June 19 in observance of Juneteenth. Photo courtesy of Randall Museum The museum is located in the Corona Heights neighborhood in the heart of San Francisco.
articles.title: Randall Museum offers discounted workshops, free admission throughout June

articles.text: David Hen r y Hwang’s award-winning satirical play Yellow Face is playing on Shotgun Players’ Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through June 14. Yellow Face is a semi-autobiographical play featuring the author Hwang as the protagonist, DHH, mounting his 1993 play Face Value. DHH inadvertently casts a white actor in the role of an Asian character while taking a stance against racial misrepresentation in the media. The play’s themes include questions of race and of the interaction between media and politics. “This isn’t just a play about a single identity. It’s about how we perceive identity itself,” said Director Daniel Eslick. “My team and I are excited to create a space where audiences can reflect on their own perceptions. ‘Asian American’ is such a complex and layered term, but Hwang offers us a vessel to begin unpacking what that really means.” Inspired by real-life events, the comedy also explores themes of hypocrisy and the complexities of identity politics for second and first-generation Americans. “There are so many subplots to explore,” Eslick added. “Failed allyship versus expected allyship, Asian-American intersectionality, political relations with China, and many more come to the forefront in Hwang’s dense text. It all brings me to the question, ‘What is Allyship?’” Shotgun Players Artistic Director Patrick Dooley said the “whipsmart play … effortlessly juggles all these issues in a way that challenges us to consider our own responsibility and complicity.” “The fear and mistrust of China and its corresponding xenophobia that had somewhat cooled in the early 20th century is back on the front burner. And on a more metatheatrical level, the frustrations of artists from historically marginalized communities have taken center stage and demanded a reckoning with the American Theater,” Dooley added. Yellow Face premiered in 2007 and has since been hailed for its humor and social critique on race, politics and media. Hwang’s play won an Obie Award for Playwriting and a Pulitzer Prize nomination. The play’s run has been extended due to popular demand. Tickets are currently available for showtimes June 11 through 13. Wednesday and Thursday performances begin at 7 p.m.; Friday, and final Saturday, June 13 performances begin at 8 p.m. Tickets are available at www. shotgunplayers.org or by calling the box office at 510-841-6500 x 303. Cast of Shotgun Players’ production Yellow Face Photo by Robbie Sweeny
articles.title: Shotgun Players’ Yellow Face extended through June 14

articles.text: Dwelling, 2014, by Yuan Goang-Ming (b. Taipei, 1965) A large-scale exhibition featuring digital artwork by Yuan Goang-Ming, one of the foremost Taiwanese artists active in the international media art scene, is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through July 7. Goang-Ming is considered a pioneer of video art in Taiwan and has worked with the digital art medium since 1984. He received the Hsiung-Shih Art Award for the Best New Artist for his video and sculptural work Out of Position (1987) when he was still in art school in 1988. He went on to receive a master’s degree in media art from the Academy of Design, Karlsruhe Germany in 1997 and has exhibited internationally across Asia, Europe, and America since. The Asian Art Museum exhibition Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War features numerous works that debuted in GoangMing’s critically acclaimed exhibition representing Taiwan at the 60th Venice Biennale. The largescale exhibition is displayed in the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion and is the artist’s first North American solo show. “The generational anxiety of this artist known as the ‘father of Taiwanese video art’ offers Photo courtesy of Asian Art Museum a timely message,” said Abby Chen, curator of contemporary art at the Asian Art Museum. “As Yuan strives to locate a sense of home and belonging, his visions of an unstable world convey a relatable yearning for safety and peace.” A free docent-led tour of Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War will be held this Sunday, May 31. No advance reservation is needed. To join the tour, meet at the exhibition entrance on the ground floor at 11 a.m. Admission to Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War is required. To learn more, visit https:// exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/everyday-war/.
articles.title: Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War on view at Asian Art Museum through July 7

The Museum’s live animal exhibit, Wild in California, offers an up-close look at California’s natural wildlife and is one of its most popular displays. Every Saturday morning, visitors can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Lyra and Scarlet have been rehabilitated by staff and are now animal ambassadors for the museum. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. Visit https://randallmuseum. org to learn more. The Museum is open every Tuesday through Saturday, 10 am to 5 pm. Randall Museum will be closed on June 19 in observance of Juneteenth. Photo courtesy of Randall Museum The museum is located in the Corona Heights neighborhood in the heart of San Francisco.

And it’s also at this point that what was hopefully a benign miscommunication between the two friends begins to evolve into something more sinister. When Sean does return he is not quite as perplexed as is Stephanie, commenting that Emily can be “like a ghost,” present but not present. Finally, after another day passes and they are convinced she is not on a work-related assignment somewhere, Sean calls the police to report Emily missing. And it’s at this point that the plot proves increasingly irresistible, filled with turns and twists, involving incest, adultery and murder. But know that it’s the superb performances of Lively and Kendrick that is the connecting tissue that keeps A Simple Favor engrossing. articles.text: Like its predecessor, Peter Rabbit, Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway is a computer-animated hybrid, based on the much-loved books by Beatrix Potter. Kids love this rabbit, and The Runaway has an energetic, wack-a-mole, convoluted plot, set in great part in London and not the familiar Windemere farm. The story opens with the marriage of Beatrix (Rose Byrne) and Thomas (Domhall Gleeson), who, due to the efforts of Bea, are now living in relative harmony with the farm animals, most especially Peter (James Corden) and Thomas, whose trust of Peter is still a work in progress. Bea and Thomas have been working on a series of books that feature tales about the denizens of the McGregor farm. They receive a letter in the mail from a London publisher Nigel Basic-Jones (David Oyelowo). He wants to take Bea’s charming local stories commercial, a proposal that causes some concerns for the couple. But out of curiosity and to put to rest their questions about the methods to be used by Nigel, they take a meeting in London with the publisher, bringing with them not only Peter, but the whole crew: Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), Cotton Tail (Aimee Horne), and cousin Benjamin (Colin Moody). Peter, as it turns out, is not happy about the way he is portrayed in the stories, characterized as a bit of a rogue; Nigel refers to him as a “bad seed,” even villainous. So, in a pique, he leaves the group, only to hook up with some bad company, headed up by a rabbit named Barnabas (Lennie James). And so begins a series of adventures that take Peter first to Barnabas’ hideout where he learns that there’s a plan afoot to carry out a vegetable/dried fruit heist from the local farmers market. As it turns out, their carefully formed plans turn into a mess, wherein Peter and his clan get swept up by the Pet Pound, then freed, and head back to the farm where Peter seeks out the help of Thomas. They plan to return to London and defeat the underhanded works of Barnabas. Peter Rabbit 2 is exciting, slapdash, and even prankish, much to the delight of the kids who are happily watching events unfold, with tight corners gotten into and, of course, gotten out of. It’s all a lot of fun and the real-life animation is once again superb. Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Directed by Will Glick. With voices of James Gorden, Rose Byrne and Domhall Gleeson. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG. Released in 2021. Streaming on Hulu/Fandango/prime/apple tv. A scene from Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway

The story opens when a mother canine and her small litter are taken to the animal shelter by a malevolent dogcatcher. Out of the shadows appears the face of a pint-sized pooch, watching as the family is carted off. He is a mixed-breed dog who lives on the street, searching for food. In his travels, he meets up with Carter and Frankie. They try and feed him some strawberries, but he is cautious and timid. He quickly realizes that the kids will not hurt him and so he follows them home. Carter spots the little guy outside, and decides to bring him inside, though uncertain of their mom’s reaction, They hide him under a pile of stuffed animals. Frankie wants to name him after Benjamin Franklin, which naturally gets shortened to Benji. When Whitney discover Benji, she insists that the kids take the stray back where they found him. articles.text: The Berkelium String Quartet made its debut in the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday evening. Its founder, violinist Dan Flanagan, is a man of many interests. First and foremost, he is a violinist of high musical attainments which include deep thinking and musical intelligence. At the same time, he is an art historian and artist. As such, his concerts, entitled The Bow and the Brush, give audiences a fascinating insight into music and art history. At the very beginning of Sunday’s concert, Flanagan explained why his quartet is known as the Berkelium String Quartet. In case you didn’t know, Berkelium is an artificially created element discovered in Berkeley in 1949. Some concerts are composed of music only. Flanagan on the other hand conceives his concerts on a wide panorama. Thus, his concerts combine music and history in a fascinating way. It’s hard to imagine any college professor who has a more interesting way of presenting music and art. Sunday’s concert began with one of Flanagan’s original string quartets, which was inspired by the Claude Monet painting “The Water Lilies.” All of Flanagan’s ‘s verbal introductions are brief and to the point. Monet‘s painting of the water lilies was projected for the audience to see, and then the music began. There was The Berkelium String Quartet presented an outstanding concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday evening. In addition to a fascinating look into art history, the members of the string quartet performed with a virtuosity of highest attainments. The members of the Quartet are: violinists Dan Flanagan and Karen Shinozaki Sor, violist Jacob Hansen-Joseph, and cellist Michael Graham. GOOD THROUGH JUNE 2025 GOOD THROUGH JUNE 2025

It was as if a MUSICAL GOURMET The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet new string Quartet by Debussy or Ravel had been discovered. The music was truly impressionistic. It had all of the dissonance of the impressionistic era and yet it had a total center. Very impressive indeed: floral essence on the surface with a restless current beneath. Next came Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 6. A delightful mood was set from the outset. The very essence of Beethoven was expressed. Beethoven’s musical language paired drama alongside humor. The composer’s multi- faceted invention was played in a brilliant and elegant way. The performers made everything look easy. After intermission came Schubert’s monumental “Death and the Maiden” String Quartet. As I listened to the performance, I noticed that the performers presented the music with every aspect of dynamics and tone color as well as artistic nuances of all kinds. Virtuosity in the interest of music. All in all it was a delightful experience. articles.text: It was a warm afternoon on Cinco de Mayo when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their monthly discussion at the Community Hall. The readers were there to talk about Cloudstreet by Australian writer Tim Winton. The novel was published in 1991 and has been called a classic. It has received several awards and was included in 2022 on the “Big Jubilee Read” list of 70 books by British Commonwealth authors. It has also been adapted into a stage play and a television miniseries. Cloudstreet tells the twenty-year long story of two poor, working-class Australian families, the Pickles and the Lambs. The Pickles family are struggling to rebuild their lives after being struck by disaster, when they inherit a big house called Cloudstreet in a suburb of Perth in Western Australia. After the father squanders the money that came with the inheritance, the family takes in the God-fearing Lambs as tenants for some income. The Lambs have suffered catastrophes of their own but are determined to survive. They open a grocery store on the ground floor of the house. Cloudstreet relates the families’ mostly shared post-war experiences from 1944 to 1964. They include drunkenness, adultery, death to resurrection, marriage, and birth. In the end, they are bonded together in this unique house. Cloudstreet was an excellent book group selection because some of the readers loved it, some liked it but had issues, and some readers disliked it so much they couldn’t finish it. For those with their thumbs up, it was “a great read” and “entrancing.” They enjoyed following the generations and their journeys. The book really is a journey. It follows the families’ challenges, their misfortunes, and their failings that result in generational trauma. The book’s occasional magical realism and supernatural events were left for reader interpretation. They also liked the cultural and character development. The possible motivations behind characters’ actions also generated an interesting discussion. This is an important book for Australians and readers with personal experiences in the country could especially relate to the story. Cloudstreet was not right for everyone. Some didn’t like the characters and couldn’t relate to them and it was hard to keep track of all the people. The “sadness after sadness” was difficult and not enjoyable. The language was annoying, and the ending was predictable. The start was “painful” and the story was “like a soap opera.” It made sense that the story was made into a television miniseries. However, the reactions of other readers were mixed. There were many layers and voices in the story that were engaging. Parts of the story may have been confusing, but others were interesting, and the ending was satCloudstreet by Tim Winton isfying with a good feeling and message. This is a story of the importance of family and community, and that was something everyone agreed upon. With their discussion complete, the group turned their attention to the selection of their next book. They had previously selected How We Got to Now by Steven Johnson for June and The Immortalists by Chloe Benjamin for July. After Darby Gregg’s presentation of three memoir candidates for August, the readers selected Tender At The Bone: Growing Up At The Table by Ruth Reichl. . The group’s next discussion will be on June 2 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate, Tegisyer at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. articles.text: Before the walkers started, they were reminded that next Wednesday, May 28th, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan will give the walkers a preview of the community evacuation exercise that is planned for the Scenic/ Blair Avenues neighborhood on June 14th. Additionally, the group has been invited by the Recreation Department to walk again in the City’s 4th of July Parade and is planning on doing it. For the first part of the morning, Nancy Kent, the City’s Parks & Project Manager, was going to give the group a tour of the Dracena Park Reforestation Project. After she finished, the walkers would cross El Cerrito Avenue and see Jean Hansen’s CA native garden. Hers was the only Piedmont garden on this year’s East Bay “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour“ earlier in May. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, May 28, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Dracena Park By Dick Carter Before the walkers started, they were reminded that next Wednesday, May 28th, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan will give the walkers a preview of the community evacuation exercise that is planned for the Scenic/ Blair Avenues neighborhood on June 14th. Additionally, the group has been invited by the Recreation Department to walk again in the City’s 4th of July Parade and is planning on doing it. For the first part of the morning, Nancy Kent, the City’s Parks & Project Manager, was going to give the group a tour of the Dracena Park Reforestation Project. After she finished, the walkers would cross El Cerrito Avenue and see Jean Hansen’s CA native garden. Hers was the only Piedmont garden on this year’s East Bay “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour“ earlier in May. The walkers headed out on Magnolia Avenue and went past what Phil Witte calls “Piedmont’s Pool of the Future.” Workers were busy, progress is visible, and the walkers seemed confident it will be completed someday. The group went across Hillside Avenue and enjoyed views of San Francisco through spaces between the street’s beautiful homes. The walkers safely crossed Oakland Avenue at the stop light, went on Blair Avenue to Dracena Avenue and the entrance to Dracena Park. At the top of the park Nancy was waiting for them. She told the group the City did an aerial inventory and found there are approximately 9,000 public trees and about 3,000 to 4,000 street trees in Piedmont. However, the aromatic ceders, Douglas firs, and some other species are dying. Many trees and other plants which thrived in a moderate climate with plenty of rain every winter are suffering and dying in our increasingly hot, windy, warming climate. The Dracena Park Reforestation Project is a city-led effort to remove dead trees and reforest with native plants and trees that require less moisture and can hopefully thrive in a hotter climate. Approximately 30 trees have been removed recently. The new trees include coastal live oaks, western dogwoods, redbuds, and big leaf maples. The City is planning for 50 years and planting trees that will be able to thrive in a dryer, warmer, future Piedmont. After this overview, Nancy took the walkers to an upper park path and area where some of the reforestation had been done. Two new, flowering western dogwoods were in the center of an open area. Some of the group’s K-9 best friend owners noted the foxtail weeds in the area can get stuck in their pets’ eyes, ears, and noses and create health problems. Nancy understood the issue, but said the City has a policy of not using chemical sprays in its parks for control and she plans to ask the gardeners to cut back the grasses containing these weeds. Nancy took the group through the park to another newly replanted area near the popular tot lot. For one last park stop, Nancy showed the walkers a recently planted big leaf maple near the park’s restroom. Jean Hansen’s garden was the only Piedmont garden on the East Bay’s 2025 “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour” this year. Their tour is conducted on the first Saturday and Sunday of May each year. Jean told the walkers that her front garden is 98% native. The front garden was installed in 2008, and the back and side gardens were installed in stages, beginning in 2013. Jean was inspired by the initial “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour,” and she wanted to redesign her front yard which was inhabited by grass and camellias at the time, She replaced them with natives that include Coffee Berries, Manzanitas, Clevelandii Sages, Ribes, Epilobium (CA fuchsia), Irises, Heuchera, and more. They complement her rustic home and provide habitat for wildlife. Jean only has to water these native plants about once a month. They flourish on the slope that leads up to the house. Jean replaced a small lawn in the back garden with a native, mow-free bunchgrass lawn. The side and backyard have a variety of co-mingling edibles and natives. The gardens were designed collaboratively by Jean and several gardeners. She took the walkers up the side path to the backyard where the group also enjoyed its native beauty. After their visit, the walkers climbed up El Cerrito to Magnolia and back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu There was a good turnout of 47 walkers and five K-9 best friends last week. pages.text: Wednesday, May 28, 2025 31 Memorial Day Continued from page 1 Refreshments were served before and after the event. The Master Florist Association provided red and white roses for guests. The event began with an introduction by Mountain View Cemetery CEO Jeff Lindeman. Music then followed from the David Hardiman Trio as well as a short performance by the Piedmont Highlanders Drum and Pipe trio. Scout Troop 6 led the presentation of colors and pledge of allegiance. Then, Matt Camacho, bassist for the metal band Forbidden, played a bass guitar rendition of “The Star Spangled Banner.” Cemetery Trustee and the Reverand John Sutton, a Mountain View trustee, gave an invocation, followed by a proclamation and words by Cemetery Docent Dennis Evanosky. This year’s ceremony felt the watchful weight of history, marked by the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War era, and the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. “These milestones offer a powerful lens to view the enduring meaning of a day like today,” said guest speaker Master Sergeant Tranquilino Herrera. “... While these two anniversaries represent distinct conflicts separated by time and circumstance, they are united by the common thread of sacrifice that underpins Memorial Day.” Closing remarks were given by Kristie Ly, Customer Service Manager at Mountain View Cemetery. Ly thanked the cemetery staff and honored 101-year old Jack Costello as the oldest veteran in attendance and a purple heart recipient. Throughout the program, local choral group Tosca led the crowd in vocal arrangements of “My Land ‘Tis of Thee,” “This is My Country,” and “This Land is Your Land.” At the conclusion of the ceremony, the Piedmont Highlander Drum and Pipe trio played Doves are released on Memorial Day at a ceremony at Mountain View Cemetery. articles.text: Piedmont Police recently arrested two suspects involved in a residential burglary on May 15 in the 100 block of Olive Avenue. The suspects entered a garage and stole a 2012 Vespa motor scooter and two E-bikes. Piedmont Police Detective Jorge Faucher and Officer Jasdeep Singh immediately began their investigation and identified a suspect vehicle. The unoccupied vehicle was located in a motel parking lot on West MacArthur Boulevard. Piedmont Police searched the suspects’ motel room which revealed the stolen E-bikes and a loaded firearm. One suspect was on probation and the other had four outstanding felony warrants. Both suspects were arrested and booked into Santa Rita Jail. The recovered property was returned. Piedmont Police Detective Jorge Faucher and Officer Jasdeep Singh (right) return the stolen bikes back to their owners. Frankie can identify them and so they kidnap the kids, forcing them into a van. Benji, who has been outside waiting, sees this taking place and chases after the van, all the way to the robbers’ hideout, a large, decaying plantation house. Watching the kids being taken into the house and seeing that the men own a mean-looking Rottweiler, Benji hurries back to Grant and Frankie’s home where he tries to convince Whitney and a friendly cop, Lyle (Jerod Haynes), to follow him back to the hideout. Of course, the children in the audience are rooting for Benji. There are harrowing moments, chases, and the challenge to outwit the bad guys in order to rescue the kids. The children in the audience will be riveted to the story, and definitely will fall in love with Benji. Benji. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously Monday night, May 18th, to approve new passes for the community pool and membership pricing for Piedmont’s community pool. The Pool Advisory Committee recommended the type and pricing of membership passes after three meetings and feedback from Isaac Sports Group. The key goals for the Committee were to offer incentives for annual pass purchases with priority for Piedmont residents, and to break even on operation costs. The new plan will allow families to add additional members to annual and summer passes at a lower fee. The flexible “Build-aPass” pricing model includes four base categories before other family members are added on: • Adult ($891) • Senior ($668) • Youth ($668) • Family ($1,337) Piedmont residents can look forward to extra benefits, including lower prices, extra guest passes, earlier registration for pool programs, and additional single-use guest passes. Non-residents will pay a 40% higher price for annual and summer passes, as well as slightly higher prices for single-day use. Once completed, the community pool is intended to operate on a “cost recovery” model. If revenues from pass sales, dropins, classes, and rentals fail to cover the cost of running the pool, money from the City’s General Fund would need to be used to fund pool operations. Major revenue sources toward this cost recovery include annual pool pass purchases, drop-in fees, swim lessons, and facility rental fees. Isaac Sports Group estimated that cost recovery should be achieved by 2029 when it is estimated pool revenue to at least break even. The last pool update in City Council chambers reported June 2 as the expected completion date for pool construction, not accounting for weather delays and four weeks of systems testing. Pool Fees and Financial Assistance “It’s expensive to go to this pool. If somebody wants to go to this pool on a Saturday afternoon, it’s going to cost them twenty bucks, plus or minus,” said PAC Chair Steve Roland at Monday’s Council Meeting. “Seems like a lot. I was uncomfortable with that the whole time – I’m still uncomfortable with it.” Fortunately, it seems that programs may be in development to ensure that any resident that simply cannot afford the pool fee will still be able to enjoy the upcoming aquatic center. “We’re going to look for tools and ways to get people in, especially to get them in to see the pool before they purchase a pass,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. Roland also mentioned the possibility of applying the Recreation Department’s Financial Assistance Program to help families afford pool access. Although currently the program applies to fee assistance with recreation programs, the program does not currently apply to the pool. “It doesn’t come up a lot, so I think that’s why it’s never really been revised in the recent past,” said Putzer. “...it should be an item that the Rec. City Council approves passes for new pool By Tony Simons Piedmont City Council voted unanimously Monday night, May 18th, to approve new passes for the community pool and membership pricing for Piedmont’s community pool. The Pool Advisory Committee recommended the type and pricing of membership passes after three meetings and feedback from Isaac Sports Group. The key goals for the Committee were to offer incentives for annual pass purchases with priority for Piedmont residents, and to break even on operation costs. The new plan will allow families to add additional members to annual and summer passes at a lower fee. The flexible “Build-aPass” pricing model includes four base categories before other family members are added on: • Adult ($891) • Senior ($668) • Youth ($668) • Family ($1,337) Piedmont residents can look forward to extra benefits, including lower prices, extra guest passes, earlier registration for pool programs, and additional single-use guest passes. Non-residents will pay a 40% higher price for annual and summer passes, as well as slightly higher prices for single-day use. Once completed, the community pool is intended to operate on a “cost recovery” model. If revenues from pass sales, dropins, classes, and rentals fail to cover the cost of running the pool, money from the City’s General Fund would need to be used to fund pool operations. Major revenue sources toward this cost recovery include annual pool pass purchases, drop-in fees, swim lessons, and facility rental fees. Isaac Sports Group estimated that cost recovery should be achieved by 2029 when it is estimated pool revenue to at least break even. The last pool update in City Council chambers reported June 2 as the expected completion date for pool construction, not accounting for weather delays and four weeks of systems testing. Pool Fees and Financial Assistance “It’s expensive to go to this pool. If somebody wants to go to this pool on a Saturday afternoon, it’s going to cost them twenty bucks, plus or minus,” said PAC Chair Steve Roland at Monday’s Council Meeting. “Seems like a lot. I was uncomfortable with that the whole time – I’m still uncomfortable with it.” Fortunately, it seems that programs may be in development to ensure that any resident that simply cannot afford the pool fee will still be able to enjoy the upcoming aquatic center. “We’re going to look for tools and ways to get people in, especially to get them in to see the pool before they purchase a pass,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. Roland also mentioned the possibility of applying the Recreation Department’s Financial Assistance Program to help families afford pool access. Although currently the program applies to fee assistance with recreation programs, the program does not currently apply to the pool. “It doesn’t come up a lot, so I think that’s why it’s never really been revised in the recent past,” said Putzer. “...it should be an item that the Rec. articles.text: A letter from Piedmont’s Fire Chief When a wildfire hits, your actions matter. The decisions you make – and how quickly and confidently you make them – will save time, save stress, and maybe save your life. That’s why I’m asking you to mark your calendar now and plan to take part in our citywide Wildfire Evacuation On the morning of June 14, Piedmont’s firefighters and police will be practicing a real-world evacuation scenario with residents in the Blair/Scenic neighborhood. Just like in a real wildfire, we won’t be everywhere all at once. So while this drill is happening, we’re asking the rest of Piedmont to grab a cup of coffee, find a place you like to focus for a while, and complete an at-home activity with your household. Afterwards, trade your slippers for shoes and join us at the Fire Station for a community debrief and conversation. Talking Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan through what we experienced – what worked, what didn’t, and what we learned – is how first responders process our own exercises. It’s also how we improve as a community. I know everyone is busy. But in the time it takes to sip a cup of tea, you can gain the skills to ensure your family is ready and save critical minutes in a future A pair of firefighters canvas the Blair and Scenic neighborhood to inform residents about the upcoming drill. Chief Brannigan gives a resident information on the upcoming wildfire evacuation exercise on June 14. emergency. We’ve designed your at-home exercise to be simple, quick, and impactful. No preparation is needed. All you need is 30 minutes with the people you live with and a willingness to talk through a realistic wildfire scenario that we provide. We’ll give you clear instructions and discussion prompts — things like: What route would you take if roads were closed? Who grabs the pets? Where will you go if you can’t come home? Just like our firefighters who train every day, this exercise is about building muscle memory so that if a real evacuation happens, you’ll know what you need to do and can execute your evacuation plan quickly and confidently. Practicing helps fill gaps in your plan, gives everyone a role, and makes your response faster and calmer. This year’s event builds on the success of our 2022 evacuation exercise, which we conducted in the Maxwelton neighborhood. We used what we learned from that experience to re-write the City’s Emergency Operations Plan and fine-tune our coordination with partner agencies. Participating in our at-home activity on June 14 will allow you to do the same. Think about how good it will feel to move from the anxiety of “I don’t want to think about it” to the confidence of “I know what to do if the worst happens.” Wildfire risk in Piedmont is real – so is your ability to prepare. Please save the date and plan to join us on June 14. You’ll walk away safer, more confident, and better prepared – and you’ll be helping make Piedmont stronger for everyone. articles.text: Business owners can now apply for, renew, and pay annual tax for their City of Piedmont business license entirely online. The new tool replaces a cumbersome paper-based process, providing community members a faster, simpler way to manage business licensing and rental taxes. Business owners no longer need to download forms, write checks, or visit City Hall in person. Through the new online portal, business owners can: • Apply for a new business license • Pay their annual business license tax, including rental business tax • Close their City of Piedmont business or rental account • Update contact information and business details All actions and payment history are stored in one place, accessible 24/7 from any device. Community members who need assistance using the online system can get help by calling a dedicated support number at (510) 250-1975 or by visiting City Hall, where staff can assist business owners with completing the process using the public online service kiosks located in the lobby. Licenses required for all businesses operating in Piedmont All businesses operating in Piedmont – including rental property owners – must have a valid business license. This includes, but is not limited to: • Home-based businesses (includes 1099 self-employment) • Online storefronts or “influencers” with a Piedmont business address • Landlords operating longterm or short-term rentals • Contractors and consultants working in Piedmont, even if located elsewhere Businesses that fail to obtain a license are subject to late fees and penalties. Learn more about licensing requirements and compliance at piedmont.ca.gov/BusinessCompliance. Part of a broader effort to modernize services The launch of online business licensing continues Piedmont’s work to make City business more accessible and user-friendly. This system joins the NextRequest public records portal, Piedmont Police CitizenConnect online incident map, and eTRAKiT online building and planning permit portal in a growing collection of digital services. Building on these efforts, a new City website is currently in development and scheduled to launch later this year.
articles.title: City launches online Business License application

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting residents to complete a short survey to help ensure new construction in Piedmont reflects the design qualities the community values most. The City is extending the deadline to complete the design standards survey to June 2, in order to give more residents and design professionals the opportunity to have a voice in what new housing in Piedmont will look like. This survey is an opportunity for community members to share what architectural styles, design elements, and site features they want to see reflected in new housing in your neighborhood. Responses will be used to inform “objective design standards” that govern new housing – including ADUs and SB9 projects – in Piedmont. The survey asks about: • What would your biggest concerns be if a new home or major addition was built next door to you? • How important are design elements like building height, window placement, exterior materials, and screening of utility equipment? • How important is it that additions and ADUs match the style and period of the original home? The survey should take about 10 minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ ODSSurvey. Responses will be accepted through June 2. About Objective Design Standards State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing projects, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards – those that require no subjective judgement or interpretation by public officials. The Objective Design Standards initiative aims to create clear, measurable, and enforceable rules governing design elements like articulation and massing, providing residents, property owners, and developers clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. In Piedmont, objective design standards already exist for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and multi-family and mixed-use developments. This initiative is developing new objective standards for one-to-four unit residential development and updating the existing standards for other housing types. A video introduction to Objective Design Standards is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ODSBasics. For more information, visit the project website at piedmont. ca.gov/ODS.

City launches online Business License application By Tony Simons Business owners can now apply for, renew, and pay annual tax for their City of Piedmont business license entirely online. The new tool replaces a cumbersome paper-based process, providing community members a faster, simpler way to manage business licensing and rental taxes. Business owners no longer need to download forms, write checks, or visit City Hall in person. Through the new online portal, business owners can: • Apply for a new business license • Pay their annual business license tax, including rental business tax • Close their City of Piedmont business or rental account • Update contact information and business details All actions and payment history are stored in one place, accessible 24/7 from any device. Community members who need assistance using the online system can get help by calling a dedicated support number at (510) 250-1975 or by visiting City Hall, where staff can assist business owners with completing the process using the public online service kiosks located in the lobby. Licenses required for all businesses operating in Piedmont All businesses operating in Piedmont – including rental property owners – must have a valid business license. This includes, but is not limited to: • Home-based businesses (includes 1099 self-employment) • Online storefronts or “influencers” with a Piedmont business address • Landlords operating longterm or short-term rentals • Contractors and consultants working in Piedmont, even if located elsewhere Businesses that fail to obtain a license are subject to late fees and penalties. Learn more about licensing requirements and compliance at piedmont.ca.gov/BusinessCompliance. Part of a broader effort to modernize services The launch of online business licensing continues Piedmont’s work to make City business more accessible and user-friendly. This system joins the NextRequest public records portal, Piedmont Police CitizenConnect online incident map, and eTRAKiT online building and planning permit portal in a growing collection of digital services. Building on these efforts, a new City website is currently in development and scheduled to launch later this year. Weekly delivery to homes in Piedmont and online access is available by subscription. Call 510-652-2051 for information or go to piedmont-post.com/subscribe. Piedmont Post at your door and online The Piedmont Post remains available online to all subscribers, no matter where they live. To have access to the online Post, type piedmont-post.com for a Google search. The entire edition is online. You must log in and use your password. Then readers may scroll from top to bottom as if reading the printed version from left to right. The City of Piedmont’s Planning & Building Department hosted its 29th annual Design Awards on Wednesday, May 14, honoring four of PIedmont’s most ambitious home projects. The event, taking place at Piedmont Community Hall, also hosted its second year of Sustainability Awards, a separate category honoring homeowners in Piedmont who have dedicated their houses to zero-waste, carbon-neutral, and sustainable designs. Light appetizers and refreshments were served before the awards presentation. “I think everyone here in this room really plays a role in this gorgeous built environment that we live in and the place we call home in Piedmont,” said Mayor Betsy Andersen. “I’m glad to be here tonight to honor all of you and appreciate you and thank you so much for a gorgeous community.” • Excellence in Comprehensive Remodel with Integrate Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) The first award went to homeowners David Lee and Lisha Liang of 224 Greenbank Avenue. Architect Steven Shirley and contractors Jose Pena and Jose Jimenez were also honored. • Excellent Second Story Addition Homeowners Kevin Ma and Liana Wu of 47 York Drive were honored along with architect Ethan Anderson and contractor Silvio Dobrovat. • Excellence in Historically Consistent Renovations The homeowners of 205 Crocker Avenue were honored, along with designer Robin Pennell, designer Chelsea Sachs, designer Alexis Davis Millar, contractor Doug Wolfe, contractor Julie De Bourbon, contractor Michael Waxman, and landscaper John Vasquez. Planning Commissioner Raffi Zaroukian, contractor Scott Cameron, architect Edward W. articles.text: Creamcheese is 1-year-old mixed breed dog who was found as a stray and brought to Oakland Animal Services by a helpful Oaklander. Creamcheese is gentle with other dogs, but since she is a youngster she is full of energy and would do best with another energetic dog or as a solo dog. Oakland Animal Services volunteers adore her. On a recent field trip with a volunteer she walked well on leash and cheerily greeted all of the people and dogs she met. Creamcheese weighs about 60 pounds. You can see a video of her outing and more photos of her on Oakland Animal Services website. Come meet her this week at Oakland Animal Services on Thursday from 12 - 7 p.m., or on Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Meet Creamcheese is 1-year-old mixed breed dog at Oakland Animal Services. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Creamcheese must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s proposed FY2025-26 budget is now available for review. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. The proposed FY2025-26 budget maintains existing service levels and staffing levels citywide, prioritizing high quality service delivery, fiscal responsibility, and planning for the future while bringing several multi-year major projects to completion, including the City’s new community pool, dispatch center relocation, and Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Budget Advisory Committee to review proposed budget on May 20 The City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee will meet to discuss the proposed budget next week on Tuesday, May 20, at 6:00 p.m. in the City Council Chambers. Community members are welcome to attend and speak at the meeting. After their review, the Committee will provide a letter to City Council with their findings and recommendations in advance of budget adoption. The City Council will hold public hearings on the proposed budget on June 2 and 16. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Piedmont High School gathered its best and brightest 12th grade students on Monday, May 19, for the annual Senior Awards Ceremony. The event in the Alan Harvey Theater honored standout achievements of the class of 2025 by presenting 36 awards. Students were not told in advance which award they had been selected for. New this year, students were allowed to sit in the audience with family and friends until being called on stage. The change added to the excitement and allowed the seniors more comfortable accommodations than in previous years when they sat on the stage for the duration of the evening. “I would urge you to get their autographs now, while you still can,” said Principal David Yoshihara. Winners of PHS Senior Awards Staff Photos Piedmont Post intern Sophie Hess won the Outstanding Journalist Award and also Outstanding Senior in Drama Department. She is shown with sister Phoebe, mother Stephanie, and father Drew. Kasper Jansson, Dean Olliphant, Aman Jajodia, Ayaan Jajodia, and Oliver Greenebaum are all smiles with their certificates in hand after the ceremony. Piedmont Certificate in Spanish winner Megan Foster (left), with Honors Spanish teacher Tracy Garcia-Barron, AP Spanish teacher Deysi Sahagon, and Spanish for Excellence Trophy winner Dean Olliphant (right) Hayley Adams (right) presents the Associated Student Body Plaque to Friedie Schickendanz & Genevieve Hiller. Hiller (left) also won the Daughters of the American Revolution Good Citizens Award. Parents, faculty, and students in the Alan Harvey Theater give a round of applause for the evening’s winners.

articles.text: At the May 14 School Board Meeting, Piedmont Unified School District recognized 28 students receiving the State Seal of Civic Engagement. The students participated in a civic action project in the community and met the five criteria areas defined by California to earn the The seal is an emblem that will be displayed on students’ transcripts or diplomas, awarded to those who demonstrate excellence in civic education and participation. Two students spoke of their experiences during the meeting and explained how this project fostered a newfound commitment to civic engagement The State Seal of Civic Engagement creates a meaningful and attainable goal for students interested in government, increasing civic engagement, and student voice in the community. This program was created by the state legislature based upon Assembly Bill 24. California legislatures have identified the voice of students as a critical component to improving education systems and ensuring the student body supports by district decisions. Five criteria for Seal • Be engaged in academic work in a productive way. • Demonstrate a competent understanding of US and California government. • Participate in a local civic engagement project. • Demonstrate civic knowledge and skills through self-reflection. • Exhibit character traits that reflect civic-mindedness. Recipients of the State Seal of Civic Engagement were honored in City Hall by the Piedmont School Board.
articles.title: State Seal of Civic Engagement awarded to 28 students

Navigating the Campus Guided tours and games help students feel at home in their new school, so they can walk in on the first day with confidence. Building Connections Friendships start here. Two students spoke of their experiences during the meeting and explained how this project fostered a newfound commitment to civic engagement The State Seal of Civic Engagement creates a meaningful and attainable goal for students interested in government, increasing civic engagement, and student voice in the community. This program was created by the state legislature based upon Assembly Bill 24. California legislatures have identified the voice of students as a critical component to improving education systems and ensuring the student body supports by district decisions. Five criteria for Seal • Be engaged in academic work in a productive way. • Demonstrate a competent understanding of US and California government. • Participate in a local civic engagement project. • Demonstrate civic knowledge and skills through self-reflection. • Exhibit character traits that reflect civic-mindedness. Recipients of the State Seal of Civic Engagement were honored in City Hall by the Piedmont School Board. articles.text: Six Piedmont High School students and four parents visited China during the school’s Spring Break, April 4-13, led by Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia and Havens 1st grade teacher Hofsa Shurbaji. The trip included stops in Chengdu, Xi’an, and Beijing, allowing the group to soak up all the culture of ancient and modern China along the way. This was the first trip to China organized by a Piedmont teacher in 10 years, and Xia started planning and preparing one year in advance. The stop in Beijing included a school exchange visit at Beijing Etown Academy, and sightseeing in the Forbidden City and Tiananmen Square. Local transportation on bikes, buses and taxis was arranged by a cultural exchange company, and the group slept in hotels. Beijing is 1,100 miles northeast of Chengdu, with Xi’an in between. For long trips between cities, the students rode high-speed trains. “Students not only had the opportunity to learn the language in an immersive environment, but they were also able to experience Chinese culture and gain a deeper understanding of both ancient and modern China,” said Xia, who teaches Mandarin at both Piedmont High and Piedmont Middle School. articles.text: Photos courtesy of Piedmont Swim Team Nik Costello (left), Owen Blanford, Asher Takazawa and Cole Carnazzo competed for Piedmont High in the in the 200 medley relay and 400 freestyle relay at the State Swimming Championships. In a milestone moment for Piedmont High School athletics, the boys swim team made what is believed to be it’s first-ever relay appearance at the CIF State Swimming and Diving Championships at Clovis West High School on Friday, May 9. The team earned its spot at last week’s North Coast Section (NCS) Championships, qualifying for both the 200-yard medley relay and the 400-yard freestyle relay and earning the right to compete at one of the most competitive high school swim meets in the country. On Friday, four Highlanders – Owen Blanford (senior), Cole Carnazzo (sophomore), Nik Costello (junior), and Asher Takazawa (sophomore) – took on the state’s fastest swimmers at the Clovis Olympic Swim Complex. In the 200 medley relay, the team posted a time of 1:33.84, finishing 23rd out of 40 teams. Later, in the 400 freestyle relay, they clocked a 3:07.38, placing 21st out of 40. While only the top 18 teams advanced to the finals, the Highlanders came impressively close. They proved they could hold their own against powerhouse programs from across the state. With three of the four relay members set to return next season, Piedmont isn’t just celebrating what it accomplished this year, it’s setting the stage for what comes next. Owen Blanford (left), Asher Takazawa, Cole Carnazzo and Nik Costello with an underwater photo at the CIF State Championship.
articles.title: Piedmont High relay swim team makes historic debut at State Championships

articles.text: It was another successful meet for Piedmont High’s track and field team at the North Coast Section Bayshore Area Championships on Saturday, May 19 at Vallejo High School, qualifying in 18 different events for the NCS Meet of Champions with top-six finishes. PHS won four events throughout the day, including Sebastien Swain in the 800, Miguel Long in the long jump, the boys’ 4x400 relay team, and Nia Kim in the 100 hurdles. Long had a big day, qualifying for the NCS Meet of Champions in four different events. His long jump of 22 feet, 3.75 inches won in a field of 23 athletes, improving his personal record by one inch set last week at the WACC Championship. He also finished second of 20 in the triple jump with a distance of 44 feet, 7.75 inches, was fourth of 21 in the 300 hurdles in 42.36 seconds, and was fifth of 15 in the high jump in 5 feet, 10 inches. “Miguel outscored 29 of the 36 Bayshore teams on his own, he's going to be a decathlete in college, so it makes sense. He'll focus exclusively on the long and triple jump at the meet of Champs, since we think that's his best chance of getting to the state meet,” said PHS coach Pouyan Assadi. Swain won the 800 in a field of 24 with a time of 1:54.55, which puts him just three seconds back of the school’s all-time record by Piedmont Hall of Famer Gordon Johnson in 1988. Swain is only a sophomore and has a lot of momentum building. He was also ran the anchor leg of the 4x400 team with Maddox Ma, Sam Shelby, and Rehan Mumtaz. They won the event with a sizzling time of 3:28.75 against 14 other teams. “Tactically, Seb executed his race to perfection. That's saying a lot since he's run the 800 like a vet since day one. articles.text: Piedmont, the No. 8 seed and underdog, came inches away from winning the Division 2 North Coast Section Championship game for the second time in school history. On Thursday, May 18, they lost 8-7 in sudden-death overtime to No. 4 College Park. In a gritty performance, the Falcons won the opening faceoff of OT, turning it up field to quickly score the winner. “In a draw, it’s a fast break situation and they ran a great scheme. They were running cutters all day and one just got in. But hat’s off to our players, they played a great game and excellent defense. We matched up girl to girl,” said PHS coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders came inches away from victory. With a shooting space opportunity with just 40 seconds left, Peyton Watson’s shot attempt clanged off the crossbar in a 7-7 deadlock. “I’m always worried about taking the last shot, but we held the ball for a good three minutes. It didn’t work out. It was so close, so close. It hit the crossbar and that’s usually a really good shot,” Watson said. Things were going well for Piedmont which opened the first quarter with a 4-1 lead before Staff Photos Peyton Watson’s shot attempt hit the crossbar in the final seconds of the fourth quarter. the Falcons stormed back in the second quarter with four straight goals to take a 5-4 advantage into halftime. Schickedanz and Watson connected in the fourth quarter to give PHS a 7-6 lead with 8:26 left, but College Park scored the equalizer three minutes later. “I’m really proud of us,“ said senior leader Schickedanz. “The fact that we went down and regained the lead speaks to the resiliency of our team. Even if it wasn’t the result we wanted, we were able to keep it at a tie and give ourselves a chance to win,”. Despite the loss, Piedmont’s Friedie Schickedanz scored three goals and had an assist against College Park. Chloe Graham scored one goal and helped win three draws. quest for the NCS title is a testament to the team’s development. In early season, the Highlanders struggled to maintain possession when transitioning their defense into the attack. As the season progressed, PHS became dependable in possession, more patient, and found they were able to fluidly conduct their attack. “Instead of pushing through defenders, we started turning around and passing to the open girl. That’s one thing that really changed – just being patient when trying to move the ball,” Watson said. This year’s Piedmont team contrasted considerably with the team of 2019. That squad had a handful of players who went on to play in college: Zoe Torok (University of Chicago), Lily Keville (Pitzer), Elie Cole (William & Mary), Widdy Tevis (Trinity), Maria del Rosario Chan (U.S. Coast Guard Academy), and Sadie Tschider (Smith College). “We didn’t have any girls playing club lacrosse and in 2019, we were filled with superstars. This team had to rely on each other. They had a lot of grit, worked hard, and learned, learned, learned. We coached this team up and they were so receptive to it. It’s a very different team, but boy were they hard working,” Chan said. articles.text: Baseball team avoids upset in 7-6 win over No. 15 Archie Williams Piedmont High’s comeback kids were at it again on Tuesday, May 20 in the opening round of the Division 3 North Coast Section baseball playoffs. As the No. 2 seeded team, the Highlanders avoided an upset at Humphries Diamond, beating No. 15 Archie Williams in comeback fashion. The result marked the team’s sixth comeback victory of the season. They won 7-5 over Acalanes on February 28 after trailing 5-4, trailed 4-3 against Encinal on March 27 before winning 8-5, were also down 5-3 to Head-Royce before winning 7-5 on April 9, and beat Alameda 8-7 on April 18 after falling behind 7-4. “We get our offense late in games. Maybe it’s just us getting acclimated to the pitcher. You’re going to need clutch performances in the playoffs,” said coach Eric Olson. Piedmont trailed 6-1 after the second inning, but began chipping away. They rallied to put themselves one run down 6-5 with three runs in the bottom of the fourth inning, and went ahead with a pair of runs in the bottom of the fifth inning. Piedmont senior Will Parker smacked the game-winning run on a single to right field to score Diego Delventhal. Junior pitcher George Bishop also had a clutch performance on the mound after entering in the second inning. He struck out seven batters in 5.1 innings of shutout baseball. The Highlanders will host Northgate in the NCS Quarterfinals on Friday, May 23 at Witter Field. No. 10 Northgate is 17-7 after upsetting No. 7 Bishop O’Dowd 9-2 on Tuesday night. Game Recap Trailing 6-0 after the top of the second inning, Piedmont got its first run when freshman Jonah Cha-Foster hit a two-out single to score Jordan Vo, who led off with a walk. PHS scored again the following inning when Vo drew a one-out walk with the bases loaded, but PHS struck Staff Photos Will Parker hit the game-winning single in the bottom of the fifth inning against Archie Williams. George Bishop was the winning pitcher with 5.1 innings of work, five strikeouts, and allowing no earned runs. Diego Delventhal scored the gamewinning run for Piedmont. out twice with three runners stranded. Piedmont’s big three-run fourth inning all came with two outs. After Cha-Foster and Delventhal opened with walks, Shafer Dando was hit by a pitch with two outs. With Brandon Dicke at the plate, Cha-Foster and Delventhal scored on the same wild pitch. Then, Dicke slugged an RBI double to the right field fence, making it a 6-5 deficit. In the bottom of the fifth, Jack Meyjes drew a leadoff walk. With one out, Delventhal cracked a ground ball through the middle of the infield. On his horse was Meyjes, wheeling all the way around from first to home to tie the game up at 6-6. After Delventhal made his way to third, Parker smacked a single of his own to score Diego. Bishop stayed in the game at pitcher and retired three of four batters in the top of the sixth and the seventh. Final stats: Delventhal went 2-for-3 with an RBI, two runs, and a walk. Lagios went 1-for-4 with a run. Parker went 2-for-3 with an RBI. Dando scored once. Dicke went 1-for-4 with a double and an RBI. Vo had a run, RBI, and drew three walks. Meyjes scored once and drew two walks. Cha-Foster went 1-for-3 with a run, RBI, and a walk. pages.text: Wednesday, May 21, 2025 13 Girls lacrosse team falls in NCS finals By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont, the No. 8 seed and underdog, came inches away from winning the Division 2 North Coast Section Championship game for the second time in school history. On Thursday, May 18, they lost 8-7 in sudden-death overtime to No. 4 College Park. In a gritty performance, the Falcons won the opening faceoff of OT, turning it up field to quickly score the winner. “In a draw, it’s a fast break situation and they ran a great scheme. They were running cutters all day and one just got in. But hat’s off to our players, they played a great game and excellent defense. We matched up girl to girl,” said PHS coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders came inches away from victory. With a shooting space opportunity with just 40 seconds left, Peyton Watson’s shot attempt clanged off the crossbar in a 7-7 deadlock. “I’m always worried about taking the last shot, but we held the ball for a good three minutes. It didn’t work out. It was so close, so close. It hit the crossbar and that’s usually a really good shot,” Watson said. Things were going well for Piedmont which opened the first quarter with a 4-1 lead before Staff Photos Peyton Watson’s shot attempt hit the crossbar in the final seconds of the fourth quarter. the Falcons stormed back in the second quarter with four straight goals to take a 5-4 advantage into halftime. Schickedanz and Watson connected in the fourth quarter to give PHS a 7-6 lead with 8:26 left, but College Park scored the equalizer three minutes later. “I’m really proud of us,“ said senior leader Schickedanz. “The fact that we went down and regained the lead speaks to the resiliency of our team. Even if it wasn’t the result we wanted, we were able to keep it at a tie and give ourselves a chance to win,”. Despite the loss, Piedmont’s Friedie Schickedanz scored three goals and had an assist against College Park. Chloe Graham scored one goal and helped win three draws. quest for the NCS title is a testament to the team’s development. In early season, the Highlanders struggled to maintain possession when transitioning their defense into the attack. As the season progressed, PHS became dependable in possession, more patient, and found they were able to fluidly conduct their attack. “Instead of pushing through defenders, we started turning around and passing to the open girl. That’s one thing that really changed – just being patient when trying to move the ball,” Watson said. This year’s Piedmont team contrasted considerably with the team of 2019. That squad had a handful of players who went on to play in college: Zoe Torok (University of Chicago), Lily Keville (Pitzer), Elie Cole (William & Mary), Widdy Tevis (Trinity), Maria del Rosario Chan (U.S. Coast Guard Academy), and Sadie Tschider (Smith College). “We didn’t have any girls playing club lacrosse and in 2019, we were filled with superstars. This team had to rely on each other. They had a lot of grit, worked hard, and learned, learned, learned. We coached this team up and they were so receptive to it. It’s a very different team, but boy were they hard working,” Chan said.
