articles.text: Build It, Launch It, Make It! 11th Annual Maker Faire Returns Sunday The 11th annual Piedmont School Maker Faire returns to the Piedmont High School campus this Sunday, May 18, 11:00 a.m. - 3:00 p.m. Come celebrate K-12 Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts & Math (S.T.E.A.M.) education for the Piedmont community and beyond. Organized by Piedmont Makers, this beloved event will showcase more than 80 projects featuring the S.T.E.A.M. creativity, passion, and effort of makers in our community. Many of these projects are created by Piedmont students. From robotics and rocketry to handcrafted art and engineering marvels, the Faire celebrates the power of STEAM through creativity, collaboration, and invention. This isn’t just a showcase— it’s an experience. Families and curious minds of all ages can dive into dozens of hands-on activities, from returning fan favorites like Maker River, Air Rockets, and the Nerdy Derby to exciting new experiences like Mini Golf Links, fresh apple juice pressing, and even making your own paintbrushes and jewelry. For the sustainably minded, there are opportunities to bring your old electronics to be repaired and swap STEAM toys. Musical guests are the Piedmont High School Jazz Combo, Pied mont Middle School Orchestra groups, and Camino’s Jazz. Food will also be available at the Faire, including delicious lunch options from Chef Robert Dorsey and Boba Tea from Tea on Piedmont. Free tickets are available at www.piedmontmakers.org. Secure your tickets in advance to avoid the lines at the Faire.
articles.title: 2025 School Maker Faire on May 18

articles.text: Piedmont botanical artist Bonnie Bonner, also known as Joanne Palamountain, will demonstrate how to create Bug Hotels for pollinators using renewable, found materials during the 2025 Piedmont School Maker Faire. The Bug Hotels — along with hundreds of other STEAM projects and demonstrations — will be open to the public on the Piedmont High School campus Sunday, May 18, from 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. Bug Hotels are hanging garden art that provide protection for beneficial insects. Like organic litter found naturally on the forest floor, reclaimed plant matter offers pollinators and other helpful insects a place to feed, rest, propagate and hide from predators. Essential to our ecosystem, native wasps, beetles, lacewings and ladybugs are among the tenants that take up residence in the hidden hollows and tunnels. Bug hotels are ready to hang indoors or outside. These sustainable shelters foster habitats that support biodiversity and remind the public that insects need our help. They also highlight the simple beauty of nature. You can find more than 50 of Bonnie’s Bug Hotels hanging in Piedmont backyard gardens and front porticoes. View more on her website gallery at: BonniesBotanicalArt.com/bug-hotels Bonnie Bonner makes one-of-kind insect habitats as hanging garden art from seed pods and other recycled plant matter.

articles.text: Sixty-two students, mentors, and family members travelled to Houston in April for the FIRST World Championship. This April, 50,000 people and 600 teams from 18 countries converged on Houston for the FIRST World Championship in robotics. During the four-day competition, Highlander Robotics — Team 8033 — earned the Engineering Excellence Award for their robot, “Kelpie.” The team faced a tough qualification round in the 75-team Johnson Division, with three close matches ending in narrow losses (159–160, 225–221, 180–181). Despite finishing 43rd in qualifications with a 3–7 record, they were selected 14th overall in the playoff draft by the fifth-seeded alliance. The team ultimately finished fifth in the double-elimination playoff bracket. In judged awards, the Highlanders received the “Excellence in Engineering” honor, which recognizes a professional approach to the design process and consistent high-performance operation. With the competition season concluded, Highlander Robotics now ranks in the top 3% of all teams worldwide. Next up for the team is an open house and recruiting session during the Piedmont School Maker Faire. On May 18, the team will open the doors of the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at 2 p.m. to prospective students, parents and community members. The event offers a chance to tour the lab, meet the dedicated mentors and students behind the award-winning team, and learn how to get involved. Founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert, Highlander Robotics includes 55 students from 17 high schools across the region. The team is based at the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information, visit the team online at frc8033.com. Team Captain Vaughn Khouri (left) tests Kelpie on the practice field alongside Software Lead Athena Li. Kelpie extends to over 6-feet tall to score 16” kick balls into a net. “Kelpie” (8033) picks up 4-inch PVC game pieces from the ground with its end-effector. Romir Sharma checks out Kelpie between rounds in the Highlander pit.

articles.text: Seven Girl Scouts in Troop 33426 will be formally recognized on Wednesday, May 28, for completing their Gold Award projects – Anna Lavin, Carolina Romanczuk, Coral Yeh, Julia Montes, Maile Matubrew, Sabrina Olliphant and Sonja ten Grotenhuis. The community is invited to celebrate with the troop and enjoy refreshments in the Piedmont Community Center starting at 6:45 p.m. The Gold Award is the highest achievement a Girl Scout can earn, comparable to an Eagle project. All projects require a minimum of 80 hours and Scouts spend years preparing and making decisions on their project. Troop 33426 was created in 2012 when the girls were in kindergarten. Thirteen years later, they are celebrating their completed journey through Girl Scouts. Along the way the girls have enjoyed everything from crafts and service, to backpacking and earning badges on a multitude of subjects, including Adulting 101 and most recently a “make your own badge”, which the troop named Urban Adventurer. En route to earning their Gold Awards, the girls also earned Bronze Awards, Silver Awards, Service Awards and Leadership Awards. For more information about Girl Scouts contact Buffy Yeh at yeh4mom@yahoo.com. engaging and accessible. and two water features. tel: 510-658-2588 www.piedmontfuneralservices.com 5000 piedmont ave., oakland, ca (fd#2210)

articles.text: Sabrina Olliphant: A Journey Through Time: The History of Earth. This was a detailed timeline and interactive lesson plan to teach students about major events in Earth’s geological history. She developed a giant timeline poster, event markers, and a classroom activity used by the Lawrence Hall of Science’s outreach programs to make learning about Earth’s 4.5-billion-year history Maile Matubrew: Art Mindfulness program at Berkeley High School. The goal was to provide a safe space for people to do art, de-stress, and learn how to manage stress and anxiety creatively and constructively. She led workshops to educate others on stress, mindfulness, and self-care; she also led various art activities to practice creative stress management. Carolina Romanczuk: PHS Campus Beautification Team, a club she founded that focuses on creating a more welcoming campus. The club combines the ideas and needs of the administration, students and teachers with the financial support from the PHS Parent Club. Hands-on service from the students included the renovation of planters on campus with donated succulents. Sonja ten Grotenhuis: Meditation Garden at the Piedmont Community Church. This is a space for reflection and meditation at the church. With the help of many, she turned a previously barren space into a beautiful sanctuary. The space includes a maze Julia Montes: Livestock Protection for Malawi. Through the organization Vijana Africa, she addressed the food security issue of a refugee camp in Dzaleka that empowers women experiencing poverty. She organized construction of animal enclosures for rabbit and pig farming to protect the livestock and contribute to the women’s economic empowerment and self-reliance. Coral Yeh: Monitoring the Humpback Whales to Protect the Ocean. Coral created an educational program about humpback whales and their importance in the ocean in order to create an awareness and responsibility toward them. The organization Whalefall will use her project to teach students preparing to go to the Dominican Republic to monitor humpback whales. As part of Coral’s research she swam and photographed humpbacks at the Silver Bank, Dominican Republic. Anna Lavin: completed a Silver Award Project: Guinea Pig Education Website. She and a partner built a website to educate people on guinea pig abandonment and how to properly care for them. Guinea pig populations can get out of control when people buy them without doing research. Lavin’s project addressed the issue by providing people with the correct knowledge of care and connecting owners with shelters so they could adopt. articles.text: Shelby, Long qualify in 4 events; Kim wins 100 hurdles Piedmont High’s track and field team had a tremendous showing at the 2025 Western .Alameda County Conference Championship meet on Wednesday and Friday, May 7-9. With top-six finishes, Piedmont officially qualified in 24 events for the North Coast Section Bayshore Area Championship at Vallejo HS on Saturday, May 17. The Highlanders won four league titles: Nia Kim in the 100 hurdles, Andrea Martin in the shot put, Sebastien Swain in the 1600, and the boys’ relay team of Maddox Ma, Eric Venner, Ben Gerber, and Rehan Mumtaz in the 4x400. Kim, a first-year varsity member, won her event in 15.62 seconds in a field of 20 hurdlers. She also placed second of 15 in the high jump with a height of five feet even. Kim ran the first leg in the 4x100 relay team with Ella Yasar, Kyla Williams, and Claire Aubrecht, which placed second of 10 teams in 49.76. She also ran the first leg in the 4x400. The team with Aubrecht, Daniela Lucaccini, and Yasar finished second of 10 in a time of 4:07.99. Nia, a senior, has been a breakthrough for the track and field team in her first-year as a varsity athlete. She elected to join the squad after previously competing in gymnastics. “I did gymnastics for a long time before this. I’ve always been pretty fast, so when I knew I was done with gymnastics, I wanted to try out. I honestly thought I would just do sprints, I didn’t expect to do hurdles or relays,” Kim said. She found her athleticism from gymnastics translated well to the track. Now nearing the end of her only year competing at the high school level, Kim is a league champion. “The first time I tried hurdles, it was just for fun because my friends were trying it. My first one didn’t go very well, but after that, I thought I could get it Photo by Becky Spies Nia Kim. a first-year varsity athlete won the league title in the 100- meter hurdles. Staff photos Sebastien Swain won the 1600 meters and just missed winning the 800. down. Coach P saw it and told me to keep working at it. It’s really exciting to win. First of all, I never thought I’d be doing hurdles, so to be good at them and be able to have great coaches, it’s amazing,” Kim said. Martin has been another breakthrough athlete. A basketball star as a freshman, she broke her own school record in the shot with a distance of 34 feet, 1.5 inches to take firstplace out of 36 athletes. She also placed fourth in the high jump at 4 feet, 10 inches. Distance runner Swain, a sophomore, qualified in two events, winning the 1600 with a time of 4:21.01 in a field of 54 runners. He also came narrowly close to winning the 800, finishing second of 47 in 1:57.33, falling to Bishop O’Dowd’s James Prater by .08 of a second. The boys’ 4x400 relay team of Ma, Venner, Gerber, and Mumtaz finished in 3:31.83 against nine other teams. They beat O’Dowd for second place by .23 of a second. Piedmont senior Sam Shelby had a big day, qualifying in four different events. He finished fifth of 50 in the 100-meter sprint in 11.28 seconds, was third of 41 in the 200 in 22.26, and was second of 45 runners in the 400 in 49.89. He ran the second leg of the 4x100 relay team with Mumtaz, Ma, and Venner, which placed second of 10 in 42.88. His times in the 200 and 400 marked personal records. His time of 22.26 in the 200 broke Kyle Dalton’s 2013 school record of 22.36. He is now .02 of a second behind Kevin Hogan’s school record set 66 years ago in the 220-yard event of 22.24. “I’ve had that number on my wall all season. It’s a big deal for me personally; just to know I accomplished that goal is a huge weight off my shoulders. It was a big moment for me,” Shelby said. Shelby missed most of his junior track season due to an injury. With that, he circled 2025 as his year to produce. “Last season was definitely not what I wanted it to be. This year was about getting done what I knew I could do after being prevented from doing that last season. I appreciate the opportunity just to do it,” Shelby said. Here’s a rundown of other marquee results of athletes who qualified for the Bayshore Championship this coming weekend: Girls Results In the 300 hurdles, Yasar placed third of 19 in 49.72. Saniyah Johnson was second in the shot put with a distance of 32 feet, 2 inches, and also placed fourth of 29 in the discus in 96 feet. Shayna Chau was second of five in the pole vault in 8 feet. Leighton Mand was fourth of 37 in the 1600 in 5:25.80. Skylar Best placed fifth of 37 in the 800, clocking a 2:23.56. Alina Shahid

articles.text: Piedmont High junior Lucas Smolko continued his strong season at the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, May 9-10 at Vintage High School in Napa. He reached the singles championship match before losing in three sets to Head Royce’s Dylan Donovan, 5-7, 6-1, 6-3. Smolko was the bracket’s No. 2 seed, while Donovan was No. 1. Smolko’s finals appearance marked the second of his Piedmont High career after reaching the 2023 title match as a sophomore. Lucas is fresh off his backto-back WACC Singles title he won the previous weekend, which made him the first Piedmont athlete to do so since Kaelli Thiel in 2012 and 2013. To reach this year’s title match, Smolko opened with a 6-3, 6-1 win over Sonoma Academy’s Alex Sae. Later on in the opening day, Lucas defeated Head Royce’s Jackson Stowell 6-2, 6-2. Smolko returned to the semifinals on Saturday, defeating San Domenico’s Toby Sadzeck in three sets by battling back after a first-set loss, 2-6, 6-1, 6-1. “I started off really slow, it was really warm that day and I was a little out of sorts in the beginning. He was a pretty defensive player and was mainly just getting balls back and standing behind the baseline. I was a little too defensive early and in the second set, I started being more aggressive,” Smolko said of the match. Then in the finals against DonStaff Photos Lucas Smolko reached the D2 NCS Individual Tournament singles finals where he lost in a heated three sets to Head Royce’s Dylan Donovan. ovan, Smolko fought to an extra game in the first set to win 7-5, but lost the next two. Playing with a gusty wind, Donovan did well with an underhand serve that produced a low enough bounce to prevent Lucas from taking powerful return shots. “I actually started slow and was down 5-1 in the first set. I wound up winning the first set 7-5, so I was in control for a while. But the wind really picked up and my opponent was serving a slice underhand. It was really difficult to go up against because his serves were staying super low,” Smolko said. Since starting his Piedmont career, Smolko has won the league championship twice and a finals Lucas Smolko won his opening two matches in straight sets. His final two matches went to three sets. Lucas Smolko hopes for a rematch against Head Royce’s Dylan Donovan in the NCS Team Tennis tournament.
articles.title: Lucas Smolko reaches NCS finals

The boys’ 4x400 relay team of Ma, Venner, Gerber, and Mumtaz finished in 3:31.83 against nine other teams. They beat O’Dowd for second place by .23 of a second. Piedmont senior Sam Shelby had a big day, qualifying in four different events. He finished fifth of 50 in the 100-meter sprint in 11.28 seconds, was third of 41 in the 200 in 22.26, and was second of 45 runners in the 400 in 49.89. He ran the second leg of the 4x100 relay team with Mumtaz, Ma, and Venner, which placed second of 10 in 42.88. His times in the 200 and 400 marked personal records. His time of 22.26 in the 200 broke Kyle Dalton’s 2013 school record of 22.36. He is now .02 of a second behind Kevin Hogan’s school record set 66 years ago in the 220-yard event of 22.24. “I’ve had that number on my wall all season. It’s a big deal for me personally; just to know I accomplished that goal is a huge weight off my shoulders. It was a big moment for me,” Shelby said. articles.text: Photos by JC Curran Piedmont ended its season with a 10-6 loss to No. 4 seed Foothill in the D2 NCS tournament. Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team’s season came to an end on Tuesday, May 6 in the first round of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs. As the No. 13 seed, the Highlanders lost to No. 4 Foothill 10-6 on the road in Pleasanton. Piedmont held a 5-2 lead through the first half, but was limited to just one goal in the second half. The result concludes PHS’ season at 4-11 in a transition year under first-year head coach Paul Pappas. Looking ahead, Piedmont will return the bulk of its premier starters, including freshman Jax Thayer, sophomore Connor Fredericks, and juniors Ian Nguyen, Timmy Kalamas, and P.J. Brayer. “It’s just trying to get them comfortable and confident. Guys are getting better and that’s all we can ask for,” coach Paul Pappas said. 10-6 loss to No. 4 Foothill Piedmont led 3-1 through the first quarter and 5-2 by halftime. However the Highlanders were limited to just one goal in the third quarter and were held scoreless in the final going. During that span, Foothill put up four goals in each of the third and fourth quarters. In the first quarter, Fredericks got Piedmont on the board first with 5:26 left. Fredericks turned around to win the ensuing faceoff, leading to Brendan Devine scoring just 40 seconds later. Foothill got its goal with 2:31 left, but Piedmont answered when Fredericks got his second goal with 37 seconds left—up 3-1. Devine scored another goal with 8:55 to go in the second quarter, giving Piedmont a 4-1 lead. Foothill got one back with 4:32 left, but PHS responded with Brayer launching in a shot with 2:49 to go—giving Piedmont a 5-2 lead going into the break. However, the comeback was on in the third quarter for Foothill. After over half of the third quarter ran out, the Falcons stormed back with two straight goals at 5:57 and 5:17, making a one-goal deficit. Devine scored Piedmont’s last goal with 1:38 left in the third to make it 6-4. But after that, Foothill scored twice in the final 30 seconds. After scoring with 27 seconds left, the won the following faceoff to score just 22 seconds later— knotting things up at 6-6. In the fourth quarter, Foothill got the go-ahead with 9:36 to play. They scored three more goals at the 6:42, 5:57, and 3:29 marks to propel them to a 10-6 victory. Final stats: Devine scored three goals. Fredericks scored twice and won eight face offs. Brayer scored once and scooped three ground balls. Goalie Gus Von Metzsch was busy, recording 15 saves. Brendan Devine scored three goals against Foothill. Goalie Gus Von Metzsch was busy in the pipes, recording 15 saves.

articles.text: When a high school pitcher is dealing his best quality all season, it’s sometimes difficult to get out from under. That was the case in Monday, May 12’s Western Alameda County Conference Semifinals at Humphries Diamond, where No. 2 seeded Piedmont lost 6-0 to No. 3 Encinal, whose pitcher Kyle Cooke nearly threw a perfect game with no hits allowed, 10 strikeouts, and one walk. “He pitched a great game. That’s the third time we’ve seen him this year and he’s beaten us twice. He was really on his game mixing up his pitches. We were definitely off of our timing and he deserves the credit. He’s a really quality pitcher,” coach Eric Olson said. The loss is a testament to Staff Photos Piedmont’s baseball team looks ahead to the North Coast Section tournament. Pitcher George Bishop, a junior, throws against Encinal. Will Ferriera throws to second base with a Jets’ runner in a pickle. the WACC Foothill Division’s quality. Piedmont split games with Encinal, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, and regular season champs Castro Valley. Piedmont similarly walked into last year’s WACC Tournament with the top seed, but lost to Alameda in the semifinals. Despite the loss, the Highlanders look to recapture 2024’s magic when they reached the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship game and the D4 CIF NorCal title game. “We went on a run last year. It’s just about playing the best baseball at the right time,” Olson added. “It’s not always the best team who wins, it’s the team that plays the best to win. Encinal played way better than us today, but we can flip that script. We have 15 wins this season and were second-place in this really tough league.” PHS goes into the NCS playoffs with a 15-9 overall record. This year’s NCS format does not account for school size, meaning Piedmont could be placed in the Div. 2 or Div. 3 brackets. “We’re going to get thrust up in a tough bracket because of the teams we’ve played this year. We know we can win. You just have to execute when your time is called. You have to be at your best when your best is needed,” Olson said. 6-0 loss to Encinal Encinal scored individual runs in the top of the first, third, and fourth innings. The Jets then piled on three runs in the top of the sixth thanks to a three-run bomb over the left field fence by Matan Antebi. Piedmont didn’t get its first runner of the game until the bottom of the sixth when freshman Jonah Cha-Foster reached first base when Encinal’s first baseman dove for a ground ball, but couldn’t hang on. Markos Lagios drew a walk in the bottom of the seventh and advanced to second base with one out on a wild pitch. Lagios then made his way to third base on a ground out by Jordan Vo. Final stats: Lagios drew a walk. George Bishop pitched two-thirds of an inning, striking out one. Diego Delventhal pitched one inning, allowing one hit. NEXT UP The North Coast Section playoff seeding will be announced this Sunday, May 18. First round games will be played on Tuesday or Wednesday, May 20-21.

articles.text: Hannah Joerger, a freshman, went 2-for-4 with an RBI. Staff Photos Piedmont’s softball team bowed out in the first round of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division playoffs on Monday, May 12 with a 7-4 loss to Mt. Eden in Hayward. Despite the loss, it was a good response by Piedmont after losing to the same team 12-1 earlier this season. Against the Monarchs, PHS had a good day at the plate with eight hits. Freshman Hannah Joerger had one of her strongest games, recording two hits and an RBI. Samantha Ronen led the Highlanders with two RBIs. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 13-10 overall. With a positive winning percentage, the Highlanders will receive a birth in the North Coast Section playoffs. NCS seeding will be announced on Sunday, May 18 with the first round of action slated for Tuesday or Wednesday, May 20-21. 7-4 loss to Mt. Eden Mt. Eden scored once in the bottom of the first, but Piedmont took a 2-1 lead in the top half of the second. However, the lead was short-lived with the Monarchs tacking on a pair of runs in the bottom half. From there, Mt. Eden scored once in the bottom of the third, two more in the fourth, and one more in the bottom of the fifth. Piedmont made things interesting with two runs in the final inning in the top of the seventh, but that’s all they could get. In the Piedmont’s two-run top of the second inning, Sa’Mara Levi led off by getting hit by a pitch. Next up was freshman Edie Elmquist, smacking a triple to the left field fence to tie things up at 1-1. Joerger then brought in Elmquist from third with a single to left field. PHS could’ve scored more in the inning, but stranded the bases loaded. With two outs, Sophena Tuli hit a double to left field, then Eunice Kouadio was hit by a pitch. Angelina Wu hit an infield single to load the bases, but Tuli was caught trying to steal home after a wild pitch. Down 7-2 in the top of the seventh, Wu reached first on an error with one out. Miya Fujimoto then slugged a double to left field, bringing Wu to third. Ronen reached first on an error by Mt. Eden’s second baseman, allowing Wu and Fujimoto to score. Levi followed up with a one-out single, but Mt. Eden got out of the jam by getting Piedmont’s next two hitters out. Final stats: Joerge went 2-for-4 with an RBI. Ronen went 1-for-4 with a double and two RBIs. Wu went 1-for-4 with a run scored. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with a double, one run, and a walk. Levi went 1-for-3. Elmquist went 1-for-4 with a triple, RBI, and a run. Tuli went 1-for-2 with a double. Pitching was Fujimoto. She threw six innings, striking out four. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-10 overall) will play in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs on Tuesday or Wednesday, May 20-21. Samantha Ronen went 1-for-4 with a double and two RBIs. Edie Elmquist, a freshman, went 1-for-4 with a triple, RBI, and a run scored.

articles.text: Boys’ 200 medley & 400 free relay teams qualify for State Piedmont High’s swim team traveled to the Concord Community Pool for the 2025 North Coast Section Championship on Thursday and Saturday, May 8-10. The Highlanders competed in 13 different events. Enjoying success, the boys’ 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams did well. In the 200 medley, Nik Costello, Cole Carnazzo, Asher Takazawa, and Owen Blanford reached the NCS finals on Saturday finals to finish fifth of 16 teams with a time of 1:33.24. Their time automatically qualified them for the State Championship on May 16-17 at Clovis West High School. Dima Secor replaced Costello for the 400 freestyle relay, which finished seventh of 16 teams in Saturday’s final with a time of 3:07.68. Their time also gained them an automatic qualification to the State meet. It marks one of the few times that the school has had two relay teams at State. Also reaching the finals, Secor qualified in two events Secor in two events. He was 10th of 16 in the 100 freestyle in 46.97, and was 15th in the 200 Individual Medley in 1:55.28. His time in the 100 free gained an CIF State consideration time. Costello also reached two different finals. He was 12th of 16 in the 50 free with a CIF consideration time of 21.38. He was also Piedmont’s boys’ team’s 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams qualified for State at the NCS Championship. Pictured are Owen Blanford (left), Cole Carnazzo, Asher Takazawa, Dima Secor, and Nik Costello 12th of 16 in the 100 free in 47.10. Blanford was 14th of 16 in the 100 butterfly, clocking a State consideration time of 50.83. Piedmont’s 200 yard freestyle relay team of Evan Byun, Secor, Zafar Majid, and Carnazzo was ninth of 16 in 1:27.58, gaining another CIF consideration time. For the girls’ team, freshman Cynthia Wu was 12th of 16 in the 100 backstroke with a CIF consideration time of 58.50. Other Results The girls’ 200 medley relay team of Wu, Isla McCardell, Samantha White, and Charlotte Zhang was 28th of 39 teams in 1:57.36. The same foursome finished 36th of 40 in the 200 free relay in 1:46.96. Blanford was 25th of 39 in the 200 free in 1:44.21. Takazawa was 19th of 40 in the 100 back, clocking a time of 53.07. Carnazzo was 20th of 39 in the 100 breast, 58.82. NEXT UP Piedmont travels to Clovis for the CIF State Swimming Championship on Friday and Saturday, May 16-17. Friday events start at 1:00 p.m. and Saturday events begin 10:30 a.m.

articles.text: 8th graders Travers Kemp (8th) and Dylan Wallway were joined by sixth grader Elijah Simon to run the 4x400 relay at the league track meet at King Middle School on May 8. It was the last event of the night, and there were not enough runners for PMS to field an 8th grade boys team, so Kemp and Wallway (who had just finished running the 200 and mile, respectively), recruited Simon, a 6th grader who had finished his 200 not long before. He happily stepped up and helped Piedmont place 2nd in the event. “Despite the late hour, the empty stands, and their exhaustion after five hours of competition, they had a great race. All the runners gave everything they had left in the tank,” said coach MInori Tsuge. Even with only three racers (Travers ran both the first and last legs), the boys finished in 2nd place for the 8th grade teams, and 3rd out of 12 teams overall. “The support they gave to each other is what we are looking for in coaching the students. We are so proud of them,” said co-coach Christine Chapon. Travers Kemp (8th) (left), Elijah Simon (6th), and Dylan Wallway (8th), shown after running the 4 x 400 Relay on May 8

articles.text: Cyclist Jasper Schuetz of the Piedmont Mountain Bike team clinched the Junior U19 Boys title in the 2025 Grasshopper .Adventure Series on May 10. It is considered Northern California’s premier mixed-terrain cycling competition. The series stretches from January 26 to May 10 and is known for its challenging blend of gravel, pavement, and dirt courses to test riders across multiple events. The races take place in Northern California, in Ukiah, Maxwell, Sonoma County, and Duncan Mills, CA on public roads, private trails, and through public parks. The Grasshopper Adventure Series, now in its 28th year, is celebrated for pushing cyclists through some of Northern California’s most demanding terrains. Each event offers a unique course, combining various surfaces to challenge participants’ versatility and endurance. Schuetz secured 46 points Jasper Schuetz was fifth of 32 riders at Stafford Lake. Photos courtesy of Piedmont MTB Jasper Schuetz (middle) recently was crowned champion of the Grasshopper Adventure Series U19 Division. at the Low Gap event on January 26, followed by 55 points at Huffmaster on February 22, and capped off with a commanding 60-point performance in Ukiah on April 27, culminating in a total of 161 points. He already clinched the title by his last race on May 10th at King Ridge in Duncan Mills, which was a distance of 91 miles with 9,116 feet of elevation gain. The ride featured steep climbs, technical descents, winding roads, and a coastal ride from Bodega Bay to Timber Cove. This combination of results placed him at the top of the Junior U19 Male category. He will be racing with the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team at the NICA NorCal Championships at Six Sigma Winery in Lower Lake County this Sunday, May 18. pages.text: Wednesday, May 14, 2025 15 Piedmont swim team competes at NCS Championship Boys’ 200 medley & 400 free relay teams qualify for State By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s swim team traveled to the Concord Community Pool for the 2025 North Coast Section Championship on Thursday and Saturday, May 8-10. The Highlanders competed in 13 different events. Enjoying success, the boys’ 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams did well. In the 200 medley, Nik Costello, Cole Carnazzo, Asher Takazawa, and Owen Blanford reached the NCS finals on Saturday finals to finish fifth of 16 teams with a time of 1:33.24. Their time automatically qualified them for the State Championship on May 16-17 at Clovis West High School. Dima Secor replaced Costello for the 400 freestyle relay, which finished seventh of 16 teams in Saturday’s final with a time of 3:07.68. Their time also gained them an automatic qualification to the State meet. It marks one of the few times that the school has had two relay teams at State. He was also Piedmont’s boys’ team’s 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams qualified for State at the NCS Championship. articles.text: The San Francisco Botanical Garden in the city’s Golden Gate Park will host a photography workshop with local photographer Mark Citret on Sunday, May 18. The workshop is open to visitors of all levels of photographic experience. Citret, a San Francisco native, began photographing in 1968 and in the 1980’s produced a large body of work titled “Unnatural Wonders,” his personal survey of architecture in national parks. Citret’s latest collection of works, entitled Structural Beauty: Photographs of the San Francisco Botanical Garden, captures the physical beauty of plants through black and white photographs, his preferred medium. Citret received both his BA and MA in Art from San Francisco State University, and has taught photography at the University of California Berkeley Extension since 1982. Structural Beauty: Photographs of the San Francisco Botanical Garden is on display at the Helen Crocker Magnolia photo by Mark Citret Russell Library in the San Francisco Botanical Garden through the end of May. Workshop attendees must bring their own camera or camera-equipped smartphone. Ticket-holders meet at the San Francisco Botanical Garden’s main gate at 10 a.m. Gardens of Golden Gate Park Members may attend the event at a 20% discount. Contact membership@gggp.org to receive the discount code. To purchase general admission tickets, visit https://gggp.org/event/ plant-photography-workshopwith-mark-citret/.
articles.title: SF Botanical Garden hosts Plant Photography Workshop with Mark Citret May 18

articles.text: The San Francisco Opera orchestra will perform a free concert at historic Saint Joseph’s Arts Society in San Francisco on Saturday, May 17. Advanced registration is required. The afternoon performance, entitled SoundCheck, features music from The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Benjamin Britten’s classic introduction to the instruments, sounds and personalities of the orchestra. Orchestra musicians will also perform Henry Purcell’s original theme from the play Abdelazer, which inspired Britten’s famous composition, and Richard Wagner’s Siegfried Idyll. San Francisco Opera Music Director Eun Sun Kim will conduct the full orchestra for this performance, suitable for families and music lovers of all ages. Attendees are encouraged to move about the iconic space to experience the varied sounds of the orchestra from different perspectives. Saint Joseph’s Arts Society, founded by Ken Fulk in 2018, was established to celebrate and promote arts, design and culture in the San Francisco Bay Area. St. Joseph’s Arts Society is located in a revitalized National Historic Landmark former church, providing an intimate setting for the San Francisco Opera’s free concert. SoundCheck begins at 2:30 p.m. at Saint Joseph’s Arts Society at 1401 Howard Street in the SOMA neighborhood of San Francisco. Doors open at 1:30 p.m. and attendees may purchase drinks at a cash-only bar. Limited seating will be available on a first-come, first-served basis. To register, visit thethirdplace.is/ event/soundcheck. St. Joseph’s Arts Society in San Francisco
articles.title: SF Opera orchestra performs free concert on May 17

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) presents the world premiere of hip-hop musical Co-Founders at Strand Theater in San Francisco Thursday, May 29. The play runs through Sunday, July 6. Directed by Jamil Jude, the play follows an underrated young Oakland coder named Esata who “hacks” her way into a competitive startup accelerator in San Francisco, the world’s tech mecca. As Esata and her loved ones get priced out by Silicon Valley billionaires, Esata forms an unlikely partnership with a prep-school dropout in a field where the privileged few make millions while others struggle to survive. “This is a musical love letter for the community… [from] the Valley to Vallejo,” said A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “I am thrilled that A.C.T. will premiere this Bay story. Strand Theater is sure to be the place this Spring to feel big joy with this big local can-do story born of necessity and drive, creativity and passion. Created by local playwrights and artists RyanNicole Austin, Beau Lewis, and Adesha Adefela, Co-Founders features a catchy Photo by Michaela Schulz Co-Founders creative team Beau Lewis, Adesha Adefela, and RyanNicole Austin score that draws inspiration from the Bay Area’s hip-hop scene, as well as soul, gospel, funk, jazz, R&B, and more. “I’m thrilled to launch Co-Founders right here in the Bay, my home and heart,” Austin said. “This show is an ode to our region, celebrating a spirit of innovation so vibrant, resilient, and determinant it blooms through concrete like dandelions. Co-Founders is both a loving critique and an invitation for today’s visionaries to reflect deeply on the future they’re building.” The cast of Co-Founders includes Adefela and Austin, as well as Austin Dean Ashford, Rolanda D. Bell, Jordan Covington, B. DeVeaux, Aneesa Folds, Roe Hartrampf, Keith Pinto, Deanalís Arocho Resto, Tommy Soulati Shepherd, and Ryan Torres. Post-show discussions with the creative team are held on June 17 and 22, and July 2. A revamped pre- and post-show party celebrating LGBTQ+ pride within the theater community will be held June 18 before and following the 7:30 p.m. performance. To purchase tickets, call the box office at 415-749-2228 or visit www.act-sf.org/cofounders to purchase online.
articles.title: A.C.T. presents world premiere of Co-Founders May 19

articles.text: Diana Ross, The Pointer Sisters and Marley sons are headliners Stern Grove Festival, San Francisco’s longest-running free music festival, begins on Sunday, June 15. Diana Ross, The Pointer Sisters and Damian and Stephen Marley are among the top headliners this year. The amphitheater at Sigmund Stern Grove in San Francisco hosts ten weeks of admission-free concerts every year beginning in June and running through August. Reservation is required and is given on a first-come, firstserve basis. Last year’s festival drew 90,000 attendees over the course of two months. The festival, now in its 88th season, opens June 15 with performances by Oakland-based retro-soul group The California Honeydrops. The San Francisco Symphony will perform a special show on Sunday, July 6 with special guest Taimane, an American ukulele virtuoso and composer. The Big Picnic Weekend, the festival’s annual fundraiser, ends the summer-long festival with performances by Damian and Diana Ross headlines the 88th Stern Grove Festival. Stephen Marley, the multi-Grammy-winning artists and sons of the legendary Bob Marley, and Motown icon Diana Ross. Ross rose to fame as the lead singer of the 1960s pop group the Supremes and earned the title “Queen of Motown Records.” She began her solo career in the 1970’s, launching iconic hits like “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” “Touch Me in the Morning,” “I’m Coming Out,” and “Love Hangover.” Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites.The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. of summer performances. Visit https://www.sterngrove.org to reserve tickets.
articles.title: Stern Grove Festival begins June 15

articles.text: The 42nd San Francisco Jazz Festival, an annual three-week music festival produced by nonprofit organization SFJAZZ, kicks off on Friday, June 13 at the Miner Auditorium. Headliners include Charles Lloyd Sky Quartet, Stanley Clark and Gonzalo Rubalcaba and Patrice Rushen. This year’s revamped festival features 35 concerts across multiple stages June 13 through 15 at the SFJAZZ Center and festival tent, and includes food trucks, a beer garden, local wine vendors, art, and vinyl merchanchanise for purchase throughout venues each day. About twelve performances take place daily. “I’m so thrilled to share America’s greatest art form with the Bay Area and the world with our revamped festival,” said SFJAZZ Executive Artistic Director Terence Blanchard. “We are going to bring the best artists and most exciting music of our time, along with new music and arts and crafts.” Performing this year is a collection of both local musicians and Grammy-winning legacy artists, including Kurt Elling, Don Was & The Pan Detroit Ensemble, Braxton Cook, Sachal Vasandani, Lakecia Benjamin, Kassa Overall, Mark Lettieri Group, and Salami Rose Joe Louis. Full access VIP passes, 3-day passes, single-day passes, and venue specific passes are now available. All ticket holders will have access to both the festival Street Market on the corner of Oak St. and Franklin St., and the Community Art Market on the 2nd Floor Lobby of the SFJAZZ Center. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/2025-summer/festival/overview/ to purchase tickets. Saxophonist Charles Lloyd kicks off the festival on Friday, June 13.
articles.title: Three-day San Francisco Jazz Festival kicks off June 13

articles.text: Piedmont resident Joel Sidney performed on guitar with the Spectrum Bluegrass Band to a near capacity audience for the Light Up the Blues concert on April 26 at the 5,900-seat Los Angeles Greek Theatre. Joel is a graduate of Piedmont High School and received a B.A. degree from the University of California in Berkeley. Other band members included Joy Louise Williams (guitar), John Frizzell (mandolin), Jesse Katz (bass) and Max Schwartz (banjo). The band played three songs including two bluegrass standards, “On and On” and “Blue Moon of Kentucky” and one song composed by Williiams, “Majestic Breed.” The 4-hour concert was headlined by performances from the legendary Stephen Stills and Neil Young as well as other famous artists including Billy Idol, Cat Power, Linda Perry, Chris Stills, Nathaniel Rateliff, and Rufus Wainwright. The Light Up the Blues concert was sponsored by and benefited Autism Speaks (www. autismspeaks.org), a non-profit organization dedicated to creating an inclusive world for all individuals with autism throughout their lifespan. The Spectrum Bluegrass Band was sponsored by the California Bluegrass Association though its new initiative, Spectrum Bluegrass (https://californiabluegrass.org/ spectrum-bluegrass/) which is dedicated to connecting neurodiverse people through bluegrass music. Spectrum Bluegrass is starting with an Autism Chapter with a goal to ease the challenges and amplify the enjoyment of bluegrass for autistic people by creating an active community where they explore new pathways to express themselves and connect. Spectrum Bluegrass Band performed at the Light Up the Blues concert. Band members are Joy Louise Williams (left), Joel Sidney, John Frissell, Jesse Katz, and Max Schwartz San Francisco Bach Choir The very next day, the San Francisco Bach Choir conducted by Magen Solomon presented a concert in First Church Berkeley. First on the program came a Mass written by Marianna Martines (1744-1812). This composition was written when she was only 16 years old. I had never heard of her. A genius like this… and totally unknown. When listening to music it’s often helpful to begin with a clean slate. There was a Mozartian clarity thoroughly embracing the spirit of the classic era. It seems that Marianna Martines was highly respected early on and then became forgotten. If this work is any indication, it will be a pleasure to hear other works by her. The San Francisco Bach choir was directed by Magen Solomon, who also conducted the Jubilate Baroque Orchestra. Solomon’s conducting was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. As a result, the performance was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. Martha Stoddard, the conductor of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra visited with me for a little while during the intermission. She told me that the PCO will play a concert Saturday afternoon, May 17 at 4:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Diluvian String Quartet A familial responsibility encouraged me to attend the Diluvian string Quartet concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts that same afternoon. Son Raphael is the violist. They have a new cellist. While listening to any concert, I form my own opinions. At the same time, I listen to what members of the audience say, and I even engage them in conversation, asking for their opinions. Some of the observations were in complete agreement with mine. They observed that the tone of the Diluvian String Quartet is like wine of a rare vintage… mellow and well-balanced.
articles.title: Joel Sidney performs at Light Up the Blues concert

articles.text: Can there be too much of a good thing? In music, we have the term ma non troppo, which means “but not too much”. I assume this means that musicians have a good amount of equilibrium. What is difficult is making the choice at the banquet table. It is a pleasure to see how child prodigies grow into mature artists. That was the case at Piedmont Piano Company on Friday evening when two of the outstanding young talents from our area presented an exciting concert. Melissa Lam is a cellist of high attainment… snd still a high school student. She was joined by pianist and composer Eric Tran. The concert featured Sonata by Mendelssohn and Rachmaninov. It is hard to imagine better compositions. What we heard was a sublime interpretation. Tran introduced the works with a little bit of levity – and then the two of them played. They did not need to warm up. They were hot from the start. The performance gave me goosebumps. In my notes, I wrote the word “thrilling“ and then added an exclamation point. This was classic Mendelsohn. It encapsulated ardent and playful leprechauns, playful but evil fairies, a love song and bees in the garden. Both the Mendelssohn Sonata, and the Rachmaninoff Sonata have a universality. The performance expressed this nature, causing the listener to be transported to another world. The two young musicians play with the wisdom of the ages. They have a diabolical intensity and make everything look so easy. In my dictionary, that defines “virtuosity”. Pianist Eric Tran and cellist Melissa Lam take their curtain calls after a masterful concert on May 9 at Piedmont Piano Company.

pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, May 14, 2025 Joel Sidney performs at Light Up the Blues concert Piedmont resident Joel Sidney performed on guitar with the Spectrum Bluegrass Band to a near capacity audience for the Light Up the Blues concert on April 26 at the 5,900-seat Los Angeles Greek Theatre. Joel is a graduate of Piedmont High School and received a B.A. degree from the University of California in Berkeley. The Light Up the Blues concert was sponsored by and benefited Autism Speaks (www. autismspeaks.org), a non-profit organization dedicated to creating an inclusive world for all individuals with autism throughout their lifespan. First on the program came a Mass written by Marianna Martines (1744-1812). This composition was written when she was only 16 years old. I had never heard of her. A genius like this… and totally unknown. When listening to music it’s often helpful to begin with a clean slate. There was a Mozartian clarity thoroughly embracing the spirit of the classic era. It seems that Marianna Martines was highly respected early on and then became forgotten. If this work is any indication, it will be a pleasure to hear other works by her. The San Francisco Bach choir was directed by Magen Solomon, who also conducted the Jubilate Baroque Orchestra. Solomon’s conducting was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. As a result, the performance was gracious, encouraging and intelligent. Martha Stoddard, the conductor of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra visited with me for a little while during the intermission. She told me that the PCO will play a concert Saturday afternoon, May 17 at 4:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Diluvian String Quartet A familial responsibility encouraged me to attend the Diluvian string Quartet concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts that same afternoon. Son Raphael is the violist. They have a new cellist. While listening to any concert, I form my own opinions. At the same time, I listen to what members of the audience say, and I even engage them in conversation, asking for their opinions. Some of the observations were in complete agreement with mine. They observed that the tone of the Diluvian String Quartet is like wine of a rare vintage… mellow and well-balanced. This concert builds upon the community of composers, living and not. Through it, you’ll meet familiar faces and meet some new ones, all of whom will make you feel like you’re reuniting with long-lost friends. Stacey’s contemporary chamber music expertise shines. Tickets at https://tickets.berkeleysymphony.org/TheatreManager/1/online?performance=577. Saturday, May 24, 4:00 p.m. San Francisco Mandolin Octet Concert The San Francisco Mandolin Octet presents a concert entitled Originals, a celebration of music composed specifically for mandolin ensemble, led by virtuoso Achille Bocus and featuring members of the San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra. The program showcases works by Italian virtuoso Raffaele Calace, bringing to life the distinct sound of an eight-piece ensemble rarely heard in today’s concert halls. From Calace’s Serenata Gaia and Sogno to works by Ballerini, Kok, and more, the Octet invites listeners into a musical world where the mandolin takes center stage. For advance tickets visit https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6648585. Saturday, May 24, 7:30 p.m. Benicia Chamber Players Concert For almost 20 years, the Benicia Chamber Players have aimed to cultivate a community of local and other world-class professional musicians with a love of playing chamber music who are dedicated to sharing that love with audiences. Here, a pair of matched cello trios present For the Love of Music and Words: String Sextets and Concerto by Bacewicz, Schoenberg and Strauss, to include the Bacewicz Concerto for Orchestra, the Strauss Capriccio, Op. 85, and Arnold Schoenberg’s Verklärte Nacht (Transfigured Night), Op. 4. With two violins, two violas, and two cellos, this program is guaranteed to satisfy lovers of stringed instruments. For advance tickets please visit https://www.eventbrite.com/e/1350060941619. Students with ID are admitted free. Sunday, May 25, 7:00 p.m. Berkelium String Quartet Concert A new chamber ensemble of celebrated Bay Area musicians based in Berkeley, the Berkelium String Quartet performs a concert, Bow and the Brush, at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The quartet, consisting of Dan Flanagan and Karen Shinozaki Sor, violins; Jacob Hansen Joseph, viola; and Michael Graham, cello; will perform Flanagan’s Water Lilies, inspired by Monet’s masterpiece, followed by iconic string quartets by Beethoven and Schubert, performed alongside projections of period paintings. The performance will be followed by a reception. Tickets are $30 and May 13, and may be purchased in advance at: https:// www.berkeliumquartet.com/events-1, or at the door with cash or Venmo.

articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Octet will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, May 24. The theme: “Originals: Music Made for Mandolins.” According to Achille Bocus, music director and concert soloist, “the concert will feature music specifically written to highlight the mandolin’s shimmering, expressive sound. It will be an afternoon of original music made specifically for mandolins, with no adaptations and no transcriptions, just authentic compositions that showcase mandolins in their purest form.” At the heart of the program are works by Raffaele Calace, one of the most brilliant and virtuosic mandolin composers of all time. His compositions, full of drama, passion, and astonishing technique, reveal the mandolin’s exceptional capacity for classical expression and virtuosity. Alongside Calace, the octet will showcase other pieces created for small mandolin ensembles with works that highlight the instrument’s unique, sparkling sound and demonstrate the depth of its classical repertoire. It’s an opportunity to hear musical treasures rarely heard in concert halls, and promises to be a distinctive musical experience. The San Francisco Mandolin Octet is an offshoot of the larger San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, which has performed to appreciative audiences in Piedmont since 2017. The ensemble plays a combination of classical orchestral pieces transcribed for mandolins, mandolas, and guitars, as well as a selection of more popular and contemporary pieces. The family-friendly concert will begin at 4:00 p.m. on Saturday, May 24. Admission is $25 general in advance, and $30 cash/ check at the door. Tickets may be purchased at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6648585

articles.text: Benicia Chamber Players presents the season finale of its 2024–2025 series on May 24 at 7:30 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts with a program of visionary and virtuosic string ensemble works. The program includes Arnold Schoenberg’s Verklärte Nacht, Richard Strauss’ Capriccio, and Grażyna Bacewicz’s Concerto for String Orchestra (1948). Schoenberg’s late-Romantic tone poem vividly brings Richard Dehmel’s haunting verse to life, exploring despair, forgiveness, and redemption through love. Strauss’ Capriccio, subtitled “A Conversation Piece for Music,” poses the timeless question: which holds greater power—words or music? Composed during World War II, it offers a poignant, lyrical escape. Bacewicz’s vibrant concerto, one of her masterpieces, fuses neoclassical clarity with modern intensity, marked by propulsive rhythms, haunting melodies, and a fiercely original voice that defies easy classification. This concert is free for students. Musicians: Maya Cohon, violin; Heeguen Song, violin; Nao Kubota, viola; Dmitri Yevstifeev, viola; Brady Anderson, cello; Evan Kahn, cello.

articles.text: Tom Hanks and Helena Zengel in News of the World News of the World is an extraordinary, neo-western, adapted from the Paulette Jules 2016 novel. It is set in Texas in 1870, three years after the end of the Civil War. Confederate veteran Captain Jefferson Kyle Kidd (Tom Hanks), once a printer, now makes his improbable living by travelling from Texas town to Texas town reading the news, stories gleaned from newspapers from both near and far, standing stage center in candle-lit rooms, saying, “I read the news to anyone with ten cents and the time to hear it.” His audience is comprised of rough-hewn settlers, many still coming to terms with the defeat of the South. Many of those standing before him either can’t read, or spend every waking hour in physical labor; yet, all remain eager to hear the news of the world. As we soon come to realize, Captain Kidd is not only a respected man of letters, but also a storyteller and entertainer, and an enthusiastic, at times jocular reader of what could simply be the dry words on a page of newsprint. His mission is not only to inform but to capture the imaginations of his audience. On a trip to another town he discovers an overturned wagon on the side of the road. Investigating, he sees the body of a black freedman, hanging from a tree. Hiding nearby, among the brush, he spots a terrified young white girl (Helena Zengel), 12, dressed in Native American clothes, her blond hair bluntly cut. She is able to speak only Kiowa. He discovers some identifying papers in the wagon that say that she is German, her name is Johanna (she later explains that she is called Cicada), and she was abducted as a youngster and her parents killed. A passing Union patrol captain, after examining the documents, instructs Kidd to take her to the next town where

articles.text: After watching A Bag of Marbles (reviewed in the April 30th edition), what came to mind was that the Holocaust (also referred to as the Shoah), has been the subject of countless narrative films as well as a canon of what is described as Holocaust literature. Some works still use the Shoah only as a general referent or as a context (The Pianist, White Bird, The Boy in the Striped Pajamas, Sarah’s Key). And then there are films that portray the reality of the Holocaust in the starkest, most cruel and unrelenting detail, displaying am absence of humanity that is still impossible to comprehend. Though I had viewed director Steven Spielberg’s film Schindler’s List when it was first released and nominated for 12 Oscars in 1993, I recently watched it on Prime and found it still to be extraordinary. It is a work of art that transcends mere storytelling. It is profoundly evocative, at times grimly compelling, while implicitly asking countless questions regarding how and why the Holocaust could ever have taken place? Of course, it isn’t the intent of a narrative film such as Spielberg’s, adapted from the 1982 prize-wining book by Thomas Keneally, to offer answers; rather, its intent is to show through characters and dialogue and settings/imagery the all of it, Liam Neeson and Ben Kingsley in Schindler’s List

articles.text: The family friendly My Dog Skip, is a captivating story that focuses on the touching relationship between a 9-year-old boy, Willie Morris (Frankie Muniz), and his dog, a spunky Jack Russell Terrier that Willie names Skip. The film is set in Yazoo, Mississippi. The year is 1942. Willie, small for his age, is a lonely kid, often bullied by his larger classmates, especially a tough trio who take every opportunity to give him a hard time. He also has a standoffish relationship with his dad, Jack (Kevin Bacon), a gruff man, even bitter, who lost a leg in the Spanish Civil war. But it is his mom, Ellen (Diane Lane), who does her best to make Willie happy and often suggests to Jack that a dog would be the perfect companion for their isolated son. Willie of course agrees, pleads for a dog, but Jack firmly resists. Willie is about to have a birthday, even sends out invitation to his classmates, but on the day of the scheduled party only his grandparents show up, and his grandmother gives him a bowtie. But unbeknownst to Jack, Ellen brings to the party a small box and inside is a sweet little terrier pup, which delights Willie, and angers Jack. But Ellen prevails. There are, of course, subplots. One involves thuggish moonshiners who use an abandoned burial vault in the local cemetery to hide their illegal hooch. And there’s the bullying trio who dare Willie to stay all night among the tombstones while telling him that he should be on the look out for a witch who wanders about. articles.text: Hailee Steinfeld and Hayden Szeto in The Edge of Seventeen To capture the essence of being an adolescent, or as one critic called it, “The unbearable lightness of being a teenager,” is no easy thing. But The Edge of Seventeen, written and directed by Kelly Freemon Craig, is a coming-of-age story that is pitch perfect and gets it just right. The narrative stars Hailee Steinfeld portraying Nadine Byrd, 17, a junior in high school, whose bursting emotions swing from sweet to awkward to mean, while comprising a period in her life that can be intensely moving, disturbing, and funny. In voice over, Nadine explains she’s had a couple of seriously difficult years following the unexpected death of her father from a heart attack. The only person she feels she can turn to for comfort and understanding is her long-time best friend (since elementary school), Krista (Haley Lu Richardson). But when Krista begins dating Nadine’s super jock quarterback older brother, Darien (Blake Jenner), a senior, (Nadine walks in on them in Darien’s room) she is crushed and feels abandoned, and thus begins what will be her emotional meltdown. Perhaps think roller coaster. Neither her mom (Kyra Sedgwick), nor her favorite English teacher, Mr. Bruner (Woody Harrelson), are sympathetic. Her mom has issues, and Mr. Bruner, laconic as always, refuses to get pulled into Nadine’s drama as she obsesses over every emotional self-esteem speed bump and detail of her adolescent life. v i o l i n C o h o n , a S o n g , u e n e g e v i o l i n H N a o K u b o t a , v i o l a n K a h n , c e l l o E v a e e v , v i o l i n y A n d e r s o n , c B r a d e l l o 3 PM Sunday May 25, 2025 Community Congregational Church Piedmont Center for the Arts 1305 W 2nd Street Benicia, CA To purchase tickets, visit beniciachamberplayers.com

articles.text: Marolyn Stanley passed away peacefully at her home on the morning of January 30, 2025, at the age of 96. A fourth-generation Californian, Marolyn Jane Hoffman was born in 1928, the daughter of Ethel and Verne Hoffman of Lodi, California. Her family lived on a ranch east of Lodi in Acampo. Her mother, Ethel Jack Hoffman, was born on the Lodi property in 1898. Marolyn was raised there along the Mokelumne River with two older brothers, Verne Jr. and Robert. Her father, Verne, was a farmer and also served in the California State Senate. The family grew peaches and cherries, as well as Tokay grapes for which the Lodi region was well known. Every summer the family spent time at their summer cabin at Meeks Bay in Lake Tahoe. Marolyn attended Bruella School, a small elementary schoolhouse about a mile from her home. She was a 4H girl and rode her horse Bessie to school. The story goes that the horse would take herself home. She attended Lodi High School where she excelled in her studies. In 1946 she enrolled at the University of California, Berkeley, and graduated with a Bachelor of Arts degree in the class of 1950. While at Cal, Marolyn joined the Alpha Delta Pi sorority, where she made lifelong friends. Cal football was at a high-water mark during those years, and she remained a devoted Cal fan throughout her life, always serving on her class planning committee. After graduating, she worked in interior design for Macy’s in San Francisco where she met the love of her life, Paul Stanley, a San Francisco native. The two of them met on a blind date and had such a wonderful time, they decided that first evening to get married. Marolyn and Paul wed in the design. This was always reflected in her homes, gardens, and style -and in the way she approached the world. She was an award-winning floral designer with a deep passion for flowers, often incorporating tropical blooms into her stunning arrangements. She was among the earliest exhibitors in The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s Bouquets to Art show, where she showcased her work for 16 consecutive years. Before that, she served on the museum’s flower committee. Her love for gardening and floral design was evident throughout her life, as she created unforgettable centerpieces and décor for charity events, as well as for family and friends, always exceeding expectations. In her seventies, Marolyn expanded her artistic pursuits to quilting. Her beautiful modern quilts, many featuring bright tropical and floral designs, were displayed at numerous quilt shows across the West. Marolyn will always be cherished for her calm and steadfast presence, her quiet wisdom, and her sly, unexpected sense of humor. In her later years she enjoyed the frequent visits and time spent with all of her children and grandchildren. She will be forever missed and remembered for the colorful life she led and shared with others. Marolyn is survived by her beloved husband, Paul; her four children, Bob (Joyce), Patricia, Douglas (Julia), Jane (Bert); and her loving grandchildren, John, Carolyn, Christine (Scott), Jessica, Charlotte, Robby, Jeff (Erin), Brian and cat Kali. The family will be forever grateful to her wonderful caregivers, Celia, Tally, Lani Angela and Angela. Memorial services will be private. articles.text: The True Story of Tamara De Lempicka & the Art of Survival is a visually stunning and sweeping feature documentary that traces the life and survival of the renowned painter through her powerful paintings – from her rise to international stardom in 1920s Paris, to her move to the United States in 1940, fleeing the rise of fascism, and her revival in the current art market. Tamara de Lempicka was the preeminent Art Deco painter, known for her high-gloss sensual nudes and portraits of high society during the Jazz Age. She was marginalized and gained notoriety for her romantic liaisons with her models and her indulgent, decadent lifestyle, but she was much more. The writer, director and producer of the film is Julie Rubio. She is a dynamic storyteller and is passionate about bringing to light the narratives of those often overlooked. As the president of Women in Film SF Bay Area, Rubio dedicates herself to empowering and elevating women in the film industry, fostering a supportive community for female filmmakers. Her most notable work, the critically acclaimed East Side Sushi, won accolades at 16 film festivals and garnered nominations for Cinema Tropical’s 2016 Best Latino Film of the Year and Mexico’s Diosa de Plata award for Best Picture. East Side Sushi, filmed in the Bay Area, is a compelling narrative of a single Latina mother’s pursuit of a better life and achieved widespread distribution through Samuel Goldwyn Company, Sony Home, HBO North America, and Netflix, where it became a trendsetter in popular and drama categories. Rubio’s latest movie, The True Story of Tamra De Lempicka & the Art of Survival will be shown at the Grand Lake Theater this weekend for three days only: • Saturday, May 17, 12 noon • Sunday, May 18, 12 noon • Monday, May 19, 4:15, 6:45, & 8:55 pm Purchase tickets online at Grand Lake Theater (https:// www.renaissancerialto.com/ Tamara.php)

pages.text: Wednesday, May 14, 2025 25 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers smell the roses By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group headed to the Morcom Rose Garden a few days in advance of Mother’s Day for the group’s annual visit. The group crossed Grand Avenue and went up Jean Street to the garden where its history was shared. The Rose Garden is in a natural bowl on a 7.5- acre site that was purchased by the City of Oakland in 1911 and named the Linda Vista Park. Local Oakland residents had petitioned and promised to contribute $8,000 for it. However, the best park entrance was through land in Piedmont. The Piedmont City Council joined the effort in June 1911 by acquiring Piedmont lots at the southern corner of Olive and Oakland Avenues to provide a “handsome entrance.” In 1913 it was proposed that the park be converted into a zoological garden. A number of animal offers were received. Golden Gate Park offered elk and buffalo. F. M. “Borax” Smith offered a number of llamas from his large herd on his East Oakland estate, but the park directors decided not to have animals. Linda Vista Park’s conversion to a rose garden was a project of the Oakland Businessmen’s Garden Club in 1930 with the support of the City. It was originally known as the Municipal Rose Garden. Work began on the garden in 1931 and the first rose was planted on January 27, 1933. The garden opened officially on May 28, 1933, and work was completed in 1935 with Depression era funding. The park’s name was changed in 1954 to honor former Oakland Mayor Fred Morcom, who served from 1931 to 1933. The park has been refurbished at least twice, in the 1950s and 1990s, with many of the old roses, some going back to the 19th century, regrafted on new rootstock. There is a “No Dogs Allowed” sign at the park entrance, but on last year’s walk a park staff person told the walkers that dogs on leaches were okay. So, Jack Fischrup’s K-9 best friend Kojak also went in with the walkers to see the roses. The group stopped at the central reflecting pool and cascade steps where more information was shared. The garden’s design was inspired by gardens in Italy. The park has over 2,400 rose bushes in three areas. There are winding walkways with a reflecting pool across from a 14-step cascade that goes down the hillside to the west and an octagonal wedding terrace above with more rose beds. The essential design has changed little in the park’s nearly 90-year history. However, in the early 2000s, Oakland city workers’ hours to maintain the garden were reduced. A group of volunteers, the “Dedicated Deadheaders,” was organized to help keep the garden beautiful. They work every Wednesday and Saturday. Christian Boyle of the Oakland Department of Public Works is in charge of the garden, and he provided additional information about its history. Christian said wild turkeys are less frequent than in the past, but geese tried to make the garden a home. Their droppings made them unwelcome and he scared them off. Deer are a challenge, too. They have visited the garden and nipped buds, which explained some bushes’ lack of flowers. Wild onions are a problem too. The garden does not use chemicals, and this provides a “healthy garden,” but weeds are an issue. A study is currently being conducted by Merritt College students on weed suppression techniques. In the early 2000s “The Mothers’ Walk” was created above the reflecting pool to a Florentine oval garden at the north end of the park. There are brass plaques in the cement with the names of women honored each year in an annual Mother’s Day ceremony. The walkers appreciated Christian’s friendly, impromptu presentation and asked him to be part of their group photo at the cascade steps. Then the walkers splintered off on the paths to see different sections of the garden. The beds of roses on Mother’s Walk were especially beautiful. The group took their time and then retraced their route back to the Exedra at their own pace. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. articles.text: and April Gruber Shalev On April 24, the Cancer League, Inc. hosted its 10th annual Spring Soirée event at Trader Vic’s in Emeryville. The “shopping for survivorship” event raised an estimated $156,000 for ground-breaking cancer research, thanks to generous sponsors, attendees, in-kind donors, and over 20 vendors that donated 25% of their proceeds from the evening’s sales. The Bay views and beautiful Polynesian décor at Trader Vic’s were the perfect backdrop to this year’s Soiree as 200 guests gathered for a Mai Tai reception, hors d’oeuvres and a choice of two sumptuous buffet dinners. Upon their arrival VIP attendees received a fresh Hawaiian lei from Oakland Flower Mart. A fabulous raffle included items donated from Cavallo Point, Veronica Beard, and Ariel Gordon Jewelry. Guests also enjoyed tarot readings by Adriana Bels Systemic Tarot. Event co-chairs Sasha Bainer and April Gruber Shalev executed a flawless night of shopping, mingling and most importantly fundraising to support early-stage, cutting-edge cancer research that truly impacts treatment and patient therapies. “Spring Soiree was a huge success this year,” said Bainer. “Not only was the party fabulously fun but we also beat our fundraising goal. Trader Vic’s was the perfect backdrop for a festive upbeat evening. We are grateful for our guests who shopped and sipped in support of cancer research and for all the sponsors, donors and vendors who joined us in our effort. April and I are so honored to have been the stewards of Soiree again this year and to help a cause that is so dear to our hearts.” The lead sponsors were Dan and Stacey Case Family Foundation and Gloria Gruber. Additional sponsors included Sasha Bainer, Mary Jane Lowenthal, Sally O’Neal and April Gruber Shalev. Cancer League is thankful to the vendors, sponsors, in-kind donors, and attendees for making this year’s Spring Soirée a huge success. “A huge shout out to everyone who supported the Cancer League at this year’s Spring Soiree!” said Cancer League President Jenna Caldwell.” Everyone from our sponsors, in-kind donors, vendors who graciously donated 25% of Co-chairs, April Gruber & Sasha Bainer Danielle Horowitz, Kristin Odegaard, Brooke Wall, Cancer League President Jenna Caldwell, Lisa Sauer & Julia Mehra Geraldine Vayson, Rachelle Hebrard, Beverly Roberts Charles and Tamara Vayson Giscela Delventhal and Tonya Antonucci Mai Tai Cocktails Kia Moore Designs their night’s proceeds and everybody who just came out for a fun-filled evening of sipping and shopping! We couldn’t continue to support our mission of seeding the cure without their generosity and support.” Save the date for Caner League’s signature holiday event, The Holly Ball, on Friday, April and Gloria Gruber December 5th, 2025. About Cancer League The Cancer League is a San Francisco Bay Area nonprofit that funds groundbreaking cancer research at its early stages. Since its inception in 1973, it has raised and donated over $5 million toward the fight against cancer organization.

articles.text: More than 100 guests gathered at George Mark Children’s House, a pediatric hospice in San Leandro, on May 2 for an unforgettable afternoon with beloved Star Wars characters. The special occasion brought Star Wars magic to children facing serious medical conditions. Now in its fourth year, Star Wars Day has become a cherished tradition for the George Mark community. This year’s celebration featured a special collaboration with Rancho Obi-Wan (ranchoobiwan. org), home to the world’s largest privately owned Star Wars memorabilia collection. In honor of the 20th anniversary of the movie Revenge of the Sith, Rancho ObiA patient has fun with Star Wars droids R2-D2 and Chopper. Wan curated a themed display of collectibles, toys, and promotional items. “For us, Rancho Obi-Wan has always been about helping to build a sense of community among fans of all ages,” said Ann Neumann, its president. “We help spread the fun and inspiration that Star Wars provides.” “We hope we brought some joy to George Mark Children’s House and helped create memories the families will hold close by sharing the love of a galaxy far, far away,” said founder Steve Sansweet. “It’s hard to put into words what it means to see the joy this day brings to our families,” said Shekinah Eliassen, CEO of George Mark Children’s House. “The Force was strong, but even stronger was the sense of community and love.” The celebration also included visits from Darth Vader, Chewbacca, General Leia, Stormtroopers, and fan-favorite droids R2-D2 and Chopper — thanks to volunteers from the Golden Gate Garrison of the 501st Legion, the Endor Base of the Rebel Legion, and the Bay Area Droid Builders. Guests enjoyed terrarium-making, caricatures, crafts, and toy giveaways, supported by Rancho Obi-Wan and Starlight Children’s Foundation. “Our mission is to provide the best quality of life for children with serious medical conditions,” said Kyle Amsler, Child Life Specialist at George Mark. “A day like this is all about joy – giving families a chance to create extraordinary memories together.” For many the experience was deeply emotional. “One mom came up to me with tears in her eyes and just said thank you,” said Events Coordinator Ricky Resurreccion. “She told me how much it meant to see her daughter so happy and to have a day that felt magical. Moments like that remind us why creating these kinds of experiences matter. It’s a validation that what we do goes beyond fun; it’s deeply meaningful.” A George Mark Children’s House patient with the movie’s galactic good guys A peek inside the Rancho Obi-Wan display area of Star Wars memorabilia A child poses with Neel, a character from Star Wars: Skeleton Crew.

articles.text: Piedmont kids and families brought their bikes to the first ever Gear Up Bike Festival last Saturday, May 10, from noon to 4:00 p.m. at the Havens School The festival provided information on bike maintenance and safety, as well as a bike swap that gave away five helmets and eight bikes to members of the community. Over 100 attendees visited the inaugural event, which began with a family biking workshop by Bike East Bay. The event also featured a Mister Softee ice cream truck, a bike obstacle course by the Piedmont Police Department and Piedmont Scouts, pedal-powered blender smoothies by Piedmont Scouts, and pedal-powered spin art by inventor group Rock the Bike. Visitors were also able to test ride E-bikes from electric bike shop The New Wheel. Oakland Trek ran a bike maintenance table at the event to help and inform attending cyclists, and an additional class teaching kids how to be safe on bikes. The event’s bike swap gave kids and adults a way to bring outgrown bikes, equipment, and parts to swap with other families. As part of the bike swap, the event gave away five helmets and eight bikes, donated from listings on Buy Nothing facebook groups. Bike to Work Day The event was organized by Piedmont parent Daniel Sherman as a way to help publicize the upcoming Bike to Work Day on May 15. The Bay Area biking event encourages people to bike to work, school, or anywhere they need to go. “When you bike, you’re connected to your environment and the people around you,” said Sherman. “You’re aware of what’s going on, and you’re not going from one box (your house) to the next box (your car) to the next box (your classroom). Instead you’re interacting with people, you’re paying attention, it gives kids autonomy, independence and pride.” Sherman and his family enjoy cycling to get around and encourages others to try it as well. “The Gear Up event was great, but look forward to May 15,” said Sherman. Kids and parents attend a family biking workshop by Bike East Bay at the festival. Kids make pedal-powered spin art with inventor group Rock The Bike. Pedaling the bike turns a wheel, and kids pour in paint to create patterns. Two children maneuver through an obstacle course at the Gear Up Bike Festival. The pedal-powered spin art hangs to dry. Oakland Trek offered bike repair and maintenance advice at their table. Piedmont Scouts gave out pedal-powered smoothies from a bicyclepowered blender. An array of bikes were contributed to the bike swap to help kids get into cycling for free.

Instead you’re interacting with people, you’re paying attention, it gives kids autonomy, independence and pride.” Sherman and his family enjoy cycling to get around and encourages others to try it as well. “The Gear Up event was great, but look forward to May 15,” said Sherman. Kids and parents attend a family biking workshop by Bike East Bay at the festival. Kids make pedal-powered spin art with inventor group Rock The Bike. Pedaling the bike turns a wheel, and kids pour in paint to create patterns. Two children maneuver through an obstacle course at the Gear Up Bike Festival. The pedal-powered spin art hangs to dry. Oakland Trek offered bike repair and maintenance advice at their table. Piedmont Scouts gave out pedal-powered smoothies from a bicyclepowered blender. An array of bikes were contributed to the bike swap to help kids get into cycling for free.
