Schindler’s List Continued from page 20 asking only that the audience not look away. Shindler’s List has at its center German industrialist Oskar Schindler (Liam Neeson), initially portrayed as a war profiteer. Arriving in Krakow, Poland in 1939, he joins the Nazi Party and lavishly cultivates high-ranking officers who will help him to find captive Jewish labor needed for his factory. It is only when he witnesses the mass killing of the Jews forced to live in the Krakow Ghetto that he comes to comprehend the true meaning of what was abstractly referred to as “the final solution.” Schindler’s journey from that moment is both transformative and horrifying. As an aside, Spielberg chose to film Schindler’s List in black and white, adding a documentary and unforgiving motif to the story. There is, however, one exception. A small girl wearing a red coat appears, walking with her parents, heading, we assume, to Krakow’s railroad station where she along with countless others will be forced onto cattle cars and transported to a death camp. She does appear again, briefly, and that moment is wrenching and heartbreaking, beyond all understanding. As is Schindler’s List. Schindler’s List. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Liam Neeson, Ben Kingsley, Ralph Fiennes. 3 hrs., 15 min. Rated R. Released in 1993. Now streaming on Netflix/prime/apple/Fandango. articles.text: centrality of Tabitha’s good works and acts of charity to the well-being, the identity, of their community. These were gifts, values and attributes that key could not let die or do without. They were practices, that without, they would not truly be followers of Jesus. Without good works and acts of charity there was no reason for their community to exist. Without these there was no there, there. This was true of the church in Joppa long ago. It remains true even in families, churches and communities of all sorts today and it is often the mothers in our midst that bring good works and acts of charity to life. It is also true that in families, churches and communities in which good works and acts of charity are alive and well, mothers are best supported in the work they do, less out on a limb of compassion all by themselves, less left to teach their children all alone, less left to care in an uncaring world without any support in that caring. We know that there are Tabitha’s among us. We need them. We also know that as the resurrected Tabitha would not live forever, they will not live forever. We need always to be teaching, training, planning for and organizing the next generation of Tabithas. Thank you this Mother’s Day 2025 to our mothers for being Tabitha’s to us, for keeping good works and acts of charity alive. And Church, let’s resolve to be a Tabitha community, a community that supports mothers in their essential work while teaching the next generation of church what the essentials of following Jesus really are, good works and acts of charity. The committee’s selection aims to pick someone who has contributed to the community, which Bowers has been recognized for. Earlier this year, Bowers was honored by the San Francisco District Attorney’s office with the Hometown Hero Award for his efforts in community engagement and his work partnering with residents and local schools to address gun violence. “I think the awards are an incredible honor. They really are. I always get the feeling when I get an award - my initial response is, you know, I’m just doing my job to the best of my ability,” said Bowers. Bowers moved to Piedmont in search of a healthy and meaningful work-life balance. With good schools for his children and a community that emphasizes volunteering, Piedmont was “just too good of an opportunity to pass up” for Bowers and his family. At times, his kids were able to drop by to enjoy lunch together with him in his office. “I’ve really grown to really appreciate being here for the past eleven years,” said Bowers. “It’s been meaningful professionally, and it’s been meaningful from a personal standpoint.” Bowers joined the Piedmont Police Department as a Captain in 2014 after 18 years of work with the San Jose Police Department. Nine years ago he succeeded his mentor, Chief Rikki Goede, with whom he worked in San Jose. Bowers has served as Police Chief through times of great social change, including the Covid-19 pandemic. “It’s been an honor and a privilege to be the Piedmont Police Chief,” said Bowers. “To the Piedmont community, I say thank you, it’s been a good ride. I’ll still see folks around town as my youngest finishes high school, but I’m really excited about the future of this organization and the future of this city.” Humble by nature, Bowers models the ideal attitude for a public servant and leader in the community, and his character and kind perspective should be prime examples for this year’s parade theme: “Traditions Thrive in 2025.” Big Climb Continued from page 1 “It was just super touching to see Russell on FaceTime and then have his wife and his two boys there,” said McNulty. “For them to see the impact that that organization has had on research and care and the survivor stories for them to hear, I think that was really reassuring and helpful,” said McNulty. These were gifts, values and attributes that key could not let die or do without. They were practices, that without, they would not truly be followers of Jesus. Without good works and acts of charity there was no reason for their community to exist. Without these there was no there, there. This was true of the church in Joppa long ago. It remains true even in families, churches and communities of all sorts today and it is often the mothers in our midst that bring good works and acts of charity to life. It is also true that in families, churches and communities in which good works and acts of charity are alive and well, mothers are best supported in the work they do, less out on a limb of compassion all by themselves, less left to teach their children all alone, less left to care in an uncaring world without any support in that caring. We know that there are Tabitha’s among us. We need them. We also know that as the resurrected Tabitha would not live forever, they will not live forever. We need always to be teaching, training, planning for and organizing the next generation of Tabithas. Thank you this Mother’s Day 2025 to our mothers for being Tabitha’s to us, for keeping good works and acts of charity alive. And Church, let’s resolve to be a Tabitha community, a community that supports mothers in their essential work while teaching the next generation of church what the essentials of following Jesus really are, good works and acts of charity. articles.text: Girls from across the Bay Area gathered at Witter Field on Sunday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s annual “Play Like a Girl” event, a free day of hands-on activities designed to inspire girls to get involved in sports. Now in its fourth year, the event featured 29 interactive stations where girls ages two to 28 could try sports ranging from field hockey and flag football to roller derby. Each station offered equipment, space to play, and guidance from experienced athletes and coaches. Information on local classes, camps and leagues was also available for participants interested in continuing with a sport after the event. This year’s event also included Q&A sessions and meet-andgreets with two high-profile athletes: former WNBA player Layshia Clarendon and five-time Olympic gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant. Sports Participation Linked to Long-Term Benefits Organizers emphasized the long-term benefits of playing sports, citing research showing that girls who participate in athletics often experience improved physical and mental health, academic achievement and career outcomes. Families enjoy playing field hockey at Play Like a Girl 2025. Photos by Sophie Hess
articles.title: Girls play sports and meet pro athletes at annual Play Like a Girl event

articles.text: I have long contended that the world’s most visible Christians are the Pope and the President of the United States of America. Both have great impact on the quality of life on our planet and both, on a daily basis, are observed and evaluated by people in every continent, country, county and city on this pale blue dot that we call home. While the President of the United States does not have to be a Christian, and the U.S. Constitution prohibits religious tests for holding office, every president has, even in some nominal way, identified with Christianity. This means that, in the eyes of billions of people, she or he is a walking, talking, living and breathing representative of my faith tradition. Even though I am not a Roman Catholic, I profess to belong to the catholic (universal) church. BEAZY ROMAN, 3rd grade I want to plant rosemary and maybe some daisies. ADRIENNE HONG, 3rd grade I want to plant rosemary and it would be nice to have a lemon tree, so we can make more lemonade for the Girl Scouts. Religion Corner - Main The world’s most visible Christians By Pastor Jim Hopkins I have long contended that the world’s most visible Christians are the Pope and the President of the United States of America. Both have great impact on the quality of life on our planet and both, on a daily basis, are observed and evaluated by people in every continent, country, county and city on this pale blue dot that we call home. While the President of the United States does not have to be a Christian, and the U.S. Constitution prohibits religious tests for holding office, every president has, even in some nominal way, identified with Christianity. This means that, in the eyes of billions of people, she or he is a walking, talking, living and breathing representative of my faith tradition. Even though I am not a Roman Catholic, I profess to belong to the catholic (universal) church. As such the pope, like the president, is a walking, talking, living and breathing representative of my larger faith tradition. It goes without saying that I am far from enamored with the way the current president represents Christianity. I am, however, very appreciative of the way the late Pope Francis represented our faith. His expansive vision, his concern for the vulnerable, his commitment to creation care, his gentle ways were laudable. With me, many are hopeful that the next pope will share his values and commitments. Which brings me to Steph Curry. I am not suggesting that he be president or pope. I am arguing that he too is one of the world’s most visible Christians and one who represents the essential values of my faith very well. As we are in the midst of the 2025 NBA playoffs, Curry is the focus of a monumental amount of media coverage. His play is analyzed. His health is evaluated. His demeanor is scrutinized. His comments are deconstructed. His character is dissected. In every area he comes across as skilled, honest, trustworthy, humble, confident and admirable. My wife, Karen, is a huge Steph Curry fan and she updates me regularly about what he is saying and what is being said about him. If there is Steph news, I don’t need to search for it on the internet. articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School Board on May 2. Dear PUSD Board of Education members and administration, Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) is a parent-led group that works collaboratively with PUSD, other parent organizations, and the broader community to support and raise awareness for families of children with disabilities and learning differences. We want to extend our sincere appreciation for your continued dedication to supporting all students’ education and well-being. We are especially grateful for the open communication and partnership we’ve had with Jean Fagin and Ariel Dolowich this year. As part of our ongoing efforts and in alignment with PIE’s founding mission to enhance educational opportunities for students with disabilities and learning differences, we are proud to offer grants to PUSD teachers. This year, we awarded nearly $7,000 in grants to 14 teachers across all PUSD schools—from preschool to high school. The funds supported a wide range of resources, including curriculum materials, database memberships, field trips, classroom furniture, and supplies such as sensory tools and graphing calculators. We collaborated closely with Jean Fagin to make sure that the most critical needs were addressed. We are deeply grateful to the many community members whose generous support and donations made these grants possible. In addition to the teacher grants, we launched our firstever Benefit Concert, featuring a local band made up of Piedmont parents. The concert raised over $4,000, with all proceeds benefiting the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Sidekicks program. Sidekicks trains local teens to support safe, fun, and inclusive after-school classes and summer camps for neurodivergent schoolaged children. We are excited about what we’ve been able to accomplish this year and look forward to continuing our collaboration in service of inclusive education in Piedmont. With appreciation, -Betty Rojas PIE Board President For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Construction has begun on a series of pedestrian, bicycle and ADA improvements along a stretch of Grand Avenue between Fairview and Greenbank avenues, part of a broader city plan to improve roadway safety and stormwater drainage. The Grand Avenue Repavement Project, which launched April 23, will include the installation of pedestrian bulb-outs, high-visibility crosswalks, ADA-compliant curb ramps, and permanent traffic-calming islands. The project will also re-pave the roadway once infrastructure improvements are completed. Construction is expected to continue through August. City officials say the project targets multiple intersections with known safety concerns. Pedestrian enhancements will be added at Grand and Greenbank, while new bicycle infrastructure — including a turn box and a flashing beacon activated by push button — will be added at Grand and Linda. At Grand and Fairview, the city will introduce its first bioswale — a landscaped drainage feature designed to filter stormwater runoff and reduce flooding. Native, drought-tolerWorkers and heavy machinery make room for improvements on the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. ant plants such as salvia, sea lavender, coyote mint and California gray rush will be installed as part of the bioswale landscaping. The Piedmont City Council awarded the construction contract to Rapid Grading Solutions in January for $1.41 million, with a total project budget of approximately $1.56 million. Funding includes a $500,000 grant from the Alameda County Transportation Commission. The work is part of the city’s ongoing implementation of its 2021 Safer Streets Plan, which identified the Grand/Linda and Grand/Greenbank intersections as high-priority locations for safety upgrades. In recent years, similar improvements have been completed on Oakland Avenue, where bulb-outs and flashing beacons were added at the Oakland/Howard and Oakland/Sunnyside intersections in 2022, and at Oakland/ Jerome and Oakland/El Cerrito in 2024. A new grant application is pending for additional safety work on Moraga Avenue. If approved, the project would install bulb-outs, high-visibility crosswalks and flashing beacons at four intersections: Moraga with Ramona, Highland, Mesa and Red Rock Road. A view of construction on Grand Ave. and Sunnyside Ave. A worker guides traffic around the roadside construction on Grand and Linda Avenues.

articles.text: City Council meets to discuss the plan to increase Civic Center parking. From left to right: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, City Attorney Deepa Sharma, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Councilmember Jennifer Long, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, and City Clerk Anna Brown. City Council voted unanimously on Monday, May 5, to approve a plan that will expand parking in the Civic Center area, reconfigure the Havens Elementary School drop-off zone, and convert a portion of Bonita Avenue into a one-way northbound street. The discussion on Civic Center parking began March 17, when city staff presented a “maximum” parking plan to address long-standing space constraints. The topic returned for further discussion on April 21. Councilmembers reviewed results from a survey of more than 500 residents. About half said they found parking in the area “somewhat” or “very” difficult. More than 80% reported typically staying less than two hours during a visit. The newly approved plan will convert the Civic Center segment of Bonita Avenue to one-way traffic, adding diagonal parking along one side. Parking will be distributed among two-hour spaces and designated employee spaces usable by both city and Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) staff. The plan includes: • 36 spaces with a 30-minute limit • More than 80 two-hour spaces • Over 120 employee-designated spaces • 13 ADA-compliant spaces • Four electric vehicle charging spots • 10 spaces reserved for police and public safety “What we’re proposing today, in the traffic world, this is considered a minor alteration,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “This is something that has been ongoing. What Bonita Avenue resident Daniel Roberts urges City Council to delay their decision until more safety data is available. we’re talking about are solutions to help remedy something which has been a problem for many decades.” The changes come after years of disruption to the Civic Center parking layout. Parking was reduced during construction of the high school’s STEAM building and theater, followed by further losses due to the new community pool project in 2023 and ongoing work on the police department’s 911 dispatch center. Changes to Havens Drop-Off Area The approved plan will also reconfigure the Havens Elementary School pick-up and drop-off zones. Based on traffic counts and input from PUSD staff, the city will remove the existing Bonita Avenue drop-off area and expand designated spaces on Highland Avenue. Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues will become one-way northbound. On the Havens side of the street, current parallel parking will be converted to diagonal parking, creating up to 17 new spaces. During public comment, PUSD Superintendent Jennifer Hawn acknowledged the tradeoffs. “Losing that Bonita drop-off and pick-up zone is challenging,” she said. “When we’re talking about Havens, we’re talking about a projected 477 students.” The drop-off area for Piedmont Middle and High School will remain unchanged to accommodate delivery trucks and student pick-ups. Residents Raise Safety Concerns Several residents asked the Council to delay the vote pending further analysis of pedestrian and traffic safety. “I really would like to see safety studies,” said Bonita Avenue resident Daniel Roberts. “My sister-in-law was hit on Highland as a child crossing the street. We don’t want that to happen again.” Gonzales emphasized that the proposed design meets all safety requirements. “We wouldn’t propose it if it was unsafe,” he said. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan confirmed that fire vehicles could still access the restriped roads following a review of clearance guidelines and a field test using cones. The Council approved the parking plan with minor adjustments to space placement and a slight increase in employee parking. A formal review of the changes is scheduled for May 2026. The proposed parking scenario from the May 5 Council meeting. City Council approved the plan with some changes to placement and slight increases to designated employee parking.
articles.title: City Council approves plan to increase parking in Piedmont’s Civic Center

pages.text: Wednesday, May 7, 2025 5 City Council approves plan to increase parking in Piedmont’s Civic Center City Council meets to discuss the plan to increase Civic Center parking. From left to right: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, City Attorney Deepa Sharma, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Councilmember Jennifer Long, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, and City Clerk Anna Brown. By Tony Simons City Council voted unanimously on Monday, May 5, to approve a plan that will expand parking in the Civic Center area, reconfigure the Havens Elementary School drop-off zone, and convert a portion of Bonita Avenue into a one-way northbound street. The discussion on Civic Center parking began March 17, when city staff presented a “maximum” parking plan to address long-standing space constraints. The topic returned for further discussion on April 21. Councilmembers reviewed results from a survey of more than 500 residents. About half said they found parking in the area “somewhat” or “very” difficult. More than 80% reported typically staying less than two hours during a visit. The newly approved plan will convert the Civic Center segment of Bonita Avenue to one-way traffic, adding diagonal parking along one side. Parking will be distributed among two-hour spaces and designated employee spaces usable by both city and Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) staff. The plan includes: • 36 spaces with a 30-minute limit • More than 80 two-hour spaces • Over 120 employee-designated spaces • 13 ADA-compliant spaces • Four electric vehicle charging spots • 10 spaces reserved for police and public safety “What we’re proposing today, in the traffic world, this is considered a minor alteration,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “This is something that has been ongoing. What Bonita Avenue resident Daniel Roberts urges City Council to delay their decision until more safety data is available. we’re talking about are solutions to help remedy something which has been a problem for many decades.” The changes come after years of disruption to the Civic Center parking layout. Parking was reduced during construction of the high school’s STEAM building and theater, followed by further losses due to the new community pool project in 2023 and ongoing work on the police department’s 911 dispatch center. Changes to Havens Drop-Off Area The approved plan will also reconfigure the Havens Elementary School pick-up and drop-off zones. Based on traffic counts and input from PUSD staff, the city will remove the existing Bonita Avenue drop-off area and expand designated spaces on Highland Avenue. Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues will become one-way northbound. On the Havens side of the street, current parallel parking will be converted to diagonal parking, creating up to 17 new spaces. During public comment, PUSD Superintendent Jennifer Hawn acknowledged the tradeoffs. “Losing that Bonita drop-off and pick-up zone is challenging,” she said. “When we’re talking about Havens, we’re talking about a projected 477 students.” The drop-off area for Piedmont Middle and High School will remain unchanged to accommodate delivery trucks and student pick-ups. Residents Raise Safety Concerns Several residents asked the Council to delay the vote pending further analysis of pedestrian and traffic safety. “I really would like to see safety studies,” said Bonita Avenue resident Daniel Roberts. “My sister-in-law was hit on Highland as a child crossing the street. We don’t want that to happen again.” Gonzales emphasized that the proposed design meets all safety requirements. “We wouldn’t propose it if it was unsafe,” he said. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan confirmed that fire vehicles could still access the restriped roads following a review of clearance guidelines and a field test using cones. The Council approved the parking plan with minor adjustments to space placement and a slight increase in employee parking. A formal review of the changes is scheduled for May 2026. The proposed parking scenario from the May 5 Council meeting. City Council approved the plan with some changes to placement and slight increases to designated employee parking. articles.text: When students and parents show up, their voices need to be respected (TPH) Editorial Staff (Originally published April 24 at TPHnews.com/22067) Piedmont is a public school district. That means it receives government dollars, its employees are government employees, and it answers to citizens. Like jury duty, the Miranda warning, and elections, public school districts have to do it by the books– the name of the game is protocol. That means the Board of Educations has to be open to public comment. On the way into City Hall, one can pick up a 3 x 5 card, write their name, and be afforded 150 seconds to speak their mind. Last issue, TPH encouraged its readers to take advantage of this tool. The Editorial Board agreed that civic engagement of this variety plays an utterly essential role in the democratic process. Unfortunately, the March 26 Board of Education meeting dampened our enthusiasm about due process. During the meeting, several community members used their rights to defend the elementary school band program from any cuts. An email sent out earlier that week raised alarm among PUSD musicians and catalyzed the collective action. Among the speakers were heartfelt parents, students, and teachers, expressing their concern for a beloved program they believed to be under threat. After everyone who wanted to speak had done so, members of the board took time to acknowledge the concern. It became apparent that the board and the community were operating with different sets of information. The board members expressed frustration and disappointment at what they perceived as attacks from the public. “We should not all be here in this state of distress and disarray right now, and it caused a level of drama that I find very disappointing.” “If we cannot discuss possible changes, then we cannot do anything, we cannot do our jobs. And if any potential change comes with pitchforks, then it’s going to be very difficult for us to do anything.” “A lot of this angst and frustration is for naught.” The Editorial Board found this response disheartening. The role of public elected officials is to carry out the wishes of the public. Part of that includes listening to the wishes of the public. When members of a public school district attend a public meeting and use public time in a public building to defend something that they are afraid to lose, they are not touting pitchforks. This isn’t a shocking or upsetting situation, it’s exactly what was in the job description. Complete and utter transparency at every step of the process can feel frustrating, but the district shouldn’t be run like a business. Efficacy and efficiency come second to public engagement. We ask that the members of the board respect that public outcry is part of the deal. Things will get ugly sometimes, but that’s the role the public sometimes takes. The administrators’ role is to not take it personally.
articles.title: For the Board of Education, Feedback Is Part of the Assignment

articles.text: Education As members of the Piedmont Board of Education, we want to assure our students and community stakeholders that you are being heard. We listen to every comment and we read every letter you send. We appreciate the passion and care that our community brings to Board meetings – it is a foundational strength of our community. Having been parent volunteers ourselves, we understand the desire to engage and the need to be heard. We welcome community engagement and recognize that effective governance often involves difficult conversations and decisions that not everyone will agree with. In recent months, there has been strong advocacy around several issues. We understand the frustration when people feel unheard or when a decision doesn’t go their way. However, a different outcome doesn’t mean you weren’t heard. In addition, the Board and administration sometimes work with information that isn’t public yet. In some cases, a decision hasn’t been made, and in others, sensitive topics require confidentiality. We don’t aim to withhold information. A good example of this was the March 26th Board meeting. Earlier this year, our elementary teachers told us they wanted to improve performing arts programming. In response, we asked the superintendent to move forward with the process, and a committee of elementary educators got to work discussing and ultimately proposing improvements to our elementary performing arts programming. Before their recommendations were brought to the Board, a couple of teachers – without all of the information – communicated to students and parents that a decision had been made to cut band from the elementary music program and urged them to speak out. As a result, many stakeholders showed up at the March 26th meeting upset about a staff-led decision that was still in process. Naturally, this led to confusion and frustration. As Board members, our concern that night was not with those who spoke up; it was with the fact that inaccurate information had been circulated. We are grateful to students and parents who took time to speak about the elementary music program because your voices, opinions, and experiences are all essential to our work. However, it is our hope that these exchanges take place with mutual respect and some level of trust. The community elected us to bring about a number of changes in the district – and in recent months, we have done just that. Public service is complex, and many decisions involve difficult tradeoffs. Our role is to consider all available information and make the best decision we can for the district as a whole. In the case of the elementary music program, information was not ready at the March 26th meeting, but was ready at the April 23rd meeting when the Board approved the recommendation from our teachers. It is our love of and deep respect for our community, students, schools, and public education as an institution that drove us to serve on the all volunteer PUSD School Board. It is what motivates us to show up for difficult conversations and to make hard decisions. Yet, we too are human and get frustrated. Criticism is difficult to manage when it is rooted in misinformation or miscommunication. Our objective is not to shut down dissenting voices but to engage in fruitful, productive conversations that drive us towards our shared objective: ensuring all our students continue to receive the high quality education that they deserve. In partnership, Lindsay Thomasson, Board President Ruchi Medhekar, Board Vice President Susy Struble, Board Trustee Max Roman, Board Trustee Michael Malione, Board Trustee

After leaving California on April 2, the American group traveled 20 hours to begin their week with host families. On the first day of school abroad, the American students and chaperones were greeted with a welcome lunch. The school in Spain, IES Mendiño, is in the city of Redondela and students attend class from 8:30 a.m.-2:00 p.m. After Friday some of the American students went on excursions with their host families. articles.text: How parents can make it count When Maya, 22, was asked to name her clearest childhood memory, she skipped the homework, the carpools and even her tenth-birthday cake. “It’s the night we slept in the backyard to watch a meteor shower,” she said. While those “Mountain Memories” were momentous in mind and heart, the “Valleys” make up most memories – both are valuable to “unblur” their childhood. What the study covered Over 20 years, I conducted 2+ hour conversations with more than 1,000 adults aged 19-30 from over 30 countries (25 percent international; mixed socioeconomic backgrounds). They answered dozens of open-ended prompts ranging from “What rituals were meaningful to you?” to “List your ten most salient memories from ages 8-18.” The result is a map of childhood recollection that parents can turn into an action plan. The mountains Planned and unplanned milestones. First concerts, graduation road-trips, a spontaneous camping night in a thunderstorm, as well as births, deaths and other life-course jolts, dominate narrative space. These episodic spikes are remembered in cinematic detail decades later—especially when photographs or keepsakes exist to cue retrieval, a phenomenon long supported by memory research. The valleys Small rituals with big footprints. Weekly pancake breakfasts, Friday-night board-game marathons, and bedtime readalouds form the gentle terrain in-between. Interviewees recalled the fact that these rituals simply happened, far more than they recalled what was said during them—evidence that predictability, not polish, drives emotional resonance. Developmental psychologists have repeatedly linked family rituals to greater well-being and resilience in youth. The surprising blanks Overarchingly, adults remembered far less of their childhood than you might imagine; after the “big events,” the rest of upper grade school onward was summarized by them in under 30 minutes! Childhood is largely a blur before age seven. Most respondents remembered very few specific memories before third grade, a pattern that matches “childhood amnesia” findings in cognitive science. But that isn’t always or necessarily true . . . keep reading. Group activities such as sports seasons were also stored in “collapsed” form—people remembered the vibe, not the playby-play, unless a single pivotal moment (the championship goal) broke through. Action plan: where attention beats perfection The data suggest two leverage points: anchor the calendar with a handful of big, well-documented adventures, and weave in a dozen-plus micro-rituals that happen with metronomic reliability. Below is menu parents can mix and match – take some picks, AND create your own. How to use the table: 1. Pick at least one ritual from each row to cover multiple memory “channels” (sensory, spatial, narrative, values-based). 2. Lock them onto the calendar—consistency, more than elaborateness, is what etches them into long-term memory. 3. Add lightweight documentation (a single photo, a 30-second voice memo) to give future adults the cues that science shows can unlock richer childhood stories. For the mountain moments – vacations, graduations, first concerts – lean into spectacle and documentation: stage a quirky group photo, record a short reflection video on the spot, and print a few images for the fridge. Photos are not vanity; they become the retrieval keys that unlock richer narratives later in life. The takeaway of simple rituals and treating the occasional milestone like the festival it is, parents trade ephemeral logistics for memories that outlast childhood’s inevitable blur. In a word, it is attention not extravagance that etches family into story. Randall Grayson P.h.D (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about summer program, family camps, and twoweek sessions can be found at www.campaugusta.org. Food & Kitchen Bonding Sunday pancake bar Gratitude jar at dinner One‑song kitchen dance‑off Turns a daily necessity into a multisensory micro‑celebration. Repetition builds scent‑ and music‑linked memory cues with almost zero extra cost. Outdoor & Nature Adventures Solstice sunrise hike First‑snow cocoa walk Neighborhood night hike Annual photo‑scavenger hunt Novel landscapes plus mild exertion elevate adrenaline and dopamine, deepening autobiographical encoding; seasonal anchors give the brain temporal hooks. Milestones & Memory‑ Making Birthday interview video New‑school‑year time capsulea Hand‑written postcards on trips Flags major transitions and collects physical artifacts that function as potent retrieval cues decades later. Growth & Connection Rituals Monthly “yes day” Quarterly volunteer day “Big fail” celebration night Cousins’ trivia showdown Builds agency, empathy, and shared mastery; normalizes failure as a bonding experience and spotlights family values in action. Creative Expression & Storytelling Seasonal story circle by firelight Home talent showcase evening Shared creation yields highly specific, emotion‑laden memories; artistic products become tangible mnemonic anchors. Mind‑Body Well‑Being Rituals Couples predictable bodily movement with reflective practice, reinforcing awareness—shown to enhance mood regulation and memory consolidation.

articles.text: Kids and families can bring their bikes and helmets to the Havens Blacktop to enjoy a free Bike to School Festival on Saturday, May 10, from 12:00-4:00 p.m. Attending families will be able to enjoy a family biking workshop by Bike East Bay, starting when the event kicks off at noon. A Mister Softee ice cream truck is expected at the event at 1:30 p.m. The event will feature a Bike obstacle course by the Piedmont Police Department, pedal-powered blender smoothies by Piedmont Scouts, and pedal-powered spin art by inventor group Rock the Bike. Attendees will be able to test ride family E-bikes from electric bike shop The New Wheel. For families looking to teach their kids about bike riding, Oakland Trek will be offering bike maintenance help. There will also be a bike swap at the event for both kids and adults to bring outgrown bikes, equipment, and parts to swap with other families. Knitting & Crochet Circle with Susan Segal! Monday, May 12 — 11:00 a.m. –1:00 p.m. Join us every second and fourth Monday of the month for a delightful early afternoon of yarn, needles, and good company at our Adult Knitting & Crochet Circle! Settle into a warm and inviting space where creativity and conversation intertwine. If you need assistance with anything or have questions, Susan is here to help. articles.text: In 2023 Piedmont Fire Department celebrated winning three awards at the Big Climb in Oracle Park, a fundraiser for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. The four-man team earned fastest team, fastest individual, and top fundraising team. Pictured are Nicholas Christ (left), Brian Protheroe, Capt. Justin McNulty, and Anthony Renteria. Piedmont Fire Department will participate in the Big Climb on Saturday, May 10, a race traversing through the upper deck of San Francisco’s Oracle Park as a fundraiser for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society (LLS). The department’s third year of participation in the event means more this year as one of its own members, Engineer Russ San Filippo, was diagnosed with leukemia in December. Captain Justin McNulty and the department have so far raised $5,895 and need some additional support to reach their $10,000 fundraising goal. Participating this year are Capt. McNulty, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Lucas Romero, and Nadder Shehadeh. In their first two years of participation, 2023 and 2024, PFD won all three categories of competition. McNulty is the twotime fastest individual, and the team has won two years in a row as the fastest team and top first responder fundraising team. Piedmont’s firefighters have added extra training to their ordinary workout regiments by running the bleachers at Witter Field. The grueling Big Climb race goes up and down each of the 28 sections in Giants stadium’s steep upper deck. “You’re burning, your lungs are on fire, but that’s nothing compared to what these people had to go through, and their battles and tribulations. So it’s a good motivator,” explained McNulty. The Big Climb takes place in 13 cities across the country annually in iconic locations including Citi Field in New York and Philadelphia’s Subaru Park. Last year’s event occurred during an unusual springtime San Francisco downpour. Despite the elements, over 3,000 climbers participated to support LLS. LLS has invested over $1.8 billion since 1949 towards fighting and curing leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, and other blood cancers. Overall, the 5-year relative survival rate for leukemia has more than doubled from 34% (1975-1977) to 70% (2013-2019). Donate to the Piedmont Fire Department’s Big Climb page at https://pages.lls.org/bigclimb/ gba/bigclimbsf 25/PiedmontFireDepartment. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community. “My grandson just said his first words, Dude. . . ‘tax shelter’.”

Piedmont High tennis player Lucas Smolko, a junior, got the job done, winning his second consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title in the league individual tournament on Saturday, May 3 at Chabot College in Hayward. He becomes the first athlete at PHS, boys or girls, to win back-to-back WACC titles since the league’s inception in 2012. In the championship match, Smol ko defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Neo Chai in three sets, dominating the first and third sets toward a 6-1, 4-6, 6-2 win. It was a windy day at Chabot, especially in the second and third sets. “I was playing well in the first set, there was very little wind and I was moving my feet. Then the wind picked up in the second set and I stopped moving my feet as well and started missing forehands I was hitting in the first set. In the third set I just adjusted my movement and tried to get more top spin,” Smolko said. Smolko was the top seed in the tournament and also won the WACC Player of the Year award. He defeated O’Dowd’s Ollie Pakzad in the first , 6-1, 6-3, won 6-1, 6-2 over Castro Valley’s Advaith Sathyan in the quarterfinals, and then beat Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar, 6-3, 6-0 in the semifinals. His title win against Chai was a rematch of last year’s WACC singles finals. The two also faced one another twice in this year’s regular season, both of which Smolko won. “We know each other pretty well. It’s definitely a different dynamic than playing someone I have no experience against,” Smolko said. Smolko is set to play in this year’s Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament at Vintage High School in Napa on Friday and Saturday, May 9-10. He reached the semifinals in last year’s singles bracket. The freshman duo of Joey Assalian and Ben Davis put on a strong display in winning the consolation doubles. After falling 6-1, 6-0 in the first round to No. 4 seed Marcello Sacnelari and Olive Liao, the pair defeated Castro Valley’s Elijah Song and Dylan Kwan 8-3 and then defeated teammates from Piedmont Hunter Fasteau and Luca LaForte 8-6 in the consolation semifinals. In the consolation finals, the pair beat Alameda’s Kyle Banducci and Keenan Chan in straight sets 6-4, 6-3 after falling behind early in the first set. “Throughout the tournament, we played a lot of good opponents. We realized we just have to be aggressive. I think our teamwork in that regard definitely improved,” Assalian said “We realized we were over-hitting and missing volleys. We started approaching more, hitting it a little lighter and just being more consistent,” Davis said. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont fell to the Dragons in the WACC Tournament semifinals, and now look ahead to the North Coast Section playoffs. The Highlanders’ boys’ lacrosse team was eliminated from the Western Alameda County Conference tournament in the semifinals, falling 11-5 to rival Bishop O’Dowd at Witter Field on Wednesday, April 30. PHS beat the Dragons 8-7 during the regular season on April 4. “We needed to find the opportunity to show who we really are and tonight wasn’t it. O’Dowd played a really good game and deserved to win,” said first-year Piedmont coach Paul Pappas. Piedmont started well, ending the first quarter in a 2-2 deadlock. But as turnovers began piling up O’Dowd piled on shots. The Highlanders committed 17 turnovers on the night. “We had a good week of practice, but any time you’re in playoffs, the nerves are going to be a bit different. When you have a young team, things can change,” Pappas said. The hope is the younger leaders on the roster, like junior Ian Nguyen and Timmy Kalamas, along with sophomore Connor Fredericks, will learn from the year’s struggles. “It’s just trying to get them comfortable and confident. Guys are just paying their dues and getting better, that’s all we can ask for. These losses hurt, but we’re getting better,” Pappas said. Connor Fredericks scored two goals against Bishop O’Dowd. PHS received the No. 13 seed in the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs and faced No. 4 Foothill yesterday, Tuesday, May 6. Results were not complete by Post time. 11-5 loss to O’Dowd O’Dowd scored the game’s first goal with 8:26 left on a low shot. After back and forth possessions, Ian Nguyen tied it at 3:38. After Timmy Kalamas sent a shot on target, BOD turned possession to score with 2:16 on the clock. Piedmont tied the match at 1:21 with a man-advantage when P.J. Brayer found Connor Fredericks for a goal. But from there, the Dragons went on to score back ahead near the midway mark of the second quarter with 6:16 left six straight goals through the second into the third quarter. In the second, Kalamas had an early shot on target, but O’Dowd scored with 8:47 on the clock. Brendan Divine had a shot on frame on the next possession, but PHS committed a turnover which led to an O’Dowd goal 20 seconds later with 6:16 left. After that, BOD forced a turnover in transiTimmy Kalamas looks to make a play against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Honorable Mentions: Will Parker & Peyton Watson We’re awarding Miguel Long and Nia Kim of the track and field team our Athletes of the Month awards for April, while Will Parker of the baseball team and lacrosse player Peyton Watson were named honorable mention. Miguel Long, who competes in the jumping events for Piedmont’s track and field team, had an amazing month of April. He competed in the prestigious Arcadia Invitational on Saturday, April 12, placing 13th of 18 athletes in the triple jump with a distance of 43 feet, 7 inches. One week earlier, Long won the Stanford Invitational with a leap of 45 feet, 8.5 inches. He also won the Del Campo Decathlon on April 19 in a field of 19 athletes. Nia Kim is having a breakout senior season for the track and field team. In April, Kim won three different 100-meter hurdles races and four high jump events. Perhaps her best showing was at the Clash of the Titans at Skyline High on April 26. At the meet, Kim won the 100 hurdles in 15.58 seconds in a field of 22, setting a school record in the process. She also won the high jump with a height of 5-feet-0 in a field of 10. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team split its last pair of games against Berkeley, bringing their record to 14-7 and 5-3 against Western Alameda County Conference teams. They are in second place in league and have two games remaining in the regular season. The Highlanders beat the Yellowjackets 4-2 on Wednesday, April 30 at Humphries Diamond, but lost 10-1 two days later in Berkeley. Their win on Wednesday featured another late response by Piedmont’s comeback kids. Trailing 2-1 entering the bottom of the sixth, Piedmont tacked on three runs to take a 4-2 lead. It was Piedmont’s fifth comeback victory of the season. They won 7-5 over Acalanes on February 28 after trailing 5-4, trailed 4-3 against Encinal on March 27 before winning 8-5 , were also down 5-3 to Head-Royce before winning 7-5 on April 9, and beat Alameda 8-7 on April 18 after falling behind 7-4. “We get our offense late in games. Maybe it’s just getting acclimated to the pitcher. We’ll take it at any time but I’d like for us to get runs a little earlier,” said coach Eric Olson with a laugh. Jordan Vo drove in Piedmont’s game-winning hit in the bottom of the sixth inning with a twoRBI single. “My coach told me I had to go up the middle and I just pushed it that way. I reacted to the fastball outside; it was exciting,” Vo said of his game-winning hit. Entering as the closer in the top of the seventh was junior Diego Delventhal, who retired three of four batters he faced. It marked Delventhal’s fourth pitching save of the season despite being Olson’s regular shortstop. Delventhal used a combinaStaff Photos Jordan Vo drives in the game-winning run against Berkeley. Diego Delventhal throws a curveball as he picks up his fourth save of the season in a game with Berkeley. tion of fastball, changeup, and curveball as if he was a primary pitcher. “I didn’t think it would be my role coming into the season, but I’ve embraced it. My mentality is to just throw strikes, I want to pick up my guys for having such great games. I want to get ahead in the count and spot my curveball,” Delventhal said. 4-2 over Berkeley Berkeley scored twice in the top of the fourth to take an iniJack Meyjes celebrates scoring a run against Berkeley. tial lead. In the bottom of the fifth, Vo hit a one-out single and advanced to second on a passed ball. Freshman Jonah Cha-Foster drove a single to right field to bring Vo to third. Berkeley’s pitcher then tried to pick off Cha-Foster at first base, which led to a throwing error that brought Vo in to score. In the bottom of the sixth, Lagios led off with a single and took second on a wild pitch. Will Parker then hit an RBI single to tie the game at 2-2. After Lagios advanced on a balk and Jack Meyjes drew a two-out walk, also advancing on a wild pitch. That’s when Vo hit his two-RBI single to take a 4-2 lead. Delventhal stepped to the mound as the closer, forcing a groundout and strikeout before Berkeley gained a two-out single. Diego then struck out the final batter of the game. Final stats: Vo went 2-for-3 with two RBIs and scored a run. Lagios went 2-for-3 with a run scored. Parker went 2-for-3 with an RBI. Delventhal gained the save with two strikeouts and allowed one hit. 10-1 loss to Berkeley Berkeley scored once in the bottom of the first, four in the third, four more in the fifth, and once in the bottom of the sixth. Piedmont’s only run came in the top of the sixth. Final stats: Parker went 2-for-4 with a double. Lagios went 1-for-4. Shafer Dando went 1-for-3. Vo went 2-for-3. articles.text: Piedmont swimmers win 25 medals Piedmont High School’s swim team turned in a stellar performance at this year’s WACC Championships. Led by Head Coach Adrien Downey, the Highlanders walked away with an impressive 25 varsity medals, awarded to the top six finishers in each event. Key Performances While the medal count was impressive, Coach Downey emphasized the importance of key efforts from swimmers who didn’t medal but contributed significantly to the team’s point total. Simon March-Cunningham and Elles Krieckhaus each added 11 crucial points across two events. articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery will host its annual fundraising gala on Saturday, May 17, at 5 p.m. Guests are invited to immerse themselves in the vibrant beauty of the nursery’s dry garden landscape during a relaxed outdoor evening featuring refreshments, live music, and an auction of rare, curated plants. Nursery staff will also share insights into the garden’s drought-tolerant and climate-adaptive species. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in water-wise gardening and an early advocate for sustainable plant practices. The nonprofit’s mission is to preserve her legacy for public education and enjoyment, supported in part by events such as the annual gala. Currently in bloom are a range Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery Gala guests are invited to enjoy live music and drink in Ruth Bancroft’s gardens. of succulents and cacti, including Yucca brevifolia, Xanthorrhoea preissii, Aloe vaombe, and more. Sponsorships and individual tickets are available for purchase online. For more information and to buy tickets, visit https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/ gala-celebrating-the-lush-drygarden/ Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery Rare arid-friendly plants are available for auction during the evening gala.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft Garden Gala is May 17

articles.text: Erin Gleeson, author of Watercolor Feast, guides beginners in creating watercolor artwork inspired by Filoli’s gardens. Join chef and New York Times bestselling author Erin Gleeson at Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside on Friday, May 16, in creating stunning waterpiece art inspired by the historic venue’s flora and fauna and Gleeson’s new book Watercolor Feast. Watercolor Feast is a beginner-friendly watercolor book with step-by-step instructions to paint an array of specific fruits, vegetables, and flowers as well as beautiful menus and plate settings. The book concludes with eight pages of watercolor paper for users to test their new skills. Tickets include a copy of Gleeson’s book, all materials needed to watercolor including paper, watercolor paints, watercolor brushes, general admission and light refreshments. Two classes will be held in the morning and afternoon of Friday, May 16; one class begins at 10 a.m., the second class begins at 2 p.m. Visit https://filoli.org/events/ parties/#watercolor-garden-party to purchase Watercolor Garden Party tickets.
articles.title: Paint with NYT author Erin Gleeson at Filoli May 16

articles.text: Bouquets to Art, de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser featuring the finest floral arrangements, opens at the museum on Monday, June 2 featuring over 150 floral designers featured. The weeklong exhibition and annual display of artwork-inspired bouquets off icially launches on the evening of June 2 with an opening-night reception and luxury raffle, and then is open to the public during regular museum hours from June 3 through 8. Floral designers from the Bay Area and beyond will converge at the de Young for the annual Bouquets to Art to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Now in its 41st year, the exhibition is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events and will expand to include the Legion of Honor this year as part of the Fine Arts Museum’s 100th-anniversary celebrations. The fundraiser and exhibition draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the opening reception and raffle, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/bouquets-to-art-2025. Courtesy of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Museum patrons view an exhibit at de Young’s Bouquets to Art 2024.
articles.title: Bouquets to Art opening reception is June 2 at de Young

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest youth orchestra in California, will feature two of its top student musicians in a spring concert on Saturday, May 17, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The concert is part of YPSO’s 88th season and marks the 36th year under music director David Ramadanoff, a veteran Bay Area conductor and educator. Ramadanoff, a former assistant conductor of the San Francisco Symphony under Seiji Ozawa, has led YPSO since the late 1980s. The orchestra includes 80 musicians between the ages of 11 and 18, representing a wide stretch of the Bay Area from Napa to Fremont. This spring’s program features classical works from Mozart to Rachmaninoff, as well as solo performances by violinist Carolyn Ren and cellist Donghu Kim—two winners of the orchestra’s annual Concerto Competition. Ren, 16, will perform the third movement of Wieniawski’s Violin Concerto No. 2, a Romantic-era piece with sweeping melodies and brisk technical runs. “It’s such an exciting concerto, especially with all the fast spiccato and playful energy,” she said. Kim, 17, will take on Tchaikovsky’s Variations on a Rococo Theme, a nod to the Classical style of Mozart that emphasizes subtlety and ornamentation over sheer virtuosity. “It’s about finding the right color and phrasing in every variation,” he said. The program will open with Mozart’s Magic Flute Overture and close with Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances, the Russian composer’s final orchestral work. In addition to the concert, YPSO will launch its annual online auction fundraiser on May 17. The auction, which runs through the end of the month, aims to raise $10,000 to support scholarships, outreach programs and operating costs. Items up for bid include gift certificates, musical instruments, and experiences with Bay Area artists and venues. Parents say the program offers more than music education. “YPSO has given my daughter not just the chance to play amazing music, but also to be part of something larger than herself,” said Christina Lee, a parent from Oakland. “It’s rare to find a program that challenges kids musically while also teaching them leadership and collaboration.” An open rehearsal is scheduled for Friday, May 16, from 6 to 9 p.m., offering prospective students and families a behindthe-scenes look at the final preparations. Admission is free, and student tickets to the concert are available at no charge with a valid student ID. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO was the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The idea came from local harpist Clarabelle Bell, who was inspired by a youth orchestra in Portland, and realized by violinist and conductor Jessica Marcelli. More information and ticket reservations are available at ypsomusic.org/events. The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra.
articles.title: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra holds 88th Spring Concert on May 17

articles.text: Photo by Kevin Berne Asia Jackson, David Moore and Anna Sharpe in Aurora Theatre Company’s Crumbs from the Table of Joy Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Lynn Nottage’s acclaimed Crumbs from the Table of Joy is playing on the Aurora Theatre stage in Berkeley now through May 25, with post-show discussions held May 14 and 22. Directed by Elizabeth Carter, Nottage’s play follows the Crump family as they relocate from Pensacola, Florida, to Brooklyn following the death of the family matriarch. The play is told through the eyes of 17-year-old Ernestine Crump and focuses on the arrival of communist-leaning Aunt Lily, who challenges the family’s dynamics and beliefs. The play navigates the complexities of race, religion, and societal expectations during the 1950’s. When the play was first presented Off-Broadway at the Second Stage Theatre in 1995, Nottage said she chose the 1950’s because it was a time of significant social change. “Everything I had seen was in black and white,” she said at the time. “And I wanted to make it colorful. So I started writing Crumbs from the Table of Joy to try to understand that era.” Nottage is the first woman in history to win two Pulitzer Prizes for Drama, and her plays, including Crumbs from the Table of Joy, have been produced widely in the United States and throughout the world. Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello called Nottage “one of the most significant American playwrights working today,” “We’re honored to bring this early work of hers, showcasing all her insight and passion, to the Aurora stage. And I’m thrilled to welcome back director Elizabeth Carter,” Costello said. The Aurora Theatre production features Jamella Cross as Ernestine Crump, Asia Jackson as Lily Ann Green, David Moore as Godfrey Crump and Carrie Paff as Gerte Shulte. Two performances per week, Wednesday evenings and Sunday matinees, are mandatory mask-required performances. For all other performances, masks will be encouraged but not required. Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/crumbs to purchase tickets and view showtimes.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre Crumbs from the Table of Joy ends May 25

articles.text: The smash-hit musical biopic A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical comes to San Francisco’s Golden Gate Theatre for a limited engagement from Tuesday, June 3, through Sunday, June 22. Created in collaboration with Diamond himself, the musical tells the true story of a kid from Brooklyn whose meteoric rise led him to become an American rock icon. “Some of my most thrilling nights have been while I was on tour, bringing my music to audiences across the world,” said Diamond. “Having A Beautiful Photo by Jeremy Daniel Nick Fradiani as ‘Neil - Then’ (center) and ‘The Noise’ in A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical Noise go on tour is an honor, and I can’t wait for audiences across North America to experience this show. I hope they enjoy it as much as I have.” Featuring classics like “America,” “Forever in Blue Jeans” and “Sweet Caroline,” the show stars Nick Fradiani—winner of American Idol in 2015—who went on to release his debut album Hurricane in 2016, including the hit single “Beautiful Life.” Fradiani is joined by a cast that includes Tony nominee Robert Westenberg (Neil Diamond – Now), Hannah Jewel Kohn (Marcia Murphey), Lisa Reneé Pitts (Doctor), Michael Accardo (Bert Berns/Kieve Diamond), Tuck Milligan (Fred Weintraub/Tommy O’Rourke), Kate A. Mulligan (Ellie Greenwich/Rose Diamond), and Tiffany Tatreau (Jaye Posner). The Neil Diamond Musical is produced by Ken Davenport and Bob Gaudio. “I couldn’t imagine a more perfect way to honor [Diamond’s] legacy than having A Beautiful Noise touring North America, visiting the same cities where he gave so many people so much joy,” said Davenport. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.broadwaysf.com/ events/a-beautiful-noise/golden-gate-theatre/calendar.
articles.title: ‘A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical’ Comes to Golden Gate Theatre June 3

articles.text: Festival Opera board members at the Spring Soirée: Timothy Evans (left), Nina Bancroft Dickerson, Claudia Terry, Megan Dey-Toth, Jennifer Kwock-Lau, Zachary Gordin, Dr. Vivian Wing, Susie Hanson, and Keegan Dwyer Piedmont Center for the Arts hosted Festival Opera’s Spring Soirée on Saturday, May 3 at 4:00 p.m. for an evening of music and celebration inspired by the legendary Parisian musical salons. Founded in 1991, Festival Opera is a Bay-Area based opera company with the mission to advance the operatic art form and to build community by producing culturally rich and diverse programming to enlighten, educate, and entertain at the highest artistic standard. Past leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp, Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony, and is currently led by baritone, conductor and impresario Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera first began performing at PCA in 2020, producing recitals and other events that were scaled to fit the venue’s intimate chambers. Now, Festival Opera presents a series of salonstyle concerts at PCA each season, encouraging the community to attend performances and meet the artists at receptions after each event at the venue. “It really is the perfect size and space to experience this special type of performance, where the audience can be close to the musicians and get involved with the music and text in a very intimate way,” said Gordin. Attendees of the Spring Soirée enjoyed the company of fellow opera lovers, patrons and artists while sipping wine, sampling sweet and savory treats from Siren Sisters Kitchen, and enjoying a live performance. According to Gordin, the Spring Soirée was a resounding success – both as a fundraising event and musically. “The artists we presented were sensational,” said Gordin. “Soprano Shawnette Sulker, mezzo-soprano Courtney Miller, and pianist Daniel Lockert wowed the audience with gems from the opera and art song repertoire.” The silent and live auctions offered an array of treasures such as jewelry, bottles of fine wines, performing arts tickets, and fine dining experiences for patrons to take home. Gordin complimented PCA as a community space and for the quality of its events. “Piedmont residents have a unique opportunity to witness the world-renowned artists and varied programs we present in their own backyard. PCA offers the community a beautiful space where performing and visual arts happen, and a vehicle for getting involved and ensuring that the arts can endure and thrive,” Gordin said. Daniel Lockert (left) plays piano as soprano Shawnette Sulker and mezzo-soprano Courtney Miller prepare to sing. Attendees at the Piedmont Center for the Arts engage in Festival Opera’s Spring Soiree Live Auction.

Friday, May 9, 2025, 7:00 p.m. Melissa Lam & Eric Tran Cello/Piano Duo This performance will take place at: Piedmont Piano Co., 1728 San Pablo Ave., Oakland “Young in years, but that belies the level of her artistry” – Piedmont Post. Melissa Lam, a talented cellist with the San Francisco Choral Society Orchestra and principal cellist of the San Francisco Symphony Youth Orchestra, has performed at major venues like Davies Symphony Hall. In 2023 and 2024, she earned critical acclaim for her two solo recitals at Piedmont Center for the Arts. In April 2023, Melissa was honored as the guest soloist for Elgar’s Cello Concerto at the Town and Gown Club’s annual luncheon in Berkeley. She has secured top honors in several prestigious competitions, and continues to be inspired by her mentor, Eric Tran, who has won top awards from multiple U.S. and international competitions. This world-class duo will perform Rachmaninoff’s Cello Sonata and Mendelssohn’s Cello Sonata No. 2. Tickets are available at the door or in advance from https://www.eventbrite. com/e/1264469174339. We found her and are so excited to make our debut as a newly reformed group. The program will include Mozart’s “Dissonant” Quartet, Smetana’s Quartet “From My Life” and “Phantasy” by Imogen Holst. Saturday, May 17, 7:30 p.m. Insight Chamber Players Concert Insight Chamber Players and Angela Han Art will present Journey of 1000 Miles, a multimedia chamber music concert spotlighting compositions by immigrant Asian women performed by Leah Froyd, violin & viola; Zoe Lee, cello; and Dana-Marie Chan, piano. Artist Angela Han will create a live painting inspired by the composers of the evening, Jean Ahn, Yangfan Xu, and Juhi Bansal. This concert is featured in the United States of Asian America Festival - Critical Refuge, hosted by the Asian Pacific Islander Cultural Center and supported by the NEA, the SF Arts Commission, and others. Pay with donations at the door or reserve your seat at https://www. zeffy.com/en-US/ticketing/journey-of-1000-miles-may-17th. Sunday, May 18, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Concert Curated by flutist Stacy Pelinka, Connections will explore the music of Kaija Saariaho, Chris Castro, Kay Rhie, Jen Wang, and Louise Farrenc to complete this season’s Chamber Music Series. This concert builds upon the community of composers, living and not. Through it, you’ll meet familiar faces and meet some new ones, all of whom will make you feel like you’re reuniting with long-lost friends. Stacey’s contemporary chamber music expertise shines. pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, May 7, 2025 Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts Festival Opera Spring Soirée Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts Festival Opera board members at the Spring Soirée: Timothy Evans (left), Nina Bancroft Dickerson, Claudia Terry, Megan Dey-Toth, Jennifer Kwock-Lau, Zachary Gordin, Dr. Vivian Wing, Susie Hanson, and Keegan Dwyer By Tony Simons Piedmont Center for the Arts hosted Festival Opera’s Spring Soirée on Saturday, May 3 at 4:00 p.m. for an evening of music and celebration inspired by the legendary Parisian musical salons. Founded in 1991, Festival Opera is a Bay-Area based opera company with the mission to advance the operatic art form and to build community by producing culturally rich and diverse programming to enlighten, educate, and entertain at the highest artistic standard. Past leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp, Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony, and is currently led by baritone, conductor and impresario Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera first began performing at PCA in 2020, producing recitals and other events that were scaled to fit the venue’s intimate chambers. Now, Festival Opera presents a series of salonstyle concerts at PCA each season, encouraging the community to attend performances and meet the artists at receptions after each event at the venue. “It really is the perfect size and space to experience this special type of performance, where the audience can be close to the musicians and get involved with the music and text in a very intimate way,” said Gordin. Attendees of the Spring Soirée enjoyed the company of fellow opera lovers, patrons and artists while sipping wine, sampling sweet and savory treats from Siren Sisters Kitchen, and enjoying a live performance. According to Gordin, the Spring Soirée was a resounding success – both as a fundraising event and musically. “The artists we presented were sensational,” said Gordin. “Soprano Shawnette Sulker, mezzo-soprano Courtney Miller, and pianist Daniel Lockert wowed the audience with gems from the opera and art song repertoire.” The silent and live auctions offered an array of treasures such as jewelry, bottles of fine wines, performing arts tickets, and fine dining experiences for patrons to take home. Gordin complimented PCA as a community space and for the quality of its events. “Piedmont residents have a unique opportunity to witness the world-renowned artists and varied programs we present in their own backyard. PCA offers the community a beautiful space where performing and visual arts happen, and a vehicle for getting involved and ensuring that the arts can endure and thrive,” Gordin said. articles.text: Tickets are still available for Berkeley Symphony’s annual Spring Gala on Saturday, May 10, celebrating the legacy of its fourth Music Director, Maestro Joseph Young, at the Unitarian Universalist Church in Kensington. Young first guest-conducted the Berkeley Symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute and was later appointed as music director following the success of that debut—his first directorship. In November 2024, the symphony announced that Young will conclude his tenure at the end of the current season. He led the orchestra through the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent arts venue closures, launching digital programPhilharmonic, Orquesta Sinfónica RTVE, the Liverpool Philharmonic, and the Louisville Orchestra. The 2025 gala will be hosted by Dianne Nicolini, midday host at KDFC Classical California, and feature performances by Berkeley Symphony musicians and guest artists. Guests will enjoy a hilltop reception with sweeping Bay Area views, hors d’oeuvres, an open bar, and a three-course dinner catered by Carrie Dove Catering. Guests can sponsor a table or purchase individual tickets, starting at $500. articles.text: Nosy neighbors. They can be a pain—but what if one of them witnesses murder right on your block? That’s the question famed movie director Alfred Hitchcock explores in his classic thriller, Rear Window. And what if his nosy hero is played by James Stewart? And what if his girlfriend is played by Grace Kelly? And what if the murderer discovers he’s been discovered? It’s all right up there on the screen — how can an audience resist? One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s next showing is indeed Rear Window, based on an ingenious Cornell Woolrich short story. Released in 1954, it centers on a recuperating news photographer, L.B. Jeffries (Stewart), who gradually comes to believe he’s witnessed a crime. Confined to a wheelchair after an accident that’s put one of his legs in a cast, he fights boredom by staring out his rear window, secretly peering with a telephoto lens and binoculars into neighboring apartments. He becomes fascinated by odd goings-on in one in particular—why is Lars Thorwald’s wife suddenly gone missing? Is the burly Thorwald mailing parts of her out of town by UPS? Assisted by girlfriend, Lisa Fremont (Kelly) and a friendly cop (Wendell Corey), Jeffries doggedly investigates, putting both himself and Lisa in peril. Hitchcock directs all this deftly, helped by a cast that includes wry and irresistible Thelma Ritter as his nurse, and Raymond Burr, who would go on to play Perry Mason and Ironside on TV, as Thorwald. Rear Window will be screened on Thursday, May 8th, at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is encouraged and can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the Marilyn Monroe classic, The Seven Year Itch, to be screened on June 12th. Alfred Hitchcock’s Rear Window will be screened on Thursday, May 8th, at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.

articles.text: Shakespeare’s great comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor begat Verdi’s final opera “Falstaff”. It was an incredible formula for success. Both the play and the opera are unique. Opera Modesto featured Verdi’s opera Falstaff for its final production this season. It was a pleasure to attend and was worth a trip to Modesto. Verdi was renowned for his operatic tragedies. He admired the works of Shakespeare and drew on that great English author for his inspiration. At the age of 80 the great Italian composer decided to retire. That didn’t sit well with his admirers. They enticed him to write one more opera. “Let your final work be a comedy. We know that you love Shakespeare. Set Falstaff to music. You can conclude the opera by saying, ‘He who laughs last laughs best.’” Verdi thought this was a great idea and got to work immediately. Falstaff is a mass of contradictions. His character is a big, fat blowhard. A highly placed phony, also. The curious thing is that he is highly successful… at failure. Throughout the opera, there is considerable wordplay with puns, misdeeds, and misleads. The sum of these contradictions becomes a comedic masterpiece. The play by Shakespeare is glorious and so is the opera by Verdi. The opera was an instant success of sorts; and then a failure of sorts. Famous orchestra conductor Toscanini reintroduced it, and it has been a success ever since. In the production by Opera Modesto, the audience was treated to a superb performance. Their theater is beautiful and so was the staging and the entire performance. The orchestra was both efficient and inspired and the performers were absolutely first class. Curtain calls at the end of the opera Falstaff by Verdi in a production by Opera Modesto. The performance was beautiful from beginning to end.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, May 7, 2025 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Café Society a nugget by Woody Allen By Chris Honoré Woody Allen has made 46 films, some iconic. My initial assumptions about Café Society were that while it would be mildly entertaining, with moments that would bring about a smile, it wouldn’t be, say, Midnight in Paris. Certainly not Annie Hall or Manhattan. As it turned out, and I understand that any reaction to a film is ultimately subjective and will touch individual moviegoers in very personal ways (good and bad), Café Society was, at least for me, a wonderful surprise. Of course, some might walk away from this film and observe that it is Woody-lite. But I would disagree. Set in the 1930s, during the Great Depression, the film is steeped in Hollywood’s golden era. It’s a palm tree, boulevard-lights postcard that says, “Wish you were here.” Café Society is gorgeous to behold: the period dress, the décor, its tones and ubiquitous golden glow captivating, the interior shots of Hollywood studios so very stylish and elegant, opulent Spanish tiled mansions, breathtakingly long town cars polished to mirror shines, all of it with an overlay of sepia color, shot by the gifted cinematographer, Vittorio Storaro. The film is Woody’s homage to Hollywood during a period that lends itself to being romanticized and certainly idealized. Add Gershwin 78 rpm vinyl songs and Kristen Stewart and Jesse Eisenberg in Café Society you’re there. So completely there. While Café Society has been billed as a comedy. This is, after all, Woody Allen, master of the incisive one-liner, dialogue perfectly crafted while he agonizes about imagined maladies. But in reality it is, a love story between a young and naïve transplanted New Yorker, Bobby Dorman (Jesse Eisenberg), who ventures west to California to start a new life and hopefully find work with his uncle, s successful Hollywood agent, Phil Stern (Steve Carrell). It’s in Stern’s office that he meets Vonnie (Kristen Stewart), a young beauty who came west to act but found getting inside the industry tent all but impossible. For Bobby, it’s love at first glance. She’s stunning, innocent yet streetwise, as well as generous. And so, as Bobby struggles to find his west coast sea legs, supported by Phil and his circle of contacts, a triangle is offered up in a surprising reveal. Meanwhile uncle Ben (Cory Stoll) is intent on getting into the nightclub business and burying those who stand in his way in cement coffins at construction sites. Actually, Ben is a good guy, endearing in a kind of remorseless, gangster kind of way. In one of Woody’s great lines in the film, spoken, I believe, in voice over by Woody himself, he quotes and then embellishes Socrates, commenting that “The unexamined life is not worth living. But the examined life is no bargain.” Somehow that sentiment is perfect as Bobby struggles to find love and his place in New York, Hollywood, and once again back in New York. What is so appealing about this movie is that while there is an unspoken melancholy that frames the story, what is missing in Woody’s manic insecurities; instead, he (in the persona of Bobby) is gently reflective. The tale is familiar, yet it is told in a fresh and appealing way, underscoring that when it comes to matters of the heart, the heart trumps intellect, for better or worse. Woody also returns to his familiar and signature theme: regret. And he reiterates that from that emotion is evinced a resulting sadness, constructed of memories, that though they may fade, there still remain those unexpected moments when a time or a decision or a person now long gone will cause us to stop and gaze off into the distance and contemplate what might have been. This very brief interlude is compounded by the realization that life moves us on, inextricably, and that what once was can never be again, no matter how deeply we wish it were otherwise. And it is that sense of lingering sadness, a realization dearly purchased, that threads it way through Café Society and makes so much of this film sublime. Café Society. Written and directed by Woody Allen. Starring Jesse Eisenberg, Kristen Stewart, Blake Lively. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2016. Now streaming on prime/ Netflix.
