articles.text: From the world renowned Japanese Studio Ghibli, The Secret World of Arrietty was co-written by two of its principal storytellers, Hiromasa Yonebayashi and Hayao Miyazaki. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule, even law, is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, alas, the Borrowers, they believe, are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure to be sure for she is fascinated by the sheer size of the bean world, something she views in all its gigantic splendor and potential danger. articles.text: Britt Robertson and Asa Butterfield in The Space Between Us Let’s be honest, the tween/teen crowd is exactly the demographic for which The Space Between Us It is a tender teenage love story that finds its sweet spot. The premise is that Gardner (Asa Butterfield) is, unexpectedly, born on Mars. His mother, an astronaut, dies giving birth. Hence, he grows up on Mars in a very controlled and insulated environment. Fast forward 16 years and Gardner is feeling very much like an adolescent, acting out with a million dollar Mars rover and insisting to his coach (and the folks that matter) that he wants above all to go to earth, a place he’s only been told about. What the adults don’t know is that he has been emailing a young girl, Tulsa (Britt Robertson), sharing feelings and images on their computers (I know, Mars to earth and back, well, it’s a stretch). Their attraction has grown. So Gardner not only wants to see earth, he wants to see Tulsa. And he wants to search for his dad, who he has never met. And thus begins his journey. He finds Tulsa, and she joins him in his search for his dad, which morphs into quite a tender adventure. Meanwhile, an unhappy NASA crowd is in the hunt for Gardner; they’re not pleased with him being out and about on his own. What he doesn’t know is that earth is not only strange and vastly different from Mars, but is also a possible threat to his health. His caretakers want desperately to find him and get him back into a controlled gravity environment. I’d judge that The Space Between Us will have the tweens and teens in its pocket from the start, all the way to the money shot at the end. There’s great music, and a nice love story, with lots of good acting on the part of Robertson and Butterfield, who have youthful chemistry. The Space Between Us. Directed by Peter Chelsom. Starring Asa Butterfield, Britt Robertson and Gary Oldman. 2 hrs., Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ YouTube.

It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule, even law, is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, alas, the Borrowers, they believe, are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure to be sure for she is fascinated by the sheer size of the bean world, something she views in all its gigantic splendor and potential danger. But, as it turns out, she is also drawn into Shawn’s personal world and is soon discovered by the bean boy. articles.text: Lisa Anne Gaston, a wonderful wife, mother, grandmother, teacher and friend passed peacefully on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia, surrounded by her family and a few of her closest Born on an Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi, and having lived in Atlanta for the past 36 years, Lisa Anne was known for her southern charm but was a true (and emphatic) California girl at heart. She spent her childhood in Piedmont, California, where she graduated from Piedmont High School in 1975. The only child of two pioneering physicians – Dr. Harper Gaston, a dedicated cardiologist, who founded the Kaiser Permanente Southeast Medical Group, and Dr. Anne Gaston, one of the very first female, board-certified neonatologists – Lisa Anne was raised with wit, determination and a passion for learning. She pursued her undergraduate studies at Bryn Mawr College, where she majored in political science. Her years at Bryn Mawr were some of her most treasured. She cherished the century-old traditions and made lifelong friends, many of whom she remained in touch with all of Never one to shy away from a challenge, she then moved to Washington D.C., earning both a Master’s Degree in Foreign Service and International Development, as well as a Juris Doctor in International Law and Legal Studies at Georgetown Lisa Anne’s professional journey was as diverse as it was impressive. She began her career practicing law in New York, California and Georgia. Once in Atlanta, she transitioned into television, where she became Vice President of Public Affairs at Turner Broadcasting. Her work creating “Interact Atlanta” earned her multiple Emmy Awards and paved the way for her eventual move to Georgia Public Broadcasting, where she was recognized as one of the “Women Making a Mark” by Atlanta Magazine. It was during her broadcasting years that she Former Piedmont resident Lisa Anne Gaston died on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. met her great love and husband of 25 years, Michael Reff. In the next chapter of her life, Lisa Anne discovered her truest calling: teaching. Earning yet another Masters Degree in Education from Agnes Scott College, she spent nine cherished years teaching English and Literature at Central Gwinnett High School. With a deep love for books and a passion for writing, she inspired her students to find confidence in their writing and empowered them to discover their own voice. She loved her students, and they loved her in return. In her final days, she received an outpouring of love and gratitude from many of her past students who shared the many ways in which Lisa Anne influenced and changed the course of their lives. Lisa Anne’s life was filled with adventure and travel with her husband, Michael, and her two daughters, Allison and Hayley Harper. She was known for her radiant smile, sharp intellect, and gift for finding joy and beauty in the everyday. She never hesitated to speak her mind, stood strong in her convictions, and moved through life with an unwavering sense of self and a deep belief in angels and the power of prayer. She loved her family, her two grandsons, and her golden retrievers. Lisa Anne was a fighter and despite a near 20-year battle with heart complications, maintained a positivity that was palpable to all she encountered. Her health challenges unfortunately pulled her away from the classroom and kept her adventures closer to home. These limitations never broke her infectious and indomitable spirit and in spite of them, she remained engaged with and even expanded her social community. Lisa Anne had friends far and wide and worked hard to maintain those connections, no matter the distance. Lisa Anne is survived by her beloved husband, Michael Reff, her two daughters, Allison Stalla (Zeid Stalla) and Hayley Swarbrick (Andrew Swarbrick), her two grandsons, Ben Stalla and Grayson Swarbrick, and many friends both near and far. Her life was a testament to the power of perseverance, the joy found in every moment, and the importance of loving deeply and boldly. She would be honored to be forever carried in the hearts of those who knew her. A funeral was held at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland on April 27, 2025, followed by a Continued Celebration of Life at Signature Studios in Roswell, Georgia on May 1, 2025. In lieu of flowers, the family encourages donations to Girls, Inc. of Greater Atlanta (www. girlsincatl.org), where Lisa Anne volunteered for many years.

pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, May 7, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers take time to smell the flowers The Wednesday Walkers wanted to see the new bridge over Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park last week, but a wonderful thing about spring flowers is that they come in waves with some blooming early and others later. Rhododendrons are one of the later flowers. They had just started to pop around Piedmont and some homes on the 100 block of La Salle Avenue have large, mature, beautiful rhododendrons that were worth a special trip to see. So, the rhododendrons were the morning’s destination. The Morcom Rose Garden and the Bushy Dell Creek Bridge could wait. The group headed out going up Highland Avenue knowing that there would be other rhododendrons and more wonderful flowers in front yards along the way to see. On Sheridan Avenue the walkers had their first rhododendron sighting and there were also dogwoods with delicate white petals, horse chestnuts with fuchsia-colored buds, cherry trees and white blossoms, purple wisteria, and even red roses to enjoy. The group went up Wildwood Avenue, through the shaded Hall Fenway, and on Crocker Avenue they found the petite, yellow Lady Banks roses that covered an iron front fence. Towards the end of the block, just before Sea View Avenue, there were spectacular white and pink rhododendrons in two front yards. Rhododendron is a very large genus of about 1,024 species of woody plants. They are found most commonly in acidic and infertile growing conditions and can be either evergreen or deciduous. Most species are native to eastern Asia and the Himalayan region, but smaller numbers occur elsewhere in Asia, and in North America, Europe, and Australia. Their name comes from Ancient Greek with “rhodon” meaning “rose” and “dendron” meaning “tree.” Rhododendrons have no final size and can grow almost indefinitely. They range from dwarf, ground-hugging varieties, which may reach 16 inches, to giant tree-like specimens as tall as 20 feet or more. Most species have brightly colored flowers which bloom from late winter through to early summer. It is the national flower of Nepal, the state flower of both Washington and West Virginia, the state flower of Nagaland, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, and Himachal Pradesh in India, and the provincial flower of Jeju in South Korea and Jiangxi in China. The smaller azalea makes up two subgenera of rhododendron. The large, white, and fuchsia-colored ones on La Salle made a beautiful background for a group photo. The morning was still young, so the walkers continued up La Salle, past Indian Road, and climbed up the rarely visited La Salle Court cul de sac. At the top of its hill is an 8,500 square foot white mansion built in 1925 with a pool on the right side. One walker said it looked like a “mini–Claremont Hotel.” It was another thing of beauty in a morning that had been filled with it. It was now time for the group to retrace their steps and make their return to the city center via La Salle, St. James Drive, and Hampton Road, enjoying more spring flowers along the way. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. On Monday, the group took a trip to Santiago to visit the famous Santiago de Compostela Cathedral the final destination of the Way of St. James, a Catholic pilgrimage route, since the 9th century. On Tuesday school life resumed through Thursday. During this time students learned about the small ways of the culture they were sampling, Piedmont students had to adjust to 10 p.m. dinners and later times to rest. Redondela is a conservative coastal town, PHS teacher Sahagon explained, where the Americans enjoyed plenty of seafood, potatoes, meat, vegetables and maybe “a nice homemade soup.” The stated goal was to improve their Spanish language fluency. Sahagon said she noticed marked improvement in the students’ confidence and ability following the immersion crash course in speaking Spanish. “The students mentioned that they learned to be patient and go with the flow when things didn’t work out the way they wanted it, and also to understand different perspectives and see different cultures,” Sahagon said. On Friday the group took a train to Madrid where they spent two nights before heading home Sunday. While there they tried dancing to flamenco music and agreed that their favorite food was churros con chocolate. The popular treat is consumed for breakfast and dessert. The trip was a wild success by most markers, and Sahagon estimated that 80% of the participants continue to communicate with their Spanish partners. Organizing the trip was a year and a half in the making for Sahagon and Piedmont educators, offering lessons of what hopefully may be the start of an annual cultural tradition. “It was a very nice experience and I’m very happy to maybe organize it if parents want to do it again,” said Sahagon. articles.text: Pat Leicher, mother of Adam (PHS ’99) and Anne (PHS ’03), recently returned from a trip to Chile. The trip focused on Easter Island and the Atacama Desert. There are hundreds of these statues, called Moai, carved in volcanic crater and made between 1000 and 1600. If the Moai has eyes, like this one, it means that the spirit is still in the statue. If there are no eyes, the spirit has gone on to Paradise. Kiran Bawa Continued from page 1 Director for the City of Oakland, where she implemented innovative budget balancing measures to expand services while addressing ongoing financial obligations. She also served as Manager of Capital Planning & Grants at AC Transit, where she was responsible for the District’s $500 million capital budget. Bawa was drawn back to Piedmont by the engaged community and the City’s thoughtful approach to long-term financial planning, noting that she particularly looks forward to working with the City Council and the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee to develop the City’s annual budgets. “I’m passionate about the budget process because it’s how we bring community priorities to life,” said Bawa. “Piedmont’s commitment to transparency and collaboration makes it a privilege to return. I’m honored and deeply grateful for the opportunity. As Finance Director, Bawa will oversee citywide finance functions, including accounting, payroll, auditing, purchasing, investments, and the development of the City’s annual budget. The City engaged executive recruitment firm Peckham and McKenney to conduct a search to fill the position last year after Finance Director Mike Szczech announced his intention to retire in January 2025. Since January, Interim Finance Director Lisa Malek-Zadeh has overseen Finance Department functions on a temporary basis. With Malek-Zadeh’s term with the City now concluded, Szczech is anticipated to return on a limited basis through July 1 to support the budget process. articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board unanimously approved changes to elementary and middle school curriculums at a board meeting on Wednesday, April 23. The changes give 7th and 8th graders the option of taking a year of World Language next year and begin a restructuring of performing arts in elementary school. Next year, 4th graders will have Theater Arts but not instrumental music, and 5th graders will receive more hours of music instruction in smaller classes. expedited curriculum adoption, staffing alterations and a reworking of the master schedule. “I know that this has come about more quickly than some other curricular changes have in the past,” said Board President Lindsay Thomasson. She added that the proposal was “really strong” and “very student-centric.” World Language Next school year (2025-26) year, all 7th and 8th graders will have the option to select a full year of World Language instruction as an elective, most likely in Spanish, Mandarin and French. In the following year, 2026-2027, all 5th and 6th graders will have exposure to World Languages. articles.text: Families enjoyed a fun and informational time at Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day and Earth Day celebration last Thursday, April 24, at Piedmont Community Hall. Hosted by Piedmont Public Works Department and the Park Commission, the event was highlighted by the announcement of this year’s Heritage Trees and owl naming contest. Twenty-two California native plants and trees were given to the raffle winners. The annual event, which began in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces, as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The event featured informational tables from Piedmont Fire Department and the City’s Sustainability Division where guests could make environmentally-minded pledges and learn about wildfire prevention, clean water programs, and Piedmont’s induction cookware lending program. Attendees enjoyed an Aloha photo booth, voted on the names of a pair of owls living in Dracena Park, and tried out electric leaf blowers courtesy of Piedmont Scout Troop 11. Raffle winners were called periodically throughout the event, allowing kids and adults alike opportunities to win stuffed

articles.text: Diplomat and legal scholar Jeff Bleich spoke to a packed house at the home of Ellen and Pete Wilson on Wednesday, April 16. The event was organized by the Community Engagement Committee of the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF). Bleich spoke about the fall in democracy worldwide. His current book updates Machiavelli’s The Prince for modern times. Bleich’s illustrious legal career includes clerking for the Chief Justice of the United States, serving as President of the State Bar of California, and providing special counsel to President Obama. He was the point man in California for Obama’s successful election as U.S. President and served as U.S. Ambassador to Australia, senior advisor to the director of National Intelligence, and chair of the California State University Board of Trustees. His works focus principally on democracy, international relations, and constitutional law. A long time resident of Piedmont, Bleich is currently a fellow at Stanford’s Center for Advanced Study in Behavioral Sciences where he is working on two books. The first is an update of progressive prescriptions from the 2nd industrial revolution in the United States to reform and restore functioning Democracy in America. articles.text: When Piedmont’s school board met on April 23, the school district’s Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) program received strong votes of confidence from District leaders. Elise Marks’ opening remarks as Teacher Union President highlighted Piedmont’s resilient stance against a federal ban on K-12 DEI programs. The meeting’s presentation of the evening came from DEIB Director, Jean Takazawa, who reported on, the growth, impact and success of Piedmont’s DEIB programs. “We are doing these things, these are our norms now, we actually are in full implementation,” said Takazawa. The original deadline for the federal K-12 DEI ban by the Federal government was set for April 24. The Federal Department of Education claimed Title 6 of the Civil Rights Acts is being violated by the presence of such programs and demanded certification from states to continue receiving federal education funds. At that time last week, California was one of 16 states that declared it will not provide certification to the federal government. articles.text: Project Peace, a nonprofit based in Walnut Creek, has announced that Dr. Katharine Hayhoe will serve as keynote speaker at an event hosted by Piedmont Community Church on May 18, 2025, from 4 to 5:30 p.m. Hayhoe, an atmospheric scientist, is chief scientist for The Nature Conservancy and a distinguished professor and endowed chair at Texas Tech University. Her work focuses on the impacts of climate change on people and the planet. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department’s Play Like a Girl returns this weekend for a free day of hands-on activities, live demonstrations, and inspiring role models – all designed to get girls interested in playing sports. The free event takes place on Sunday, May 4, from 10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. at Witter Field. Now in its fourth year, Play Like a Girl invites girls from ages 2-18 throughout the Bay Area to try sports from field hockey to flag football to roller derby with support from skilled athletes and coaches. If a girl wants to continue exploring a sport, there will be information available about classes, leagues, and camps. Play Like a Girl+ 2025 will feature a meeting with former WBNA player Layshia Clarendon and 5-time Olympic swimming gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant. Lifelong benefits of sports Participation in sports builds skills that support girls throughout their lives, teaching leadership, discipline, and teamwork. Girls who participate in sports experience lower rates of depression and higher self-esteem than their non-athlete peers. Research has shown a direct link between participation in sports and better educational opportunities, positive health outcomes, and improved career outcomes for girls: • Girls who participate in sports are significantly more likely to graduate high school compared to non-athletes. • Overall, young girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. • Girls who participate in high school sports have higher rates • of labor force participation and earn 7% higher wages than non-athlete peers. In a 2013 study of 821 senior managers and executives, 94% of female executives reported playing organized sports after primary school. Play Like a Girl+ is made possible by the support of title sponsor Dress Best for Less and many Piedmont athletic organizations hosting stations, including the PHS women’s basketball team, PHS flag football team, Piedmont DEVO mountain biking team, Piedmont junior running club, Piedmont Baseball & Softball Foundation, Piedmont Soccer Club, PMS Sports, Piedmont swim club, and the PHS track & field team. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/PlayLikeAGirl for details, to register, or to sign up to volunteer. A father helps his daughter with a golf swing at last year’s event.
articles.title: Play Like a Girl invites Bay Area girls to try new sports

articles.text: City Council study sessions have begun for a walkthrough of the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, a housing plan that provides space for 199 new housing units in Piedmont. The first study session took place on Monday, April 28, with the next study session taking place tonight, Wednesday, April 30, at 5:30 p.m. at Piedmont High School Library. The aim of these study sessions is to provide a “first look” overview of the recently released Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Using the big picture vision as a starting point, the April 28 study session focused on the mechanics of implementing the Specific Plan once it’s been adopted. The April 30 meeting will offer a deep dive into the built environment, as defined in the draft document, covering roadway improvements, building design, landscaping, and infrastructure. The study sessions mark the beginning of an extensive public review period and series of meetings before the Council is expected to consider adoption of the Specific Plan next fall. This public review period also includes the following meetings: • June 4, 2025: Park Commission • June 18, 2025: Recreation Commission • August-September 2025: Public hearings at Planning Commission and City Council Community members are encouraged to attend the study sessions. For those unable to join, presentation materials will be available on the project website after the meeting. Multifamily Housing in Moraga Canyon The product of study and community engagement beginning in summer 2023, the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan outlines a vision for a new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon that would: • bring new housing to Piedmont, creating opportunities for people of all income levels • enhance recreational amenities through an expanded sports field and new hiking trail • improve road safety with a new bike lane, sidewalks, and traffic signal at Red Rock Road • model best practices in wildfire resistant construction and landscaping The Draft Specific Plan details development locations, site improvements, and infrastructure requirements for the construction up to 199 units of new housing on City-owned land in Moraga Canyon, 60 of which would be affordable to lower income households. The document anticipates development of multifamily residential buildings between four and six stories and includes two options for where these buildings could be located – either on the north side or the south side of Moraga Avenue. It includes 10 chapters, each one addressing a single topic in detail, with subjects ranging from overall site vision to circulation and traffic safety improvements to building and landscape design. The final chapter outlines an implementation strategy and options for project financing. The Draft Specific Plan is available for download and review at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP. Submit comments online or by mail Community members can offer comments on the Draft Specific Plan: • online at piedmont.ca.gov/ MCSPComments • by email to MoragaCanyonNews@piedmont.ca.gov • by mail to: Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 The City Council is expected to consider adoption of the Specific Plan in fall 2025, following a recommendation from the Planning Commission. Learn more about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan and view video and materials from past meetings and events at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP.
articles.title: City Council study sessions offer in-depth look at Moraga Canyon Housing Plan draft

articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) will hold a community meeting tonight, Wednesday, April 30, at Havens Library at 7:00 p.m. Everyone is invited to attend. The meeting will provide an opportunity to discuss recent attacks nationally on diversity, equity, and inclusion. Businesses such as Google, Target, Walmart, Meta, and Uber have rolled back their initiatives. Schools have been threatened with funding cuts if they don’t end their programs. People are being targeted because of the color of their skin, gender, religion, beliefs, and immigration status. Attendees will be encouraged to share concerns and brainstorm ideas on how the community can respond.
articles.title: PADC to hold community meeting on Equity tonight

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to help shape an initiative to develop “objective design standards” for new housing in Piedmont by completing a short online survey. State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing projects, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards – those that require no subjective judgement or interpretation by public officials. The Objective Design Standards initiative aims to create clear, measurable, and enforceable rules governing design elements like articulation and massing, providing residents, property owners, and developers clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. This survey is an opportunity for community members to help shape the standards by sharing their preferences and priorities. The survey asks: • How important is architectural consistency within neighborhoods? • What architectural elements are the most important, regardless of style? • How important are building and site features like porches, balconies, low fences, and open front yards? • What would your biggest concerns be if a new home or major addition was built next door to you? The survey should take about 10 minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ ODSSurvey. Responses will be accepted through May 19. Feedback will help ensure new construction respects the design qualities that residents value most. In Piedmont, objective design standards already exist for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and multi-family and mixed-use developments. This initiative is developing new objective standards for one-to-four unit residential development and updating the existing standards for other housing types. A video introduction to Objective Design Standards is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ODSBasics. For more information, visit the project website at piedmont. ca.gov/ODS. articles.text: Betty C. Howard Award winners acknowledged at Volunteer Reception City officials and staff applaud City volunteers at the annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception. Piedmont City officials gathered to honor outgoing Commission and Committee volunteers, Betty C. Howard award recipients Gail Lombardi and Carrie Villa, and longtime Police Department volunteer Stanley Silverman at a Volunteer Appreciation event in Piedmont Community Hall last Tuesday, April 22. The event began with an introduction by Mayor Betsy Andersen, followed by a recognition of outgoing Commission and Committee volunteers. “I love looking out and seeing our amazing volunteers,” said Mayor Andersen at the start of the ceremony. “You all give so much to our community. Piedmont would not be the place that it is without your effort and time and love for one another and for our community.” Now in its 46th year, the Betty C. Howard award was created in 1979 by then Recreation Director Mark Delventhal as a way to honor volunteers and staff members for their dedication. The award was named after former Recreation Department Secretary Betty Howard, who worked for the department for 30 years. Two Betty C. Howard awards are given each year – one for the Outstanding Volunteer and another for Outstanding Staff. articles.text: Dr. Stephen Main, Minister of Music at Piedmont Community Church, is set to have his original cantata, The Image, performed in New York on Wednesday, June 4, at 6:30 p.m. at Trinity Church, Wall Street. Born and raised in New York City, Main studied violin, piano, organ, theory and composition at Oberlin Conservatory, where he received his Bachelor’s Degree of Music in Organ Performance. At the same time, he earned a B.A., M.A., and Ph.D. in Religious Philosophy from the University of Chicago. As a composer, Main’s work includes numerous published choral and orchestral works, regular commissions, and film scores. He has also received the John Ness Beck Award for outstanding achievement in choral composition. Main’s cantata was first unveiled at Piedmont Community Church in June 2023 with choir and full orchestra. Based on an original concept and many conversations with choir member Joe Scherer, Main composed the music and wrote the verse. “The western philosophical and theological idea of the image of God, the imago Dei as it’s called in Latin... has been a foundation for western ideals of democracy,” explained Main about the impetus of his composition. Main’s cantata is now set to play at the historical East Coast venue, Trinity Church on Wall Street. Founded in 1697, this pre-revolutionary church contains the gravesite of Alexander Hamilton. The Image has been added to Trinity Church’s Spring Concert Series, which is free to the public and will be livestreamed internationally. However, in order to fit into this year’s schedule, Piedmont Community Church was asked to pay for the orchestra – a cost of $40,000. “It came to their attention long after they’d already budgeted their year,” explained Main about Trinity Church. “And like a lot of Stephen Main, Music Director and Composer at Piedmont Community Church churches, they write their budgets and then it’s all secured.” Working with Piedmont Community Church, Trinity Church offered to cover the cost of the choir, rehearsals, insurance, technical audio staff, publicity and more in order to fit them into the church’s Concert Series schedule for 2025. Piedmont Community Church has raised more than $18,000 toward the cost of the orchestra as of April 22, and is accepting donations on their website or through mailing a check to the church noting “The Image”. Some church members will be traveling to New York to be at the concert live, and there will be a watch party at the Community Church for the concert. For residents wanting to see Main’s choral and orchestral work in person, Main encourages community members to check out the performance of another one of his pieces, Where Everything is Music. This piece will be performed at the Community Church on June 1, the Sunday right before Main flies to New York to help Trinity Church with The Image. “What I’m hoping happens from ‘The Image’ is that I would love it to redound to the glory of Piedmont,” said Main. “because I really believe in Piedmont Church and I’m very proud of my musicians.”
articles.title: Stephen Main cantata The Image headed to New York

articles.text: May can be a challenging month for students. Endurance to get through the school year is flagging, yet there are still significant hurdles to overcome before the promise of summer arrives. Whether you have a student taking AP exams, facing looming finals, or exhibiting a raging case of Senioritis (regardless of their age), here are some strategies for parents to help manage May stress. Communication is key Anyone with school-aged kids can relate to the idea that “May is the new December.” May is the month of dance recitals, band concerts, end-of-season sports banquets, and more. While it is fun to celebrate the hard work of our kids and their classmates, it can be exhausting. Taking some time now to read the backlog of emails and mark the important dates on your calendar can help avoid last-minute scheduling disappointment. Having a conversation with your high schooler now about time management in May will allow you both to identify issues while there is still time to resolve them. Ask your student to tell you about their plans for preparing for tests and finals. Remind them that even though we’re nearing crunch time, there is still time to schedule help with the teacher or an academic tutor. If there are family obligations during May that include your teen, let them know as soon as possible. Show your support Both AP tests and finals feel very high stakes to students. If your schedule allows, offering a healthy breakfast or a ride to school could help your student feel supported on a really stressful day. These simple gestures can help calm a stimulated amygdala and allow your student’s brain to focus rather than be derailed by testing stress. Students who are finishing 8th or 12th grade may be anxious about their transition to high school or college. Acknowledging that these feelings are valid goes a long way to helping your child feel better about the uncertainty of change. The end of the school year is always filled with big emotions. Here’s to getting through May with as much joy and as little stress as possible! Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Karen is a former college professor and an experienced coach. For more information please visit www. studysmarter.com, email info@ studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.

articles.text: Piedmont Adult School celebrated 50 years of education on Thursday, April 24, in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The birthday celebration reunited instructors past and present and highlighted a half century of programming embodying the example of learning for life. Adult School Director Shannon Fierro welcomed instructors and students alike at the celebration. Instructors with more than 25 years of teaching at the school were given gold apples and certificates. The school was founded in Bagpipe teacher Lynne Miller with wife Gail Miller at the celebration Adult School Director Shannon Fierro (left) is pictured with Mike Oatey and school board member Michael Malione. Photos by Jana Branisa Piedmont Adult School celebrated 50 years on Thursday, April 24, in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. 1975 by Dale Porter. Veteran instructors from the early years included Jacqui Birdsong-James, an aerobics and strength training instructor since 1977. Birdsong-James said the event brought back memories of students and teaching. She told the Post about her favorite change to aerobic instruction over the years. “In 1977 we used 33 LP records, so I had to bring a huge record player. Later we used tapes. Now it is perfect; we have a JBL speaker and my phone,” she said. Lynne Miller, the bagpipe instructor since 2003, was among the veteran teachers being honored. He credits his wife with starting his enjoyment of playing and teacher bagpipes. She gave him a bagpipe early in their 50-plus year marriage. An aerobics teacher since 1983, Alycia Lai-Clemens said it was nice to be recognized as a longtime instructor. “I love my students – they are loyal, intelligent, interesting, well-traveled, friendly, welcoming to new students, and have become my exercise family. Many students have attended 25 or more years, and many are friends outside of class,” Lai-Clemens said. articles.text: Piedmont Girl Scout Troop 33521 will host a scavenger hunt on Saturday, May 10, from 3:00- 5:00 p.m. The event, SCOUT MISSION: EMERYVILLE, will start at Emeryville Public Market (5959 Shellmound Street) before participants embark on a scavenger hunt foot-race around Emeryville’s popular spots. Attendees will create teams of two to five to compete through the streets of Emeryville, solving their way through engaging (and edible) clues for a chance at a prize. Community members will be able to challenge their brain and body while discovering new spots in Emeryville, all while supporting their local Girl Scout troop. At the end, there will be treats and a winner ceremony. This scavenger hunt race is a fundraiser hosted and created by Piedmont 9th graders in Girl Scout Troop 33521. Everyone ages seven and up is welcome – you do not need to be a Girl Scout to participate. Kids under 13 will need an adult chaperone. Cost is $20 per person, with a discount for multiple groups. articles.text: Wildwood fourth graders piled aboard a school bus in the early morning of April 17 for a field trip to Sacramento. Once in the state’s capitol, classes split up to take a tour of the Capitol before coming back for a self-guided scavenger hunt at Sutter’s Fort. Parent chaperones drove in separate cars and met the bus full of fourth graders and teachers at the West Entrance of the Capitol. It was students’ first school field trip on a bus. Jennifer Kessler’s class went into the building to take the tour while Martin Lewis’ class made sketches of the building. Sketchers noted the number of columns, windows and Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom, justice and law, in their drawings. While on the tour, they learned that there was supposed to be a grand staircase entrance on the west side, but it was never completed leaving visitors a grand portico instead. “I felt so immersed in the history of the capitol building. Our docent did a tremendous job of presenting fun, enticing and captivating facts as he took all of our students through the Treasury room, the main hallways with the detailed paintings of past governors, as well as the details of the chamber. The tour flew by because of how interactive it was,” said parent chaperone Jess Nisenbaum. After the tour, the fourth graders gathered together for a photo in front of the Capitol and then hopped back on the bus to drive to Sutter’s Fort State Park, where they ate lunch on the lawn, played card games, infection tag, chess and jumped rope. At Sutter’s Fort the fourth graders divided into small groups to find items on their scavenger hunt lists and write down what they noticed about each item. Some areas they visited included the blacksmith shop, the doctor’s office and the weaving room. Many of the spaces provided services and goods for the travelers who had Sutter’s Fort as their final destination on the California trail. The fourth graders ended their long day of learning about California history with a bus ride home and arrived back at Wildwood School around 4:00 p.m. Ayla Martinez (left) and Vera Kriss stand in front of the west entrance of the Capitol. articles.text: This group designed a biological solution to target the Chytrid fungus, which is found in waterways worldwide and is responsible for the extinction of almost 100 frog species. To stop the spread of this deadly fungus, the team planned to use mycovirus induced gene silencing to target its reproductive structures. By stopping the translation of mRNA for the SAS-4 protein of the fungi’s flagella, they could inhibit its motility and prevent it from being able to spread to new colonies of frogs. “We developed this idea because of the increasing effects the Chytrid fungus is having on frog species due to anthropogenic activities and climate change. With the implementation of our solution, we could effectively protect these keystone species and their surrounding environments,” their project stated.

The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inducted six former athletes and two teams on Saturday, April 26 at PHS’ Alan Harvey Theater, marking the first year they’ve entered two full teams. Inductees included Courtney Gault Azad from the Class of 1999 (basketball, softball, tennis), Jim “Truck” Cullom of the Class of 1942 (football), Robby Inch from the Class of 2010 (football, lacrosse), Catey McCreary from the Class of 1983 (basketball, softball), Casey Morris from the Class of 2008 (basketball), and Lauren Remer of the Class of 2013 (soccer, track). Teams inducted featured the 2003-2004 and 2004- 2005 girls’ basketball teams, and the 1976 football team. Founded in 2003 by the late Ken Rawlings and Pete Anderson, and led for many years by former PHS basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame honors athletes, coaches, administrators, and community members for outstanding contributions to Piedmont High School athletics. • Courtney Gault Azad, Class of 1999 Honors for Gault started the induction ceremony. A member of the Class of 1999, Gault was a three-sport athlete in tennis, softball and basketball at Piedmont High. She was a four-time All-League recipient in softball and two-time recipient in Basketball. As a pitcher, she threw four no-hitters during her four years as a varsity starter. Gault was introduced by former teammate Julie Skaff. “She deserves this honor both because of her athletic accomplishments and her positive impact on the community,” Skaff said. As a senior, Gault led the softball team to the Division 2A East Bay NCS Championship game, where they fell 7-3 to Dublin. In basketball, she averaged a double-double. Gault went on to attend UCLA and worked in their Athletic Department as a recruiter from her sophomore to senior year. “My teammates were synonymous with my best high school memories. Not just the wins, but even the losses created lifelong friendships,” Gault said. • Jim “Truck” Cullom, Class of 1942 Cullom was a two-year starter on Piedmont High’s legendary football teams, which finished ranked No. 1 in the United States in 1941 and No. 2 the previous year in 1940. He left school early to enlist in World War 2 with the Marine Corps and returned to play football and rugby for the University of California, taking his storied career to the NFL’s Washington Commanders and the New York Yanks. Accepting on the behalf of “Truck” was his son, John Collum, a longtime coach of the PITS rugby team. “My dad loved Piedmont. There was never a question in his or my mom’s mind that they were going to raise their family in Piedmont. My dad, more than anything else, was loyal. He was always loyal to his family, friends, Piedmont and Cal,” John Collum said. On the gridiron, Collum was on the offensive line on Cal’s historic teams under coach Lynn (Pappy) Waldorf from 1947-1949, appearing in two Rose Bowls. His teams were famously known as, “Pappy‘s Boys”. He later re-enlisted to the Marine Corps to serve in the Korean War and returned to Cal as an assistant coach for their rugby team. “Truck” was inducted into the Cal Athletics Hall of Fame in 1995. • Robby Inch, Class of 2010 Inch was a two-sport athlete in football and lacrosse. He was a three-year varsity letterman in lacrosse and played two years of varsity football. He was introduced by former lacrosse coach Jerem Stothers. “He was a great teammate and excelled in both football and lacrosse. He was unstoppable one-on-one to the cage and always looked like a running back running down field. He was guarded by the top defender on every team. If they didn’t, it was over for them. But if they did, it was still over,” Stothers said. As a senior, Inch earned USA Lacrosse High School All American honors, was named the Bay Shore Athletic League MVP, and set a single-season for points scored with 67 goals and 39 assists. PHS went 14-8 in 2010 and reach the NCS Quarterfinals. He also led the football team in touchdowns as a junior and senior. He continued his lacrosse career at Santa Clara University, playing all four years. He went on to complete his MBA degree at Columbia University in 2020. “In sixth grade, I became obsessed with lacrosse. I had amazing teammates, like our goalie Connor Sweeney, who would join me at Witter Field to ‘practice.’ He basically stood in the goal and I would hurl lacrosse balls at him,” Inch said with a laugh. • Catey McCreary, Class of 1983 McCreary was a trend-setter in the Piedmont athletic commuCatey McCreary, Class of 1983, was a trendsetter for early women’s sports at PHS. Robby Inch, Class of 2010, was a star on the football and lacrosse teams. 6 individuals, 2 teams inducted into Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame By Jonathan Comeaux The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inducted six former athletes and two teams on Saturday, April 26 at PHS’ Alan Harvey Theater, marking the first year they’ve entered two full teams. Inductees included Courtney Gault Azad from the Class of 1999 (basketball, softball, tennis), Jim “Truck” Cullom of the Class of 1942 (football), Robby Inch from the Class of 2010 (football, lacrosse), Catey McCreary from the Class of 1983 (basketball, softball), Casey Morris from the Class of 2008 (basketball), and Lauren Remer of the Class of 2013 (soccer, track). Teams inducted featured the 2003-2004 and 2004- 2005 girls’ basketball teams, and the 1976 football team. Founded in 2003 by the late Ken Rawlings and Pete Anderson, and led for many years by former PHS basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame honors athletes, coaches, administrators, and community members for outstanding contributions to Piedmont High School athletics. • Courtney Gault Azad, Class of 1999 Honors for Gault started the induction ceremony. A member of the Class of 1999, Gault was a three-sport athlete in tennis, softball and basketball at Piedmont High. She was a four-time All-League recipient in softball and two-time recipient in Basketball. As a pitcher, she threw four no-hitters during her four years as a varsity starter. Gault was introduced by former teammate Julie Skaff. “She deserves this honor both because of her athletic accomplishments and her positive impact on the community,” Skaff said. As a senior, Gault led the softball team to the Division 2A East Bay NCS Championship game, where they fell 7-3 to Dublin. In basketball, she averaged a double-double. Gault went on to attend UCLA and worked in their Athletic Department as a recruiter from her sophomore to senior year. “My teammates were synonymous with my best high school memories. Not just the wins, but even the losses created lifelong friendships,” Gault said. • Jim “Truck” Cullom, Class of 1942 Cullom was a two-year starter on Piedmont High’s legendary football teams, which finished ranked No. 1 in the United States in 1941 and No. 2 the previous year in 1940. He left school early to enlist in World War 2 with the Marine Corps and returned to play football and rugby for the University of California, taking his storied career to the NFL’s Washington Commanders and the New York Yanks. Accepting on the behalf of “Truck” was his son, John Collum, a longtime coach of the PITS rugby team. “My dad loved Piedmont. There was never a question in his or my mom’s mind that they were going to raise their family in Piedmont. My dad, more than anything else, was loyal. He was always loyal to his family, friends, Piedmont and Cal,” John Collum said. On the gridiron, Collum was on the offensive line on Cal’s historic teams under coach Lynn (Pappy) Waldorf from 1947-1949, appearing in two Rose Bowls. His teams were famously known as, “Pappy‘s Boys”. He later re-enlisted to the Marine Corps to serve in the Korean War and returned to Cal as an assistant coach for their rugby team. “Truck” was inducted into the Cal Athletics Hall of Fame in 1995. • Robby Inch, Class of 2010 Inch was a two-sport athlete in football and lacrosse. He was a three-year varsity letterman in lacrosse and played two years of varsity football. He was introduced by former lacrosse coach Jerem Stothers. “He was a great teammate and excelled in both football and lacrosse. He was unstoppable one-on-one to the cage and always looked like a running back running down field. He was guarded by the top defender on every team. If they didn’t, it was over for them. As a senior, Inch earned USA Lacrosse High School All American honors, was named the Bay Shore Athletic League MVP, and set a single-season for points scored with 67 goals and 39 assists. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team capped off its dual meet season on Friday, April 25 with a spirited performance, as the boys’ varsity team secured a 92-78 victory over Castro Valley while the girls’ varsity team narrowly fell, 84-82 . Despite mixed results in the pool, the evening was a resounding success as the team came together to honor its seniors. “Our biggest highlight was having so much of our team there to celebrate our seniors in their last-ever high school dual meet,” said head coach Adrien Downey. “They put a lot of work into creating posters and sending them off in style. Despite being at another team’s pool, we made it feel like home for a few minutes under the banners and balloons.” The Junior Varsity squads continued their strong season with standout performances. Rabia Mahmood impressed once again, showcasing her versatility with an expanding lineup of events. Rylan Patty delivered exceptional relay splits, and Elles Krieckhaus turned heads by winning the 50-yard butterfly and 500-yard freestyle back-to-back – events he doesn’t typically compete in. “JV’s performances were solid up and down the lineup,” Downey said. “But more than anything, their attitude and enthusiasm, especially during the relays, really stood out.” Overall the night was a meaningful one. Family, friends, and teammates filled the deck with cheers, hugs, and gratitude for the seniors who have been the heart of the program for years. Next, Piedmont heads to the West Alameda County Conference (WACC) Championships, where the stakes will be even higher. The meet will crown team champions for both girls and boys and offer a pathway to postseason competition, including the North Coast Section (NCS) Championships and the State Championships. “It’s a true all-hands-on-deck moment for us,” Downey said. “Depth becomes even more important, and it opens opportunities for our entire roster to contribute to the outcome. We’re excited for what’s ahead.” Piedmont honored its nine seniors on the roster for Senior Night. Pictured are Coach Adrien Downey, Julia Montes, Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Evan Byun, Owen Blanford, Simon March-Cunningham, Inaya Majid, Anna Caputo, Tyler Dacanay, Leo Hurwitz, and Principal David Yoshihara.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team rolled through last week with a pair of clean wins. They recently beat Alameda 6-1 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Wednesday, April 23 and handled Marin Academy 5-1 in Kentfield the previous day. Piedmont has just one regular season match remaining, today against Drew HS. They are set to play in the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, May 2-3. Junior singles starter Lucas Smolko aims to defend his WACC singles title from last year. “We are peaking at the right time with two good wins last week. We won three out of four singles matches and two of three doubles against Marin Academy, both of our doubles wins were in third-set tiebreakers. Against Alameda, we won all of our singles matches. The highlight of doubles was a come-from-behind win for Robert [Piniella] and Joey [Assalian],” said coach Jim Landes. After the WACC Tournament, the North Coast Section will host its singles and doubles individual tournament on May 9-10, while the NCS Team Championship will run May 13-17. 6-1 victory over Alameda Winning the first match of the day was Smolko at No. 1 singles in straight sets, 6-1, 6-2. Soon after, Nick King at No. 3 singles reeled in a 7-5, 6-2 win. After that, Alameda claimed its only match of the day at No. 2 doubles, where Luca LaForte and Hunter Fasteau fell 7-6 (7-4), 6-2. The No. 2 doubles team of Piniella and Assalian then won its three-set match 3-6, 6-2, 6-2 to give PHS its third win of the afternoon. The clinching win came from No. 1 doubles, where Will Tenney and Gianluca Bini Staff Photos Lucas Smolko had straight-set wins at No. 1 singles against Marin Academy and Alameda. articles.text: Piedmont High kept in the thick of the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division regular season title race, splitting games with league leaders Castro Valley last week. The Highlanders lost 5-0 at Humphries Diamond on Wednesday, April 23 but defeated the Trojans at their home field 3-2 two days “They pitched a helluva ballgame [on Wednesday] and got the hits when they needed it. We left some guys on base. Pitching, defense, and timely hitting – that’s baseball. You have to come through when your name is called. We’re getting opportunities,” coach Eric Olson said. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 13-6 overall and 4-2 against league competition. They are one game behind Castro Valley at 5-1 and are tied for second with Encinal with a 4-2 Piedmont has four league games left in its season. They have a two-game series remaining with Berkeley on April 30 and May 2, and they close the season with a series with Bishop O’Dowd on May 6-8. The Trojans also have four league games left against Encinal and Alameda. PHS can split the regular season banner if teams finish with an identical record. Piedmont can assure itself a first-round home bid in North Coast Section by winning the league’s tournament on May 13-15. 3-2 win over Castro Valley Castro Valley went ahead initially with one run in the bottom of the first, but Piedmont answered with two runs in the top of the second. PHS extended its lead to 3-1 in the top of the fourth, while the Trojans scored its final run in the bottom of the fifth. With one out, Piedmont’s Jack Meyjes, Jordan Vo, and Michael Martin drew three straight walks to load the bases. That’s when freshman Jonah Cha-Foster hit a hard ground ball to first base, but the Trojans’ infielder botched the catch allowing Meyjes to score. Markos Lagios then drew a twoout walk to score Vo, but that’s all Piedmont could get out of the inning. On the mound, Meyjes struck out the side the following inning and retired nine of 10 batters before CV’s next run. In the top of the fourth, Piedmont loaded the bases once again with two outs after Diego Delventhal hit a single while Lagios and Will Parker drew walks. Delventhal then made his way home on a wild pitch, making it 3-1. Castro Valley got its final run Staff Photos Jack Meyjes struck out six batters in six innings in Piedmonts 3-2 win over Castro Valley. on a solo homer in the bottom fifth and stranded a runner on second base. Delventhal picked up the save, striking out two in the bottom of the seventh. Final stats: Delventhal went 1-for-4 with a run. Lagios had an RBI and drew two walks. Parker went 1-for-3 with a walk. Shafer Dando went 1-for-4. Brandon Dicke went 1-for-3 with a walk. Meyjes went 1-for-3 with a run. Vo went 1-for-3 with a double, a run, and a walk. Martin drew two walks. Cha-Foster had an RBI and a walk. Meyjes threw six innings, striking out six and allowed one earned run. Delventhal earned the save, striking out two. Will Parker had three hits in the two-game series, including two Diego Delventhal scored the game-winning run against Castro Valley. He also earned the save by pitching the final inning.

We left some guys on base. Pitching, defense, and timely hitting – that’s baseball. You have to come through when your name is called. We’re getting opportunities,” coach Eric Olson said. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 13-6 overall and 4-2 against league competition. They are one game behind Castro Valley at 5-1 and are tied for second with Encinal with a 4-2 league record. Piedmont has four league games left in its season. They have a two-game series remaining with Berkeley on April 30 and May 2, and they close the season with a series with Bishop O’Dowd on May 6-8. The Trojans also have four league games left against Encinal and Alameda. PHS can split the regular season banner if teams finish with an identical record. Piedmont can assure itself a first-round home bid in North Coast Section by winning the league’s tournament on May 13-15. 3-2 win over Castro Valley Castro Valley went ahead initially with one run in the bottom of the first, but Piedmont answered with two runs in the top of the second. PHS extended its lead to 3-1 in the top of the fourth, while the Trojans scored its final run in the bottom of the fifth. With one out, Piedmont’s Jack Meyjes, Jordan Vo, and Michael Martin drew three straight walks to load the bases. That’s when freshman Jonah Cha-Foster hit a hard ground ball to first base, but the Trojans’ infielder botched the catch allowing Meyjes to score. Markos Lagios then drew a twoout walk to score Vo, but that’s all Piedmont could get out of the inning. On the mound, Meyjes struck out the side the following inning and retired nine of 10 batters before CV’s next run. In the top of the fourth, Piedmont loaded the bases once again with two outs after Diego Delventhal hit a single while Lagios and Will Parker drew walks. Delventhal then made his way home on a wild pitch, making it 3-1. Castro Valley got its final run Staff Photos Jack Meyjes struck out six batters in six innings in Piedmonts 3-2 win over Castro Valley. on a solo homer in the bottom fifth and stranded a runner on second base. Delventhal picked up the save, striking out two in the bottom of the seventh. Final stats: Delventhal went 1-for-4 with a run. Lagios had an RBI and drew two walks. Parker went 1-for-3 with a walk. Shafer Dando went 1-for-4. Brandon Dicke went 1-for-3 with a walk. Meyjes went 1-for-3 with a run. Vo went 1-for-3 with a double, a run, and a walk. Martin drew two walks. Cha-Foster had an RBI and a walk. Meyjes threw six innings, striking out six and allowed one earned run. Delventhal earned the save, striking out two. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse will close out its 2024-25 season with The Sound of Music, premiering May 23 and running through June 29. The production, directed by Danny Cozart, is fun for all ages and provides a story of both hope and resistance, with a collection of favorite songs like “My Favorite Things,” “Do-Re-Mi,” and “Sixteen Going on Seventeen.” The musical, based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers, premiered years before the widely-popular 1965 American musical drama film The Sound of Music, produced and directed by Robert Wise. The Sound of Music opened on Broadway at the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre on November 16, 1959, with music by Richard Rodgers and lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II. Cozart said the beloved, timeless musical is one of his alltime favorites that “continues to become more relevant day by day.” “The themes we are looking to explore in this production are the choices a person must make when the different structures of society [including] family, religion, and the state, are imposing conflicting demands on them.” Cozart said. “Our focus for this production is to drive home the real-world consequences of political action and the impact on a family trying to stay together in the face of looming tyranny.” In addition, the show delves into themes of loss, found family, reconnection, and emotional presence, he added. Cast includes Marah Sotelo as Maria Rainer, Teressa Foss as Mother Abbess, Chloe Angst as Sister Berthe, Sage Alberto as Sister Margaretta, Akshaya Lakshmi as Sister Sophia, Robert Lopez as Captain Georg Von Trapp and Phillip Leyva as Franz. A cast of young musicians will perform the musical’s key songs. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 (extension 351) or visit www. berkeleyplayhouse.org. Showtimes vary. Marah Sotelo is Maria Rainer in Berkeley Playhouse’s production The Sound of Music, premiering May 23.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse’s The Sound of Music premieres May 23

articles.text: Randall Museum, a children’s arts, science and nature museum in San Francisco, has an extensive list of free workshops next month designed for kids of all ages from toddlers to teenagers. The museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department and offers free admission while providing high-quality science and art classes moderated by museum staff, San Francisco Rec and Park employees and various resident natural scientists and zoologists at a low cost. below. May 3 - Cross Stitch Workshop Randall Museum’s science and nature program coordinator Katherine Galeas Veliz moderates a cross stitching workshop ideal for ages 12 and up on Saturday, May 3, from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. Galeas Veliz will share her love and knowledge of the art of cross stitching and guide young participants through completing a simple stitch design. All levels of skill are welcome and beginners with no cross stitch experience are encouraged to participate. The class is designed to teach the basics of cross stitching and participants are invited to take home their completed project. All materials are included with $25 workshop admission. May 10 & 17 - Threadless Pine Needle Basketry Children aged 11 and up can visit Randall Museum May 10 and 17 for a two-day workshop to learn techniques for coiling, at Corona Heights, searching for San Francisco’s diverse avian creatures. Participants are encouraged to bring their own binoculars on this two-hour excursion, geared for beginning to intermediate birders, in order to catch a glimpse of several habitats on the museum’s campus, each of which is enjoyed by different bird species. Meet in the Randall Museum’s Parking Lot at 199 Museum Way in San Francisco at 8 a.m. on Saturday, May 17, to join the flock. Every Saturday in May - Meet the Animals In addition to a rotating list of art and science workshops, the museum also offers popular yearround exhibits open to the public throughout the week. The Museum’s live animal exhibit, Wild in California, offers an up-close glimpse of California’s natural wildlife. Resident animals at Randall Museum include Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, and a longtailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Lyra and Scarlet have been rehabilitated by staff and are now animal ambassadors for the museum. At 11:30 a.m. every Saturday in May, visitors can join an open discussion about the museum’s wildlife ambassadors and learn more about resident creatures and the staff who care for them. Visitors of all ages will have the opportunity to meet some of the animals up-close and are encouraged to ask questions to learn more about California’s native wildlife. Photo courtesy of Randall Museum Take a cross stitch workshop at Randall Museum on May 3, moderated by the museum’s science and nature program coordinator and cross stitch enthusiast Katherine Galeas Veliz. weaving, and shaping a basket using traditional but lesser-known methods and materials. The class is designed to guide basket makers of all skill levels through the fundamentals of weaving a pine needle basket, from preparing the natural, locally-sourced pine needles to shaping and finishing a unique creation to bring home. Participants will also learn about the cultural and historical significance of pine needle basketry at this two-day immersive workshop that’s perfect for middle school aged children. Both workshops begin at 12 p.m. Cost is $65 per person for both workshops which includes all materials. May 17 - Birding the Hill Randall Museum’s birder-in-residence guides museum visitors on the third Saturday of each month through the hill Photo courtesy of Randall Museum Meet animals up-close and learn more about them from resident zoologists every Saturday in May.
articles.title: Randall Museum offers arts, science workshops for kids throughout May

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oaktown Jazz Workshops’ Performance Ensemble The Oaktown Jazz Workshops’ Performance Ensemble performs live this Friday at OMCA. The Oaktown Jazz Workshops’ Performance Ensemble takes the stage at Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) this Friday, May 2, with a dynamic group of young musicians performing a mix of jazz classics alongside professional master musicians and alumni youth mentors. The event launches OMCA’s “Friday Nights” series next month. “Friday Nights” is a free community-gathering evening event series held every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Oaktown Jazz Workshops, founded in 1994, is a non-profit, community based, cultural education organization dedicated to passing on the tradition of jazz music to young people and elevating the next generation of professional musicians and educators. Musicians performing this Friday are aged 14 to 18. The Oaktown Jazz Workshops Performance Ensemble regularly performs at local events including Oakland’s Art and Soul Festival, The Oakland Symphony’s Independence Day Celebration, and The Port of Oakland’s Community Day in Jack London Square. At 5:15 p.m., drag performer Per Sia will read If I Built a School by Chris Van Dusen. In this imaginative book, a boy creates his dream school from classroom to playground, offering fun for the whole family and especially young children. Per Sia is one of the originators of the famed Drag Queen Story Hour in San Francisco, and she currently works as a head teacher for first grade at an after-school arts program in the city. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live jazz music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-oaktown-jazz-workshops-performance-ensemble/ to learn more. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony’s popular “Lights, Camera, Music!” series, featuring a film screening accompanied by live orchestra, continues with Peter Jackson’s fantasy-adventure saga Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers May 8 through 10. The sequel to the Golden Globe-nominated The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers follows the continuing quest of Frodo and the Fellowship to destroy the One Ring. The musical score for The Two Towers was composed, orchestrated, and conducted by Howard Shore, who also composed the music for the other two films in the Lord of the Rings series. The sequel’s score features music performed by the London Philharmonic Orchestra, London Voices, the London Oratory School Schola and several vocal and instrumental soloists, including soprano Isabel Bayrakdarian and Irish fiddler and violinist Dermot Crehan, who also played the Hardanger fiddle with Rohan themes. Ludwig Wicki conducts the symphony with musicians accompanied by the Pacific Boychoir Academy. Cocktails and light refreshments inspired by the film will be available for purchase at the Davies Symphony Hall bar. Thursday, May 8 and Friday, May 9 performances begin at 7:30 p.m.; Sunday, May 10 performance begins at 2 p.m. Ticketing is limited. Visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/lord-of-the-rings to purchase tickets. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Symphony Rings: The Two Towers.
articles.title: SF Symphony performs Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers score May 8 - 10

articles.text: A large-scale exhibition featuring digital artwork by Yuan Goang-Ming, one of the foremost Taiwanese artists active in the international media art scene, is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through July 7. Goang-Ming is considered a pioneer of video art in Taiwan and has worked with the digital art medium since 1984. He received the Hsiung-Shih Art Award for the Best New Artist for his video and sculptural work Out of Position (1987) when he was still in art school in 1988. He went on to receive a master’s degree in media art from the Academy of Design, Karlsruhe Germany in 1997 and has exhibited internationally across Asia, Europe, and America since. The Asian Art Museum exhibition Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War features numerous works that debuted in GoangMing’s critically acclaimed exhibition representing Taiwan at the 60th Venice Biennale. The largescale exhibition is displayed in the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion and is the artist’s first North American solo show. “The generational anxiety of this artist known as the ‘father of Taiwanese video art’ offers a timely message,” said Abby Chen, curator of contemporary art at the Asian Art Museum. “As Yuan strives to locate a sense of home and belonging, his visions of an unstable world convey a relatable yearning for safety and peace.” A free docent-led tour of Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War will Yuan Goang-Ming be held tomorrow, Thursday, May 1, at 5 p.m. No advance reservation is needed. To join the tour, meet at the exhibition entrance on the ground floor at 5 p.m. Admission to Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War is required. To learn more, visit https:// exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/everyday-war/. Photo courtesy of Asian Art Museum Everyday War, 2024, by Yuan Goang-Ming (b. Taipei, 1965). Single-channel video with sound; 10:33 min.
articles.title: Tawianese video artist Yuan Goang-Ming exhibition now on view at Asian Art Museum

The event launches OMCA’s “Friday Nights” series next month. “Friday Nights” is a free community-gathering evening event series held every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Oaktown Jazz Workshops, founded in 1994, is a non-profit, community based, cultural education organization dedicated to passing on the tradition of jazz music to young people and elevating the next generation of professional musicians and educators. Musicians performing this Friday are aged 14 to 18. The Oaktown Jazz Workshops Performance Ensemble regularly performs at local events including Oakland’s Art and Soul Festival, The Oakland Symphony’s Independence Day Celebration, and The Port of Oakland’s Community Day in Jack London Square. At 5:15 p.m., drag performer Per Sia will read If I Built a School by Chris Van Dusen. In this imaginative book, a boy creates his dream school from classroom to playground, offering fun for the whole family and especially young children. Per Sia is one of the originators of the famed Drag Queen Story Hour in San Francisco, and she currently works as a head teacher for first grade at an after-school arts program in the city. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live jazz music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-oaktown-jazz-workshops-performance-ensemble/ to learn more. articles.text: 1883 (Season 1), is an extraordinary, richly produced episodic origin series that is, from the opening introductory scenes, relentlessly engaging, wonderfully cast and superbly acted, the writing and the photography inspired. We soon come to realize that episodic storytelling can transcend the familiar two-hour cinema format, which has, for more than a century, defined the movie-going experience. The series is set during those early post-civil war years when the nation and its denizens are just beginning to recover from the trauma and loss of what was a lethal and divisive Civil War. The opening scene is of a man, Shea Brennan (Sam Elliot), sitting alone on the porch of his farmhouse, lost in grief. He goes inside, carries his lifeless daughter (small pox we assume) upstairs, places her on a bed next to her deceased mother, and grimly returns to the front of the house and throws a kerosene lamp through a window. He stands back watching all that he cares about consumed by fire. The narrative then cuts to Ft. Worth, Texas, 1883, referred to as “Hell’s Half Acre,” the wide dirt street, bordered by stores, a saloon, is teeming with hardscrabble people, wagons, horses, all seeming on the verge of chaos and lawlessness. It’s there that we’re introduced to James Dutton (Tim McGraw), arriving alone in Ft. Worth in a covered wagon. His appearance is frayed, heavily bearded, well armed, clearly not intimidated by what he sees. He’s in Ft. Worth to await the arrival of his wife, Margaret (Faith Hill), teenage daughter, Elsa (Isabel May), and young son, John (Rick Audie), arriving by train from Tennessee. We soon learn that the Dutton family intends to travel by wagon West in search of land and a new life. Circumstances lead to James meeting Shea (aka Captain, his rank in the Union Army), and reluctantly agrees to travel with but not join Shea’s wagon train, comprised of Slavic and German immigrants, their wagons laden with all that they possess, and incapable of understanding what the journey before them will entail. At their core all they know is that they will never, no matter the cost, return to the repression Gratiela Brancusi, Sam Elliott and LaMonica Garrett in 1883

articles.text: Batyste Fleurial and Dorian Le Clech in A Bag of Marbles The film, A Bag of Marbles, is based on the memoir/novel by Joseph Joffo. It is 1942 in German occupied France during WWII. At the story’s center are two young Jewish brothers, Joseph (Dorian LeClech) and Maurice (Batyste Fieurial) Joffo. The narrative begins with preteen Joseph, sitting on the concrete steps of a library, examining his much cared for collection of marbles kept in a cloth bag. It is late winter and he is waiting for Maurice. When Maurice, the older of the two, finally arrives, the two cross a busy Paris street and stop at their father’s barbershop. Smiling, they purposefully stand in front of a sign in the window that says that the shop is for Jews only. Unaware, two German officers enter and ask for a trim. The boys follow. For their mother Anna (Elsa Zylberstein) and father, this ominous directive hastens the decision that it is time for them to leave Paris. articles.text: Pom Poko is an unusual film perhaps best suited for older tweens, teens, and adults. Its audience may be those who find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that has, for decades, been the signature of Studio Ghibli. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poko is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. If there is a weakness it resides in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine, thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog, with huge pouches (aka testicles). These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting in which they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals). The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, on the outskirts of Tokyo, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes in 1990 when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the warlike chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous but often lack focus, and are, on occasion, leavened by slapstick. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and even kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. Pom Poko. Directed by Isao Takahata. Animé from Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. Released in 1994. Streaming on prime/MAX/apple tv/Fandango.
