articles.text: Ewan McGregor in Christopher Robin Christopher Robin is a live-action/animated fantasy film inspired by the books of A.A. Milne, replete with the iconic illustrations of E.H. Shepard. If I had to select an ideal age for this movie I would pick older kids and tweens, despite the strong animated opening. The tale begins with a young Christopher Robin in 100 Acre Woods with his friends Winnie the Pooh, Piglet, Tigger et.al. The lad is about to leave for boarding school, and the gang is giving him a farewell tea party. Christopher comforts Winnie (Jim Cummings), reassuring the honey-loving bear that he will never forget him. And so begins the transition from animation to live-action. As it turns out, the boy has a difficult time in school, his father unexpectedly dies, and he soon puts the 100 Acre Woods behind him. He grows up (now played by Ewan McGregor), marries an architect, Evelyn (Hayley Atwell), has a daughter, Madeline (Bronte Carmichael), and serves in WWII. After the war, he finds a demanding job with Winslow Luggage Co. as an efficiency expert, working long hours while increasingly neglecting his family. In other words, Christopher is losing perspective, putting his work before everything else, including a promised family vacation. This commitment to his job takes the story to that one day when Christopher is sitting on a bench in London’s Langdon

articles.text: The séance is about to begin. Please join us. We don’t need a medium nor a trance. There will be no dark shadows – just the pleasure of memories. April 21st is the anniversary of the victory by Sam Houston in the battle of San Jacinto. Every history student knows the name Sam Houston. As a leader, he was first class in the military, and as an able politician. He was also an excellent diplomat, and he enjoyed a good reputation in business also. Biographies of him list his allies as well as his victories over his enemies. Likewise, the names of his friends are also listed. Strangely, one of his most important allies is never mentioned. One of the things that made Sam Houston so adept was his skill in finance; he sought healthy business aspects for his fledgling republic of Texas. It was in finances that he connected Sam Houston with a German named Heinrich Franz Fischer. Born in Germany, he was from the same generation as Sam Houston. Before Fischer arrived in Texas, he traveled throughout Europe, acquiring business expertise, and he became an excellent linguist. When he arrived in Texas, he Americanized his name to Henry Francis Fisher. Curiously, there were many, many generations which had the same name. I was fortunate to know the last of these men. He was born in Houston in 1889 and died in Santa Monica in 1964. This last Henry Fisher lived by the beach and so he was known as Henry Fisher Del Mar. He became one of the finest violinists anywhere. In addition, he was a living history book and a great storyteller. Along the way, he became a friend of the noted race car driver Barney Oldfield. This guy was one of the great characters of all time. His accomplishments included being the first person to drive a race car faster than 60 miles an hour. That was a great accomplishment in the early 1900s. His flamboyance established racecar driving as an important sport. He never won the Indianapolis 500 but that hardly mattered because everybody in the country knew Barney Oldfield driving the Peerless “Green Dragon” at Lakeside Track in San Diego, California, in April 1907

Henry Fisher Del Mar spoke of his friendship frequently. This connection resulted in a collection of classic automobiles including an Auburn, a Cord, and a Stutz. Around 1906 the entire Fisher family moved to Berlin where Henry studied at the Berlin Hochschule, the outstanding conservatory in all of Germany. Young Henry Fisher was enrolled in the class of the illustrious Joseph Joachim. The person who made the greatest impression on him was the Spanish virtuoso violinist Pablo de Sarasate (1844-1908). He spoke of him very often during my violin lessons. His words of wisdom made a big impression on me. For example, Sarasate was asked “how can you play so fast?” The great violinist responded: “I keep my fingers directly above the strings. Another thing, keep your movements to a minimum.” These words of advice are marvelous. The young generation would serve itself much better if they would remember what Sarasate said. The wonderful memories remain vivid. Looking back on it, I remember the stories of the great musicians and of Barney Oldfield. Despite Henry Fisher’s fabled historical past, he never mentioned his famous predecessors in Texas. Our séance is coming to a close. Immerse yourself in an intimate concert featuring favorite Festival Opera artists, set against the backdrop of the beautiful Piedmont Center for the Arts. Revel in the company of fellow opera lovers, patrons, and artists, as we sip wine, sample sweet and savory treats by Siren Sisters Kitchen, and share in the magic of live performance. The Spring Soirée promises to be a memorable experience, a gathering of minds and hearts with the power of music. The event will feature an exciting array of silent and live auction items to bid on, as well as a paddle raise in support of Festival Opera. Don’t miss this opportunity to witness the human voice in its most vibrant form and celebrate the launch of our 2025 season. pages.text: Wednesday, April 30, 2025 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Linda Dog Run By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group likes to go to places of interest around town, and last week there were a couple of things on the west side of town to see. They decided to see the Linda Park Off Leash Dog Area that is being closed and the Linda Pickleball Courts that are being resurfaced. There was a big turnout of 54 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday to check them out. However, before the group went off to see these places, they had a special, pre-walk event. Piedmont’s sidewalks are often uneven and sometimes dangerous. Walker Peggy Shultz is a physical therapist and 30 minutes before the group’s regular start time she shared strategies and actionable items to maintain stability and keep the walkers from falling. She followed these thoughts with some simple fall prevention exercises. The City Council had been considering the closure of the Linda Beach Off Leash Dog Area. City staff had been contacted by the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board on February 6th about a complaint regarding soil and animal excrement washing down the city’s storm drains. It could have cost the City as much as $66,000 per day in fines if this issue was not addressed. The Linda Park Off-Leash Area was designated by a City ordinance in December 2000. It was often closed during periods of heavy rainfall when the soil became muddy and unstable. According to City staff, the area’s sloped hillsides may never have been a good fit for dogs. Staff had recommended the City Council approve the area’s permanent closure, and the council members voted unanimously on April 7th to move forward with it. A second, final reading was on April 21st, the Monday before the group’s walk last week. The Council did pass the closure, and the ordinance will go into effect in 30 days. Some walkers spoke against the closure and the group was interested in seeing the area. Additionally, the Piedmont Public Works Department began a project to resurface and restripe the Linda Pickleball Courts on April 7th. The project will repair and restripe the courts’ surface and remove two trees whose roots were causing uneven surfaces. The courts will be closed for about two months and should reopen this summer. They are across Linda Avenue from the dog area and the walkers could see both on their walk. Continuing up Oakland Ave. the walkers came to the Linda Park Trail with the closed dog area. Chuck Oraftik told the group that this trail was once part of the Key System 11 Train Line route and right-of-way. The 11 went from Oakland Avenue to Piedmont Avenue during the first half of the 20th Century. The group then had a conversation about the City’s closure process and possible dog run alternatives. It was noted that the Dracena Park dog run is getting a lot of use by large dogs and showing wear on its slopes. The closed Linda Park area’s hillside appeared to have been hydro seeded with fertilizer to protect the soil from further erosion and get vegetation growing on the bare ground. The walkers went up to Linda Avenue, passed a big bed of beautiful California lilac and California poppies in the park, and started down Linda. They passed Beach School students on the playground and crossed Linda to get a closer look at the Pickleball resurfacing project. At Grand Avenue the walkers went to the crosswalk at lights at Fairview Avenue. They returned to the Exedra via Dale Avenue, Nova Drive, and a safe climb up Magnolia Avenue after sidewalk inspections of three City projects and excellent fall prevention suggestions from Peggy Shultz. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu to register or contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: The Indie Next List has fresh reading recommendations every month. Check out their newest iteration of hot-off-the-press literature recently published by respected writers. The Indie Next List of new releases is curated by independent bookstore owners and staff of only new releases. April’s list has extra helpings of Science Fiction and Historical Fiction. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. Wild and Wrangled: Rebel Blue Ranch #4 Paperback, Romance “I have been so eager for Dusty and Cam’s story, and this delivered the perfect ending to the series. Dusty is the definition of the perfect man written by a woman, and witnessing their relationship finally come to fruition was worth the wait.” —Amy Dickinson, Book Ends Winchester, Winchester, MA Say You’ll Remember Me Romance “Once again, Abby Jimenez brings us a love story we can root for. There’s always something more to her romances than just the romance. Jimenez puts just as much care and thought into the rest of the story, giving the reader so much more to savor.” —Layne Van Boxtel, Reads by the River, Waterford, WI Heartwood Schuster, Fiction “Heartwood is a mesmerizing novel that captures the precariousness of being alive. articles.text: New York Life Insurance Company and New York Life Insurance and Annuity Corporation The first image that often comes to mind when people think about long-term care is an elderly person sitting alone in a depressing nursing home. The misconceptions about what longterm care involves and peoples’ images of the most common care settings are understandable, since long-term care insurance originally started as nursing home insurance four decades ago. However, it has evolved into a much more flexible solution that allows you to receive care in a variety of settings. Most of us want the ability to age at home, in a familiar setting surrounded by family and our favorite things. The fact is, 90 percent of adults who need long-term care services receive assistance at home or in another community setting.1 If the level of care you need evolves over time, most longterm care insurance policies not only allow you to transition to a nursing home, but some may also provide you with support during the transition. Since you can’t predict the care you might eventually need, it’s important to have the flexibility to choose the setting that best fits your needs at any given time. Many long-term care policies available today can provide you with a choice of where you want to receive care, including: • At home, with the help of a home health aide or in some cases a family member or friend to assist with daily activities • In a community setting, such as adult day care services • At an assisted living facility, where you can receive help with transportation and meals • In a nursing home, if you need around-the-clock care Each of these options provides a different level of care depending on how much assistance you need. Receiving care at home is the most popular and preferred option, and some policies even provide benefits that allow you to make home modifications that can help you stay at home longer. Policies that provide home care allow you to receive care from a professional, or possibly a friend or family member if informal care is covered. While most people hope they won’t ever need to worry about long-term care, the reality is Americans have almost a 70 percent chance they will need some type of long-term care assistance after age 65.2 Women are even more at risk, primarily because they tend to live longer. The thought of not being able to care for yourself can be difficult and creating a strategy for care can be daunting. However, it’s best to not let long-term care preparation get pushed aside, because your age and health both factor into whether you’ll qualify for insurance and how much you’ll pay for coverage. have the peace of mind that you’ve taken the steps to help protect your family from the financial and emotional impact of a long-term care event. Take the time to research available options, decide how much coverage you need based on estimated costs, and create a strategy that will give you the flexibility to choose where and how you receive care. articles.text: On their latest excursion, the Piedmont Seniors ventured to the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek to enjoy The Neil Diamond Concert Experience, starring Rob Garrett, otherwise known as “The King of Diamonds.” Garrett, a longtime Las Vegas performer and Legends in Concert alumnus, captured the presence, passion, and energy of the iconic Neil Diamond in all his glory. Garrett has performed everywhere from Las Vegas to Honolulu, New York to Berlin, and has been a Neil Diamond tribute artist for more than 30 years. He and his top-notch show band took a break from their full-time Las Vegas residency to bring their award-winning show to venues across the country. His tribute to the legendary singer was unparalleled as he belted out favorites like “Sweet Caroline,” “Hot August Night,” “Cracklin’ Rosie,” “I Am...I Said,” “Song Sung Blue,” and many more live-in-concert hits. After the performance, the Piedmont Seniors headed to Peony Garden restaurant in Walnut Creek, where they enjoyed a variety of family-style Chinese dishes to satisfy every appetite. The service was outstanding, with each server extremely attentive and eager to please. All in all, it was a delightful outing for a lucky group of seniors! To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors and their activities, including monthly meetings, or to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors’ Coordinator, Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov or call 510/420-3070 for more information. pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, April 30, 2025 Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama, I’m about to get a new laptop, and I want to get all the information from my old Mac to the new. Is it something that I can do myself? Or is it something that I need professional help to do? I’m pretty savvy with technology, but I’m no expert. Goeff, Piedmont Dear Geoff, If you’re feeling up to it, you can absolutely set up your new Mac yourself—and if you run into trouble, AppleCare can walk you through it at 1-800-275-2273. I’ll explain one of the easiest ways: using Migration Assistant. First, place your old Mac and your new Mac next to each other. Make sure the old Mac is powered on, connected to Wi-Fi, and ideally plugged into a power source. Then, turn on the new Mac. As you go through the setup assistant, you’ll choose your language, your country, and either enable or skip accessibility options. You’ll connect to your Wi-Fi network, enter the password, and accept Apple’s privacy notice. Soon, you’ll reach a screen asking if you want to transfer information to this Mac. Choose the option to transfer from a Mac, Time Machine backup, or startup disk. Now it’s time to open Migration Assistant on your old Mac. You’ll find it in the Applications folder, inside the Utilities folder. Open it, click Continue, and enter your computer login password (the one you use for downloads, not your Apple ID password). Then select “Transfer to another Mac.” If you have a Thunderbolt cable—and the right adapter if needed—you can connect the two machines directly, which will make the process much faster. If not, using Wi-Fi works too, although it will be slower. On your new Mac, you should soon see your old Mac appear. Select it. A six-digit code will show up on both screens; check that they match and click to confirm. You’ll then see a list of information you can transfer, such as your applications, documents, and settings. In most cases, you’ll want to leave everything selected. Click Continue, and the migration will begin. If you have non-Apple software, you’ll need to re-enter your login information afterward (e.g., Microsoft Office, Adobe Creative Cloud). You may also need to re-enter your email passwords. The transfer can take anywhere from a couple of hours to most of the day, depending on how much data you have and whether you are using a cable or Wi-Fi. Once it’s finished, your new Mac should look and feel a lot like your old one. If you are transferring from a Time Machine backup instead, the process is very similar. Plug in the backup drive when prompted, and Migration Assistant will recognize it and guide you through selecting the most recent backup. Some people prefer to skip transferring everything and set up their Mac fresh, especially if their old computer had glitches or other issues. If you use iCloud, you can easily restore your contacts, calendars, photos, documents, passwords, and bookmarks by signing in with your Apple ID. You would then need to manually reinstall any non-Apple software, like Microsoft Office, Chrome, or Zoom. This method gives you a clean start, although you will need to manually move over anything not stored in iCloud, such as a music library. Each approach has its pros and cons. If something goes wrong during the migration, you can restart and try again. And even if you didn’t purchase AppleCare, Apple provides free phone support for the first few months after buying a new Mac. And of course, if it ever feels overwhelming, you can always call the MacMama! Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: It’s never too soon nor too late to start thinking about your future. Visualizing your future and planning for it are certainly within your control. Small steps taken today help make your big plans happen. If you’ve followed my blogs, you might remember that whenever we travel, we take the time to explore the local real estate market—whether by touring homes or engaging with local experts. Real estate is not just a hobby for us; it’s a passion that has been part of our lives for nearly 35 years, and it never gets old. I often tell homeowners and buyers that it’s never too early to plan for the future. Last October, we scheduled a ski trip for March. At the time it seemed so far in advance, but as time passes, we realize just how quickly the days fly by. And March came before we knew it. If we hadn’t booked the trip when we did, we would have missed the ski season entirely. Planning for your future life goals, vacations and real estate alike, it’s never too early to educate yourself, plan, and set goals. Whether you’re buying, selling, moving up, downsizing, or relocating, initiating the conversation early is key. Just as we booked our ski trip in advance, ensuring we enjoyed the slopes this season, the same principle applies to real estate—timing is everything. Whether you’re looking to buy or sell tomorrow or in the foreseeable future, we’re here to provide guidance. We offer complimentary evaluations and home audits, including insights on system enhancements and cosmetic upgrades. Feel free to reach out to schedule a personal consultation. I assure you’ll gain valuable insights from our 35 years of experience, and we’re eager to help make your next chapter as smooth as possible. Join us for our upcoming Presentation and Workshop on Saturday, May 10th, from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. at 342 Highland Avenue, in Piedmont. Professional service providers will discuss their areas of expertise, sharing how they can assist seniors and their families as they transition into the next exciting phase of life—whether that’s aging in place gracefully or finding the ideal senior community filled with activities and support. Here are five key takeaways you can expect from the workshop: 1. Understanding the current real estate landscape for seniors. 2. Strategies for home modifications to enhance comfort and accessibility. 3. Insights into various senior living options and communities. 4. Tips for navigating the emotional and logistical aspects of moving. 5. Resources available to support seniors and their families during transitions including financing, long term care insurance and estate planning. pages.text: Wednesday, April 30, 2025 27 Small steps taken today help make your big plans happen By Debbi DiMaggio It’s never too soon nor too late to start thinking about your future. Visualizing your future and planning for it are certainly within your control. Small steps taken today help make your big plans happen. If you’ve followed my blogs, you might remember that whenever we travel, we take the time to explore the local real estate market—whether by touring homes or engaging with local experts. Real estate is not just a hobby for us; it’s a passion that has been part of our lives for nearly 35 years, and it never gets old. I often tell homeowners and buyers that it’s never too early to plan for the future. Last October, we scheduled a ski trip for March. At the time it seemed so far in advance, but as time passes, we realize just how quickly the days fly by. And March came before we knew it. If we hadn’t booked the trip when we did, we would have missed the ski season entirely. Planning for your future life goals, vacations and real estate alike, it’s never too early to educate yourself, plan, and set goals. Whether you’re buying, selling, moving up, downsizing, or relocating, initiating the conversation early is key. Just as we booked our ski trip in advance, ensuring we enjoyed the slopes this season, the same principle applies to real estate—timing is everything. Whether you’re looking to buy or sell tomorrow or in the foreseeable future, we’re here to provide guidance. We offer complimentary evaluations and home audits, including insights on system enhancements and cosmetic upgrades. Feel free to reach out to schedule a personal consultation. I assure you’ll gain valuable insights from our 35 years of experience, and we’re eager to help make your next chapter as smooth as possible. Join us for our upcoming Presentation and Workshop on Saturday, May 10th, from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. at 342 Highland Avenue, in Piedmont. Professional service providers will discuss their areas of expertise, sharing how they can assist seniors and their families as they transition into the next exciting phase of life—whether that’s aging in place gracefully or finding the ideal senior community filled with activities and support. Here are five key takeaways you can expect from the workshop: 1. Understanding the current real estate landscape for seniors. 2. Strategies for home modifications to enhance comfort and accessibility. 3. Insights into various senior living options and communities. 4. Tips for navigating the emotional and logistical aspects of moving. 5. Resources available to support seniors and their families during transitions including financing, long term care insurance and estate planning. Meet The Presenters: • Debbi DiMaggio, DiMaggio Betta Group, Corcoran Icon Properties | Real Estate Advisors for the Generations • Kimberly Sweeney, Moving Angels, Certified Senior Move Manager, Collectibles Advisor • Liz Lummis O’Neil, New York Life Insurance Company (Long Term Care Insurance) • Isaac Kim, Wealthy Management | Tax Deferred Exchange • Esther Kestenbaum, Preferred Placement • Mele Shavers | Authentic Home Care (Aging In Place) • Zach Griffin, Mortgage Consultant • Shane Barnard, Estate Planning Attorney Sponsored By: Dylan Sanders, AMS Relocation | Bekins Moving Company, Experts in Moving Older Adults We look forward to seeing you there! He discussed strategies and tactics used by autocratic regimes, the necessity for accurate information and a well-informed public, and many more topics that would be featured in his future book. Bleich also offered an informal lesson on the history of Machiavelli’s The Prince to provide background during his talk. Machiavelli’s book, a sort-of manual on ruling through fear and an iron fist written in an “extraordinarily brutal form,” was used by Bleich to provide insight to modern political problems – including the nationally-covered El Salvador deportations, the blanket pardon of January 6 insurrectionists, and dramatic increases to violent threats against public officials (particularly those who disagree with the president). Ending on a message for Piedmont High School’s Senior Class, Bleich stressed that America only has a democracy for as long as its people can keep it. Bleich was the guest speaker at the high school’s graduation ceremony in 2022. “It’s up to them,” said Bleich about the youth of Piedmont. “If they are good citizens, if they take their civic duties responsibly, if they do things like this… and have that kind of engagement on civic affairs, then we’ve got a fighting chance.” “All it takes is a protester holding up a sign, you know. articles.text: Tonight’s school board meeting, April 23, at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall, is likely to put in motion many impactful changes for the school, including approval for layoffs and changes to curriculum. The meeting is open to the public and can be participated in via zoom at https://us06web. zoom.us/j/84656989857. Of considerable public interest on the agenda will be the board’s recommendation for changes to music, performing arts and foreign language programs at elementary and middle school levels. The board is seeking approval of a full year of foreign language (World Languages) for 7th graders. The board also plans to recommend the following for the next school year: 60 minutes a week for 4th Grader in Theater Arts; one hour a week for 5th Graders in Arts, Band, and Orchestra. The Performing Arts Planning Committee is referring to next year as a “bridge year,” with a team using the time next year to help build a permanent plan for subsequent years. These changes will be up for board approval. “Fifth grade students will have the same number of hands-on instrumental music minutes in 5th grade that they currently have in 4th and 5th grade combined due to the amount of time required to transition, set up, and take apart instruments,” the board document states. “The class size of the instrumental music groupings will also be reduced by half; two music teachers will allow for more individualized feedback.” A presentation will be made with an update on the district’s work on Diversity Equity Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB). The work includes numerous Restorative Justice Circles at all school levels and the training of 68 students to lead group Circles. The growth of the affinity mentorship program is seen as a bright spot in the district’s work. During tomorrow’s school board meeting the district will finalize the layoffs of two veteran Human Resource Managers, Suzanne Binder and Kimberly Randlett. In the board background document, the district states they “either did not request a hearing or specifically waived their right to a hearing.” Although not on tomorrow’s agenda, community members, parents and students are likely to speak at the start of the meeting to challenge a March 27 decision by Athletic Director Tyler Small to not renew the contract of Dan Chubbock, the high school girls’ soccer coach for 17 years.

articles.text: At its meeting on Monday, April 21, Piedmont City Council approved an ordinance that will permanently close the Linda Park Off-Leash Dog Area. After listening to public comment from several impassioned residents, City Council voted unanimously to close the Off-Leash Dog Area. The Ordinance will go into effect 30 days after the decision. The topic was brought forward quickly when City Staff was contacted by the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board on February 6, regarding a citizen complaint about Linda Park’s Off-Leash Dog Area. The complaint, raising concerns about soil and animal excrement washing down the City’s storm drains, could cost the City as much as $66,000 per day in fines if it does not take action to address the Water Board’s request. The Off-Leash Area was designated by City ordinance in December 2000, and is often closed during periods of heavy rainfall when the soil becomes a risk to park-goers. articles.text: The fourth annual Piedmont Food Fest brought more than 1500 guests, and a dozen food trucks from the larger Bay Area together for an idyllic afternoon of music, food, and fun on Saturday, April 19. Sunshine greeted everyone in Piedmont Park, and the accompanying breeze made the afternoon a runaway success in bringing a bountiful multi-cultural celebration to Piedmont. Seven vastly differing musical acts and performances took the main stage in the park, requiring a schedule to get it all in. People from all over the Bay Area were able to grab all sorts of food originating from kitchens across the globe and then sit and enjoy an equally diverse array of entertainment, from acapella rap to Tahitian dance and jazz. Food Fest founder Roger Tsai had his fingerprints all over the event, from acquiring performers and sponsorships down to the website and marketing. “It’s about learning and discovering new things and being able to enjoy that with one another,” said Tsai. “We’re perfectly situated in the Bay Area to host.” Tsai gave credit to the many volunteers who helped make Picnic blankets cover the grass in Piedmont Park under the Magnolia tree at Food Fest 4.
articles.title: Food Fest 4 puts Piedmont on the map

articles.text: Editor: It has been several weeks since the Piedmont Post reported on the firing of long time Piedmont High School girls soccer head coach Dan Chubbock. Many parents of current players have written to school administration to petition for his reinstatement, only to be told that “much thought” has been put into the decision- making process and will stand as is. How much thought could that have been if key stakeholders in the program – the current varsity players and their parents – were not consulted? In addition Athletic Director Tyler Small commented to some players who spoke to him the day of the firing that Coach Chubbock created a “negative team culture.” This was a very disrespectful comment to make, considering that there was no consultation with those closest to the program. I don’t know the motivations of AD Small. Perhaps he has certain plans for PHS athletics and this is the first step, but getting rid of a successful, well-liked coach and justifying it with unsubstantiated issues is not the way to go cancer research. articles.text: Editor: I have known Coach Dan Chubbock since my first year with Piedmont Soccer Club in elementary school. He is a coach who truly cares about his players and always wants them to succeed. Dan made my years on the varsity so memorable, and I will cherish the time I got to play for Piedmont High School forever. He is caring, always smiling, and makes every practice fun. He truly created the most positive girls’ high school soccer environment I’ve heard of. Dan led us to win the. North Coast Section championship in 2023 and tp second place in League the next year. He never stopped believing in us. That is why we were competitive against the state champions Archbishop Mitty and how we beat O’Dowd with a last-minute senior night goal last year. Dan has been here for 17 years. He built the competitive reputation of the girls’ soccer program. It saddens and shocks me to know he was let go without notice or discussion with the players. He is such a key part of all our communities. In no way did he deserve this. I know I will miss him, and so will the rest of the team. –Eliza Hammond
articles.title: Dan Chubbock a winning coach who cares

articles.text: Editor: Coach Dan Chubbock’s commitment and dedication have been the foundation of Piedmont High School’s girls’ soccer team’s success over the past 17 years. During my two years on varsity, he made my high school soccer experience even more meaningful and memorable than I could have imagined. He always brought positivity, laughter, and a competitive spirit that pushed us to grow and succeed. Regardless of the outcome of our games, Coach Dan had a unique ability to make us better on and off the field. It saddens me that the team culture and soccer program that Dan and many players have built over the years may not exist next year unless he is brought back. Being a part of the Piedmont High School soccer team has truly been one of my favorite parts of high school, and I am disappointed that our school felt the need to change it. Bring back Coach Dan. –Elia Kwong PHS Junior
articles.title: We want coach Dan Chubbock

articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) will hold a community meeting on Wednesday, April 30 at Havens School Library at 7:00 p.m. Everyone is invited to attend. The meeting will be an opportunity to discuss the recent attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion. Businesses such as Google, Target, Walmart, Meta, and Uber have rolled back their initiatives. Schools have been threatened with funding cuts if they don’t end their programs. And people are being targeted because of the color of their skin, gender, religion, beliefs, and immigration status. Additional opportunities to learn about the Draft Specific Plan are planned in the coming months, including presentations to the City’s Park Commission and Recreation Commission. Multi-family Housing in Moraga Canyon The Draft Specific Plan details development locations, site improvements, and infrastructure requirements for the construction up to 199 units of new housing on City-owned land in Moraga Canyon, 60 of which would be affordable to lower income households. The document anticipates development of multifamily residential buildings between 4 and 6 stories and includes two options for where these buildings could be co-located – either on the north side or the south side of Moraga Avenue. It includes 10 chapters, each one addressing a single topic in detail, with subjects ranging from overall site vision to circulation and traffic safety improvements to building and landscape design. The final chapter outlines an implementation strategy and options for project financing. The City Council is expected to consider adoption of the Specific Plan in fall 2025, following a recommendation from the Planning Commission. Submit comments online, by email, or by mail. Community members can offer comments on the Draft Specific Plan: • online at piedmont.ca.gov/ MCSPComments • by email to MoragaCanyonNews@piedmont.ca.gov • by mail to: Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Residents can learn more about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan and view video and materials from past meetings and events at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP. The City of Piedmont has released a public review draft of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, a housing plan that provides space for 199 new housing units in Piedmont. Community members can now review and share comments on the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP. New Moraga Canyon housing helps meet requirements for the City’s Six Cycle Housing Element Implementation. The Housing Element, required by state law, was adopted by the city in March 2023. The Housing Element requires the city to plan for new housing based on state guidelines, although the city is not responsible for the housing’s construction. The product of study and community engagement beginning in summer 2023, the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan outlines a vision for a new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon that would: • bring new housing to Piedmont, creating opportunities for people of all income levels • enhance recreational amenities through an expanded sports field and new hiking trail

articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department is putting on their Pop-up Putt Putt in the Park event in the Community Hall parking lot this Sunday, April 27, from noon to 4:00 p.m. Community members are welcome to play a free round of mini-golf in an all-ages course of City-created and community-created holes. Last year’s inaugural course drew more than 400 people to play mini-golf in the park and enjoy the Spring weather. This year, residents are encouraged to enjoy a picnic in the park, check out a Mobile Golf Simulator sponsored by ACE Kids Golf, and dance to music by a DJ. The 18-hole pop-up miniature golf course features a mix of holes designed by the City and the community. Community holes will be awarded with prizes for: Best overall, most creative, most clever, and best use of recycled materials. Families enjoy a mix of City-created and community-created holes at the 2024 Putt Putt in the Park. Children play at community designed courses at last year’s Putt-Putt event. An online petition with more than 300 signatures called for not closing the area, An in-person petition was presented with over 75 more signatures, and several residents voiced their concerns to the City Council. “As a taxpayer, I happily voted for the $7 million bond for schools and the $20 million bond for the pool. So not checking in and saying ‘it’ll cost this much’ just seems, frankly, rushed,” said resident David Hsu at Monday’s Council meeting. Following confirmation of the closure, Public Works staff will move forward with hydroseeding of the hillside, an erosion control measure that forms a protective shell over the soil, allowing vegetation to begin to regrow. Concurrently, the City plans to soon begin a sustainability and stewardship evaluation of all City parks and open spaces. This study will examine current management practices and existing park uses, including off-leash dog areas, with the aim of developing recommendations for how to best meet the community needs throughout Piedmont. “I know this is not the result that many of you wanted to hear this evening,” said Mayor Andersen after the vote to close the park. “As Councilmember Ramsey said, please participate in the upcoming review of sustainability in all our parks as that will include a dog component.”

articles.text: While you may already be familiar with small personal conservation actions, like recycling and turning off the lights, we know that sustained, lifelong action is more closely tied to individuals who see themselves as part of nature. Forging your nature identity starts with listening and observing, science skills that California Academy of Sciences educators are fostering in youth locally and nationally. Gregg Castro, cultural director for the Association of Ramaytush Ohlone in San Francisco and one of the Academy’s Indigenous partners, shares how this manifests in his community, “Native people see things in aggregate, in a network, in relationship to each other. We aren’t apart from nature, either. That’s a fundamental viewpoint that we’re working on with the Academy,” he said. “You can’t detach yourself from nature. You’re a part of it. So why don’t we just dive in, and learn what it means to be a part of that network?” The Academy’s Student Education Program is doing just that, shaping positive science identities and fostering community connections for nearly 70,000 K-5 students in San Francisco and throughout the US with hands-on field trips and interactive distance learning webinars each year. In the Academy’s backyard of Golden Gate Park one such program encourages students to listen to the environment and share what they hear. Equipped with their senses and a small bag containing the same scientific tools used by Academy biologists in their field work, the students set out. And there’s so much to observe: from the Redwoods that line their walking path to the great horned owls and coyotes regularly spotted in the nearby meadow. Academy educators encourage students to appreciate breathing in the same air as our tree “neighbors,” and highlight how humans are in relationship with nature by urging students to see humans, plants, and animals as sharing the same habitat. During hands-on exploration, students express awe, surprise, focus, and excitement upon uncovering even the most miniscule of insects, often feeling attached to the creatures they observe. Students leave the program with a new way of looking at the natural world and the knowledge that they can observe it anywhere, all they have to do is listen. Listening is highly critical in shifting your perspective and building a relationship with nature, but is often overlooked. The good news is you can start from anywhere. From April 25-28 the global community science event City Nature Challenge provides an excellent opportunity to explore and document the natural world wherever you are, from backyards to beaches and everywhere in between. Grab a friend or simply step outside with your curiosity– the natural world awaits. Solitaire Miguel us an Education Specialist with the School and Youth Programs at California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park Educator Lindzy Bivings leads an elementary school class in nature observation and exploration in the Academy’s outdoor Wander Woods classroom.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom You are nature – Growing a lifelong relationship with the natural world

Tickets are also available online at Phsdanceconcert.ludus. com/index.php Mackenzie Seto-Nguyen Photo by Julie Reichle Thinking Outside the Classroom You are nature – Growing a lifelong relationship with the natural world By Solitaire Miguel While you may already be familiar with small personal conservation actions, like recycling and turning off the lights, we know that sustained, lifelong action is more closely tied to individuals who see themselves as part of nature. Forging your nature identity starts with listening and observing, science skills that California Academy of Sciences educators are fostering in youth locally and nationally. Gregg Castro, cultural director for the Association of Ramaytush Ohlone in San Francisco and one of the Academy’s Indigenous partners, shares how this manifests in his community, “Native people see things in aggregate, in a network, in relationship to each other. We aren’t apart from nature, either. That’s a fundamental viewpoint that we’re working on with the Academy,” he said. “You can’t detach yourself from nature. You’re a part of it. So why don’t we just dive in, and learn what it means to be a part of that network?” The Academy’s Student Education Program is doing just that, shaping positive science identities and fostering community connections for nearly 70,000 K-5 students in San Francisco and throughout the US with hands-on field trips and interactive distance learning webinars each year. In the Academy’s backyard of Golden Gate Park one such program encourages students to listen to the environment and share what they hear. Equipped with their senses and a small bag containing the same scientific tools used by Academy biologists in their field work, the students set out. And there’s so much to observe: from the Redwoods that line their walking path to the great horned owls and coyotes regularly spotted in the nearby meadow. Academy educators encourage students to appreciate breathing in the same air as our tree “neighbors,” and highlight how humans are in relationship with nature by urging students to see humans, plants, and animals as sharing the same habitat. During hands-on exploration, students express awe, surprise, focus, and excitement upon uncovering even the most miniscule of insects, often feeling attached to the creatures they observe. Students leave the program with a new way of looking at the natural world and the knowledge that they can observe it anywhere, all they have to do is listen. Listening is highly critical in shifting your perspective and building a relationship with nature, but is often overlooked. The good news is you can start from anywhere. From April 25-28 the global community science event City Nature Challenge provides an excellent opportunity to explore and document the natural world wherever you are, from backyards to beaches and everywhere in between. Grab a friend or simply step outside with your curiosity– the natural world awaits. articles.text: In his final year of teaching fourth graders at Wildwood School, Martin Lewis took his students on a final field trip to explore the early California mission in Sonoma. Twenty-six students in Lewis’ class carpooled with parent chaperones to learn about California History at the mission on April 1. Lewis’s class visited General Vallejo’s house and stable to start the trip. A state park docent presented information about General Vallejo and how the Mexican government gave him 66,000 acres of land, and how he lost it all when it was taken over by Americans. The class also walked by the military barracks that Vallejo built on the way to visit Mission Solano, where a park ranger provided a tour of the chapel and told them the history of how it burned down and has been rebuilt over the years. The docent also described life as a native person working for the mission. A plaque outside the mission lists the names of people who died while working at the mission. If a name has an asterisk next to it, it was the name of a child. Lewis asked students to remember a name and write it down on a piece of paper once back in their classroom, to remember the kids. After lunch students enjoyed playing in the Sonoma Plaza. Students read the plaque of a statue in the plaza that describes the history of the bear flag and how California was once its own country for 25 days in 1846. Lewis has been teaching at Wildwood since 2007 and will retire at the end of the school year. Photos by Carolyn Pan 4th grade students explore General Vallejo’s home. articles.text: Kids will have a chance to climb up in Public Works’ trucks, complete a tree-themed art project, and possibly win a new book to take home at Piedmont’s annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration tomorrow, Thursday, April 24, from 4:00-6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The annual event, which dates back to 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. This year’s event will feature: • Public Works big trucks: Works staff uses daily in their work to keep Piedmont’s trees and public spaces healthy and beautiful. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the trucks. • Arts & crafts: Park Commissioners will be on hand to assist little ones with their creations. • Owl naming contest: A photo exhibit and naming contest will highlight raptors living in Piedmont Parks, including a nesting pair of great horned owls that have taken up residence in Dracena Park. Community members can share name suggestions online in advance at piedmont.ca.gov/ DracenaOwls. • Raffle: Kids can enter to win a Lego set or children’s book related to Arbor and Earth Day themes. New this year, a raffle for adult attendees will offer an opportunity to take home a California native plant for your garden. • Electric leaf blower demos: Gas powered leaf blowers are not allowed in Piedmont, but clean, quiet electric alternatives can get the job done. Attendees can try one for themselves at the event. The event will also include informational tables from the Piedmont Fire Department and the City’s Sustainability Division. 2025 Heritage Trees announcement The Arbor Day celebration will also feature the announcement of the current winners of the Heritage Tree designations. As many as five new trees in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces will join the 30 existing Heritage Trees. The winners will be announced at the event tomorrow. The Heritage Tree program, now in its seventh year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. This year, the City received nine nominations for Heritage Trees. This year’s trees were nominated by: • Cameron Wolfe, Jr. & Karen Sullivan: Island Oak (Quercus tomentella) in Mountain/Bellevue traffic circle • Tom Ramsey: Oak tree at Community Pool construction site • Dick Carter and Walking on Wednesdays group: Southern magnolias on Artuna Avenue adjacent to lower Dracena Park • Jack and Sharona Fischrup: California buckeye in Dracena Park • Shari Fujii: Plum trees lining Huntleigh and Lexford Roads • Lisa Gardner and David Hitchcock: Crepe myrtle in front of 1053 Harvard Road • Justin Zucker: Cherry trees on Lake Avenue in front of Beach Elementary School • Mary Louise Morrison: Redwood trees behind the bleachers at Coaches Field • Anonymous, in honor of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation: Flowering chestnuts along Highland Avenue (an early PBF project) For more information contact Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont. ca.gov. articles.text: Highlanders establishing selves as the comeback kids Piedmont’s baseball team swept its two-game series with Alameda, beating the Hornets 5-1 in Alameda on Wednesday, April 16, and winning a thrilling 8-7 game in walk-off fashion at Humphries Diamond two days later on Friday, April 18. PHS also hosted Oakland Tech on April 19 and lost 13-6. Piedmont’s walk-off win over Alameda came down to Diego Delventhal with two outs and the bases loaded. Working it to a 3-2 count, including fighting off a pair of pitches with foul tips, Delventhal hit the ball high off of the fence to bring in Michael Martin from third with the winning run. “I wasn’t going to strike out there. I was just battling and trying to get my pitch. He threw me Staff Photos Diego Delventhal roars after slugging the walk-off win against Alameda. Will Parker had eight hits in the last three games. Piedmont players celebrate the game-winning run in its 8-7 win over Alameda. an inside fastball and I turned on it,” Delventhal said of the moment. It became another late-inning comeback by Piedmont. They defeated Acalanes 7-5 on February 28 after trailing 5-4 in the sixth inning. PHS was also behind 4-3 to Encinal in the fifth inning before winning 8-5 on March 27. They trailed HeadRoyce 5-3 entering the bottom of the sixth inning before winning 7-5 on April 9. “I have a short memory as a coach; we just take it one at a time. Whenever you’re in that situation, it’s desperation. We were going to make sure that we didn’t bail them out by swinging at bad pitches. We just tried to keep the line moving with quality at bats,” said coach Eric Olson. “Our goal was to get the first guy on base and Markos [Lagios] did a great job of that. We faced their pitcher before and knew he was kind of wild. He walked a few guys, made some mistakes, and we kept hitting the ball hard,” senior Will Parker added. The pair of wins improves Piedmont’s record to 12-5 overall and 3-1 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division teams. Beating Alameda means the Highlanders are one game behind Castro Valley (4-0) in the race for the league championship for a second consecutive year. Piedmont faces Castro Valley this week for a two-game series on April 23-25. “It’s a good win. We swept Alameda last year and it’s important to do it again. We’re on the right track; we just have to keep rolling,” Delventhal said. “They way I see it, we can only lose three league games. Last year, we barely won league after going 7-3. So, we know we can’t lose many games. Every game is important,” Parker mentions. 5-1 win over Alameda The game was scoreless until Piedmont tacked on one run in the top of the fourth before piling on four runs in the top seventh. Final stats: Delventhal went 1-for-2 with one RBI and walk. Markos Lagios went 1-for-2 with a double, one run, and walked twice. Parker went 2-for-4 with one RBI and a run. Shafer Dando went 1-for-4 with an RBI. Michael Martin went 1-for-2 with a run and stolen base. Jack Meyjes went 1-for-3 with an RBI and a walk. On the mound, Will Ferreira pitched 6.1 innings for four strikeouts and allowed one earned run. 8-7 barnburner over Alameda Piedmont scored two runs in the bottom of the third inning and led 4-1 after the bottom of the fourth. Alameda tied with three runs in the top of the fifth and led 7-4 the following inning. Piedmont scored four runs to win it in the bottom of the seventh. In the game-winning bottom seventh, Lagios and Parker smacked back-to-back singles, and then Dando drew a walk to load the bases. With one out, Michael Martin hit a hard grounder that ate up the second baseman, reaching on an error and scoring Lagios. Jordan Vo was then hit by a pitch to score Jimmy Lagios, who entered as a pinch-runner for Parker—making it 7-6. Ferreira then walked to score Dando, tying it at 7-7. Delventhal stepped to the plate with two outs. After two foul-tips in a 3-2 count, Diego turned on a pitch to slug the ball to the right field wall. Martin jogged home for the game-winning run. Final stats: Delventhal went 3-for-5 with a double, two RBIs, a stolen base, and scored a run. Markos Lagios went 1-for-3 with a run. Parker went 3-for-4 with an RBI. Dando went 1-for-2 with a run, RBI, and a walk. Martin had a run and RBI. Ferreira had an RBI, run, and two walks. Jonah Cha-Foster went 3-for-4 with two runs and an RBI. 13-6 loss to Oakland Tech Piedmont scored three runs in the bottom of the first and led 4-2 after the bottom of the second, but the Bulldogs scored five runs in the top of the third and never relinquished the lead. PHS added single runs in the bottom fifth and seventh. Final stats: Delventhal drew four walks and scored three runs. Lagios went 2-for-3 with a double, RBI, and run scored. Parker went 3-for-4 with three RBIs and two runs. articles.text: Miguel Long continued his strong senior season, winning the 2025 Del Campo Multi-Meet decathlon. Piedmont High senior Miguel Long continued his breakout season by winning the decathlon at the 2025 Del Campo Multi-Meet on Friday and Saturday, April 18-19. His score of 5,369 points topped the next-best athlete, Tim Libell of Bella Vista, by nearly 300 points. Long becomes the second PHS student to win the event after Parker Terrill won the same decathlon with a score of 5.964. Terrill went on to become the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2022. “I’ve been patiently waiting for Miggy’s hot streak to slow down but he just keeps going. He wants to get onto a great college team while also making it to the state meet, so we’re trying to find a balance between getting tons of reps and workouts in for his triple jump while also training him beyond the bare minimum for all decathlon events,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Competing in a field of 19 athletes at Del Campo, he won the long jump with a distance of 21 feet, 3 inches, won the high jump with a leap of 6 feet, .75 inches, and won the 110 meter hurdles in 16.69 seconds. Long also finished second in the 100 meter dash in 11.58 seconds, was third in the 400 in 55.36 seconds, third in the discus with a distance of 89 feet, 3 inches, and tied for third in his pole vault debut in 10 feet. He was also impressive in the shot put, placing fourth at 35 feet, 3 inches, and was fourth in the 1500 in 5:14.13. He was seventh in the javelin toss, recording a distance of 86 feet. “Training both depth and breadth when he only has so much energy and when we only get so much access to certain facilities is tough. He’s giving everything he can so we hope it all works out,” Assadi said. WACC League Meet Piedmont also competed in a WACC Meet at Mt. Eden in Hayward on Wednesday, April 16. PHS faced Alameda, winning both girls’ and boys’ meets. The boys’ team won eight events on the afternoon. Sam Shelby won the 200 in 22.84 in a field of 27 runners. Eric Venner won the 400 in 53.89 against 17 other runners. Sebastien Swain won the 3200 in 9:52.46 in a field of seven athletes. PHS’ 4x400 team of Venner, Shelby, Dean Olliphant and Maddox Ma won in 3:38.81 against two other teams. Gus Von Metzsch won the shot put with a distance of 38 feet, 4 inches against 13 athletes. Colby Hong won the discus in 105 feet in a field of 15. Long won the high jump in 6 feet 2 inches against nine others and the won the triple jump in 40 feet, .5 inches in a field of five. The girls’ squad also won eight events throughout the day. Caroline Taylor won the 1600 in a field of 13 with a time of 5:42.33. Amalia Gray won the 3200 against one other athlete, clocking a 12:34.87. Nia Kim won Miguel Long totaled 5,369 points to win the Del Campo decathlon. He becomes the first since Parker Terrill in 2022 to win the event for Piedmont High.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team came out of last week with two wins in three Western Alameda County Conference matches. They defeated Castro Valley 5-2 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Tuesday, April 15 and swept Hayward 7-0 at home the next day, but lost to Berkeley 5-2 at the Berkeley Tennis Club on Thursday, April 17. The Highlanders had to compete without several starters, including No. 2 singles starter Nate Welch and doubles starter Kasper Jansson, who were traveling with the school robotics team to the national championships in Houston. “We didn’t have Nate throughout the week due to the big Robotics event in Houston and we were a little handicapped against Berkeley because Kasper also went. Still, we got revenge on Castro Valley and had chances to win against Berkeley,” coach Jim Landes said. Their victory over Castro Valley avenged an early-season 4-3 loss to the Trojans, while Piedmont came narrowly close to turning things around against Berkeley with two three-set matches. The Berkeley match came down to the last matches on the courts. Will Tenney battled at No. 3 singles. After losing the first set, he won the second and forcing an extra game in the third, but lost 6-2, 4-6, 7-5. Staff Photos Lucas Smolko reeled in wins over Berkeley and Castro Valley at No. 1 singles. At No. 1 doubles, Gianluca Bini and Luca LaForte similarly lost the first set, won the second, but couldn’t find the same momentum in the third, falling 6-2, 5-7, 6-2. “Willie played a very good match. After splitting the first two sets, he dug too deep a hole in the third and had to come back from 5-2 down. He played some great offensive tennis then, approaching the net almost every point and tied it up. But at 5-all, he ran out of gas and lost the next two games. Luca and Gianluca also had a very long contest losing the first but coming from behind to win the second before going down in the third. They played great at times but couldn’t sustain it long enough,” Landes said. 5-2 loss to Berkeley Berkeley won the first three matches of the day to establish some momentum.. Nick King lost at No. 2 singles 6-0, 6-4, Torsten Olsen and Ryan Ehtashami fell 6-2, 6-3 at No. 3 doubles, and then Hunter Fasteau and Robert Piniella lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 2 doubles. Freshman Emilio Misra brought home Piedmont’s first win of the day at No. 4 singles, winning in straight sets 6-2, 7-5. Tenney then fell in his close three-set match, 6-3, 4-6, 7-5 to give Berkeley its clinching fourth win. After Bini and LaForte lost 6-2, 5-7, 6-2 at No. 1 doubles, Smolko finished the day with a clean 6-1, 6-0 win at No. 1 singles. Will Tenney had a heated three-set loss against Berkeley. Gianluca Bini hits a forehand against Berkeley. He played at No. 1 doubles against Berkeley and No. 2 doubles versus Castro Valley.
articles.title: Piedmont wins 2 of 3 league matches; loss to Berkeley mars clean sweep

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team had a victorious week with consecutive wins at Witter Field, defeating Acalanes 15-4 on Tuesday, April 15 and Rancho Cotate 18-9 on Thursday, April 17. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 8-7 overall with one match left in its regular season. The Highlanders’ win over Acalanes was against a Division 2 North Coast Section foe, while Rancho Cotate plays in Division 1. The games were led by the strong performances of Peyton Watson and Friedie Schickedanz against Rancho Cotate with six goals apiece in both games. The pair often combined to win possession out of the face-off circle, accounting for nine victories on the draw. “Rancho Cotate was a signature win for the girls. Peyton Watson probably played one of her best games - Friedie set up 50-50 balls for her on the draw circle and Peyton just beat her opponent to the ball time and time again,” said PHS coach Carlton Chan. “The girls probably played their cleanest game of the year with few turnovers, patience on offense, and great defense,” explained Chan. Piedmont will travel to Miramonte in Orinda for its regular-season finale tonight, April 23. With a 4-1 league record, PHS goes into the Western Alameda County Conference tournament with the No. 2 seed and will host No. 3 Berkeley in the first round of post-season playoffs on Wednesday, April 30. The Highlanders defeated Berkeley 10-8 on March 28. With a win against Berkeley, the Highlanders will likely face arch rival Bishop O’Dowd for the league title for a second straight year on Friday, May 2. Piedmont has been designated as this year’s championship hosts. 15-4 win vs. Acalanes; 11-0 at halftime Piedmont held Acalanes scoreless in the first half and went into halftime holding a commanding 11-0 lead. With the large advantage, PHS was able to kill the clock in the third and fourth quarters, scoring three goals and one respectively. PHS established a 6-0 lead through the first quarter, includStaff Photos Peyton Watson scored six goals against Acalanes and Rancho Cotate. ing three goals by Watson, two goals by Chloe Graham, and one by Schickedanz. They added five more in the second quarter with two by Watson and three consecutive by Schickedanz before halftime. Schickedanz, Watson, and Graham scored three more in the third, while Schickedanz got Piedmont’s final goal of the game. Final stats: Watson scored six goals, won seven draws, and scooped one loose ball. Schickedanz had six goals, won five face-offs, and gathered one ground ball. Graham had three goals. Goalie Sophie Santander recorded six saves. 18-9 win over Rancho Cotate Piedmont jumped out to an 8-3 lead in the first quarter and Friedie Schickedanz also scored six goals.
articles.title: Piedmont bashes Acalanes & Rancho Cotate

articles.text: Staff Photos Ian Nguyen (left) and Connor Fredericks celebrate a goal. Nguyen scored three goals, Fredericks scored twice and won nine face-offs. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team split its last two matches on the road against upper Division 1 North Coast Section opponents. They recently defeated Dublin 9-3 on Monday, April 21, and lost 7-3 to Rancho Cotate in Rohnert Park on Saturday, April 19. The team has two regular season matches left before the Western Alameda County Conference tournament on Wednesday, April 30. With a game with University tonight, April 23, and Novato on April 25, Piedmont has played all of its league matches and concludes its WACC schedule with a 3-1 record. Given the No. 2 seed in the four-team bracket, PHS will face rivals Bishop O’Dowd at Witter Field on April 30. PHS recently defeated O’Dowd 8-7 on April 4 on a last-second goal by Timmy Kalamas. 9-3 victory over Dublin Piedmont held Dublin without a single goal until they scored all three of its goals in the third quarter. PHS led 2-0 through the first quarter and 4-0 by halftime. They made it 7-3 in the third quarter, while adding on two more goals in the final going. It actually took Piedmont a bit to get on the board, not scoring its first goal until 1:34 remained in the opening quarter when Ian Nguyen sent in a shot. PHS made quick work to make it 2-0 with Connor Fredericks winning the faceoff, leading to long stick midfielder P.J. Brayer rocketing in a shot just 30 seconds later. In the second quarter, Fredericks scored after a minute and a half to give PHS a 3-0 lead. Kalamas later scored with 2:37 left. Dublin scored its first goal 22 seconds into the third quarter, but PHS responded by Fredericks winning the faceoff followed by Nguyen scoring just 10 seconds later. Dublin scored the next two goals to make it 5-3 with 7:24 left, but it was the last time they got on the board. From there, Nguyen scored again with 6:42 left and Fredericks scored with 5:38 left—7-3. In the fourth, Brendan Divine netted one with 7:04 left, while Kalamas got the game’s final goal with 4:58 on the clock. Final stats: Nguyen scored three goals and gathered two loose balls. Kalamas scored twice and had one assist. Fredericks scored twice, logged an assist, two ground balls, and won nine face-offs. Brayer scored once and grabbed three ground balls. Goalie Gus Von Metzsch had six saves. 7-3 loss to Rancho Cotate Piedmont trailed 3-0 through the first quarter and 6-1 by halftime. PHS scored twice in the third to make it a 7-3 deficit, while both teams went scoreless in the fourth. Final stats: Fredericks, Devine, and Nguyen scored individual goals. Brayer had one assist and gathered three loose balls. Von Metzsch logged nine saves and three ground ball recoveries. articles.text: Piedmont High swimmers brought serious energy to a high-intensity meet against Berkeley, with the varsity boys sweeping every event in a 100–70 win. “Overall, the meet was exciting and fun,” said Head Coach Adrien Downey. “The team seating was a little cramped and old-school, but we had front-row seats to the action, and the cheering and energy was a lot better.” Though the varsity girls lost 105–64 and the JV boys fell 106–40, Downey emphasized the strong individual performances across the board. “Our varsity boys created a lot of momentum right out of the gate in the first relay, and sustained it by winning every single event of the meet,” Downey said. “Asher Takazawa gave us an early lead in the 200 medley relay with a lifetime best in the 50 back, then dominated the 200 IM and 100 back. Cole Carnazzo showed even more reasons why he’s one of the most versatile and reliable swimmers in the conference. His wins in the 100 fly and 500 free were not only impressive performances in themselves, but he beat Berkeley’s fastest swimmer which helped secure the team victory for us.” JV boys also impressed: “Zayd Mahmood, Dean Kvoriak, Rylan Patty, and Theo Ferguson all showed major speed improvements. They held their own against a much deeper squad.” On the girls’ side, Downey noted the team stepped up under tough circumstances. “All our girls swam varsity to cover injuries and illness, and they stayed focused. Cynthia Wu had her best meet of the year, giving us a chance in the medley relay with her excellent backstroke, plus wins in the 50 free and 100 back. Abigail Jacoby raced smart and with heart, and came back with a dominant 100 free after a tough 200 IM. Isla McCardell swam several great races, but none more exciting than her upset victory in the 100 breaststroke win.” Piedmont faces Castro Valley on Friday in their final dual meet before WACC and NCS. Goff placed 100th of 326 athletes in Cadet Men’s Foil by winning four of six pool matches and winning one match in the direct elimination round before losing in his second showing. Of his pool matches, Goff closed with a win over a “hard” rated opponent. He finished 198th of 358 in the Junior Men’s Foil event, winning three of six pool matches before losing in the direct elimination round. He defeated one “hard” rated opponent in his pool matches. Goff has racked up 40 wins this year with just 19 losses, giving him a sterling win ratio of 69.8 percent. “Nathaniel ran into a really high seed but had a good Junior Olympics. He’s doing well, he comes here for tournaments and then returns to the UK,” explained Piedmont coach David Sinkkonen. Kulkarni finished 210th of 232 in the Cadet Women’s Foil and 219th of 246. Despite losing her pool matches, she faced all “very hard” rated opponents and scored well in several matches. She is having an impressive year with 40 wins thus far, improving from 16 wins in 2023/2024. “Myra has really worked hard. She had a rough year last year, but her wins have gone up. She’s made a lot of improvement; I have high hopes for her,” coach Sinkkonen said. COZMX Fencing ROC/RJCC/ RYC Piedmont had several athletes represented at the Stockton event, including PMS 8th grader Maya Dvoiris, elementary students Nina Stock and Ian Stock, along with Piedmont home-schooled resident Eliot Schamp. Dvoiris was 27th of 62 in the Y-14 Women’s Foil category and 34th of 45 in the Cadet Women’s Foil event. In the Y-14 category, Dvoiris won three of six pool matches and won once in the direct elimination round before falling in her next match. Her direct elimination win was a 15-11 victory over a “very hard” rated opponent. In the Cadet event, she won two of five pool matches before losing in the direct elimination round. Dvoiris is also seeing an improvement in wins, already accomplishing 44 wins this year after finishing with 29 in 2023/2024. “Maya’s had a good year. She’s had some lovely results,” Sinkkonen said. articles.text: Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster, currently running at the War Memorial Opera House, presents four dynamic contemporary dance works from the oeuvre of Hans van Manen, the renowned Dutch choreographer. A modernizing force in classical ballet, Van Manen is known for his minimalist storytelling and maximal impact. Over a prolific career — he’s now 92 — Van Manen has created more than 150 ballets and worked with every major Dutch company, including Nederlands Dans Theater and Dutch National Ballet, where he remains a resident choreographer. The evening opened with Grosse Fuge, a physically demanding piece that explores gender roles and power dynamics, set to Beethoven’s stormy string quartet. Four pairs of dancers engage in a kinetic dialogue — dancing for each other, with each other, even against each other — and moving fluidly between defiance and surrender, assertion and ambiguity. The women, costumed in understated nude-colored leotards, seem to downplay the beauty traditionally associated with femininity. The men, by contrast, wear long, flaring black skirts that create a striking contrast with their bare torsos, emphasizing the force and sweep of their movements; midway through the piece, they tear them off to reveal black boxer briefs, their prominent belt buckles becoming points of visual tension, balance, and connection. After a sequence of gender-defined quartets and playful duets, the push-and-pull of attraction and rejection culminates in a sensual ensemble, each couple celebrating its presence in the world. It’s a technically demanding piece that requires not only individual precision but a deep sense of ensemble awareness. Jennifer Stahl and Max Cauthorn, Wona Park and Wei Wang, Nikisha Fogo and Aaron Robison, and Dores André and Fernando Carratalá Coloma delivered that rare combination of virtuosity and cohesion. Lighting design by Jan Hofstra was a particular delight, with a single neon line projected onto the backdrop, framing the movement in a stark, modernist glow. Photo by Chris Hardy Nikisha Fogo and Aaron Robison in van Manen’s Grosse Fuge The opening piece was followed by Variations for Two Couples, a 2012 quartet originally created for Dutch National Ballet’s 50th anniversary. Set to music by Benjamin Britten and others, the ballet continues Van Manen’s exploration of human connection, where choreographic focus is on relationship nuance. Frances Chung and Joseph Walsh danced alongside Jennifer Stahl and Adrian Zeisel, offering a compelling performance marked by a refined understanding of space and musicality. Classical lines gave way to idiosyncratic gestures—head bobs, prowling—that earned laughter from the audience. The beauty of abstract storytelling lies in its openness: we’re invited to write our own narratives, guided but never dictated by the choreographer’s intent. The third piece, Solo, offered a playful reprieve for those craving something more concrete. Set to the music of Bach, it’s a tightly structured work full of humor, energy, 0and rapid-fire exchanges. Cavan Conley, Victor Prigent, and Alexis Francisco Valdes tackled its virtuosic demands with style and wit. Dressed in slouchy purple shirts and grey tights, they bounded through cascades of pirouettes and lunges, their athleticism matched by an easy charm. The audience, clearly engaged, responded with spontaneous applause mid-phrase—a testament to the piece’s infectious spirit and the dancers’ crisp delivery. It was the perfect lead-up to the evening’s finale. 5 Tangos, the program’s final piece, was inspired by Van Manen’s visit to a flamenco performance in Madrid. Set to the music of Astor Piazzolla, it premiered in 1977 and hasn’t lost a bit of its edge. Dancers in bold red-and-black costumes set the tone immediately: drama, elegance, fire. A staple of contemporary ballet repertoires worldwide, 5 Tangos is both a crowd-pleaser and a masterpiece. Pointe shoes replace tango heels; Spanish inflections in Piazzolla’s score blend seamlessly with ballroom accents, creating a rich musical and physical tapestry. As in all Van Manen’s choreography, the emphasis is on movement — on the beauty of line, gesture, and spatial dialogue. Dores André and Esteban Hernández led the cast with elegance and intensity, while Thamires Chuvas, Kamryn Baldwin, Jihyun Choi, and their partners brought texture and variety to the ensemble. Esteban Hernández’s solo stood out as a highlight of the night: passionate, precise, and thrilling to behold. With its flair and poise, 5 Tangos brought the evening to a triumphant close, a celebration not only of Van Manen’s remarkable legacy, but of San Francisco Ballet’s depth, range, and contemporary spirit. Dores André and Esteban Hernández in van Manen’s 5 Tangos Photo by Chris Hardy

articles.text: Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts museums of San Francisco, is currently exhibiting more than 250 personal photographs by Paul McCartney in a never-before seen collection entitled Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm through July. The exhibition includes the Beatles’ songwriter and singer personal captures as well as video clips, archival materials and more that offer a behind-the-scenes look at the meteoric rise of one of the world’s most celebrated and popular bands. Images span December 1963 through February 1964 and chronicle the Beatles’ journey to megastardom. Photographs were taken by McCartney with a single-lens reflex camera, which were introduced in the 1950’s as part of a new generation of handheld cameras. Sally Martin Katz, Legion of Honor Assistant Curator of Photography, said that McCartney acquired the camera in 1963 at a time “when many were experimenting with this newly popularized medium.” “The technology of the 35mm handheld camera allowed for a spontaneity in picture-taking, leading to the emergence of a snapshot aesthetic that embraced imperfection,” Katz said. “McCartney’s pictures reflect this new spirit in photography, as well as the literal blur of travel that The Beatles were experiencing, rapidly moving from one place to another.” Katz added that the exhibition, which includes photographs printed for the first time, captures “Beatlemania in full force.” “They depict the frenzied crowds chasing the band down the New York City streets, for example, and the swarms of people greeting them at the Miami airport,” she said. “The Beatles were at the eye of the storm they created: thousands of eyes were looking to capture that storm, and McCartney, with his camera, returned their gazes.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/paul-mccartney-photographs to learn more. Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm exhibition display at Legion of Honor, San Francisco

articles.text: Guest speaker is former NYT Correspondent John J. Geoghegan Journalist John J. Geoghegan Treasure Island Museum welcomes former Special Correspondent for the New York Times John J. Geoghegan this Saturday, April 26, to discuss the mystery surrounding the “Ghost Blimp” that lifted off from the island in 1942 and was discovered off the shore of Ocean Beach with crew members missing. According to historical accounts, at 11:15 a.m., several hours after the airship lifted off from Treasure Island, it reappeared near Fort Funston and briefly made contact with the ground at Ocean Beach, causing damage to the airship. It then drifted over San Francisco and crashed on Bellevue Avenue in Daly City. No traces of the airship’s crewmen, Lieutenant Ernest DeWitt Cody and Ensign Charles Adams, have ever been found. Cody and Adams were declared legally dead in 1943, and theories regarding their whereabouts arose following the incident but have not been founded. Geoghegan, specializes in reporting on unusual inventions that fail in the marketplace despite being innovative, will offer findings based on research he conducted for his recent book When Giants Ruled the Sky: the Brief Reign and Tragic Demise of the American Rigid Airship. He served as an on-camera expert for a Smithsonian Channel documentary based in part on his research for When Giants Ruled the Sky. Geoghegan also served as a guest lecturer at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business, UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business and Kansas University’s School of Journalism and Communications. In this speaker series event, he recounts the “Ghost Blimp” story using rarely seen photographs and first-person accounts to explain the mystery surrounding the airship’s wreckage. The event begins at 10:30 a.m. at the Treasure Island Museum this Saturday, April 26. Attendance is free and open to all, but registration is recommended. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/ ghost-blimp-the-enduring-mystery-of-the-l-8 to learn more and register.. Treasure Island Museum
