articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will present its Spring Concert on Saturday, May 17, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. As part of YPSO’s 88th season, this concert marks the 36th season under the leadership of Maestro David Ramadanoff, whose dedication has shaped generations of young musicians. A native of Cleveland, Ohio, Ramadanoff studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony under Seiji Ozawa. With a distinguished career in music education, he remains deeply committed to nurturing young talent, carefully selecting programs that highlight the diversity of the orchestra’s musicianship and showcase works from a wide range of musical eras and composers. This season, YPSO’s talented ensemble of 80 musicians, ages 11 to 18, represents cities across the Bay Area, from Napa in the north to Fremont in the south. Concert details The evening will open with Mozart’s Magic Flute Overture, a piece full of brilliant energy and theatrical flair. A favorite among musicians for its precision and technical clarity, it is often performed as a test of an orchestra’s cohesion and dynamic control. For YPSO musicians, this piece has been a particular favorite this season for being both technically challenging and exhilarating to perform. YPSO will then showcase the winners of its annual Concerto Competition. This competition provides a unique opportunity for students to step into the spotlight and perform as soloists with the full orchestra. This season, three outstanding musicians earned the honor, and two of them, violinist Carolyn Ren and cellist Donghu Kim, will be featured. Carolyn Ren (violin) will perform Wieniawski’s Violin Concerto No. 2, Op. 22, Mvt. 3. a technically dazzling piece known for its playful character and virtuosic passages. Donghu Kim (cello) will perform Tchaikovsky’s Variations on a Rococo Theme, known for its wide range of colors and emotions. The concert will conclude with Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances, the composer’s final orchestral work. YPSO Annual Online Auction Fundraiser YPSO will launch its annual online auction, running from May 17–31. The goal is to raise $10,000 to support YPSO’s music education programs, scholarships, and outreach efforts, ensuring that high-quality orchestral training remains accessible to young musicians across the Bay Area. The auction will feature an exciting selection of items, including concert tickets, unique local experiences, fine dining gift certificates, musical instruments, and more. Community members are encouraged to participate and bid, directly supporting YPSO’s mission while taking home fantastic offerings. For more details, to donate an auction item, or to discuss sponsorship opportunities, please contact ypso@ypsomusic.org. Open Rehearsal As part of its tradition, YPSO invites community members to an open rehearsal on Friday, May 16 at the final dress rehearsal before the concert. Drop in anytime between 6:00 PM and 9:00 PM to experience the orchestra in action as they make final preparations for their performance. This event is open to prospective families, relatives unable to attend the concert, and teachers with young musicians interested in joining YPSO. Please register here: tinyurl.com/ypso-open-reh. Free student tickets are available for students with valid ID. Reserve tickets online at www. ypsomusic.org/events. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is California’s oldest youth orchestra and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra.

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts will host Festival Opera’s Spring Soirée, an evening of music and celebration inspired by the legendary Parisian musical salons of the past, on Saturday, May 3, from 4:00-7:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: Mark Morris Dance Group will perform Pepperland, with choreography set to the Beatles’ iconic album Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall May 9 through 11. Pepperland was created by artistic director and choreographer Mark Morris at the request of the City of Liverpool to kick off its Sgt. Pepper at 50 Festival in 2017. The work features an original score by composer Ethan Iverson inspired by the songs “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band”, “With a Little Help From My Friends”, “A Day in the Life”, “When I’m Sixty-Four”, “Within You Without You”, and “Penny Lane” off the studio album. “I was just a child [when the album was released]. As a very young person, I was dazzled and confused by the music. I loved it and I loved The Beatles,” Morris said. “Fifty years later, with contemporary eyes and ears, we are presenting a comment and a rethinking of this profound cultural artifact with all of the imagination, surprise, humor, and bizarrity intact.” Iverson joins the Mark Morris Dance Group performing on piano with an ensemble of musicians including Clinton Curtis (vocals), Sam Newsome (saxophone), Jacob Garchik (trombone), Chris McCarthy (keyboard), Rob Schwimmer (theremin), and Vinnie Sperrazza (percussion). Friday and Saturday performances, May 9-10, begin at 8 p.m. The Sunday, May 11 performance begins at 3 p.m. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 pm and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 pm. Pepperland premiered at the City of Liverpool’s Sgt. Pepper at 50 Festival.

articles.text: Before he made his debut directing Wind River, Taylor Sheridan was a screenwriter of considerable talent, known for taut storytelling and signature dialogue as demonstrated in the extraordinary Paramount+ streaming series 1883 and 1923. He also wrote screenplays for the film Sicario and the Oscar nominated Hell or High Water. Wind River, the name of an Indian reservation in Wyoming, proves to be a remarkable film. It opens with a teenage Native American girl (Kelsey Asbille) running across a snow-covered meadow with the dim glow of the moon. White- capped mountains are in the distance. She struggles, panic evident with every breath. She falls, and kneels, her gloveless hands clutching the snow. Her feet are bare, her only protection a blue parka. Finally, she falls and remains still, her lungs having frozen from the bitter and unforgiving cold, and she chokes on her own blood. She was running from something, desperate to escape. What caused her to flee to a certain death is the essence of this engaging story. She is discovered the next morning by U.S. Fish and Wildlife tracker Cory Lambert (Jeremy Renner) while hunting for a mountain lion that had been killing reservation livestock. articles.text: Amanda Peet and Dermot Mulroney in Griffin & Phoenix I recently came across Griffin & Phoenix, a film now streaming on YouTube. It looked interesting and I read the brief summary of the plot. I was familiar with the two actors, Amanda Peet, who I recalled is always memorable as is Dermot Mulroney. The film seemed interesting, and the opening scene has Griffin (Dermot Mulroney), late 30s, sitting across from a doctor who delivers a decidedly detached diagnosis: he has a constellation of cancerous lesions throughout his chest. In response to his questions, she grimly tells him that there is nothing that can be done to save his life. He has one, perhaps two years to live. Cut to Griffin sitting in a university class – the subject matter is death and dying. And it is in that lecture hall, with an uninspired professor standing at a podium, that he meets Phoenix (Amanda Peet). Suffice it to say, they meet cute. However, to go any further would be to deprive the audience of the opportunity to watch unfold what turns out to be an unexpected and moving love story carried by two superb actors. I will mention that the interaction between them is quick and well written and possesses an edge of humor and reparté that continues. Their relationship grows while exhibiting a touching chemistry. Griffin and Phoenix is extraordinary, deeply human, while never maudlin. Griffin and Phoenix. Directed by Ed Stone. Starring Amanda Peet, Dermot Mulroney, Sarah Paulson. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated PG 13. Released in 2006. Now streaming on YouTube.

articles.text: Ponyo, written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, is a visual treat, displaying a hand-drawn style that is reminiscent of early Disney, the colors vibrant while creating a soft, less delineated, yet pleasing effect. Ultimately the success of Ponyo, at least for an American audience, rests with its narrative, which is a tad convoluted, at least for younger moviegoers. At its center, the film is a love story between a young boy, Sosuke (Frankie Jonas), and a small fish, Ponyo (Noah Cyrus). When Sosuke rescues Ponyo from the sea (she is trapped in a glass jar), she falls in love with him and wills herself to become human. Her decision has countless unintended consequences, involving her father, Fujimoto (Liam Neeson), a King Neptune of sorts, and her mother, Gran Mamare (Cate Blanchett). And so the film spins off into a tsunami-like storm that results in Sosuke setting out, with Ponyo, to find his mother (Tina Fey). While Disney enthusiastically promoted Ponyo to American audiences as one more animated feature, it is, in sum, a much different film, different in tone and dialogue from the signature Disneyesque fare. In Japan, animation, also known as animé, is not just the province of children. Adults are completely taken with the genre, as they are with magna, which are illustrated stories, drawn in black and white. Magna comics can look like phone books, can be lengthy serials, and are read intensely by a broad spectrum of Japanese society. It is likely that Miyazaki had two audiences in mind when he wrote and directed Ponyo, resulting in a story that seems more slated for an older audience than children ages 6 to 9. Like most children’s films, it does end with a moral – value loyalty, love and family above all else. But these lessons are lost in the complexity of the dialogue and the plot, tilting the narrative toward a slightly older viewing audience. Ponyo. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With voices of Noah Cyrus, Liam Neeson, Cate Blanchett. Animation by Studio Ghibli. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated G. Released in 2008. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/MAX/apple tv/Roku. articles.text: Ruby Barnhill and Mark Rylance in The BFG The BFG (big friendly giant), based on Roald Dahl’s children’s book, proves to be a gentle, beautifully imagined film that captures the power of enchantment that only film can fully create, especially when crafted by director Steven Spielberg. Visually, it is wondrous to behold and with the aid of CGI, Mark Ryance (from Bridge of Spies) is transformed into an enormous giant whose face is deeply creased by smiles, possesses enormous ears, and eyes that capture the sparkle and joy of his job. He’s Merlin, an alchemist, a gentle soul who lives in an out-of-plumb house and visits, beneath a canopy of stars, the dream tree where he captures small whizzing stars/ dreams (not unlike Tinkerbell) and bottles them for later. It is a stunning scene, breathtaking in all aspects. And what does he do with those glowing, luminous stars? At night, when all are sleeping, BFG goes forth from giant land, stealthily visiting the city, and with his trumpet-like, spiraling horn, that has attached a bottle of captured dreams, he blows them, one at a time, into the mouths of kids and adults. It’s on one such outing that he is spotted by 10-year-old Sophie (Ruby Barnhill), a plucky, precocious orphan who climbs out of bed and stands on a narrow balcony staring at this enormous creature in complete disbelief. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Lisa Anne Gaston died on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. Lisa Anne Gaston, a wonderful wife, mother, grandmother, teacher and friend passed peacefully on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia, surrounded by her family and a few of her closest friends. Born on an Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi, and having lived in Atlanta for the past 36 years, Lisa Anne was known for her southern charm but was a true (and emphatic) California girl at heart. She spent her childhood in Piedmont, California, where she graduated from Piedmont High School in f 1975. The only child of two pioneering physicians – Dr. Harper Gaston, a dedicated cardiologist, who founded the Kaiser Permanente Southeast Medical Group, and Dr. Anne Gaston, one of the very first female, board-certified neonatologists – Lisa Anne was raised with wit, determination and a passion for learning. She pursued her undergraduate studies at Bryn Mawr College, where she majored in political science. Her years at Bryn Mawr were some of her most treasured. She cherished the century-old traditions and made lifelong friends, many of whom she remained in touch with all of her life. Never one to shy away from a challenge, she then moved to Washington D.C., earning both a Master’s Degree in Foreign Service and International Development, as well as a Juris Doctor in International Law and Legal Studies at Georgetown University. Lisa Anne’s professional journey was as diverse as it was impressive. She began her career practicing law in New York, California and Georgia. Once in Atlanta, she transitioned into television, where she became Vice President of Public Affairs at Turner Broadcasting. Her work creating “Interact Atlanta” earned her multiple Emmy Awards and paved the way for her eventual move to Georgia Public Broadcasting, where she was recognized as one of the “Women Making a Mark” by Atlanta Magazine. It was during her broadcasting years that she met her great love and husband of 25 years, Michael Reff. In the next chapter of her life, Lisa Anne discovered her truest calling: teaching. Earning yet another Masters Degree in Education from Agnes Scott College, she spent nine cherished years teaching English and Literature at Central Gwinnett High School. With a deep love for books and a passion for writing, she inspired her students to find confidence in their writing and empowered them to discover their own voice. She loved her students, and they loved her in return. In her final days, she received an outpouring of love and gratitude from many of her past students who shared the many ways in which Lisa Anne influenced and changed the course of their lives. Lisa Anne’s life was filled with adventure and travel with her husband, Michael, and her two daughters, Allison and Hayley Harper. She was known for her radiant smile, sharp intellect, and gift for finding joy and beauty in the everyday. She never hesitated to speak her mind, stood strong in her convictions, and moved through life with an unwavering sense of self and a deep belief in angels and the power of prayer. She loved her family, her two grandsons, and her golden retrievers. Lisa Anne was a fighter and despite a near 20-year battle with heart complications, maintained a positivity that was palpable to all she encountered. Her health challenges unfortunately pulled her away from the classroom and kept her adventures closer to home. These limitations never broke her infectious and indomitable spirit and in spite of them, she remained engaged with and even expanded her social community. Lisa Anne had friends far and wide and worked hard to maintain those connections, no matter the distance. Lisa Anne is survived by her beloved husband, Michael Reff, her two daughters, Allison Stalla (Zeid Stalla) and Hayley Swarbrick (Andrew Swarbrick), her two grandsons, Ben Stalla and Grayson Swarbrick, and many friends both near and far. Her life was a testament to the power of perseverance, the joy found in every moment, and the importance of loving deeply and boldly. She would be honored to be forever carried in the hearts of those who knew her. A funeral will be held at Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland on April 27, 2025 at 12:30pm, followed by a Continued Celebration of Life at Signature Studios in Roswell, Georgia on May 1, 2025 at 7pm. In lieu of flowers, the family encourages donations to Girls, Inc. of Greater Atlanta (www. girlsincatl.org), where Lisa Anne volunteered for many years.

articles.text: Wednesday, April 16 was the 7th anniversary of the Walking on Wednesdays group and it was celebrated by a record turnout of 70 walkers and six K-9 best friends at Mountain View Cemetery with a special walk. The walkers met in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum for a tour by Dennis Evanosky, a docent who has written two books on the history of the cemetery. He pointed out his “three girlfriends” right above them in mausoleum’s façade. They are statues of ancient Greek women that represent life and how well and long it is lived. pages.text: Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers celebrate 7th anniversary By Dick Carter Wednesday, April 16 was the 7th anniversary of the Walking on Wednesdays group and it was celebrated by a record turnout of 70 walkers and six K-9 best friends at Mountain View Cemetery with a special walk. The walkers met in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum for a tour by Dennis Evanosky, a docent who has written two books on the history of the cemetery. He pointed out his “three girlfriends” right above them in mausoleum’s façade. They are statues of ancient Greek women that represent life and how well and long it is lived. Evanosky noted the last one is holding a scissors. The cemetery’s main mausoleum was built in 1928 in a neo-classical design. Five buildings were added to this central section of the cemetery through 1933, but the cemetery’s history goes much further back. In the early 1860s a group of 12 businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and mayor of Oakland from 1867 to 1869, decided the area needed a private cemetery. Two public cemeteries existed, but they were not well maintained, and the group wanted something better for their own final resting places. In 1863 they bought 200 acres of fields “well out of town,” far from the center of Oakland at a cost of $13,000, and the Mountain View Cemetery was established. Twenty-six acres were added later for its current size of 226 acres. Evanosky told the story of renowned landscape architect Fredrick Law Olmsted, who designed the cemetery in 1863. Olmsted most significantly designed New York’s Central Park, as well as much of the UC Berkeley and Stanford University campuses. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. Actually, two Fredrick Olmsteds designed the cemetery. Olmsted created the original portion and his son, “Rick,” designed a second portion further up the hill in the 1940s. There are three types of cemeteries within Mountain View, the grand, old mausoleums of early times, the monuments and headstones for more common folk, and the later in-ground plaques that make grass cutting easier. The number of people buried in the cemetery is unknown. In the early days, poor people 26 26 Wednesday, April 23, 2025 Features were sometimes buried in unendowed areas and a Strangers’ Plot and not recorded. People of every race are buried at Mountain View. Plots initially ranged in price from $2 to $10, and the first burial was $8 for three spots. It is estimated there are about 180,000 graves in the cemetery with room for about that many more. The group went up the main road to “Millionaires’ Row,” which was not part of Olmsted’s plan. The walkers stopped at the large mausoleum of Edson Adams, for whom Adams Point near Lake Merritt is named. Then it was up the hill to the humble grave of Julia Morgan, the architect of Hearst Castle, Chapel of the Chimes, Berkeley City Club, and many Piedmont homes. She lived from 1872 to 1957, never married, and was buried with nine others in a family plot. Her name is just one of the ten on the marker. She wanted to be “quietly tucked away with my own.” Evanosky also said the young Julia’s family was on their way to Hawaii when they stopped in Oakland, found they liked it, and decided to stay. Millionaires’ Row is a section of the grandest, most elaborate crypts that house some of the cemetery’s most famous and wealthy residents. These were successful businessmen most of whom came to California around 1850. They did not use picks and shovels during California’s gold rush to make their fortunes but rather sold the miners items needed to mine for gold. The walkers were told the histories of Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli, and others. The group stopped in front of “Borax” Smith’s mausoleum which also houses his wife, Mary, and her friend Jane Sather, who had Sather Gate built in her husband’s memory as the entrance to the UC Berkeley campus. The walkers made their way back down the hill to their cars where they expressed their thanks to Dennis Evanosky for a most enjoyable, informative tour of a beautiful place on a special day. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Frederic Vignobles On a cool, misty morning, we set out from Santa Cruz and drove north on back roads. The fog draped the Coastal Redwoods as we wound our way through the tiny towns of Ben Lomond and Boulder Creek. We were heading for Rhys Vineyards, located on a ridge line in the northern most reaches of the Santa Cruz Mountain Appellation. RHYS VINEYARDS Rhys was founded in the 1990s by Kevin Harvey, an avid student of wine, enology, geology, and viticulture. He was intrigued by the idea of growing Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in meticulously selected sites which mirrored the terroir of Burgundy and making complex, Old World style wines. To ensure integrity with his vision, Rhys planted estate vineyards, most in the Santa Cruz mountains, from the ground up, bringing careful attention to rootstock, clone selection, and vine density. Rhys is 100% organic and dry farms its mature vineyards. It has a minimalist winemaking style - all in pursuit of making beautiful wines that express the unique essence of each estate vineyard. After several years of making highly regarded Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Kevin was inspired to take on a second project – bringing Italian varietals to Northern California with the same attention to terroir. He chose Nebbiolo, the red grape best known for Barolo and Barbaresco, and two lesser known varietals from the slopes of Sicily’s Mount Etna – Nerello Mascalese and Carricante. He found the optimal growing conditions for these varietals at Centennial Mountain. With vineyards at 2000’ elevation in the mountains of northern Sonoma County and 15 miles from the Pacific Ocean, Rhys’s sister winery is now blazing a trail for these Italian varietals. Rhys Centennial Mountain project Rhys makes a complex and lively Chardonnay. When we arrived, we were greeted by Rose Lacey, our knowledgeable and gracious guide, who then ushered us into the estate home adjacent to the underground winery and our tasting began. Sophie Sharabi grew up on the Mount Eden Estate.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School shield was designed in 1922. Piedmont is a small town with deep traditions. Here are three traditions that are over 50 years old. One of the long-standing traditions dates to the construction of the first Piedmont High School in 1921. The High School opened with an expected enrollment of 250 students. At the end of the first week, there were 360 students and 400 students by the end of the first semester. These students came from 14 secondary schools. In order to create a cohesive student body, the 1922 Clan-OLog – the year of the school’s first graduation class, tells us that the Rob Roy, as the school’s mascot, began in 1959. He appeared at each football game with the cheerleaders and pom-pom girls. This Scottish theme is still strong in many aspects of the school. The school’s athletic teams are called the Highlanders, sometimes Scots. T he 1924 Clan- O -Log describes the students’ thoughts on naming the first yearbook in 1922. “From the Scotch [sic], we have coined the word Clan-OThe Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling during halftime at a 1961 Piedmont football game. student body officers selected the school colors and the school motto. They also designed the school shield and created the Clan-O-Log that first year. They chose purple and white as the school colors. As noted on the High School’s website, “Royal purple symbolizes regality and suggests to all Piedmont students, the necessity of learning to rule their lives and ambitions by the mastery of their own thoughts and actions. White represents purity and suggests that true PHS students will strive to be pure in thought, speech, and act.” The student body officers then chose the school’s motto, “Achieve the Honorable,” meaning that all students demonstrate academic and personal integrity in their work. Students worked together to design the school shield with classic symbols of a winged sandal (athletic ambitions), torch (scholastic achievement), the helmet of knighthood (bravery, courtesy, honor), Minerva (patron goddess of wisdom) and the open book that shows knowledge is open to those who will learn. These were intended to address all aspects of student life. Log, Clan standing for the students and Log meaning history.” The yearbook was to be a record of all the students. The Piedmont Highlander is the student newspaper. Sweatshirts and T-shirts are printed with “Highlanders.” The Highland Fling Spring Carnival dates to 1922, and the Alpha Clan honor society began in 1924. The school’s fight song was adapted from “On, Wisconsin” with Scottish references: A Scottish Theme The students also chose a Scottish theme. Piedmont is a highland, like Scotland. The Scots were never conquered, hence the Piedmont spirit to never give up. We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Bold and bonny bunch! We eat thistles for our breakfast, Granite for our lunch, Munch, munch, munch … We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Come from Highlands brown … So fight, Piedmont, Fight till every foe is down! In the 1960s, the Scottish Highland theme was at the High School football games. Rob Roy became the official school mascot in 1959 and was on the field during all the games. At halftime, the Kiltie Band played, and the Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling. Today, the words to the fight song have been changed from “fighting Clansmen” to “fighting Scotsmen.” The yearbook name was changed from “Clan-O-Log” to “The Pride” in May 2018. Bird Calling Contest The Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest has been a beloved tradition since 1963 when a student approached biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck and asked, “Can we do something to liven things up around here?” Waxdeck gave the students an assignment to select a bird, give a report on that bird and give its authentic bird call. The raucous bird calls drew the attention of students in nearby classrooms who came to see what the noise was. What began as an exercise quickly outgrew his classroom and moved to the home economics classroom, a larger space. One year later it was moved to the school auditorium. The contest evolved into a highly competitive contest with elaborate skits and (sometimes) costumes. The top winners were flown to the Johnny Carson Show in Burbank, and later the Late Night Show with David Letterman in New York to perform their bird calls. This television exposure brought international attention to the Bird Calling Contest and to the community of Piedmont. Television performances ended when Letterman retired in 2015. Today, after 55 years, the Bird Calling Contest continues to fill the Alan Harvey Theater at the High School each spring. Fourth of July Parade Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade officially began in 1965 when Recreation Commissioner Dick (Pear) Johnson decided to start a city-wide parade. Years before, his El Cerrito Avenue neighborhood had been celebrating the 4th of July with their own bicycle parade, watermelon eating contest and water balloon toss. Johnson thought it was too quiet in Piedmont in the summer and expanded his neighborhood parade to a city-wide event on Highland Avenue, the main thoroughfare. Over the years the parade has grown to include bands, antique cars, floats, horse patrols, unique groups including the Balloon Platoon of tubby sailors, and the all-important neighborhood entries. The post-parade music program in the park fills the lawn with picnickers, and many residents end their day at block parPiedmont biology teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck arranged each year to have a friend, a commercial artist, create a fanciful, distinctly original poster to promote that year’s Bird Calling Contest.

Program Highlight: Piedmont Police Exploring Post Four years ago, Lucas C. joined Piedmont’s Police Exploring program with a friend. It was a decision that would alter the course of his life. Lucas became interested in Exploring after reading that it was one of very few youth programs that offered the opportunity to get involved with law enforcement. Now a senior at Piedmont High School, Lucas is preparing for college – and a career as a police officer. “Exploring has been an experience like nothing else,” Lucas says. “My friends who have completed the police academy have all said this program was the most useful thing they did to prepare. You learn how to talk to people, how to write. You learn people skills and teamwork, which are helpful even if you don’t decide to go into police work.” Lucas likes that the Piedmont Police post has him doing things out in the community like ridealongs and monitoring the Turkey Trot and the Harvest Festival. He says the program has trained him to handle himself in a range of situations from traffic stops to crime scene investigations and hostage negotiations. Lucas encourages others to consider the program as an opportunity to gain life skills. “Definitely do it!” he says. “You’ll get to see another side of law enforcement and all the effort that goes into keeping the community safe. For me, I even found my career.” Council Membership Totals 206 Cub Scouts ages 5-10 293 Scouts BSA ages 11-17 144 Venturing ages 14-20 659 Total Youth Served 16 Explorers Piedmont Police Exploring Post & Piedmont Service Club 364 Registered Volunteers

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department’s veteran Engineer Russ San Fillipo, was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia last December, and has been aggressively fighting the blood cancer ever since. The news comes in advance of the Piedmont Fire Department’s preparation for their third annual participation in the Big Climb, a stair-climbing race in the upper deck of Giant’s Oracle Park which is a fund-raiser for the nonprofit Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. The fundraising is even more important this year with one of their own leaders directly battling cancer. San Fillipo, a soft spoken man, with an ear for the guitar, was shocked upon the diagnosis. Fillipo, 57, is a distance runner and in fire-fighter shape. “It kind of started off as a sore throat and I thought I was just getting a cold, I didn’t really think much of it. Basically the sore throat wasn’t going away. It just kept getting worse,” said San Fillipo. He was initially diagnosed with mono, but then his blood work showed his white blood cell that are going through your mind like, how it’s going to affect your family,” said San Fillipo. So far he has been responding well to the treatment. He has gone through three rounds of chemotherapy since the diagnosis. Each start at the hospital but the majority of the three week treatments are at home. His latest round of chemo was in March. The battle with cancer looks different on a daily basis for him; sometimes his blood counts are low and he stays home, but other days he is feeling good and can go out with a mask to watch one of his son’s sports events. Russ and his wife Kelly and children live in Pacific Grove near Monterey. The Fire Department, a family in its own right, is bonding around their 23-year veteran Engineer. “He’s just very humble and soft spoken, one of those genuine people who nobody has a bad thing to say about,” said Captain Justin McNulty. McNulty who was in the Fire Academy with San Fillipo and was hired by Piedmont Fire Dept. at the same time as San Fillipo 23 years ago. By Jay Russell Piedmont Fire Department’s veteran Engineer Russ San Fillipo, was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia last December, and has been aggressively fighting the blood cancer ever since. The news comes in advance of the Piedmont Fire Department’s preparation for their third annual participation in the Big Climb, a stair-climbing race in the upper deck of Giant’s Oracle Park which is a fund-raiser for the nonprofit Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. The fundraising is even more important this year with one of their own leaders directly battling cancer. San Fillipo, a soft spoken man, with an ear for the guitar, was shocked upon the diagnosis. Fillipo, 57, is a distance runner and in fire-fighter shape. “It kind of started off as a sore throat and I thought I was just getting a cold, I didn’t really think much of it. Basically the sore throat wasn’t going away. It just kept getting worse,” said San Fillipo. He was initially diagnosed with mono, but then his blood work showed his white blood cell Piedmont Firefighter battles leukemia that are going through your mind like, how it’s going to affect your family,” said San Fillipo. So far he has been responding well to the treatment. He has gone through three rounds of chemotherapy since the diagnosis. Each start at the hospital but the majority of the three week treatments are at home. His latest round of chemo was in March. The battle with cancer looks different on a daily basis for him; sometimes his blood counts are low and he stays home, but other days he is feeling good and can go out with a mask to watch one of his son’s sports events. Russ and his wife Kelly and children live in Pacific Grove near Monterey. The Fire Department, a family in its own right, is bonding around their 23-year veteran Engineer. “He’s just very humble and soft spoken, one of those genuine people who nobody has a bad thing to say about,” said Captain Justin McNulty. RELIGION CORNER Innocent and inconvenient By Pastor Jim Hopkins “Certainly this man was innocent.” Luke 23:47b In Luke’s gospel Jesus speaks from the cross three times. His courageous words are: • “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” • (To one who was crucified with him) “Truly, I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” • “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Following his last cry he breathed his last and one of the Roman soldiers who had carried out the crucifixion declared, “Certainly, this man was innocent.” The soldier’s declaration echoes through history a witness to Jesus fundamental goodness as does the reality that this innocent one was, and is, very inconvenient to many. He was inconvenient to the Temple authorities who feared his popularity. He was inconvenient to Pontius Pilate who feared he would lead a popular uprising. He was inconvenient to Herod Antipas who feared him as a potential rival. He was inconvenient to the crowd that feared standing up to the powers that be in order to support him. He is inconvenient to many of us for he represents a God who suffers, a God we are not sure that we want. In her book “God In Pain: Teaching Sermons on Suffering,” Barbara Brown Taylor speaks to this inconvenient reality, “Christianity is the only world religion that confesses a God who suffers. It is not a popular idea, even among Christians. We prefer a God who prevents suffering, only that is not the God we have got. What the cross teaches us is that God’s power is not the power to force human choices and end human pain. It is, instead, the power to pick up the shattered pieces and make something holy out of them – not from a distance, but right close up.” Jesus is inconvenient because, rather than preventing suffering, he suffers with us and bids us to “take up your cross and follow me.” This is not a message of popular appeal. This is not the promise of wealth, prestige and security. This is not a gospel of prosperity. This is not a theology of self-improvement. This is not cheap grace. This is a costly, demanding, heart-rending, heart-changing way. articles.text: Kids will have a chance to climb up in Public Works’ big trucks, complete a tree-themed art project, and maybe win a new book to take home at Piedmont’s annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration, hosted by Piedmont Public Works and the Piedmont Park Commission. The event will take place on Thursday, April 24, from 4:00-6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The annual event, which dates back to 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. • • • This year’s event will feature: Public Works big trucks: Works staff uses daily in their work to keep Piedmont’s trees and public spaces healthy and beautiful. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the trucks. Arts & crafts: Park Commissioners will be on hand to assist little ones with their creations. Owl naming contest: A photo exhibit and naming contest will highlight raptors living in Piedmont Parks, including a nesting pair of great horned owls that have taken up residence in Dracena Park. ComChildren will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of Public Works’ trucks. munity members can share name suggestions online in advance at piedmont.ca.gov/ DracenaOwls. • Raffle: Kids can enter to win a Lego set or children’s book related to Arbor and Earth Day themes. New this year, a raffle for adult attendees will offer an opportunity to take home a California native plant for your garden. • Electric leaf blower demos: Gas powered leaf blowers are not allowed in Piedmont, but clean, quiet electric alternatives can get the job done. Try one for yourself at the event. The event will also include informational tables from the Piedmont Fire Department and the City’s Sustainability Division. Heritage Trees announcement The Arbor Day celebration will also feature the announcement of the 2025 class of Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its seventh year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. This year, the City received nine nominations for Heritage Trees. Anyone with questions, contact Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont. ca.gov. Kids enjoy fresh popcorn at the City’s 2024 Arbor and Earth Day Celebration. articles.text: Come to Cat town and meet Pluto and Mars. Meet 1-year-old Pluto and 4-year-old Mars, a playful and affectionate bonded pair of boys looking for a home together. These best friends love to wrestle, chase toys, and even eat and nap together. As shy cats, they’ll benefit from a patient adopter who’ll give them time to feel safe. They thrive in a calm, quiet home, and once they settle in, each has uniquely adorable traits you’ll quickly fall in love with. Mars, a white and brown tabby, asks for affection with headbutts or by gently brushing up against your legs as he walks by. He’s known for using these approaches to flirt with visitors, before flopping over and rolling away. This charming boy also loves scrambling after toys. Although a bit more reserved, Pluto, an orange tabby, is often the first to explore, moving through his surroundings with quiet curiosity. He loves to stalk after his toys, and is a true cuddle buddy, eagerly curling up in a familiar lap for a gentle petting session. Want to meet this duo? Complete an Adoption Inquiry form for a free matchmaking appointment, or book a visit to meet all of Cat Town’s adoptable cats at their cat cafe, located at 2869 Broadway in Oakland. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org.

articles.text: The Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program is offering grants of up to $6,000 for community-based projects that help prevent stormwater pollution and improve the health of local watersheds, creeks and the San Francisco Bay. Eligible projects include litter reduction efforts, public outreach and education about clean water issues, public art installations and stormwater detention initiatives. One past recipient is I Heart Oakland-Alameda Estuary, a group of water sports enthusiasts who use their skills and equipment to organize cleanups in areas of the Oakland-Alameda Estuary that are otherwise inaccessible by foot. Other grant-funded projects have included the removal of microplastics from Albany Beach, a cleanup of Sausal Creek in Oakland, and the production of a short film titled Doing Our Part to Clean Up San Francisco Bay. The deadline for submissions is May 9, 2025, at 5:00 p.m. Projects must be implemented in Alameda County. For details and to download the application packet, visit www.cleanwaterprogram.org/grants. articles.text: Piedmont resident Jean Hansen will be showing her garden for the third time in this year’s Garden Tour. The award-winning Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour returns Saturday and Sunday, May 3–4, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., inviting community members to explore more than 50 water-conserving native plant gardens across Alameda and Contra Costa counties. In addition to showcasing native gardens, 25 of the homes will also participate in a Green Home Showcase, featuring ecofriendly technologies such as solar panels and battery systems, induction stoves, and electric heat pumps. This year’s tour includes the garden of Piedmont resident Jean Hansen. Her landscape, designed to complement her rustic 1912 home, is filled with California native plants that provide food and shelter for local bees, birds and butterflies. Attendees will learn how to design native gardens with yearround color and interest, support wildlife, reduce water usage, and protect both family health and the environment by gardening without pesticides. The tour also highlights practical steps homeowners can take to electrify their homes and reduce carbon emissions. California native plants are naturally adapted to local soil and climate conditions, making them low-maintenance and water-efficient. They are also more effective than non-native species at supporting native birds, butterflies and other wildlife. articles.text: Josh Bernstein, a 3-time contestant and proud member of Piedmont High’s class of 1975, achieved local – and briefly national – fame that year with his stirring, second-place portrayal of the Bald Eagle at the Leonard J. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest. His commitment to the role included a freshly shaven head for aerodynamic realism, and his performance was one of the rare news items to ever make Walter Cronkite laugh on the CBS Evening News. For a teenage bird impressionist, it was the equivalent of winning an Emmy, a Peabody, and possibly a fish. Josh has since traded feathers for floss as a longtime practicing dentist, where he’s spent decades perfecting the beautiful whirring call of the high-speed drill. He’s also been raising a lively flock of his own three children and two grandchildren, including his daughter Mavra, who proudly served as M.C. of the Birdcalling Contest during her senior year at Piedmont High. Back home in the hills of Piedmont, Josh lives among a vibrant avian chorus of owls, crows, whippoorwills, woodpeckers, wild turkeys, and chickens – though none have been brave enough to challenge him to a call-off. When not in the office or the backyard, he’s often out in open water, marathon swimming alongside seagulls, pelicans, and great blue herons, pondering which bird might next be worthy of emulation. Now returning to the Bird Calling Contest as a judge, Josh brings a legendary ear, decades of dedication, and the rare distinction of having once cracked up the most trusted man in television with a birdcall. Let the squawking commence. The 56th Annual Bird Calling Contest poster was designed by PHS student Layla Miguel-Reed. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: Judge profiles – Leonard J. Waxdeck Birdcalling Contest

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit of Piedmont Scout Council, is hosting a discussion panel this Saturday, April 19 for 9th graders. It will be held in the middle school multi-purpose room at 5:00 p.m. The panel, titled “What I wish I knew before I went to high school,” aims to provide information to soon-to-be graduates of middle school and their parents. The event is being organized by the Piedmont Community Service Crew co-presidents Elena O’Connell and Stephanie Lee as a service to the community. They will be the event moderators for a panel five crew members who will share insights and tips on the transition from middle to high school. They will also talk about the values of being in Piedmont Community Service Crew and how being a member has added to their own personal growth in ways beyond being just a convenient and social way of gaining service hours. There will be time for parents and students to ask questions. 8th grade parents are encouraged to respond to the following form to share their thoughts and concerns about the transition to high school, and to show their interest in attending: https://forms. gle/E6ZC57P2AmRWo3p89 For more information about Piedmont Community Service Crew, visit their website at http:// www.pcservicecrew.org or contact crew advisor Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net.
articles.title: Teen Community Service Crew hosts panel for PHS incoming freshmen this Sat.

articles.text: The Piedmont community is invited to join the Piedmont High School (PHS) English Department and freshman parent representatives for the Ninth Grade I-Search Celebration and public viewing on Tuesday, April 22, from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. in the Piedmont Middle School multipurpose room. These 15 to 30 plus-page documents represent more than nine weeks of intensive work focused on writing, research, and thoughtful reflection. Every freshman has completed a guided research project as part of the I-Search curriculum, demonstrating their growth as writers, thinkers, and investigators. The projects offer compelling insight into what students are curious about in the world and how they communicate their findings. Each student conducted an interview to deepen their understanding of their chosen topic and form original conclusions. Freshman English teachers Jamie Mockel, Wade Wilgus, and Eduardo Wolbert recognize the valuable support the Piedmont community has offered throughout the students’ research journeys and invite everyone to come view the final work. Come explore student research on topics ranging from the benefits of gene editing and the drive of an athlete to the rise of flag football and the economics of climate change. These projects are thoughtful, relevant, and deserving of a broader audience beyond the classroom. Questions can be directed to English department member, Beth Black at bblack@piedmont. k12.ca.us.
articles.title: Celebrate PHS Freshmen at I-Search Night on April 22

articles.text: Fifty years of education will be celebrated by the Piedmont Adult School (PAS) on Thursday, April 24, in the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) from 6:30-8:00 p.m. The public is invited to join the 50th anniversary party honoring lifelong education in Piedmont with snacks, a presentation and a chance to mingle with students and teachers. The community is invited to the free event with food, drinks, and mingling from 6:30-7:00 and a brief presentation at 7:00 honoring some of PAS’s veteran instructors. Instructors Susan Schnellbacher (Italian), Dennis Mockel (Excel and Photography), and Jacqui Birdsong-James (strength training) have been teaching at the adult school since the mid-70s, and will be in attendance along with many other favorite instructors that have made critical additions to the course offerings and culture of the school. Shortly after being founded in 1975, PAS expanded its offerings to include progressive English as a Second Language (ESL) classes, citizenship classes, General Education Diploma (GED) test preparation, California DMV-approved traffic school classes, and a High School Diploma Program (HSDP) for adults. articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center astronomer Gerald McKeegan has a few tips for stargazing, planet-watching and observing points of interest in the night sky. McKeegan co-hosts free telescope viewings every Friday and Saturday evening at Chabot alongside other professional and volunteer astronomers, making the center a go-to destination for skywatchers across the Bay Area. Here’s what McKeegan says to watch for in the coming weeks: • Jupiter and Mars are still visible in the evening sky for the next few weeks. • Around 9:30 p.m., look east • • for a bright, yellowish star— Arcturus, a giant star 37 lightyears away. Arcturus appears in the early spring sky and remains visible throughout the summer. The Big Dipper is easy to spot in the northeastern sky after 9 p.m. This familiar star pattern is part of the constellation Ursa Major, or the Big Bear. Telescope season for globular clusters is beginning. These dense, spherical groups of hundreds of thousands of stars are among the oldest in our galaxy—about 12 billion years old. The clusters orbit • the Milky Way’s center in a region known as the galactic halo. There are roughly 160 globular clusters orbiting our galaxy, and they offer a stunning sight through a telescope. Also visible is the faint constellation Corona Borealis, or the Northern Crown. Known to some Native American traditions as the “Campfire Circle,” it usually goes unnoticed—except this year, when it could make headlines. Within the constellation lies T Coronae Borealis (T CrB), a faint star nearly 3,000 lightyears away. Though it appears as a single star, it’s actually a binary system, with two stars orbiting each other. One of the stars is a white dwarf, a small, dense, extremely hot remnant of a once-larger star. It’s pulling gas from its companion, a red giant. When enough gas accumulates on the white dwarf’s surface, a nova occurs—a nuclear explosion that dramatically increases the system’s brightness. T CrB is expected to undergo such a nova event soon—possibly this spring or summer—for the first time in 80 years. The explosion will cause the star to brighten by a factor of nearly 2,000, making it briefly visible to the naked eye. The event will be tracked by telescopes worldwide as the star brightens in hours and fades slowly over weeks. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. Sky over Chabot Conrad Jung

articles.text: Council Considers Expanded Signage Rules for Yards, Public Spaces The Piedmont City Council on Monday, April 7, held a public hearing and introduced the first reading of an ordinance to update the city’s rules on signage in both residential lawns and public areas. The proposed ordinance, based on recommendations from the Planning Commission’s March 10 public hearing, includes a series of changes aimed at clarifying regulations and streamlining approvals. The council voted unanimously to increase the number of allowable non-commercial signs per property from two to five and approved a list of special city events that can post signs in public rights-of-way. The proposed updates seek to: • Define categories of signage; • Streamline the review process for city-initiated events; • Expand temporary sign locations on public property; • Clarify rules around construction signs; and • Establish enforcement procedures. Residents would be allowed up to five non-commercial signs— such as political, graduation, or nonprofit messages—and one construction sign per contractor or design professional. Non-commercial signs would have a maximum display period of six months. Event signs would need to be removed within 10 days after the event. To ensure compliance with First Amendment protections, “all non-commercial signs are treated the same by the law”. The ordinance also spells out prohibited signs, including those that mimic traffic control devices, animated or moving signs, roof signs, balloons or inflatables, and ground signs over 15 feet tall. The City is also proposing a formal process to allow signage on public property, including Piedmont Park and 801 Magnolia Ave., home to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Signs posted by the City would be exempt from permits and standards. Officials also plan to launch a program to manage signage for city-sponsored events in specific locations. Currently, the Public Works Director can issue permits for signage across Magnolia Avenue at Highland Avenue, at the Piedmont Corporation Yard, and on fencing at city recreation facilities such as Coaches Field, Beach Playfield, Hampton Field, the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and the city pool. Proposed updates would add bridge railings near Piedmont Community Hall and other rightof-way areas for approved events. The new list of eligible events includes the Piedmont Food Fest, Oktoberfest, the Pumpkin Patch, Turkey Trot, and Christmas Tree Lot. City Council would review and update this list annually. During the hearing, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier questioned how enforcement would work under the six-month rule. “So I take my sign down after six months and then, two days later, I put it back up…” she asked. “That would be fine,” replied Associate Planner Gopika Nair. Kevin Jackson clarified the city’s approach to enforcement: “The city will not be removing signs from private property. The enforcement there would be sending notice to that property owner that they are not in compliance and requesting that they bring their property into compliance by removing that sign, and then following up through a nuisance if they fail to do that.” Jackson added that the City does remove unauthorized signs from public property and will hold them for retrieval by the original poster. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said he is developing a one-page summary of the proposed signage program. “The idea is that less is more,” he said. “We want to have something that’s simple, that is clear… has locations, has types of events that we would consider, and also sign size that [the Council] would consider and durations that are typical.” Associate Planner Gopika Nair (left), City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, City Attorney Deepa Sharma, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Mayor Betsy Smegal-Andersen, Councilmember Jennifer Long, Councilmember Tom Ramsey, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, Deputy City Clerk Lisa Argue, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. articles.text: Photos by Becky Spies Miguel Long competed at the 2025 Arcadia Invitational, the premier meet in California in the spring track and field season. Piedmont High senior Miguel Long continued his strong season at the 2025 Arcadia Invitational, which is considered among the most prestigious meets of the spring track and field season. articles.text: Layth Haddawy qualified for the USPA National Championships for a second straight year. Piedmont High junior Layth Haddawy continued his power lifting career at the United States Powerlifting Association National Tested Get Bent’s Spring Break in Oakland on April 5. In the Age 16-17 category at 148 pounds, Haddawy lifted a combined total of 1,085 pounds – 352 pounds in the squat, 248 pounds on the bench press, and a 485- pound dead lift. Haddawy last competed in the USPA National Championships in July, when he had a combined weight of 932 pounds. He increased his squat by 43 pounds, his dead lift 66 pounds, his bench 44 pounds, resulting in his combined weight jumping 153 pounds. But after the National Championships in July, an MRI revealed Haddawy had suffered a fracture in his pelvis. “This was my first time competing since I fractured a part of my pelvis and had to take months off from lifting. I wanted to try and qualify for the National meet and test myself on what I could do after my injury. I wanted to take ambitious third attempts and it resulted in getting a slightly lower total, but I still qualified in the event I wanted to reach,” Haddawy said. After fighting through nagging pain he figured out something was wrong. Testing revealed an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. “At first, I didn’t realize my injury was as big a deal as it turned out to be. I probably made it worse by trying to lift lighter weights and adjust my form to what didn’t hurt. But I realized I wasn’t getting better, so I underwent an MRI. It revealed part of my hamstring muscle tore off a segment of the bone in my pelvis. It happened in August and I didn’t start my rehab until October,” Haddawy said. Haddawy last competed in the 132-pound division, adding 16 pounds to his frame. He thinks the added weight is giving him more power after battling a difficult weight-cut in his previous division. “I’ve been reassured by how stronger I’ve gotten since I’ve come back in a higher weight class. As I got toward the end of competing in the 132 weight class, I was walking around about 6-7 pounds heavier than where I was competing. In 148, I’m walking around just four pounds heavier, so I still have decent room to grow in this weight class,” Haddawy said. The Get Bent’s Spring Break competition officially marked Layth’s one-year anniversary as a competitive power-lifter. “I’ve learned a lot about competing, how to train, what to do, and what not to do. I’ve really learned how to go about things Layth Haddawy competed at the USPA Tested Get Bent’s Spring Break on April 5.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team closed the Concord Varsity Tournament with a win on Wednesday, April 9, defeating neighboring the Head-Royce Jayhawks 7-5 at Concord High School. The victory avenged Piedmont’s first loss of the season on March 7 when they lost to Head-Royce 7-1. Piedmont returns from Spring Break with a 10-4 overall record and the bulk of its Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division schedule ahead. Piedmont is currently 1-1 against league competition as they look to defend last year’s regular season first-place title. The Highlanders, Castro Valley, and Alameda have played the fewest number of league games thus far. CV leads the Foothill at 2-0, while Berkeley is 3-1, Encinal is 2-2, Bishop O’Dowd is 2-4, and Alameda is 0-2. The fate of the regular season title is still up in the air with Piedmont having two-game series’ remaining against Alameda, Castro Valley, Berkeley, and O’Dowd. 7-5 win vs. Head-Royce PHS took an initial 1-0 lead in the bottom of the second and held a 2-1 lead following the next inning. But Head-Royce tacked on three runs in the top of the fourth and one more in the fifth to take a 5-2 lead. That’s when Piedmont scored once in the bottom of the fifth before jumping ahead with a powerful four-run bottom sixth. Piedmont got its first run on a two out rally. Brandon Dicke hit a single and advanced all the way to third on a throwing error. Dicke then scored on another throwing error, this time by HR’s Staff Photos Diego Delventhal got the save on the mound against Head-Royce with two strikeouts in the final inning. pitcher. After allowing a run, Piedmont got back to the front when Will Parker hit a one-out single to score Markos Lagios. The Jayhawks then scored three runs and the top fourth and one more the next inning, up 5-2, but the comeback was on from there. In the bottom of the fifth, Will Ferriera led off with a triple to right field, and then scored on a wild pitch with one out—making it 5-3. Piedmont’s big four-run bottom of the sixth inning started with a leadoff double by Shafer Dando followed by Michael Martin drawing a walk. With one out, Jordan Vo grounded into a field’s choice, allowing Dando to score and reaching first in the process. Ferriera then drew a walk and with two outs, Delventhal was hit by a pitch to score Martin and tie up the ballgame at 5-5. From there, Lagios roped a line drive to the center field wall to bring around Vo and Ferreira, giving PHS its 7-5 lead. Delventhal took the mound for the save in the top of the seventh. After walking the first two batters, Diego put down the next three batters in order via a strikeout, fly out, and another strikeout to claim the save. Final stats: Lagios went 2-for-3 with two doubles, two RBIs, a run, walk, and a stolen base. Parker went 1-for-4 with an RBI. Dando went 1-for-3 with a double and a run scored. Dicke went 1-for-3 with a run. Vo went 1-for-2 with an RBI, run, walk, and a stolen base. Ferreria went 1-for-1 with a triple, two runs scored, and a stolen base. Martin scored a run and drew a walk. On the mound, Enzo Ong was the winning pitcher with one inning of work and two strikeouts. Delventhal earned the save with two strikeouts. George Bishop, a junior, started with four innings of work, striking out two. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-4 overall, 1-1 league) travels to Alameda tonight, April 16, for a 7:00 p.m. game. They also host Alameda on Friday, April 18 at 4:00 p.m. Markos Lagios hit a two-run double in the bottom of the sixth inning for the go-ahead runs against HeadRoyce. articles.text: Staff Photos Miya Fujimoto went 3-for-4 with two triples and scored three runs against Oakland Tech. Piedmont High’s softball team fell short in its return from Spring Break on Monday, April 14, falling by two runs in a high-scoring 9-7 game at Oakland Tech. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 5-5 as they enter the final month of their regular season. Oakland Tech scored nearly all of its runs on errors by Piedmont’s defense. The Bulldogs had only one hit on the afternoon, while the Highlanders slugged 11 of their own but still came up short. The difference was committing four errors. “If we can clean up our errors, we’ll be alright. We’ve given up a lot of runs from errors this season. If we clean those up, some results could be different,” coach Gene Denard said. Despite the loss, Piedmont is still 2-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline B teams and are currently atop the division. Piedmont still has league games remaining against Tennyson, Hayward, and San Lorenzo. 9-7 loss to Oakland Tech Piedmont took an initial 1-0 lead in the top of the first, but Tech answered with one run in the bottom of the second before slamming on five runs in the bottom of the third and another two runs in the bottom of the fourth. PHS added two runs in the top of the fifth, while Oakland Tech got its final run in the bottom of the sixth. Trailing 9-3, the Highlanders made a valiant effort to comeback on the top of the seventh, adding four runs. In the top of the first, Miya Fujimoto led off with a single. Fujimoto then stole second and advanced to third on a dropped third strike. Sa’Mara Levi then Sa’Mara Levi went 3-for-4 with a double, two RBIs, and a run scored on Tech.

articles.text: The collegiate basketball and swimming seasons came to end in recent months. This week we take a look at a pair of siblings who just concluded their college seasons: Luke Harris of Carleton College, and A.J. Harris of Emory University. LUKE HARRIS Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, just finished his senior season at Carleton College. He finished at the team’s leader in several categories, including 538 points scored, 103 free throws, 200 field goals made, and 914 total minutes. With Harris leading the show, the Knights went 18-10 and reached the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference Finals before losing to Saint Johns of Minnesota. Harris earned All-Conference honors for the third consecutive season, was an All-Region selection by the National Association of Basketball Coaches, and academic All-District. He averaged 19.2 points per game and scored a team-high of 22 in the MIAC Finals. As a sophomore, Harris helped lift Carleton College to the MIAC Conference championship with an 86-76 win over St. Johns where the guard scored 19 points. He departed from Piedmont High as another all-time great, finishing with over 1,200 points and was three-year starter in three mightily successful years, going 21-11 as a sophomore, won the 2020 D4 NCS Championship that finished 24-6, while the team went 11-5 in the pandemic shortened 2021 season. We named Harris the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2021. Photo courtesy of Carleton College Athletics Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, finished his senior season at Carleton College. A.J. HARRIS Emory University A.J. Harris, PHS Class of 2023, finished his sophomore year on Emory University’s men’s Photo courtesy of Emory University A.J. Harris, PHS Class of 2023, helped Emory University reach the Elite Eight of the DIV. 3 NCAA Tournament. basketball team in Atlanta. The Eagles finished its season 23-6 and reached the Elite Eight of the Division 3 NCAA Tournament before falling to Wesleyan University 61-58 in overtime. Harris appeared in all 29 games for 825 minutes, scoring 336 points by shooting 45 percent from the field and 33 percent from 3-pointers, to go along with 149 rebounds, 43 assists, 42 steals and seven blocks. Harris notched a career-high of 28 points on December 30 in a 77-71 win over Union College. He finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s All-Time leading scorer with 1,570 points after playing in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID-19. Harris was named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year alongside Berkeley’s Samir O’Brien. We named Harris the Posts’ 2023 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. articles.text: Two-time Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Lynn Nottage’s acclaimed Crumbs from the Table of Joy comes to the Aurora Theatre stage in Berkeley April 26, running through May 10. Directed by Elizabeth Carter, Nottage’s play follows the Crump family as they relocate from Pensacola, Florida, to Brooklyn following the death of the family matriarch. The play is told through the eyes of 17-year-old Ernestine Crump and focuses on the arrival of communist-leaning Aunt Lily, who challenges the family’s dynamics and beliefs. The play navigates the complexities of race, religion, and societal expectations during the 1950’s. When the play was first presented Off-Broadway at the Second Stage Theatre in 1995, Nottage said she chose the 1950’s because it was a time of significant social change. “Everything I had seen was in black and white,” she said at the time. “And I wanted to make it colorful. So I started writing Crumbs from the Table of Joy to try to understand that era.” Nottage is the first woman in history to win two Pulitzer Prizes for Drama, and her plays, including Crumbs from the Table of Joy, have been produced widely in the United States and throughout the world. Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello called Nottage “one of the most significant American playwrights working today,” “We’re honored to bring this early work of hers, showcasing all her insight and passion, to the Aurora stage. And I’m thrilled to welcome back director Elizabeth Carter,” Costello said. The Aurora Theatre production features Jamella Cross as Ernestine Crump, Asia Jackson as Lily Ann Green, David Moore as Godfrey Crump and Carrie Paff as Gerte Shulte. Preview nights are April 26-27, and 29-30. Opening night is Thursday, May 1 at 7 p.m. The play runs through May 10. Two performances per week, Wednesday evenings and Sunday matinees, are mandatory mask-required performances. For all other performances, masks will be encouraged but not required. A streaming of Crumbs from the Table of Joy performances will be streamed online May 20-25 for audiences to enjoy in their homes. Streaming performances will run concurrently with in-person performances. Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/crumbs to purchase tickets and view showtimes. articles.text: Cast of Here There Are Blueberries pictured at the Wallis Annenberg Theater in Beverly Hills. Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production of Here There Are Blueberries, written by Moisés Kaufman and Amanda Gronich, continues at the Roda Theatre stage through May 11. The play takes place in 2007 and opens in the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, where a mysterious album featuring Nazi-era photographs arrives at the desk of an archivist. Museum curators begin to unravel shocking truths behind the images and what they reveal about the historical tragedy and our own humanity. Here There Are Blueberries tells the story of these historical photographs and is based on true events. The play was a 2024 Pulitzer Prize Drama finalist and is performed on Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s stage following a run at the Wallis Annenberg in Beverly Hills. Cast includes Scott Barrow, Nemuna Ceesay, Delia Cunningham, Luke Forbes, Barbara Pitts, Jeanne Sakata, Marrick Smith, Grant James Varjas, Anna Shafer and Sam Reeder. Post-show discussions are held following April 18, April 24 and April 29 performances, guided by members of Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s artistic team. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/here-there-are-blueberries/ for showtimes and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Opera San Jose (OSJ) will present the Northern California premiere of Hector Armienta’s Zorro this Saturday, April 14, closing out the company’s 41st season. The production stars tenor Xavier Prado as Diego de la Vega and Zorro and soprano Maria Brea as Ana Maria Soza, with Latino stage director David Radamés Toro making his OSJ debut and Conductor Jorge Parodi returning to OSJ after his debut last season on Rigoletto. Armienta’s opera about the famed masked vigilante marries humor and suspense and comes alive with mariachi, flamenco and corrido music. Set in an early 1800s Spanish colony, this new work follows the adventures of a nobleman who defends the poor and enslaved while hiding his true identity behind a black mask. “I can’t wait to bring Zorro to our audiences. This mesmerizing opera blends stunning orchestration with high drama, delivering an enthralling experience for both regular opera-lovers and newcomers to the form,” Opera San José General Director Shawna Lucey said. “From the fierce brass fanfares to the rich strings and sonorous woodwinds, the score pulses with adventure, romance, and suspense. With thrillingly challenging vocals and nonstop momentum, Zorro takes us on a heart-pounding ride.” Xavier Prado as Diego de la Vega and Zorro and soprano Maria Brea as Ana Maria Soza in Opera San Jose’s Zorro Zorro is the second Spanish-language opera to be presented on OSJ’s mainstage following last season’s production of Florencia en el Amazonas. “So many in our community speak Spanish in the home, and we have been delighted to welcome new audiences who are excited to hear works they can instantly follow,” Lucey said, adding that many California public school students study the history of the state and its early settlements, and will gain insight on that era while watching Zorro. “This production will provide an outstanding, and wildly dramatic, look at the political dynamics of that era, making it a great introduction for younger audiences,” she said. The performance will run approximately two hours and thirty minutes with one intermission. Join OSJ staff for a pre-show discussion at 1:00 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. Zorro is showing on select dates April 19 through May 4. Visit https://www.operasj.org/ productions/zorro to learn more and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Opera San Jose closes season with Armienta’s Zorro this Saturday

articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is launching a series of monthly nighttime events beginning this Friday, April 18, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. Beginning April 18 and running monthly through December, FMCAC will host outdoor markets that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid will provide more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. Night Markets are held on the following dates: April 18, May 30, June 27, July 18, August (Date TBA), September 5, October 17, November (Date TBA), and December 12, 2025. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2025/. pages.text: Wednesday, April 16, 2025 19 Fort Mason Night Market launches this Friday By Allyson Aleksey The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is launching a series of monthly nighttime events beginning this Friday, April 18, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. Beginning April 18 and running monthly through December, FMCAC will host outdoor markets that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid will provide more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. articles.text: The episodic journey of the Dutton family begins in Ft. Worth, Texas. The year is 1883. It concludes in Montana where James Dutton and family, wife Margret and young son John, settle on the land that will become the Yellowstone Ranch. 1923 is the sequel to 1883, and, like its prequel, it is wonderfully cinematic, a rich production, character-driven, and the writing by Taylor Sheridan is extraordinary. It is also superbly acted (led by Harrison Ford as Jacob Dutton and Helen Mirren in the role of Cara Dutton). Unlike 1883, which is linear, 1923 is comprised of three integrated vignettes, each an evocative, stand-alone story meant to create a compelling context and rich history of that singular year. Season 1 focuses on Spencer Dutton (Brandon Sklenar), Harrison Ford and Helen Mirren in 1923 nephew of Jake and Cara Dutton, veteran of WWI, and now working for the British Protectorate. He has recently arrived in Nairobi where he meets Alexandra (Julia Schloepfer), the reluctant fiancé of a titled Englishman. She is traveling with a group of upper class Brits on safari. Their encounter at a hotel bar, a wonderful scene, quickly becomes an intense love story wrapped in a harrowing journey. The episodes that follow focuse on Jake and Cara and their struggle to sustain the Dutton Ranch, confronting drought, an ongoing battle for grazing rights, and encroaching sheepherders. And there is the ruthless, amoral, wealthy Donald Whitfield (Timothy Dalton), intent on acquiring mineral-rich land including Yellowstone.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Nineteen Twenty-three (1923) a superb story

articles.text: It’s 1926. The setting for The Danish Girl is Copenhagen, Denmark. Two artists, Einar Wegener (Eddie Redmayne) and his wife, Gerda (Alicia Vikander), married some six years, live a contented, bohemian life, both in search of galleries that will carry their work. Einar, a landscape painter, is finding more success than Gerda, who has thus far confined herself to portraits of wealthy burghers. Their connection, through touch and gaze, reflects a sustained intimacy, revealing in countless subtle ways a relationship that they both cherish as they stand before easels, working, basking in the soft early morning Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander in The Danish Girl light, or reveling in the luminescent glow of late afternoon that filters through the diaphanous curtains of their bedroom. Looking out the wood-framed windows of their starkly furnished flat is a view of a busy harbor filled with working boats, their cinnabar and white sails often partially raised, swaying ever so slightly in the wind. The Danish Girl is replete with achingly gorgeous moments, not only between Einar and Gerda, but horizons framed by pink sunsets and bucolic hills obscured by orange and red wildflowers, each image suffused with color and beauty. Together they share life’s continuum, a kaleidoscope of small and not so small changes. But the depth and breath of their marriage, a touching and visible bond, is seemingly inviolable.
articles.title: The Danish Girl a fascinating journey into the unknown
