articles.text: Briefly, let’s discuss demographics. If memory serves, when I was 10-12-years-old, on the cusp of adolescence, I had some 1,000 comic books, most were stacked in corners or in my closet with a few newbies on my nightstand. I worshipped at the shrine of superheroes, met with similarly obsessed friends, and spent hours trading, reading, and discussing who was faster, stronger and the best bet to save mankind when push came to shove. Batman was a gadget-driven guy who could all but defy gravity. But Superman, well, he was indestructible, could fly, and had x-ray vision. Both were incredibly strong and resourceful. My money was on Superman, plus I could never get enough of his origin story. The reason I mention demographics is that my friends and I were the target audience for DC and Marvel Comics. Their source material and imaginative characters have, for more than a decade, dominated a segment of the big tent/blockbuster movie business. Keep in mind that there is a kind of Harry Potter reading experience involved with comics. My friends and I waited impatiently for the next installment of these larger-than-life characters who possessed powers we could only dream of having. Harry had a wand of magic. Superman could leap tall buildings and was faster than a speeding bullet. Batman was “the Bat” and had one bad outfit and a cool car. What has happened in Hollywood is the creation of a perfect nexus of CGI and the superhero. Filmmakers, using computers and green screens, can now craft any special effect imagined by the writers, and take the young audience to places that are beyond thrilling, so seamless is the technology. Naturally, there have been multiple incarnations of Batman and Superman (and countless other heroes), for which the fanboys and fangirls (Wonder Woman and Supergirl) have been endlessly grateful. Having shared all of the above, this brings us to Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice. First of all, from the perspective of the youngsters, this was a terrific movie: Gotham/Metropolis, two superheroes with abandonment issues (each lost his parents when young), both crusaders for justice and the American way in a world that can be decidedly dystopian. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Castle in the Sky Castle in the Sky is a swashbuckling, Indiana Jones steampunk adventure that also manages to weave into its narrative a subtle ecological message. But above all it’s for kids and there are few slow moments. From the get-go, the story is gripping and in the first opening scenes there’s a kidnapping attempt of a young orphan girl Sheeta (Anna Paquin) by a secret, nefarious agent called Muska (Mark Hamil). She is flown via airship to a military fortress, but on the way the ship is attacked by a cohort of air pirates, led by captain Dola (Cloris Leachman). The reason for the raid is to steal a precious, mysterious amulet that Sheeta wears around her neck, a gift to her from her grandmother. During the attack, Sheeta falls from the ship and instead of crashing to earth she floats gently down into the arms of a dreamy teenage boy, Pazu (James Van Der Beek). Together they set out on a hold your breath, hide from the pirates adventure, a quest that leads them to a floating mythical, steampunk island called Laputa that hovers just above earth. Its source of power is a crystal, not unlike Sheeta’s amulet. Sheeta and Pazu are scrappy, courageous protagonists who relish getting into and out of sequential jams. The story is fast-paced and while there is gunplay, and the bad guys and designated villains bite the dirt, so to speak, Miyazaki is never relies on gratuitous, wham-bang, shots-fired action drama. It’s all in service of a let’er rip story. Castle in the Sky is no exception. It’s pure fun fantasy. pages.text: Wednesday, April 16, 2025 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS Castle in the Sky a wonderful adventure from Studio Ghibli Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice: Can it get any better than this? By Chris Honoré Briefly, let’s discuss demographics. If memory serves, when I was 10-12-years-old, on the cusp of adolescence, I had some 1,000 comic books, most were stacked in corners or in my closet with a few newbies on my nightstand. I worshipped at the shrine of superheroes, met with similarly obsessed friends, and spent hours trading, reading, and discussing who was faster, stronger and the best bet to save mankind when push came to shove. Batman was a gadget-driven guy who could all but defy gravity. But Superman, well, he was indestructible, could fly, and had x-ray vision. Both were incredibly strong and resourceful. My money was on Superman, plus I could never get enough of his origin story. The reason I mention demographics is that my friends and I were the target audience for DC and Marvel Comics. Their source material and imaginative characters have, for more than a decade, dominated a segment of the big tent/blockbuster movie business. Keep in mind that there is a kind of Harry Potter reading experience involved with comics. My friends and I waited impatiently for the next installment of these larger-than-life characters who possessed powers we could only dream of having. Harry had a wand of magic. Superman could leap tall buildings and was faster than a speeding bullet. Batman was “the Bat” and had one bad outfit and a cool car. What has happened in Hollywood is the creation of a perfect nexus of CGI and the superhero. Filmmakers, using computers and green screens, can now craft any special effect imagined by the writers, and take the young audience to places that are beyond thrilling, so seamless is the technology. Naturally, there have been multiple incarnations of Batman and Superman (and countless other heroes), for which the fanboys and fangirls (Wonder Woman and Supergirl) have been endlessly grateful. Having shared all of the above, this brings us to Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice. First of all, from the perspective of the youngsters, this was a terrific movie: Gotham/Metropolis, two superheroes with abandonment issues (each lost his parents when young), both crusaders for justice and the American way in a world that can be decidedly dystopian. In this flick Superman is considSee Batman v Superman on page 29 A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Castle in the Sky By Chris Honoré Castle in the Sky is a swashbuckling, Indiana Jones steampunk adventure that also manages to weave into its narrative a subtle ecological message. But above all it’s for kids and there are few slow moments. From the get-go, the story is gripping and in the first opening scenes there’s a kidnapping attempt of a young orphan girl Sheeta (Anna Paquin) by a secret, nefarious agent called Muska (Mark Hamil). She is flown via airship to a military fortress, but on the way the ship is attacked by a cohort of air pirates, led by captain Dola (Cloris Leachman). The reason for the raid is to steal a precious, mysterious amulet that Sheeta wears around her neck, a gift to her from her grandmother. During the attack, Sheeta falls from the ship and instead of crashing to earth she floats gently down into the arms of a dreamy teenage boy, Pazu (James Van Der Beek). Together they set out on a hold your breath, hide from the pirates adventure, a quest that leads them to a floating mythical, steampunk island called Laputa that hovers just above earth. Its source of power is a crystal, not unlike Sheeta’s amulet. Sheeta and Pazu are scrappy, courageous protagonists who relish getting into and out of sequential jams. The story is fast-paced and while there is gunplay, and the bad guys and designated villains bite the dirt, so to speak, Miyazaki is never relies on gratuitous, wham-bang, shots-fired action drama. It’s all in service of a let’er rip story. Castle in the Sky is no exception. It’s pure fun fantasy. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Nan Wright Winn died on February 24, 2025 in Waltham, MA. Born Nancy True Phillips on March 21, 1935 in Annapolis, MD, she was the daughter of Rear Admiral Richard Helsden Phillips and Betty Mackenzie Seaman Phillips. Due to her father’s career in U.S. Naval Intelligence, she traveled extensively throughout Britain and Europe as a young child. When her parents divorced in 1947, she began attending boarding schools in the U.S. & Switzerland, finally settling in at St. Agnes Episcopal School in Alexandria, VA, and graduated from their high school in 1953. During this period, her mother married Hal James Wright who became President of Creole Petroleum Corporation (Standard Oil) in Caracas, Venezuela. Traveling to and from South America as a minor became an issue, due to her last name being different from her parents, so the U.S. State Dept changed her name to Nan Wright. When attending St. Agnes, she became a Girl Scout and earned the highest award at the time, the Curved Bar. Scouting made an impact on Nan where she was a Scout leader multiple times and cultivated a life of service to others. She was a Lifetime member of the Girl Scouts. Always unconventional, her planned debutante presentation was cancelled because, unknown to her parents, in January 1957 she signed up as a commissioned Naval officer (Ensign) prior to her graduation in June 1957 from Mills College in Oakland. As a Lieutenant, she was an Occupational Therapist in the USNR Medical Service Corps with Top Secret clearance. She was an Maynard, MA. She worked as an occupational therapist, specializing in geriatric rehabilitation. She presented papers as a speaker at several worldwide OT conferences. She was a member of the American Occupational Therapy Association & the British Occupational Therapy Association. Every ancestral generation of her family has chosen to serve their country by active duty as naval officers since 1742 in the U.S. & Great Britain. After moving to MA to be near her cousins, she joined the National Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution where she found a welcome group of friends. She held the position of State Chair DAR Service to Veterans, in addition to frequently acting as a liaison for the NSDAR Old Concord Chapter to the Edith Nourse Rogers Memorial Veterans Hospital in Bedford, MA. She especially enjoyed making lap quilts for veterans in wheelchairs. Nan cared about volunteerism, her country, her faith, and her family. She was a parishioner at Trinity Episcopal Church, Concord, MA. Nan is survived by her daughter Sarah Elizabeth Winn Garcia and spouse Jose Garcia, son Andrew Mackenzie Winn and spouse Mirna Winn, four grandchildren, Isabel Winn, Robert Winn, William Winn and George Winn, and cousin Susan Corey and her spouse Donald Corey. She is predeceased by her grandson, Thomas Michael Garcia. Special thanks from Sarah and Andrew to Donald Corey, Peter Corey, and Brooke Corey. An interment with military funeral honors and a memorial service are pending. Nan Wright Winn died in Waltham, Massachusetts on February 24, 2025. She was 89. It was at SURF Division 1221 that she met her husband LCDR John Greeley Winn II, who she married on December 27, 1964 at the Treasure Island Naval Station in San Francisco. They were divorced in 1992. Nan received an honorable discharge from the Navy when she became pregnant with her first child. Nan & her family lived in Montclair and then moved the family to Piedmont in 1974, where she lived for three decades. articles.text: Jacque Price of Jacque Price Art chats with patron of Montclair Village Art Walk. The Montclair Village Art Walk celebrates its 48th year this April, featuring more than 50 artists from the Bay Area and beyond. Hosted by the Montclair Village Association, the free, open-air event will take place Saturday and Sunday, April 26–27, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., along the sidewalks of Montclair Village and the Oakland Hills. Visitors can enjoy a stroll through this outdoor art gallery and shop for gifts—for themselves, loved ones, or even the office. A special feature on Saturday is Picnic on the Plaza, from 1 to 4 p.m., with food available from local restaurants and a live performance by Rustwood Revival from 12:30 to 3:30 p.m. Kids can enjoy the Oakland Fire Department’s Random Acts Parade Rig and free face painting by Lily’s Arte. On Sunday, attendees can explore the art walk as well as stop by La Salle’s farmers market for fresh produce and local treats from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Glass garden designs of Moira Barker, Moira’s Glass Art, brightens the sidewalk to patrons’ delight at the Montclair Village Art Walk. articles.text: • Megan Brown – Megan Brown Ceramics Megan Brown creates functional and modern ceramic tableware, home décor, and jewelry inspired by California’s natural beauty. “Each piece is one of a kind and thoughtfully designed to be both visually striking and satisfying to hold,” she says. Her process includes hand-painting, carving, and applying intricate tape designs to create textures that invite touch and elevate everyday use. • Swann Freslon – Swann Paints A mixed-media abstract artist, Swann Freslon draws inspiration from her global travels, nature, and personal connections. “Through my abstract art, I aim to explore the process of letting go—of releasing both my own emotions and those of the viewer,” she says. “I use the power of color to mesmerize the soul.” • Jeannie Haydon – Jeannie Haydon Creative Jewelry Jeannie Haydon has worked with metal and jewelry since she was 12. “I create mixed metal jewelry and sculpture inspired by the world around me,” she says. Her work features innovative textures and designs, often incorporating found objects from the street. With over 30 years of experience, she produces sculptural jewelry that’s built to last. • Galit Perez – Cartera Galit Perez designs and handcrafts leather bags, beginning each piece with a cardboard blueprint. She selects each leather hide for color and thickness, then cuts, sews, and embosses the final product with her signature logo. “The leather bags are charming and practical, crafted to seamlessly transition from professional to casual settings,” she says. articles.title: Spring Blooms Shine on ‘Walking on Wednesdays’ Tour

pages.text: Wednesday, April 16, 2025 25 Features Walking on Wednesday By Richard F. Carter Sunshine, spring flowers and a cheerful crowd made for a perfect morning on April 3, as the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group set out in search of seasonal blooms. Spring Blooms Shine on ‘Walking on Wednesdays’ Tour The group’s mission? A 2.5- mile flower walk through Piedmont and Crocker Parks and surrounding streets, timed to catch the city’s fleeting spring blooms at their peak. The tour started at the Exedra’s vase, where tulips — though slightly past their prime — were still lovely, albeit nibbled by curious critters. From there, the group climbed Highland Avenue to the park stairs by the bus stop. Towering cherry trees along the way, cloaked in white and pink blossoms, evoked comparisons The Wednesday walkers enjoyed the cherry blossoms of Piedmont Park at the recently renovated HighlandGuilford steps. to the famed spring displays in Washington, D.C. While the origin of those trees remains unclear, members noted that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation has contributed to city landscaping since 1964, including projects at the Hall Fenway, Cherry Walk, and the Community Center. Next, the group descended the steps to the circular flower bed in front of the Community Hall, where a Yulan magnolia — native to China — had finished blooming. In its place, a generous bed of pink and white tulips was still on full display. The path continued to the Cherry Walk above the Tea House, flanked by Japanese maples — another beloved feature of the city’s designated Heritage Trees. New Heritage Trees will be announced during the Park Commission’s Arbor Day celebration on April 24 at the Community Hall. The Cherry Walk led to the recently renovated Highland-Guilford steps, which now serve as a stately entrance to the Tea House, Cherry Walk and Piedmont Park. The 2023 renovation, funded in part by $82,000 from the Beautification Foundation and $5,000 from the Piedmont Garden Club, replaced old concrete and railroad ties with elegant landings and walkways. With cherry blossoms as a backdrop, the group attempted a photo — though not everyone could squeeze into the frame. The walkers then crossed Highland Avenue and headed up Sierra Avenue, where more tulips awaited. At the end of Sierra, the group crossed Sheridan Avenue, spotting chestnut trees with fading red blooms and three graceful dogwoods in nearby front yards. Turning onto Wildwood Avenue and through the Hall Fenway, they admired more cherry trees and white calla lilies — a reminder that Easter is near. Calla lilies, native to southern Africa, now grow across the globe. In Crocker Park, walkers stopped at a path-side copper beech, also called a purple beech — another Heritage Tree. Known for its deep purple leaves in spring and copper tones in fall, the tree can live 150 to 300 years. After a short stroll up Hampton Road and Sea View Avenue, the group reached the Reich family home, a seasonal floral highlight. This year’s tulips and daffodils didn’t disappoint, and a second group photo was snapped — with everyone fitting in this time. On La Salle Avenue, the group checked on a row of rhododendrons just beginning to bud — a good reason to return in a few weeks. They looped around Mandana and Crocker Avenues near the Oakland border before heading back into Piedmont, enjoying the blooms from a reverse view. It was a colorful, fragrant, and heartwarming spring morning — a floral tour through what one walker fondly called “a big park called Piedmont.” The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420- 3070 for more information. There was a large turnout of 56 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra. Among those participating were Bill Ahern, Kat Lang, Cathy Layman, Mark Davis, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Tom Lehrkind, Nancy Lehrkind, June Yee, Edith Lee, Carolyn George, Alissa Quan, Priscilla Wanerus, Laura DuDell-Foley, Debbie Powell, Peggy Shultz, Stella Houston, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Tina Sum, Jasmine Cai, Noemi Alvarado, Sherry Jacobs, Liz Dalrymple, Margie Richardson, Chuck Oraftik, Margaret Leunig, Jim Kellogg, David Haecker, Julia Chin, Phil Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Lori Austin, Phil Witte, Ken Moy, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Matt Gerhardt, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Greg Slatoff, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kuo, Nancy Olsen, Denny McGee, Larry Olsen, Lois Price, Karen Palmer, Irene Thompson, Lisa Euphrat, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Mike Gallant, Vicki Trimbach, and Dick Carter. I recently opened a Ridge Petite Sirah from 1985 and it was a baby showing no age at all. This wine cries out for a grilled leg of lamb. • 2023 Ridge Geyserville This wine adds 18% Carignane, 9% Petite Sirah and 3% Alicante Bouschet to the Zinfandel. The Geyserville shows tremendous character, it has hints of violets, currants and raspberries with a rich spice box note as well as leather and earth. The perfect companion to grilled burgers or portabello mushrooms. • 2023 Ridge Zinfandel Paso Robles This 100% Zinfandel from the Benito Dusi ranch offers classic briery, mineral, spicy Zinfandel aromas. On the palate, the wine is dense, rich, and full-bodied, with copious quantities of glycerin, abundant plum/blueberry fruit, low acidity, and a fleshy, succulent finish. It’s a gorgeous Zinfandel to drink over the next five years. • 2022 Ridge Estate Cabernet Sauvignon The grapes come from the famed Montebello Vineyard with 9% Petite Verdot and 5% Merlot blended in with the Cabernet Sauvignon. It has compelling aromas of cherry, blueberry, hibiscus and violet. The full-bodied palate features complex, layered flavors framed by grainy tannins and tons of fresh acidity, and it has a long, fragrant finish. This will improve with cellar age and reach full maturity in ten to fifteen years. • 2023 Ridge Lytton Springs It is hard to choose between the many outstanding Ridge Zinfandels but in most years Lytton Springs usually stands out to me. This bottling is blended with 14%Petite Sirah and 7% Carignane, 2% Alicante Bouschet and 1% Mataro.. This beautiful and compelling wine shows blackberries, graphite, leather and tar notes. The wine boasts fabulous balance in an extroverted style that is hard to resist. It is built to last and will easily develop over ten years in the cellar. • 2023 Ridge Three Valleys (Best Value) This is a blend of five grapes with Zinfandel making up 71%. Unlike most of Ridge wines which are single vineyard the Three Valleys is made from a variety of vineyards from across the state. It is a lighter, softer style of wine but still retains great character and interest. It is soft and supple on the finish making for smooth and easy drinking upon release. articles.text: Spruce, a male mountain lion and the 30th rescue by Oakland Zoo, was safely transported to his new home at the Birmingham Zoo on April 4. He was rescued in January along with his siblings, Fern and Thistle, and has received care from Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital and animal care staff, thanks to donor support. Spruce will now live with his new companion, Juniper, a female rescue cub. The decision to relocate Spruce to the Birmingham Zoo was based on the compatible personalities of both cubs. The future locations for Fern and Thistle have not yet been determined. Oakland Zoo partnered with the Birmingham Zoo and FedEx to transport Spruce to Memphis, Tennessee. Over the past month, animal care staff at Oakland Zoo trained Spruce using positive reinforcement techniques to help him acclimate to the crate used for travel. “He did an amazing job shifting right into the crate for his early morning flight last Friday,” said Angela Gibson, zoological manager at Oakland Zoo, who accompanied Spruce on the flight to ensure his safety and well-being. Upon arrival in Memphis, they were met by Mollye Nardi and Amy Toman, curators at Birmingham Zoo. “We are excited that a wonderful home has been found for Spruce,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. “Though we are quick to respond when called into action, we hope measures will be implemented to prevent Oakland Zoo from needing to rescue these animals so often in the future. Coexistence is essential for the survival of this species. The zoo is committed to enhancing connectivity, nurturing coexistence, and advocating for policy initiatives to protect pumas, pets and people across the Bay Area.” Spruce and Juniper have already been introduced in their nighthouse. Keepers have observed them cuddling, playing, chirping — a form of mountain lion communication — and getting to know each other. They will remain in the nighthouse while acclimating to their new environment. Once they are ready, they will move into the Birmingham Zoo’s Wojciechowski Cougar Crossing Habitat, which opened to the public on March 19. Mountain lions in California face increasing threats from vehicle collisions, wildfires and habitat encroachment. These dangers lead to more frequent human-wildlife conflict, prompting zoos such as Oakland and Birmingham to care for orphaned mountain lions. “He and Juniper have already had positive interactions under the guidance of Birmingham Zoo and Oakland Zoo animal care professionals,” said Chris Pfefferkorn, president and CEO of Birmingham Zoo. “The cougar cubs, along with two adult bobcats, now live in a new facility designed to allow the cats to explore and display natural behaviors.” For more information about the rescued cubs, Oakland Zoo’s Mountain Lion Rescue Program and the Birmingham Zoo, please see the FAQ below. Where was Spruce and his siblings found? What happened to their mother? Fern (female), Thistle (male), and Spruce (male) were found in Portola Valley, San Mateo County. California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) believes the mother of these three cubs was the same female lion hit by a car on Portola Valley Road about 0.3 miles from where Fern, Thistle, and Spruce were found. While there were many witnesses of the mountain lion after it was hit, the carcass has since disappeared and is still being investigated. Why can’t the cubs be released to the wild? In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother to learn survival skills. Because Fern, Thistle, and Spruce are so young, they lacked those skills and could not be returned to the wild. How are new homes for mountain lions rescued by Oakland Zoo chosen? CDFW selects locations with the animals’ welfare and wellbeing in mind. The Zoo cares for the cubs and then assists CDFW with transporting them to appropriate institutions. Why couldn’t the cub trio be introduced to Oakland Zoo’s resident mountain lions? Many factors are considered when introducing animals – personalities, age, AZA’s Species Survival Plan recommendations, etc.– and all decisions are made with the animal’s welfare and wellbeing in mind. The trio was determined not to be the perfect match for Oakland Zoo’s resident mountain lions and Briar, another rescued puma the Zoo is caring for. How is Spruce’s separation from his siblings like what this species experiences in the wild? articles.text: An enthusiastic group of 21 readers gathered at the Piedmont Community Hall on April 7 for the First Mondays Reading Group. The focus of the evening was Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz, and the opportunity to meet with the author. Hershovitz, a professor of law and philosophy and director of the Law and Ethics Program at the University of Michigan, joined the group via phone thanks to a personal connection. Group member Phil Witte, whose daughter Margo is a graduate student at Michigan, arranged the call. The book, Hershovitz’s debut, explores deep philosophical questions through conversations with his two young sons. From the time they were toddlers, Hershovitz noticed the boys asking questions that philosophers have wrestled with for centuries. “Every kid­ – every single one – is a philosopher,” Hershovitz writes. “They stop when they grow up. Indeed, it may be that part of what it is to grow up is to stop doing philosophy and to start doing something more practical.” Through playful, real-life exchanges, the book addresses topics ranging from the right to drink soda and whether it’s okay to swear, to bigger questions about truth, knowledge, race, gender and the existence of God. Hershovitz argues that kids’ questions deserve serious consideration, and that adults can learn a great deal by thinking with them. The group’s reaction was mostly positive. Many readers praised the author’s voice and humor, calling the book accessible, engaging and thought-provoking. One member compared the tone to the Pogo comic strip, while another said it inspired them to read more philosophy. Several said they planned to gift the book to their now-adult children — especially those with young kids — as a parenting guide with a philosophical twist. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, April 16, 2025 First Monday Reading Group dives into philosophy — with a little help from the author By Dick Carter An enthusiastic group of 21 readers gathered at the Piedmont Community Hall on April 7 for the First Mondays Reading Group. The focus of the evening was Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz, and the opportunity to meet with the author. Hershovitz, a professor of law and philosophy and director of the Law and Ethics Program at the University of Michigan, joined the group via phone thanks to a personal connection. Group member Phil Witte, whose daughter Margo is a graduate student at Michigan, arranged the call. The book, Hershovitz’s debut, explores deep philosophical questions through conversations with his two young sons. From the time they were toddlers, Hershovitz noticed the boys asking questions that philosophers have wrestled with for centuries. “Every kid­ – every single one – is a philosopher,” Hershovitz writes. “They stop when they grow up. Indeed, it may be that part of what it is to grow up is to stop doing philosophy and to start doing something more practical.” Through playful, real-life exchanges, the book addresses topics ranging from the right to drink soda and whether it’s okay to swear, to bigger questions about truth, knowledge, race, gender and the existence of God. Hershovitz argues that kids’ questions deserve serious consideration, and that adults can learn a great deal by thinking with them. The group’s reaction was mostly positive. Many readers praised the author’s voice and humor, calling the book accessible, engaging and thought-provoking. One member compared the tone to the Pogo comic strip, while another said it inspired them to read more philosophy. Several said they planned to gift the book to their now-adult children — especially those with young kids — as a parenting guide with a philosophical twist. The title Nasty, Brutish, and Short also sparked discussion. The phrase, coined by philosopher Thomas Hobbes to describe life without government, was debated. Did it really apply to Rex and Hank? According to the book’s cover, the boys said yes — but added, “we’re not British.” Not everyone in the group was charmed. A few found the stories overly cute or cringeworthy. One reader said the tone made them feel like a bad parent. Another thought the author was trying too hard and stopped reading after 30 pages. After about 45 minutes of discussion, Witte placed the call to Hershovitz. He confirmed that the kid dialogue was accurate — if sometimes reconstructed — and said the stories often serve as warm-up material for his university classes. Don’t expect a sequel, though. The boys, now nearing their teenage years, are more conscious of privacy. “Are you going to put this in a book?” Hank now asks when a philosophical moment arises. Still, Hershovitz isn’t done writing. His next book, How to Change the Past, is due out later this year. And Hank has clearly figured out his dad’s method: when a tough question comes up, he turns it around and asks, “What do you think?” That, says Hershovitz, is the whole point. The group wrapped up by confirming future selections: Cloudstreet by Tim Winton for May, How We Got to Now by Steven Johnson for June, and — after a presentation by Lois Price — The Immortalists by Chloe Benjamin for July. With business concluded, the readers stepped outside the Community Hall to take a group photo in the spring sunshine. The group’s next discussion will be on May 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. Participating last month were Lisa Euphrat, Rebecca Schnier, Laura Goldman, Lois Price, Rich Seigel, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Phil Witte, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Martin Levy, Melba Yee, discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, Karin Fetherston, Peggy Shultz, Pat McMahon, Nadean Guffanti, Sarah Johnson, June Yee, Bella Almanzan, Bob Hall, and Dick Carter. articles.text: A pair of great horned owls have taken up residence in Dracena Park. The Piedmont Park Commission is inviting community members to share ideas to name a pair of great horned owls that have taken up residence in Dracena Park. Suggestions may be submitted online at piedmont.ca.gov/DracenaOwls. The winning names will be selected by members of the Park Commission and announced at the City’s annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration on Thursday, April 24, 4:00-6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Wildlife: part of a healthy park ecosystem Piedmont’s parks don’t just support people – they are shared spaces where local wildlife find shelter, food, and nesting grounds. Owls nesting in City parks is a sign of a healthy, thriving ecosystem. Owls play an important role in balancing the local environment, helping manage rodent populations naturally and maintaining ecological harmony. The owl-naming contest invites community members to connect more deeply with the natural world. Especially for kids and families, giving the owls a name can encourage curiosity about all the wildlife supported by Piedmont’s urban forest, which is home to raptors, songbirds, pollinators, and more. Forming connections with wildlife at a young age can spark a lifelong interest in conservation and stewardship. For more information, contact Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City holds contest for naming nesting owls in Dracena Park

Students, parents and community members engaged in a protest of the dismantling of the federal Department of Education. Piedmonters showed up in “red for Ed,” and brought signs supporting public education, and the national programs that stand on the chopping block. Support was garnered via the rally and subsequent group walk-in to school sites. Teachers spoke up for federal programs like IDEA, Title I, and Title IX. The Department of Education was founded in 1980. It distributes federal funds to K-12 schools, particularly to support students with disabilities and those from low-income families. articles.text: Following a clear mandate from the school board and strong support from Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, Piedmont Unified School District is preparing for one of its most ambitious program expansions in recent years. Funds have been allocated to add new offerings in world languages, performing arts, and advanced academic coursework—changes aimed at better preparing students for an increasingly competitive college admissions landscape. But as the district looks to move swiftly on these enhancements, teachers—the ones tasked with turning plans into reality— are urging a more deliberate approach to ensure quality and sustainability. With summer less than two months away, the 2025- 2026 master schedule remains in flux. For high school students, new offerings include the rigorous AP Capstone pathway, AP Physics C, a restored Vocal Music program, and dual enrollment through Berkeley City College for Calculus III. At the middle school level, 7th graders will now have access to Level 1 classes in Spanish, French, and Mandarin. This marks a return to a more robust foreign language offering after a recent shift removed language classes to accommodate a new Health course. At the elementary level, the district is exploring the possibility of expanding performing arts and introducing world language instruction, 100 minutes per week, for 4th and 5th graders. The proposal has raised logistical concerns from educators, who are supportive of enriching the curriculum but mindful of existing time constraints. “Teachers are supportive of these changes, but also recognize the complexity of making room for all these programs without losing the best of what we offer students now. And the proposed speed of the changes—having everything ready by fall—also caught teachers by surprise,” said teacher union President Elise Marks. “Walk-in” Rally............... 1 Editorial cartoon.............. 2 Salvation Army ............... 3 Food Fest. ...................... 4 Schools......................... 6 PHS Play Dracula............. 8 Scout Council Dinner......... 9 PPD Blue...................... 11 Sports. ......................... 12 Art & Entertainment . ........ 16 Musical Gourmet ............ 18 PCA events.................... 19 Movies. ........................ 20 Blair Park History............ 22 Wine Corner.................. 23 Wed. articles.text: The City of Piedmont celebrated the 100th anniversary of the dedication of Piedmont Community Hall and the Exedra on Friday, April 4, at Community Hall. The evening transformed the historic hall into a pop-up history exhibit, featuring photos, newspaper clippings, and archival video that took residents on a journey through the city’s past. The event also included live period music, birthday cake, and refreshments. Community Hall and the Exedra were originally dedicated on April 3, 1925, as part of architect Albert Farr’s 1922 Civic Center master plan. The plan envisioned a library, museum, municipal market square, underground streetcar tunnel, and a new City Hall on Guilford Place—but only the Community Hall and Exedra were ultimately built. Piedmont resident and historian Cameron Wolfe offered historical context to attendees about the significance of the Exedra and Community Hall. “The Greeks referred to an ‘Exedra’ as a structure that would provide a place for people to gather behind it and have conversation and fellowship together,” A Piedmont resident reads about the history of Piedmont’s public architecture.

articles.text: The Salvation Army’s 10th Annual Gala, The Way Out 2025 – A Night for Others, reached unprecedented heights this year, raising a remarkable $532,000— breaking all previous records and providing vital resources for those in need across Alameda County. Held at the elegant Claremont Country Club, the sold-out event was a stirring celebration of generosity, community, and the transformative power of the Salvation Army’s life-saving programs. A centerpiece of the evening was the presentation of the Volunteer of the Year Award to Alice Waters, the legendary chef, restaurateur, and champion of sustainable food practices. Waters, best known as the founder of Chez Panisse in Berkeley and a pioneer of the farm-to-table movement, has spent her career advocating for healthy food systems and educational initiatives like the Edible Schoolyard Project, which empowers children to learn about food production and nutrition. In her deeply personal acceptance speech, Waters shared a moving story of her childhood, recounting how, growing up with three sisters, her family could never afford new clothes. It was the Salvation Army thrift store that provided them with everything they needed—a testament to the profound and lasting impact the organization has had on her life. Lt. Col. Bettie Love (LEFT), Alice Waters, Kate Addiego, and Gala co-chair Debbie Kelley. The evening was further electrified by a thrilling auction, which included an exclusive dinner at Chez Panisse with Waters. In a heartwarming display of generosity, she not only extended the offer to include two more guests but also allowed the auctioneer to sell it twice—raising an incredible $25,000 in the process. This stunning gesture was just one of many ways the event brought the community together in support of the Salvation Army’s mission to break the cycle of poverty, homelessness, and hunger. A particularly emotional moment came when Jeff Taylor, a beneficiary of the Salvation Army’s programs, took the stage Lt. Col. Bettie Love (left) at the podium with Alice Waters. to share his powerful personal testimony. His story of overcoming adversity through the organization’s support moved the audience to tears and served as a poignant reminder of the essential role these services play in transforming lives. “This record-breaking event is a testament to the power of community,” said Debbie Kelley, chair of the gala committee and a member of the advisory board. “When we come together and give just a little, we can achieve so much. Tonight, we’ve shown that we can truly make a difference in the lives of individuals and families in need through compassion and generosity.” The funds raised will support the Salvation Army’s crucial programs across Alameda County. These programs provide shelter, food, education, and vocational training to those in need. With five properties across the county—including the only family shelter in the area that accepts boys over the age of 12—the Salvation Army continues to be a beacon of hope for thousands. For more information on The Salvation Army’s ongoing work or to contribute, visit www.alamedawayout.org. A handful of auction items are still available for sale, including a week at Cal’s Lair of the Bear Family camp. The auction page can be found at https://sadeloro2025.ggo.bid/bidding/package-browse. articles.text: Doesn’t it seem like you just paid your property taxes recently? If so, that’s because you did. The prior installment was due on December 10, 2024, and here it is – only four months later – that the Tax Collector is knocking at your door. Owners of real property in California pay property taxes twice a year, with the second installment due on April 10th. Missing the deadline is a very expensive mistake, since you will incur a penalty of 10% plus a $10 fee. If you don’t pay by June 30th, things start to get worse very quickly. Trust me on that. You can send a check, along with your 2nd payment voucher, or pay by phone. However, most people find it more convenient to pay online. The Alameda County Tax Collector’s secure URL for making payments is: https://www.acgov.org/propertytax/index.htm If you want to use a credit card and get those frequent flyer miles, you can do so, but you pay a 2.5% processing fee (the money does not go to the county). A direct debit to your bank account does not incur any additional charges. Although there are several electronic payment services (PayPal and Venmo, to name a few) in common use these days, the Tax Collector has a specific warning about PayPal on its website: NOTICE TO TAXPAYERS USING PAYPAL At this time, we are strongly discouraging the use of PayPal for your property tax payments. Using this method of payment may result in late fees and costs. With our current technology, we can only accept full payments for property taxes; partial payments are not allowed. articles.text: Piedmont City Council held a first reading at their Council meeting on Monday, April 17 for an ordinance that would permanently close the Linda Beach OffLeash Dog Area. The Ordinance would go into effect 30 days after a second reading on April 21. The topic was brought forward quickly when City Staff was contacted by the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board on February 6, regarding a citizen complaint about Linda Park’s Off-Leash Dog Area. The complaint, raising concerns about soil and animal excrement washing down the City’s storm drains, could cost the City as much as $66,000 per day in fines if it does not take action to address the Water Board’s request. Staff recommended that City Council approve the closure of Linda Park’s off-leash area, and the Council voted unanimously to move forward with the closure of the off-leash area. Concurrently, the City will begin a study with the intention to look at how the City can be a good steward of Piedmont’s parks, with an eye toward all uses that serve the needs of the community – including off-leash dog uses. “Staff takes tremendous pride in maintaining our public spaces. That’s something that we’re very proud of,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We maintain these spaces not just in the fashion that it keeps them open to the public but keeps them vibrant and well managed… when we fail to achieve that in one of our spaces, it’s not just frustrating to the public – it’s tremendously frustrating to staff, because our goal is to keep spaces open and keep them working well.” The Off-Leash Area was designated by City ordinance in December 2000, and is often closed during periods of heavy rainfall when the soil becomes muddy and unstable. According to City Staff the area’s sloped hillsides may never have been a good fit for dogs. “Over time we have seen clear evidence of soil erosion. There’s been deterioration of the ivy ground cover, exposing soil and tree roots, and it’s been very evident that active dog play and off-leash dog use has prevented vegetation from regrowing at the area as well,” said Sustainability Program Manager Denise Ergun. The topic will return to City Council for a second reading at their Monday, April 21 meeting later this month. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales addresses the City Council.
articles.title: Linda Park off-leash dog area to close for good?

The event will include timed egg hunts grouped by age: • 2 years: 9:45 a.m. • 3 years: 10:00 a.m. • 4-5 years: 10:15 a.m. • 6-7 years: 10:30 a.m. The cost of the event is $10 per participant. Kids aged two and under are admitted free. Advance registration is strongly encouraged. articles.text: The Cancer League will have its annual Spring Soiree at Trader Vic’s in Emeryville on Thursday, April 24, at 6 p.m. with a VIP reception at 5 p.m. Titled Sip & Shop for Survivorship, the event invites guests to spend an evening of shopping, mingling and supporting early-stage cancer research. The Cancer League’s Spring Soirée event is an annual pop-up boutique. One hundred percent of the funds raised at this event will directly help ‘seed the cure’ for cancer, by supporting early-stage cancer research. At this year’s event, attendees will be able to browse through high-end attire accessories and goods provided by local Bay Area merchants and artisans. Attendees will enjoy drinks and hors d’oeuvres while mingling with friends in a fun and refreshing environment. articles.text: Piedmont Adult School (PAS) will host a 50th anniversary celebration on Thursday, April 24, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from 6:30 to 8:00 p.m. The event marks 50 years of educational programming at PAS, and the public is warmly invited to attend. The free community event will include food, drinks, and mingling from 6:30 to 7:00 p.m., followed by a brief presentation. articles.text: Over the past few years, we’ve lost something precious—something many of us didn’t even realize we were missing until it was gone. Community. Not the kind you “follow” or “like” online, but the kind where someone borrows a cup of sugar, where kids ride bikes together down the block, where spontaneous laughter rings out over a shared meal. COVID accelerated this disconnection, but even before the pandemic, our shared spaces were already eroding. Busy schedules, digital distractions, and modern life have chipped away at our instinct to gather. But here’s the thing: rebuilding community doesn’t require a huge event or perfectly planned retreat. It just takes intentionality—and a bit of creativity. Creative Simplicity Is the Key We don’t need to add more to our plates—we need to reframe what’s already there. Here are a few easy, creative ways to cultivate real connection: • The Block Party Potluck: Don’t overthink it. Pick a day, put flyers in a few mailboxes or group texts, and ask people to bring a dish. Add chalk for the kids and a Bluetooth speaker for ambiance. Community will take care of the rest. • Cross-Pollination Gathering: Email 4-5 people from different parts of your life— maybe a coworker, a neighbor, a parent from your kid’s school—and invite them over for wine, tea, or dessert. Let them know the goal: meet someone new, share a story, and just be present. • Creative Shared Moments: Host a craft night, a book swap, a backyard open mic, or even a puzzle-and-popcorn evening. The activity isn’t the point. The point is to gather. • The Five-Minute Favor: Not all connection happens through events. Text someone you haven’t talked to in a while. Offer to run an errand for a busy neighbor. Ask your barista how their week’s been. Micro-acts of community build macro belonging. We’re All Craving It The magic of community isn’t in the epicness—it’s in the shared experience. And now, more than ever, we have to choose to create those experiences. When we do, we tap into something deeply human. Something healing. Something joyful. So what’s your version of a creative community moment? Start small. Stay real. And let it grow. Nina Meehan is a Communication and Creativity Coach and Speaker. https://ninameehan. com/ A block party is a great example of establishing community.
articles.title: Reclaiming community through creative connection

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group announced that it will return to Mountain View Cemetery on April 16 for a special 7th Anniversary Spring Tour, led by author and longtime cemetery docent Dennis Evanosky. This will be Evanosky’s third tour with the group, following well-attended walks in April 2023 and 2024. A historian for the Alameda Post newspaper, Evanosky has “history in his blood” and has written two books about Oakland’s history: Oakland’s Laurel District and Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery. He has also authored books on Alameda and San Francisco. The April 16 event coincides with the Walking on Wednesdays group’s 7th anniversary. Their first walk took place on April 18, 2018, and a return visit to the cemetery—known for its vibrant spring flowers and expansive views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco—offers a meaningful way to mark the occasion. Instead of meeting at their usual location at the Exedra at Magnolia and Highland Avenues in Piedmont, participants will gather in front of Mountain View Cemetery’s main mausoleum. The tour will begin at 10:30 a.m. and is expected to last about 90 minutes. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. There is no charge for the event, and free parking is available on the streets inside the cemetery. For more information, contact activity leader Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Friday, April 4 reawakened perhaps the school’s best rivalry between Piedmont High and Bishop O’Dowd’s boys’ lacrosse teams. The Highlanders defeated the Dragons 8-7 with Timmy Kalamas scoring the game-winner with just 3.6 seconds left, ending a six-game losing streak. In an exhilarating ending, O’Dowd tied the match at 7-7 with 34 seconds left. Sophomore Connor Fredericks won the faceoff, leading to Kalamas scoring in short distance to put the game away. “There were just 20 seconds left and I knew we had one shot. I waited for the clock and took my opportunity. I saw they overcommitted, so I rolled back and went for the goal from there,” Kalamas said of the play. Fredericks claiming the faceoff was a catalyst in the victory. He finished the night 10/18 on draws and lost the preceding faceoff before the final goal. It’s been unusual for Fredericks to lose more than a couple of attempts throughout Piedmont’s nine matches. But taking a line from Apple TV’s Ted Lasso, he kept the memory of a goldfish, and moved on from any frustrating moments. “I knew the pressure was on and that we needed to get down on offense; it led to a great possession by Timmy. I struggled on the face-off whistle a few times, but keeping a goldfish memory really helped to just focus on the next faceoff. Thinking makes you slower,” Fredericks said. It marked the biggest win of first--year coach Paul Pappas’ career, receiving the honorary Gatorade bath after the final buzzer sounded. The PHS Class of 2020 graduate never lost a single match against the Dragons during his playing career, and now his streak remains alive. “Th is why you come back and coach; it was emotional and fun as heck. I’m so proud of them for not giving up and embracing when things got difficult. I’m still undefeated against O’Dowd, just seeing the team happy means Staff Photos Timmy Kalamas (18) runs to midfield after scoring the game-winning goal against Bishop O’Dowd. Connor Fredericks (left) and Timmy Kalamas celebrate a goal against O’Dowd. everything to me,” Pappas said. The victory was a big moment for the Highlanders, showing their most control in possession since former coach Al Yu’s departure in 2023. “We just started doing the little things right and what we’ve been practicing all week. If you win possession and keep possession, you’re going to win a lacrosse game. The attitude switched from playing scared to playing heads-up lacrosse and really pushing for that win,” Pappas said. Senior goalie Gus Von Metzsch was a sophomore on that squad which reached the D2 NCS Championship and won the WACC league championship against O’Dowd. 8-7 over O’Dowd Both teams remained tied 1-1 through the first quarter with a goal from Ian Nguyen, but O’Dowd held PHS scoreless in the second to hold a narrow 2-1 lead at halftime. In the third quarter, the Dragons extended the gap to 3-1 with 9:13 left, but that marked the start of a six-goal scoring run for the Highlanders. From there, Fredericks assisted Nguyen for a goal with 8:21 remaining. After a shot was saved by Von Metzsch, Piedmont scored in transition with 7:02 on the clock. O’Dowd then had a near two-minute possession without a shot, leading to Von Metzsch critically scooping a ground ball near his own goal—turning it into a goal by Brendan Divine with 4:34 left to tie the match at 4-4. Piedmont made quick work of the next possession with Fredericks Head coach Paul Pappas, a PHS Class of 2020, stays undefeated against O’Dowd after finishing his playing career perfect against the Dragons.
articles.title: Lacrosse team slays Dragons with late goal by Kalamas

articles.text: Miguel Long wins Triple Jump Photos by Becky Spies Miguel Long stands next to his winning mark in the triple jump at the Stanford Invitational. Members of Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Palo Alto for the Stanford Invitational on Saturday, April 5, competing in eight events throughout the day. The Stanford Invitational brings together some of the best runners throughout the state and is considered among the most prestigious track events on the West Coast. “The Stanford Invitational is such a fun weekend, where elite high school competition from California and neighboring states and we get to warm up and race alongside top tier college athletes. The crowd is engaged, the races lived up to the hype, and everyone keeps their eyes open for runner celebrities. It’s the who’s who of NorCal and beyond. It’s so, so fun to watch,” said PHS coach Pouyan Assadi. It marked a remarkable performance by senior jumper Miguel Long, who won the Triple Jump with a distance of 45 feet, 8.5 inches in a field of 18 athletes. Coach Assadi praised Long for having a “Mamba Mentality.” “Miggy’s been a points scoring machine since he was a sophomore, but what he’s doing now is different. I figured he’d do well at Stanford but to win it is next level. I’ve always called him the Kobe Bryant of the team since he takes on every challenge we give him and he demands more,” Assadi said. Long will now compete at another prestigious event in the United States, the Arcadia Invitational on April 11-12, which attracts competition from all over the country. “Arcadia will be a good challenge for him since it’s literally the best jumpers in the US, so let’s see if he steps it up again,” Assadi said. articles.text: Will Parker hit an RBI triple against Arroyo. Staff Photos Photo by Chuck Wolf George Bishop (middle) is congratulated by assistant coach Evan Haarz for a strong outing. The freshman threw a complete game shutout against Arroyo. Piedmont’s baseball team won two of its last three games, bringing their record to 9-4 overall. The Highlanders shut out Arroyo 5-0 in San Lorenzo on Thursday, April 3, beat Concord 6-1 at the Concord Classic Varsity Tournament on Saturday, April 5, and lost to Encinal on Monday, April 7 in the Concord tournament. Freshman pitcher George Bishop had a huge performance in Piedmont’s shutout of the Dons, throwing a complete game shutout. He becomes PHS’ second ninth grader to throw a complete game shutout, joining classmate Massimo Mittone. Piedmont’s loss to Encinal marks their third meeting. The Jets and Highlanders split their two regular season games, but Monday’s game does not count as a league game because it was in a tournament. 5-0 over Arroyo Piedmont broke the 0-0 deadlock with three runs in the top of the third and added one more the following minute. The Highlanders added one more in the top of the seventh. Bishop allowed just four hits on the day. He retired the first six batters before allowing his first hit and retired Arroyo’s final six hitters in order. In the three-run third inning, Staff Photos Freshman Jonah Cha-Foster had two RBIs and scored twice in Piedmont’s win over Concord.
articles.title: Baseball team wins two of last three games

articles.text: 3-1 loss to Berean Christian in non-league game Piedmont’s softball team split its last two games. They dominated Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline foe San Lorenzo 17-7 at Witter Field on Thursday, April 3, but lost narrowly 3-1 to Berean Christian also at home two days earlier. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 4-4 overall while they are 2-0 against league opponents. In Thursday’s game, Piedmont did it without star player Miya Fujimoto and answered an early 5-0 deficit in the first inning, winning by the 10-run rule in the bottom of the sixth. “We’re getting better every game. Today, we made two early errors that led to five runs. We just had to settle down and get into a rhythm,” coach Gene Denard said. Coming back to the lineup for her third game since recovering from an injury is Sa’Mara Levi, providing the Highlanders some power to their batting order. “I feel good coming back and I’m having fun this season. My knee is still a little hurt, but I’m fine and I’m playing,” Levi said. Playing shortstop was freshman Edie Elmquist, lining up in a critical role as a first-year varsity player. “It’s inspiring to come onto this team and just put forth the work. We weren’t ready at the start of the game today missing Miya, but we just had to know we’re up for this. We took care of business after that,” Elmquist said. 17-7 over SLZ After falling behind 5-0 in the top of the first, Piedmont added two runs in the bottom half and then took a 6-5 lead in the bottom of the second. PHS added three runs in the bottom third and exploded for five runs in the fourth. After scoring one run in the fifth inning, they solidified the 10-run rule in the bottom of the sixth with two runs. In their 2-run first inning, Elmquist led off with a single. Samantha Ronen brought her in with a double, while Levi smacked a triple to score Ronen. The next inning, PHS loaded the Staff Photos Sa’Mara Levi is back in the lineup after missing early games due to an injury. bases with one-out, leading to Ronen hitting a 2-RBI single, followed by Hannah Joerger hitting another 2-RBI single to give them a 6-5 lead. SLZ tied 6-6 in the top of the third, but Piedmont scored three thanks to a Eunice Kouadio stealing home on a botched pitch, then Ronen and Joerger hit a pair of RBI singles. Piedmont big five-run inning featured Navorro and Ronen hitting RBI singles, Elmquist scored on a passed ball, then Ronen scored on a dropped third strike. Joerger brought in Levi on an error by the Grizzlies’ defense, making it 14-7. Edie Elmquist, a freshman, is starting at shortstop.
articles.title: Piedmont bashes league foe SLZ 17-7

They dominated Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline foe San Lorenzo 17-7 at Witter Field on Thursday, April 3, but lost narrowly 3-1 to Berean Christian also at home two days earlier. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 4-4 overall while they are 2-0 against league opponents. articles.text: It was a barnburner of a game, the Piedmont girls’ lacrosse team lost to rival Bishop O’Dowd 16-15 at the Dragons’ field in Oakland on Friday, April 4. The Highlanders are still 4-1 against Western Alameda County Conference teams entering Spring Break. “The girls never gave up. We were down the entire game but never out. We were able to score two in the waning minutes to get the game within one but could not win possession and O’Dowd burned out the clock,” coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont had to compete fight without several starters, allowing Dragons’ star player Lucy Yu – the daughter of former PHS boys’ coach Al Yu – to score nine of BOD’s goals. They’ll likely get one more chance with O’Dowd in the WACC Tournament. “It was disappointing but with the spring break we were missing lot of starters on defense which really hurt us. Lucy scored almost all the goals and we pinned three on her. That was a hard task missing our defenders. We will Photos by Sophie Hess Peyton Watson scored seven goals against the Dragons. Photo by Todd Marshburn Olive Litwin scored a goal against O’Dowd. Photos by Sophie Hess Friedie Schickdandz had five goals and one assist against Bishop O’Dowd. have another bite of the apple in WACC playoffs,” Chan said. 16-15 to O’Dowd O’Dowd led 5-3 through the first quarter while both teams traded goals in the second quarter with the Dragons leading 10-9 by halftime. Bishop O’Dowd took a 13-12 lead into the fourth quarter, but Piedmont couldn’t pull ahead with three goals apiece. In the first quarter, O’Dowd came out with a two goal lead in the first minute, but Friedie Schickedanz helped pull Piedmont back with a pair of scores at 10:25 and 6:52. BOD then scored three unanswered goals to lead 5-2 with 4:11 left, while Jameson Sanford pulled one back with 1:50 remaining, 5-3. Peyton Watson scored a few minutes into the second quarter, down 5-4, but O’Dowd’s Yu scored the next two goals. Schickedanz made it a 7-5 deficit with 5:43 left, then Yu scored again 40 seconds later and BOD scored again on its next possession, up 9-5 with 4:29 left. Piedmont then scored three straight to make it a 9-8 deficit with 1:48 left with goals by Watson, Schickedanz, and Watson again. O’Dowd got one more, but Olive Litwin netted one with 11 seconds left. Both sides played with strong defense in the third. Watson broke through with 4:40 left to tie it at 10-10, but O’Dowd scored three times in the final minutes. Watson scored again with 12 seconds left to make it 13-11 in favor of O’Dowd. Yu scored again for O’Dowd 48 seconds into the fourth quarter, but Chloe Graham answered a couple of minutes later. After another O’Dowd goal with 8:24 left, Watson answered 20 seconds later on the next possession, making it 15-13. BOD got its last goal with 6:55 left, while Watson scored with 2:40 left after back and forth possessions. Schickedanz pulled it to a single-goal deficit with 1:21 left, but O’Dowd got ahold of possession on the next draw and killed out the clock. Final stats: Watson scored seven goals and scooped five balls out of the draw. Schickedanz scored five goals, one assist, and helped win three draws. Graham had one goal, helped win one draw, and scooped one loose ball. Sanford scored once. articles.text: Honorable Mention: George Bishop & Samantha Ronen This week, we are naming Miguel Long of the track and field team as our boys’ Athlete of the Week, and Saniyah Johnson of track and field as our girls’ Athlete of the Week. Earning honorable mentions are George Bishop of the baseball team and softball player Samantha Ronen. Miguel Long made a lasting impression at the prestigious Stanford Invitational on Saturday, April 5. Recording a triple jump of 45 feet, 8.5 inches, Long won the event over 17 other toplevel athletes. His mark is currently 3.5 inches shy of Nikka Piterman’s school record of 46 feet set in 2011. Saniyah Johnson is a junior at PHS and, with basketball, is a two-sport athlete. She recently set a school record in the shot put with a distance of 32 feet, 6.5 inches at a WACC Meet on April 2 at Arroyo. She snapped Kylie Hilton’s 2018 record of 31 feet, 8.5 inches. Honorable Mentions Freshman George Bishop earns an honorable mention for recording a complete game shutout in Piedmont’s 5-0 shutout of Arroyo on April 3. Bishop recorded eight strikeouts, walked one, and allowed just four hits in the 7-inning game. Samantha Ronen earns an honorable mention for leading the softball team past San Lorenzo in a 17-7 win. She stepped in as pitcher with Miya Fujimoto out, recording eight strikeouts over all seven innings. She also made a big impact with the bat, going 4-for-4 with a double, five RBIs, and scored three runs. He recently elected to enter the transfer portal and is seeking his new school. Murphy led the entire CCAA with an average of 20.5 points per game and a .395 3-point shooting percent. They also competed in the 26th Annual Spring Golf Classic at Monarch Bay. Most recently on April 2 at Lake Chabot Golf Course Piedmont shot a collective score of 219 strokes, beating Encinal’s 229 but falling by just five strokes to Alameda at 214. On March 26, Piedmont shot 212 at Monarch Bay in San Leandro, toppling Arroyo’s 291 but narrowly falling by five strokes to Castro Valley’s 207. Piedmont finished 12th of 27 schools also finished 12th of 27 schools at the Spring Gold Classic. They closed the day with 407 strokes in the 18-hole tournament. Sophomore Derek Lee was Piedmont’s low medalist in all three matches. He shot a 36 at Lake Chabot, a 37 at Monarch Bay tri-match, and a 71 at the Spring Golf Classic. Here’s a recap of both tournaments. Wright finished with a 46, while Henry Pfister had a 47. Lee shot a birdie on the fifthhole 374 yard par 4, where he hit a nice chip onto the green before sinking a putt from a few feet. Monarch Bay Tournament Lee finished with Piedmont’s best round, once again, shooting a round of 37 strokes, which was good enough for +2 over par. Wright was next best with a 42, Bloemker shot a 44, Julien Porter also finished with 44, while Pfister was one stroke back with 45. Spring Golf Classic Piedmont finished with a round of 407 strokes to finish 12th of 27 teams. Lee led the way with a round of 71, which was even-par on the day. Porter shot a 79, Bloemker finished in 85, whole Vankleek and Wright both shot round of 86. Lee was among the lowest scores of the day. articles.text: Free Community Day is this Sunday, Apr. 13 Ruth Asawa: Retrospective, the first posthumous retrospective of the groundbreaking work of California modernist Ruth Asawa, is now on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA). Organized by SFMOMA and the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the exhibition features more than 300 works of art, including the looped-wire hanging sculptures for which Asawa is best known. The retrospective also includes drawings, prints, paintings, and archival materials drawn from both public and private collections. “Ruth Asawa: Retrospective is deeply aligned with SFMOMA’s vision to be both local and global—presenting Bay Area artists with profound significance that also have the potential to be highly impactful and relevant on an international scale,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “This exhibition provides an opportunity to celebrate the legendary Ruth Asawa, who was both a widely acclaimed artist and a hometown inspiration whose impact can be very much felt today.” Spanning more than six decades, the exhibition highlights how Asawa’s longtime San Francisco home and garden served as inspiration for her artistic practice, public sculpture commissions, and tireless advocacy for arts education in the city. The retrospective is co-curated by Janet Bishop, Thomas Weisel Family Chief Curator and Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. “It is an immense privilege to present the full range of Ruth Asawa’s life’s work through this retrospective,” said Bishop. “Not only was Asawa an exceptionally talented artist—among the most distinguished sculptors of the 20th century and a major contributor in so many other mediums—but she lived her values in everything she did, modeling the importance of the arts and opening up creative opportunities for others at every turn.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective will remain on view through Sept. 2. SFMOMA will offer free admission on Saturday, April 13, to celebrate the exhibition with interactive programming and performances for younger visitors. Admission is also free for residents of the nine Bay Area counties on the first Thursday of each month. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415.357.4000 for more information. articles.text: 1st place: “Beeline to the Blossoms” by Marilyn Wear The California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition came to a close this past week following a successful and warmly received run at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The vibrant water-media show featured works by 85 national and international artists, selected by award-winning artist Michael Holter. Of those, 22 pieces received awards chosen by renowned Bay Area artist Gary Bukovnik. During the opening reception, Bukovnik shared insight into the challenge of judging such a high-caliber exhibition. “This exhibition was possibly the most difficult art show for me to judge. There is so much excellence,” he said. When asked about his judging criteria, he added, “Well, aside from my own personal biases—the nature of being human—I like to see that people are able to express their ideas.” The top three awards were presented as follows: • First Place – CWA Gold Award ($2,300): Beeline to the Blossoms by Marilyn Wear • Second Place – CWA Silver Award ($1,800): Orange Blossoms by Chris Krupinski • Third Place – CWA Bronze Award ($1,400): Emigrant Lake Hike by Linda Erfle In addition to juried prizes, attendees of the five-week exhibition were invited to vote for the People’s Choice Award, which was also awarded to second-place winner Chris Krupinski. If you missed the show, you can still see the paintings on CWA’s online gallery at https:// bit.ly/55thShow. If you have any questions or would like more information on a painting, please email sales@californiawatercolor.org. articles.text: Maestro Joseph Young Berkeley Symphony will celebrate the legacy of its fourth Music Director, Maestro Joseph Young, at its 2025 Spring Gala on Saturday, May 10, at the Unitarian Universalist Church in Kensington. Young first guest-conducted the symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute and was soon invited to become its next music director—his first appointment in that role—following the success of that initial concert. In November 2024, the symphony announced that Young will conclude his tenure at the end of the current season. During his leadership, Young guided the orchestra through the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic and widespread performing arts venue closures. He launched digital programming initiatives and secured key grants to promote diversity and equity within the orchestra’s staff and musician ranks. In the 2024–25 season, Young has continued to grow his national and international profile with debuts and return engagements at the National Philharmonic, Orquesta Sinfónica RTVE, the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic, and the Louisville Orchestra, among others. The 2025 gala will be hosted by Dianne Nicolini, midday host on KDFC Classical California, and will include live performances by Berkeley Symphony musicians and special guest artists. The evening will feature a hilltop reception with sweeping views of the Bay Area, along with hors d’oeuvres, an open bar, and a three-course dinner catered by Carrie Dove Catering. Guests can sponsor a table or purchase individual tickets, starting at $500. To learn more or make a sponsorship gift, email Gillian Eorwyn, Director of Development and Communications, at georwyn@berkeleysymphony.org or call 510-841- 2800.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony to Honor Music Director Joseph Young at 2025 Spring Gala

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is honoring the legacy of esteemed Dutch choreographer Hans van Manen with a mixed-bill program titled Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster, on stage now through April 19 at the War Memorial Opera House. The program features a selection of van Manen’s most acclaimed ballets, including Grosse Fuge, Variations for Two Couples, Solo, and, making its San Francisco premiere, 5 Tangos. Curated by San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo, the program showcases a blend of classical and contemporary styles, set to music by composers such as Astor Piazzolla, Bach, and Beethoven. “Hans van Manen is the most important choreographer of the Dutch tradition, and we are thrilled to bring four works from his oeuvre to San Francisco,” Rojo said. “His legacy is unparalleled, shaping what we think of now as the signature Dutch style. What appears to be simple choreography is actually quite difficult to perform.” Rojo added that the works “[focus] on musicality and powerful exchanges of energy between humans, [and] allow the ComPhoto by Lindsey Rallo Dores André and Esteban Hernández in van Manen’s 5 Tango’s pany to showcase their charisma, top-tier virtuosity, and individuality.” “It’s a wonderful opportunity to witness SF Ballet’s dancers take on a uniquely European style,” she said. Dores André, Max Cauthorn, Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, Jasmine Jimison, Wona Park, Jennifer Stahl, Joseph Walsh, and Wei Wang make their role debuts as Principal dancers in ‘Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster.’ Performance showtimes vary. Tickets are available for purchase at www.sfballet.org or by calling Ticket Services at 415-865-2000, open Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. - 4 p.m.
articles.title: SF Ballet honors Hans van Manen legacy in ‘Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster’

articles.text: Registration for free event is recommended San Francisco Opera’s highly anticipated Bohéme Out of the Box returns to Sausalito in Marin County on Saturday, April 26, and Sunday, April 27. The company’s acclaimed musicians and singers will perform an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème just steps from downtown Sausalito’s picturesque waterfront, with sweeping views of San Francisco Bay as a backdrop. This 70-minute traveling production is performed live on a mobile stage crafted from a repurposed shipping container and features musical excerpts from La Bohème sung in Italian. English narration will be available through guests’ cell phones. Originally conceived as part of San Francisco Opera’s 100th anniversary season, Bohéme Out of the Box continues to engage audiences across the Bay Area, with recent performances in Hayward and San Ramon. Sausalito guests are encouraged to pack a picnic or enjoy food and beverages from the many nearby restaurants along Bridgeway. Chairs will be available on a first-come, first-served basis at the parking lot performance site, but attendees are welcome to bring their own seating. Both performances begin at 2 p.m. and will take place in the parking lot adjacent to the Sausalito Center for the Arts. Guests are also invited to visit the gallery space, which will be showcasing work from more than 250 artists participating in Marin Open Studios. Bohéme Out of the Box is presented in partnership with the Sausalito Paks and Recreation Department and the Sausalito Center for the Arts. Families with young children are invited to participate in free “First Act Workshops” 30 minutes prior to each performance. Bohème Out of the Box is a free event. Registration at sfopera.com/box is now available and encouraged but not required. San Francisco Opera’s free production is performed on a mobile stage made from a repurposed shipping container.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera’s “Bohème Out of the Box” returns to Sausalito

articles.text: Music education for kids is so important. It helps to start young, whether singing or playing an instrument. This fact was brought home to me when I attended a musical program of first graders. It was an impressive, all encompassing, one hour program of singing and recitations. The kids even sang in different languages. The expressions of joy on their faces spoke volumes. These days, gigantic events get all of the publicity. We need to consider the smaller venues. The musical salon was “the” place for many of the great names of the past. Franz Schubert was at his best in the drawing room. Royalty was very active in the employment of court musicians for that very reason. They employed some of the most famous musicians of all time. Names like Paganini, Chopin and Liszt are just a few. These musical salons were at least as popular as the larger concert venues. It is no surprise, therefore, that some very interesting things happened at these concerts. For example. at one musical soirée a Parisian Contessa engaged Franz Liszt list to play some of Chopin’s music for her guests; Chopin was one of the guests. This played in his grand manor. When the applause had subsided, the Contessa asked Frederick Chopin, the composer, what he thought of the performance. Wouldn’t you know it, Chopin was highly critical of the competitor’s performance. He didn’t like it at all, and he expressed his opinions in a commanding tone of voice. The poor Contessa was flabbergasted. She asked Chopin if he would perform the music the way he wanted it played. He suggested that the entire audience assemble in a week and he would play the proper way. He made another stipulation: he wanted to play in complete darkness. The following week everyone was present and Chopin seated himself at the piano. The lights were extinguished and the audience was told to close their eyes. Chopin performed exquisitely. When he finished, the lights were brought back, and the audience opened its eyes. What they saw was shocking to say the least. Chopin was not at the piano at all. Seated at the piano was Franz Liszt. Chopin and Liszt had pulled off one of the great musical stunts of all time. It is my firm belief that the Contessa was part of this ruse because Chopin and Liszt were consummate gentlemen, and they would not embarrass their hostess. One more story bears repeating. articles.text: This April join Berkeley Symphony on A Viennese Sojourn. This concert, curated by violinist René Mandel, invites listeners to spend an afternoon transported to eighteenth-century Vienna. The program, comprised of favorites from Mandel’s childhood in his half-Austrian family, includes the charming and romantic Serenade by Ernst Von Dohnányi, Maria Theresia von Paradis’s sweet Sicilienne for cello accompanied by string quartet, and Franz Schubert’s lush and lyrical String Quintet in C major.
