articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is launching a new series of monthly nighttime events beginning Friday, April 18, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was developed following the success of an inaugural December night market that drew more than 10,000 attendees. Beginning April 18 and continuing monthly through December, FMCAC will host outdoor markets that transform its iconic waterfront campus into a lively showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place—a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s president and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” Off the Grid will feature more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event, while attendees can enjoy performances by local DJs, participate in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC’s collections. West Coast Craft—founded in San Francisco in 2013 to provide a platform for independent artists and designers—will also take part. Known for one of the largest arts fairs in the country, West Coast Craft traditionally hosts its annual summer event at FMCAC. Artisans who appear at that festival will be invited to showcase and sell their work at the monthly Night Market. “This new market is an exciting evolution of what we started back in 2010 with the original Off the Grid festival [in San Francisco],” said Matt Cohen, founder of Off the Grid. “This time around, we’re expanding our offerings to include both crowd favorites and emerging food creators, plus joining forces with West Coast Craft and FMCAC to offer an interactive shopping, dining, artistic, and community experience—a perfect blend that is quintessentially San Francisco.” Paulina Nassar, co-founder of West Coast Craft, said the collaboration creates “an incredible opportunity for our community of artists and designers to connect with their customers in a new, vibrant format—shopping from exceptional vendors while enjoying the arts programming and amazing dining options that make Fort Mason a unique destination.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. Night Markets are held on the following dates: April 18, May 30, June 27, July 18, August (Date TBA), September 5, October 17, November (Date TBA), and December 12, 2025. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2025/. Fort Mason’s inaugural night market in December 2024 drew over 10,000 attendees.
articles.title: Fort Mason launches “Night Market” events April 18

articles.text: Saturday, April 12, 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. Oakland Art Association Exhibition Don’t miss the artists’ opening reception for this stunning juried exhibition of Oakland Art Association’s members’ works, titled The World Around Us. For the next eight weekends starting April 12, until June 1, 2025, the gallery will be open and staffed with member artists from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday, except April 20 and May 10. There is no charge. Active since 1957, OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties.. pages.text: Wednesday, April 9, 2025 19 Fort Mason launches “Night Market” events April 18 By Allyson Aleksey The Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is launching a new series of monthly nighttime events beginning Friday, April 18, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was developed following the success of an inaugural December night market that drew more than 10,000 attendees. Beginning April 18 and continuing monthly through December, FMCAC will host outdoor markets that transform its iconic waterfront campus into a lively showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place—a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s president and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” Off the Grid will feature more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event, while attendees can enjoy performances by local DJs, participate in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC’s collections. West Coast Craft—founded in San Francisco in 2013 to provide a platform for independent artists and designers—will also take part. Known for one of the largest arts fairs in the country, West Coast Craft traditionally hosts its annual summer event at FMCAC. Artisans who appear at that festival will be invited to showcase and sell their work at the monthly Night Market. “This new market is an exciting evolution of what we started back in 2010 with the original Off the Grid festival [in San Francisco],” said Matt Cohen, founder of Off the Grid. “This time around, we’re expanding our offerings to include both crowd favorites and emerging food creators, plus joining forces with West Coast Craft and FMCAC to offer an interactive shopping, dining, artistic, and community experience—a perfect blend that is quintessentially San Francisco.” Paulina Nassar, co-founder of West Coast Craft, said the collaboration creates “an incredible opportunity for our community of artists and designers to connect with their customers in a new, vibrant format—shopping from exceptional vendors while enjoying the arts programming and amazing dining options that make Fort Mason a unique destination.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. Night Markets are held on the following dates: April 18, May 30, June 27, July 18, August (Date TBA), September 5, October 17, November (Date TBA), and December 12, 2025. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2025/. articles.text: I did not expect to laugh, let alone smile at what I assumed would be a shallow tale about four old friends who bask in the soft glow of the affluent L.A. burbs. I saw the trailer, a brief scene of these wonderful actors from the 70s, sitting in a fantasy kitchen making quick work of the novel Wild by Cheryl Strayed: “She hiked. She lost her boots. She did heroin.” Next would be, surprise!, Fifty Shades of Grey, brought to the group by Vivian (Jane Fonda), a book that immediately evokes resistance from the other three women, Diane (Diane Keaton), Carol (Mary Steenburgen), and It’s at this point that I jettisoned my prejudice and began to be won over by what proves to be a very funny movie. Way beyond Book Club is bawdy, ribald, delightfully honest, but rarely indulges in unnecessary raunchy humor. Most of the time it is just flat-out funny and 104 minutes of loosely connected vignettes, focusing on the individual women who are all bright, successful, with a nexus of loneliness in the Book Club is not a hot air balloon; rather it conveys how much fun these four actors are having – call it a hoot – as they inhabit their characters who are exchanging thoughts regarding sex (or lack thereof), aging, and, of course, men. Each is a master of the stylized apercu, while Candice Bergen, Jane Fonda, Diane Keaton, and Mary Steenburgen in Book Club rejecting any semblance of yielding. These are not women who accept the condescending moniker, “Senior Citizen”; rather, they are vital and brimming with warmth and good will for one another, and for life in general. They’re great to hang out with, which they’ve been doing regularly for 40 years. Actually E.L. James’ 50 Shades is but a catalyst and not a novel they will ever take the time to discuss, at least not in the literary sense. React to, sure. Sharon does say, with conviction, putting bondage and carnality aside, “it’s simply a love story.” Right. The novel does, however, frame the film’s central story and prompts each of them to pause and ponder what might be missing in their personal lives, especially in regards to men and their sexuality. Concerning the men (Craig T. Nelson, Andy Garcia, Richard Dreyfus and Don Johnson), they are incidental, their rough edges nicely sanded down. The point is that this is a movie about women, well past middle age, and how they cope with their lives, replete with lots of wonderful brio. Book Club. Directed by Bill Holderman. articles.text: It’s been over 25 years since Jurassic Park roared onto screens—Steven Spielberg’s masterful adaptation of Michael Crichton’s novel about dinosaurs resurrected through genetic engineering. The original film was a seismic hit, combining the spectacle of blockbuster action with the primal thrill of horror. The image of a raptor’s unblinking eye or a torso dangling from its jaws still lingers in pop culture memory. At its core, the Jurassic series, like Jaws before it, taps into a timeless fear: a predator unleashed, and humans rendered helpless in the face of nature’s ancient power. That sense of overwhelming vulnerability is the franchise’s enduring magic. And while every installment since has varied in tone and scale, together they’ve built a surprisingly durable—and consistently thrilling— cinematic universe. The latest chapter, Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom, is the second film in the new trilogy that began with Jurassic World. The setup is simple: Isla Nublar, once the site of a fully functioning dinosaur theme park, has been abandoned after its inevitable collapse. Now, a once-dormant volcano is about to erupt, threatening the remaining dinosaurs. Claire (Bryce Dallas Howard) and Owen (Chris Pratt) are recruited by aging philanthropist Benjamin Lockwood (James Cromwell) to rescue the animals and transport them to a safe, human-free sanctuary. But not all is as it seems. Lockwood’s assistant, driven by greed, has other plans—namely, auctioning off the dinosaurs to the highest bidders. articles.text: From Up on Poppy Hill was written by Hayao Miyazaki, fat her of d i rector Goro Miyazaki, and is based on the manga story by Tetsuro Sayama. Absent the fantastical, devoid of that floating sense of the surreal so often embedded in Studio Ghibli’s animated features, Poppy Hill is a touching, straight-forward, unsentimental coming-of-age story about a strong-willed 16-year-old girl named Umi (Sarah Bolger) who meets and become much enamored with Shun (Anton Melchin), a member of a geeky group of boys who inhabit an aging wreck of a building out of which they run a newspaper of which he is the editor. The story is set in Yokohama, over looking a sweeping bay. The year is 1963, and Japan is only just beginning to fully emerge from the devastation wrought by WWII. Umi, whose father was lost at sea, and her mother is presently studying in America, helps her grandmother (Jamie Lee Curtis) run a boarding house. She is responsible for much of the cleaning and shopping while attending a nearby high school and struggling to keep up with her schoolwork. In the opening scenes, we see Umi raising a flag in homage to her much missed father. She is spotted by Shun who works on his father’s tugboat. A scene from Miyazaki’s From Up on Poppy Hill Umi soon meets Shun and learns about his and his friends’ resistance to the razing of an old building they occupy as part of urban renewal. The struggle is between reverence for the past and the urge by officials to move toward a new, more modern Japan. The Olympics is slated to arrive in Japan in 1964. Umi joins Shun and friends in a campaign protesting the removal of the building and the more time she and Shun spend together the deeper their connection grows, and soon the story finds that tentative teenage romance sweet spot. However, not atypical for Studio Ghibli, screenwriter Hayao Miyazaki introduces a plot curve that causes Umi and Shun deep consternation, information that they find all but impossible to resolve. Of course, the hand-drawn animation of Up on Poppy Hill is as good as any work produced by the Studio, the characters are appealing, the background images wonderfully created. Also not surprising, is that the story stresses the power of goodness while being, in its special way, light and breezy and filled with youthful idealism leavened by a certain wistfulness. It is both inspirational and enjoyable. From Up on Poppy Hill. Directed by Goro Miyazaki. Written by Hayao Miyazaki. With voices of Sarah Bolger, Anton Melchin, and Jamie Lee Curtis. pages.text: Wednesday, April 9, 2025 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS From Up on Poppy Hill another gem from Miyazaki By Chris Honoré From Up on Poppy Hill was written by Hayao Miyazaki, fat her of d i rector Goro Miyazaki, and is based on the manga story by Tetsuro Sayama. Absent the fantastical, devoid of that floating sense of the surreal so often embedded in Studio Ghibli’s animated features, Poppy Hill is a touching, straight-forward, unsentimental coming-of-age story about a strong-willed 16-year-old girl named Umi (Sarah Bolger) who meets and become much enamored with Shun (Anton Melchin), a member of a geeky group of boys who inhabit an aging wreck of a building out of which they run a newspaper of which he is the editor. The story is set in Yokohama, over looking a sweeping bay. The year is 1963, and Japan is only just beginning to fully emerge from the devastation wrought by WWII. Umi, whose father was lost at sea, and her mother is presently studying in America, helps her grandmother (Jamie Lee Curtis) run a boarding house. She is responsible for much of the cleaning and shopping while attending a nearby high school and struggling to keep up with her schoolwork. In the opening scenes, we see Umi raising a flag in homage to her much missed father. She is spotted by Shun who works on his father’s tugboat. A scene from Miyazaki’s From Up on Poppy Hill Umi soon meets Shun and learns about his and his friends’ resistance to the razing of an old building they occupy as part of urban renewal. The struggle is between reverence for the past and the urge by officials to move toward a new, more modern Japan. The Olympics is slated to arrive in Japan in 1964. Umi joins Shun and friends in a campaign protesting the removal of the building and the more time she and Shun spend together the deeper their connection grows, and soon the story finds that tentative teenage romance sweet spot. However, not atypical for Studio Ghibli, screenwriter Hayao Miyazaki introduces a plot curve that causes Umi and Shun deep consternation, information that they find all but impossible to resolve. Of course, the hand-drawn animation of Up on Poppy Hill is as good as any work produced by the Studio, the characters are appealing, the background images wonderfully created. Also not surprising, is that the story stresses the power of goodness while being, in its special way, light and breezy and filled with youthful idealism leavened by a certain wistfulness. It is both inspirational and enjoyable. From Up on Poppy Hill. Directed by Goro Miyazaki. Written by Hayao Miyazaki. With voices of Sarah Bolger, Anton Melchin, and Jamie Lee Curtis. Fallen Kingdom Continued from page 20 rian estate, where they’re stored in cages beneath the manor in preparation for sale. Claire and Owen, along with allies Zia (Daniella Pineda) and Franklin (Justice Smith), sneak onto the evacuation boat and follow the dinosaurs to the mainland. What follows is a dark, gothic turn for the franchise, as the action shifts from jungle to mansion. The Lockwood estate, filled with dioramas and dinosaur bones, becomes a new kind of haunted house—only the monsters are very much alive. Of course, chaos ensues. Dinosaurs escape. Chaos deepens. The film also keeps with the franchise’s tradition of including young protagonists. Here, Lockwood’s granddaughter Maisie (Isabella Sermon) delivers one of the movie’s most chilling moments: frozen in bed, blanket pulled to her chin, as an Indoraptor—a genetically engineered predator—slowly taps its claw across the floor beside her. It’s the kind of scene that will burrow into the minds of younger viewers, just as the shark fin did in Jaws. And that’s the point. These films are meant to thrill, especially for a younger audience looking to be spooked in all the right ways. As co-writer Colin Trevorrow—who directed Jurassic World—put it in an email exchange: “We have a responsibility to appeal to everyone around the world. These movies don’t belong to America, they’re global, and they need to incorporate universal themes that can connect with a hugely diverse audience. It’s not just about age. It’s diversity of experience, of context. Many movies have the luxury of appealing to one group. We have to think about everybody.” Fallen Kingdom is a classic “bridge” film—setting the stage for the final chapter of the trilogy. “We can’t get to where we’re going without this,” Trevorrow added. “The dynamic between the characters has completely shifted by the end of this story. The equilibrium of the planet has been altered. Nothing will ever be the same for them, or the world they live in.” The challenge ahead? Making the third film feel fresh while honoring the themes that have carried the franchise this far. But Jurassic was never just about spectacle—it’s always been about fragility, the illusion of control, and the terrifying beauty of nature unchained. Like the woman in Jaws taking a midnight swim, we never quite know what’s circling beneath the surface—until it’s too late. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Directed by J.A. Bayona. He failed to let go of the line and rose with the balloon - 300, 600, 900 feet up in the air. The tether failed. It was a terrible sight to see little Bertram dangling from the line and holding on for his life while balloonist Charles Conlon attempted to return the balloon to earth. Unfortunately, Bertram’s strength gave out before the balloon could descend, and he fell to his death. His body was found a half mile away on farmland in the Montclair hills. The public lost its taste for balloon ascensions in Blair Park after little Bertram’s death, and the ascensions in Blair Park ended shortly thereafter. What Became of Blair Park? As fine as the intentions of the park operators were, Blair Park seems to have encountered problems almost immediately. In 1892, the Oakland Tribune reported that “gamblers had things their own way up at Blair Park” and described prospering shell games. Citizens were also concerned that the planned casino would attract “scum and hoodlum.” In 1896 the Board of Directors of Mountain View Cemetery complained that “the balloon ascensions on Sundays from Blair Park is [sic] becoming a great nuisance, attracting a great crowd of the hoodlum element and causing a disturbance in the Cemetery Grounds.” They called on the Sheriff to protect the cemetery grounds and arrest trespassers. The fate of Blair Park was tied to the fiscal success of the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company. In 1892, electric trolleys were replacing the cable cars and competing for ridership. Due to the great expense of building the cable line, the Piedmont Cable Company went into receivership in 1893, and the assets were sold at auction in 1895. Walter Blair’s heirs continued to own the park land, but it was heavily mortgaged. In 1897 all of Blair’s 235 acres, including Blair Park, were for sale. Mountain View Cemetery bought 1-1/2 acres on the northern edge of the park. In 1901, the Cable Company announced that it was abandoning the park and that it would not reopen that spring. By 1902, Frank C. Havens and the Realty Syndicate owned the park land. The park was set for development. Throughout these last years, Blair Park continued to operate. Voters approved the purchase of Dracena and Linda Parks, but not Blair Park. In 1917, new homes began to appear on the Blair Park site. Builder Guy Taylor built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue, both shingled and stucco styles. He returned in 1922 to build at least 6 more bungalows. As you drive along Moraga Avenue today, you can see the similarities that many of these homes share. Blair Park Today The early sketches show Blair Park in a grove of eucalyptus trees. Walter Blair thinned some of these trees to make paths and picnic areas. The Cable Company thinned more trees to make room for their attractions. Finally, more eucalyptus were thinned when the houses were built along Moraga Avenue. Today, the former grove of eucalyptus is just a narrow row of trees along the cemetery border. Lombardi To attract more riders on their cable car line to Piedmont, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company built a Bandstand for concerts, a Tea House, Maze, Venetian Canal and small amusements for children. As the Cable Company failed to make a profit and was going into receivership in 1893, they added balloon ascensions to attract more riders on their cable cars. Hot Air Balloon Ascensions There was always an element of excitement and danger with the hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park, and they drew many visitors. By 1896, there were balloon ascensions every Sunday and on the 4th of July. Balloonists were considered daredevils, and for 25 cents visitors could ride up with the balloonist. Most of the balloon ascensions at Blair Park were aerial gymnasts, “dressed in spangles and tights” and doing “hair raising” stunts on a trapeze suspended from a captive balloon. It was exciting to watch the balloon fill with hot air. Young boys were allowed to hold the anchor lines as the balloon filled. As the aerialist climbed into the balloon basket, the balloon handler ordered the boys to “Let Go!” Visitors watched in awe as the balloon rose over their heads. One particularly daring aerialist hung upside down from the trapeze bar as it ascended. After several acrobatic stunts on the bar, the aerialist finished with a parachute drop from a height of 1000 feet. The balloon was on a long tether, and the balloon manager pulled it back to earth at the end of the show. One Sunday a balloon ascension ended fatally. For years we have run into Miro Tcholakov at various wine events, mostly the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers tastings. We have always been impressed by his wines so it is great to have an opportunity to go into depth and analyze his wine portfolio. Miro grew up in a wine-making family in Bulgaria and studied winemaking there. In 1990 he was accepted into an exchange program that gave him the opportunity to work as an intern and learn the wine business from the inside out. He landed at Dry Creek Winery in Sonoma County and spent 9 years there, ending up as Assistant Winemaker. In 1999 he was hired to be winemaker at Trentadue Winery in Sonoma. In addition to making the Trentadue wines in 2001 he started his own wine label, Miro, and made the wines at the Trentadue facility. The Miro wines are sourced from a variety of vineyards around the state, wherever he can find good grapes. “So many vineyards, too little time,” Miro laments. Though he makes a wide range of varietals, he fell in love with Zinfandel and Petite Sirah which have continued to be his specialties under both Trentadue and Miro labels. Miro has served on the board of the Zinfandel Advocates and Producers association as well as the P.S. I Love You group that promotes Petite Sirah. Additionally, Miro has become an in-demand judge at wine competitions, participating in judging about 10 wine competitions a year. After coming to the U,S, Miro took classes in enology at UC Davis but he has for the most part left that “schoolbook” winemaking behind. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Springtime means brunch time for many of us. And finally, we are slated for some dry and sunny days to gather with family and friends. I often make a frittata for our Sunday brunch. It’s usually in a 12-inch skillet to savor leftovers the next day. I’ve modified a springtime favorite to bake in muffin tins for individual servings, ideal for entertaining and your brunch spread. Advance notes: It’s important to liberally grease each muffin cup, even if for “nonstick” pans. If well buttered or oiled, the muffins are removed easily. Omit this if using parchment liners. I add the salmon, asparagus pieces (saving the tips for topping), crumbled cheese and chives into the egg mixture; just as I do for a large frittata. For mini-frittatas, carefully fill each cup with about the same amounts of everything in each. If you want to be more precise, layer the fillings before adding the egg mix as follows: asparagus pieces, salmon pieces, crumbled cheese and lastly chives on top. Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Serves 12 INGREDIENTS • 10 large eggs • 1/2 cup whole milk • 4 ounces cold smoked, sliced sockeye salmon • 12 stalks asparagus, about the diameter of a pencil. • 2.5 ounces goat cheese, crumbled (about 1/3 cup) • 1/4 cup fresh chives, cut into 1/4-inch lengths • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste • 2 teaspoons olive oil, extra-virgin • Vegetable oil spray or butter for greasing the muffin tins. Omit if using parchment liners. INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 12-cup muffin pan by liberally greasing each cup or use parchment liners. Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 425°F. Cut a 1-1/2 inch length of the asparagus tips off, then cut the remaining stalks into 1/2-inch pieces to measure a generous one-half cup of pieces. Heat the 2 teaspoons of olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Add all the asparagus pieces and sauté until just tender. Remove from heat and set aside. Separate the asparagus tips from the 1/2-inch pieces, the tips will be used to decorate the tops of each frittata. Cut the smoked salmon into 1/2-inch squares by first cutting the entire piece of adhered sliced salmon in half lengthwise. Stack the two pieces atop each other, then cut in 1/2-inch strips lengthwise. Turn the strips 90-degrees and cut these strips crosswise in 1/2-inch increments. Gently separate the slices. It’s OK if there are a few of the thin slices stick together. Whisk together the eggs, milk, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Add the salmon, asparagus pieces, cheese, and chives and stir to evenly distribute. (Optional: see the advance note above to layer the filling.) Divide evenly among muffin cups, leaving about 1/4-inch from the rim. Bake for 10 minutes, then remove the muffin pan to place an asparagus tip atop each mini frittata. Return to the oven, continue baking until the frittatas are lightly browned, set in the center, and puffed up. Total baking time is about 18 – 20 minutes. (Their puffy splendor is temporary, as they will fall to about even to the rim upon removal from the oven.) Transfer the muffin pan to a wire rack and cool for 10 minutes. Use a small silicone spatula to loosen around the edges and bottoms of each tin. Remove gently and serve warm. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on April 5, 2023.

articles.text: • 2022 Petite Sirah, $38 Petite Sirah is a lesser known and often overlooked varietal. It dates back to the late 19th century in France, where it was created by Francois Durif as a hybrid of Syrah and Peloursin. It is called “Petite” because of its dense, small grape clusters which produce dark colored, powerful wines with lots of tannin. This 2022 wine from Miro was our favorite of the evening. Striking, dark purple in hue, it opens with a complex nose of blueberry, vanilla oak, violets, and hints of tar. Huge body, full of dark fruit coupled with ample tannins. Well-structured and deeply satisfying, this wine is a gem and will benefit from a decade in the cellar. Serve it with aged Gouda, barbecued ribs, or grilled lamb. The Miro Petite Sirah is his finest wine.

Zinfandel is one of Miro’s specialties. • 2022 Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve Pine Mountain Vineyard $52 Hailing from a vineyard on Cloverdale Peak the wine shows a touch of vanilla oak on the nose giving way to cassis, blueberry and leather. The medium-bodied palate features ripe, savory flavors structured by strong tannins on the finish. This wine could use time in the cellar to soften up a bit. • 2022 Cabernet Sauvignon Hitchcock Vineyard, Chalk Hill, $42 This wine is an enjoyable, ready to drink Cabernet with enough complexity to make it interesting. It opens with blackberry, cedar, and floral notes followed by rich, sumptuous fruit on the palate, soft tannins and a smooth finish. Well balanced. It would pair beautifully with prime rib or steak. Photo by Deborah Quok Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas By Deborah Quok Springtime means brunch time for many of us. And finally, we are slated for some dry and sunny days to gather with family and friends. I often make a frittata for our Sunday brunch. It’s usually in a 12-inch skillet to savor leftovers the next day. I’ve modified a springtime favorite to bake in muffin tins for individual servings, ideal for entertaining and your brunch spread. Advance notes: It’s important to liberally grease each muffin cup, even if for “nonstick” pans. If well buttered or oiled, the muffins are removed easily. Omit this if using parchment liners. I add the salmon, asparagus pieces (saving the tips for topping), crumbled cheese and chives into the egg mixture; just as I do for a large frittata. For mini-frittatas, carefully fill each cup with about the same amounts of everything in each. If you want to be more precise, layer the fillings before adding the egg mix as follows: asparagus pieces, salmon pieces, crumbled cheese and lastly chives on top. Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Serves 12 INGREDIENTS • 10 large eggs • 1/2 cup whole milk • 4 ounces cold smoked, sliced sockeye salmon • 12 stalks asparagus, about the diameter of a pencil. • 2.5 ounces goat cheese, crumbled (about 1/3 cup) • 1/4 cup fresh chives, cut into 1/4-inch lengths • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste • 2 teaspoons olive oil, extra-virgin • Vegetable oil spray or butter for greasing the muffin tins. Omit if using parchment liners. INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 12-cup muffin pan by liberally greasing each cup or use parchment liners. Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 425°F. Cut a 1-1/2 inch length of the asparagus tips off, then cut the remaining stalks into 1/2-inch pieces to measure a generous one-half cup of pieces. Heat the 2 teaspoons of olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Add all the asparagus pieces and sauté until just tender. Remove from heat and set aside. Separate the asparagus tips from the 1/2-inch pieces, the tips will be used to decorate the tops of each frittata. Cut the smoked salmon into 1/2-inch squares by first cutting the entire piece of adhered sliced salmon in half lengthwise. Stack the two pieces atop each other, then cut in 1/2-inch strips lengthwise. Turn the strips 90-degrees and cut these strips crosswise in 1/2-inch increments. Gently separate the slices. It’s OK if there are a few of the thin slices stick together. Whisk together the eggs, milk, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Add the salmon, asparagus pieces, cheese, and chives and stir to evenly distribute. (Optional: see the advance note above to layer the filling.) Divide evenly among muffin cups, leaving about 1/4-inch from the rim. Bake for 10 minutes, then remove the muffin pan to place an asparagus tip atop each mini frittata. Return to the oven, continue baking until the frittatas are lightly browned, set in the center, and puffed up. Total baking time is about 18 – 20 minutes. (Their puffy splendor is temporary, as they will fall to about even to the rim upon removal from the oven.) Transfer the muffin pan to a wire rack and cool for 10 minutes. Use a small silicone spatula to loosen around the edges and bottoms of each tin. Remove gently and serve warm. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on April 5, 2023.

articles.text: The first Wednesday of April seemed to be time for the Walking on Wednesdays group to do its annual spring check of the Piedmont real estate market. Everyone seems to enjoy seeing homes that are for sale, and there was a good turnout of 38 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra. Before the group started some information on the national and local real estate market was provided. A study from Bankrate, a financial services company, reported the median price of a U.S. home listed for sale was $418,000. But an article last week in the San Francisco Chronicle said that according to Zillow data the typical high-tier home in the San Francisco metropolitan area in February 2025 was worth $1.91 million. That’s almost 4% higher than in February 2024. Low-tier home values essentially stayed flat at just over $700,000. High mortgage rates are a main driver for this. Rates are twice what they were five years ago, and they’ve kept first-time home buyers and homeowners unwilling to give up their lower mortgage rates out of the market. Wealthier buyers have the resources to make all-cash offers, or large down payments that reduce their monthly costs. Twenty-six percent of homes sold in 2024 were all cash offers. The luxury home inventory is also especially tight, even by Bay Area standards, making this part of the market more competitive. The other major factor is the stock market. Buyers with large sums in stocks, including tech employees with stock options, have benefited from the market’s performance over the last two years, and are able to purchase expensive homes. For Piedmont, Calia Homes did some research and found that based on Multiple Listing Service (MLS) data for the 20 years from 2005 to 2024, the median sales price of Piedmont homes grew 73% from $1,420,000 to $2,450,000. Over the same period, the S&P 500 delivered a total return of roughly 830%, or an average annual return of about 8.4%. Homes may not have provided the best returns over the last 20 years, but Piedmont real estate is hot. A March report by Calia Homes had 10 homes pending or being sold since February. They sold or went pending in an average of 10.8 days and sold for 15% above their listing prices. articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center invites the public to the opening of its newly renovated, 15,000 square-foot Observation Deck during its From Oakland to the Stars weekend, Saturday and Sunday, April 26-27, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The weekend kicks off exciting new features and exhibits on Chabot’s popular outdoor Observation Deck that surrounds its three world-class telescopes, providing fun, participatory opportunities for all ages to learn how observation — both on the ground and in space — are fundamental to science. Tickets are included with general admission for both days and more information may be found at https:// chabotspace.org/calendar/fromoakland-to-the-stars-observation-deck-grand-reopening-26th/. “Throughout the design process, we teamed up with our community, knowing that Chabot is a resource for Oakland and beyond,” commented Tracy Corado, Chabot’s Director of Design and Exhibits. “Local amateur astrophotographers shared their work to help visitors dive into astronomy, while Space Telescope Science Institute provided content for fun tools to explore astronomy terms. We also highlighted the incredible work of the East Bay Astronomical Society and our amazing volunteers, who keep our telescopes running. The excitement around this project really showed how much people love coming together at Chabot’s Observation Deck. We can’t wait to see how this project grows and continues to inspire our community.” Funding for the Observation Deck includes generous contributions from the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. a showcase of its high school student volunteers, the Galaxy Explorers, focusing on the latest projects that highlight their innovative work and hands-on contributions to the world of astronomy, engineering, environmental science and digital media. In addition, Chabot will host a panel discussion featuring local astrophotographers and scientists from the Space Telescope Science Institute. The weekend will From Oakland to the Stars also offer a chance to enjoy live Observation Deck music, become a “solar detective” The April 26 & 27 From through hands-on demonstraOakland to the Stars weekend is tions, take guided hikes through the official opening of Chabot’s the nearby redwoods and more. newly renovated Observation Deck—an exciting transforNewly renovated observation mation that blends astronomy, nature and hands-on learning in a beautiful outdoor interactive space. The space will feature new observation tools, engaging hands-on interactive exhibits and live pop-up demonstrations, and the opening of a special astrophotography display showcasing breathtaking images captured by amateur astrophotographers from the Bay Area. A portion of the exhibition will feature astrophotography by late Chabot astronomer Conrad Jung in honor of his years of dedication and service to Chabot and the science community. As part of the weekend celebration, Chabot will present deck Highlights of the newly renovated space include a new exhibition of Astrophotography by amateur Bay Area astronomer/ photographers with a wealth of interpretive materials focusing on what’s in the photos and why they are important. Visitors will be inspired that real people like themselves can participate in and make contributions to real science. The observation deck renovations build on seven years of enthusiastic public enjoyment of expanded outdoor facilities and amenities. In 2018, Chabot added nearly 4,000 square feet to its telescope area, creating an extremely popular addition to the Center. Since then, the deck and exhibits have dynamically underscored Chabot’s mission to inspire all ages to discover, practice and learn about science through engaging and interactive exploration and programs as well as its unique resources as a public/private education center for Oakland and the Bay Area. The observation deck and its expanded suite of interactive exhibits inspire visitors to get outside, connect with their local environment, and build observation skills in fun and innovative ways. The deck continues to provide a prime venue for field trips, campouts and viewing major celestial and terrestrial events. The exhibits highlight the local landscape and natural phenomena from the smallest seeds to the sun overhead and encourage creative and reflective observation.

Tickets are included with general admission for both days and more information may be found at https:// chabotspace.org/calendar/fromoakland-to-the-stars-observation-deck-grand-reopening-26th/. “Throughout the design process, we teamed up with our community, knowing that Chabot is a resource for Oakland and beyond,” commented Tracy Corado, Chabot’s Director of Design and Exhibits. “Local amateur astrophotographers shared their work to help visitors dive into astronomy, while Space Telescope Science Institute provided content for fun tools to explore astronomy terms. We also highlighted the incredible work of the East Bay Astronomical Society and our amazing volunteers, who keep our telescopes running. The excitement around this project really showed how much people love coming together at Chabot’s Observation Deck. We can’t wait to see how this project grows and continues to inspire our community.” Funding for the Observation Deck includes generous contributions from the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. a showcase of its high school student volunteers, the Galaxy Explorers, focusing on the latest projects that highlight their innovative work and hands-on contributions to the world of astronomy, engineering, environmental science and digital media. In addition, Chabot will host a panel discussion featuring local astrophotographers and scientists from the Space Telescope Science Institute. The space will feature new observation tools, engaging hands-on interactive exhibits and live pop-up demonstrations, and the opening of a special astrophotography display showcasing breathtaking images captured by amateur astrophotographers from the Bay Area. A portion of the exhibition will feature astrophotography by late Chabot astronomer Conrad Jung in honor of his years of dedication and service to Chabot and the science community. As part of the weekend celebration, Chabot will present deck Highlights of the newly renovated space include a new exhibition of Astrophotography by amateur Bay Area astronomer/ photographers with a wealth of interpretive materials focusing on what’s in the photos and why they are important. Visitors will be inspired that real people like themselves can participate in and make contributions to real science. The observation deck renovations build on seven years of enthusiastic public enjoyment of expanded outdoor facilities and amenities. In 2018, Chabot added nearly 4,000 square feet to its telescope area, creating an extremely popular addition to the Center. Since then, the deck and exhibits have dynamically underscored Chabot’s mission to inspire all ages to discover, practice and learn about science through engaging and interactive exploration and programs as well as its unique resources as a public/private education center for Oakland and the Bay Area. The observation deck and its expanded suite of interactive exhibits inspire visitors to get outside, connect with their local environment, and build observation skills in fun and innovative ways. The deck continues to provide a prime venue for field trips, campouts and viewing major celestial and terrestrial events. The exhibits highlight the local landscape and natural phenomena from the smallest seeds to the sun overhead and encourage creative and reflective observation. Lamb is ubiquitous on restaurant (and home) menus, and at least half the nation’s supply is imported to satisfy demand. The French claim more variety of cheeses than days in a year as they never stop telling you. Their cheeses are made from the ewe, or brebis, yielding an earthy-flavored semi-soft variety, but the region’s most famous cheeses are made from cows: the soft, ripened Camembert, the soft, creamy Pont-L’Évêque, and the cream-cheese like but with fewer calories, Neufchâtel. The cheesemaking hews to ancient methods that place top awards on terroir, its soil, where the product is grown. The French assertively protect some 290 provenanced agricultural products related to the terroir, its soil. Cheeses are one, apple cider from the Calvados region is another, as are the grapes of Bordeaux, and the bubby of the Champagne region. One sees the designation on the product label or packaging, the AOP or AOC, Appellation d’Origine Protégée/Controlée refers to its place of origin. It is an assurance of consistent quality for an agricultural product, traceable to which herd was fed on which pasture grasses on what date. Camembert is certified as made from cows in Camembert pastures, and Cognac is not any brandy – it is the brandy produced in the Cognac region. French wine has a separate register of AOP with nearly 500 appellations of origin. See Americans in Paris on page 29

The Charm of Normandy Villages Honfleur is a seaport located at the Seine estuary on the English Channel, and the city’s medieval architecture survives as a charming reminder of the long history of the Calvados region. L’Église de Sainte Catherine dates to the 15th Century and is built entirely in wood. Replicating the church in stone wasn’t possible when it was destroyed during the Hundred Years’ War. About 25 minutes west is Deauville, a seaside resort on the Channel. it’s been a holiday destination since the late 1800s and is known for its stylish residential streets, its gambling casino, horse races, golf courses, and a film festival. These are among the cities that had the good fortune to be strategically irrelevant to World War II and were not bombed as other channel cities were, such as Caen and Le Havre. The Invasion beaches The Normandy towns along the English Channel were Ground Zero in the Allied invasion that marked the entry of the United States into Europe during the Nazi occupation in World War II. In today’s Normandy, more than a dozen memorials and museums tell the collective story of the June 6, 1944, D-Day invasion by allied forces. Two museums exhibit the Omaha Beach invasion where U.S. Army troops withstood heavy machine-gun barrage before overtaking the Germans. Its story is well-known via the film Saving Private Ryan. pages.text: Wednesday, April 9, 2025 29 AMERICANS IN PARIS Continued from page 28 The Cider Route Fr a nce is k now n for cider-making, and Normandy is one of its top regions. The spirits date to the Celtic Gauls in the 1st century B.C. under Roman rule. Charlemagne in the 9th Century ordered the planting of apple trees in the north country. During World War II, many cider apple and pear orchards in Normandy were destroyed. An intensive effort rejuvenated the industry and the AOC status was granted to the cider industry. The bountiful supply of apples is evidenced on any shopping day at the produce market, and other than Golden, many varieties are unique to the continent. Several hundred alone grow only in Normandy. The ciders and cider-spirits compete based on terroir and they claim to use ancient methods, with well-guarded family secrets for extraction and fermentation. The apple growers of Calvados branded itself back in the 1880s, and what’s known as the Cider Route (or Trail) strings together the now 20 cider farms, inviting travelers to sample and purchase their product. The route connects the villages of Beuvron-en-Auge, Cambremer, Bonnebosque, Beaufour-Druval, and the Château du Breuil distillery. Bicyclists and cars frequently share the 25-mile route. Apple cider has a 3.5-5% alcohol content. Calvados is apple brandy with 40% alcohol content, which the French say is essential with crepes. The pommeau is fresh apple juice mixed with Calvados brandy. Another 20 producers offer Perry from fermented pears having 4% alcohol content. In 104 years of history, only six other Piedmont volunteers have received this recognition. “It’s a testament to everyone who helped you along the way,” said James. “No one ever becomes an Eagle Scout of any type by himself or now herself. It’s something that you do with your family, with your friends, with companions and people that may never cross paths again, and yet all of them resulted in your being on this path. And I think you carry that forward from youth to what you pursue in your adult life, knowing that it takes a village and it takes a group of people to achieve anything worthwhile in life, and you carry that forward.” At the dinner, the council also recognized other volunteers who have made a difference – in some cases for many, many years. articles.text: On Friday morning, April 4, before school, Piedmont teachers will gather together in Piedmont Park near the vase from 8:00-8:20 a.m. to stage a “Walk-in” in support of Public Education. Teachers invite the larger community – students, school staff, parents, and neighbors – to join in support of the work done by the U.S. Department of Education which is in imminent danger of being dismantled. Teachers will be wearing Red for Ed, and invite everyone to wear red, bring signs supporting public education and stand in solidarity before walking to school 10 minutes before the first bell of the day rings. The Beach and Wildwood communities are staging walk-ins at the Beach and Wildwood campuses as well. “The Department of Education gives crucial support to American students–including those with disabilities, English Learners, children who face racial and gender discrimination, and children who live in poverty,” said Elise Marks, Piedmont Teachers Union President. “I believe most residents of Piedmont understand the importance of federal support for our nations’ nearly 100,000 public schools. We understand that education is the pathway to a better life for American citizens, and the cornerstone of a healthy democracy,” said Marks during the school board meeting March 26. Marks invites the entire community to bring signs expressing support for public education: for IDEA, for Title I, for Title IX, for federal funding of college education, for students with disabilities, for trans students, and for all the students of this country.

articles.text: P i e d m o n t C o m m u n i t y Church’s (PCC) annual Mexico House Building trip over Spring break, a popular rite of passage for hundreds of teens for many years, will not occur this year. Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted sent a letter to past participants in the summer of 2024 relaying the decision to put a pause on the trip. The leader of the Mexico Trip, Director of Student Ministries Scott Kail, is no longer with the Church. It appears he retired on June 7, 2024. Kail led the trip for 19 years. Its popularity grew to include more than 200 teens and adults to build 12 homes for locals in Tijuana’s Valle de Palmas. The Aqua Team shares the shade with local residents in Valle de Palmas, Mexico, by a newly constructed home. “With the absence of [Kail’s] leadership, I am writing to let you know that we are going to push pause on the trip this coming year,” Senior Pastor Schibsted wrote. “The trip is a huge undertaking for our church. We don’t see any way that we could orchestrate the trip this year without Scott.” The restructuring of the church, without Kail, and without finding a replacement, suggests that there are other reasons causing the church to rethink the trip. Schibsted said no one from the church offered to take over leadership of the trip. “We really just questioned if sending kids for over $2000 for a mission trip was really the right thing to do,” Schibsted told the Post. Despite the complexities and the high price tag participants loved the experience. “I am a junior and have gone since my freshman year. I was looking forward to going one more year before I got to be a leader. I really hope they bring it back next year,” said Dahlia Osman.
articles.title: Mexico house-building trip for teens canceled

Despite the complexities and the high price tag participants loved the experience. “I am a junior and have gone since my freshman year. I was looking forward to going one more year before I got to be a leader. I really hope they bring it back next year,” said Dahlia Osman. See Trip Cancelled on page 8

articles.text: The Community Engagement Committee of the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) welcomes Piedmont neighbors to enjoy cocktails and conversation with former Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich at the Piedmont home of Ellen and Pete Wilson the evening of Wednesday, April 16, at 7:30 p.m. Jeff Bleich’s legal career includes serving in the White House as special counsel to President Obama, law clerk to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and president of the State Bar of California. Additionally he has served as chair of the California State University Board of Trustees, chair of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board, and as a trustee of Amherst College. Bleich also served as the United States ambassador to Australia and as a senior advisor to the Director of National Intelligence. He is an ambassadorial fellow at the University of Sydney, chairs the board of the Bleich Centre of Democracy and Disruptive Technologies in Adelaide and is a professorial fellow at Flinders University also in Adelaide. Bleich earned a BA from Amherst College, MPP from Harvard University, JD from UC Berkeley and honorary doctorates from SFSU and two Australian universities. Currently Bleich is a Visiting Scholar at Stanford’s Center for Advanced Study in Behavioral Sciences where he is completing two books. Bleich’s writings have focused principally on democracy, international relations and constitutional law. A product of public schools, Jeff and his wife, Becky Bleich, are committed to public educaPiedmont resident Jeff Bleich tion and are delighted to help raise funds for Piedmont schools. When they were not living abroad, their three children all attended Piedmont schools. Bleich’s remarks on the evening of April 16 will focus on what is behind the fall in democracy worldwide, the rise in autocracy, and his current book project updating Machiavelli’s “The Prince” for modern times. Bleich’s recent article in Persuasion offers a glimpse of how Machiavelli’s advice to autocrats explains recent events. In a March 18 article, Bleich focused his attention on the judiciary branch and the limits of Presidential power under the constitution. Tax deductible tickets are available at the Piedmont Store for $75, at https://piedmontstore. org/products/cocktails-conversation-with-jeff-bleich. Thanks to many generous donations, 100% of the proceeds raised from the event will go to supporting Piedmont Schools. articles.text: The Honorable Mary-Margaret Anderson, a retired administrative law judge with the California Office of Administrative Hearings, is now serving as chair of The National Judicial College Board of Trustees. The College is the nation’s oldest, largest and most widely attended school for judges. Judge Anderson first joined the board in 2016 and was elected by her fellow board members to serve a one- year term as chair starting in January 2025. “The mission of the NJC is to both educate and inspire the judiciary,” Judge Anderson said. “Now more than ever, we must support our nation’s judges. By doing so, we support an institution that is essential to our democracy. Without fair, impartial, competent and independent judges, democracy is impossible. I am enormously proud of the work the NJC does and to serve as its board chair.” At the Office of Administrative Hearings Judge Anderson presided over the full range of cases brought by state, county, and local agencies, including school districts, from 1997 until her retirement in 2017. Judge Anderson is a past president of the National Association of Administrative Law Judiciary (NAALJ). She also served on the Judges’ Journal Editorial Board, the quarterly magazine published by the American Bar Association’s Judicial Division, for eight years, the last two as co-chair. She is currently co-chair of the Judge Mary-Margaret Anderson Judicial Division’s Book Editorial Board. She has taught ethics, evidence, and expert evidence to new and experienced judges in a variety of settings. Judge Anderson has resided in Piedmont since 1976 with her husband Lannie Spencer. Their sons Brett and Scott attended the Piedmont schools. About the National Judicial College The National Judicial College was founded in 1963 and is based at the University of Nevada, Reno. It trains judges nationwide, improving the delivery of justice and advancing the rule of law through a process of professional study and collegial dialogue. The College offers an average of 100 courses and programs annually with more than 12,000 judges attending from all 50 states and more than 150 countries. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm
articles.title: Piedmont Judge Chair of National Judicial College

articles.text: Students in each Piedmont elementary school in grades K-3 are participating in vocal music concerts this week. Beach School’s vocal music concert occurs this Thursday, April 3 at 8:45 a.m. and Wildwood will have its performance on April 4 at 8:45 a.m. The concerts feature the music of Paul Simon, John Denver, the Beach Boys, and songs made popular by Nat King Cole, the Muppets, and Tony Bennett. Havens students performed yesterday, on Tuesday, April 1 to a large crowd in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. Vocal music instructor Adrian Behrendt introduced the songs with a theme of “Road Trip,” to students in January. “Students learned about their voice as an instrument, and to sing as a group well. [This means] listening to the group sound, blending in, and focusing their personal best for the benefit of the audience,” said Behrendt. For third grade vocal students their performances require them to sing with respect to a variety of style like folk country, light jazz, and rock & roll. Behrendt said 3rd graders felt motivated by the catchy melodies and contemporary feel. “There are few things as rewarding as hearing a full voiced, focused choir of combined classes,” said Behrendt. “And in the case of [Tuesday’s concert at Havens] three classes of around seventy-five students, pulled together in a common goal [which made] the rafters ring and [brought] a welcoming applause from the audience.”

articles.text: The first step in the annual Piedmont Bird Calling contest process, besides nailing down a date in the Alan Harvey Theater, is choosing the poster. In the early days of the Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest posters were created by professional artists. In more modern times contest organizers have turned to the talent of Piedmont High School artists. This year’s winning artist is Layla Reed-Miguel. “I am a freshman at PHS,” she said, “and one of my biggest interests is art. I am planning on taking Art every year of high school. It is my main hobby. I have never seen Bird Calling Contest before, but it looks really interesting (and I love birds). “I was inspired by the “Who’s the Biggest Bird” theme, which is why I made the birds in order from biggest to smallest (with the biggest one having the #1 ribbon and being inspired by Big Bird from Sesame Street). I also put the Exedra in the background as it is an iconic part of Piedmont. Overall, I wanted the poster to have a retro/vintage look with the border and text.” This year’s theme is “Who’s The Biggest Bird?” This is to acknowledge the extraordinary efforts of birds. The Bird Calling Contest will be on Friday, April 18 at 7:30 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School. Tickets are on sale for $20 and student tickets are $10. articles.text: The Highlander Robotics team traveled to San Francisco with its new robot “Kelpie” for its second tournament of the season. After finishing 2nd of 41 teams in qualification rounds with a 10-1 record, they went 3-1 during the double elimination playoffs to challenge the first seed alliance captained by BREAD from Redwood Shores, currently ranked 3rd in the world. They lost two straight in the best of three finals to finish second overall. In judged awards, the Highlanders won in Industrial Design. Judges noted the elegant structure and appearance, high performance on the field, and the functional and attractive use of LEDs to support the driver from across the field. The team will compete in its final Regional Tournament April 5-6 at Berkeley High School before traveling to Houston, Texas for the World Championship. The Berkeley event is free and open to the public; the community is encouraged to come cheer them on. Closed toed shoes are recommended. articles.text: Girl Scout Troop 30713, consisting of Piedmont 10th graders, hosted the Piedmont Annual Afternoon Tea and Paint at the Veterans Hall on Sunday, March 23, It was a full house. Guests enjoyed traditional Afternoon Tea treats of tea sandwiches, scones, brownies, shortbread, lemon bars and fruit cups. Following the tea, guests painted their own cups and saucers to take home for their tea collection. Creative Painting Girl Scout members of Troop 30713 hosted the annual Afternoon Tea and Paint at the Piedmont Veterans Hall on March 23. Pictured are Emma Chan (left), Skye Prata Baack, Kate Tong, Lucy Allen, and Jeannie Choi. Anne, Izzy, Bea and Millie Wheeler paint their tea cups and saucers. Guests enjoying their afternoon Tea Building Mission Trip united participants through hard work whether they were church members or not. Getting to meet and interact with families in Tijuana in need of housing delivered perspective to teens. Exchanging the comforts of Piedmont homes for tents starkly brought into focus some of the privilege Piedmonters can easily take for granted. PCC also pointed to the inability to rent trucks from their usual rental company in San Diego and to get Mexican car insurance. Car rental companies are hesitant to send their fleet to Tijuana due to a high rate of vehicles not making it back, Schibsted noted. The Post contacted a representative at Amor Ministries, the company that connects American volunteers and those in need in Mexico. An Amor representative confirmed that PCC informed them there was no one to lead the trip in 2025, as the reason for cancelling the mission trip. Amor Ministries continues to send mission trips to do the same work. They stated that sign ups have not declined significantly. The church says they are in the midst of searching for a Director of Student Ministries to replace Kail, who left nine months ago. “Once that person is hired we will begin talking about our options regarding some sort of mission trip,” said Schibsted. “Many of the reasons we cited for not having the Mexico trip this year are still present. In fact, conditions at the border have probably become more complex. We have a Mission Board who will make the decision in partnership with our youth ministries team.” If the trip is to survive, a leader must emerge to take over all of the logistics including flights, insurance, building materials, and safety. “We are evaluating. We want to do something, but it may not be that,” said Schibsted. Teens and adults with Piedmont Community Church gather last year at the home base site of the house-building project outside Tijuana, Mexico.

articles.text: You’re right: to be happy. To be healthy is #2. Right again? Yup, “happy” here doesn’t mean ephemeral pleasures, such as a tasty meal, a good cup of coffee, a ‘frivolous’ book, a movie, getting a nice car, gambling, or watching sports. Last pop quiz: If you could only ask one question to figure out if someone will be happy today, what would it be? Okay, a few possibilities popped into your mind this time, right? Let’s come back to that and offer the answer. In a Gallup World survey of 1,551,362 adults collected from 164 nations – the largest, most representative sample of the world’s population, the best predictor of the amount of positive emotions felt today was: “Did you learn something new yesterday?” Interesting, right? But, so what? Learning something is meaningful, and meaning is what creates a life of joy, which is truly what parents wish for their children, above all. In exploring how individuals find meaning in life—essentially, how they discover sustained fulfillment and joy—it is apparent that there are four cornerstones central to this pursuit: Discovery, Expression, Service, and Love. 1. Discovery: This involves a continual quest for personal understanding and the exploration of one’s desires and capacities. It’s about unraveling the layers of who we are and what we truly seek from life. 2. Expression: Stemming from the insights gained through self-discovery, expression is the process of showcasing our inner selves to the world. This can be through art, communication, or any form that allows one to convey their personal essence. 3. Service: This cornerstone asks, “How can I contribute to the betterment of others?” It is about extending oneself beyond personal needs to aid and uplift others, thereby enriching the communal human experience. Purpose is central to meaning, and after happiness and health, it is the 3rd most wished for by parents. 4. Love: Representing deep connections and affections, love may be directed towards people, places, or things. It is a profound force that drives much of human interaction and fulfillment. These cornerstones manifest differently depending on one’s life stage, cultural background, and personal circumstances. For instance, a monk might prioritize service and love, while a young adult may focus more intensely on discovery and expression. The cultural environment also plays a significant role in shaping which cornerstone predominates in an individual’s life. The people around us act as branches supporting our life’s tree, providing context and meaning. While not inherently meaningful—similar to being alone in a crowd or having numerous online contacts with few deep connections—the true value in relationships comes through these cornerstones. They help us discover ourselves, express our inner thoughts, commit acts of service, and experience love. The depth of these relationships, much like the thickness of branches, determines their impact on our lives, influencing how we find meaning and joy. However, finding and sustaining this sense of meaning is not without challenges. Fear is a significant hindrance; it stifles our ability to engage with life’s cornerstones by shifting our focus towards immediate safety and comfort. Another less obvious obstacle is the pursuit of fleeting happiness, which can distract from the deeper, more fulfilling joy that comes from engaging with our foundational cornerstones. these four cornerstones, individuals can transcend the ordinary, finding not just happiness but profound joy and fulfillment in their lives. For more resources on creating a meaningful life, visit the nonprofit organization ameaningoflife.org, a comprehensive platform dedicated to helping individuals live more purposefully and joyfully. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over 20 years and is excited to share AMeaningOfLife.org with the world.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 2, 2025 9 Thinking Outside the Classroom What is the No. 1 wish of parents for their children? By Randall Grayson You’re right: to be happy. To be healthy is #2. Right again? Yup, “happy” here doesn’t mean ephemeral pleasures, such as a tasty meal, a good cup of coffee, a ‘frivolous’ book, a movie, getting a nice car, gambling, or watching sports. Last pop quiz: If you could only ask one question to figure out if someone will be happy today, what would it be? Okay, a few possibilities popped into your mind this time, right? Let’s come back to that and offer the answer. In a Gallup World survey of 1,551,362 adults collected from 164 nations – the largest, most representative sample of the world’s population, the best predictor of the amount of positive emotions felt today was: “Did you learn something new yesterday?” Interesting, right? But, so what? Learning something is meaningful, and meaning is what creates a life of joy, which is truly what parents wish for their children, above all. In exploring how individuals find meaning in life—essentially, how they discover sustained fulfillment and joy—it is apparent that there are four cornerstones central to this pursuit: Discovery, Expression, Service, and Love. 1. Discovery: This involves a continual quest for personal understanding and the exploration of one’s desires and capacities. It’s about unraveling the layers of who we are and what we truly seek from life. 2. Expression: Stemming from the insights gained through self-discovery, expression is the process of showcasing our inner selves to the world. This can be through art, communication, or any form that allows one to convey their personal essence. 3. Service: This cornerstone asks, “How can I contribute to the betterment of others?” It is about extending oneself beyond personal needs to aid and uplift others, thereby enriching the communal human experience. Purpose is central to meaning, and after happiness and health, it is the 3rd most wished for by parents. 4. Love: Representing deep connections and affections, love may be directed towards people, places, or things. It is a profound force that drives much of human interaction and fulfillment. These cornerstones manifest differently depending on one’s life stage, cultural background, and personal circumstances. For instance, a monk might prioritize service and love, while a young adult may focus more intensely on discovery and expression. The cultural environment also plays a significant role in shaping which cornerstone predominates in an individual’s life. The people around us act as branches supporting our life’s tree, providing context and meaning. While not inherently meaningful—similar to being alone in a crowd or having numerous online contacts with few deep connections—the true value in relationships comes through these cornerstones. They help us discover ourselves, express our inner thoughts, commit acts of service, and experience love. The depth of these relationships, much like the thickness of branches, determines their impact on our lives, influencing how we find meaning and joy. However, finding and sustaining this sense of meaning is not without challenges. Fear is a significant hindrance; it stifles our ability to engage with life’s cornerstones by shifting our focus towards immediate safety and comfort. Another less obvious obstacle is the pursuit of fleeting happiness, which can distract from the deeper, more fulfilling joy that comes from engaging with our foundational cornerstones. By choosing to engage with these four cornerstones, individuals can transcend the ordinary, finding not just happiness but profound joy and fulfillment in their lives. For more resources on creating a meaningful life, visit the nonprofit organization ameaningoflife.org, a comprehensive platform dedicated to helping individuals live more purposefully and joyfully. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over 20 years and is excited to share AMeaningOfLife.org with the world. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, April 2, 2025 AP Art Show Continued from page 1 pieces of their portfolio during this show; their finished portfolios for The College Board, will consist of 10 pieces by May. Junior Kate Jumper stated, “my work explores how the experience of living with different eye conditions can be expressed.” “An AP Studio Art portfolio requires a student to design a Sustained Inquiry that is a personal interest that they follow through the year in an artistic response to an aesthetic question,” explained Art Department Chair Gillian Bailey. Junior Sasha Jerez’s work was centered around the “how symbolic doors offer moments of reflection and shape our perception of growing up.” “Since I was a little kid, I have always wished I was older and now that I am older I only wish I was little again,” Jerez wrote in her artist statement. PHS Principal David Yoshihara was among the gallery patrons, taking it all in. “I was impressed at how personal the art was to our students,” said Yoshihara. “As I read their narrative and studied the art, it Senior Carolina Romanczuk’s portfolio investigates how “photography connects our universe through circles.” Junior Hadley Hayes’s art strives to “show the imperfections in life and normalize them.” felt so real – like I was ‘there’ for some of their stories.” Senior Alan Xu hopes his works can draw attention towards species extinction, pollution and the power of trash. Xu’s salmon piece uses a piece of saran wrap with a butcher’s label of Atlantic salmon. Pieces of plastic make up the water surrounding the representation of the fish. Xu told the Post the wild variety of Atlantic salmon is nearly extinct. He found some piece of “trash” from around the house to incorporate in his pieces. “I also use a collage of trash I find, gluing them to my work to reinforce the dominance that pollution has on the ecosystems I illustrate,” stated Xu. Next up will be the All-School Art Show on Thursday, April 17, 5:30-7:30 p.m., which will include the selected works of 200 Piedmont student artist in grades 9-12. Senior Camila Work’s pieces “explore the universal experience of childhood through the use of commonly nostalgic childhood items.” The AP student art remained in the foyer for a week after the show. MHS senior Ellie Willats explores the “use of a traditional and ‘realistic’ style and medium for very modern and fantastical concepts.” Sasha Jerez had 10 pieces in the gallery, some down at stroller height, fitting for her theme of what we perceive growing up. articles.text: The Chevron gas station and car wash at the corner of Grand and Piedmont avenues is preparing for a long-anticipated reopening later this month. The business, located at 4400 Piedmont Ave., will host a grand reopening celebration within the next three weeks to mark its return to serving Piedmont-area drivers. Closed since Dec. 1, 2023 due to state regulations, the station has undergone more than a year of repairs, including the replacement of underground gas tanks and upgrades to the car wash facilities. Staff training began this week on April 1. All staff returning for training worked there prior to the closure in 2023. “That’s a testimony to the kind of people that come in there and get their car washed, because they wouldn’t come back to a place that didn’t have nice people as customers,” said owner Carla Betts. According to Betts, the car wash is fully operational, but additional improvements are planned, including the installation of two shade structures after the grand opening to provide sun protection for both staff and customers. The car wash will resume full-service cleaning options, offering both hand and machine washes. Business hours will remain the same: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Although an exact reopening date has not been announced, the celebration is expected to include balloons, music and an ice cream truck. Betts expressed appreciation for the community’s support during the closure. “I just thank them for the continual questions of ‘When are you going to open?’ They started asking those the day after we closed… and the questions have never stopped,” she said. “That just goes to show that we’ve been missed.” Workers prepare the Betts Car Wash for its opening later this month.

articles.text: Three Chevron gas stations were targeted in attempted “crash & grab” burglaries in the early morning of Tuesday, March 11. Located on Lakeshore Avenue, Redwood Road, and Moraga Avenue, the stations were all broken into within 45 minutes of each other around 3:30 a.m. The burglars, seemingly looking to steal the safe at each station, crashed cars into the stores of two of the stations and broke the window to access another. $250,000-$300,000 in estimated damages resulted from the break-ins, although the criminals escaped empty handed as police arrived. “All of the electrical stuff is gone, all of the computer driven stuff is gone, and they’ve gotten absolutely nothing,” said owner and Piedmont resident Carla Betts. “Within 45 minutes they hit three of our places and just did massive damage to the building and got absolutely nothing – they didn’t even steal a Red Bull.” It is possible the Lakeshore station’s store may not be opening again. “The store on Lakeshore is not open. And I don’t think we’re going to re-open it,” said Betts. According to Betts, the attempted burglaries fall in line with similar stories from other gas stations across Oakland and its neighboring cities. “They’re targeting any small business that they consider a soft target,” said manager Rick Draper in an interview with CBS News. “It’s just a sad thing that this is repeating itself all over the city virtually all the time.” The burglars’ escape raises questions about the effectiveness of Oakland Police Department’s no pursuit policy. “I don’t know where I stand [on the pursuit policy], because I don’t want them pursuing people and hitting a random child or a random pedestrian. That’s not fair. I care about those families. I also care about my business,” said Operations Manager Marissa Betts in an interview with NBC News.
