articles.text: Piedmont High made a shocking decision on Friday, March 28, announcing they have declined girls’ soccer head coach Dan Chubbock’s year-to-year contract after 17 years at the school. Chubbock is just two years removed from having led the Highlanders to the Division 4 North Coast Section championship in 2023. Piedmont athletic director Tyler Small issued the following statement. “Piedmont High School Athletics is dedicated to providing the best coaches for all teams each season. Coaches are hired on a seasonal basis and contracts are renewed yearly for coaches returning. At the end of each season we evaluate each program’s Staff Photos Dan Chubbock and Kesy Platt, a former assistant coach and player, following their title win in North Coast Section as a Div. 3 team. Dan Chubbock’s days as girls’ soccer coach may not be over. Dan Chubbock and the 2023 NCS Championship winning team. success with the intent of ensuring the best coaches are in place to support our student athletes on and off the playing field,”. But the story might not be done. Since the announcement, the community has rallied to reinstate Chubbock by sending comments to PHS principal Dr. David Yoshihara and school superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Chubbock made it clear he wants to be back next year. “The support has been overwhelming. If the people would like me to carry on, I’d like to continue. I’ve had no intention of stepping down from the role. I’ve been in this for 17 years, I’ve always tried to carry myself in the right way and lead the program in line with everyone,” Chubbock said. Chubbock has proven to be a community pillar in every sense. Aside from his year’s coaching the high school, he is a director of Piedmont Soccer Club and 24-7 UK Soccer Academy, which produced boys’ soccer coach Ben Russell and several former coaches including Todd Sullivan and Marcus Watson. He also coaches Chabot College’s women’s team during its fall season. A group of parents of girls’ soccer players sent the following email to the school’s administration: “We are writing to express our shock, disappointment, and anger over the non-renewal of Dan Chubbock’s contract. Our daughters play on his varsity girls’ soccer team and have found him to be a skilled, successful, and compassionate coach. Dan’s record at Piedmont has been remarkable given that Piedmont routinely competes against schools twoto-three times its size in league play… We very much would like to see Dan return as varsity coach next year and feel his dismissal was unwarranted as well as a huge loss for Piedmont.” Team captain Louisa Symkowick also expressed her disappointment over the decision, mentioning that players and parents were never consulted on the matter. “Coach Chubbock has supported me on the field during tough games and off the field during tough injuries. My sophomore year we won the NCS championship, something that hadn’t been done by a Piedmont girls’ soccer team in over 20 years. It is also wrong to cite the creation of a “negative team culture” without even speaking to the actual players on his team. If there were other problems with Dan’s performance, these should have been clearly communicated earlier in the season so they could have been addressed. It is poor form for a newly hired athletic director to abruptly fire someone who has improved the soccer program and its culture for the last Photo by Todd Marshburn Staff Photos Photo courtesy of Piedmont Soccer Club Piedmont High School’s athletic department shocked soccer fans when it declined to renew coach Dan Chubbock’s contract after 17 years. 17 years,” Symkowick said. Chubbock indicates he only had a three-minute conversation with Small about his decision. But since then dialogue has picked up. “From speaking with the school, I’m hoping there’s a possibility to return. I know the job has been posted, but I’d like to find a way to continue. In my mind, things aren’t done,” Chubbock said. Piedmont Soccer Club board member Jonathan Essner, who is a PHS Class of 1990 graduate, also voiced dismay over the school’s decision. “It’s totally a surprise and a shock, I personally cannot believe this is being handled the way it is. It’s unworthy of Dan’s commitment to this community. Dan represents the entrance of sporting life for Piedmont youth,” Essner said. The decision is the latest black mark by Piedmont High’s athletic department. Under former AD Bradley Smet, the school moved on from former football coach Jerome Johnson in 2021 and sloppily canceled their varsity football program before reinstating it after parents fought to keep it alive. The program left its league for a year, loaded the schedule with difficult teams, only to suffer extensive injuries during the season. The football team returned to the WACC and won consecutive Shoreline and Mission titles, but star players lost were overlooked by colleges. More information will be provided as the story develops. Photo courtesy of Piedmont Soccer Club The Piedmont community is rallying to reinstate Dan Chubbock as the girls’ soccer team’s head coach.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team split a pair of games of in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division with Encinal, winning 8-5 on Thursday, March 27 at Humphries Diamond but losing the next day by the exact same 8-5 score at Willie Stargell Field in Alameda. articles.text: Piedmont suffered a 14-4 loss to Berkeley. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team suffered a rough 14-4 loss to Berkeley at Witter Field on Friday, March 28. It was their fifth straight loss. The result came against last year’s Western Alameda County Conference champions and the current No. 1 team in the league. The Highlanders are 2-1 in the league and can clinch a berth in the North Coast Section playoffs by finishing with an even overall or league record. Piedmont will host Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, April 4 in a critical league match. The Dragons are 6-4, but have faced weaker teams than Piedmont’s difficult schedule, which has been wrought with D1 schools like Amador Valley, Casa Grande, Campolindo, and Berkeley. 14-4 loss to Berkeley It was actually a strong first quarter for the Highlanders, trailing 3-2 at the end of the opening 12 minutes but was held scoreless through the second and third quarters. In the first quarter, Piedmont opened the game with a goal straight out of the faceoff. Connor Fredericks won one of his 14 draws, turning it up field to long stick midfielder P.J. Brayer for a goal just 18 seconds into the game. But from there, Berkeley scored three straight goals with 9:51, 9:31, and 2:57 left in the first quarter. Piedmont got one back when Ian Nguyen scored with 28 second seconds left, but it marked the Highlanders’ last time to score until the fourth quarter. What transpired was PHS Staff Photos Goalie Gus Von Metzsch moves the ball upfield. He had 16 saves. Connor Fredericks lines up a shot. He scored twice and won 14 face-offs. struggling to move the ball in transition and maintaining possession through an aggressive press while in the attacking zone—resulting in offense relying on goalie Gus Von Metszch to move the ball toward midfield. Turnovers are an issue that has plagued the Highlanders since transitioning from former coach Al Yu following the school’s D2 NCS Championship appearance in 2023. Piedmont had a couple looks in the second quarter before BHS started to continuously force turnovers. Timmy Kalamas had a shot blocked with 6:25 left, but it led to a Berkeley goal in transition. Fredericks then had a pair of shots go wide while Gianluca Richmond had a shot hit the post with 5:15 on the clock Berkeley scored a little over a minute later. After that, Piedmont committed four turnovers without taking a shot, leading to a Berkeley goal with 18 seconds left. Brayer and Fredericks had shots go wide with 9:43 and 9:17 left, but the attack commit a costly turnover with 8:42 left, leading to a Berkeley got on the ensuing possession. Kalamas had a shot on target with 7:10 left, while Brayer and Fredericks also had shots saved four minutes later. Berkeley scored twice in the last 25 seconds before halftime. In the fourth, Piedmont got back on the board with 8:30 left, but Berkeley scored straight out of the faceoff 16 seconds later. The Jackets scored another four goals until Fredericks netted another with 40 seconds left. Final stats: Fredericks scored twice with seven ground balls and won 14/17 face-offs. Brayer scored once and gathered six ground balls. Nguyen scored once and pickd up six ground balls. Kalamas had two assists. Von Metzsch was busy with 16 saves. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team dropped a pair of matches and its match on Monday with Head-Royce was rained out. PHS lost 6-1 to Bishop O’Dowd at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Tuesday, March 25, and to Lick-Wilmerding on Friday, March 28 also at home. Piedmont’s wins in the two matches came from Lucas Smolko at No. 1 singles against O’Dowd, and at No. 1 doubles duo of Gianluca Bini and Luca LaForte won against Lick. For Smolko, he won 7-5, 7-5 over Neo Chai, who Lucas defeated in last year’s Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament for the singles title. Tuesday’s meeting could be another preview of this year’s singles final once again. “Our sole win was Lucas at #1 singles, It was a nice win because Neo is a very strong player who always gives Lucas a run for his Monday,” coach Jim Landes said. Bini and LaForte won handily in straight sets 6-2, 6-1. “Our sole victory was a beautifully played match at #1 doubles by the new team of Gianluca Bini and Luca LaForte. They trounced their opponents, they played exceptionally well. We have a lot of confidence in this duo for the remainder of the season,” Landes said. 6-1 to O’Dowd In singles, Smolko won 7-5, 7-5 at No. 1. Nate Welch lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 2, Nick King fell 6-3, 6-4 at No. 3, while freshman Emilio Misra lost in three sets at No. 4, 3-6, 6-1, 7-5. Misra had a chance to win the match at No. 4, but fell narrowly short. “Emilio split sets and then had two match points in the third, eventually losing it 7 -5. He played very well at times but just needed a little more offensive play to close it out,” Landes said. In doubles, Will Tenney and LaForte lost at No. 1, 6-2, 6-1. Kasper Jansson and Bini fell 6-3, 6-2 at No. 2, while Ben Davis and Hunter Fasteau lost in three sets at No. 3, 4-6, 6-0, 7-6 (7-4). 6-1 to Lick-Wilmerding Smolko lost at No. 1 in a heated three-set match with the 10-point super breaker third set going an extra few points, 4-6, 7-5, 13-11. “There were three matches that could have gone our way. Lucas lost 13-11 in the super breaker and had a couple of match points,” Landes said. Also in singles, Welch lost 6-3, Staff Photos Lucas Smolko won against Bishop O’Dowd but lost a close three-set match with against Lick-Wilmerding. Luca LaForte, a freshman, helped reel in a win at No. 1 doubles against Lick-Wilmerding. Joey Assalian with a forehand.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team split its last two games, which both close and both barnburners. The Highlanders defeated Berkeley 10-8 at the Yellowjackets’ home field on Friday, March 28, but lost 10-9 in overtime to Dublin at Witter Field on Tuesday, March 25. “We made a valiant effort in the waning minutes to tie the game but lost in OT. We had a lot of opportunities to win the game. The girls really gave it their all to climb out of a hole,” coach Carlton Chan said of their loss to Dublin. Piedmont is undefeated against Western Alameda County Conference opponents at 4-0 with its win over Berkeley. They enter the final month of the regular season with a match with league rival Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland this Friday, April 4. O’Dowd is currently 5-7 overall and 3-0 in league, but got obliterated by Dublin 21-8 on March 13 and are in the midst of a seven-match losing streak. 10-8 victory over Berkeley Piedmont held a narrow 4-3 lead to end the first quarter and maintained a 6-5 advantage going into halftime. Both teams added two goals in the third, still leading 8-7, while PHS held the Jackets to one goal in the final going. In the first quarter, Friedie Schickedanz won quickly after the faceoff, sending in a goal just 35 seconds into the match. Berkeley tied the match two minutes later, but Chloe Graham put PHS back up with 7:07 left. Peyton Watson then scored with 2:31 on the clock and netter another to make it 4-2 with 49 seconds left. Berkeley got one back with 35 seconds left. Berkeley scored quickly in the second quarter nearly two minutes in to tie it at 4-4. After eight minutes of back and forth possessions, Photo by Sophie Hess Peyton Watson had 3-goal hat tricks against both Berkeley and Dublin. Graham scored with 1:50 left and Watson made it 6-4 with 30 seconds left. Berkeley inched closer in the final seconds, scoring with 10 seconds before halftime. In the third, Berkeley scored twice in the first minute of action at the 11:28 and 11:02 marks after winning back-to-back draws to take a 7-6 lead. With 4:39 left, Graham tied the match with a shot in front of the net. Then with six seconds left, Luisa Cole put Piedmont back up 8-7. Olive Litwin gave Piedmont a two-goal cushion with 10:37 left in the fourth quarter, up 9-7. Berkeley quickly answered after winning the faceoff, scoring with 10:03 left, but it was their last goal of the game. With 6:13 left, Schickedanz scored Piedmont’s last goal. Final stats: Graham had three goals and gathered four loose balls. Watson scored three goals, won three draws, and scooped a ground ball. Schickedanz scored Photo by Todd Marshburn Friedie Schickedanz scored three goals against Berkeley and four against Dublin. Photo by Todd Marshburn Chloe Graham scored three times against Berkeley and twice against Dublin.

articles.text: Miguel Long sets school record in triple jump Staff Photos Piedmont celebrated its 17 seniors on the track and field roster. The league meet at Witter Field was the first at home since 2023. Piedmont High’s track and field team had two meets over the past week. The school hosted a Western Alameda County Conference meet against Berkeley and San Leandro on Friday, March 28, at Witter Field. It also brought a small group to the Castro Valley Relays on Saturday, March 29. Saturday’s event marked a historic day when senior Miguel Long recorded a triple jump of 45 feet, 7.75 inches to finish second of 11 athletes. His mark puts Long at the top of Piedmont’s alltime list of triple jumpers. Although Miguel fell short of Nikka Piterman’s 46-foot record in 2011, Piterman’s mark was aided by a 5.1 meters-per-second wind (11.4 miles per hour)— which is considered outside legal limits. “We rested Miggy for a week and focused on jump technique, and that seems to clearly be paying off. Miguel broke the all-time PHS school triple jump record and is inching toward the CIF state at-large standard. This also ranks him among the top in all of California,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. The league meet at Witter Field marked the school’s first time hosting a track and field event since 2023, after prolonged renovations last year. Piedmont’s boys and girls teams beat San Leandro and Berkeley in points. For the boys, PHS outscored San Leandro 66-61 and Berkeley 83-44. As for the girls, the Highlanders beat San Leandro 68-54 and Berkeley 90-31. “This is the first time in my tenure that the girls beat Berkeley, so that’s a huge accomplishment,” Assadi said. 400-meter run in 53.18 in a field of 13 athletes. Also winning two events was Sebastien Swain. He won the 800 in 2:03.33 against 16 others, and his 4:29.96 in the 1,600 was first of 26. Miguel Long competed in four events, winning both of his jumps. He was first of seven in the triple jump at 43 feet, 5 inches, and first of 12 in the long jump at 21 feet, 5.5 inches. articles.text: The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Archive’s (BAMPFA) West Coast engagement of Making Their Mark: Works from the Shah Garg Collection, an exhibition of one of the largest private collections of work by women artists, is on view now through April 20. Making Their Mark brings together more than seventy artworks from the Shah Garg Collection and features artists from the postwar period to the present day, as well as artists with deep ties to the Bay Area, including Mary Corse, Trude Guermonprez, Mary Heilmann, Mary Lovelace O’Neal, Elizabeth Murray, and Kay Sekimachi. Also featured are internationally distinguished artists including Lynda Benglis, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Sonya Gomes, Maria Lassnig, Joan Mitchell, Julie Mehretu, Howardena Pindell, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, and more. BAMPFA’s display is the first public presentation of this exhibition following its premiere in New York in 2023 and was assembled by the Bay Area philanthropist Komal Shah and her husband Gaurav Garg. “The significant investment in the work of women artists by Komal and Gaurav is truly inspiring and groundbreaking,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “We are so grateful that their vision dovetails with ours at BAMPFA to create public access to such excellent examples of artwork by leading artists of our time, which will generate new scholarship and new art histories for years to come.” “The Shah Garg Foundation is honored to bring Making Their Mark to an institution as brilliant as Berkeley and further educate a younger generation on the accomplishments of women artists,” said Shah. “We are filled with so much excitement at the opportunity to spotlight works that have rarely been seen before to this community. To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://bampfa.org/ making-their-mark. Making Their Mark: Works from the Shah Garg Collection installation view Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: Grand Parade is Sunday, April 20 The 58th annual Northern California Cherry Blossom Festival (NCCBF) is coming back to San Francisco’s Japantown on Saturday, April 12, with a host of activities open to the public that weekend and the following weekend. NCCBF is California’s most prominent celebration of Japanese and Japanese American culture as well as the largest Cherry Blossom Festival on the West Coast. The free festival draws over 220,000 visitors annually over two weekends in April to celebrate the arrival of spring and tout the city’s stunning sakura displays. The first Northern California Cherry Blossom Festival, formerly called the San Francisco Cherry Blossom Festival, was celebrated over three days in March 1968 after the opening of the Japan Trade Center, now Japan Center Malls, in the city’s Japantown on March 28, 1968. The festival is now organized by a group of volunteers and has grown to become one of the largest and most prominent cherry blossom festivals outside of Japan. The event features live music and cultural performances, pop-up arts and crafts by local vendors and artists, Japanese cuisine food trucks and a Sapporo beer garden. Guests can learn more information about the festival from community and sponsor information booths and participate in interactive, family-friendly activities at the Children’s Cherry Blossom Village on Post Street outside the Kinokuniya Mall. The final San Francisco screening of KINTSUKUROI, a film that follows members of the Ito family from their pre-war life in Japantown to the concentration 2019 Northern California Cherry Blossom Festival Grand Parade in San Francisco’s Japantown camps of the American West, is held on Sunday, April 13, at the Kabuki Cinema as part of the NCCBF. The festival concludes with a grand parade, the highlight of the NCCBF, which stretches over a mile from Civic Center Plaza to Japantown. The parade showcases cultural and community organizations that contribute to the continued success of the festival, and features a procession of traditional taiko drummers, dancers and decorative floats. The parade is held on Sunday, April 20, departing from San Francisco’s Civic Center Plaza at 1:00 p.m., proceeding up Polk Street to Post Street, and ending in Japantown at Post and Fillmore Streets. While Japantown is the epicenter of the upcoming festival, be sure to visit the Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park to view magnificent cherry blossom displays. Sakura blossoms are blooming in the garden and can be seen by the Main Gate, Tea House, and Drum Bridge until early April. All events are free and open to the public. Visit https://sfcherryblossom.org/schedule/ to learn more and for a full list of programming. Most events begin at 12 p.m. Cherry Blossom displays at the Japanese Tea Garden in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park

articles.text: Photo courtesy Dallas Museum of Art Kunié Sugiura, Sidewalk Palms, 1980 An exhibition featuring over 60 works by Japanese American photoartist Kunie Sugiura opens at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on April 26. Japanese native Sugiura pioneered a unique category of artistic expression by blending photography with painting, drawing and other mediums. She also experimented with the photogram technique, one of the earliest forms of photography dating back to 1839. Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, her first survey exhibition in the U.S., features over 60 artworks spanning her sixty-decades long career. “Throughout her career, Kunié Sugiura has subverted traditional notions of photography, bravely bucking trends to produce a distinctive body of work that is unmistakably her own,” said Erin O’Toole, SFMOMA’s curator and head of photography. “Sugiura’s many experiments and explorations with the photographic medium upend our notions of what photography can be,” added SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford. “We look forward to engaging our communities with KuniéSugiura’s art and are honored to open the first survey exhibition of her work in the U.S.” Sugiura moved to the U.S. in 1963 to study at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago where she was a mentee of conceptual artist and photographer Kenneth Josephson. A major retrospective of her art was on display at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum in 2018. From 1986 to 2008 she produced a column entitled “New York Report,” in which she reviewed gallery and museum exhibitions, for the Japanese-language magazine Bijutsu Techo. “I am very happy I found a way of life that has interested me and has kept my focus for so long,” Sugiura said in an interview with Cristina Chan, SFMOMA’s Managing Editor. “Over my career, I have had a few people and audiences who have supported my art. This time, I feel like more people are understanding my ideas and art.” Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting is on display from April 26 to September 14. Guests at SFMOMA’s Art Bash on April 23 will enjoy a sneak peek of the exhibition. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/kunie-sugiura-photopainting/ to learn more. ®

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony musicians perform the score of 1997 mega blockbuster Titanic this Friday and Saturday. San Francisco Symphony musicians will perform the Titanic score live alongside a screening of the film at Davies Symphony Hall this Friday, April 4 and Saturday, April 5. The 1997 mega blockbuster Titanic features an iconic score composed, orchestrated, and conducted by James Horner. The film’s immense success allowed the soundtrack to shoot to the top of the charts and sell over 27 million copies worldwide, making it one of the top 100 best-selling albums in the United States. Celine Dion’s “My Heart Will Go On”, the film’s signature song written by James Horner and Will Jennings, won the 1997 Academy Award for Best Original Song as well as the Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song in 1998. Performances are conducted by Sarah Hicks and feature vocalist Alice Zawadzki and the San Francisco Girls Chorus accompanying the orchestra. Guests will enjoy a blue Heart of the Ocean cocktail and Sweet Heart of the Ocean macarons inspired by the film, offered at the Davies Symphony Hall bar. The Friday performance begins at 7:30 p.m.; the Saturday, April 5 performance begins at 2 p.m. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/Titanic to purchase tickets, or call the box office at 415-864-6000.
articles.title: SF Symphony performs Titanic score live April 4 & 5

articles.text: Shotgun Players current production of Yasmina Reza’s Art is now extended through Saturday, April 12, with an added matinee performance and closing final performance at 8:00 p.m. Reza’s internationally-acclaimed play launched Shotgun Players 33rd season with direction by Emilie Whelan. Art, written in French and adapted to English, premiered at Comédie des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1994 and won a Tony Award for best play in 1998 and the Olivier Award for best comedy in 1997. The English-language adaptation, translated by Christopher Hampton and directed by Matthew Warchus, opened in London’s West End in 1996. Art explores dy namics between lifelong friends Serge, Marc, and Yvan as their relationships slowly unravel when Serge, played by Benoît Monin, purchases a $200,000 piece of modern art. Marc, played by David Sinaiko, questions his friend’s extravagant purchase, likening it to a mid-life crisis, while neutral Yvan attempts to mediate arguments between them. Eventually, the painting begins to symbolize Serge, Marc, and Yvan’s own perceived failures. “That painting is the first crack for the wall to come tumbling down,” Whelan said. “[Reza] bears these cracks in the wall [and] lines in the canvas through a mad hilarity. She stretches her comedy, kneads it and rolls it out to a place of absurdity, and in 2025 that feels about right.” “The play makes me think about the trade-offs we make in the intimate relationships we engage in,” Shotgun’s Artistic Director Patrick Dooley added. “Platonic [or] romantic, and how we are sometimes asked to compromise our integrity and our values in order to maintain those relationships. Would you be willing to compromise your integrity, your values, in the name of ‘art’?” Art is showing onstage at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through April 12, Wednesdays and Thursdays at 7:00 p.m., Fridays and Saturdays at 8:00 p.m. and Sundays at 2:00 p.m. Visit www.shotgunplayers.org or call the box office at (510) 841- 6500 ext. 303 to purchase tickets. You’ll be able to sit for a couple of hours in a comfortable chair in the intimate club-like environment with complimentary snacks while enjoying familiar music. Get tickets at https://bpt.me/6214927, or $30 at the door, cash or check only. Saturday, April 12, 11 a.m. - 2 p.m. Oakland Art Assn. Exhibition Don’t miss the artists’ opening reception for this stunning juried exhibition of Oakland Art Association’s members’ works — varied in style, medium, approach, and size — The World Around Us! For the next eight weekends starting April12, until June 1, 2025, the gallery will be open and staffed with member artists from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday, except closed April 20 and May 10. There is no charge to visit. Active since 1957, OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Exhibit locations include libraries, banks, John Muir Hospital, Piedmont Gardens, and local country clubs. Saturday, April 12, 3 p.m. David Martin & Bita Nejat Vocal/Piano Recital David Martin, bass-baritone, will perform Ralph Vaughan Williams’ Songs of Travel, a song cycle based on the poems of Robert Louis Stevenson. The songs tell the story of the life of a traveler, from bold young man through the arc of his life of adventure, to his final days of contemplation. articles.text: Sona Jobarteh Gambian multi-instrumentalist, singer and composer Sona Jobarteh performs at the Herbst Theatre in San Francisco this Friday, April 4. Called “a griot for a new generation of West Africans” by BBC Radio, Jobarteh is regarded as a master and a pioneer of the kora, a unique 21-string African lute. Most similar to a lute or a harp, the kora is played almost exclusively in West Africa and was first discovered in the Gambia. Music for the kora was not written until the 20th century. Songs are passed down from griots, composed of West African storytellers, singers, musicians, and oral historians. Griots also keep records of all births, deaths, marriages through the generations of the village and pass traditionally composed music down to younger generations. Gambian griot traditions date back nearly seven centuries. Jobarteh, born in London, is from one of only five principal kora-playing ‘griot’ families of West Africa and is the first female professional kora player to come from a griot family. She is the granddaughter of the griot of her line, Amadu Bansang Jobarteh, whose father migrated from Mali to Gambia. Jobarteh’s cousin is celebrated kora player Toumani Diabaté and her brother Tunde Jegede is also a renowned diaspora kora player. Jobar teh’s debut album Afro-Acoustic Soul, released in 2008, is influenced heavily by her Gambian background but also includes melodies that could be heard on more conventional European radio stations. Her second album and first solo recording Fasiya, released in 2011, highlighted her skills as a vocalist and multi-instrumentalist. She returns to SF JAZZ next month following the release of her 2022 follow-up for African Guild Records, Badinyaa Kumoo. Jobarteh performs at the Herbst Theatre, an auditorium in the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center in San Francisco’s Civic Center, on Friday, April 4. The concert begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/24-25/sona-jobarteh/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Tom Cruise, indisputably a top-tier movie star since his iconic Risky Business slide, continues his resilient career with a variety of films, though he’s best known for the Mission: Impossible franchise and Top Gun. This brings us to Knight and Day, a romantic comedy where Cruise portrays rogue government agent Roy Miller, alongside Cameron Diaz as June Havens, an unsuspecting traveler en route from Wichita to Boston. June’s suitcase, oddly, contains retro muscle car parts. A seemingly chance encounter at the Wichita airport thrusts June into a whirlwind of danger, as both good and bad people seek to kill Roy. June attempts to maintain composure, often succumbing to unconsciousness—a recurring gag that is surprisingly charming. The film, surprisingly, is entertaining. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter is a breezy, enjoyable ride. Knight and Day also features a compelling MacGuffin, an object that quickly captures attention. The film cleverly plays with audience expectations, revealing unexpected layers to both Roy and June. Their dynamic evolves beyond simple romantic comedy tropes, adding a layer of intrigue. The twists and turns keep the audience guessing, and the film’s playful tone ensures that even the most outlandish scenarios remain engaging. While the plot may seem straightforward, a closer look reveals subtle clues and motivations that add depth to the characters’ actions. The film’s strength lies in its ability to balance action, comedy, and romance without sacrificing its sense of fun. Knight and Day. Directed by James Mangold. 20th Century Studios/ Bontonfilm A.S. . articles.text: The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on a 2010 novella by Claire Keegan and nominated for an Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category, the Irish film is an unassuming, beautifully acted and photographed coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch). The film opens with Cait lying in a lush field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family where, to her shame she occasionally wets her bed and is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and her siblings. School is also a struggle, something to be endured, a place where she is often ridiculed by her schoolmates. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives her to the distant farm, saying little, and is so disengaged that when he leaves Cait with the Catherine Clinch and Carrie Crowley in The Quiet Girl couple, absent even a goodbye, he drives off with her suitcase still in the trunk of the car. It’s with this couple (it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl) she experiences a kindness and generosity, attention and concern that she has never felt before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world which is far different from the one she has known. Expecting indifference or cruelty, she discovers the opposite. Her reflexive response to life, is slowly abandoned and Cait begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated. When encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. The Quiet Girl. articles.text: Spirited Away, directed by Hayao Miyazaki, is an award-winning animated film that captivates audiences with its compelling fairytale-adventure. The film won an Oscar, a Golden Bear and an Annie Award. The narrative centers on 10-year-old Chihiro (Daveigh Chase), who is unhappy about her family’s move to the countryside. Her mother (Lauren Holly) and father (Michael Chiklis) take a wrong turn and discover what appears to be an abandoned amusement park. When her parents begin eating at a restaurant, Chihiro wanders off and meets Haku (Jason Marsden), a boy who shows her around. Upon returning, she finds her parents transformed into pigs. Haku explains that a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette), who runs a bathhouse for spirits, is responsible. He warns Chihiro to avoid Yubaba, but Chihiro learns she must work for the witch to save her parents. Chihiro’s journey through the spirit world introduces her to dragons, frog-men, a giant baby, a spidery furnace stoker and other creatures. The film focuses on Chihiro’s transformation as she learns to be brave for herself and her parents. The animation is visually rich, with each frame resembling a hand-drawn work of art. The story, rooted in Japanese mythology, may appeal more to young girls, but boys will also enjoy the mysterious spirits, particularly Yubaba. Spirited Away. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Studio Ghibli-Walt Disney. Voiced by Daveigh Chase, Suzanne Pleshette, Jason Madsen. Released in 2019. 2hrs 5min. Rated PG. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX/HULU/apple tv A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Spirited Away The Quiet Girl a quiet, lovely film By Chris Honoré The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on a 2010 novella by Claire Keegan and nominated for an Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category, the Irish film is an unassuming, beautifully acted and photographed coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch). The film opens with Cait lying in a lush field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family where, to her shame she occasionally wets her bed and is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and her siblings. School is also a struggle, something to be endured, a place where she is often ridiculed by her schoolmates. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives her to the distant farm, saying little, and is so disengaged that when he leaves Cait with the Catherine Clinch and Carrie Crowley in The Quiet Girl couple, absent even a goodbye, he drives off with her suitcase still in the trunk of the car. It’s with this couple (it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl) she experiences a kindness and generosity, attention and concern that she has never felt before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world which is far different from the one she has known. Expecting indifference or cruelty, she discovers the opposite. Her reflexive response to life, is slowly abandoned and Cait begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated. When encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. The Quiet Girl. Written and directed by Colm Bairead. Starring Catherine Clinch, Carrie Crowley, Andrew Bennett. With subtitles. Filmed with subtitles. 1 hr., 34 min. PG-13. Released in 2022. articles.text: The Piedmont Flix Fest’s selection, Amelie, directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, embodies a bellowed French charm. Amelie stars Audrey Tautou, who may remind some viewers of Audrey Hepburn. The film depicts contemporary Parisian life in Montmartre. It tells the story of Amelie Poulain, a waitress with an active imagination, who tries to improve the lives of those around her following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. The film was released in France on April 25, 2001, and received critical acclaim. Tautou’s performance, the cinematography, visuals, production design, sound design, editing, musical score, writing and Jeunet’s direction were praised. It won Best Film at the European Film Awards, four Cesar Awards, including Best Film and Best Director, and two British Academy Film Awards. It was nominated for five Academy Awards, including Best Foreign Language Film and Best Original Screenplay. The film was a commercial success. Amelie will be screened April 10 at 1 p.m. The event, sponsored by the Rec Department, is held at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The event is free and open to those over 18. Participants can drop in, but registration with the PRD is encouraged at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. Attendees may bring snacks or lunch. The Flix Fest, held on the second Thursday of each month, combines film screenings with post-film discussions at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The next film in the series is the Alfred Hitchcock thriller Rear Window, to be screened May 8.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, April 2, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers honor women’s history, local legacy By Dick Carter Last Wednesday marked the final Wednesday of March, the first Wednesday of spring, and the last chance this year for the Walking on Wednesdays group to celebrate Women’s History Month. With clear skies and a spring breeze, the occasion drew 50 walkers and six K-9 companions for their weekly gathering. Women’s History Month began in 1981 when Congress authorized the President to proclaim the week beginning March 7, 1982, as Women’s History Week. Over the next several years, Congress passed annual resolutions recognizing the week. In 1987, after advocacy from the Last week’s gathering of the Walking on Wednesdays group included Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Denny McGee, Tracy Lee, Kathlene Henrickson with K-9 best friends Finn and Frankie, Quincy Dong, Debbie Powell, Sylvia Fones, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Rick Eigenbrode, Edith Lee, Ken Moy, June Yee, Phil Witte, Laura DuDell-Foley, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lori Austin, Bob Wong, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, Alissa Quan, Helen Dong, Susan Anderson, Carolyn George, Dave DeRoche, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Liza Dalrymple, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Mark Davis, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kellogg, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Nancy Henn, Chuck Oraftik, Lois Price, Irene Thompson, Claudine Bach, Abha Kothari, Bill Ahern, Melba Yee, Lisa Euphrat, Michelle Yang, Noemi Alvarado, Vicki Trimbach, Brenda Ferrero, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Gerry Montmorency, John Kelson, and Dick Anderson who were walking with them for the first time. National Women’s History Project, March was officially designated Women’s History Month – and has been celebrated as such ever since. In Piedmont, women’s contributions to the community abound. One such story, shared during the walk, was drawn from an article by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi in the Piedmont Post. The group revisited the tale of the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls, the city’s first school. Fittingly, Lombardi was honored this March with the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Betty C. Howard Award, which recognizes dedication to the community. The award is named for Betty C. Howard, the longtime Recreation Department secretary during the mid-20th century. The walk began with a pause to admire blooming tulips around the Exedra vase, then wound through upper Piedmont Park and past Community Hall, where more tulips greeted the group. From there, walkers made their way to the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane, near the original site of Amy Requa Long’s pioneering school. In the early 1900s Long sought a quality education for her daughters and convinced her father, Isaac Requa – who made his fortune in banking, mining, and railroads – to build a one-room schoolhouse on his estate, “The Highlands.” The school eventually outgrew its modest beginnings, prompting Long to lease a home at Highland and Hazel Lane and hire teachers Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from Berkeley’s Anna Head School. As enrollment grew, Long commissioned famed architect Julia Morgan in 1908 to design a new school building on five acres of what is now Hazel Lane. The Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls officially opened in 1913, complete with classrooms, dormitories, and eventually a gymnasium. At its height, the school served students from first grade through high school and attracted girls from prominent California families. But like many institutions, the school was hit hard by the Great Depression. Enrollment fell, and the school closed in 1932. Its buildings were demolished in 1936, and the property was later developed by architect Albert Farr into what is now Ransom Gardens. The Wednesday group followed Hazel Lane to the redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane—the former entrance to the school—then continued to 141 Hazel Lane, where a Farr-designed home now stands. They posed for a group photo in front of the house and admired the area’s history, including Piedmont’s first Hazel Lane home, built in 1937 at No. 152. Miller Flowers hosts Pop-up Art Show Celebrating the Joy of Flowers for 55 years Valerie Lee (left) gives flowers and a tour to Colibri Preschool students during the pop-up art show. By Tony Simons J. Miller Flowers celebrated its 55th anniversary with a Spring open house and pop-up art show on March 21-23. It coincided with the nearby annual Tulip Exhibition at Mountain View Cemetery. The art show featured displays from 15 local artists showcasing unique oil, watercolor, and acrylic paintings. Owned by sisters Robbin and Valerie Lee, J. Miller Flowers provides Piedmont and Oakland residents with high quality flowers and arrangements. Active for special events around the Bay Area, the beloved flower shop has provided flowers for many milestones in the community. On Friday morning, dozens of paintings lined the walls and tables of the flower shop’s side room for visitors to appreciate. The artists, many of whom graduated from Piedmont High School, stood near their displays to talk to attendees about their art. “It’s intimate,” said Seana McDevitt, who attended to see some of her friends’ artwork. “It’s a nice way to hear about what got them started, why they do it, and see the art.” Near the entrance, artist Germaine DeLuca gave out greetings near her collection of landscape and still life art and answered questions about her artistic process. “I tend to be more on the sparse side, as opposed to cluttering up… I think simplicity can be beautiful. You can just have one object and have it be beautiful,” said DeLuca. Another artist, Judy Chamberlin, has her own, much different approach reflected in her art. Her brightly colored and vibrant paintings are born from a process that is “totally immersed in color.” “I paint a bright color that makes you happy in the first place, and then I mix up kind of a limited palette,” said Chamberlin. “And then I really do start with a big brush and I just start slapping it all over the place, and I let these like, really happy accidents happen, and then I sit back and I just start seeing what’s coming Artist Germaine DeLuca stands near a collection of her paintings. Judy Chamberlin in front of a vibrant display of her floral paintings out of it. … And so every time, it’s going to be something unexpected,” said Chamberlin. J. Miller Flowers Co-owner Valerie Lee was very excited to put on the event, bringing together artists in the community. “It elevates everyone’s mood, which everyone really needs right now for whatever reason,” commented Lee. “I think so many people are still feeling isolated, so to have this and people just come at their leisure, it’s really just a beautiful, joyful event.” “You can be in other cities that are the same size or larger, but you don’t get that same feeling and caring that really is unique to Piedmont,” said Lee. articles.text: Former longtime Piedmont resident Suzanne Vinson Royce passed away peacefully on March 8, 2025 near her home in Healdsburg, California after a brief illness. She was 89. Suzy was born in Oakland California on December 26, 1935, to Virginia Pearson Vinson and Eugene Mulally Vinson. She is predeceased by her husband, Richard Ernest Royce and her older sister, Nancy Vinson Rubey of Diablo. She attended Bentley School in Berkeley, Our Lady of Lourdes in Oakland, Oakland High School, and graduated from San Ramon Valley High School in Danville. Suzy attended the University of California at Berkeley where she was a member of the Chi Omega Sorority. Suzy started a small and successful manufacturing business on Piedmont Avenue. She returned to Cal to complete her studies and received a degree in Fine Arts. She worked for a time at the Philips Collection in Washington, D. C. and then returned to the Bay Area where she continued to manage her Piedmont Avenue business and work as an independent Art Consultant. Suzy was a member of the Women’s Board of the Oakland Museum and supported many Suzy Royce died on March 8 at age 89 law, Trini Amador III, along with their children, Ashley Petersen (and her family), and Trini Amador IV (and his wife and children). She is also survived by her granddaughter, Sydney Royce; her grandson, Kellan Royce, and his wife, Sabrina, and their new great-grandson, Danny; her niece, Louise Bea (San Francisco); her nephew, Reed Rubey (New York); her niece, Ginger Rubey (Denver); her brother, Tom Vinson (Piedmont); her stepbrother, Bill Champlin (Tarzana); and her stepsisters, Mimi Champlin (Castle Shannon, PA) and Sally Champlin (West Hollywood). charitable and civic organizations. Her most particular interest was in training service dogs for American veterans. She is survived by her son, Peter Hobson Royce; her daughter, Lisa Royce Amador, and son-inWe miss Suzy very much and will cherish her memory. Donations in Suzy’s memory may be made to Canine Companions, PO Box 446, Santa Rosa, California 95402 or a charity of your choice.

articles.text: Montclair Village Association Festively stroll with friends and family while sampling delicious bites and libations. This year’s Taste of Montclair Village (formerly known as the Restaurant Walk) returns Tuesday, April 8, from 4 to 8 p.m. Get a taste of the food and beverages of the Village during this annual fundraiser benefiting the Montclair Village Association (MVA), a nonprofit and business improvement district serving the community for more than 75 years. The Taste of Montclair Village is a great way to get to know the Village, try the best food and drinks of the neighborhood, and chat with members of the MVA board and district merchants. So come out and join the fun this April. Start at the Village Plaza to pick up your “passport” to participating locations in the district. The passport is your ticket to explore tasty offerings along Mountain, La Salle, Antioch and Moraga streets. Restaurants in the neighborhood will offer samples, snacks and libations to enjoy. This year’s Taste will feature plenty of restaurants, bakeries and specialty food shops from the Village, including Farmstead Cheeses & Wines, 5 Spiced Kitchen, Italian Colors and Full Belly Bakery. Patrons are welcome to stroll into participating shops hosting open houses with more food and drinks from Bay Area eateries. Before leaving, make sure to head back to the Village Plaza to enjoy your favorite samples while listening to live music at the first of the Kakui at Taste of Montclair Village new Picnic in the Plaza monthly series. Picnic in the Plaza will feature live entertainment at the Village Plaza (Antioch Court) and is sponsored by F&M Bank. The first of the series will be held in conjunction with Taste of Montclair Village and will feature music performed by the Jazz Education Ensemble Trio. Available tickets for the Taste of Montclair Village on Tuesday, April 8, include: • Adult Passport – $50 ($55.20 with processing fee) • Under 15 Passport – $20 ($23.18 with processing fee) • Package of four Adult Passports – $200 (processing fees waived, savings of $20.80) • New Supporters of the MontPhoto by Michael Walker clair Cares Club (MCC) Passport – Receive a $20 discount on a Taste passport when you sign up for the MCC – $150 ($161.90 with processing fee) As a fundraiser, the Taste of Montclair Village is a fantastic way to have fun in the Village while supporting the safety and well-being of the district. Proceeds from the tastings will go toward projects and events like the Safety Ambassador Program and the Montclair Beer, Wine and Music Festival. Taste of Montclair Village is also supported by the Montclair Cares Club, which provides additional funds and support for the MVA’s mission and operations. To learn more and purchase tickets, visit MontclairVillage.com. Yellow Door at Taste of Montclair Village Photo by Michael Walker

articles.text: An unobtrusive multi-family Piedmont building, made up of four stacked flats, each with its own separate street entry. It has the same architectural massing as the neighboring homes. This single story complex is oriented around a shared courtyard with Bay views. The nine units are really attached bungalows, each with their own separate entrance. The quality and simplicity of this flat roofed contemporary design in Piedmont suggests that it may have been designed by the important modernist architect Irving Gill. housing tract development with all homes the same size, same setbacks, and even the same color and building plans spread over acres of land. What this means is that well thought out and designed multi-family buildings with neighborhood compatible massing, building heights, materials, architectural styles, and colors can be a visual enhancement that makes for a richer, more interesting city. One of the main urban design and architectural objections to different uses, types and sizes of buildings next to each other is the abruptness of change. This is especially true in residential areas, where people live. For example, think of a new seven-story glass clad office building located in a two story residential neighborhood – clearly not appropriate. But what about a 4-story mixed use building in a 2-3 story neighborhood? What about a well designed 3-story apartment? It’s often hard to say without seeing it in context. Each case is different because each site and its local surrounding context is different and has to be evaluated as such. It occurs to me that the principal issue with denser multi-family housing is most often not more people, but instead….more cars. Will Adams was a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who lived in Piedmont for 30 years. A small, unobtrusive backyard second unit. The “outdoor room” formed by the cottage, fencing and planting is a useful amenity to this award winning “Tiny House” of 285 square feet. The famous California architect Bernard Maybeck is credited with designing this five-unit multi-family Piedmont building which seems to be a hybrid between stacked flats and attached bungalows. It responds well to the hilly site and fits in with the surrounding single-family detached homes.

articles.text: Next, the walkers headed up Requa Place, a cul-de-sac leading to the former site of The Highlands mansion, before looping back down Highland Avenue and ascending Caperton Way. They took a scenic turn onto Sheridan and Lakeview Avenues, eventually arriving at Poplar Way—a hidden lane with a street sign but no addresses or poplar trees, just a charming path behind Mountain and Lakeview homes. The walk wrapped up with a gentle descent down Mountain Avenue and along a 217-foot path to Sierra Avenue, before returning to the Exedra. It was, as always, a walk filled with camaraderie, curiosity, and community pride—this time with a special nod to the many women who have shaped Piedmont’s past. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.
